Beyond this exceptional device performance, the synergy between high carrier density and mobility clarifies the long-standing mystery regarding the distribution of electrostatically doped carriers on the SrTiO$_{3}$ surface. Specifically, it reveals the mechanisms behind the formation and continuous evolution of field domains and current filaments.

This study examines the computational complexity of decision problems concerning conjugacy within finite inverse semigroups. We present polynomial-time algorithms to determine conjugacy between two elements in such semigroups and to assess whether an inverse monoid is factorizable. Additionally, we establish a relationship between verifying conjugacy and checking membership in inverse semigroups. We demonstrate that $\sim_o$ and $\sim_c$ form partition coverings for any countable set, while $\sim_p$, $\sim_p^*$, and $\sim_{tr}$ do so for any finite set. Furthermore, we prove that determining nilpotency, R-triviality, and the existence of central idempotents in partial bijection semigroups are NL-complete problems, and we extend several complexity findings regarding partial bijection semigroups to the broader context of inverse semigroups.

Analyzing turbulence within plasmas is essential for fusion research. Although theoretical modeling has advanced significantly over the last fifteen years, a comprehensive and consistent understanding of turbulence in magnetic confinement systems like tokamaks remains elusive. Experimental investigations face difficulties due to the complex, high-speed dynamics driven by diverse processes. This study introduces a novel use of motion tracking to detect and follow turbulent filaments, known as blobs, within fusion plasmas using high-frequency video from Gas Puff Imaging diagnostics. We evaluated four baseline algorithms (RAFT, Mask R-CNN, GMA, and Flow Walk) trained on synthetic data before testing them on both synthetic datasets and real-world data from the Tokamak à Configuration Variable (TCV). The blob regimes identified through trajectory analysis align with state-of-the-art conditional averaging methods for all tested baselines, validating the accuracy of these techniques. Traditionally, high entry barriers have restricted tokamak plasma research to a limited group of specialists. By releasing a dataset and benchmark publicly, we aim to expand the field to a wider scientific and engineering community.

Environment-assisted quantum transport (ENAQT) represents a phenomenon where environmental noise paradoxically boosts transport within an open quantum system. This paper explores how a one-dimensional single-particle mobility edge can induce robust ENAQT. To this end, we examine the energy current of a generalized Aubry-Andr\'e-Harper (AAH) tight-binding model, which is connected at its boundaries to spin baths characterized by varying temperatures and dephasing noise throughout the system. Our results demonstrate that ENAQT can increase by orders of magnitude, exhibiting a nonmonotonic dependence on both the count of localized eigenstates and the magnitude of disorder. We attribute this significant enhancement to the synergistic interplay between population uniformization and localization.

In a chemical graph $G$, the transmission of a vertex $v$ is defined as the sum of its distances to all other vertices within $G$. If every pair of vertices in $G$ possesses a distinct transmission, the graph is classified as transmission irregular. It has been demonstrated that for every odd integer $n \geq 7$, a transmission irregular chemical tree of order $n$ exists. Furthermore, a specific construction method is offered to generate new instances of transmission irregular (chemical) trees. The study also characterizes two additional families of chemical graphs based on their transmission irregularity and establishes two sufficient conditions ensuring that this property remains intact when a new edge is added.

Explainable AI (XAI) has advanced significantly in clarifying how discriminative models make decisions, yet it has largely overlooked generative models that create artifacts rather than judgments. As generative AI (GenAI) matures and enters fields like software engineering, there is a growing need to understand its explainability. By employing scenario-based and question-driven design methods, this study investigates the explainability requirements of GenAI across three software engineering contexts: converting natural language to code, translating code, and auto-completing code. Through nine workshops involving 43 software engineers, we used real-world examples from leading generative AI models to identify these needs. Building on existing research, we propose four categories of XAI features tailored for generative code models and collected further design suggestions from participants. Ultimately, this work highlights human-centered approaches to uncovering GenAI explainability needs and guiding the technical evolution of XAI in new domains.

This study investigates the gravitational collapse of a barotropic perfect fluid characterized by the linear Equation of State (EoS), $p=k\rho$, within the context of general relativity. We analyze the constraints imposed on the Misner-Sharp mass function by this specific EoS, focusing on the compatibility of a specific set of quasi-linear partial differential equations derived from Einstein's field equations. Our findings indicate that consistent solutions for perfect fluid collapse with a linear EoS are generally unattainable, except in scenarios where the system of PDEs simplifies to ordinary differential equations due to additional spacetime symmetries, or in particular cases where the equations become mutually compatible. We also examine the end state of collapse without such EoS constraints. Since determining the end state for arbitrary pressures is challenging due to unknown general dynamics of the collapse, we instead analyze small perturbations to mass profiles associated with inhomogeneous dust collapse, which induce corresponding small pressure perturbations in an otherwise pressureless fluid. Numerical methods are employed to study how the visibility of singularities depends on initial conditions, both with and without these perturbations. Crucially, we observe that no incompatibility issues arise between the corresponding pair of PDEs when a linear EoS is not imposed on the matter field, contrasting sharply with the case where $k$ is fixed as a constant.

Let ${\cal{C}}_1$ represent the collection of fundamental cycles derived from breadth-first-search trees within a graph $G$, and let ${\cal{C}}_2$ denote the set of sums formed by pairs of cycles from ${\cal{C}}_1$. We demonstrate that: (1) the union ${\cal{C}} = {\cal{C}}_1 \cup {\cal{C}}_2$ includes a shortest $\Pi$-twosided cycle in any $\Pi$-embedded graph $G$; (2) ${\cal{C}}$ encompasses every possible shortest even cycle in a graph $G$; and (3) if a shortest cycle in $G$ is odd, then ${\cal{C}}$ contains all such shortest odd cycles. Consequently, this result establishes a polynomially bounded algorithm for identifying a shortest $\Pi$-twosided cycle in an embedded graph, thereby resolving an open problem posed by B. Mohar and C. Thomassen [2, pp. 112].

In traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL), the primary goal is to identify a policy that maximizes expected return. However, this objective is often unsuitable for safety-critical fields like autonomous driving or healthcare, where stochastic policies and environmental fluctuations can cause catastrophic outcomes. To mitigate these risks, Conditional-Value-at-Risk (CVaR) can be employed to encourage risk-averse behavior in learned policies. This paper introduces Adversarial Cvar Reinforcement Learning (ACReL), a new adversarial meta-algorithm designed to optimize the CVaR objective. ACReL operates through a max-min framework involving a policy player and a learned adversary, where the adversary perturbs state transitions within a limited budget. We demonstrate that as the players approach the game's equilibrium, the resulting policy converges toward the CVaR-optimal solution, with risk tolerance directly tied to the adversary's budget. By formulating the problem as a Stackelberg game, we present a gradient-based training method that facilitates the use of deep RL architectures. Empirical results indicate that ACReL achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art CVaR RL baselines in obtaining optimal policies, while also offering robust theoretical assurances.

The direct observation of gravitational waves from multiple compact binary mergers has initiated a new epoch in astronomy, enabling the potential detection of ultralight bosons—hypothetical particles predicted by extensions to the Standard Model—through their gravitational imprints. This research is especially significant because certain such particles may constitute dark matter, interacting minimally or not at all with Standard Model matter while still exerting gravitational influence. These ultralight bosons can induce superradiant instabilities in rotating black holes, generating bosonic clouds that radiate gravitational waves. This article provides an overview of these instabilities as sources of gravitational waves and evaluates the capacity of both existing and upcoming detectors to constrain potential dark matter candidates.

Gutman introduced a novel geometric framework for graph invariants, with the second Sombor index ($SO_2$) being the most fundamental, defined by the formula $SO_2=SO_2(G)=\sum_{uv\in E}\frac{|d^2_G(u)-d^2_G(v)|}{d^2_G(u)+d^2_G(v)}$, where $G = (V, E)$ represents a simple graph and $d_G(v)$ signifies the degree of vertex $v$ within $G$. This study examines the chemical utility of the second Sombor index, demonstrating its superior accuracy in predicting physicochemical properties relative to several established indices. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for the second Sombor index across all molecular trees with a fixed vertex count and identify the specific trees that attain these extremal values.

Correlation functions and entanglement offer distinct perspectives for characterizing quantum many-body systems. Although numerous correlation functions can be measured experimentally, entanglement entropy (EE)—the most fundamental metric of quantum entanglement—remains challenging to access directly. This Letter introduces a protocol to bound EE using local measurements. The method relies on local correlation matrices and specifically targets their (approximate) zero eigenvalues. For a given quantum state, each (approximate) zero eigenvalue defines a corresponding set of local projection operators. An auxiliary Hamiltonian is subsequently constructed by summing these projectors. We demonstrate that if the construction utilizes only projectors associated with zero eigenvalues, the EE of a subsystem is bounded by the ground-state degeneracy of the auxiliary Hamiltonian restricted to that subsystem. Conversely, when projectors linked to nonzero eigenvalues are incorporated, the EE is bounded by the subsystem's thermal entropy. This protocol is experimentally viable for probing exotic quantum many-body states prepared within quantum simulators.

This paper investigates the fundamental group $\pi_1(\Sigma X,\overline{x_0})$ of the reduced suspension $\Sigma X$ for any arbitrary based Hausdorff space $(X,x_0)$. We demonstrate that this group is canonically isomorphic to a direct limit $\varinjlim_{A\in\mathscr{P}}\pi_1(\Sigma A,\overline{x_0})$, where each component group $\pi_1(\Sigma A,\overline{x_0})$ is either a finitely generated free group or the infinite earring group. A key implication of this characterization is that $\pi_1(\Sigma X,\overline{x_0})$ is locally free for every Hausdorff space $X$. Furthermore, we establish that $\Sigma X$ is simply connected if and only if $X$ is sequentially $0$-connected at $x_0$.

The identification of Lyman-$\alpha$ emitting galaxies (LAEs) imposes strict limits on reionization history. In this study, we determine the characteristics of very high-redshift LAEs predicted by the only two reionization models from a previous work that align with current data on 15 independent evolving global cosmic properties, including luminous objects, the intergalactic medium, and the optical depth to electron scattering of ionized hydrogen relative to CMB photons. These models are: one featuring monotonic behavior concluding at $z=6$, as traditionally assumed, and another exhibiting non-monotonic behavior with two complete ionization events at $z=6$ and $z=10$. We discover that the Ly$\alpha$ luminosity functions for very high-$z$ LAEs differ significantly between these two scenarios. Consequently, comparing these forecasts with upcoming observations from instruments like the James Webb Space Telescope should allow us to identify the correct reionization model. Meanwhile, we compare the predicted redshift distributions and UV (or Lyman-$\alpha$) luminosities of very high-$z$ LAEs with the few objects already detected at $z>7.5$. This comparison reveals that such data are inconsistent with the single reionization scenario but fully compatible with the double reionization scenario.

It is widely recognized that the standard neutrino oscillation framework successfully accounts for a vast array of experimental data. As the field enters a new era of precision in the neutrino sector, research has pivoted to investigating sub-dominant phenomena, specifically non-standard interactions (NSI) and neutrino decay. Although these effects can theoretically coexist at high-energy new physics scales, they are typically examined in isolation. This study investigates how potential neutrino decay influences oscillation patterns when NSI are present, across various setups involving atmospheric, accelerator, and reactor neutrinos. Utilizing current constraints on both NSI and decay parameters, we determine that decay effects are negligible for atmospheric neutrinos. For the T2K accelerator experiment, the impact is trivial, while MINOS and DUNE show only marginal deviations. In contrast, the reactor experiments KamLAND, JUNO, and Daya Bay exhibit significant deviations. Consequently, the inclusion of neutrino decay can modify the limits on NSI parameters derived from reactor-based studies.

Did the expansion of agropastoralism across Eurasian founder regions rely primarily on population movement (demic diffusion) or on the spread of ideas (cultural diffusion)? This research utilizes a mathematical framework modeling regional sociocultural evolution, incorporating various diffusion mechanisms alongside local innovation and societal adaptation. By hindcasting the rise and spread of agropastoral lifestyles across 294 regions in Eurasia and North Africa, the study contrasts different scenarios of exchange between neighboring areas to assess spatiotemporal diffusion patterns. From a modeling standpoint, the findings reject the notion of a simple, exclusive reliance on either demic or cultural diffusion; instead, most regions in Eurasia experienced a blend of both processes. Moreover, the study highlights significant spatiotemporal variability in how these processes balanced out, with individual regions shifting between demic and cultural dominance over time. Only a few, likely environmentally marginal, areas exhibited a clear dominance of demic diffusion. Ultimately, the research emphasizes that diffusion processes must be analyzed diachronically rather than through a time-integrated lens.

We derive new upper bounds for the count of tangencies and orthogonal intersections within a configuration of curves. First, for a collection of $n$ algebraic plane curves, we demonstrate that the number of points where two or more curves are tangent is bounded by $O(n^{3/2})$. Specifically, if no three curves share a common tangent point, the total number of curve-curve tangencies remains $O(n^{3/2})$. Second, given a family of algebraic plane curves and a subset of $n$ curves selected from it, we prove that either the number of points where two or more curves intersect orthogonally is $O(n^{3/2})$, or the family possesses specific special characteristics. These bounds are achieved by converting the arrangement of plane curves into an arrangement of space curves, where the tangency or orthogonality of the original curves maps to intersections in space. Subsequently, we limit the number of intersections among these space curves. To address curve-curve tangency, we apply a polynomial method inspired by Guth and Katz's proof of the joints theorem. For orthogonal curve intersections, we utilize a bound established by Guth and the third author to regulate the number of two-rich points in space curve arrangements.

Nonlinear Auto-Regressive eXogenous (NARX) models represent a widely used category of nonlinear dynamical systems. To characterize the internal multivariate nonlinear mapping within these systems, polynomial basis expansions are frequently employed, resulting in P-NARX models. Utilizing fixed basis functions offers the advantage of yielding a closed-form solution for parameter estimation; however, this approach often fails to produce a sparse representation, leading to an excessive number of parameters. To address this issue, decoupling techniques have been developed specifically for reducing complex multivariate functions. Research indicates that rotating toward a novel basis can yield a more efficient parameterization, where the transformed relationship is structured such that it relies solely on single-input single-output nonlinear functions. Traditional decoupling methods are inadequate for single-output NARX models, a gap this study bridges by implementing the filtered CPD decoupling method introduced by Decuyper et al. (2021b). The proposed approach is demonstrated using data from the Silverbox benchmark, which consists of measurements from an electronic circuit realization of a forced Duffing oscillator.

This document serves as an announcement and preview of a memoir, with the complete version hosted on the American Mathematical Society's Open Math Notes repository (OMN:202109.111309). Within this memoir, I aim to present a fairly comprehensive overview of asymptotic models for water waves, focusing primarily on shallow water scenarios. While the work and its presentation draw significant inspiration from the book by D. Lannes, it expands the discussion in several key areas, specifically addressing high-order and fully dispersive models, as well as internal and interfacial waves.

This work examines solutions to a system of equations modeling the dynamic evolution of spontaneous ruptures within a prestressed, elasto-gravitational medium governed by rate and state friction laws. We introduce an iterative coupling approach utilizing a weak formulation with nonlinear interior boundary conditions, applicable to both continuous time and implicit temporal discretization via the backward Euler method. By incorporating viscosity, we regularize the problem, ensuring the convergence of the proposed scheme for the regularized solutions in both scenarios. Furthermore, we explicitly define the necessary conditions on relevant coefficients required to guarantee convergence.

This paper introduces the Heston-Queue-Hawkes (HQH) model, a novel jump-diffusion framework that integrates the established Heston model with the recently developed Queue-Hawkes (Q-Hawkes) jump mechanism. Similar to the Hawkes process, the HQH model effectively captures self-excitation and contagion dynamics. Crucially, because the characteristic function of the HQH process admits a closed-form solution, it enables the full utilization of Fourier-based fast pricing techniques, such as the COS method. Additionally, we demonstrate that by employing explicitly calculable partial integrals of this characteristic function, the dimensionality and numerical complexity of the COS method can be significantly reduced. Numerical evaluations on European and Bermudan options indicate that the HQH model generates a broader spectrum of volatility smiles than the Bates model, while maintaining a computational cost substantially lower than that of the Heston-Hawkes (HH) process.

This study is driven by the need to resolve unresolved issues in distributionally robust chance-constrained programs (DRCCP) that utilize widely adopted Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Current computational approaches for these programs often impose limiting assumptions on constraint functions and rely on expensive cross-validation (CV) or conservative measure concentration bounds to determine the size of the Wasserstein sets. Conversely, we introduce a practical DRCCP algorithm based on kernel maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) ambiguity sets, designated as MMD-DRCCP. This method effectively manages general nonlinear constraints without requiring ad-hoc reformulations. MMD-DRCCP accommodates both nonlinear and non-convex constraints, offering a proven finite-sample guarantee of constraint satisfaction with a dimension-independent convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$, which is attainable through our practical implementation. Additionally, we develop an efficient bootstrap procedure to construct precise MMD ambiguity sets for real-world applications, eliminating the need for CV. Numerical experiments validate our approach on portfolio optimization and a tube-based distributionally robust model predictive control problem featuring non-convex constraints.

A recent study suggested that the cooling rate of ancient, cold neutron stars (NS) imposes a strict upper bound on the transition rate between neutrons and mirror neutrons ($n-n'$), a constraint so tight that it would likely rule out any detection of $n \to n'$ oscillation in current terrestrial experiments. Driven by this significant implication, we re-examine the proposal and identify a previously overlooked phenomenon in nearly exact mirror models of $n \to n'$ oscillation that substantially alters this bound. Specifically, the $\beta$ decay of mirror neutrons ($n' \to p' + e' +\bar{\nu}'_{e}$) generates a dense cloud of mirror particles ($n'$, $p'$, $e'$, and $D'$) within the NS core. Through $e-e'$ scattering, facilitated by a minute milli-charge carried by mirror particles, these mirror electrons can siphon energy produced by the $n \to n'$ transition. This energy is subsequently released as undetectable mirror photons through rapid mirror bremsstrahlung, thereby weakening the previously established upper limit.

Time series forecasting is essential across diverse fields, including economics and energy systems. However, developing a forecasting model for a specific application involves a complex, iterative design process. This process typically comprises five stages: (1) data pre-processing, (2) feature engineering, (3) hyperparameter optimization, (4) selecting the forecasting method, and (5) forecast ensembling, often structured as a pipeline. To address the increasing demand for such forecasts, automating this design workflow is a promising solution. This paper examines existing literature on automated time series forecasting pipelines to determine how to streamline model design. Specifically, it integrates both Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) and automated statistical methods within a unified pipeline. The study first presents and compares automation techniques for each of the five stages. It then analyzes how these methods interact, combine, and cover the entire pipeline. For both analyses, the authors review the literature, highlight challenges, offer recommendations, and propose directions for future research. The review indicates that most studies address only two or three of the five stages. Consequently, the authors conclude that future work must holistically automate the entire forecasting pipeline to facilitate large-scale adoption of time series forecasting.

The frequent observation of bidirectional links in local cortical networks remains a central topic in debates regarding non-random connectivity. This study presents a concise mathematical analysis demonstrating that within networks where pairwise connection probabilities are symmetric ($P_{ij} = P_{ji}$), the prevalence of reciprocal connections and the presence of non-random architectures are intrinsically connected; consequently, an excess of mutually linked pairs inevitably arises whenever the network structure departs from randomness in any way.

We introduce a general approach to calculating corrections to the extremality bound and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes under arbitrary perturbations, utilizing the Iyer-Wald formalism. In this framework, corrections to the extremality bound are expressed as an integral over an effective stress tensor, which simplifies to the standard stress tensor in specific scenarios of interest. This formulation elucidates the connection between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a canonical ensemble, the weak gravity conjecture's requirement to reduce the mass of an extremal black hole necessitates a violation of the dominant energy condition by the perturbation. Furthermore, we apply this method to determine higher-derivative corrections for charged black holes in anti-de Sitter space and for Kerr black holes.

We present measurements of the gravitationally lensed secondary image—the inaugural "photon ring" in an infinite sequence—surrounding the supermassive black hole M87*, derived from simultaneous modeling and imaging of the 2017 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) data. The inferred ring diameter remained stable throughout the seven-day 2017 observing campaign and aligns with theoretical predictions, offering robust evidence that these measurements probe spacetime and strongly validating the models behind the initial EHT findings. Residual diffuse emission was observed to evolve over timescales of approximately one week. We detected a southwestern extension with high significance, consistent with a rapidly rotating, clockwise base of a jet. This finding bolsters the identification of the M87* jet as a black hole spin-driven outflow generated via the Blandford-Znajek mechanism. We provide three revised mass estimates for M87* by correlating the modeled thin ring component with bright ringlike features in simulated images; one of these estimates is only weakly dependent on the astrophysics of the emission region. All three estimates are mutually consistent and agree with previously reported values. Our most stringent mass constraint integrates data from both the ring and diffuse emission regions, yielding a mass-to-distance ratio of $4.20^{+0.12}_{-0.06}~\mu{\rm as}$ and a corresponding black hole mass of $(7.13\pm0.39)\times10^9M_\odot$, where the uncertainty in the latter is now primarily driven by systematic errors related to the uncertain distance to M87*.

Uncovering concealed geometric and topological structures within noisy datasets presents a significant challenge. The elastic principal graph serves as a computationally efficient and adaptable data approximator, functioning by embedding a graph into the data space and minimizing an energy functional that penalizes deviations of graph nodes from both data points and a pluri-harmonic configuration (an extension of linearity). This graph structure is derived from the data using a topological grammar, which, in its most basic form, generates principal curves or trees. To better handle noise and outliers, we propose incorporating a trimmed data approximation term to enhance the method's robustness. This modification preserves the original elastic graph method's computational efficiency and general convergence characteristics. Furthermore, the resulting trimmed elastic energy functional continues to act as a Lyapunov function for the optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these robust principal graphs in capturing the global structure of various complex data distributions and highlight the benefits of utilizing the trimmed data approximation term for constructing principal graphs and other common data approximators.

We present a protocol designed to solve the conformance test problem, which involves verifying whether a tested process aligns with a reference standard. In our framework, a process is defined by the set of end-products it generates, governed by a specific probability distribution. We model this scenario within the realm of hypothesis testing, focusing on cases where objects behave as pure loss channels. Theoretically, we show that a straightforward quantum strategy—utilizing accessible resources and measurement techniques such as two-mode squeezed vacuum and photon counting—surpasses any classical approach. This protocol was experimentally realized using optical twin beams, confirming our theoretical predictions and proving that a quantum advantage is achievable in realistic settings for this specific task.

The Feynman path-integral variational framework for the polaron problem\cite{Feynman1955}, combined with the related FHIP linear-response mobility theory\cite{Feynman1962}, offers a computationally accessible way to forecast frequency-resolved, temperature-dependent charge-carrier mobility and other experimental metrics in polar semiconductors. We demonstrate that the FHIP mobility theory yields non-Drude transport characteristics and exhibits excellent alignment with recent diagrammatic Monte-Carlo mobility simulations by Mishchenko et al.\cite{Mishchenko2019} for the abstract Fr\"ohlich Hamiltonian. By extending this methodology to include multiple phonon modes within the Fr\"ohlich model action, we achieve a marginally improved variational solution, as evidenced by the calculated energy. Incorporating this added complexity into the mobility theory reveals richer structural details in the frequency and temperature dependence of mobility, resulting from various phonon modes activating at distinct energy levels. Ultimately, this approach serves as a computationally efficient and fully quantitative tool for predicting polaron mobility and response in actual materials.

This article investigates the De Rham cohomology of the initial cover within the Lubin-Tate tower. Specifically, we present a purely local demonstration that the supercuspidal component embodies the local Jacquet-Langlands correspondence for ${\rm GL}_n$ by contrasting it with the rigid cohomology of certain Deligne-Lusztig varieties. The resulting representations mirror those found in $\ell$-adic cohomology when the Weil group's action is disregarded. Our approach depends on extending an excision theorem by Grosse-Kl\"onne and on a semi-stable model developed by Yoshida, for which we provide a more detailed characterization.

In Weyl semimetals, the chiral anomaly drives valley polarization—an imbalance in the occupation of valleys with opposite chirality—when parallel electric and magnetic fields are applied. This study introduces numerical methods to investigate these nonequilibrium phenomena in spatially confined three-dimensional systems subject to variable disorder potentials, providing exact solutions to leading order in both the disorder and the electric field. Applying these tools to a Weyl-metal slab reveals that valley polarization can arise even without an external magnetic field due to "chiral anomaly trapping": spatial confinement generates chiral bulk states that facilitate valley polarization similarly to those induced by a magnetic field. Although this effect stems from finite-size origins, the valley polarization can persist over macroscopic length scales provided the disorder potential is sufficiently long-ranged; under these conditions, direct inter-valley scattering is suppressed, and relaxation proceeds through Fermi-arc surface states.

This work investigates semiclassical spiky strings within de Sitter space and their associated Regge trajectories, extending previous analyses conducted in anti-de Sitter space. Specifically, we show that de Sitter acceleration imposes a maximum spin on each Regge trajectory, a feature analogous to that observed in earlier studies of folded strings. Although this constraint aids the spectrum in adhering to the Higuchi bound, it raises a significant question regarding the preservation of the mild high-energy string scattering behavior characteristic of flat and anti-de Sitter spaces. Our findings suggest that achieving an infinite spectrum of higher-spin states requires an infinite set of Regge trajectories, each possessing an increasingly larger folding number.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated exceptional few-shot learning abilities when a small number of natural language examples serve as demonstrations within a prompt, a technique known as in-context learning. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of this approach is highly sensitive to prompt formatting, the selection of training examples, and their arrangement. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel nearest-neighbor calibration framework for in-context learning. This method leverages the observation that the in-context learning process often generates incorrect labels for training instances, which serves as a valuable supervised signal for calibration. Consequently, our approach directly enhances predictions by integrating a $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$NN) classifier trained on a datastore of cached few-shot instance representations and their associated labels from PLMs. Furthermore, we incorporate adaptive neighbor selection and feature regularization modules to maximize the utility of limited support instances and minimize noise in $k$NN retrieval. Experimental results across various few-shot text classification tasks indicate that our method substantially boosts in-context learning performance, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art tuning-based methods in certain sentiment analysis scenarios.

Incentive salience attribution functions as a psychobiological mechanism that assigns relevance to potentially rewarding stimuli and actions. Although it is a vital element of the motivational system driving daily life, investigating it in natural settings is challenging. We introduce a methodology utilizing artificial neural networks (ANNs) to estimate the latent states generated by this process in scenarios where extensive behavioral data exists but experimental control is absent. Drawing on theoretical and computational insights regarding incentive salience, we constructed an ANN to predict the duration and intensity of future interactions between individuals and video games within a large-scale longitudinal dataset ($N> 3 \times 10^6$). Video games were identified as an optimal context for this approach due to their dependence on reward mechanics and their capacity to yield robust behavioral measures at scale. Compared to alternative methods, our approach generates representations that more effectively predict future behavioral intensity and approximate the functional properties of attributed incentive salience. We contextualize these results within the adopted theoretical and computational frameworks and propose that this methodology could serve as a foundational step for estimating incentive salience in large-scale behavioral research.

Given a well-known theorem by Dixmier, it is natural to treat primitive quotients of $U_q^+(\mathfrak{g})$ as quantum counterparts to Weyl algebras. This paper examines these primitive quotients specifically within the $G_2$ context and calculates their Lie algebra of derivations.

Recent advancements in image denoising have heavily relied on strong supervision from large-scale datasets; however, acquiring well-aligned noisy-clean image pairs for every specific scenario is both complex and expensive in practice. This makes applying conventional supervised denoising networks to real-world, uncurated noisy inputs difficult. While some research has tackled this issue without strong supervision, these methods often depend on impractical assumptions and cannot be directly applied to real-world scenarios. To overcome these challenges, we introduce CVF-SID, a novel and robust self-supervised denoising approach built upon a Cyclic multi-Variate Function (CVF) module and a self-supervised image disentangling (SID) framework. The CVF module generates multiple decomposed variables from the input and feeds their combination back into the system cyclically. By utilizing diverse self-supervised loss terms, CVF-SID effectively separates clean images from noise maps. Unlike methods limited to signal-independent noise models, our approach also addresses signal-dependent noise components essential for real-world applications. Moreover, CVF-SID requires no prior assumptions regarding the underlying noise distribution, enhancing its generalizability to realistic noise conditions. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that CVF-SID achieves state-of-the-art self-supervised image denoising performance, comparable to existing methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Reyhanehne/CVF-SID_PyTorch.

This research note presents explicit dynamical systems for language acquisition based on an acquisition-driven framework (Niyogi & Berwick, 1997; Niyogi, 2006), under the assumption that learners apply the Tolerance Principle (Yang, 2016) to assess rule productivity. The study examines various theoretical parameters, including population size (finite versus infinite) and the quantity of data provided by prior generations. Although simulations of these dynamics and applications to diachronic data are currently being prepared, they are excluded from this initial note.

Driven by contemporary cosmological interests, we aim to extend Einstein's General Theory of Relativity. A promising approach emerges from a novel class of teleparallel gravity known as symmetric teleparallel gravity, or $f(Q)$ gravity, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ governs fundamental interactions. These alternative gravity theories play a crucial role in addressing modern observational challenges and constructing viable cosmological models. The primary goal of this manuscript is to investigate traversable wormhole geometries within the framework of $f(Q)$ gravity. We develop wormhole solutions under three distinct scenarios: (i) assuming a specific relationship between radial and lateral pressures, (ii) incorporating a phantom energy equation of state, and (iii) adopting a specific shape function for the gravitational interaction (specifically a linear $f(Q)$ form). Additionally, we examine two wormhole configurations for the general $f(Q)$ case using two particular shape functions. For each scenario, we assess the viability of the shape functions and perform stability analyses. Our findings indicate that the Null Energy Condition (NEC) is violated in all wormhole models, confirming that these solutions are both realistic and stable. Finally, we analyze embedding diagrams and the volume integral quantifier to provide a comprehensive understanding of the wormhole geometries.

Neural network (NN) potentials are well-suited for coarse-grained (CG) modeling, offering many-body capabilities that enable highly accurate approximations of the potential of mean force and promising unprecedented simulation precision. However, CG NN potentials developed via bottom-up force matching (FM) encounter limitations due to finite data effects; they depend on prior potentials for physically valid extrapolations beyond the training domain, making the resulting free energy surface sensitive to errors in transition regions. While relative entropy (RE) minimization serves as a standard alternative for classical potentials, it has not previously been applied to NN potentials. This study demonstrates through benchmark tests on liquid water and alanine dipeptide that RE training is more data-efficient because it utilizes the CG distribution during the training process. Consequently, RE yields improved free energy surfaces and exhibits reduced sensitivity to prior potentials. Furthermore, RE learns to correct time integration errors, facilitating larger time steps in CG molecular dynamics without compromising accuracy. These results highlight the potential of adopting training objectives beyond force matching to enhance the accuracy and reliability of CG NN potentials.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers an efficient method for jointly training policies for multiple interacting agents. However, in scenarios involving complex interactions, current algorithms often struggle to accurately predict how their own actions influence others. By integrating the capacity to reason about potential responses from other agents, an agent can devise more effective strategies. This paper introduces a recursive reasoning model within a centralized-training-decentralized-execution framework to enhance an agent's ability to cooperate or compete effectively. The proposed algorithm, called the Recursive Reasoning Graph (R2G), achieves state-of-the-art results across various multi-agent particle and robotics games.

We theoretically show that the chemical reaction rate constant can be markedly inhibited by linking molecular vibrations to an optical cavity, showcasing both collective coupling and cavity-frequency modifications to the rate. When a reaction coordinate is tightly coupled to solvent molecules, the rate constant decreases because of the dynamical caging effect. We demonstrate that collectively coupling the solvent to the cavity intensifies this dynamical caging effect, resulting in further suppression of chemical kinetics. This phenomenon is even more pronounced when cavity losses are taken into account.

We introduce a novel, general mechanism explaining how collective exuberance arises among interacting agents within a broad category of Ising-like models, which have long been utilized in economics and social sciences. This mechanism is founded on the insight that socio-economic networks are inherently non-symmetric and hierarchically structured, a feature mathematically represented by a non-normal adjacency matrix. Such non-normal network structures induce transient explosive growth across a wide range of control parameters, specifically within the subcritical regime. Unlike earlier models, this framework demonstrates that achieving coordinated opinions, actions, and global macroscopic order does not necessitate fine-tuning near a critical point. We illustrate this phenomenon theoretically, through agent-based numerical simulations, and via empirical analysis of meme stocks in financial markets. Furthermore, we show that the magnitude of the bubble is directly governed by the Kreiss constant, which quantifies the degree of network non-normality. This conceptual and operational advancement improves upon existing methods for anticipating critical phase transitions by accounting for the pervasive non-normality in complex system dynamics. Consequently, our mechanism offers a comprehensive alternative to previous interpretations of instability across a vast array of complex systems, including ecological environments, social opinion dynamics, and financial markets.

The study of the cone of lower semicontinuous traces focuses on its utility as an invariant, highlighting properties such as compactness, Hausdorffness, and continuity under inductive limits. A corresponding definition for the dual cone is established, and the cone of lower semicontinuous 2-quasitraces on a (non-exact) C*-algebra is also examined. These findings are utilized to analyze the Cuntz semigroup. Specifically, it is demonstrated that for any C*-algebra absorbing the Jiang-Su algebra, the subsemigroup of purely non-compact elements within its Cuntz semigroup is isomorphic to the dual cone of the cone of lower semicontinuous 2-quasitraces. This result enables the calculation of the Cuntz semigroup for two specific classes: C*-algebras that absorb the Jiang-Su algebra and lack non-zero simple subquotients, as well as simple C*-algebras that absorb the Jiang-Su algebra.

Let $D$ represent the distance matrix of an $(n+1)$-point metric space $(X,d)$. For unweighted metric trees, the sum of the entries in $D^{-1}$ consistently equals $2/n$. These trees can be viewed as affinely independent subsets of the Hamming cube $H_n$, leading to a conjecture that $2/n$ represents the minimum possible value for such subsets. This paper validates that conjecture and provides a geometric interpretation of the findings applicable to any subset within $H_n$.

Although markerless pose estimation has gained significant attention recently, marker-based methods remain unmatched in accuracy under controlled conditions. Consequently, they are widely adopted in robotics and biomedical fields, yet traditional implementations rely heavily on heuristics and extensive parameter tuning to ensure reliability across varying environments. This paper introduces MarkerPose, a robust, real-time system designed for high-accuracy pose estimation using a stereo vision setup and a planar target composed of three circles. The system employs two deep neural networks: a SuperPoint-like architecture for pixel-level keypoint localization and classification, and a novel lightweight network called EllipSegNet for sub-pixel-level ellipse segmentation. Pose is calculated via stereo triangulation, with the detection process demonstrating resilience against low lighting and motion blur. Validation against classical computer vision techniques using a robotic arm confirms that MarkerPose achieves superior accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the system's applicability in a 3D freehand ultrasound setup, which demands precise pose estimation. The source code is accessible in Python and C++ at https://github.com/jhacsonmeza/MarkerPose.

This paper presents a novel attack on the NTRU-HPS cryptosystem based on lattice theory and Babai's Nearest Plane Algorithm. Although this approach shares significant characteristics with the traditional CVP attack on NTRU, it distinguishes itself by employing a distinct lattice rather than the standard lattice derived from the public key. The proposed attack is further demonstrated through numerous illustrative examples.

We establish a system of stochastic partial differential equations governing the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix composed of Brownian sheet entries. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sequence of empirical spectral measures for the rescaled matrices, denoted as $\left\{L_{d}(s,t), (s,t)\in[0,S]\times [0,T]\right\}_{d\in\mathbb N}$, is tight within the space $C([0,S]\times [0,T], \mathcal P(\mathbb R))$. Consequently, as $d$ approaches infinity, this sequence converges according to Wigner's semicircle law. Additionally, we derive partial differential equations that characterize the high-dimensional limiting measure.

This paper details a comprehensive investigation into the kinematic, chemical, and excitation characteristics of the giant Ly$\alpha$ emitting nebula and the associated giant \ion{H}{I} absorber linked to the $z = 2.92$ radio galaxy MRC 0943--242. Leveraging spectroscopic data from VLT/MUSE, VLT/X-SHOOTER, and additional instruments, we utilize a broad spectrum of rest-frame wavelengths (765 \AA$\,$ to 6378 \AA$\,$ at $z = 2.92$) combined with two-dimensional spatial resolution. Our analysis reveals clear signs of jet gas interactions influencing the nebula's kinematics, with radio-mode feedback driving both inflows and outflows. We propose that areas exhibiting lower ionization levels, which align spatially with radio hotspots, result from either localized compression of photoionized gas by the expanding radio source—reducing the ionization parameter—or contributions from shock heating. Furthermore, modeling indicates that the X-SHOOTER emission line spectrum is best reproduced by photoionization of super-solar metallicity gas ($Z/Z_{\odot}$ = 2.1) driven by an AGN-like continuum ($\alpha$=--1.0) at a moderate ionization parameter ($U$ = 0.018). We also identify a significant degeneracy between column density and Doppler parameter for the \ion{H}{I} absorption feature, allowing for reasonable fits across a range of log N(\ion{H}{I}/cm$^{-2}$) from 15.20 to 19.63, with optimal fits occurring near the extremes of this interval. Finally, the extended \ion{H}{I} absorber is blueshifted relative to the emission line gas, yet displays a systematic reduction in blueshift at larger radii, consistent with a large-scale expanding shell.

The human microbiome significantly influences both health and disease conditions. Next-generation sequencing technologies enable the quantification of microbiome composition, and clustering this data reveals underlying patterns across samples. While Fang and Subedi (2020) previously introduced a logistic normal multinomial mixture model (LNM-MM) for this purpose, we have developed a family of logistic normal multinomial factor analyzers (LNM-FA) by integrating a factor analyzer structure into the LNM-MM. Given that microbiome data is often high-dimensional, the LNM-FA family is particularly advantageous because assuming a small number of latent factors drastically reduces the parameter count. We estimate parameters using a computationally efficient variant of the alternating expectation conditional maximization algorithm that employs variational Gaussian approximations. The efficacy of this proposed method is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world datasets.

A method developed several years ago enables the analysis of a theory within a regime of strong perturbations. This approach yields a gradient expansion where the leading order recovers the BKL solution in general relativity. By solving the leading-order Einstein equations exactly for a spherically symmetric scenario, we assume a Schwarzschild metric subjected to a time-dependent perturbation. We demonstrate that, when the perturbation is correctly applied, the 4-velocity acquires an exponential warp factor that is consistently greater than unity. A closed-form expression for this factor is provided for a specific case, accompanied by several numerical examples.

Amid the global impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, healthcare infrastructures are transforming, leading to increased acceptance of e-health solutions. However, wearable devices frequently handle sensitive user data, exposing it to significant security and privacy threats. Furthermore, users remain concerned about device counterfeiting, which can occur during fabrication or while stored by vendors. Consequently, safeguarding personal information and verifying device authenticity have become critical challenges. To mitigate these risks, biometric authentication and Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs) must be implemented. Among various biometric modalities, Electrocardiogram (ECG) systems have gained popularity for both patient authentication and vital sign monitoring. Recently, researchers have investigated vulnerabilities within ECG biometric systems to address spoofing attempts. Additionally, since most wearables incorporate CPUs and memory, Non-Volatile Memory (NVM)-based PUFs can be integrated to prevent counterfeiting; yet, numerous studies have questioned the unclonability properties of PUFs. Therefore, a thorough examination of such attacks is essential to meet current security needs. This paper aims to offer a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art advancements in hardware security enabled by biometrics.

This study addresses one-shot visual search for object components. By providing a single reference image with labeled affordance regions, we identify semantically matching parts within a target scene. We introduce AffCorrs, an unsupervised framework that integrates pre-trained DINO-ViT image descriptors with cyclic correspondences. Utilizing AffCorrs, we locate corresponding affordances for both intra-class and inter-class one-shot part segmentation. Although this task presents greater challenges than supervised methods, it facilitates future research directions such as imitation-based affordance learning and assisted teleoperation.

We introduce PICCOLO, a streamlined and efficient algorithm designed for omnidirectional localization. The goal is to determine the camera pose of a 360-degree panorama image given a colored point cloud and the panorama itself. Our pipeline operates off-the-shelf using a single query image, eliminating the need for neural network training or the collection of ground-truth poses. Instead, we employ gradient-descent optimization to align the color of each point cloud feature with the comprehensive view of the panorama to recover the camera position. Our proposed "sampling loss" is point-cloud-centric, assessing the match at the projected location of every point, whereas traditional photometric loss is image-centric, comparing colors pixel by pixel. By shifting the focus of comparison, sampling loss effectively mitigates the severe visual distortions inherent in omnidirectional imagery and leverages the global context of the 360-degree view to address challenging localization scenarios. Evaluation across diverse environments demonstrates that PICCOLO surpasses existing omnidirectional localization methods in both accuracy and stability.

Drawing inspiration from a novel coded computation algorithm for invertible functions, we introduce Coded-InvNet, a method for creating robust prediction serving systems capable of gracefully managing stragglers and node failures. Coded-InvNet integrates recent advancements in deep learning, including invertible neural networks, Manifold Mixup, and domain translation techniques, thereby bridging significant research gaps between machine learning and systems engineering. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that Coded-InvNet surpasses existing solutions, particularly when compute resource overhead remains as low as 10%. For example, even without prior knowledge of which of ten workers will fail, our algorithm can design a backup task to accurately recover the missing prediction with 85.9% precision, representing a substantial 32.5% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art.

The CLIC Tracker Detector (CLICTD) is a monolithic pixel sensor manufactured using a modified 180 nm CMOS imaging process, enhanced with a deep low-dose n-type implant to achieve full lateral depletion. A key feature of this sensor is its small collection diode, which is crucial for minimizing input capacitance. Originally conceived as a technology demonstrator for tracking detector research within the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC) framework, the CLICTD's design holds significant relevance for future upgrades at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). The sensor is available in two pixel configurations: one featuring a continuous deep n-type implant and another with a segmented n-type implant designed to facilitate rapid charge collection. The pixel matrix comprises $16\times128$ detection channels, each sized at $300 \times 30$ microns. To reduce digital circuitry while preserving a fine collection electrode pitch, every detection channel is divided into eight sub-pixels. This paper details the characterization of the CLICTD sensor under particle beam conditions, comparing the two pixel flavours through simultaneous time-over-threshold and time-of-arrival measurements. Notably, the results demonstrate a time resolution as low as $(5.8 \pm 0.1)$ ns and a spatial resolution reaching $(4.6 \pm 0.2)$ microns. Furthermore, hit detection efficiency is observed to exceed 99.7% at thresholds corresponding to several hundred electrons.

We examine charged d-dimensional black holes confined within a cavity under extended phase space conditions, focusing on their behavior as heat engines and during Joule-Thomson (JT) expansions. Given that the phase structure of black holes in a cavity mirrors that of anti-de-Sitter (AdS) scenarios, we utilize them as the working substance to compute efficiency across both Carnot and rectangular cycles. Furthermore, we analyze the consistency of JT expansion for charged black holes in a cavity with AdS cases, ultimately determining how varying boundary conditions influence black hole thermodynamics.

This study investigates M dwarf rotation rates across various ages to set benchmarks for M dwarf gyrochronology. We analyzed a sample of 713 spectroscopically classified M0-M8 dwarfs, deriving new rotation rates from K2 light curves for 179 of them. These findings were combined with rotation data from cluster members with known ages (5–700 Myr) and field objects assumed to be older than 1 Gyr. Using Gaia DR2 parallaxes and (G-GRP) photometry, we constructed color-magnitude diagrams to compare the samples. We examined period distributions across ages using color-period plots and supplemented our analysis with H-alpha equivalent widths and tangential velocities where available to explore age dependencies. Our results indicate that the transition age from rapid to slow rotation, identified as an "elbow" in period-color plots, varies by spectral type; later spectral types transition at older ages, with M4 stars in the 700 Myr-old Praesepe cluster marking one of the oldest measured transitions. This shift coincides with a change in H-alpha activity, where objects move from rapid to slow rotation, though redder or smaller stars remain active longer. Finally, Gaia kinematic data reveal evidence of rotation stalling for late-type M dwarfs in the field, suggesting the transition to slow rotation occurs much later for mid-to-late-type M dwarfs.

The DGKT vacua represent a category of AdS$_4$ flux solutions characterized by complete moduli stabilization, parametric control, and a parametric hierarchy of scales. Notably, the specific moduli masses in these models result in integer conformal dimensions within the light spectrum of their potential holographic duals. This note examines two key features of AdS flux vacua possessing such integer conformal dimensions: first, the moduli exhibit polynomial shift symmetries dependent on spacetime; second, the dominant scaling behaviors of the central charge and the moduli can be inferred directly from the near-horizon geometry of stacks of orthogonally intersecting D-brane domain walls, which are dual to the unbounded fluxes. We demonstrate these points using several examples of parametric flux vacua in both AdS$_4$ and AdS$_3$ contexts.

This study introduces a new approach for gathering survey data in the aftermath of natural disasters, integrating it with device-based mobility metrics to analyze demographic outcomes. There is growing interest within the demographic field in leveraging social media as a cost-effective platform for measuring difficult-to-access demographic indicators. Building on prior research that utilized Facebook targeted ads to study low-income shift workers, immigrant assimilation, global fertility, and migration stocks, we present a rapid-response survey distributed directly through the Facebook app to assess post-disaster demographic and economic impacts. By combining these survey responses with Facebook Displacement Maps, we evaluate the validity and underlying drivers of observed behavioral patterns. Specifically, we deployed this survey following the 2019 Australian bushfires to investigate resident displacement, testing key hypotheses regarding displacement decisions and demographics. Our findings reveal significant gender disparities in displacement timing, decision-making, and access to protective gear like smoke masks. The paper concludes with a discussion of the resulting research and policy implications.

Let $G$ be a finite group acting on a set $X$, where $\delta_k(G,X)$ represents the fraction of elements in $G$ possessing exactly $k$ fixed points in $X$. Denoting the symmetric group on $[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ as $\mathrm{S}_n$, we consider the permutational wreath product $A\wr B$ for subgroups $A\le\mathrm{S}_m$ and $B\le\mathrm{S}_n$. This construction admits two natural actions, for which we derive explicit formulas regarding $\delta_k(A\wr B,[m]{\times}[n])$ and $\delta_k(A\wr B,[m]^{[n]})$. We demonstrate that when $k=0$, these proportions are dense within the intervals $[\delta_0(B,[n]),1]$ and $[\delta_0(A,[m]),1]$. Additionally, we offer estimates for $\delta_0(G,[m]^{[n]})$ concerning subgroups $G$ of $\mathrm{S}_m\wr\mathrm{S}_n$ that contain $\mathrm{A}_m^{[n]}$.

We present a variational approximation of the Ambrosio-Tortorelli type for brittle fracture energies in piecewise-rigid solids, addressing both geometrically nonlinear and linearized elasticity scenarios.

Minimizing output fluctuations in thermal machines is a critical objective for both classical and quantum technologies. We demonstrate that leveraging collective effects within open quantum systems enables the creation of highly consistent many-body quantum machines. Specifically, we examine quantum Otto engines modeled as $n$ spins jointly coupled to thermal reservoirs. Our findings indicate that these collective interactions can markedly decrease fluctuations in output work, measured by high reliability ($r$) and low thermodynamic uncertainty. Unlike independent engines, our collective counterparts exhibit a quadratic improvement in reliability $r$. These results strengthen the argument for the practical development of realistic collective quantum thermal machines.

Precise segmentation of cardiac anatomy is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning, yet it faces significant hurdles due to limited annotated data and variability across different medical centers and imaging vendors, which hampers advanced deep learning models. This study introduces a fully automatic approach to segment cardiac structures—including the left and right ventricular blood pools and the left ventricular myocardium—within MRI volumes. Our method employs a semi-supervised learning framework that utilizes unlabelled MRI timeframes through label propagation and applies style transfer to mitigate inter-center and vendor variance, thereby enhancing segmentation robustness. Evaluated in the M&Ms Challenge 7, our approach achieved a second-place ranking among fourteen competing teams.

This paper introduces URanker, a ranking-based underwater image quality assessment (UIQA) method built upon an efficient conv-attentional image Transformer. Specifically for underwater imagery, we introduce (1) a histogram prior that encodes color distribution as tokens to capture global degradations, and (2) dynamic cross-scale correspondence to model local degradations. The final prediction relies on class tokens from multiple scales, ensuring a comprehensive analysis of multi-scale dependencies. Utilizing a margin ranking loss, URanker accurately ranks underwater images from the same scene enhanced by various UIE algorithms based on visual quality. To support this, we provide the URankerSet dataset, which includes results from diverse UIE algorithms and their corresponding perceptual rankings for training purposes. Beyond URanker's strong performance, we demonstrate that a simple U-shape UIE network achieves promising results when supervised by our pre-trained URanker. Furthermore, we propose a normalization tail that significantly boosts UIE network performance. Extensive experiments confirm the state-of-the-art efficacy of our approach, and we discuss the key design elements. Finally, our dataset and code will be made publicly available.

We introduce an efficient mechanism for generating an invisible axion through Peccei-Quinn symmetry breaking at a low energy scale. The proposed model includes, alongside standard model fermions and gauge bosons, a single gauge boson, an up-type vector-like quark, two Higgs doublets, and two Higgs singlets. The physical Peccei-Quinn global symmetry emerges from two distinct global symmetries linked by the new gauge symmetry; each symmetry acts exclusively on either the right-handed top quark or the left-handed new quark, thereby circumventing the domain wall problem. Due to electroweak and new gauge interactions, the Higgs doublet responsible for top quark mass and the Higgs singlet responsible for new quark mass contribute only minimally to the axion. Consequently, the axion decay constant is significantly enhanced by a factor determined by the vacuum expectation values of the four Higgs scalars.

By integrating hydrodynamic and field theoretic approaches, we construct a comprehensive theory describing phonons as Goldstone bosons in crystals, liquids, and glasses. This framework relies on non-affine displacements and the resulting relaxation of Goldstone phases. We establish a connection between the conservation status of specific higher-form currents and the characteristics of the underlying deformation field—non-affinity—which governs molecular motion under applied stress. Specifically, the single-valued nature of the deformation field corresponds to the conservation of higher-form charges that quantify topological defects. Our formalism predicts, from first principles, the existence of propagating shear waves in liquids above a critical wave-vector, offering the first derivation of this phenomenon based on fundamental symmetries. This same perspective explains the "positive sound dispersion" observed in longitudinal sound. Crucially, our theory posits that the primary collective relaxation timescale for liquids and glasses (the $\alpha$ relaxation for glasses) is determined by the phase relaxation time, which is not inherently tied to the Maxwell time. Furthermore, we develop a non-equilibrium effective action using the in-in formalism on the Schwinger-Keldysh contour, reinforcing this conceptual framework. In conclusion, our work indicates that the essential distinction between solids, fluids, and glasses lies in their associated generalized higher-form global symmetries and topological structures, with the Burgers vector of displacement fields serving as a topological order parameter that differentiates the ordered solid phase from amorphous phases (fluids and glasses).

This paper examines the valuation of exchange options under two dynamic models for log-prices: the established variance gamma process and the recently proposed variance gamma++ process by Gardini et al. [19]. Specifically, we derive a Margrabe-style formula for the standard variance gamma model and formulate an "integral-free" expression for the variance gamma++ variant. Additionally, we demonstrate the construction of general multidimensional extensions of the variance gamma++ process that maintain both mathematical and numerical tractability. Finally, we apply these models to German and French energy power markets by calibrating parameters with real market data and evaluating exchange options using the derived closed-form formulas, Fourier-based methods, and Monte Carlo simulations.

Through the application of topology, we demonstrate the presence of novel unidirectional modes within compressible, rotating, and stratified fluids. Their origin is linked to the violation of time-reversal symmetry caused by rotation and the breaking of vertical mirror symmetry due to stratification and gravity. We emphasize the significance of the nontraditional component of the Coriolis force, which arises from a rotation field tangent to the surface. Unlike horizontally trapped equatorial waves generated by the traditional, surface-perpendicular component of the Coriolis force, we identify vertically trapped modes confined along interfaces separating regions with differing stratification characteristics. Furthermore, we establish that these modes represent generalized atmospheric Lamb waves, where the direction of propagation is determined by the nontraditional part of the Coriolis force.

Enhancing the reliability of line segment detectors under motion blur is a critical challenge for practical applications like visual SLAM and 3D reconstruction. Current detection methods suffer significant performance drops when attempting to accurately identify and localize line segments in motion-blurred conditions. Although event data offers strong complementary properties to standard images—providing minimal blur and high-temporal-resolution edge awareness—it holds potential for improving robust line segment recognition. To address this, we propose leveraging the complementary information from both images and events. Our approach begins with a general frame-event feature fusion network designed to extract and combine detailed image textures with low-latency event edges; this network comprises a channel-attention-based shallow fusion module and a self-attention-based dual hourglass module. Subsequently, we employ two state-of-the-art wireframe parsing networks to detect line segments on the fused feature maps. Additionally, we introduce two datasets, FE-Wireframe and FE-Blurframe, which contain pairwise motion-blurred images and events for both synthetic and realistic scenarios. Extensive experiments on these datasets validate the effectiveness of our method. On the real-world dataset, our approach achieves a mean structural average precision (msAP) of 63.3% when using a model pre-trained on FE-Wireframe and fine-tuned on FE-Blurframe. This represents an improvement of 32.6 and 11.3 points over models trained exclusively on synthetic or real data, respectively. The code, datasets, and trained models are available at: https://levenberg.github.io/FE-LSD

This study addresses the k-sparse recovery challenge: constructing an m × n matrix A that allows the efficient recovery of a signal x' from its measurement Ax, such that the ℓ₁-distance ||x - x'||₁ is bounded by a constant C times the optimal ℓ₁-distance to any k-sparse vector. While it is established that matrices with this property exist with only O(k log(n/k)) rows, this paper demonstrates that this bound is tight. This result remains valid even in a more general randomized framework, where A is a random variable and the recovery algorithm must successfully reconstruct any fixed x with constant probability over the choice of A.

Association rule mining represents a prominent area of data mining research, with applications spanning from grocery basket analysis to highly interpretable classification systems. However, classical algorithms for this task suffer from significant drawbacks, including inefficient execution times, high memory consumption, and an excessive number of generated rules. Meta-heuristics, widely applied to various optimization challenges, offer a viable alternative. This study has two primary goals: first, to evaluate the performance of current state-of-the-art meta-heuristics on association rule mining using their multi-objective variants optimized for support, confidence, and cosine; and second, to introduce a novel algorithm designed to efficiently extract rules from massive datasets by exploring a vast solution space, inspired by the species diversity of the Cambrian Explosion. By benchmarking this new approach against 20 existing algorithms across 22 real-world datasets, we demonstrate that it yields superior results and outperforms several leading methods.

To address the challenges of high Doppler spread in 6G wireless systems, Orthogonal Time Frequency Space (OTFS) modulation has been introduced. This phenomenon occurs when signals reflected by rapidly moving objects, such as high-speed vehicles, cause Inter-Carrier Interference (ICI). While current advanced OTFS detectors struggle to maintain an acceptable Bit-Error-Rate (BER) as the count of mobile reflectors—and consequently the level of ICI—increases, this paper presents a new solution: the Bayesian-based Parallel Interference and Decision Statistics Combining (B-PIC-DSC) OTFS detector. Designed for high ICI environments, the B-PIC-DSC detector iteratively eliminates interference using PIC and DSC schemes while incorporating Bayesian probability measures to refine transmitted symbol estimates. Simulation results demonstrate that, compared to existing state-of-the-art detectors, the proposed method achieves a BER below $10^{-5}$ at Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNR) exceeding 14 dB, even under severe ICI conditions.

Positive definite functions on spheres have garnered growing attention across various mathematical and statistical disciplines. Specifically, Schoenberg sequences within the spectral representation of these functions have been extensively investigated by numerous mathematicians recently. This paper establishes a set of relationships between Schoenberg sequences defined on both real and complex spheres of varying dimensions. We further demonstrate these findings by detailing an application to strict positive definiteness.

We introduce two general approaches to enhance semi-supervised learning (SSL). The initial approach incorporates weight perturbation (WP) into current "consistency regularization" (CR) frameworks, utilizing variational Bayesian inference (VBI) for implementation. The second approach introduces a new consistency loss termed "maximum uncertainty regularization" (MUR). Unlike standard consistency losses that focus on perturbations near data points, MUR actively identifies "virtual" points located further away that yield the highest prediction uncertainty. This mechanism enables MUR to enforce smoothness across a broader region of the input-output manifold. Experimental results demonstrate significant reductions in classification errors for various CR-based methods when augmented with VBI, MUR, or both.

We present a new distributed rendering technique designed to deliver high-fidelity graphics for thin-client gaming and VR environments. Since mobile devices often lack the processing power required for real-time ray tracing, our solution utilizes hardware-accelerated cloud servers to handle this computationally intensive task, streaming the results back to the client via remote rendering. By employing a distributed hybrid rendering strategy, we combine the strengths of both the client and server: the client performs rasterization locally, while the server offloads ray tracing. Leveraging the low-latency capabilities of 5G networks, this collaboration ensures effective communication, maintaining interactive frame rates while producing superior visuals. Ultimately, this approach offers better image quality than local rendering and faster performance than traditional remote rendering.

Multisplit is a versatile parallel primitive that reorganizes input data into contiguous buckets or bins based on a programmer-defined categorization function. Because efficient multisplit operations are currently absent on GPUs, developers typically resort to sorting as a workaround. This can be done by first generating an auxiliary array of bucket IDs and sorting the data accordingly, or, when smaller buckets correspond to smaller keys, by sorting the input directly. However, both existing approaches are inefficient: the first involves costly data movements, while the second wastes resources by sorting elements within each bucket. This paper introduces a parallel model and several implementations for the multisplit problem, specifically targeting scenarios with a small number of buckets (up to 256). We leverage warp-synchronous programming and emphasize warp-wide communication to minimize branch divergence and memory consumption. Additionally, we hierarchically reorder input elements to optimize global memory access coalescing. Testing on a GeForce GTX 1080 GPU demonstrates a peak throughput of 18.93 Gkeys/s (or 11.68 Gpairs/s) for key-only (or key-value) multisplit operations. Furthermore, we show how multisplit serves as a foundational component for radix sort. Our multisplit-based sort implementation achieves performance comparable to the fastest existing GPU sort routines, handling 32-bit keys and key-value pairs at throughputs of 3.0 Gkeys/s and 2.1 Gpairs/s, respectively.

This study introduces a compact model for a 14 nm CMOS FinFET-based Resonant Body Transistor (fRBT) designed to operate at 11.8 GHz, aiming to support next-generation RF generation, filtering, clocking, and sensing. The model development is guided by an analysis of the device's phononic dispersion characteristics, which reveals polarization exchange resulting from the periodic structure of the back-end-of-line (BEOL) metal PnC. To represent the resonance cavity, an eigenfrequency-based extraction method suitable for electrostatic force transduction resonators was employed. Additionally, the drive and sense transistors within the fRBT are modeled using augmented versions of the BSIM-CMG (Common Multi-Gate) model. This framework ensures seamless integration with foundry-provided process design kits (PDKs) and circuit simulators while offering flexibility regarding transduction mechanisms and device architectures. Finally, the model's accuracy was confirmed by comparing its behavior with RF measurement data from fabricated fRBT devices under various operating conditions, successfully demonstrating the first complete model for this class of resonant device integrated directly into the CMOS stack.

The unique chance to measure black hole and neutron star merger properties, such as mass and spin, with exceptional precision comes from gravitational waves. Achieving this requires theoretical signal models that are both highly accurate and computationally efficient. However, incorporating complex physics like higher-order multipoles and relativistic spin-induced orbital precession increases model complexity and computational cost, creating a major bottleneck for parameter inference. A common strategy to address this is constructing fast surrogate models based on slower, original waveforms. This paper demonstrates that combining traditional surrogate techniques with artificial neural networks can produce accurate, highly efficient emulations of multipolar time-domain waveform models for precessing binary black holes. Applying this approach to the state-of-the-art SEOBNRv4PHM model, we achieved significant speed gains: our neural network surrogate, SEOBNN_v4PHM_4dq2, generates a single waveform for a 44 solar mass binary (starting at 20Hz) in just 18ms on a standard CPU. This represents a two-order-of-magnitude improvement over the original SEOBNRv4PHM model. Furthermore, GPU acceleration allows for simultaneous batch generation, further enhancing speed. Even without GPU support, this drastic reduction in generation cost can shorten inference times from weeks to mere hours.

Recursive path ordering (RPO) is a fundamental instrument in term rewriting for establishing termination. We re-examine its formulation through specific rules applied to trees (or equivalent terms) that incorporate a 'star' control symbol, indicating a requirement to reduce the tree (or term) within the defined order. This approach yields "star games," which are highly effective for demonstrating termination across various rewriting problems. For example, applying the most basic star game to finite unlabeled trees provides a straightforward proof of the termination of the renowned Hydra battle, bypassing the conventional reliance on ordinals. Furthermore, we present an alternative methodology for constructing star games based on a proof technique by Buchholz, refined by van Oostrom, which results in a quantitative interpretation of the star control symbol. The paper concludes by outlining several open questions and potential avenues for future research.
