Leveraging the VRMOM estimator, we formulate a general distributed inference algorithm capable of resisting Byzantine failures. Theoretically, our algorithm demonstrates a rapid convergence rate requiring only a constant number of communication rounds. Furthermore, we establish an asymptotic normality result to facilitate statistical inference, marking the first such normality result in the context of Byzantine-robust distributed learning to our knowledge. Simulation results are also included to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

A gaseous time-projection chamber (TPC) capable of reconstructing the $z$ coordinate for nuclear recoil tracks has been developed for dark-matter searches and $\alpha$-particle imaging under low radioactivity conditions. TPCs utilizing sheet-resistor field cages offer the potential to detect both charge and photons generated by tracks, provided the sheet resistor allows visible light transmission, enabling drift length determination via the time difference between these signals. In this study, the optical transmittance of sheet resistors was measured at $24.5\pm0.1_{\rm stat}\pm0.6_{\rm syst}\%$ for $\rm {CF}_4$ gas scintillation light using an $\alpha$-particle source. Approximately 20 photoelectrons were observed for a 5.3~MeV$\alpha$ particle in $\rm CF}_4$ gas when a sheet resistor was present. The study further discusses the feasibility of detecting lower-energy tracks by estimating the number of observable photoelectrons using multi-alkali-cathode phototubes and SiPMs sensitive to near-infrared light.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g$ over an algebraically closed field $k$, and let $G$ be a connected reductive group defined over $k$. A $G$-torsor is termed essentially finite if it can be reduced to a finite group, extending the concept of essentially finite vector bundles to any reductive group $G$. We establish that every such torsor is strongly semistable with torsion degree. Furthermore, we investigate the density of the $k$-rational points of essentially finite $G$-torsors of degree $0$, denoted $M_{G}^{\text{ef},0}$, within the set of all semistable degree $0$ $G$-torsors, $M_{G}^{\text{ss},0}$. Our results demonstrate that for $g=1$, the inclusion $M_{G}^{\text{ef},0}\subset M_{G}^{\text{ss},0}$ is dense. However, when $g>1$ and $\text{char}(k)=0$, we prove that for any reductive group of semisimple rank 1, the set $M_{G}^{\text{ef},0}$ is not dense in $M_{G}^{\text{ss},0}$.

Question answering (QA) models are widely recognized for leveraging data biases, such as language priors in visual QA and positional biases in reading comprehension. Although recent debiasing techniques improve out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, they often incur significant losses in in-distribution (ID) performance, limiting their use to scenarios where the test distribution is pre-known. This paper introduces Introspective Distillation (IntroD), a novel approach that optimizes both OOD and ID performance in QA tasks. Our primary contribution lies in blending the inductive biases of both distributions by introspecting whether training samples belong to the factual ID domain or the counterfactual OOD domain. Experiments on visual QA benchmarks (VQA v2, VQA-CP) and the SQuAD reading comprehension dataset show that IntroD matches the competitive OOD results of existing debiasing methods while maintaining or even surpassing ID performance compared to non-debiasing baselines.

Biological systems are frequently represented using ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with constant parameters. Nevertheless, factors like cell signaling or drug treatments can shift the cellular state, creating multi-mode dynamics that are best described by hybrid automata featuring distinct nonlinear behaviors across various operational modes. This paper presents a model checking-based framework capable of modeling and analyzing both single- and multi-mode biological systems. We address the core challenge in systems biology—determining parameter values that ensure a model exhibits desired behaviors—through bounded model checking. By employing delta-decision procedures to solve satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) problems, we circumvent the undecidability inherent in reachability issues. The proposed framework supports various analytical tasks, including model calibration and falsification, therapeutic strategy discovery, and Lyapunov stability analysis. We validate these approaches through case studies involving prostate cancer progression, cardiac cell action potentials, and radiation-induced diseases.

This research addresses rank aggregation, aiming to derive a consensus ranking from a collection of individual lists, with a specific focus on scenarios involving extreme lists where only the top or bottom positions are known. To handle missing data in these extreme cases, we impute absent ranks using the average value and extend Spearman's $\rho$ to accommodate such constraints. Our primary contribution is the development of a non-parametric rank aggregation estimator grounded in multivariate extensions of Spearman's $\rho$, which quantifies correlation across multiple ranked lists. Defined via copulas, this multivariate formulation reveals that the geometric mean of normalized ranks maximizes correlation, inspiring a weighted geometric mean approach for learning to rank that yields a closed-form least squares solution. By imputing missing ranks with average values for extreme lists, we enable the application of Spearman's $\rho$. Empirical evaluations on the MQ2007 and MQ2008 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

We analyze recent work by Malaney-Weinstein titled "Economics as Gauge Theory," which was presented on November 10, 2021, at the University of Chicago's Money and Banking Workshop. Specifically, we simplify the technical mathematics used in their work to make it more accessible to a broader audience. Additionally, we address the conjectures raised by Malaney-Weinstein, demonstrating that they offer no meaningful value for calculating index numbers or inflation rates. Our conclusion is that the primary contribution of the Malaney-Weinstein work is that it serves as a striking example of how simple concepts can be obscured through an inefficient application of gauge theory.

This paper introduces an optimization-driven framework for neighborhood search that removes the necessity of defining problem-specific neighborhoods for any given (zero-one) optimization task. By integrating a generalized Hamming distance neighborhood into the problem formulation, the method naturally yields a suitable search procedure. We apply this strategy to the non-unicost set covering problem and evaluate it across 65 test instances widely recognized in existing literature. The computational findings demonstrate that our neighborhood search optimization approach achieves solution quality that is highly competitive compared to other methods documented in the field.

This study presents the initial LHC search utilizing vector boson fusion to investigate heavy Majorana neutrinos and the Weinberg operator. The analysis examines the same-sign dimuon final state using proton-proton collision data recorded at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV by the CMS detector, covering an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. The findings align with standard model predictions. Constraints on the squared mixing element between the muon and heavy neutrino are established for masses ranging from 50 GeV to 25 TeV; notably, for masses exceeding 650 GeV, these represent the tightest limits obtained from LHC searches to date. Additionally, a preliminary test of the Weinberg operator yields an observed 95% confidence level upper limit on the effective $\mu\mu$ Majorana neutrino mass of 10.8 GeV.

This paper investigates Yukawa textures within effective heterotic models by employing singular spectral data. A primary benefit of this method is the ability to decompose bundle cohomologies into smaller components, thereby isolating the segments that host zero modes capable of generating non-varying Yukawa couplings. Furthermore, it establishes a clear correspondence between Yukawa textures in heterotic models and local F-theory models, specifically regarding fields residing in the bulk or localized on 7-branes. The analysis is currently restricted to Weierstrass elliptically fibered Calabi-Yau manifolds, though the paper concludes with a proposal for extending this framework to all elliptically fibered Calabi-Yau spaces possessing rational sections.

This paper introduces a distinct category of elements, termed l elements, within algebras generated by the Cayley Dickson process. We establish criteria for the invertibility of these elements, which prove instrumental in deriving new identities that facilitate the investigation of these algebras' properties.

To achieve diverse goals such as aligning safety with human preferences and optimizing learning efficiency, recent reinforcement learning research has increasingly focused on risk functionals that consider the full distribution of returns. Building on prior work in off-policy risk assessment (OPRA) for contextual bandits—which provided consistent estimators for the target policy's return cumulative distribution function (CDF) with finite sample guarantees valid across all risk measures—this paper extends OPRA to Markov decision processes (MDPs). In MDPs, standard importance sampling (IS) CDF estimators exhibit high variance on extended trajectories due to low effective sample sizes. To address this, we integrate model-based estimation to create the first doubly robust (DR) estimator for the return CDF in MDPs. This new estimator significantly reduces variance and, under well-specified models, reaches the Cramer-Rao lower bound. Furthermore, downstream estimates for many risk functionals benefit from reduced bias and variance. We also establish the first minimax lower bounds for off-policy CDF and risk estimation, showing they match our derived error bounds up to a constant factor. Finally, experiments across various environments confirm the precision of our DR CDF estimates.

The discovery of an increasing number of two-dimensional superconductors within the layered van der Waals (vdW) family has so far been constrained by the small sample volumes, limiting characterization primarily to electrical transport. Consequently, measuring the diamagnetic response of the superfluid to magnetic fields—a hallmark of superconductivity—has remained elusive. In this study, we employ a local magnetic probe to directly assess the superfluid response in the gate-tunable superconducting state of MoS$_2$. Our results indicate that while the backgate voltage alters the superconducting transition temperature non-monotonically, both the low-temperature superfluid stiffness and normal-state conductivity increase monotonically with voltage. In certain devices, we observe direct evidence consistent with a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition, whereas others exhibit a broadened, shallow onset of superfluidity. These findings suggest that disorder plays a critical role in shaping the superconducting properties of MoS$_2$. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that magnetic property measurements are feasible for vdW superconductors and reveals that their superfluid response deviates significantly from simple BCS-like behavior.

A basin of attraction is defined as the collection of initial conditions that converge to a particular asymptotic state within a specific dynamical system. In this work, we present a classification of the most prevalent basins in nonlinear dynamics utilizing basin entropy. Furthermore, we have identified significant relationships between basin entropy and other metrics employed to quantify the unpredictability linked to these basins, including the uncertainty exponent, lacunarity, and various parameters associated with the Wada property.

This study examines level statistics during the transition between delocalized and localized phases in interacting many-body systems. We revisit the joint probability distribution for eigenvalues derived from the statistical mechanics of energy level dynamics, as originally formulated by Pechukas and Yukawa. This resulting single-parameter analytic distribution is investigated numerically using Monte Carlo simulations. The higher-order spacing ratios obtained are then compared against data from various quantum many-body systems. The findings indicate that the Pechukas-Yukawa distribution aligns well with the $\beta$-Gaussian ensemble, a recently proposed single-parameter model for level statistics in disordered many-body contexts. Furthermore, the Pechukas-Yukawa distribution performs only marginally worse than the two-parameter $\beta$-h ansatz, which has previously demonstrated remarkable accuracy in reproducing the level statistics of physical systems.

Our primary objective is to elucidate Lidskii's findings regarding the decomposition of the root vector system for non-selfadjoint operators. By employing techniques from entire function theory and defining a specific Schatten-von Neumann class based on the convergence exponent, we analyze strictly accretive operators under particular norm-based conditions. Consequently, we construct a sequence of power-type contours, which contrasts with Lidskii's approach that utilized a sequence of exponential-type contours.

We examine a two-dimensional electron gas situated on a cylinder featuring a screw dislocation, focusing on how both the system's geometry and the potential deformation arising from lattice distortions influence its Landau levels. This scenario, where a deformed potential is present, is applicable to three-dimensional common semiconductors with electrons confined to a cylindrical shell. Our analysis reveals significant quantitative distinctions caused by this lattice distortion; specifically, the deformed potential reduces the effective cyclotron frequency, which consequently increases the Hall conductivity.

This study presents a comprehensive search for anomalous Higgs boson production via diphoton decays, both in isolation and in association with at least one jet, utilizing CMS data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Events are categorized using razor variables ($M_\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{R}^2$) alongside the momentum and mass resolution of the diphoton system. The results are interpreted within the frameworks of strong and electroweak supersymmetric particle production. Consequently, we exclude bottom squark pair production with masses under 450 GeV (for decays to a bottom quark, Higgs boson, and lightest supersymmetric particle with LSP mass below 250 GeV). Additionally, for wino-like chargino-neutralino production, we rule out charginos with masses below 170 GeV when the LSP mass is less than 25 GeV. Finally, in the Gauge-Mediated Supersymmetry Breaking (GMSB) scenario, we exclude charginos with masses below 205 GeV for neutralinos decaying into a Higgs boson and a goldstino LSP with a 100% branching fraction.

This study adopts specific structures for the charged and neutral mass matrices within the lepton sector, drawing inspiration from analogous patterns in up and down quark mass matrices that feature a defined number of "texture zeros." The resulting lepton mixing matrix is derived from the rotation matrices that diagonalize these mass matrices in both the neutral and charged lepton sectors. By employing texture zeros, the model minimizes spurious parameters, retaining only those essential for explaining observed charged lepton masses and neutrino oscillation parameters. Specifically, we analyzed a scenario involving five texture zeros and compared the predicted lepton mixing matrices against current neutrino sector measurements. Furthermore, we investigated the sensitivities of the independent parameters across non-equivalent model forms using simulated data from the DUNE neutrino oscillation experiment. Our findings indicate that DUNE possesses the sensitivity to detect non-zero CP-violation permitted by these models.

Autonomous systems incorporating deep learning (DL) require uncertainty quantification methods to evaluate the confidence of their predictions. However, for safe deployment in critical applications, these systems must address input uncertainty in addition to output uncertainty. By modeling a probability distribution at the input stage, uncertainty can propagate through various components, yielding a comprehensive measure of total system uncertainty. This position paper introduces a method for managing input uncertainty within Bayesian Deep Learning control policies for aerial navigation. Preliminary results indicate that this approach enhances the robustness of navigation policies when encountering Out-of-Distribution (OoD) scenarios.

Bloch and Beilinson's conjecture posits that for a smooth projective variety $X$ defined over a number field $k$, the kernel of its Albanese map consists entirely of torsion elements. This paper examines the case where $X$ is a product $C_1\times\cdots\times C_d$ of smooth projective curves, demonstrating that if the conjecture holds for any pair of curves within the product, it necessarily holds for the entire variety $X$. Furthermore, we construct numerous new instances of non-isogenous elliptic curves $E_1, E_2$ with positive rank over $\mathbb{Q}$ such that the image of the natural map $E_1(\mathbb{Q})\otimes E_2(\mathbb{Q})\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\text{CH}_0(E_1\times E_2)$ is finite, notably including the first examples where the rank exceeds one. By integrating these findings, we establish infinitely many nontrivial products $X=C_1\times\cdots\times C_d$ for which the corresponding map $\varepsilon$ also yields a finite image.

This research focuses on the local analysis of analytic constrained differential systems, also known as impasse systems, defined by $A(x)\dot{x} = F(x)$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$, where $F$ represents a vector field and $A$ is a matrix-valued function. By employing resolution of singularities techniques involving weighted blow-ups, we generalize established results regarding the topological classification of phase portraits for planar vector fields to apply to this specific class of systems. Additionally, we investigate and categorize the phase portraits of these constrained systems in the vicinity of singular points located within the impasse set, denoted as $\Delta=\{x:\det A (x) = 0\}$.

We establish a direct product theorem for the entanglement-assisted interactive quantum communication complexity of an $l$-player predicate $\mathsf{V}$. Specifically, for a distribution $p$ that is product across the input sets of the $l$ players, we demonstrate that any entanglement-assisted quantum communication protocol computing $n$ copies of $\mathsf{V}$ with communication costs below $o(\log(\mathrm{eff}^*(\mathsf{V},p))\cdot n)$ will experience a success probability that decays exponentially with $n$. In this context, $\mathrm{eff}^*(\mathsf{V}, p)$ represents a distributional variant of the quantum efficiency or partition bound proposed by Laplante, Lerays, and Roland (2014), serving as a lower bound for the distributional quantum communication complexity of a single copy of $\mathsf{V}$ under $p$. As an application, we prove that device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) can be achieved without assuming that devices cease leaking information after receiving inputs. By analyzing the DIQKD protocol from Jain, Miller, and Shi (2017), we show that when executed with devices compatible with $n$ copies of the Magic Square game, one can extract $\Omega(n)$ bits of key despite $O(n)$ bits of leakage. Our security proof is parallel, allowing honest parties to input all data simultaneously, and applies to an arbitrarily interactive leakage model where Alice's and Bob's devices may exchange information with each other and Eve in multiple rounds, provided the total communication volume remains bounded.

This paper begins with a duality principle for sequences of natural numbers that, under mild assumptions, swaps subadditive and superadditive sequences while reversing their asymptotic growth constants. We are driven to investigate this duality because it emerges naturally in two significant algebraic-geometric settings. The first setting involves Macaulay-Matlis duality, where the sequence of initial degrees for symbolic powers of a radical ideal corresponds to the sequence of Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity values for quotients by ideals generated by powers of linear forms; this concept builds upon the influential work of Emsalem and Iarrobino. We extend this duality to differentially closed graded filtrations of ideals. In a separate direction, we demonstrate a duality linking the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity values of symbolic powers of specific ideals with a geometrically motivated sequence we call the jet separation sequence. We show that this duality forms the foundation for the reciprocity between two key geometric invariants: the multipoint Seshadri constant and the asymptotic regularity of point sets in projective space.

Spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (SARPES) measures the energy-momentum dispersion of electronic states in crystalline solids alongside the spin orientation of emitted electrons, enabling the mapping of a material's band structure with spin resolution. By employing low-energy photons, this technique combines high spin sensitivity with a deeper bulk probe depth, achieved through the extended inelastic mean-free path of electrons at these kinetic energies, thereby allowing direct access to the spin structure of states at buried interfaces. In this work, we demonstrate this capability by utilizing SARPES to analyze the spin polarization of photoelectrons from a 6-nm-thick topological insulator film (Bi$_2$Se$_3$) using 8.5 eV photons. Through modeling of the expected spin structure, we show that the observed complex spin polarization represents an integrated signal from spin-polarized states at the surface, bulk, and buried bottom interface of the film. Consequently, our results enable the direct determination of the spin texture of the buried Dirac interface state. This capability is highly valuable for advanced spectroscopic investigations of spin-physics in quantum materials and spintronic devices, where spin-polarized interface states govern operational principles.

String diagrams offer an intuitive approach to proving equations between morphisms in symmetric monoidal categories through equational reasoning. This method can be expanded to handle infinite families of equations via a straightforward graphical syntax known as !-box notation. Although this significantly enhances the proof capabilities of string diagrams, earlier efforts to surpass standard equational reasoning have remained largely ad hoc due to the absence of an appropriate logical framework for diagrammatic proofs involving !-boxes. In this paper, we generalize equational reasoning with !-boxes into a complete first-order logic, denoted as !L, which includes conjunction, implication, and universal quantification over !-boxes. This logic is sufficiently robust to formally establish an induction principle for !-boxes. Furthermore, we construct a standard model for !L and demonstrate a theorem regarding non-commutative bialgebras using !L—a proof that cannot be achieved through equational reasoning alone.

Building on the concept that a primary goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target distribution of outcomes, end-effect drives are introduced as a viable method for achieving goal-directed motor learning without an explicit forward model. These drives utilize a straightforward statistical record of the current policy's effects as a resource-efficient alternative to complex forward models. When paired with a reward structure, this mechanism establishes the foundation for a lightweight variational free energy minimization framework. The primary challenge involves sustaining this simplified effect model while simultaneously updating the policy in real-time. If the prior target distribution is uniform, the approach facilitates the learning of an efficient exploration policy aligned with intrinsic curiosity principles. Furthermore, when integrated with extrinsic rewards, the method demonstrates faster training speeds compared to conventional off-policy techniques.

Driven by persistent indications of lepton-flavour non-universality in $b \to c \ell \nu$ and $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions, we investigate ditau production via the Drell-Yan mechanism at the LHC. Within the framework of models featuring third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks (LQs), we compute the full ${\cal O} (\alpha_s)$ corrections for the $pp \to \tau^+ \tau^-$ process, attaining next-to-leading order (NLO) accuracy augmented by parton showering (NLO$+$PS) through the POWHEG technique. We have developed a specialized Monte Carlo tool that calculates NLO QCD corrections dynamically during event generation, employing it to assess the quantitative effects of NLO$+$PS corrections on kinematic variables relevant to current experimental searches for non-resonant ditau signatures. Utilizing these phenomenological findings, we establish NLO-precise limits on the masses and coupling strengths of third-generation gauge vector LQs, based on the most recent LHC ditau data from approximately $140 \, {\rm fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13 \, {\rm TeV}$. This newly presented NLO$+$PS generator facilitates enhanced signal modeling, serving as a critical resource for upcoming ATLAS and CMS investigations into vector LQs in $\tau^+ \tau^-$ channels during LHC Run III and subsequent runs.

This short paper introduces a straightforward yet effective cross-lingual Word2Vec model that utilizes the Poincaré ball model of hyperbolic space, contrasting with earlier Euclidean-based approaches. Trained on a German-English parallel corpus, the model learns unsupervised cross-lingual word representations. Since hyperbolic embeddings are known to capture and maintain hierarchical relationships, we evaluated the model on analogy and hypernymy tasks. While performance on cross-lingual analogies matches that of standard Word2Vec, the hypernymy results demonstrate that the Poincaré-based model successfully extracts latent hierarchical structures from free text across languages—structures missing from Euclidean representations. Consequently, our findings indicate that preserving latent hierarchical information allows hyperbolic spaces to provide superior representations for cross-lingual embeddings.

The use of positron emission tomography (PET) is constrained in radiation-sensitive groups, such as pregnant women, children, and patients needing longitudinal scans, due to radiation exposure concerns. Lowering the radiotracer dose or scan duration to mitigate this risk reduces photon counts, thereby compromising image quality. While recent deep neural network (DNN) techniques can translate low-quality PET images—acquired with significantly reduced doses—into high-quality results by leveraging corresponding MRI data, these methods often struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differs statistically from their training sets. We introduce a novel DNN approach that incorporates (i) the fundamental sinogram physics of PET imaging and (ii) uncertainty quantification via per-voxel heteroscedasticity in the residuals between predicted and reference images. This proposed framework, termed suDNN, generates standard-dose PET images from multimodal inputs consisting of low-dose/low-count PET and multi-contrast MRI data, enhancing its robustness against OOD acquisitions. Empirical results on in vivo PET-MRI data and various OOD scenarios demonstrate that suDNN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively.

Gender bias inherent in language and text generation permeates state-of-the-art machine translation (MT) systems, as these models are trained on vast human-generated corpora. A prominent example occurs when translating gender-neutral English occupations into languages like German, which require masculine or feminine forms, forcing the MT system to make a choice. Recent studies indicate that such systems often default to stereotypical translations. In 2019, the inaugural and currently sole benchmark specifically designed to quantify gender bias in MT was released, focusing exclusively on occupational translations. This paper introduces an expanded challenge set named WiBeMT, which incorporates gender-biased adjectives and verbs alongside sentences. Comprising over 70,000 sentences, this dataset was evaluated using three commercial MT platforms: DeepL Translator, Microsoft Translator, and Google Translate. The findings reveal significant gender bias across all three systems, driven primarily by adjectives and to a lesser degree by verbs.

To accurately replicate both spikes and bursts, a comprehensive single-neuron model is essential. This study examines a simplified representation of cortical deep pyramidal cells featuring active dendrites. We propose that modeling the soma and apical tuft using just two compartments yields spike-timing predictions with negligible loss in accuracy. Built upon experimentally derived impulse-response functions, the model translates current injected into one compartment into effects felt in another. Each compartment is described by a set of non-linear differential equations and a limited number of parameters that approximate the Hodgkin-Huxley framework. The model's predictive capabilities were validated against electrophysiological data involving simultaneous noisy current injections into both the soma and apical dendrite. Our findings demonstrate that a simple two-compartment model can effectively forecast the spike times of pyramidal cells when stimulated at both locations. These results underscore the necessity of regenerating activity within the dendritic tuft to correctly capture the dynamics of layer 5 pyramidal cells under in-vivo-like conditions.

This research investigates a wireless network supported by multiple Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRSs), where several base stations (BSs) serve mobile users. The study centers on the IRS-BS association challenge, in which multiple BSs compete to manage the phase shifts of a finite pool of IRSs, aiming to maximize the long-term downlink data rate for their connected users. To address this, we introduce MDLBI, a Multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning-based framework that simultaneously optimizes BS-IRS associations and the phase shifts of IRSs assigned to specific BSs. Notably, MDLBI operates without the need for information exchange between base stations. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that MDLBI delivers substantial performance gains and exhibits scalability suitable for large-scale networking environments.

Despite gravitational waves interacting weakly with matter, their propagation is influenced by gravitational potentials. Consequently, if a source is eclipsed by a star, analyzing the resulting perturbations allows for a direct measurement of the star's internal mass distribution. This study calculates the expected Shapiro time delay, amplification, and deflection during such an eclipse, demonstrating how these effects can reveal the mass profile of the eclipsing body. Continuous gravitational waves from neutron stars are identified as the most viable candidates for detecting this phenomenon. When the Sun eclipses a distant source, the depth of the eclipse can alter the time delay by up to approximately 0.034 ms, increase the strain amplitude by about 4%, and shift the source's apparent sky position by 4 arcseconds. While accreting neutron stars with Roche-lobe filling companions are likely to produce similar time delays, the associated changes in amplitude and sky location remain undetectable. Furthermore, even for the fastest-rotating neutron stars, the time delay represents only a few percent of the gravitational wave phase, making the measurement highly difficult. However, if continuous wave sources exist just below the sensitivity threshold of current detectors, next-generation observatories will possess the precision required to observe them and detect the signature of an eclipsing star. Successfully detecting this effect would offer a novel direct method for probing stellar interiors, complementing existing techniques such as asteroseismology and solar neutrino detection.

This study addresses the adaptive control of discrete-time nonlinear systems where all states are observable. Building on a recently developed high-order tuner algorithm—originally designed for minimizing convex loss functions with time-varying regressors in identification tasks—we extend its application to adaptive control. The high-order tuner, which relies on Nesterov's algorithm, ensures bounded parameter estimation under varying regressors and achieves accelerated tracking error convergence when regressors remain constant. Our approach involves two main contributions: first, demonstrating that the dynamical error model for a specific class of plants can be causally transformed into an algebraic error model; and second, proving that utilizing this algebraic formulation allows the high-order tuner to stabilize the dynamical systems around a reference trajectory.

Semi-supervised learning, which involves training networks using both labeled and unlabeled data, has advanced significantly in recent years. However, prior research has mainly concentrated on image classification, overlooking object detection, a task that demands substantially more annotation. This study re-examines Semi-Supervised Object Detection (SS-OD) and highlights the problem of pseudo-labeling bias within this domain. To resolve this, we propose Unbiased Teacher, a straightforward yet effective method that trains a student network and a progressively improving teacher network in a mutually beneficial fashion. Complementing this approach is a class-balance loss designed to reduce the influence of overly confident pseudo-labels. Consequently, Unbiased Teacher consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods by large margins across COCO-standard, COCO-additional, and VOC datasets. Specifically, it delivers a 6.8-point absolute mAP gain over the current state-of-the-art when utilizing just 1% of labeled data on MS-COCO, and achieves approximately 10 mAP improvements over supervised baselines with only 0.5%, 1%, or 2% of labeled data on the same dataset.

Imbalanced domain learning seeks to build accurate models capable of predicting instances that, despite being scarce, are critical to the domain. While research has predominantly concentrated on classification, studies addressing regression tasks remain negligible. A primary barrier is the absence of loss functions designed to minimize errors associated with extreme or rare values. Recently, the Squared Error Relevance Area (SERA) metric was introduced; it prioritizes errors at extreme values while also considering overall performance on the target variable to mitigate severe bias. However, its efficacy as an optimization metric remains unverified. This paper investigates the impact of employing SERA as an optimization criterion in imbalanced regression scenarios. Using gradient boosting algorithms as a proof of concept, we conducted an experimental study across 36 datasets spanning various domains and sizes. The results indicate that models utilizing SERA as an objective function outperform those using standard boosting algorithms in predicting extreme values. This confirms that SERA can be effectively integrated as a loss function within optimization-based learning algorithms for imbalanced regression problems.

Addressing probabilistic inference challenges like stochastic filtering and rare event probability estimation often necessitates analyzing models subject to both initial and terminal constraints. We introduce a solution to this bridging problem specifically for the prevalent class of population-structured Markov jump processes. Our approach utilizes a state-space lumping strategy that groups states within a grid framework. The approximate bridging distribution generated by this method is employed iteratively to refine and prune irrelevant sections of the state space. Consequently, the algorithm develops a well-justified finite-state projection that ensures guaranteed lower bounds for system behavior under endpoint constraints. We illustrate the method's versatility by applying it to diverse scenarios, including Bayesian inference and rare event analysis.

The surge in COVID-19-related misinformation, termed an "infodemic," has intensified in recent years. This phenomenon displays concept drift, wherein the evolving distribution of fake news diminishes the efficacy of detection models trained on historical data. To address this, we introduce MiDAS, a multi-domain adaptive framework designed to select the most appropriate pre-trained model for new instances. MiDAS comprises two key components: a domain-invariant encoder and an adaptive model selector. By integrating various pre-trained and fine-tuned models with their respective training data, the encoder generates domain-invariant representations. Subsequently, the selector leverages the local Lipschitz smoothness of this invariant embedding space to assess each model's relevance to a given sample. In this system, highly ranked models generate predictions, while lower-ranked ones abstain. Evaluated across nine diverse datasets spanning different domains and modalities to test generalization against drifted data, MiDAS establishes new state-of-the-art results in multi-domain adaptation for out-of-distribution fake news classification.

This article examines a critical, fixed security flaw in Google Tink's Java implementation of Ed25519. The vulnerability enables remote attackers to retrieve the private key using just two Ed25519 signatures, stemming from a misunderstanding of the "final" keyword in the Java programming language. Discovered during the security review phase prior to Google Tink's official release, this incident underscores the inherent difficulties in crafting secure cryptographic code and highlights the necessity of rigorous security reviews, even for code authored by professional cryptographers.

Spin noise spectroscopy serves as an optical method for investigating spin resonances without perturbation. Initially utilized on atomic vapors to uncover details regarding nuclear magnetism and hyperfine interactions, this technique has previously been restricted in solids to carriers within semiconductor heterostructures. This study demonstrates that atomic-like spin fluctuations of Mn ions diluted in bulk CdTe and quantum wells can be detected via Kerr rotation linked to excitonic transitions. Zeeman transitions occurring within and across hyperfine multiplets are distinctly observed under zero and low magnetic fields, exposing local symmetry influenced by crystal fields and strain. The resonance linewidths approach the dipolar limit, while the high sensitivity enables the detection of only a few spins in environments where nuclear spin-induced decoherence is mitigated through isotopic enrichment. Furthermore, this capability paves the way for spin resonance microscopy with significant potential applications in biology and materials science.

We examine how twist angle and gating influence proximity-induced exchange coupling in monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides (MoSe$_2$ and WSe$_2$) van der Waals coupled to the ferromagnetic semiconductor CrI$_3$, using first-principles calculations. A model Hamiltonian focusing on the relevant band edges at the $K/K^{\prime}$ valleys is utilized to quantify this exchange. As the twist angle varies from 0° to 30°, the valence band (VB) edge exchange splitting transitions from approximately -2 to 2 meV, whereas the conduction band (CB) edge splitting remains stable near -3 meV. For WSe$_2$ and MoSe$_2$ on CrI$_3$, the exchange coupling in the VB reverses sign at roughly 8° and 16°, respectively. Notably, even when VB spin splittings approach zero, the real-space spin polarization of holes at the band edge exhibits significant non-uniformity with alternating spin-up and spin-down orbitals. Additionally, a transverse electric field of a few V/nm offers substantial tunability of the exchange coupling. Complementing our *ab initio* findings, we calculate excitonic valley splitting to establish experimentally accessible optical markers for proximity exchange. Our predictions indicate that valley splitting grows nearly linearly with the twist angle. Moreover, gating provides high tunability of the exchange interaction, enabling valley splitting adjustment from 0 to 12 meV in WSe$_2$/CrI$_3$, corresponding to effective magnetic fields of up to ~60 Tesla. These results underscore the critical roles of twist angle and gating in the practical application of magnetic vdW heterostructures.

While the internet was envisioned as a force for democratizing knowledge and fostering global understanding, the current reality falls short of this ideal. Social media platforms are increasingly dominated by misinformation, falsehoods, and conspiracy theories, creating a toxic digital environment with severe real-world consequences, including genocide, election interference, and threats to public health. In response, a frustrated public and impatient regulators are demanding a stronger countermeasure against disinformation campaigns aimed at inciting civil unrest and violence against individuals, societies, and democratic institutions. This paper presents a large-scale, domain-level analysis uncovering coordinated efforts across multiple domains to amplify misinformation. Additionally, we demonstrate how hyperlinks shared by specific Twitter users can help identify problematic domains. These findings can empower search engines and social media recommendation algorithms to systematically detect and suppress those distributing misinformation.

**Aims.** This study seeks to limit the masses and orbital separations of possible substellar companions orbiting five accelerating stars (HIP 1481, HIP 88399, HIP 96334, HIP 30314, and HIP 116063) by integrating multiple datasets gathered via diverse techniques. **Methods.** The targets were initially monitored within the SPHERE/SHINE survey, with radial velocity (RV) archival data accessible for four of the five stars. Although no companions were initially identified in these datasets, significant proper motion anomalies (PMa) detected in all stars indicated the likely presence of unseen bodies. By synthesizing PMa information with constraints from RV and SPHERE observations, we established limits on the characteristics of these hidden companions. **Results.** The analysis yielded robust constraints for HIP 1481 and HIP 88399, restricting companion masses to 2–5 $M_{Jup}$ and 3–5 $M_{Jup}$, and separations to within 2–15 au and 3–9 au, respectively. Due to large age uncertainties for HIP 96334, suboptimal observing conditions during SPHERE epochs for HIP 30314, and the absence of RV data for HIP 116063, the results for these targets are less precise; however, we still constrained the putative companions' properties within a reasonable confidence level. **Conclusions.** For all five targets, our findings suggest that the companions causing the PMa signals are accessible to future Extremely Large Telescope instruments, such as MICADO, which should easily meet the necessary contrast and angular resolution requirements. Consequently, these results further demonstrate the efficacy of multi-technique approaches for both discovering and characterizing planetary systems.

Using light-cone QCD sum rules, we determine the magnetic dipole moments for spin-$\frac{3}{2}$ baryons containing two charm quarks, two bottom quarks, or one of each. These moments provide critical insights into the internal structure and shape deformations of these particles. The calculated values are $\mu_{\Xi_{cc}^{*++}} = 2.94 \pm 0.95$, $\mu_{\Xi_{cc}^{*+}} = - 0.67 \pm 0.11$, $\mu_{\Omega_{cc}^{*+}} =- 0.52 \pm 0.07$, $\mu_{\Xi_{bb}^{*0}} = 2.30 \pm 0.55$, $\mu_{\Xi_{bb}^{*-}} = -1.39 \pm 0.32$, $\mu_{\Omega_{bb}^{*-}} = -1.56 \pm 0.33$, $\mu_{\Xi_{bc}^{*+}} = 2.63 \pm 0.82$, $\mu_{\Xi_{bc}^{*0}} = - 0.96 \pm 0.32$, and $\mu_{\Omega_{bc}^{*+}} =- 1.11 \pm 0.33$, respectively.

In recent years, Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have emerged as a leading approach for unsupervised learning of complex distributions. VAEs offer more efficient reconstruction capabilities compared to traditional autoencoders and provide superior approximations over MCMC methods. By defining a generative process through ancestral sampling across a sequence of hidden stochastic layers, VAEs function as directed graphical models. Training involves maximizing the variational lower bound, which balances the trade-off between data log-likelihood and the KL divergence from the true posterior. This work addresses the scenario of finding a point-estimate for the parameters $\theta$ of a parametric model where observations are generated by first sampling a local latent variable and then the associated observation. We employ a least squares loss function with regularization for image reconstruction, finding that this approach yields higher-quality reconstructed images and faster training times.

The Italian research institutes INFN and INAF have created a space-based X-ray polarimetry instrument utilizing an X-ray telescope to direct radiation onto a Gas Pixel Detector (GPD). This device determines the polarization angle by analyzing the emission direction of photoelectrons generated within the GPD. In this context, we demonstrate the method used to calculate the instrument's angular resolution.

Findings by Amir-Corwin-Quastel, Calabrese-Le Doussal-Rosso, Dotsenko, and Sasamoto-Spohn indicate that the one-point distribution of the KPZ equation's solution, given a narrow wedge initial condition, matches the multiplicative statistics of an Airy determinantal random point process. By extracting Taylor coefficients from both sides, we derive moment identities. We offer a straightforward, direct proof of these identities by aligning their multivariate integral representations through a combinatorial match.

Representing position is essential for creating position-aware models in Transformers. Current approaches often fail to generalize to test data with novel lengths or incur excessive computational costs. We explore shifted absolute position embedding (SHAPE) to resolve both challenges. SHAPE achieves shift invariance—a vital trait of modern position representations—by randomly displacing absolute positions during training. Our findings show that SHAPE matches the empirical performance of its counterparts while being both simpler and faster.

This work addresses the persistent challenge of local constraint conditions—specifically, the single occupation of a slave particle per site—within slave particle theory. Previous literature utilized a Lagrange multiplier field, $\lambda_i(t)$, to enforce these constraints. However, since the original Lagrange multiplier $\lambda_i$ is inherently static, treating it as time-dependent introduces redundant gauge degrees of freedom. Consequently, an additional (gauge fixing) constraint, $\partial_t \lambda_i(t)=0$, which was previously overlooked, must be imposed. This requirement grants $\lambda_i(t)$ dynamical properties. With this framework, slave particle theory can effectively dualize strongly correlated problems into well-controlled weak coupling problems. Mean field (MF) approximations become controllable, provided one verifies the stability of MF phases against $\lambda_i$ fluctuations. For instance, the superconducting (SC) state of the Hubbard model at half-filling is found to be unstable. Conversely, while the MF SC state in the $t$-$J$ model remains stable, the pairing gap may be significantly reduced by these fluctuations. This mechanism likely explains why the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) in cuprates is substantially lower than MF predictions for the $t$-$J$ model.

This work introduces accelerated approximation algorithms for generalized network flow problems, where flow exiting an edge is a constant multiple of the incoming flow, specifically in the lossy case with factors not exceeding 1. Our approach employs a standard interior-point method to address the linear programming formulation of these flows. At each iteration, the resulting system of linear equations features a symmetric M-matrix, for which we provide a solution method operating in nearly linear time; this technique builds upon the Spielman-Teng algorithm designed for diagonally dominant matrices. For a graph containing $m$ edges, our method achieves an additive $\epsilon$-approximation for both maximum and minimum cost generalized flows within $\tilde{O}(m^{3/2} \log(1/\epsilon))$ time. Across various parameter ranges, this represents a roughly $\sqrt{m}$ improvement over prior algorithms. Additionally, we demonstrate a comparable enhancement when exactly solving the standard minimum cost flow problem.

Oscillatory dynamics are widespread across both natural systems and human societies; yet, conventional two-strategy game-theoretical models have largely failed to replicate these patterns. This study demonstrates that such oscillations arise naturally when incomplete information is integrated into the cooperation evolution of a non-Markovian framework. We examine a population engaged in a prisoner's dilemma, where individuals can only probabilistically access their neighbors' payoffs and retain this data in memory for a specified duration, using these stored values to guide their choices. Remarkably, we observe that cooperation levels rarely stabilize, instead exhibiting quasi-periodic oscillations—a trend that intensifies with longer memory spans and lower probabilities of information acquisition. The underlying mechanism reveals that misperceptions regarding neighborhood payoffs drive the simultaneous growth of cooperators and defectors at different phases, thereby generating oscillatory dynamics. These results remain robust regardless of the population's structural layout. Given the pervasive nature of incomplete information, our findings offer a credible explanation for oscillatory phenomena observed in the real world.

Human Activity Recognition (HAR) has gained significant traction for embedded systems like smartwatches. While most ultra-low power HAR solutions rely on traditional Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL) remains less common despite its superior accuracy, primarily due to its high energy demands, which hinder its use in battery-powered and resource-limited devices. This study bridges the divide between on-device HAR and DL by introducing a hierarchical architecture combining a Decision Tree (DT) and a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D CNN). These classifiers function in a cascaded manner: the DT handles the simplest activities, while the CNN processes more complex ones. Experiments conducted on a state-of-the-art dataset using a single-core RISC-V microcontroller demonstrate that this hybrid approach reduces energy consumption by up to 67.7% compared to a standalone DL model while maintaining equivalent accuracy. Furthermore, the two-stage system either minimizes memory overhead (by up to 200 B) or decreases total memory usage.

We introduce a joint model designed for entity-level relation extraction from documents. Unlike existing methods that concentrate on local intra-sentence mention pairs and necessitate mention-level annotations, our model functions at the entity level. This is accomplished through a multi-task framework that leverages coreference resolution and collects pertinent signals via multi-instance learning, utilizing multi-level representations that integrate both global entity and local mention information. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DocRED dataset and delivers the first entity-level end-to-end relation extraction results for future use. Furthermore, our experiments indicate that a joint approach performs comparably to task-specific learning while being more efficient thanks to shared parameters and training steps.

News recommendation and personalization remain unsolved challenges, as increasing concern grows over excessive data collection under the guise of personalization and its use for questionable purposes. Our experience developing privacy-safe personalization tools for publishers prompted an investigation into how users perceive the intersection of privacy and personalization. Through a survey examining individual experiences and perspectives across various age groups, this paper presents key findings for the publishing community and developers. These insights aim to guide the design and implementation of next-generation news recommender systems that prioritize human-centric approaches, striking a necessary balance between personalized experiences and privacy to maximize the benefits of both.

This study investigates the application of Transfer Learning with Pretrained Audio Neural Networks (PANNs) and introduces a new architecture designed to more effectively utilize the acoustic features offered by PANNs for Automated Audio Captioning. Additionally, we present a novel self-supervised objective called Reconstruction Latent Space Similarity Regularization (RLSSR). The RLSSR module enhances model training by reducing the similarity between encoder and decoder embeddings. By integrating these two approaches, we achieve results that significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics and benchmarks on the Clotho dataset.

Traditional methods for reducing metal artifacts in computed tomography (CT) and cone beam CT (CBCT) involve substituting X-ray projection data within the metal trace with synthesized values. However, current projection or sinogram completion techniques often fail to generate anatomically consistent information to fill these gaps, leading to significant secondary artifacts, particularly when metallic implants are large. This study proposes replacing artifact-affected regions with anatomically consistent content by employing joint projection-sinogram correction combined with adversarial learning. To address metallic implants of varying shapes and substantial sizes, we introduce a novel mask pyramid network that propagates mask information across the network's encoding layers, alongside a mask fusion loss designed to mitigate early saturation during adversarial training. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed projection-sinogram correction strategies are effective, enabling the method to recover information from metal traces superiorly compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

This study employs the lattice Boltzmann method to model the gravity-driven motion of partially wetting droplets on fibers. By varying the droplet Bond number and fiber radius, we identify three distinct dynamic regimes associated with the clamshell morphology: compact droplets, droplet breakup, and droplet oscillation. In the compact droplet regime, which occurs at low Bond numbers, the droplet achieves a steady state where velocity scales linearly with the driving body force; a comparable scaling law applies to the barrel morphology. At higher Bond numbers, the droplet breakup regime results in the formation of trailing satellite droplets, a phenomenon that becomes more probable as fiber curvature increases (i.e., with smaller fiber radii). Lastly, within the droplet oscillation regime, typically observed at intermediate fiber radii, the droplet shape undergoes periodic extension and contraction along the fiber axis.

Determining nonlinear and asymmetric causal links within multivariate longitudinal datasets is a difficult endeavor with broad applications in fields such as clinical medicine, mathematical biology, economics, and environmental science. Although various methods have been developed to infer causality in complex dynamic and stochastic systems, a unified definition of causality remains elusive. This study assesses the performance of ten leading bivariate causality indices across four simulated models featuring distinct coupling mechanisms and traits. Additional experiments reveal that these methods often lack invariance to real-world transformations, including variations in data availability, standardization, scaling, rounding errors, missing values, and noise. Consequently, we recommend transfer entropy and nonlinear Granger causality as particularly robust metrics for estimating bivariate causal relationships in practical settings. Furthermore, we offer flexible, open-access Python code for both computing these methods and running the model simulations.

Recent research has focused heavily on simultaneously estimating multiple parameters, with applications spanning causal inference, multiple testing, and large-scale data analysis. While most existing methods rely on empirical Bayes techniques, we introduce a fully frequentist alternative grounded in nonparametric regression. We demonstrate that simultaneous estimation can be framed as a penalized, constrained least-squares regression problem, allowing empirical risk minimization to identify the optimal estimator within a specific class. Under mild assumptions, our data-driven decision rules achieve asymptotically optimal risk, matching the best-known convergence rates for this compound estimation challenge. Furthermore, our approach offers a new perspective on the sufficient conditions for asymptotic optimality in simultaneous estimation. In various simulation studies, our estimators perform comparably to state-of-the-art empirical Bayes methods, and our methodology is adaptable to numerous practically relevant scenarios.

This study investigates the localization characteristics of an electric field-induced tight-binding ladder network that includes backbone sites. Utilizing the Green's function formalism, we numerically determine two-terminal transport and the density of states for various configurations of atomic sites within the ladder and its backbone. Our findings suggest the potential for multiple mobility edges, which enable a switching mechanism between completely insulating and fully or partially conducting states by varying the system's Fermi energy, thereby facilitating the creation of mesoscopic or DNA-based switching devices.

Let $\mathcal{G}$ denote a locally compact étale groupoid, and let $\mathscr{L}(L^2(\mathcal{G}))$ represent the $C^*$-algebra of adjointable operators acting on the Hilbert $C^*$-module $L^2(\mathcal{G})$. This paper introduces the concept of quasi-locality for operators within $\mathscr{L}(L^2(\mathcal{G}))$, extending the metric space framework originally proposed by Roe. We establish that if $\mathcal{G}$ is both $\sigma$-compact and amenable, an equivariant operator in $\mathscr{L}(L^2(\mathcal{G}))$ resides in the reduced groupoid $C^*$-algebra $C^*_r(\mathcal{G})$ precisely when it satisfies the quasi-locality condition. Consequently, this offers a practical method for characterizing elements of $C^*_r(\mathcal{G})$ through the lens of coarse geometry. Our primary technique involves analyzing operators in $\mathscr{L}(L^2(\mathcal{G}))$ via their slices, adhering to a philosophy analogous to computer tomography. As applications, we recover a theorem by \v{S}pakula and the second author from the metric space context and derive novel characterizations for reduced crossed products and uniform Roe algebras associated with groupoids.

Many critical graph data processing tasks involve information derived from both node attributes and graph topology. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are built to leverage these two data sources, they often fail to optimally balance their utility or integrate them in a universally applicable way, where universality implies independence from assumptions regarding graph homophily or heterophily. To address this, we propose a novel Generalized PageRank (GPR) GNN architecture that adaptively learns GPR weights to jointly optimize the extraction of topological and feature information, irrespective of whether node labels exhibit homophilic or heterophilic patterns. These learned weights automatically adjust to the specific node label distribution and are independent of initialization methods, ensuring superior performance on challenging label patterns. Additionally, this approach prevents feature over-smoothing—which makes features nondiscriminative—without necessitating shallow network architectures. Our theoretical analysis of the GPR-GNN method is supported by new synthetic benchmarks generated via the contextual stochastic block model. We further evaluate our architecture against several state-of-the-art GNNs on node classification tasks using established homophilic and heterophilic datasets. The results indicate that GPR-GNN achieves significant performance gains over existing methods on both synthetic and real-world benchmark data.

This paper demonstrates that, provided specific conditions are met regarding their Fourier-Bohr coefficients, the Eberlein convolution of a measure possessing pure point diffraction spectra with one exhibiting continuous diffraction spectra yields zero.

Determining whether a quantum state $\hat \rho$ is nonclassical (meaning it cannot be described as a mixture of coherent states) is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantum optics, largely because many nonclassicality witnesses depend nonlinearly on $\hat \rho$. Specifically, measuring the quadrature coherence scale to detect nonclassicality typically necessitates full state tomography. We introduce a practical experimental method to directly measure this quantity using a straightforward linear interferometer with two independent, identical copies of the state $\hat \rho$, combined with photon number detection. Interpreted as an extension of the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect, this result demonstrates the broad utility of multicopy interferometry for avoiding state tomography in quantum optical applications.

The Catalan numbers $C_n$ represent a thoroughly investigated sequence that serves as the solution to numerous combinatorial problems. Among the various extensions of these numbers, the Fuss-Catalan and Hypergraph Catalan numbers have been subjects of study. This paper examines their synthesis, termed Hypergraph Fuss-Catalan numbers, offering combinatorial interpretations alongside a description of their generating function.

Describing the excitation of an autoionizing resonance by intense radiation demands a theoretical framework that extends beyond the standard transition probability per unit time. This necessitates a time-dependent approach that accounts for all characteristics of the radiation source, including pulse temporal shape, duration, and stochastic properties, particularly for pulses that are not Fourier limited. Free electron lasers operating at short wavelengths serve as a prime example, as they are the sole sources capable of delivering the requisite intensity. Given current experiments utilizing such sources, this study presents a systematic analysis of an isolated autoionizing resonance. Our findings reveal that intensity, pulse duration, and field fluctuations interact to generate unexpected excitation profiles that cannot be described using the conventional Fano profile. Specifically, the influence of intensity fluctuations introduces significant theoretical challenges, several of which are addressed in this work.

While radiologists utilize Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems to identify malignancies and characterize pulmonary fibrosis and other chronic conditions, the development of imaging techniques for quantifying infectious diseases has not kept pace. There is a pressing need to develop advanced CAD systems that can detect and measure specific patterns associated with respiratory infections, such as influenza, bacterial pneumonia, and tuberculosis. One such distinctive pattern is Tree-in-bud (TIB), characterized by bronchial structures that appear thickened and are surrounded by clusters of micro-nodules. Automatically detecting TIB patterns is difficult due to their faint boundaries, noisy visual appearance, and small lesion size. This paper introduces two novel methods for the automatic detection of TIB patterns: (1) a rapid localization technique leveraging local image scale information, and (2) a Möbius invariant feature extraction approach based on learned local shape and texture properties. A comparative evaluation of these methods was conducted using a dataset comprising 39 CT scans from laboratory-confirmed human parainfluenza (HPIV) viral bronchiolitis cases and 21 normal lung CTs. Experimental results indicate that the proposed CAD system achieves a high detection rate with an overall accuracy of 90.96%.

This study examines the dynamics of a three-species system that includes the Allee effect, specifically investigating its role in generating extreme events. We observe that the Allee effect transforms regular periodic behavior into chaos. Additionally, the system displays unbounded growth in the vegetation population once the Allee parameter exceeds a critical threshold. Our most significant result is the identification of a critical Allee parameter beyond which the likelihood of extreme events becomes non-zero across all three population densities. While the Allee effect has a minimal impact on extreme events in the predator population, the prey population exhibits a sharp rise in the probability of such events after a specific threshold, and the vegetation population similarly generates extreme events under strong Allee effects. Finally, we analyze the impact of additive noise on these phenomena. We find that noise suppresses the unbounded vegetation growth caused by the Allee effect. More notably, we demonstrate that stochasticity significantly reduces the probability of extreme events in all three populations; indeed, at sufficiently high noise levels, no extreme events are observed. This indicates that noise can mitigate extreme events, which may have important implications for understanding their observability in natural systems.

Embedded systems are ubiquitous across numerous domains today. In mixed-criticality settings such as automotive applications, Industry 4.0, and drone operations, these systems must execute real-time software with strict timing and safety requirements concurrently with a full-featured operating system. This is typically achieved through virtualization techniques utilizing hardware extensions; however, such extensions may not satisfy specific security and safety needs or might be unavailable. A prominent example is the RISC-V architecture, which is rapidly gaining adoption in mixed-criticality applications but currently lacks hardware virtualization support. To address this, the paper introduces VOSySmonitoRV, a mixed-criticality solution designed for RISC-V platforms. VOSySmonitoRV enables the secure, isolated co-execution of two or more operating systems by operating at the highest machine privilege level. Furthermore, the study employs a specific benchmark to evaluate system performance in mixed-criticality contexts, focusing on metrics such as interrupt latency and context switch duration.

Recent advances in explicit step-truncation tensor methods have shown great promise for solving initial value problems associated with high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs). Nevertheless, the interplay between stiffness and non-linearity can impose strict time-step limits, potentially rendering explicit approaches computationally impractical. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel family of implicit rank-adaptive algorithms designed for the temporal integration of nonlinear evolution equations on tensor manifolds. These methods operate by executing a single time step using a standard scheme, followed by an implicit fixed-point iteration that incorporates a rank-adaptive truncation onto the tensor manifold. Because implicit step truncation relies solely on tensor arithmetic, it is easy to implement and can leverage efficient, scalable parallel computing strategies. We present and discuss numerical results for the Allen-Cahn, Fokker-Planck, and nonlinear Schrödinger equations, demonstrating the efficacy of these implicit step-truncation tensor integrators.

We have created an automated tool for classifying OB stars into their specific sub-types. Our methodology employs the standard Random Forest (RF) algorithm, Probabilistic RF (PRF), and a novel KDE-RF approach that integrates Kernel-Density Estimation with RF. These models were trained using Equivalent Width (EW) measurements of diagnostic absorption lines derived from high-quality spectra in major Galactic (LAMOST, GOSSS) and extragalactic (2dF, VFTS) surveys, utilizing known spectral types and luminosity classes. Results indicate an overall accuracy of approximately 70% across all methods, with full performance per spectral class requiring the complete set of 17 spectral lines. When applied to various observational datasets, the classifier demonstrated effectiveness for both isolated massive stars and the massive companions in Be X-ray binaries. Furthermore, we introduced a streamlined 10-feature scheme suitable for large datasets with lower signal-to-noise ratios. The consistent performance across different models underscores the robustness and reliability of the RF algorithm for early-type star classification. Achieving a ~70% accuracy is significant given the complexity of the multi-class problem, the intrinsic scatter in EW distributions within spectral classes, and the heterogeneity of the training data sourced from surveys with varying observing strategies. Additionally, our approach is versatile, accommodating data of differing quality and formats (such as absolute or normalized flux), remaining agnostic to luminosity class and largely independent of metallicity.

This study examines the intergenerational shape dynamics of individual *Caulobacter crescentus* cells by integrating advanced imaging methods with theoretical modeling. We quantify changes in pole-to-pole length, cross-sectional width, and medial curvature using highly precise contour measurements. Our dataset encompasses over 250 cells spanning approximately 10,000 total generations, ensuring high statistical reliability. Both our empirical data and the proposed model indicate that constriction begins early in the cell cycle and is governed by the timescale of exponential longitudinal growth. Leveraging extensive growth and contour data, we constructed a minimal mechanical model that accurately describes cell shape dynamics and proposes that the asymmetric division plane arises from the distinct mechanical properties of stalked versus swarmer poles. Additionally, we demonstrate that the asymmetry in division plane positioning is inherited across generations. These findings are interpreted within the framework of current molecular insights regarding the shape, growth, and division of *C. crescentus*.

For a Galois number field $K$, the P\'olya-Ostrowski group consists of the subgroup within the ideal class group of $K$ generated by all strongly ambiguous ideal classes. A field $K$ is defined as a P\'olya field if its corresponding P\'olya group is trivial. This paper establishes an explicit relationship between the order of P\'olya groups and Hasse unit indices in real biquadratic fields by leveraging results from \cite{Bennett, Zantema}.

A fundamental requirement for grasping sheaves on elementary toposes is demonstrating the equivalence between (Lawvere-Tierney) topologies on a topos and closure operators defined on it. While this standard theorem is typically presented concisely—often omitting details and offering little guidance on visualizing complex axioms and proofs—these notes aim to provide a comprehensive and visual exposition. Following the conventions outlined in "On my favorite conventions for drawing the missing diagrams in Category Theory" [Ochs2020], we consistently depict properties such as stability under pullbacks using identical diagrammatic shapes.

Furthermore, these notes serve as an experiment in proving the correspondence between closure operators and topologies using "archetypal cases," ensuring the proofs are easily adaptable to the general scenario. The first archetypal case involves "toposes with inclusions," a variation of "toposes with canonical subobjects" discussed in [Lambek/Scott 1986]; notably, all toposes of the form $\mathbf{Set}^\mathbf{C}$ (where $\mathbf{C}$ is a small category) fall into this category, allowing concepts like subsets and intersections to be formalized intuitively. We establish the correspondence for toposes with inclusions first, then demonstrate how to extend these proofs to arbitrary toposes. The second archetypal case consists of toposes of the form $\mathbf{Set}^\mathbf{D}$, where $\mathbf{D}$ is a finite two-column graph. In this context, we illustrate how to visualize all LT-topologies and formally define a method for incorporating visual intuition into proofs regarding toposes, a concept linked to various "Category Theory for children" techniques described in the aforementioned conventions paper.

In superconductors without inversion symmetry, supercurrent flow generates a non-zero magnetization, which is the core mechanism behind non-dissipative magneto-electric effects, or the Edelstein effect. A fundamental question for electrons possessing both spin and orbital moments concerns the orbital contribution to these effects in conventional spin-singlet superconductors featuring Rashba coupling. Remarkably, we discover that the supercurrent-induced orbital magnetization exceeds spin-induced magnetization by more than an order of magnitude, resulting in a colossal magneto-electric effect. This induced orbital magnetization is sign-tunable; the sign flips when the Fermi level approaches avoiding crossing points in the Brillouin zone or under superconducting phase inhomogeneities, creating domains with opposing orbital moment orientations. Consequently, these orbital-dominated magneto-electric phenomena exhibit distinct signatures detectable in both the bulk and at the system's edges, suggesting they are a general characteristic of multi-orbital superconductors lacking inversion symmetry.

Neural architecture search (NAS) has recently gained significant traction in both academic and industrial sectors. Although these methods have yielded impressive empirical results, most current NAS algorithms remain computationally prohibitive due to the expensive iterative stochastic gradient descent (SGD) training required. To address this, we introduce Random-Weight Evaluation (RWE), an efficient alternative for rapidly estimating network architecture performance. By training only the final linear classification layer, RWE slashes the evaluation time from hours to mere seconds. When embedded within an evolutionary multi-objective framework, RWE successfully identifies a set of high-performance architectures on CIFAR-10 with state-of-the-art results in under two hours of search time on a single GPU. Furthermore, ablation studies on rank-order correlations and transfer learning experiments on ImageNet confirm the robustness and effectiveness of the RWE approach.

This work establishes the relaxation-time limit from the Quantum-Navier-Stokes-Poisson system to the quantum drift-diffusion equation within the framework of finite energy weak solutions, without imposing any assumptions on the limiting solution. The proof utilizes suitably scaled a priori bounds derived from energy and BD entropy estimates. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how these estimates yield Fisher entropy and free energy estimates corresponding to the diffusive evolution in the limit. As a secondary result, the main theorem also offers an alternative proof for the existence of finite energy weak solutions to the quantum drift-diffusion equation.

This note provides two affirmative solutions to Tingley's problem within specific subspaces of function algebras. First, we demonstrate that any surjective isometry mapping the unit spheres $S(A)$ and $S(B)$ of two uniformly closed function algebras $A$ and $B$ on locally compact Hausdorff spaces extends to a surjective real linear isometry from $A$ onto $B$. Second, we investigate surjective isometries between the unit spheres of two abelian JB$^*$-triples, which are represented as spaces of continuous functions defined by $$C^{\mathbb{T}}_0 (X) := \{ a \in C_0(X) : a (\lambda t) = \lambda a(t) \hbox{ for every } (\lambda, t) \in \mathbb{T}\times X\}$$, where $X$ is a (locally compact Hausdorff) principal $\mathbb{T}$-bundle. We prove that every surjective isometry $\Delta: S(C_0^{\mathbb{T}}(X))\to S(C_0^{\mathbb{T}}(Y))$ can be extended to a surjective real linear isometry between these respective abelian JB$^*$-triples.

In an anharmonic potential, classical mechanics predicts a renormalization of the oscillatory bare frequency, while statistical mechanics indicates that anharmonicity induces a correction to the heat capacity of an ideal gas. When both frequency and heat capacity are expanded perturbatively in terms of their respective characteristic length scales, their expansion coefficients exhibit a direct order-by-order correspondence. This finding contradicts the intuitive expectation that the renormalized frequency would appear in statistical mechanics as a single, isolated parameter.

Dialogue systems can utilize large pre-trained language models and external knowledge to create fluent and informative replies. Nevertheless, these models often generate hallucinations unsupported by the source input, significantly limiting their practical use. The disparity between external knowledge and dialogue context complicates representation learning and source integration, further exacerbating unfaithfulness. To address this and produce more reliable responses, this paper introduces RHO ($\rho$), which leverages linked entity and relation predicate representations from a knowledge graph (KG). We propose (1) local knowledge grounding to merge textual embeddings with their corresponding KG embeddings; and (2) global knowledge grounding to enable multi-hop reasoning capabilities through an attention mechanism. Furthermore, we develop a response re-ranking strategy based on traversals of KG sub-graphs to enhance conversational reasoning. Experiments on OpenDialKG demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in both automatic and human evaluations, particularly in reducing hallucinations (a 17.54% improvement in FeQA).

Traditional subclassification of Seyfert galaxies relies on visual inspection or the flux ratio between Balmer and forbidden lines. However, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated successful classification capabilities. In this study, we constructed a one-dimensional CNN model to differentiate Seyfert 1.9 spectra from Seyfert 2 galaxies. Our model achieved an accuracy exceeding 80% in distinguishing these two types and identified an additional sample of Seyfert 1.9 galaxies that had been overlooked by visual inspection.
