Utilizing worm Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate surface criticality at an emergent superfluid-Mott insulator transition within the Villain representation, a system thought to link classical and quantum O(2) critical models. Our findings reveal a special transition characterized by thermal and magnetic renormalization exponents of $y_t=0.58(1)$ and $y_h=1.690(1)$, respectively, aligning closely with recent estimates from discrete spin variable models. The presence of extraordinary-log universality is confirmed by the two-point correlation critical exponent $\hat{q}=0.58(2)$ and the renormalization-group parameter $\alpha=0.28(1)$ derived from superfluid stiffness; these values satisfy the scaling relations of extraordinary-log critical theory and reproduce the logarithmic finite-size scaling observed in the critical superfluid stiffness of the open-edge quantum Bose-Hubbard model. Consequently, our results connect recent findings on surface criticality in classical statistical mechanical systems [Parisen Toldin, Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 135701 (2021); Hu $et$ $al.$, $ibid.$ 127, 120603 (2021); Parisen Toldin $et$ $al.$, $ibid.$ 128, 215701 (2022)] with those from the open-edge quantum Bose-Hubbard model [Sun $et$ $al.$, Phys. Rev. B 106, 224502 (2022)].

Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) represents the variable radio, near-infrared (NIR), and X-ray emission resulting from accretion onto the supermassive black hole at our galaxy's center. Our study examines a comprehensive dataset spanning submillimeter wavelengths (incorporating new simultaneous NIR observations), NIR, and X-ray energies (2–8 keV). We find that submillimeter fluctuations lag behind NIR variations by approximately 30 minutes. Furthermore, an approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) analysis of the X-ray first-order structure function reveals significantly reduced power at short timescales compared to the NIR. Given the observed NIR-X-ray correlations alongside this reduced short-timescale X-ray variability, the fluctuations can be modeled as two strictly correlated stochastic processes, where the X-ray component acts as a low-pass-filtered version of the NIR process. This NIR-X-ray connection supports a straightforward radiative model consisting of a compact, self-absorbed synchrotron sphere with a high-frequency cutoff near NIR frequencies, complemented by a synchrotron self-Compton component at higher frequencies. When fitted to structure functions across submillimeter, NIR, and X-ray bands, this model successfully reproduces observed flux densities, statistical properties of all light curves, and inter-band time lags. The resulting fit yields physically reasonable parameters, including a magnetic field strength of $B\approx13$ G, a source size of $L \approx2.2R_{S}$, and a high-energy electron density of $n_{e}\approx4\times10^{7}$ cm$^{-3}$. Additionally, we provide an animation of typical light curves and publicly release the parameter chains from our Bayesian analysis, along with the model implementation and visualization code.

Accurate 3-D pose estimation of surgical instruments is essential for achieving automatic scene understanding in robotic minimally invasive surgery. While robotic systems can theoretically supply joint values, this data is rarely utilized in operating rooms because of potential unreliability, restricted access, and the extensive calibration time required, particularly for continuum robots. Consequently, standard 3-D pose estimation typically relies on external tracking systems. Recently, image-based methods have emerged as promising, non-invasive alternatives. Although many existing image-based approaches demonstrate high accuracy, they generally suffer from either complex iterative optimization per image—rendering them unsuitable for real-time use—or a heavy dependence on large sets of manually annotated images for training. This paper introduces a self-supervised image-based method that utilizes imprecise kinematic data from the robot exclusively during the training phase. To eliminate the need for time-consuming manual annotations, the problem is framed as an auto-encoder, strategically constrained by a physical model of the robotic instruments and surgical camera to separate image background from kinematic content. Validation conducted on semi-synthetic, phantom, and in-vivo datasets using a flexible robotized endoscope demonstrates promising results for real-time, image-based 3-D pose estimation of surgical tools.

This study introduces a robust method for scaling registration of $m$-dimensional point sets. Unlike rigid transformations, scaling registration cannot be directly modeled using a standard least squares function because the scale factor creates an ill-posed problem. To address this, the paper develops a new objective function structured as a rational fraction, with the least squares error in the numerator and the squared scale factor in the denominator. By prioritizing the scale factor, this formulation mitigates the ill-posed nature of the problem. The resulting objective function is solved using a proposed scaling Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm to derive the optimal scaling transformation. Furthermore, this algorithm is adapted for practical scenarios involving partially overlapping point sets. Validation on public datasets and its application to merging grid maps of varying resolutions confirm that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both efficiency and robustness.

Grid computing environments necessitate novel tools and strategies for identifying cybersecurity threats and executing autonomous responses without human oversight. Additionally, these systems require mechanisms to isolate and track job payload activities to safeguard users and uncover malicious behavior. This paper proposes an integrated security monitoring framework combining Security by Isolation using Linux Containers with Deep Learning techniques to analyze real-time data within virtualized High-Throughput Computing infrastructure, aiming to detect and prevent intrusions. A dataset tailored for malware detection in grid computing is introduced, alongside the application of generative methods employing Recurrent Neural Networks to enhance the dataset's quality. We present Arhuaco, a prototype implementation of these proposed methodologies, and empirically evaluate its performance. The findings demonstrate that Arhuaco surpasses existing Intrusion Detection Systems used in grid computing. This research was conducted on the ALICE Collaboration Grid, which is part of the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid.

This project contributed to the DCASE 2022 Competition (Task 6), which comprised two subtasks: (1) Automated Audio Captioning and (2) Language-Based Audio Retrieval. The first subtask required generating textual descriptions for audio samples, whereas the second aimed to identify matching audio samples within a fixed dataset based on a given description. Both subtasks utilized the Clotho dataset. Evaluation metrics included BLEU1, BLEU2, BLEU3, ROUGEL, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE, and SPIDEr for captioning, and R1, R5, R10, and mARP10 for retrieval. We performed several experiments modifying baseline models for these tasks. Our final Automated Audio Captioning architecture achieved performance close to the baseline, while our Language-Based Audio Retrieval model outperformed its counterpart.

Quantum parametric amplifiers are conventionally created by functioning near a dynamical instability. In contrast, we propose a broader approach that achieves quantum-limited, high-gain amplification without relying on such instability. Our fundamental mechanism, which relies on photon-number-conserving dynamics involving squeezed photons, facilitates the creation of diverse one- and two-mode amplifiers that bypass inherent gain-bandwidth limitations. Specifically, we examine a configuration capable of performing ideal single-mode squeezing in transmission with no reflection. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of this system, accounting for pump depletion, and report on experimental results from a superconducting quantum circuit implementation.

This study examines a multispecies extension of the porous media equation applied to cancer modeling, where distinct species denote various cell types, such as healthy and tumor cells. Each population's density evolves according to a continuity equation driven by a velocity field derived from a pressure gradient determined by the aggregate cell density. Consequently, the model forms a complex system of coupled hyperbolic and parabolic equations; individual species fail to regularize over time, allowing discontinuities to emerge and persist. While the existence of weak solutions was recently established, numerous significant issues remain unresolved. A key open problem is determining whether initially separated populations can intermingle. This paper addresses this by constructing solutions that demonstrate non-mixing. We achieve this by establishing both forward and backward Lagrangian flows along the pressure gradient—a contribution of independent value given the gradient's insufficient regularity for standard regular Lagrangian flow theory. By leveraging the porous media equation's structure, we show that irregular components of the pressure gradient can be disregarded. With these flow maps defined, proving that the populations do not mix becomes a direct consequence.

This study introduces a regression-based market designed for wind agents to monetize data exchanges for wind power forecasting. Current data market research typically frames data disclosure as a binary decision or adjusts data quality according to the gap between bid and offer prices. Consequently, these approaches either penalize data sellers by overestimating their willingness to share information or disadvantage buyers by supplying insufficiently useful data. In contrast, our proposed regression market calculates payments using the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso). This method empowers buyers to identify valuable features while allowing sellers to set individualized payment thresholds. Case studies utilizing both synthetic and real-world wind data confirm that this approach reduces overall losses for purchasing agents and generates extra financial gains for selling agents.

Although sentiment and emotion analysis have received significant attention, the connection between sarcasm and emotion remains largely uninvestigated. Sarcastic utterances often conceal diverse underlying emotions; for instance, "I love being ignored" masks sadness, whereas "my mobile is fabulous with a battery backup of only 15 minutes!" conveys frustration. Identifying the specific emotion behind sarcasm is a challenging yet critical task. This study addresses the detection of emotions within sarcastic statements, an area we believe has not been previously explored. Leveraging the recently released MUStARD multimodal sarcasm detection dataset, which was initially annotated with nine emotions, we identified and corrected 343 erroneous labels out of a total of 690. We expanded the dataset's size and enriched it with emotion labels alongside valence and arousal scores, key metrics for emotional intensity. Furthermore, we categorized each sarcastic utterance into one of four sarcasm types—Propositional, Embedded, Likeprefixed, and Illocutionary—to advance the field. Extensive experiments utilizing multimodal fusion models (combining text, audio, and video) established a new benchmark for exact emotion recognition in sarcasm, surpassing existing state-of-the-art sarcasm detection methods. We have made the dataset, complete with diverse annotations, and the associated code publicly available for research at: https://github.com/apoorva-nunna/MUStARD_Plus_Plus.

Liquid democracy can be naturally represented graphically through a delegation graph. Consequently, the strategic dynamics of liquid democracy can be analyzed as a game played on these delegation graphs, termed the liquid democracy game. Our primary finding is that this game offers bicriteria approximation guarantees concerning both rationality and social welfare. Specifically, we demonstrate that the price of stability for $\epsilon$-Nash equilibria in the liquid democracy game is precisely $\epsilon$.

Although derivative-free approaches have empirically succeeded in reinforcement learning for planning through contact, this contrasts with the known fragility of classical gradient-based optimization in such environments. This paper investigates the source of this discrepancy and proposes ways to enhance gradient-based methods by incorporating a stochastic view of dynamics. Leveraging randomized smoothing, we analyze sampling-based gradient approximations and formalize them as a "gradient bundle." We demonstrate that substituting the gradient with the gradient bundle effectively mitigates the rapid fluctuations caused by non-smooth contact dynamics, whether modeled via implicit time-stepping or penalty methods. Furthermore, we integrate the gradient bundle into iLQR for optimal control, creating a new algorithm that achieves superior convergence compared to exact gradients. When combined with a convex implicit time-stepping formulation for contact, our approach enables tractable solutions for manipulation tasks involving planning through contact.

This study proposes a numerical scheme for approximating evolving interface problems in parabolic equations, utilizing the abstract evolving finite element framework introduced by Elliott, Ranner, and others (2021). A suitable weak formulation is established to facilitate the application of evolving finite elements capable of handling moving interfaces. The paper derives optimal order error bounds for arbitrary order evolving isoparametric finite elements and concludes with numerical experiments on a model problem that confirm the observed convergence rates.

The recent triumph of transformer architectures in natural language processing has spurred significant interest within the computer vision community. These models are increasingly replacing traditional convolutional operators to capture long-range dependencies, a strategy that has yielded state-of-the-art results across numerous tasks. This trend has extended to 3D vision, where transformers are being integrated into 3D convolutional neural networks and multi-layer perceptrons. While existing surveys cover transformers in vision broadly, the distinct data representations and processing requirements of 3D data necessitate a dedicated focus. This paper provides a comprehensive review of over 100 transformer-based methods addressing various 3D vision tasks, including classification, segmentation, detection, completion, and pose estimation. We examine transformer designs tailored for diverse 3D data representations and highlight the key contributions of these methods for each application. Furthermore, we evaluate their competitiveness by comparing their performance against standard non-transformer approaches on 12 benchmarks. The survey concludes by outlining open challenges and future directions for transformers in 3D vision. Additionally, we maintain an updated repository of relevant papers and their implementations at: https://github.com/lahoud/3d-vision-transformers.

This research investigates the asymptotic learning rates associated with linear and log-linear aggregation rules for belief vectors within a distributed hypothesis testing framework. Our findings demonstrate that agents achieve exponential convergence to the truth under both fusion strategies, with the log-linear approach yielding a superior rate. Furthermore, we analyze the disparity in these rates by considering network connectivity and information diversity, and we derive closed-form solutions for specific scenarios involving federated structures and exchangeable networks.

We introduce a discrete Darboux-Lax framework to generate auto-Bäcklund transformations and build solutions for quad-graph equations that may lack 3D consistency. Using the Adler-Yamilov system—connected to the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation [19]—as a case study, we develop an auto-Bäcklund transformation for this discrete model, establish its superposition principle, and apply these tools to derive one- and two-soliton solutions for the Adler-Yamilov system.

A Dalitz plot analysis of $B^0 \to \eta_c(1S) K^+\pi^-$ decays has been conducted using data from $pp$ collisions recorded by the LHCb detector at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=7,~8$, and $13$ TeV, amounting to a total integrated luminosity of $4.7~\text{fb}^{-1}$. The data are well described by a model that includes an exotic resonant state with the $\eta_c(1S) \pi^-$ configuration. This exotic resonance is observed with a significance exceeding three standard deviations, exhibiting a mass of $4096 \pm 20~^{+18}_{-22}$ MeV and a width of $152 \pm 58~^{+60}_{-35}$ MeV. Both $J^P=0^+$ and $J^{P}=1^-$ spin-parity assignments remain consistent with the experimental results. Furthermore, this study presents the first measurement of the branching fraction for $B^0 \to \eta_c(1S) K^+\pi^-$, yielding $\displaystyle \mathcal{B}(B^0 \to \eta_c(1S) K^+\pi^-) = (5.73 \pm 0.24 \pm 0.13 \pm 0.66) \times 10^{-4}$, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical, systematic, and external branching fraction limitations, respectively.

We present a perturbative approach to determine all moments of the first-passage time distribution for stochastic one-dimensional processes influenced by both white and colored noise. These non-Markovian processes are fundamental to the study of thermal active matter, comprising self-propelled particles undergoing diffusion. The perturbation theory expands around a Markov process, treating the self-propulsion effect as negligible relative to thermal fluctuations. To demonstrate the method, we apply it to active thermal particles in two scenarios: (i) within a harmonic trap and (ii) on a ring. For both cases, we compute the first-order correction to the moment-generating function of first-passage times, thereby deriving all moments. Finally, our analytical findings are validated against numerical simulations.

This paper introduces Adam-Hash, an adaptive and dynamic multi-resolution hashing data structure designed for efficient pairwise summation estimation. For a dataset $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, a binary function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\times \mathbb{R}^d\to \mathbb{R}$, and a query point $y \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the Pairwise Summation Estimate is defined as $\mathrm{PSE}_X(y) := \frac{1}{|X|} \sum_{x \in X} f(x,y)$. The objective is to construct a data structure that, for any dataset $X$, can approximate $\mathrm{PSE}_X(y)$ for any query $y$ in time sub-linear to the dataset size $|X|$. While previous research has addressed only static datasets with independent queries, this work presents a hashing-based PSE structure capable of handling the more practical dynamic scenario, which permits point insertions, deletions, and replacements. Furthermore, Adam-Hash demonstrates robustness against adaptive PSE queries, where an adversary selects subsequent queries $q_j$ based on the results of prior queries $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_{j-1}$.

Using second-principles simulations, we investigate the emergence of Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phases in (PbTiO$_3$)$_3$/(SrTiO$_3$)$_3$ superlattices. When the tensile epitaxial strain exceeds a threshold of $\epsilon = 0.25\%$, local dipole moments are confined to the film plane, rendering the polarization effectively two-dimensional. Analyzing the distance-dependent decay of dipole-dipole correlations, alongside the temperature-dependent distribution and density of defects, confirms the presence of a BKT phase within a specific temperature range between the low-temperature ordered ferroelectric state and the high-temperature disordered paraelectric phase ($T_{\rm BKT}$). This intermediate phase is defined by quasi-long-range order, evidenced by a power-law decay of correlations, and the formation of tightly bound vortex-antivortex pairs whose density arises from thermal activation. The proposed superlattice model and its mechanical boundary conditions are experimentally viable, paving the way for the first experimental detection of these novel topological phases in ferroelectrics.

A nanopatterning approach is introduced that enables structure height control within the tens of nanometers and achieves a lateral resolution at least three times superior to the writing beam's point spread function. This technique depends on initiating polymerization through highly inefficient energy transfer from a fluorescent dye molecule following single-photon absorption. The process follows a distinct sequence: the dye adsorbs onto the substrate surface at a concentration exceeding that of the bulk, where illumination triggers polymerization; this leads to the formation of isolated islands that coalesce into a uniform structure via percolation, continuing to grow until the light source is halted. This percolation mechanism possesses a threshold that provides the necessary nonlinearity to fabricate structures surpassing the diffraction limit.

Estimating the entropy of discrete random variables is a cornerstone challenge in information theory and its associated disciplines. While this task has broad applications across statistics, machine learning, and data compression, numerous estimation techniques have emerged over time. Despite notable advancements, most existing approaches falter when sample sizes are small relative to the variable's alphabet size. This paper presents a practical extension of McAllester and Statos (2020) that addresses this limitation by leveraging the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks (DNNs) for cross-entropy estimation to achieve higher accuracy. Additionally, we propose a family of estimators for related information-theoretic metrics, including conditional entropy and mutual information. We demonstrate that these estimators are strongly consistent and evaluate their efficacy across diverse scenarios: large alphabet entropy estimation, mutual information estimation, conditional mutual information estimation for independence testing, and transfer entropy estimation. Across all tested configurations, our proposed estimators outperform existing methods.

**Background:** The structural nature of the Hoyle state—a highly $\alpha$-clustered state at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$—has been a long-standing topic of contention. Determining whether the system consists of three weakly interacting $\alpha$-particles in the 0s orbital, forming an $\alpha$-condensate, relies on analyzing the decay branches of this state. **Purpose:** To identify the direct decay of the Hoyle state into three $\alpha$-particles, bypassing the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, researchers examine the energy distribution of the resulting three $\alpha$-particles. This study details the break-up mechanism of the Hoyle state using a novel experimental method. **Method:** Employing beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy of $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ with the TexAT (Texas Active Target) TPC, the experiment achieves high sensitivity in measuring the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio, effectively eliminating pile-up event contributions. **Results:** Applying a Bayesian approach via a likelihood function to assess direct components reveals that the direct contribution is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level (C.L.). This finding aligns with previous studies, indicating that a small non-sequential component with a decay fraction of approximately $10^{-4}$ is the most probable scenario. **Conclusion:** For the first time, the non-sequential component of the Hoyle state decay has been measured in an almost medium-free reaction. The derived upper limit matches prior research and confirms the method's sensitivity to absolute branching ratios. Future investigations must integrate these measurements with robust microscopic theoretical models of decay dynamics to further explore the hypothesis of the Hoyle state as an $\alpha$-condensate.

Code review, which identifies and locates defects and quality issues, is vital for software quality control. Among the factors affecting software quality are code smells, yet their detection rates during modern code reviews remain underexplored. To examine how code smells are identified in contemporary reviews, the suggested actions by reviewers, and the subsequent responses from developers, we conducted a study analyzing reviews from four large open-source projects within the OpenStack (Nova and Neutron) and Qt (Qt Base and Qt Creator) communities. We manually inspected 25,415 code review comments, selected via keyword searches and random sampling, and identified 1,539 instances related to code smells. Our analysis revealed that: 1) code smells are infrequently flagged in code reviews; 2) these smells typically stem from violations of coding conventions; 3) reviewers generally offer constructive feedback, including refactoring recommendations to eliminate smells; 4) developers usually adhere to these recommendations and implement the changes; 5) fixing identified smells typically takes developers less than a week; and 6) the primary reason developers ignore identified smells is that they deem the issues unworthy of fixing. Our findings suggest that: 1) developers should strictly adhere to project coding conventions to prevent introducing code smells; 2) review-based detection is viewed as a trustworthy method by developers, largely because reviews are context-sensitive (reviewers, being part of the development team, have better awareness of the code context); and 3) program context must be fully considered when deciding whether to immediately fix an identified code smell.

We examine a setup involving two interacting classical particles, each coupled to an on-site potential and a Langevin thermal bath. We analytically determine the heat current flowing through the system under a temperature gradient, specifically for weak nonlinear interactions. We investigate the conditions necessary for the diode effect to appear when the temperature difference is reversed. Despite the minimal complexity of this two-particle diode, a complex dependence on system parameters is revealed. Furthermore, insights applicable to long particle chains are derived, including how flux varies with interfacial stiffness and force types, as well as the temperature dependencies required for rectification. These analytical findings serve as a tool to predict the distinct roles that various forms of nonlinearity and asymmetry play in thermal conduction and rectification.

This work aims to define a weak solution for the master equation governing potential mean field games and demonstrate existence and uniqueness under broad conditions, notably without imposing monotonicity constraints on the coefficients. The central approach involves interpreting the master equation conservatively and adapting existing arguments for hyperbolic systems—originally derived from Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations—to an infinite-dimensional framework. Specifically, the master equation is treated as an infinite-dimensional system defined on the space of probability measures, formally representing the derivative of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation linked to the underlying mean field control problem. To facilitate the analysis, periodicity of the coefficients is assumed, enabling the representation of probability measures via their Fourier coefficients. Consequently, the study primarily consists of reformulating both the master equation and the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation as partial differential equations acting on these Fourier coefficients. Ultimately, the paper establishes the existence and uniqueness of displacement semi-concave functions that solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation in a generalized sense, which subsequently yields the existence and uniqueness of functions solving the master equation in a weak sense while satisfying a weak one-sided Lipschitz inequality. Additionally, a novel result is presented proving the uniqueness of optimal trajectories for the associated mean field control problem for almost every starting point, relative to a suitable probability measure on the space of probability measures.

Idealized models of protoplanetary disks and giant planet formation suggest that a planet's atmospheric composition can reveal its birthplace within the disk. Recent observations of the hot Jupiter WASP-77 Ab indicate sub-solar carbon and oxygen abundances, yet a solar C/O ratio. Assuming the host star, WASP-77 A, has solar abundances, these atmospheric values might imply the planet formed interior to the water ice line by accreting carbon-depleted gas, with minimal later accretion of planetesimals or core erosion. However, we have comprehensively modeled WASP-77 A to refine our characterization of WASP-77 Ab. Our findings reveal that the host star's photospheric carbon and oxygen abundances are actually super-solar with a sub-solar C/O ratio; consequently, the planet's atmosphere possesses significantly sub-stellar carbon and oxygen levels but a super-stellar C/O ratio. This discrepancy suggests WASP-77 Ab likely accreted its envelope beyond the water ice line. Although numerous theoretical complexities have been identified in these idealized models, the potential for non-solar abundances in protoplanetary disks complicates even advanced formation theories. Therefore, we argue that interpreting giant planet atmospheric ratios is only meaningful when compared against the potentially non-solar mean compositions of their parent disks, as recorded in the photospheric abundances of their solar-type host stars.

This study investigates the dynamical behavior of {\it Topologically Anosov} plane homeomorphisms. We demonstrate that a Topologically Anosov homeomorphism $f:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ which arises as the time-one map of a flow is conjugate to a homothety. Furthermore, we derive findings for scenarios where the nonwandering set of $f$ consists solely of a fixed point, or when there exists an open, connected, simply connected proper subset $U$ satisfying $U \subset \mathrm{Int}(\overline {f(U)})$ and $\cup_{n\geq 0} f^n (U)= \mathbb{R}^2$. In the general setting, we establish a structure theorem regarding the $\alpha$-limits of trajectories with empty $\omega$-limits (or conversely, the $\omega$-limits of trajectories with empty $\alpha$-limits), and we prove that any basin of attraction or repulsion is necessarily unbounded.

Axion-like particles (ALPs) represent a well-motivated category of particles embedded within a more comprehensive ultraviolet theory. This study introduces and demonstrates the incorporation of both ALPs and standard axions into Heavy Hadron Chiral Perturbation Theory (HH$\chi$PT) through a model-independent effective Lagrangian approach. This framework is particularly advantageous for analyzing transitions that preserve heavy quark flavor. In the case of light ALPs, constraints on their couplings (or specific combinations thereof) are found to be largely independent of the ALP mass. Furthermore, radiative and leptonic decays of heavy vector mesons into corresponding heavy pseudoscalar mesons offer some of the most rigorous limits on ALPs, especially regarding diagonal couplings.

Statistical models form the backbone of machine learning and are widely applicable to various downstream tasks. These models rely on free parameters, which are usually estimated from data using maximum-likelihood estimation or its approximations. However, a significant challenge arises when applying these models to real-world datasets: they are typically designed for fully observed data, yet practical datasets often contain missing values. The theoretical framework for estimating parameters from incomplete data resembles that of latent-variable models, where techniques like variational inference (VI) are powerful. Nevertheless, unlike standard latent-variable models, parameter estimation with missing data frequently involves computing exponentially many conditional distributions of the missing variables, rendering conventional VI methods intractable. To bridge this gap, we introduce variational Gibbs inference (VGI), a versatile new method for estimating parameters of statistical models from incomplete data. We validate VGI on both synthetic and real-world estimation tasks, successfully applying it to important models such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) and normalizing flows. Although general-purpose, the proposed method achieves performance that is competitive with or superior to existing model-specific estimation techniques.

We develop a comprehensive age-of-infection epidemic framework incorporating two transmission routes: symptomatic and asymptomatic infections. We derive the basic reproduction number, $\mathcal{R}_0$, and derive the corresponding final size relation. Our analysis demonstrates that the proportion of total accumulated symptomatic cases to asymptomatic cases is governed by the symptomatic ratio $f$, representing the probability of an infected individual eventually exhibiting symptoms. Furthermore, we construct and analyze a generalized age-of-infection model that includes disease-related mortality alongside the dual infection pathways. We investigate the final size relation within this context and establish both upper and lower bounds for the ultimate epidemic magnitude. Additionally, multiple numerical simulations are conducted to validate the analytical findings.

Detection-efficiency mismatch remains a prevalent challenge in practical quantum key distribution (QKD) systems. Existing security proofs addressing this issue typically depend on either assuming a single-photon source at the transmitter or a single-photon input at the receiver, both of which limit the range of potential eavesdropping strategies considered. This study provides a rigorous security proof that eliminates these constraints, thereby resolving a critical issue and demonstrating the security of QKD under detection-efficiency mismatch against general attacks in the asymptotic limit. Specifically, we extend the decoy-state method to accommodate scenarios involving detection-efficiency mismatch.

Multi-exposure fusion (MEF) is a technique for combining multiple images of the same scene captured with varying exposure settings into a single output. Existing MEF algorithms typically merge these images by selectively choosing the best-exposed portions from each input. We introduce a new multi-exposure fusion pipeline that incorporates noise reduction. Our approach leverages Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) processing and the inherent multi-image characteristics of MEF. We propose a unified strategy for fusion and denoising that utilizes spatio-temporal patch selection and collaborative 3D thresholding. This overall method enables simultaneous denoising and fusion of the image set without the need to reconstruct individual denoised exposures, resulting in a highly efficient process.

Detecting faces remains a persistent challenge in computer vision, aiming to precisely locate human faces within uncontrolled settings. Despite recent advancements in machine learning that have leveraged data-driven deep-learning models to achieve remarkable accuracy [70], significant technical obstacles persist due to factors like pose, lighting, resolution, occlusion, and viewpoint [44]. However, a crucial limitation affecting both performance and the social responsibility of these systems is the inherent diversity of human appearance. Each individual's look reflects unique aspects of their heritage, identity, experiences, and self-expression. Consequently, concerns arise regarding how well current systems handle variations in facial size and shape, skin tone, body modifications, and ornaments. To address this, we assembled the Distinctive Human Appearance dataset, which captures low-frequency appearances often underrepresented in existing collections. By evaluating state-of-the-art face-detection models against this dataset, we found that these algorithms struggle to generalize across such diverse appearances. Assessing and characterizing the current capabilities of these models is essential to accelerating research and development toward fairer and more accurate face-detection systems.

This paper provides an algebraic characterization of the syntax and operational semantics for a class of simply-typed languages, including PCF. We define simply-typed syntax, which involves variable binding and reduction rules, as the initial object within a specific category of models, utilizing a universal property. To achieve this, we integrate techniques from two prior studies: the first modeled syntactic translations between languages with varying type sets as initial morphisms in a category of models, while the second characterized untyped syntax with reduction rules similarly as an initial object. By combining these earlier approaches, we characterize simply-typed syntax with reduction rules as the initial object in a category. The resulting universal property defines an operator for specifying translations between languages over potentially different type sets; these translations are semantically faithful by design.

As an illustrative example, we enhance a previously established translation from PCF to the untyped lambda calculus to incorporate reduction in both the source and target languages. We introduce appropriate reduction rules to define the semantics in both languages. By equipping the untyped lambda calculus with the structure of a PCF model, the principle of initiality generates a translation from PCF to the lambda calculus that remains faithful regarding the specified reduction semantics. This article represents an extended version of a paper originally published in the proceedings of WoLLIC 2012.

We present an implementation of the Extended Tower Number Field Sieve (ExTNFS) and document computations performed in a 512-bit medium-characteristic finite field Fp4. Our results demonstrate that sieving within a box (orthotope) to gather relations for ExTNFS remains efficient even in four dimensions.

We establish an elliptic curve $E/\mathbb{F}_q(t)$ and examine the family $\{E\otimes\chi_D\}$ formed by twisting $E$ with quadratic Dirichlet characters. It is demonstrated that the one-level density of their $L$-functions exhibits orthogonal symmetry for test functions whose Fourier transforms are supported within $(-1,1)$. Consequently, we derive an upper bound of 3/2 for the average analytic rank. By partitioning the family based on the sign of the functional equation, we find that at least 12.5% of the curves possess rank zero and at least 37.5% have rank one. These figures contrast with the Katz and Sarnak philosophy, which anticipates both percentages to be 50% and the average analytic rank to be 1/2. Finally, we calculate the one-level density for $E$ twisted by Dirichlet characters of order $\ell\neq 2$ coprime to $q$, revealing a unitary symmetry with support restricted to $(-1/2,1/2)$.

The ADMM-based interior point method (ABIP, Lin et al., 2021) is a hybrid algorithm that effectively merges the interior point method with first-order techniques to enhance performance in large-scale linear programming. Unlike the standard interior point method, which depends on expensive Newton steps, ABIP utilizes the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to approximately solve the barrier penalized problem. In this study, we present an improved version of ABIP with several enhancements. First, we introduce new implementation strategies designed to accelerate ABIP's performance for linear programming. Second, we extend ABIP to address the broader class of linear conic programming problems and derive the corresponding iteration complexity. Finally, we perform extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets to empirically validate the advantages of our developments. Specifically, the enhanced ABIP achieves a 5.8x reduction in the geometric mean of run time across 105 Netlib LP instances and performs competitively against state-of-the-art open-source solvers on a wide range of large-scale problems. Furthermore, it demonstrates comparability with commercial solvers on certain specific datasets.

We introduce a method for pruning a random recursive tree by prioritizing vertices with high degrees. Specifically, we order the $n$ vertices of the tree in descending order of their degrees, denoted as $(v^{(i)})_{i=1}^{n}$ such that $deg(v^{(1)}) \geq \cdots \geq deg (v^{(n)})$. The cutting process sequentially removes these vertices starting from $v^{(1)}$ through $v^{(n)}$, retaining only the root-connected subtree after each deletion. The procedure terminates once the root itself is selected for removal. Let $X_n^{targ}$ represent the total number of steps required; we demonstrate that this value is upper bounded by $Z_{\geq D}$, the count of vertices with degrees equal to or exceeding that of the root. Our analysis reveals that the first-order growth of $X_n^{targ}$ is bounded above by $n^{1-\ln 2}$, a rate significantly lower than that achieved when vertices are removed uniformly at random. More precisely, we establish that $\ln(Z_{\geq D})$ exhibits logarithmic growth with respect to $n$ asymptotically and derive its limiting probabilistic behavior. Furthermore, we show that the $k$-th moment of $\ln(Z_{\geq D})$ scales proportionally to $(\ln(n))^k$.

Recent advancements in theory and computation have yielded a novel understanding of symmetry-breaking instabilities in two-dimensional dynamic fracture. Central to this progress is the recognition of two intrinsic length scales near the crack tip—a nonlinear elastic scale $\ell$ and a dissipation scale $\xi$—which are absent in classical crack theory. Specifically, it has been established that brittle materials in 2D exhibit an oscillatory instability at high propagation velocities $v$, with a wavelength scaling linearly with $\ell$. At even higher velocities and loading levels, a tip-splitting instability occurs, findings that align with experimental data. In this study, we utilize phase-field models of brittle fracture to characterize the oscillatory instability through three key properties: (i) It persists even without near-tip elastic nonlinearity (in the limit $\ell\!\to\!0$), where the wavelength is governed by the dissipation length scale $\xi$, demonstrating that the instability fundamentally relies on an intrinsic length scale arising from the breakdown of linear elasticity, regardless of whether this stems from nonlinear elasticity or dissipation. (ii) It represents a supercritical Hopf bifurcation, characterized by oscillation amplitudes that vanish at onset. (iii) It remains largely unaffected by the fracture energy $\Gamma(v)$, which is regulated by a dissipation time scale. These findings confirm the universal nature of oscillatory instabilities in ultra-high speed 2D cracks. Furthermore, we present evidence suggesting that the ultra-high velocity tip-splitting instability is governed by the maximum rate of elastic energy transport within the crack tip region. Lastly, we detail the numerical implementation of the phase-field fracture approach employed.

This study analyzed 89 A- and F-type members of the Pleiades open cluster, comprising five escaped members. We determined projected rotational velocities ($v \sin i$) for 49 stars, confirming that stellar rotation broadens the main sequence in the color-magnitude diagram. Leveraging time-series photometry from NASA's TESS Mission (and one star from Kepler/K2), we identified $\delta$ Scuti pulsations in 36 stars. Notably, the fraction of pulsating stars within the instability strip is unusually high (exceeding 80%), and their effective temperature range aligns well with theoretical models. However, the varied characteristics of their pulsation spectra show no correlation with stellar temperature, casting doubt on the utility of the $\nu_{\text{max}}$ relation for $\delta$ Scuti stars, particularly in young populations. Furthermore, incorporating $\delta$ Scuti stars from the Kepler field reveals that the instability strip shifts toward the red with increasing distance due to interstellar reddening. In summary, this research highlights the effectiveness of combining Gaia and TESS observations for investigating pulsating stars in open clusters.

This study estimates convergence rates for fixed-point iterations involving a specific class of nonlinear operators, partially inspired by convex optimization challenges. We define the generalized averaged nonexpansive (GAN) operator with a positive exponent and analyze the convergence behavior of its fixed-point iteration. The proposed GAN framework is less restrictive than standard averaged nonexpansiveness but more restrictive than basic nonexpansiveness. We demonstrate that iterating a GAN operator with a positive exponent converges to its fixed point, with the local convergence rate (based on the distance between successive iterates) determined by the exponent's range. Specifically, we prove that if the exponent is positive and strictly less than 1, the iteration achieves an exponential global convergence rate (based on the distance between an iterate and the solution). Additionally, for GAN operators that are also H$\ddot{\text{o}}$lder regular, we derive a global convergence rate dependent on both the generalized averaged nonexpansiveness exponent and the H$\ddot{\text{o}}$lder regularity exponent. Finally, we apply this theoretical framework to three common convex optimization problems in data science to design fixed-point iterative algorithms and evaluate their convergence characteristics.

We illustrate a method for mapping the phase diagram of a two-dimensional quantum many-body system without relying on prior physical insights, utilizing deep \textit{anomaly detection} applied to ground states derived from infinite projected entangled pair state (iPEPS) simulations. As a case study, we analyze the 2D frustrated bilayer Heisenberg model, which features two first-order and one second-order quantum phase transitions. Our findings indicate that achieving a qualitatively accurate representation of transition lines requires only data from the cost-effective simple update optimization. Furthermore, results can be enhanced by post-selecting ground states based on their energy values, despite the computational expense of contracting the tensor network once. Additionally, we demonstrate that the conventional wisdom suggesting "more training data yields better results" does not apply to this specific learning task; in fact, a single training example may suffice. This challenges the perceived necessity of neural network optimizations for such tasks, showing that for the specific model and dataset examined, a straightforward geometric analysis is adequate.

Numerous magnetic confinement fusion applications demand the efficient computation of surface integrals featuring singular integrands. Common singularity subtraction methods are often difficult to implement and yield only low-order accuracy. Conversely, this work demonstrates that the Kapur-Rokhlin quadrature scheme is ideally suited for logarithmically singular integrals arising in toroidally axisymmetric confinement systems; it is both straightforward to implement and high-order accurate. As an example, we illustrate the application of this quadrature scheme to efficiently and accurately compute the normal component of the magnetic field generated by the plasma at the plasma boundary using the virtual casing principle.

This paper proposes a straightforward method for calculating the Jacobian group of the $Y$-graph $Y(n; k, l, m)$. Specifically, for the case $Y(n; 1, 1, 1)$, we explicitly determine the group's structure. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for the count of spanning trees in $Y$-graphs using Chebyshev polynomials and provide their asymptotic behavior.

Conventional measures for assessing image processing effectiveness fail to capture the full scope of modern techniques, especially those driven by deep learning. In engineering applications, scientists and engineers require transparent metrics to validate their design choices. By utilizing Blind/Referenceless Image Spatial Quality (BRISQUE), Structural Similarity (SSIM) indices, and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) to evaluate images before and after processing, we can meaningfully quantify quality enhancements and identify the minimum recoverable quality threshold for a specific method.

The LHCb detector investigates J/psi and Upsilon meson production in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV. These mesons are identified through their decay into mu+mu- pairs, with signal yields extracted by fitting the invariant mass distributions of these muon pairs. The analysis covers a rapidity interval of 2.0 < y < 4.5 and a transverse momentum range of 0 < p_T < 14(15) GeV/c for the J/psi and Upsilon mesons. Measurements are reported for the production cross-sections of both mesons and the fraction of J/psi mesons originating from b-hadron decays, as functions of their transverse momentum and rapidity.

This paper introduces a primal-dual gradient flow algorithm designed for distributed support vector machines (DSVM). The framework considers a network of computing nodes, where each node processes a portion of a large dataset through horizontal partitioning. These nodes are modeled as dynamical systems governed by Arrow-Hurwicz-Uzawa gradient flow dynamics, which are derived from the Lagrangian formulation of the DSVM problem. First, the study demonstrates that these nodes function as passive dynamical systems. Subsequently, utilizing Krasovskii-type candidate Lyapunov functions, the authors prove that the nodes asymptotically converge to the optimal primal-dual solution.

Recent studies have identified the clathrate hydride \emph{Fm}\={3}\emph{m}-LaH$_{10}$ as an exceptional superconductor, exhibiting a critical temperature ($T_c$) exceeding 250 K under compression of hundreds of gigapascals (GPa). While researchers aim to lower the stabilization pressure while retaining this high $T_c$ in the LaH$_{10}$ phase, the structure suffers from significant instability at lower pressures, causing a sharp decline in superconductivity. To address this, we examined the phase stability and superconducting properties of \emph{Fm}\={3}\emph{m}-LaH$_{10}$ by implementing chemical pre-compression via the partial substitution of La with Ce atoms, utilizing both experimental and computational approaches. To precisely characterize the synthesized material, we employed a lanthanum-cerium alloy with a 1:1 stoichiometric ratio. X-ray diffraction and Raman scattering analyses confirmed the stabilization of \emph{Fm}\={3}\emph{m}-La$_{0.5}$Ce$_{0.5}$H$_{10}$ within the 140–160 GPa range. Superconductivity with a $T_c$ of 175$\pm$2 K at 155 GPa was verified through the detection of zero electrical resistance and corroborated by theoretical modeling. These results offer valuable insights for future investigations into a wide range of hydrogen-rich hydrides.

Orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) modulation has recently gained attention as a promising waveform for 6G networks, particularly in high-mobility environments. This paper explores the integration of OTFS with non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). Current approaches for OTFS-NOMA equalization and detection, such as MMSE with successive interference cancellation (MMSE-SIC), exhibit limited performance. Furthermore, iterative methods designed for single-user OTFS using low-complexity least-squares solvers cannot be directly applied to NOMA due to multi-user interference (MUI). Addressing these challenges, we propose a low-complexity equalization and detection framework for OTFS-NOMA. The suggested method employs an iterative process where each step applies an LSQR-based equalizer followed by a new reliability zone (RZ) detection scheme. This scheme identifies reliable user symbols and utilizes interference cancellation to mitigate MUI. Numerical results show that our proposed approach significantly outperforms the existing MMSE-SIC benchmark in terms of symbol error rate (SER). Additionally, our findings highlight that carefully selecting RZ thresholds is crucial for optimizing the algorithm's performance.

In stereoscope-based Minimally Invasive Surgeries (MIS), dense stereo matching is crucial for 3D reconstruction, AR, VR, and navigation. Despite many Deep Neural Network (DNN) proposals, traditional prior-free methods remain prevalent in the industry due to the scarcity of open-source annotated datasets and limitations in task-specific pre-trained models. Currently, no prior-free stereo matching algorithm can achieve real-time performance on non-GPU hardware for MIS. This paper introduces the first CPU-based real-time prior-free stereo matching algorithm designed for general MIS applications. It achieves an average processing speed of 17 Hz on 640×480 surgical images using a single-core CPU (i5-9400). Additionally, the method demonstrates slightly superior accuracy compared to the widely used ELAS algorithm. The approach utilizes a patch-based fast disparity search on rectified stereo images, incorporating a proposed coarse-to-fine Bayesian probability framework and a spatial Gaussian mixed model to assess patch probabilities across scales. Furthermore, an optional probability density function estimation technique quantifies prediction variance. Extensive experiments confirm the method's ability to resolve ambiguities caused by textureless surfaces and photometric inconsistencies arising from non-Lambertian reflectance and low-light conditions. The estimated probability effectively balances patch confidence across different scales. Compared to the baseline ELAS in MIS, this method offers similar or higher accuracy with fewer outliers while operating 4–5 times faster. The source code and synthetic datasets are accessible at https://github.com/JingweiSong/BDIS-v2.

This paper demonstrates that no nonconstant Goussarov-Polyak-Viro finite-type invariants remain invariant under the virtualization move. Consequently, it follows as a direct corollary that none of the Birman coefficients of the Jones-Kauffman polynomial possess GPV finite-type properties.

Over the past few decades, statisticians have frequently employed Threshold Autoregressive (TAR) models for non-linear time series forecasting, valuing their simplicity and mathematical characteristics. Conversely, the forecasting community has recently favored general-purpose tree-based regression algorithms, such as forests and gradient-boosting, for their user-friendliness and predictive accuracy. This paper investigates the intrinsic links between TAR models and regression trees, leveraging this relationship to define a hierarchical TAR model as a global regression tree known as SETAR-Tree. Unlike standard tree-based models that often prioritize general tasks and rely on averaging at leaf nodes, we present a forecasting-oriented tree algorithm that trains global Pooled Regression (PR) models within the leaves. This approach enables the capture of cross-series information while incorporating time-series-specific splitting and stopping criteria. The tree's depth is regulated through a statistical linearity test typical of TAR models and by assessing the percentage of error reduction at each split. Consequently, the proposed model minimizes the need for external hyperparameter tuning and delivers competitive performance out of the box. Furthermore, we utilize this algorithm to construct a forest that aggregates forecasts from a diverse ensemble of SETAR-Trees. Evaluation across eight publicly available datasets demonstrates that our proposed tree and forest models significantly outperform state-of-the-art tree-based algorithms and forecasting benchmarks across four distinct metrics.

This paper introduces our investigation into the $T\bar{T}$-deformation of non-relativistic complex scalar field theory. By employing perturbation theory and the method of characteristics, we derive a closed-form expression for the deformed Lagrangian. Additionally, utilizing the Brillouin-Wigner perturbation theory within a suitable regularization framework, we calculate the precise energy spectrum of the resulting deformed free theory.

Providing robust support to inertial navigation systems (INS) in environments where GNSS signals are unavailable is essential to mitigate navigation errors that accumulate due to the inherent drift and bias of inertial sensors. A common method for achieving this involves matching geophysical measurements—such as gravity, gravity gradients, or magnetic data—against a known geo-referenced map. While conceptually straightforward, this map-matching process is difficult because the measurements are noisy, their spatial locations are uncertain, and they may correspond to multiple locations on the map (a non-unique solution). This paper introduces a probabilistic multiple hypothesis tracker designed to resolve the map-matching problem and enable robust INS aiding. Our method addresses the issue both locally through probabilistic data association and temporally by integrating platform kinematic constraints into the tracker. The resulting map-matching output is fused with the navigation system using an unscented Kalman filter. Furthermore, we introduce a statistical metric for local map information density, termed map feature variability, which is used to weight the output covariance of the proposed algorithm. The efficacy and robustness of this approach are validated through a navigation scenario utilizing gravitational map matching.

We present a Virtual Reality (VR) one-on-one tutoring platform designed to enhance anatomy instruction. In this setup, a student explores the human skull base using a fully immersive VR headset, while an instructor guides them via a semi-immersive zSpace. These systems are networked to synchronize every action between the teacher and student. The instructor benefits from various tools to direct the learning journey, such as controlling the student's navigation or adding real-time annotations, thereby enriching the educational experience. Built on the \textit{Unity} game engine, the system was evaluated through a qualitative user study. The results confirm that this one-on-one tutoring model is viable and establish a strong foundation for future research into shared virtual environments for teaching anatomy.

Although neural networks offer a promising approach for parameterizing sub-grid-scale physics, such as moist atmospheric convection, in coarse-resolution climate models, their limited interpretability and reliability hinder broad adoption. Specifically, the reasons why these networks frequently induce severe instability when coupled with atmospheric fluid dynamics remain unclear. This study presents tailored interpretive tools designed for parameterization tasks. First, we evaluate the nonlinear sensitivity of neural networks regarding lower-tropospheric stability and mid-tropospheric moisture, two key drivers of moist convection. Second, we integrate the linearized response functions of these networks with simplified gravity-wave dynamics to analytically determine phase speeds, growth rates, wavelengths, and spatial structures. To validate these methods' versatility, we apply them to two distinct neural network sets: one trained using a super-parametrized Community Atmosphere Model (SPCAM) and another using a near-global cloud-resolving model (GCRM). Despite the SPCAM simulation exhibiting a warmer climate than the cloud-resolving model, both networks forecast enhanced heating and drying in moist, unstable conditions, aligning with observational data. Furthermore, spectral analysis indicates that instability arises when global climate models are coupled with networks supporting unstable gravity waves possessing phase speeds exceeding 5 m/s, whereas standing unstable modes do not lead to catastrophic failure. Leveraging these tools, we analyze the disparities between SPCAM- and GCRM-trained networks and identify strategies to incrementally enhance their coupled online performance.

Causal systems define the localization of relativistic quantum entities that adhere to special relativity and elementary causality. By limiting the classification to real mass and finite spinor systems, we identify that, excluding certain unitarily equivalent cases, the sole irreducible causal systems are Dirac and Weyl fermions. Their wave equations emerge directly from the requirement of causal localization. Detailed analysis of bounded, localized Dirac and Weyl wavefunctions reveals that at light speed, the carriers contract in the past and expand in the future. For any spatial direction, there exists a specific moment marking the transition from contraction to expansion. States characterized by a later transition time shrink into a delta-strip when boosted in the opposite direction. Leveraging a density result for these late-change states, we demonstrate that all Dirac and Weyl wavefunctions undergo Lorentz contraction, a phenomenon examined in depth. Furthermore, we investigate whether a causal system generates a representation of causal logic, thereby enabling localization in proper space-time regions instead of merely on spacelike hyperplanes. It is shown that the logic derived from the spacelike relation admits no representations, whereas the logic from the non-timelike relation generally does, provided a specific condition is met: the existence of a projection-valued measure on every non-timelike, non-spacelike hyperplane, representing the high-boost limit of spacelike localization. Both Dirac and Weyl systems satisfy this condition, extending their localization to all non-timelike hyperplanes and revealing deeper properties of causal systems. Notably, the bounded localized eigenstates of projections onto non-spacelike flat strips correspond to these late-change states.

Accurate computational modeling and simulation tools are essential for accelerating the discovery of materials capable of storing hydrogen (H₂) under specific pressure and temperature conditions. In prior work, we introduced the H2Bind275 dataset, comprising equilibrium geometries and evaluating 55 density functionals (Veccham, S. P.; Head-Gordon, M. J. Chem. Theory Comput., 2020, 16, 4963--4982). Since accurately modeling the entire potential energy curve (PEC), beyond just equilibrium structures, is critical, we expanded this dataset to H2Bind78x7 by adding 389 new points. These new points include two compressed and three elongated geometries sampled along 78 PECs for H₂ binding. Our assessment of 55 density functionals against this larger, more comprehensive dataset identified the top performers for H₂ binding applications: PBE0-DH, $\omega$B97X-V, $\omega$B97M-V, and DSD-PBEPBE-D3(BJ). While incorporating Hartree Fock exchange generally enhances functional performance, this improvement is not consistent across the entire PEC. We recommend using $\omega$B97X-V and $\omega$B97M-V due to their robust performance across both geometries and energies. Furthermore, we identified B97M-V and B97M-rV as the most effective semi-local density functionals for predicting H₂ binding energies at equilibrium geometries.

We demonstrate that any Peano continuum possessing uncountably many local cut points qualifies as a topological fractal. This finding builds upon recent developments and offers a partial resolution to a conjecture proposed by Hata. Furthermore, we examine the quantity of mappings required to reveal the underlying structure of a topological fractal.

This paper presents a novel dataset designed to advance research in instance segmentation for irregularly shaped objects. We observe that while such objects are prevalent in daily and industrial contexts, they have been largely overlooked in instance segmentation due to a scarcity of relevant data. To address this gap, we introduce iShape, a comprehensive dataset featuring six sub-datasets—one real-world and five synthetic—each representing a distinct scene of a typical irregular shape. In contrast to existing datasets focused on regular objects, iShape presents significant challenges to current algorithms, including extensive bounding box overlaps, extreme aspect ratios, and numerous connected components per instance. Benchmarking popular methods on iShape reveals a dramatic performance decline. Consequently, we propose ASIS, an affinity-based instance segmentation algorithm that explicitly integrates perception and reasoning to handle Arbitrary Shape Instance Segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that ASIS surpasses state-of-the-art methods on iShape. The dataset and source code are accessible at https://ishape.github.io.

This work presents the inaugural instances of closed, 7-dimensional Riemannian manifolds possessing G_2 holonomy that are homeomorphic yet not diffeomorphic, marking the first such examples among closed Ricci-flat manifolds. These structures arise from the twisted connected sum construction applied to Fano 3-folds with Picard ranks of 1 and 2. The distinct smooth structures are identified using the generalized Eells-Kuiper invariant, which was previously introduced by the authors in arXiv:1406.2226.

This text serves as the first of a two-part series introducing a novel application of the separation of variables method to the Clebsch integrable case of the Kirchhoff equations. The approach introduces two key innovations: first, separating coordinates are derived by solving Kowalewski separability conditions rather than being conjectured; second, the resulting quadratures offer what appears to be a new generalization of the standard Jacobi inversion problem within algebraic geometry. Part I details the Kowalewski conditions and their application to the Clebsch case, demonstrating that the newly constructed separating coordinates yield quadratures involving Abelian differentials on two distinct non-hyperelliptic curves, each possessing a genus exceeding the dimension of the invariant tori. In Part II, these quadratures are reinterpreted as a fresh generalization of the standard Abel-Jacobi map, with an inversion procedure based on theta-functions developed. Notably, this theta-function solution differs from F. Kötter's earlier findings because the theta-functions employed here utilize a different period matrix.

We examine a charged scalar field within a uniform external magnetic field set against the near-horizon geometry of a Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli black hole that includes torsion. By deriving an analytical solution to the associated Klein-Gordon equation, we identify quasi-stationary states for this system. This solution yields a complex spectrum, revealing that both the real oscillation frequency and the decay time of the modes are functions of the external magnetic field's strength as well as the geometric background parameters. Specifically, increasing the magnetic field intensity causes the amplitude of the real oscillation modes to diminish while extending the decay time. Furthermore, these findings suggest that the geometric background remains stable under this perturbation.

This research investigates the projective freeness and Hermiteness of algebras comprising complex-valued continuous functions on topological spaces, as well as Stein algebras and commutative unital Banach algebras. The study establishes novel sufficient cohomological conditions on the maximal ideal spaces of these algebras that ensure these properties hold. These theoretical findings are supported by nontrivial examples. Drawing upon Borsuk's shape theory, the paper introduces a new class $\mathscr{C}$ of commutative unital complex Banach algebras, which serves as an analogue to local rings in commutative algebra; notably, the projective tensor product with algebras from $\mathscr{C}$ maintains both projective freeness and Hermiteness. The work compiles various examples of algebras within class $\mathscr{C}$ and other projective free and Hermite function algebras, including Douglas algebras, finitely generated algebras of symmetric functions, Bohr-Wiener algebras, algebras of holomorphic semi-almost periodic functions, and algebras of bounded holomorphic functions defined on Riemann surfaces.

Previous physical adversarial examples for camera-based computer vision relied on visible artifacts, such as stickers on stop signs, colored borders on eyeglasses, or 3D-printed objects with distinct textures. This approach implicitly assumes that perturbations must be visible for a camera to detect them. In contrast, we introduce a novel method for generating physical adversarial examples that remain invisible to the human eye. Instead of altering the victim object with visible modifications, we manipulate the light illuminating the object. We demonstrate how an attacker can engineer a modulated light signal to adversarially illuminate a scene, inducing targeted misclassifications in state-of-the-art ImageNet deep learning models. Specifically, we leverage the radiometric rolling shutter effect found in consumer cameras to generate precise striping patterns in captured images. While these patterns look like normal illumination to human observers, the camera records striped images that force machine learning models to produce the attacker's desired classification. Through extensive simulations and physical experiments using LEDs, we achieved targeted attack success rates of up to 84%.

Collaborative filtering remains one of the most impactful approaches in recommender systems, with methodologies ranging from matrix factorization to graph convolutional techniques. Drawing inspiration from the recent advancements in GF-CF and diffusion models, we introduce a novel blurring-sharpening process model (BSPM). Like diffusion models, BSPMs operate on a philosophy where new information is generated after the original data is perturbed and subsequently recovered. However, because diffusion models and our BSPMs address distinct types of information, their optimal perturbation and recovery mechanisms differ fundamentally, resulting in unique model structures. Our concept not only theoretically encompasses numerous existing collaborative filtering frameworks but also surpasses them in Recall and NDCG metrics across three benchmark datasets: Gowalla, Yelp2018, and Amazon-book, achieving the highest accuracy among them. Furthermore, our method boasts one of the fastest processing times ever recorded in this domain. Future enhancements hold significant potential, particularly through the design of superior blurring (perturbation) and sharpening (recovery) processes beyond those currently implemented.

Explaining the presence of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with masses exceeding $10^8\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$ at redshifts greater than 6 remains a significant hurdle for contemporary astrophysics. While multi-wavelength studies of quasars (QSOs) at $z\gtrsim6$ indicate that their average accretion mechanisms resemble those of lower-redshift counterparts, QSOs exhibiting anomalous properties offer valuable clues about the rapid growth of SMBHs in the early universe. We report on X-ray follow-up observations (XMM-Newton, 100 ks) of the $z\approx6$ quasar J1641+3755, which appeared exceptionally bright in a 2018 Chandra survey. However, J1641+3755 was undetected in a 2021 XMM-Newton observation, suggesting its X-ray flux dropped by a factor of at least 7 within a brief period of approximately 115 rest-frame days, establishing it as the most variable QSO at $z>4$. Additionally, we acquired rest-frame UV spectroscopic and photometric data using the LBT and compared them with archival records. Unexpectedly, our analysis reveals that J1641+3755 brightened in the rest-frame UV between 2003 and 2016, yet showed no significant variation from 2016 to 2021. Its rest-frame UV spectrum contains multiple narrow absorption lines, several of which likely originate from an intervening system at $z=5.67$. The variability of J1641+3755 could stem from intrinsic accretion rate fluctuations, a minor obscuration event, gravitational lensing by an intervening object, or an unrelated X-ray transient in a foreground galaxy in 2018. By examining all QSOs at $z>6$ with multiple X-ray observations separated by more than 10 rest-frame days, we identified an increased prevalence of strongly variable objects (varying by a factor $>3$) compared to quasars at later cosmic epochs. This result may reflect the unique physics governing fast accretion in high-redshift quasars.

The \emph{Gutman index}, denoted $Gut(G)$, was originally defined for connected undirected graphs $G$. This note applies that concept to the underlying graphs of the family of Jaco graphs (which are inherently directed) and presents a recursive formula for the \emph{Gutman index} $Gut(J^*_{n+1}(x)).$ Furthermore, we calculate the \emph{Gutman index} for the trivial \emph{edge-joint} formed between Jaco graphs.

Our research team is creating a remote online assessment tool that evaluates hand movement characteristics linked to aging, accessible from any research center. Participants complete this test from their own computers using webcams to capture hand motion data. However, gathering high-quality video is difficult, particularly for older adults lacking technical experience. A critical component of our data collection is the automated and precise identification of instruction adherence and gesture consistency across various devices, a necessity given the anticipated scale of thousands of participants. We have developed a hand gesture detector with a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.782, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. Our work involved processing 20,000 images from these tests and manually labeling 6,450 to identify distinct gestures. This study offers three primary contributions: first, a comparative analysis of different network architectures for gesture detection; second, the successful enhancement of classification accuracy for similar gestures through the integration of attention layers; and third, the creation of two datasets containing 20% blurred images to assess network resilience against noisy data, demonstrating that our proposed network maintains superior performance in such conditions.

In supervised learning, gathering labeled data for predictive models is often expensive, whereas obtaining vast amounts of unlabeled data is typically straightforward. Active learning addresses this by adaptively selecting samples for labeling, thereby achieving high-precision models at a reduced cost. This paper outlines the fundamental settings of active learning and examines recent research trends, with a specific focus on developing acquisition functions for sample selection, theoretical advancements in active learning algorithms, and stopping criteria for sequential data collection. Additionally, the paper presents application examples within material development and measurement.

The increasing need for mental health assistance has underscored the global and Chinese significance of conversational agents as human-like supporters. These tools can enhance access to care while lowering associated costs. Support provided by such agents generally falls into two categories: cognitive and emotional. Current research predominantly focuses on developing agents grounded in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) principles, which utilize predefined templates and exercises to deliver cognitive aid. However, studies regarding emotional support via these agents remain scarce. Furthermore, since most existing agents operate in English, there is a critical need for research within the Chinese context. This study evaluates the efficacy of Emohaa in alleviating mental distress symptoms. Emohaa is a conversational agent that offers cognitive support through CBT-based exercises and guided dialogue, alongside emotional support by allowing users to express their feelings. The experiment involved 134 participants divided into three groups: Emohaa (CBT-based), Emohaa (Full), and a control group. Results indicated that users of Emohaa showed significantly greater improvements in mental distress symptoms compared to the control group. Additionally, the inclusion of emotional support yielded a complementary benefit, particularly in reducing depression and insomnia. Given these findings and the high satisfaction levels reported by participants, we conclude that Emohaa is a practical and effective instrument for mitigating mental distress.

Building on the proposal in Phys. Rev. D 98, 103023 (2018) regarding the detection of dark matter (DM)–electron interactions through hydrogen-atmosphere pulsating white dwarfs (DAVs) in globular clusters, this comment refines the analysis. While the original study suggested a testable parameter space of $5 \mathrm{GeV} \le m_{\chi} \le 10^{4} \mathrm{GeV}$ and $\sigma_{\chi,e} \ge 10^{-40} \mathrm{cm}^{2}$, our calculations establish a precise lower bound for the testable DM mass of approximately $1.38 - 1.58 \mathrm{GeV}$, contingent upon the scattering cross section $\sigma_{\chi,e}$. This finding not only provides a robust minimum mass limit for the scenario but also delineates a definitive upper mass threshold for future investigations.

The thermal evolution of neutron stars is investigated within the $f(R)=R+\alpha R^{2}$ framework of gravity. We begin by outlining the equations governing stellar structure and evolution for a spherically symmetric spacetime containing a static perfect fluid. Subsequently, we provide numerical results regarding neutron star structures derived from four different nucleonic equations of state and various gravity theories, where the parameter $\alpha$ spans from zero (corresponding to General Relativity) to approximately $10^{16}$ cm$^2$. We highlight specific model properties critical to thermal evolution, including the threshold masses for direct Urca neutrino emission, the core volume permitting this process, crust thickness, and surface gravitational acceleration, all of which influence the observable effective temperature. Furthermore, we numerically solve the thermal evolution equations to explicitly examine the effects of modified gravity. Our findings indicate that uncertainties in dense matter microphysics—such as core chemical composition and superfluid/superconducting properties—as well as astrophysical uncertainties regarding surface layer composition, exert a significantly stronger influence than potential modifications to gravity within the studied $f(R)$ family. Consequently, within this specific theoretical framework, conclusions from prior studies on neutron star thermal evolution remain largely unaffected by gravitational alterations. Conversely, this suggests that neutron star cooling models may not serve as an effective means to constrain deviations from Einstein's theory unless those deviations are substantially more profound than those permitted by the $f(R)=R+\alpha R^{2}$ model.

Contemporary autonomous vehicles depend significantly on mechanical LiDAR for environmental perception.
