Notably, we identified a pronounced sensitivity of the transmission amplitude to the geometry-phase $\phi = \tan^{-1} \alpha$ inherent in $\alpha-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattices. We anticipate these results will be instrumental in developing Dirac cone-based tunneling transistors for ultrafast analog RF applications and in controlling tunneling currents via potential barriers within one-dimensional scatterer arrays.

This paper introduces a new information processing architecture designed for the safe, deep learning-driven visual navigation of autonomous systems. This architecture supports a predictive control algorithm grounded in perceptual attention, integrating model predictive control (MPC), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and uncertainty quantification techniques. The core innovation is employing MPC to learn how to focus attention on pertinent areas of visual input, enabling the system to identify unsafe conditions more quickly. Specifically, MPC learns to select regions of interest within input images, which generate control actions alongside estimates of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty for the attention-aware visual data. These uncertainty estimates are then utilized to assess the safety of the network controller under current navigation scenarios. The architecture and algorithm were validated on a 1:5 scale terrestrial vehicle. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses prior approaches in the early detection of unsafe conditions, particularly when novel obstacles appear in the environment. Furthermore, this architecture represents an initial step toward applying deep learning-based perceptual control policies in safety-critical domains.

This paper introduces a numerical procedure for integrating non-autonomous linear delay differential equations. The method employs spectral discretization of the delayed component to convert the original problem into a matrix linear ordinary differential equation, which is then solved using numerical integrators derived from the Magnus expansion. This algorithm is applicable to periodic cases, enabling the accurate computation of both characteristic multipliers and the solution itself. Furthermore, the approach can be extended to handle specific quasilinear delay equations.

Safety-critical decision-making systems powered by machine learning depend on highly reliable and certain predictions. To address this, such systems can be enhanced with a "reject option," enabling them to decline inputs where the model's confidence is insufficient. While rejecting uncertain samples is crucial, it is equally vital to provide explanations for these rejections. Although the field of eXplainable AI (XAI) has produced numerous explanation techniques, explaining reject options remains a nascent area with limited existing research. This work introduces the use of semifactual explanations—a type of example-based method not yet widely adopted in XAI—to clarify why samples are rejected. We present a conceptual framework for applying semifactual explanations to any reject option and empirically assess a specific implementation within a conformal prediction-based reject option system.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective in supervised feature extraction for node-level and graph-level classification by propagating node features across edges and learning transformations under label supervision. However, standard GNNs typically assume the graph structure is fixed, neglecting the underlying formation of edges. This paper proposes a graph generative process that models edge generation as the aggregation of node interactions within overlapping communities, where each community contributes to edges via a logical OR operation. Leveraging this model, edges are decomposed into a sum of community-specific weighted edges, which define distinct community-aware GNNs. We introduce a variational inference framework to jointly train an inference network that partitions edges into communities, learns these community-specific GNNs, and employs a predictor GNN that integrates them for final classification. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness in learning discriminative representations for both node-level and graph-level classification.

Recent studies on Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) focus on segmenting highly concealed items within intricate environments, where their small size and fuzzy appearance render them visually indistinguishable. However, existing single-view COD detectors struggle with background distractors, making it difficult to fully capture the blurred boundaries and variable shapes of these hidden objects. To address these challenges, we introduce a behavior-inspired framework known as the Multi-view Feature Fusion Network (MFFN), which emulates human strategies for locating indistinct objects by simulating observations from various angles, distances, and perspectives. The core concept involves generating multiple observational viewpoints through data augmentation to serve as diverse inputs. MFFN effectively captures essential boundary and semantic details by comparing and fusing features extracted from these multi-view inputs. Furthermore, the network leverages the interdependencies between views and channels. This is achieved through a two-stage attention mechanism, the Co-attention of Multi-view (CAMV), which utilizes complementary information across different views, and a locally iterative Channel Fusion Unit (CFU) designed to explore channel-wise contextual clues within diverse feature maps. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches when trained on the same dataset. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/dwardzheng/MFFN_COD.

CuTeO$_4$ has been suggested as a crystallographically unique but electronically analogous counterpart to superconducting cuprates. Magnetization data spanning 2 to 300 K reveal low-dimensional antiferromagnetic correlations with an exchange constant $J = 148(7)$ K. Below approximately 50 K, an upturn in magnetization signals enhanced ferromagnetic correlations, accompanied by neutron powder diffraction evidence of diffuse magnetic scattering at $Q \approx 0.6$ \si{\angstrom^{-1}}. A Warren line shape analysis determines a magnetic correlation length of $\xi = 4.5(9)$ \si{\angstrom} at 40 K, which increases to $\xi = 10.1(9)$ \si{\angstrom} at 10 K. Specific heat measurements show a significant linear temperature dependence ($\gamma = 8.3$ mJ/mol-f.u/K$^2$) below 5 K. Collectively, these findings suggest a low-dimensional, antiferromagnetic spin glass state. Structural modeling of the diffraction data identifies layered stacking disorder, which explains the absence of long-range magnetic order and aligns with theoretical predictions of its two-dimensional character. In contrast to cuprates, no substantial dopability was observed in this wide-band-gap, yellow insulator.

This study examines feebly interacting massive particle dark matter, where its production is notably influenced by phase evolution and complex thermal corrections to the vector boson. We compute freeze-in mechanisms to derive the accurate dark matter relic abundance by systematically cataloging all viable $1 \leftrightarrow 2$ and $2 \leftrightarrow 2$ interactions. Furthermore, we assess the gravitational waves generated by first-order phase transitions and cosmic strings.

Although deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit impressive performance, recent research has highlighted their susceptibility to adversarial examples (AEs)—carefully perturbed inputs intended to deceive targeted models. While the literature offers numerous effective methods for generating these AEs, various defense strategies have also emerged to counter this threat. However, existing defenses often lack generalization, performing well only against specific attacks rather than across a broader range. This paper introduces a two-stage framework to defend DNN classifiers against adversarial samples, comprising a dedicated detector and a denoising module. The detector identifies AEs by analyzing natural scene statistics (NSS), which are shown to be altered by adversarial perturbations. The denoising component utilizes a block-matching 3D (BM3D) filter, guided by an optimal threshold determined by a convolutional neural network (CNN), to map detected adversarial samples back to their original data manifold. Extensive evaluations on three standard datasets—MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet—demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art defenses, enhancing robustness against multiple attacks in black-box, gray-box, and white-box scenarios. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/kherchouche-anouar/2DAE

In critical software systems, testers face significant time and resource demands due to the persistent emergence of defects, some of which are severe enough to compromise system integrity. To alleviate this burden, numerous machine learning models have been developed to automatically forecast defect severity by analyzing documented reports. Unlike conventional methods, this study introduces a metric-based Software Defect Severity Prediction (SDSP) model that employs a self-training semi-supervised learning strategy to classify defective modules. This approach leverages a combination of labeled and unlabeled data, utilizing a decision tree classifier to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled instances; the resulting predictions are promising because the self-training process effectively assigns appropriate class labels to these instances. While extensive research has addressed prediction methodologies and approaches, a gap remains in estimating project-specific attributes derived from these models. To address this, we propose five project-specific metrics—Risk-Factor (RF), Percent of Saved Budget (PSB), Loss in Saved Budget (LSB), Remaining Service Time (RST), and Gratuitous Service Time (GST)—to capture project outcomes based on the predictions. Consistent with traditional metrics, these measures are derived from the observed confusion matrix and are utilized to evaluate the impact of the prediction model on the software project.

The CDF-II collaboration's recent determination of the $W$-boson mass stands out as notably heavier than the Standard Model forecast. We investigate this discrepancy within the scale-invariant Two-Higgs-Doublet-Model (SI-2HDM) featuring a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry designed to suppress flavor-changing-neutral-currents (FCNCs). In this framework, the Higgs boson corresponds to the classically massless scalon, which acquires mass through radiative corrections, rendering it naturally light. Furthermore, the scale symmetry enhances the model's predictivity compared to a generic 2HDM. We demonstrate that the oblique parameters, which rely on the masses of the charged scalar ($M_{H^\pm}$) and the CP-even ($M_h$) or CP-odd ($M_A$) neutral scalars, are sufficiently large to explain the $W$-boson mass anomaly. Additionally, viable parameter spaces exist within the SI-2HDM mass spectrum that remain consistent with current collider constraints on charged Higgs bosons and neutral scalars.

Kagome lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnets exhibit significant sensitivity to structural disorder perturbations. Although Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) serves as an ideal local probe for studying these disorder-induced phenomena, traditional one-dimensional NMR data often display broad distributions that obscure the intrinsic behavior of pristine kagome quantum spin liquids from disorder effects. This study introduces a two-dimensional NMR acquisition method applied to Zn-barlowite (Zn$_{0.95}$Cu$_{0.05}$)Cu$_{3}$(OD)$_{6}$FBr, enabling the correlation between low-energy spin excitation distributions and local spin susceptibility. We provide evidence for the progressive formation of domains featuring local spin polarization, driven by 5% Cu$^{2+}$ defect spins occupying interlayer non-magnetic Zn$^{2+}$ sites. At 2~K, these spin-polarized domains comprise approximately 60% of the sample volume, where gapless excitations resulting from interlayer defects dominate the low-energy spin excitation spectrum within the kagome planes.

Let $R_q(r,n)$ represent the $r$th order Reed-Muller code of length $q^n$ defined over $\Bbb F_q$. We address two algebraic inquiries concerning this code. First, we define $H_q(r,n)$ as the quotient $R_q(r,n)/R_q(r-1,n)$. For $q=2$, a known "duality" exists between the actions of $\text{GL}(n,\Bbb F_2)$ on $H_2(r,n)$ and $H_2(r',n)$ where $r+r'=n$; however, this property does not generally hold for arbitrary $q$. We demonstrate that a slightly adjusted duality statement remains valid when $q$ is prime or when $r < \text{char}\,\Bbb F_q$. Second, let $\mathcal F(\Bbb F_q^n,\Bbb F_q)$ be the $\Bbb F_q$-algebra of all functions from $\Bbb F_q^n$ to $\Bbb F_q$. It is established that for prime $q$, the Reed-Muller codes form the exclusive chain of $\text{AGL}(n,\Bbb F_q)$-submodules within $\mathcal F(\Bbb F_q^n,\Bbb F_q)$, implying that $H_q(r,n)$ is an irreducible $\text{GL}(n,\Bbb F_q)$-module in this case. For general $q$, $H_q(r,n)$ is not necessarily irreducible; instead, we identify all its submodules and the factors comprising its composition series. These factors constitute an explicit family of irreducible representations of $\text{GL}(n,\Bbb F_q)$ over $\Bbb F_q$.

We present an adaptive tree search algorithm capable of identifying high-scoring outputs across translation models, regardless of the search objective's form or structure. As a deterministic variant of Monte Carlo tree search, this approach allows for the investigation of novel models without the constraints typically imposed to ensure decoding tractability, such as autoregressivity or conditional independence assumptions. When applied to autoregressive models, our algorithm exhibits distinct biases compared to beam search, facilitating a fresh analysis of how decoding bias influences these models. Empirically, we demonstrate that our method discovers outputs with significantly superior model scores relative to beam search in autoregressive settings and outperforms reranking techniques in models where scores do not decompose additively with respect to output words. Additionally, we analyze the correlation between various translation model objectives and BLEU scores. Our findings indicate that while certain standard models are poorly calibrated and gain from beam search bias, other more robust models—specifically autoregressive models optimized for expected automatic metric scores, the noisy channel model, and a newly proposed objective—benefit from increased search depth via our proposed decoder. Conversely, the beam search bias restricts the improvements achievable from these objectives. Consequently, we argue that as models advance, their potential gains may be obscured by an over-reliance on beam search or reranking-based methods.

Although unbiased machine learning models are crucial for numerous applications, bias is a human-defined notion that can differ depending on the specific task. When provided solely with input-label pairs, algorithms often lack the necessary information to separate stable (causal) features from unstable (spurious) ones. However, since related tasks frequently exhibit similar biases, we can exploit this observation to build robust classifiers in transfer learning scenarios. In this study, we explicitly guide the target classifier by informing it about the unstable features present in source tasks. Specifically, we create a representation that captures these unstable features by contrasting various data environments within the source task. To ensure robustness, we cluster the target task data based on this representation and minimize the worst-case risk across these clusters. We tested our approach on both text and image classification problems. Empirical results show that our algorithm successfully maintains robustness on the target task, performing well in both synthetically generated and real-world environments. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/YujiaBao/Tofu.

Network alignment, which involves identifying corresponding nodes across different networks, is a critical challenge in numerous application areas. We introduce CAPER, a multilevel framework that Coarsens input graphs, Aligns these coarsened versions, Projects the alignment results back to finer levels, and Refines the final solution. CAPER enhances the performance of various existing network alignment algorithms by ensuring consistency across multiple graph resolutions: matches identified at finer levels must also hold at coarser levels. Furthermore, CAPER significantly speeds up slower alignment methods by enabling them to operate on smaller, coarsened graph versions, with only a modest overhead from linear-time coarsening and refinement steps. Experimental results demonstrate that CAPER improves upon diverse network alignment methods by increasing accuracy by an average of 33% and/or reducing runtime by an order of magnitude.

Structural DNA nanotechnology has progressed significantly, enabling the design of highly complex structures, largely driven by automated design and simulation tools. However, existing software (such as NUPAK, cadnano, and OxDNA) is typically task-specific. Ideally, a unified environment would integrate these DNA tools with non-DNA utilities, such as those for modeling electromagnetic fields within gold nanoparticle-based zero-mode waveguides on a DNA breadboard. Such a platform would streamline DNA nanotechnology design and facilitate the application of its principles to build high-performance materials and devices from non-DNA components.

In this work, we introduce a small programmatic tool as a step toward constructing such an environment for designing arbitrary nanostructures. Specifically, we demonstrate how this tool was employed to develop an Integrated Computational Materials Engineering (ICME) framework for DNA nanotechnology, supporting the hierarchical design, simulation, and visualization of any DNA nanostructure. Additionally, we illustrate the design and modeling of mode profiles and band structures in hybrid DNA-nanoparticle materials by integrating the tool with Maxwell solvers.

For a manifold with boundary equipped with a discrete group action, we examine the operator algebra formed by components of the Boutet de Monvel algebra—specifically pseudodifferential boundary value problems—and shift operators defined on the manifold and its boundary. Assuming specific constraints on the group action, we define a Chern character for the symbols of elliptic operators within this algebra, taking values in a de Rham-type cohomology associated with the fixed point manifolds. Consequently, we derive an index formula expressed through this Chern character.

We report ALMA band 7 (339 GHz; 0.89 mm) observations of gas and dust in the protoplanetary disk surrounding the very low-mass star ZZ Tau IRS, achieving a spatial resolution of 0.25 arcseconds. The position-velocity diagram for $^{12}$CO $J=3\rightarrow2$ indicates a dynamical mass for ZZ Tau IRS of approximately 0.1 to 0.3 solar masses. The disk exhibits a total flux density of 273.9 mJy, implying a dust mass between 24 and 50 Earth masses. The dust emission map reveals a ring at 58 au and an azimuthal asymmetry at 45 au with a position angle of 135 degrees. Characteristics of this asymmetry, such as its radial width, aspect ratio, contrast, and flux contribution, closely resemble those found in intermediate-mass stars (~2 solar masses) like MWC 758 and IRS 48. This similarity suggests a common origin for the asymmetry in ZZ Tau IRS, despite the host star being roughly ten times less massive. Additionally, our data suggest a potential misalignment between the inner and outer disk regions. Collectively, these findings indicate evidence of giant planet formation at a scale of ~10 au within a few million years. If confirmed, this would challenge current core accretion models, which predict that forming such planets around very low-mass stars is exceptionally difficult.

Given the widespread consumption of vertical videos on mobile devices, we introduce a framework to enhance the visibility of horizontal content through automated horizontal-to-vertical (H2V) conversion. This proposal includes our H2V framework and a newly created, accurately annotated H2V-142K dataset. The framework combines video shot boundary detection, subject selection, and multi-object tracking to ensure the preserved subject remains intact during conversion, with subject selection being the critical component. To accomplish this, we developed a Rank-SS module that identifies human objects and selects the primary subject based on location, appearance, and saliency cues. Subsequently, the system automatically crops the video around this subject to transform horizontal footage into vertical format. To construct and evaluate the framework, the H2V-142K dataset provides dense subject bounding box annotations for 125 videos (comprising 132,000 frames) and 9,500 covers. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional saliency-based approaches in subject selection and delivers promising overall H2V conversion quality. By releasing both the dataset and our methodology, we aim to facilitate future advancements in horizontal-to-vertical video conversion.

This paper serves as a note on the recently introduced tensor degree of finite groups, a numerical invariant that extends the concept of commutativity degree via the nonabelian tensor square. We establish two inequalities linking the tensor and commutativity degrees of finite groups, thereby indirectly examining their structural properties.

Data collected via tools like TACC Stats tracks resource utilization across nodes in high-performance computing environments. We introduce techniques to analyze this data for assessing system performance and detecting anomalies. The fundamental approach involves modeling the data as a three-way tensor representing compute nodes, usage metrics, and time. By treating the reconstruction error between the original tensor and its low-rank decomposition as a scalar metric, we can monitor system performance in real-time. This error statistic facilitates anomaly detection based on the premise that routine system behavior can be effectively approximated by a low-rank tensor. We validated the algorithm using system logs, demonstrating that the identified performance anomalies align with critical errors recorded in those logs. The results utilize data from the 2013 operations of the Lonestar4 system at the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC).

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning (SSL) have demonstrated its potential for extracting meaningful semantic representations from images for classification. This study investigates the applicability of SSL to Fine-Grained Visual Categorization (FGVC), a task that involves distinguishing between visually similar subcategories. The challenge in FGVC arises from small inter-class differences and large intra-class variations, a problem further compounded by the scarcity of annotated labels for such fine-grained data. SSL offers a solution by providing additional supervision to enhance learning without incurring the cost of extra annotations. Our baseline model achieves $86.36\%$ top-1 accuracy on the CUB-200-2011 dataset using random crop augmentation for training and center crop augmentation for testing. This work explores the efficacy of various pretext tasks—specifically rotation, Pretext Invariant Representation Learning (PIRL), and Deconstruction and Construction Learning (DCL)—for FGVC. The rotation task encourages the model to learn global features, potentially at the expense of subtle details, whereas PIRL, utilizing jigsaw patches, aims to highlight discriminative local regions but often fails to localize them accurately. In contrast, DCL excels at learning local discriminative features, surpassing the baseline with a top-1 accuracy of $87.41\%$. By forcing the model to attend to local object parts and reconstructing them to learn part correlations, DCL proves highly effective. We conducted extensive experiments to validate these findings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/mmaaz60/ssl_for_fgvc.

This study examines how strong magnetic fields influence the hadron-quark phase transition point at zero temperature. The hadronic phase is modeled using a relativistic mean field (RMF) approach, while the quark phase is described via a density-dependent quark mass model (DDQM). Compared to non-magnetized matter, we find that the transition point shifts toward higher pressures and, generally, higher chemical potentials. Additionally, we analyze phase transitions capable of supporting hybrid stars.

Advanced adversarial threats, including membership inference and model memorization, can compromise federated learning (FL) and expose sensitive private information. Local differentially private (LDP) methods are increasingly favored because they offer robust privacy guarantees and natively accommodate data distributions, surpassing other differentially private (DP) solutions. Nevertheless, current DP techniques rely on the assumption that the FL server is either honest or semi-honest (acting honestly while attempting to extract maximum information), rendering these approaches impractical and unreliable in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, in industrial contexts such as healthcare, distributed entities like hospitals already operate local machine learning models, a scenario known as the cross-silo setting. Existing solutions lack scalable mechanisms for privacy-preserving FL within such environments, particularly when involving untrusted parties. This paper introduces LDPFL, a novel local differentially private FL protocol designed for industrial applications. LDPFL ensures operation with untrusted entities while enforcing stronger privacy protections than current methods. Additionally, it demonstrates high FL model performance (reaching up to 98%) even with minimal privacy budgets (e.g., epsilon = 0.5), outperforming existing techniques.

Transition metal silicides such as $\beta$-RhSi, known for their chiral cubic structure, have recently been shown to host exotic multifold topological excitations. In this study, we demonstrate that the topological properties of RhSi persist in its orthorhombic $\alpha$-phase, which features multiple Dirac nodes situated near the Fermi level ($\varepsilon_F$) with a negligible presence of trivial carriers. We present a symmetry analysis, examine band connectivity via group representations along high-symmetry paths, and detail the band structure, focusing on the Dirac points and nodal lines near $\varepsilon_F$. Experimental data from the de Haas-van Alphen effect confirms a Fermi surface consistent with theoretical calculations. Specifically, we identify an elliptically shaped nodal line located just below $\varepsilon_F$ around the $S$-point on the $k_y-k_z$ plane, formed by the intersection of two inverted Dirac cones. Since the two Dirac points of the involved Kramers degenerate bands are separated by only 5 meV, an accessible magnetic field could potentially induce a crossing between the spin-up state of the upper cone and the spin-down state of the lower cone, offering a plausible explanation for the anomalies detected in magnetic torque measurements.

Event cameras offer distinct benefits over traditional RGB cameras, enabling new solutions for visual tasks in demanding environments characterized by rapid motion, high dynamic range, and strict power limitations. However, unlike established image and video compression techniques, current event compression methods remain insufficient for practical use. The primary obstacle lies in the unique structure of event data: a stream of asynchronous tuples containing 2D coordinates, timestamps, and polarity (indicating brightness increases or decreases). Because events capture only temporal changes, they inherently lack the spatial structure essential for effective compression. To overcome this, we introduce a novel compression algorithm utilizing a quad tree (QT) segmentation map generated from adjacent intensity frames. This map establishes 2D spatial priorities within the 3D space-time volume. During encoding, events are first aggregated temporally to create polarity-based histograms. These histograms are then variably sampled using Poisson Disk Sampling, guided by the QT segmentation map to prioritize spatially significant areas. Subsequently, differential encoding handles spatial information, run-length encoding processes polarity data, and Huffman encoding generates the final bitstream. Our proposed Poisson Disk Sampling based Lossy Event Compression (PDS-LEC) algorithm optimizes rate-distortion trade-offs. On average, it achieves over 6x compression, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

Data programming (DP) has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to manual data labeling. In this approach, users define \emph{labeling functions} (LF)—heuristic rules that generate noisy labels for data subsets, often with intricate dependencies. A label model is subsequently trained on these functions to infer the true class labels. However, the impact of label model misspecification on downstream classifier performance remains largely unexplored. This represents a critical knowledge gap for practitioners, especially because the interdependencies among LFs are frequently neglected in practical DP implementations. We investigate modeling errors arising from structural over-specification. Furthermore, we establish new theoretical bounds on this error and demonstrate empirically that it can be significant, even when the assumed structure appears logical.

Remote state estimation of large-scale distributed dynamic systems is vital for Industry 4.0 applications. This study addresses the transmission scheduling challenge within such remote estimation systems. Initially, we establish key structural characteristics of the optimal sensor scheduling policy operating over fading channels. Leveraging these theoretical insights, we construct a structure-enhanced deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed to optimize system scheduling and minimize the overall estimation mean-square error (MSE). Specifically, we introduce a structure-enhanced action selection mechanism that prioritizes actions adhering to the established policy structure, thereby exploring the action space more efficiently and boosting the learning performance of DRL agents. Additionally, we implement a structure-enhanced loss function that imposes penalties on non-compliant actions, guiding the DRL agent to rapidly converge toward the optimal policy structure. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed structure-enhanced DRL algorithms reduce training time by 50% and decrease remote estimation MSE by 10% to 25% compared to standard benchmark DRL algorithms. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the derived structural properties are applicable to a broad spectrum of dynamic scheduling problems extending well beyond remote state estimation.

The symmetry of matter, ranging from finite entities such as molecules and atomic clusters to extended structures like periodic and aperiodic crystals, is characterized by point and space groups. This framework is extended to magnetic materials, where atomic constituents exhibit binary properties, such as the "up" or "down" states of spins or magnetic moments. This text defines magnetic groups—also referred to as antisymmetry, Shubnikov, Heesch, Opechowski-Guccione, dichromatic, 2-color, or black-and-white groups—detailing their structure, notation, and providing illustrative examples of their enumeration. Furthermore, it examines the resulting selection rules or extinctions observed in neutron diffraction experiments and briefly outlines further generalizations to color and spin groups.

Zero-shot intent detection (ZSID) seeks to handle continuously emerging intents without relying on annotated training data. However, current ZSID approaches face two key challenges: they struggle to model the relationship between seen and unseen intents, and they fail to effectively recognize unseen intents within the generalized intent detection (GZSID) framework. A fundamental cause of these issues is the inability to learn representations for unseen intents during the training phase. To overcome this, we introduce a new framework that leverages unseen class labels to generate Class-Transductive Intent Representations (CTIR). Specifically, the model is enabled to predict unseen intents during training by using their corresponding label names as input utterances. Building on this, we propose a multi-task learning objective that fosters the distinction between different intents, alongside a similarity scorer that more accurately assesses connections among them. CTIR is straightforward to implement and can be seamlessly integrated with existing methods. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that CTIR significantly enhances baseline system performance.

For any pair of Hermitian matrices $A$ and $B$, the Golden-Thompson inequality \cite{golden1965lower, thompson1965inequality} asserts that $$ \mathrm{tr}\left[ \exp{(A+B)} \right] \leq \mathrm{tr}\left[ \exp{(A)}\exp{(B)} \right]. $$ We now present a detailed derivation of this result based on the approach by Sutter et al. (2017).

This study examines two-player stochastic games on finite graphs played over infinite rounds. These games extend Markov decision processes (MDP) by introducing an adversarial player and extend deterministic two-player games by incorporating stochasticity. The game's result is defined as a sequence of state distribution vectors. We focus on synchronizing objectives, where the probability mass must concentrate on a target set of states, evaluated under four conditions: always, once, infinitely often, or eventually (always after some point). Winning is categorized as "sure" (accumulated probability equals 1) or "almost-sure" (probability approaches 1 arbitrarily closely). We provide algorithms to determine the set of winning distributions for each objective mode. Our results establish that deciding these objectives is PSPACE-complete for "once" and "infinitely often," and PTIME-complete for "always" and "eventually." These complexity bounds align closely with those found in the MDP special case. However, the algorithms and proofs are significantly more complex than for deterministic games, even when the graph itself is non-stochastic. This increased difficulty stems from an imperfect information dynamic: the games are not determined, requiring randomized strategies, and when combined with graph stochasticity, finite-memory strategies are generally insufficient for achieving the "infinitely often" objective.

We introduce a sophisticated field formulation of quantum Fisher estimation theory designed to inherently handle complex statistics regarding complex parameters. This framework establishes new complex iterations of key estimation theory concepts, including Fisher information matrices and Cramér-Rao bounds, which depend on these complex parameters. This approach proves valuable in scenarios where quantum states are characterized by complex parameters, such as in coherent or squeezed states. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of this theory through its application in quantum communication utilizing coherent states.

We present SToRM, a new generative smoothness regularization model designed to reconstruct dynamic image data from highly undersampled measurements. This framework models the image time series as a smooth, non-linear transformation of low-dimensional latent vectors that encode cardiac and respiratory phases, implemented via a deep convolutional neural network (CNN). Distinct from conventional CNN methods that rely on large fully-sampled datasets unavailable in this context, our approach jointly optimizes the CNN generator parameters and latent vectors directly from undersampled data using stochastic gradient descent. To ensure a smooth manifold, we penalize the generator's gradient norm, while penalizing temporal gradients of the latent vectors enforces smoothness in the time series. Key advantages include a substantial reduction in memory requirements compared to analysis-based SToRM models and the spatial regularization provided by the CNN architecture. Additionally, we propose efficient progressive strategies to lower the algorithm's computational complexity.

Stochastic variance-reduced optimization techniques are recognized for their global convergence but often exhibit slow local convergence, particularly when moderate to high accuracy is required. To address this limitation, we introduce a hybrid acceleration scheme designed for proximal variance-reduced stochastic optimization algorithms. This proposed method integrates a rapidly converging local algorithm, such as a quasi-Newton method, with a globally convergent variance-reduced stochastic algorithm like SAGA or L-SVRG. The global convergence of our hybrid approach relies on specific safeguard conditions that determine whether a step from the fast local method is accepted. We demonstrate that the sequence of iterates produced by this hybrid scheme converges almost surely to a solution of the optimization problem. Additionally, numerical experiments indicate that the hybrid acceleration scheme achieves significantly faster convergence compared to standard stochastic variance-reduced optimization algorithms.

This article introduces a novel deep learning architecture called JDNN, designed to approximate numerical solutions for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs), with a specific capability to handle high-dimensional equations. By employing orthogonal Jacobi polynomials as activation functions, the Jacobi Deep Neural Network enhances both the accuracy and stability of solving these equations. To address computational complexity, the method applies finite difference time discretization. Furthermore, the approach leverages Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) to expedite the learning process through neural network platforms. Numerical experiments comparing this scheme with existing methods demonstrate its efficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical problems.

Using video microscopy, we identified a two-step glass transition in monolayers of colloidal ellipsoids. The transition associated with rotational degrees of freedom occurred at a lower density compared to that of translational degrees of freedom. In the intermediate regime between these two transitions, the ellipsoids exhibited orientational glass behavior. As the system approached either glass transition, the fastest-moving particles in both rotational and translational supercooled liquids moved cooperatively, organizing into clusters characterized by power-law size distributions. Consequently, the mean cluster sizes diverged according to a power law near the transitions. Furthermore, these clusters formed in distinct locations: translational clusters primarily within pseudo-nematic domains, while rotational clusters formed mainly around the domain boundaries.

We present the identification of eight previously unknown quasars within a single extragalactic field, centered at RA=$08^h58^m08.2^s$, Dec=$01^o32'29.7''$ and spanning five degrees, discovered during LAMOST's commissioning run on December 18, 2009. These objects exhibit $i$-band magnitudes ranging from 16.44 to 19.34 and redshifts between 0.898 and 2.773. While none were detected in the SDSS spectroscopic survey, six of them (those with redshifts below 2.5) had been selected as quasar targets by SDSS. Seven of the eight new quasars satisfy a recently proposed selection criterion that utilizes both near-infrared and optical colors, with the sole exception being one source lacking near-IR $Y$-band data. Notably, two of these quasars reside in the "redshift desert" ($z$ from 2.2 to 3.0), demonstrating the efficiency of the new criterion in recovering quasars that possess optical colors similar to stars. Despite challenges encountered during LAMOST's commissioning phase, we successfully identified an additional 38 known SDSS quasars in this region, with $i$ magnitudes from 16.24 to 19.10 and redshifts spanning 0.297 to 4.512. These findings suggest that a significant portion of quasars may have been overlooked in prior surveys. We also discuss the implications of these results for future LAMOST quasar surveys.

Building task-oriented dialogue systems efficiently and deploying models across diverse domains at scale presents two major challenges. To address these, this paper introduces a novel manual-guided dialogue scheme where an agent learns tasks from both dialogue interactions and accompanying manuals. These manuals are unstructured texts that direct the agent's interaction with users and databases. By leveraging this approach, the scheme lessens reliance on fine-grained domain ontologies, enhancing the models' flexibility to adapt to various domains. Additionally, we present MagDial, a fully-annotated multi-domain dataset designed to support this framework. MagDial defines three subtasks: instruction matching, argument filling, and response generation, which align with human agent behavior patterns. Experimental results indicate that the manual-guided scheme improves both data efficiency and domain scalability. The dataset and benchmark will be made publicly available to facilitate future research.

Inspired by recent experimental findings, we performed microscopic calculations of the quasiparticle self-energy and spectral function for doped graphene exhibiting sublattice symmetry breaking. Our systematic analysis employs the many-body G$_0$W approach, built upon the random phase approximation and a continuum model of massive Dirac equations for graphene. We provide extensive computations of both the real and imaginary components of the quasiparticle self-energy under conditions of gap opening. Additionally, we present findings regarding the spectral function, renormalized Fermi velocity, and band gap renormalization of massive Dirac fermions across a wide spectrum of electron densities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that mass generation in graphene suppresses the plasmaron peak in spectral weight.

This study presents Submillimeter Array (SMA) observations of H2CO and N2H+ emission in the disks surrounding the T Tauri star TW Hya and the Herbig Ae star HD 163296, achieving a resolution of 2"-6". We analyze the spatial distribution of these molecules relative to the CO freeze-out region. In HD 163296, the H2CO and N2H+ emission peaks are significantly offset from the continuum center, which marks the star's location. Utilizing an established model of the disk's physical structure, we demonstrate that the H2CO data are accurately reproduced when the molecule is primarily located in the cold outer disk. Specifically, a model placing H2CO exclusively beyond the CO snow line (estimated at 160 AU) aligns well with the observations. Furthermore, the average excitation temperature of H2CO, derived from two transitions observed in these two disks and a broader sample from the DISCS program, matches the CO freeze-out temperature of 20 K. Additionally, we find a strong correlation between H2CO and N2H+ line fluxes across the disk sample, suggesting these species form together. Collectively, these findings indicate that H2CO and N2H+ generally exist only in cold regions where CO depletes onto dust grains; this is consistent with the rapid destruction of N2H+ by gas-phase CO and the *in situ* formation of H2CO via the hydrogenation of CO ice. Under this scenario, H2CO, CH3OH, and N2H+ emission should manifest as rings with an inner edge defined by the CO midplane snow line, a prediction that can be directly tested using higher-resolution and more sensitive ALMA observations.

We examine two BF formulations of gravity with a negative cosmological constant: the Plebanski and MacDowell-Mansouri theories. Although both yield the standard Einstein equations in the bulk, they produce different expressions for edge charges. We explicitly calculate the asymptotic charges for both frameworks using AdS-Schwarzschild, AdS-Kerr, and AdS-Taub--NUT solutions. Our results indicate that while charges diverge in the Plebanski theory, they remain finite in the MacDowell-Mansouri theory. Additionally, we demonstrate that for arbitrary asymptotically AdS spacetimes, the MacDowell-Mansouri asymptotic charges, action, and symplectic form are all finite. Consequently, the MacDowell-Mansouri theory of gravity in asymptotically AdS spaces requires no counterterms.

Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) is widely used to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE), yet empirical evidence indicates that IPTW estimators are vulnerable to misspecification of the propensity score model. To mitigate this, researchers have suggested estimating propensity scores by directly optimizing pre-treatment covariate balance. Although these approaches demonstrate strong empirical performance, their theoretical properties regarding the selection of balancing conditions remain underexplored. To address this gap, we analyze the asymptotic bias and efficiency of the IPTW estimator utilizing the Covariate Balancing Propensity Score (CBPS) method under local model misspecification. Based on this analysis, we derive optimal covariate balancing functions and propose an optimal CBPS-based IPTW estimator. This estimator exhibits double robustness, remaining consistent for the ATE if either the propensity score or outcome model is correctly specified. Furthermore, when both models are correctly specified, the proposed estimator achieves local semiparametric efficiency. To further relax parametric constraints, we extend the method using a sieve estimation approach, demonstrating that the resulting estimator is globally efficient under significantly weaker assumptions and possesses a reduced asymptotic bias compared to existing estimators. Finally, we assess the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators through simulations and empirical studies, with an open-source software package available for implementation.

Local Fisher discriminant analysis serves as a localized alternative to standard Fisher discriminant analysis and is widely recognized as a supervised dimensionality reduction technique. The `lfda` R package facilitates this analysis, supporting various extensions like kernel and semi-supervised local Fisher discriminant analysis. Additionally, it offers visualization tools that enable users to inspect dimension reduction outcomes using `rgl` for three-dimensional rendering or `ggfortify` for two-dimensional plots styled with `ggplot2`.

High-dimensional Ising models ($d\ge 5$) exhibit mean-field critical exponents. Nevertheless, the finite-size scaling of susceptibility $\chi$ at the critical temperature is sensitive to boundary conditions. Specifically, periodic boundaries yield $\chi\propto L^{5/2}$, whereas removing $5L^4$ edges to impose free boundaries results in $\chi\propto L^2$. This study demonstrates that eliminating only $L^4$ edges along a single direction is sufficient to achieve the $\chi\propto L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, removing $L^3$ edges appears to produce an intermediate scaling regime, estimated at $\chi\propto L^{2.275}$. Additionally, we investigate the effects of edge deletion on the distributions of energy and magnetization.

Utilizing sensors to monitor behavior in smart homes provides valuable insights into residents' long-term health and independence. While Passive Infrared (PIR) motion sensors are common, they often fail to capture the complete duration of movement, require a direct line of sight, and necessitate visibility to the occupants. In contrast, Channel State Information (CSI) offers a cost-effective, unobtrusive method for radio sensing that not only tracks motion but also yields rich data. We have created a new, self-calibrating motion detection system that processes CSI data on an off-the-shelf Raspberry Pi 4. This system leverages correlations between CSI frames to perform variance analysis via our algorithm, enabling precise measurement of the full duration of a resident's activity. Tests across various real-world settings confirm the system's efficacy, demonstrating accurate detection of activity start and end times for movements of varying intensities and locations.

This research addresses the localization of multiple forced oscillation (FO) sources and the estimation of their properties—frequency, phase, and amplitude—based on noisy phasor measurement unit (PMU) data. At each source location, the input oscillation is modeled as a summation of unknown sinusoids, which establishes a linear relationship between measurements and inputs at specific sinusoidal frequencies within the frequency domain. These frequencies are identified by applying a threshold to the empirical spectrum of the noisy data. Leveraging the sparsity of both FO locations and the number of sinusoids per location, the location recovery task is formulated as an $\ell_1$-regularized least squares problem in the complex domain, known as complex-LASSO. We solve this optimization numerically using the complex-valued coordinate descent method and demonstrate its effectiveness on the IEEE 68-bus (16-machine) and WECC 179-bus (29-machine) systems.

Understanding sequential information relies fundamentally on narrative sensemaking, a process supported by narrative maps—visual frameworks that help analysts navigate this task. These maps enable users to grasp the overarching narrative, discover novel event relationships, and model connections between storylines. This study investigates how analysts create and utilize narrative maps to establish design guidelines for an interactive visualization tool that enhances sensemaking. Through two experiments using a dataset of news articles, we extract insights applicable to designing narrative maps, extraction algorithms, and visual analytics tools. The paper offers three main contributions: an analysis of how analysts construct these maps, a user evaluation of specific map features, and a set of design guidelines. Our findings propose strategies for designing maps and algorithms that facilitate useful interactions. We discuss these insights, guidelines, and potential implementation challenges. Key highlights include the recommendation to avoid redundant connections inferable via the transitive property of events, thereby reducing map complexity. Additionally, maps should incorporate multiple cognitive connections between events, such as topical and causal links, to mirror the strategies analysts employ during sensemaking.

Building upon Kotzig's 1968 work on transition systems, Krivelevich, Lee, and Sudakov introduced a broader concept of incompatibility systems to analyze the robustness of Hamiltonicity in Dirac graphs. For a graph $G=(V,E)$, an incompatibility system $\mathcal{F}$ consists of a collection $\mathcal{F}=\{F_v\}_{v\in V}$, where each $F_v$ is a set of edge pairs in $G$ sharing vertex $v$. The system is termed $\Delta$-bounded if, for any vertex $v$ and incident edge $e$, no more than $\Delta$ pairs in $F_v$ include $e$. A subgraph $H$ is considered compatible with $\mathcal{F}$ if no two adjacent edges $e,e'$ in $H$ (meeting at vertex $v$) form a pair in $F_v$. Krivelevich, Lee, and Sudakov demonstrated that a universal constant $\mu>0$ exists such that any $\mu n$-bounded incompatibility system on a Dirac graph admits a compatible Hamilton cycle, thereby confirming a 1988 conjecture by H\"{a}ggkvist. This study extends these findings to high powers of Hamilton cycles, proving that for any $\gamma>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a constant $\mu>0$ ensuring that sufficiently large $n$-vertex graphs with minimum degree $\delta(G)\ge(\frac{k}{k+1}+\gamma)n$ contain a compatible $k$-th power of a Hamilton cycle under every $\mu n$-bounded incompatibility system. Furthermore, the authors provide counterexamples demonstrating that the $\gamma n$ error term is essential and cannot be entirely removed.

We present a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) designed to produce cloud reflectance fields (CRFs) based on extensive meteorological inputs, including sea surface temperature and relative humidity. Our trained model successfully creates realistic CRFs from these observations, marking progress toward a data-driven framework for stochastic cloud parameterization.

Dynamical systems where local agent interactions generate complex emergent behaviors are common throughout nature and society. This study addresses the challenge of reconstructing the unknown interaction topology (modeled as a graph) of such systems using data from their individual components (nodes). The framework accommodates scenarios where the underlying dynamical model is unspecified and where available measurements (snapshots) are independent, potentially originating from distinct experiments. We introduce GINA (Graph Inference Network Architecture), a graph neural network designed to concurrently infer the latent interaction graph and, conditioned on that structure, predict a node's observable state based on its neighbors. This approach relies on the premise that the true interaction graph enables the most accurate prediction of a node's state given its neighbors' states. We validate this hypothesis and demonstrate GINA's efficacy across diverse interaction graphs and dynamical processes.

Simultaneous Neural Machine Translation (SNMT) models begin generating the target sequence prior to fully processing the source input. Recent adaptive SNMT approaches rely on monotonic attention to determine read/write operations based on partial source and target sequences. However, insufficient information can lead to suboptimal read/write choices by monotonic attention, thereby degrading SNMT performance. Conversely, human translators excel at making these decisions by leveraging linguistic knowledge and domain expertise to anticipate upcoming words. Inspired by this human capability, we introduce a framework that enhances monotonic attention by incorporating an external language model to refine its decision-making. Experiments on the MuST-C English-German and English-French speech-to-text translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The proposed SNMT method achieves a superior quality-latency trade-off compared to state-of-the-art monotonic multi-head attention models.

The LHCb experiment conducted the initial search for the rare radiative decay $\Xi_b^- \to \Xi^- \gamma$ using data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 5.4 fb$^{-1}$. This search utilized the $\Xi_b^- \to \Xi^- J/\psi$ decay channel for normalization. No signal for $\Xi_b^- \to \Xi^- \gamma$ was observed, resulting in an upper limit of $\mathcal{B}(\Xi_b^- \to \Xi^- \gamma) < 1.3 \times 10^{-4}$ at a 95% confidence level.

Product Question Answering (PQA) has recently gained significant traction within e-commerce platforms due to its potential to serve as an intelligent shopping assistant and enhance the overall customer experience. The primary objective of PQA is the automatic generation of answers that are both relevant to the query and preserve essential product details. However, current approaches often overlook a critical feature of PQA: personalization. Providing identical, generalized summaries to every user is inadequate, as many customers prefer tailored responses that reflect their specific preferences regarding product attributes or information needs. To address this gap, we introduce PAGE, a novel method for Personalized Answer Generation that employs multi-perspective preference modeling. This approach leverages historical user-generated content to model user preferences for creating customized PQA responses. The methodology operates in three stages: first, it retrieves question-related user history as external knowledge to model knowledge-level preferences; second, it utilizes a Gaussian Softmax distribution model to capture latent aspect-level preferences; and third, it employs a persona-aware pointer network to generate answers that are customized in both content and style by incorporating individual user preferences and dynamic vocabularies. Empirical evaluations on real-world e-commerce question-answering datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques by producing informative and personalized answers, confirming that personalization significantly benefits answer generation in the e-commerce domain.

We introduce a criterion for identifying genuine entanglement in pure multiqubit states. Central to this approach is the definition of a "losing one qubit" operator, distinct from the reduced density operator; states resulting from applying this operator are termed projected states. We demonstrate that if a pure product n-qubit state cannot be decomposed into a single qubit state and a genuinely entangled (n-1)-qubit state, then all its projected states remain pure product states. Furthermore, we establish that a pure n-qubit state is genuinely entangled if it possesses at least two genuinely entangled (n-1)-qubit projected states. By iteratively applying this losing process, the detection of entanglement for pure n-qubit states is reduced to the detection of entanglement for pure two-qubit states. Additionally, we have developed a LISP program to facilitate this reduction process.

Cloud storage systems have been developed to offer a scalable, secure, reliable, and highly available data storage environment for both organizations and end-users. As service providers expand geographically, extensive storage service provision necessitates a replication mechanism. However, replication incurs significant costs for cloud storage, including expenses related to synchronization, communication, and storage among replicas. Furthermore, synchronizing replicas presents a major challenge in cloud storage, where consistency is defined as the coordination among these replicas. In this paper, we propose an extension to strict timed causal consistency by incorporating monetary costs and violation counts into cloud storage systems, which we term "extended strict timed causal consistency." Our approach supports monotonic read, read-your-write, monotonic write, and write-follow-read models by considering causal relations between user operations at the client side, while also supporting timed causal consistency at the server side. We implemented this method using the Cassandra cloud database, which supports various consistency levels such as all, one, quorum, and causal. Our method demonstrates superior performance in reducing the staleness rate, the severity of violations, and monetary costs compared to all, one, quorum, and causal consistency models.

Magnetars are young, isolated neutron stars distinguished by the universe's most powerful magnetic fields, yet the origin of these fields remains an unresolved puzzle. While dynamo action amplifying magnetic fields in fast-rotating progenitors is a leading hypothesis, it is uncertain if enough such progenitors exist to account for all observed magnetars. To resolve this, we introduce a new formation scenario where a slow-rotating proto-neutron star gains angular momentum through supernova fallback. We posit that this spin-up triggers the Tayler-Spruit dynamo, rendering other dynamo mechanisms unlikely. By combining existing research on this dynamo with fallback simulations, we developed equations modeling the coupled evolution of the proto-neutron star's rotation and magnetic field. Comparing time-integrated results for various fallback masses with analytical estimates of amplification timescales and saturation levels, we found that magnetic fields amplify within 20 to 40 seconds post-core bounce and saturate at radial intensities of $10^{14}-10^{15}$ G, covering the entire range of magnetar dipolar fields. Furthermore, comparing two saturation mechanisms indicates that magnetar-like fields can arise in neutron stars spun up to rotation periods of $\lesssim8$ ms and $\lesssim28$ ms, corresponding to fallback masses of $\gtrsim4\times10^{-2}{\rm M}_{\odot}$ and $\gtrsim10^{-2}{\rm M}_{\odot}$, respectively. Consequently, our findings suggest that magnetars can originate from slow-rotating progenitors, provided the fallback mass aligns with recent supernova simulations and yields plausible initial proto-neutron star rotation periods.

Loop Quantum Cosmology (LQC) has successfully established effective approaches to predict observable quantities across various models. Although effective dynamics have been widely explored in different contexts, a rigorous validation of these descriptions at the perturbative level remains an area needing further investigation. Most current methodologies rely on the test field approximation, which is valid only when the gravitational backreaction of produced particles can be ignored. Within LQC, the primary strategies for quantizing linear perturbations include the dressed metric, hybrid, and closed/deformed algebra approaches. This study evaluates the consistency of the test field assumption across these frameworks by calculating the ratio of energy density in gravitationally produced particles to the background energy density, thereby offering a critical consistency check for LQC's effective descriptions.

Native Language Identification (NLI) involves using supervised machine learning to train classifiers that determine an author's native language. While this field has seen extensive research and consistent performance improvements over the last decade, our work focuses on a distinct aspect: examining the internal mechanisms of NLI classifiers trained with explainable algorithms to generate explanations for their decisions. Our ultimate goal is to understand which specific linguistic features reveal a speaker's native language (L1). By applying this approach, we address both standard NLI and the less-explored task of distinguishing between native and non-native speakers. Utilizing three datasets from diverse sources—two containing English learner essays and one comprising social media posts—we investigate which linguistic characteristics (lexical, morphological, syntactic, and statistical) are most effective at identifying a speaker's L1. Furthermore, we present two case studies analyzing Spanish and Italian learners of English, detailing the specific linguistic traits that classifiers identified as critical for detecting these L1s. Overall, our research demonstrates that explainable machine learning serves as a valuable tool for th

Recently introduced for stochastic optimization tasks with uncertain parameters, Decision-focused learning (DFL) combines predictive modeling with an implicitly differentiable optimization layer, outperforming the conventional two-stage predict-then-optimize approach. Nevertheless, current DFL techniques are largely limited to convex problems or nonconvex variants that can be easily relaxed, and they often suffer from training inefficiencies caused by the need to solve and differentiate through the optimization problem at every iteration. To address these issues, we introduce SO-EBM, a general and efficient DFL framework for stochastic optimization that utilizes energy-based models. Unlike methods relying on KKT conditions to create an implicit optimization layer, SO-EBM explicitly parameterizes the original problem using a differentiable layer grounded in energy functions. To more accurately approximate the optimization landscape, we implement a coupled training objective that employs a maximum likelihood loss to identify the optimum and a distribution-based regularizer to model the overall energy landscape. Additionally, we develop an efficient training procedure for SO-EBM utilizing a self-normalized importance sampler with a Gaussian mixture proposal. Evaluations across three domains—power scheduling, COVID-19 resource allocation, and non-convex adversarial security games—demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency.

Despite achieving impressive results on various benchmarks and attracting significant scientific attention, Deep Neural Networks fail to encompass the full scope of cognition. This paper contends that, however, these architectures hold promise for cognitive robotics, particularly in their ability to represent perceptual audio and visual data. Furthermore, we pinpoint critical areas within cognitive robotics where deep neural networks have contributed minimally thus far, given the field's complex challenges. Finally, we propose that the underexplored domain of Reservoir Computing should be considered an essential component of sequential learning in this context.

Managing epidemics requires rapid and intensive data collection and management from various locations and entities. The Internet of Things (IoT) can meet this demand through its easy and scalable deployment. Effective containment also necessitates collaboration across organizations and nations. Consequently, this paper introduces the Intelligent-Health (I-Health) system, designed to unify diverse e-health entities into a cohesive national framework by facilitating secure and swift medical data exchange and storage. Specifically, we propose an edge-based automated patient monitoring scheme that enables quick detection, remote oversight, and rapid emergency response to critical incidents, including emerging epidemics. Additionally, we develop a blockchain optimization model to enhance the secure sharing of medical data among various health entities, ensuring effective service delivery. Finally, we demonstrate the system's adaptability to diverse critical events and underscore the advantages of the proposed I-Health solution.

Causal matching designs frequently result in discarded control subjects and unmodeled covariates. This article introduces "rebar," a technique that leverages high-dimensional modeling to integrate these typically excluded data points without compromising the integrity of the matching structure. Following the creation of a match, researchers utilize the remaining unmatched controls—the remnant—to train a machine learning model that forecasts control potential outcomes based on the complete covariate matrix. These predictions are then applied to the matched set to adjust causal estimates, thereby mitigating confounding bias. The study provides theoretical validation for the method's bias-reduction capabilities, supports them with a simulation analysis, and demonstrates the approach through an evaluation of a comprehensive school-level educational reform initiative in Arizona.

Physical models of rigid bodies are employed for sound synthesis across various applications, ranging from virtual environments to music production. Conventional techniques like modal synthesis typically depend on computationally intensive numerical solvers, whereas recent deep learning methods are constrained by the need for post-processing their outputs. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end framework that trains a deep neural network to generate modal resonators for specified 2D shapes and materials by utilizing a bank of differentiable IIR filters. We validate this approach on a dataset of synthetic objects, training the model with an audio-domain objective to facilitate the development of physically-informed synthesizers learned directly from recordings of real-world objects.

Deep neural networks are extensively employed to uncover the latent structures within datasets spanning various modalities, including images, shapes, and audio. Nevertheless, current models typically rely on specific architectures and objectives tailored to individual modalities. In contrast, we utilize neural fields to capture underlying structures across images, shapes, audio, and cross-modal audiovisual domains in a modality-agnostic way. We formulate this task as manifold learning, aiming to identify a low-dimensional, locally linear subspace where the data exists. By enforcing manifold coverage, local linearity, and local isometry, our proposed model, GEM, successfully learns the fundamental structure of datasets regardless of modality. This approach enables us to traverse linear regions of the manifold to produce perceptually consistent interpolations between samples. Furthermore, GEM allows for the recovery of points on the manifold, facilitating not only diverse completions of input images but also cross-modal hallucinations of audio or image signals. Finally, we demonstrate that by navigating the underlying manifold of GEM, new samples can be generated within the signal domains. Code and supplementary results can be found at https://yilundu.github.io/gem/.

Deep neural networks have proven highly effective at image classification in closed-set environments, where test data originates from the same distribution as the training data. However, traditional classifiers struggle in more realistic open-set scenarios, where they cannot handle test data belonging to classes absent from the training set. Open Set Recognition (OSR) seeks to solve this by simultaneously identifying unknown classes and distinguishing known ones. This paper introduces a novel OSR approach leveraging Vision Transformer (ViT) technology. Our method utilizes a two-stage training process: first, a ViT model is trained for closed-set classification, and second, a detection head is appended to the ViT's extracted features to compel known data representations into compact, class-specific clusters. Test samples are classified as known or unknown based on their distance to these cluster centers. To our knowledge, this is the first application of ViT for OSR. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines and achieves new state-of-the-art results.

This paper outlines a suite of computational tools for image analysis applied to brain morphometry. These technologies rely on a novel Variational Principle that generates transformations with a specified Jacobian determinant (representing local size variations) and a specified curl-vector (representing local rotations). Our primary objective is to persuade the image research community that both the Jacobian determinant and the curl-vector should be integral to every stage of image analysis. Specifically, we introduce an optimal control approach for non-rigid registration, propose a new framework for constructing average transformations, and present a robust, general method for creating unbiased templates from image sets. Computational examples are provided to demonstrate the impact of the curl-vector and to validate the efficacy of the optimal control methods for non-rigid registration and the proposed unbiased template construction technique.

This paper examines the ultraviolet behavior of 3+1 dimensional Lifshitz-type anisotropic theories involving scalar, fermion, and gauge fields with a higher-derivative structure and an anisotropy exponent of $z=3$, featuring explicit Lorentz symmetry breaking. By omitting momentum-dependent vertex operators from the action—a necessary step to prevent phenomenologically unacceptable light-cone deformations—we determine that renormalizable scalar self-interactions and Yukawa-like couplings are generally asymptotically free. However, the condition for eliminating these vertex operators conflicts with gauge symmetry; consequently, in such theories, both gauge and Lorentz symmetries emerge only below a specific energy scale $M$, which must be constrained by experimental data. Additionally, we analyze quantum corrections to the scalar mass and their implications for the hierarchy problem.

AstronomicAL is an interactive, human-in-the-loop dashboard designed for labelling and training that leverages active learning to build robust classifiers and reliable datasets. By prioritising data with high information gain, this approach enhances performance while significantly reducing the volume of data required. The platform enables users to integrate and visualise data from diverse sources, effectively managing issues such as missing or incorrect labels and class imbalance. Experts can utilise domain-specific plots and key contextual details drawn from various inputs to ensure label accuracy. Furthermore, AstronomicAL offers comprehensive exploration of the training process, including custom models and query strategies, making it suitable for both specialised classifications and general machine learning experimentation. Although demonstrated with an astronomical dataset to address immediate needs in that field, the system is versatile enough for any discipline. Finally, the ability to export a simple configuration file allows the entire layout, model, and assigned labels to be shared with the community, fostering transparency and simplifying result reproduction.

We continue to examine the relationship between scattering amplitudes for massive higher-spin particles and gravitons in specific quantum-to-classical limits and the classical gravitational interactions of spinning black holes as described by general relativity. Initially, we develop an ansatz for a tree-level gravitational Compton amplitude, restricted only by locality, crossing symmetry, unitarity, and consistency with the linearized-Kerr 3-point amplitude to all orders in the black hole's spin. Subsequently, we investigate how far a unique classical Compton amplitude can be established by comparing it with the scattering of long-wavelength gravitational waves off an exact Kerr black hole, calculated using appropriate solutions to the Teukolsky equation. Up to fourth order in spin, our results align perfectly with a previously conjectured exponential form for the tree-level Compton amplitude. At higher orders, we derive tree-level contributions from the Teukolsky amplitude through analytic continuation from a physical regime ($a/GM<1$) to a particle-like regime ($a/GM>1$). Up to sixth order in spin, we isolate a unique *conservative* component of the amplitude that remains unaffected by boundary conditions at the black hole horizon or branch choices in the analytic continuation. The remaining part of the amplitude is determined up to an overall sign, which depends on the branch choice and flips when exchanging purely ingoing and purely outgoing boundary conditions at the horizon. Additionally, we provide the resulting two-black-hole scattering angle for aligned spins within the eikonal limit. Throughout this work, we also establish connections to new applications of massive spinor-helicity variables, specifically regarding their relation to EFT operators and (spinning) partial amplitudes.

This paper investigates the frequentist characteristics of Bayesian inference applied to the stochastic block model, specifically addressing scenarios with an unknown number of communities of varying sizes. We assign a prior to the number of classes and, conditionally, to the vertex labels within the space of all possible labellings. The number of classes is allowed to increase without bound relative to the number of vertices, contingent upon the graph's sparsity. We establish non-asymptotic rates for posterior contraction, expressed as $P_{\theta_{0,n}}\Pi_n(B_n\mid X^n)\le \epsilon_n$, where $X^n$ denotes the observed graph generated under $P_{\theta_{0,n}}$, $B_n$ represents either the true parameter $\{\theta_{0,n}\}$ or, in highly sparse regimes, a ball of known radius surrounding $\theta_{0,n}$, and $\epsilon_n$ signifies an explicit convergence rate. These findings facilitate the transformation of credible sets into confidence sets. Specifically, in sparse settings, credible tests function as confidence sets, while in the very sparse case, credible sets are expanded to achieve this property. The resulting confidence levels are explicitly defined for each $n$ based on the credible level and the convergence rate. Furthermore, we examine hypothesis testing regarding the number of classes using posterior odds, demonstrating its consistency. We provide explicit upper bounds for Type I and Type II errors, along with an explicit lower bound for the statistical power of these tests.

This study calculates the structure constants for single-trace operators at strong coupling within planar $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory by employing the hexagon formalism. The analysis focuses on heavy-heavy-light correlators, where the heavy constituents are BMN operators characterized by large R-charges and finite anomalous dimensions, while the light operator is a chiral primary with finite charge. In the holographic dual, these configurations correspond to interactions between two highly boosted strings and a supergravity mode. Within the hexagon framework, binding the hexagons around the light operator requires summing over virtual magnons; we perform these sums explicitly at strong coupling for specific BMN operators. Our results demonstrate that these sums factorize into a ratio of Gamma functions and a straightforward stringy prefactor. The Gamma function ratio arises from giant mirror magnons traversing the AdS geometry, whereas the prefactor originates from small fluctuations around the BMN vacuum. The derived structure constants exhibit poles at locations anticipating enhanced mixing with double-trace operators and vanish where supersymmetry forbids the process. Furthermore, we examine the transition to the classical regime, where the light operator's length scales with the string tension, noting similarities to the Neumann coefficients found in the pp-wave String Field Theory vertex.

To clarify the geometric structure of the hypothesized room-temperature superconductor, carbonaceous sulfur hydride, under high pressure, we report findings from a comprehensive computational search of bulk C-S-H at 250 gigapascals. By employing the minima hopping structure prediction method alongside the GPU-accelerated Sirius library, we examined over 17,000 local minima featuring various stoichiometries within large simulation cells. Only 24 stoichiometries proved stable against elemental decomposition, all of which consist of carbon-doped H$_3$S crystals. Furthermore, the lack of van Hove singularities or comparable peaks in the electronic density of states across more than 3,000 candidate phases eliminates the possibility of conventional superconductivity in C-S-H at room temperature.

This study develops a high-precision relativistic theoretical framework by initially investigating the finite speed of light through coordinate transformations and subsequently expanding these analytical techniques to encompass broader relativistic phenomena. Consequently, this model advances the application of atomic interferometry for testing General Relativity.

Utilizing probe molecules to investigate the local structural and dynamical characteristics of complex systems is a long-established approach in both experimental and simulation contexts. These local probes provide access to crucial data that bulk measurements cannot readily reveal.
