To our knowledge, these covariate profiles have not previously been employed in quality measurement literature. We apply various clinically relevant covariate profiles to evaluate layered case-mix adjustment methods that sequentially combine weighting and regression modeling. This approach aims to minimize model extrapolation and accommodate provider effect modification. Through an extensive simulation study, we assess these methods and emphasize the practical value of weighting techniques that alert investigators when case-mix adjustments are infeasible without extrapolation beyond the data's support. In an analysis of cancer-care outcomes, we evaluate oncology practices across different profiles representing the diverse patient types receiving care. We demonstrate how these methods are particularly critical for high-stakes quality measurement, such as public reporting or performance-based payments, and discuss their potential application to support individual patient health decisions and facilitate personalized quality measurement.

Sensing-as-a-Service (S2aaS) represents a novel business model pattern within the Internet of Things (IoT) sector. To ensure technical viability and facilitate widespread adoption, S2aaS implementations must address significant systemic challenges, particularly concerning payment mechanisms and sensor identification. To tackle these obstacles, we suggest utilizing Bitcoin as the underlying protocol for S2aaS networks. To initiate a dialogue on the disruptive potential of Bitcoin technology for both S2aaS concepts and the IoT ecosystem at large, we examine and discuss the fundamental characteristics driving these transformations. Furthermore, we outline a conceptual scenario and detail the fundamental process of exchanging data for cryptocurrency using Bitcoin.

Generally, the Gini index does not constitute a strictly consistent scoring rule, which means optimizing it can result in erroneous decisions. This limitation arises because the Gini index relies on rank-based scoring and lacks calibration sensitivity. However, we demonstrate that the Gini index supports strict consistency when applied specifically to the class of auto-calibrated regression models.

An infinite binary sequence is considered random if it possesses every definable property that occurs with probability one under the standard measure on such sequences. Since there are only countably many definable properties, it appears that random sequences should constitute a set of full measure. However, it is possible that no random sequences exist at all, as there might not be any undefinable sets.

An ideal triangulation of a singular flat surface is defined as a geodesic triangulation where the vertices correspond exactly to the surface's singular points. Leveraging the property that for any positive length $L$, there are only finitely many geodesics of length at most $L$ connecting any two points on a surface, we demonstrate that every singular flat surface admits such a triangulation under specific conditions: either the surface has no boundary components but possesses singular points, or every boundary component contains at least one singular point. Furthermore, we establish that these surfaces contain a finite collection of geodesics linking their singular points; cutting along these arcs yields a flat disk with a non-singular interior.

This work introduces a variational framework for pressure-dependent plasticity within a time-incremental context. A new formulation of the dissipation potential enables the construction of condensed energy in a variationally consistent way. For a one-dimensional model problem, an explicit expression for the quasiconvex envelope is derived, which is found to be largely independent of the original pressure-dependent yield surface. While this model problem can be extended to higher dimensions empirically, numerical simulations demonstrate well-posed behavior with mesh-independent results.

This brief note presents a novel Menon-type identity that relates the sum of element orders to the sum of cyclic subgroup orders within a finite group. This result is derived by applying the weighted version of Burnside's lemma to a specific natural group action.

GISAXS serves as a flexible, non-contact, and non-destructive method for analyzing nanostructured surfaces. However, the shallow incidence angles inherent to this technique cause significant elongation of the X-ray beam footprint, restricting its application to samples with typical lengths of several millimeters. This limitation poses challenges for many applications where creating large target areas is unfeasible, particularly when targets are embedded within structured environments. In such cases, the oversized beam footprint captures parasitic scattering from surrounding structures, which obscures the signal from the target itself. This paper presents GISAXS measurements of both isolated and surrounded grating targets in Si substrates, covering line lengths from 50 μm down to 4 μm. For isolated targets, the study explains how scattering patterns evolve with reduced target length. Regarding surrounded targets, the signal from a 15 μm × 15 μm target grating is successfully distinguished from the 100 μm × 100 μm nanostructured background by fabricating the target with an orientation different from the dominant direction of the surroundings. This approach enables the use of GISAXS for characterizing metrology fields in the semiconductor industry, a task previously deemed impossible due to the large beam footprint.

Genome engineering is rapidly advancing and becoming increasingly accessible; therefore, developing tools to trace the origin of engineered plasmids is crucial for ensuring responsible innovation and preventing misuse. Genetic Engineering Attribution (GEA), which links sequences to their sources, would greatly assist forensic experts in this endeavor. We introduce a metric-learning-based method that ranks the most probable labs of origin while simultaneously generating embeddings for both plasmid sequences and laboratories. These embeddings facilitate downstream tasks, including clustering and serving as features for machine learning models. Our approach utilizes circular shift augmentation and achieves a 90% accuracy rate in identifying the correct lab within the top 10 predictions, surpassing all current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability for few-shot learning, attaining 76% top-10 accuracy using only 10% of the data, which outperforms the previous CNN approach with just one-tenth the dataset. Additionally, our method extracts key signatures specific to particular labs, enabling an interpretable analysis of the model's outputs.

A primary goal of cosmic-ray research involves accurately measuring the energy and chemical composition of particles at extreme energy levels. Researchers typically employ large, advanced detectors to identify atmospheric shower events with recorded energies exceeding 100 EeV. However, a Cosmic-Ray Ensemble (CRE) that develops prior to reaching Earth as a cluster of correlated particles may cover vast areas, necessitating an expanded network of detectors for discovery. The Cosmic-Ray Extremely Distributed Observatory (CREDO) offers a solution for detecting such phenomena. In this framework, even basic detectors capable of measuring only particle arrival times are effective, as they can both identify candidate CRE events and ascertain the direction of arrival.

This paper investigates cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (C-NOMA) within short packet communications utilizing finite blocklength (FBL) codes. The study evaluates decode-and-forward (DF) relaying combined with selection combining (SC) and maximum ratio combining (MRC) at the receiver. The primary objective is to maximize fair throughput in a downlink scenario through joint user pairing and resource allocation. In each pair, the user with the stronger channel serves as a relay for the weaker user, with optimal power and blocklength allocation aimed at achieving max-min throughput. The analysis begins with a single pair to explore optimal resource allocation, introducing a suboptimal algorithm that converges to a near-optimal solution. Subsequently, the problem is generalized, proposing a suboptimal C-NOMA-based user pairing strategy. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed C-NOMA scheme, under both SC and MRC, significantly enhances fair throughput compared to traditional NOMA and OMA. Furthermore, the study finds that the C-NOMA pairing scheme outperforms Hybrid NOMA/OMA in terms of average throughput, although there is a slight reduction in the fairness index.

We examine symmetric second-order differential operators with real coefficients where the associated differential equation belongs to the limit circle case at infinity. Our objective is to develop a theory for the self-adjoint realizations of these operators, drawing parallels to the theory of Jacobi operators. We define a novel concept, the quasiresolvent of the maximal operator, and leverage it to derive an explicit formula for the resolvents of all self-adjoint realizations. Specifically, this approach provides a straightforward representation for the Cauchy-Stieltjes transforms of the spectral measures, serving a function analogous to the classical Nevanlinna formula within Jacobi operator theory.

We examine a category of cosmological fluids exhibiting characteristics similar to crystalline solids subjected to isotropic deformations. Our study utilizes a modified log-corrected power-law equation of state incorporating bulk viscosity, a framework known as logotropic fluids that accounts for the late-time acceleration of the universe. To refine our understanding of the fluid's evolution, we introduce a coupling between this log-corrected power-law fluid and dark matter, investigating various interaction scenarios. By solving the resulting system of equations for the interacting modified log-power-law fluid and dark matter, we derive expressions for both the log-corrected power-law energy density and the dark matter energy density. Finally, we conduct a comparative analysis against a model featuring a nonviscous log-corrected power-law fluid that lacks interaction with dark matter.

This paper extends the Lumer-Phillips theorem to the setting of two-parameter $C_0$-semigroups of contractions by characterizing their infinitesimal generators. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions regarding the resolvent behavior of operator pairs that determine whether they generate such a $C_0$-semigroup of contractions.

Nodal points and lines within electron energy band dispersions are defined by high degeneracy occurring at specific corners or lines in the Brillouin zone (BZ). These structures also appear in the dispersion of itinerant electrons within magnetically ordered materials, which are described by anti-unitary symmetry groups known as magnetic space groups. This study presents a comprehensive catalog of magnetic space groups capable of hosting symmetry-protected nodal-point and nodal-line band structures for spin-1/2 fermions, where such degeneracies are ensured by irreducible projective representations (IPReps) of the little co-groups. The analysis focuses exclusively on magnetic space groups whose magnetic point group includes the space-time inversion operation $\tilde T=\mathcal IT$ (the combination of spatial inversion $\mathcal I$ and time reversal $T$), ensuring at least double degeneracy for energy bands at any point in the BZ. For these groups, we derive invariants to classify projective representation classes and compute all inequivalent IPReps for each class. We subsequently identify the groups and representation classes that support high-dimensional IPReps ($d\geq$4). Finally, we list the relevant magnetic space groups along with their high-symmetry points and lines possessing little co-groups with $d\geq$4 IPReps, including the associated factor systems, and discuss potential candidate materials.

There is growing acknowledgment of the value in modeling how viruses spread spatially within tissues. A prevalent method involves multicellular models, where individual cells act as distinct spatial regions interacting with a continuous virus density field. Traditionally, simulations of these models rely on discretizing the viral surface, with the level of granularity adjusted based on diffusion rates and other factors. However, the consequences of this discretization choice on system behavior have remained unexplored. This study demonstrates that when viral diffusion rates are low, the resolution of the viral surface discretization can significantly alter model outcomes, affecting both quantitative results and qualitative dynamics. We provide a detailed analysis of the underlying mechanisms and outline the constraints involved in designing and implementing multicellular viral dynamics models across various parameter settings.

Unlike Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) methods, Sequence-To-Sequence (S2S) models for Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) often struggle with errors like skipped or repeated words, particularly at sequence endings. To integrate the strengths of both approaches, we introduce the use of CTC-Prefix-Scores during S2S decoding. Specifically, our beam search penalizes paths deemed invalid by the CTC confidence matrix. Our architecture features a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) as the visual backbone, bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) cells as the encoder, and a Transformer decoder enhanced with mutual attention layers. CTC confidences are calculated on the encoder, while the Transformer handles character-level S2S decoding. We tested this configuration on three datasets: IAM, Rimes, and StAZH. On the IAM dataset, our model achieved a competitive Character Error Rate (CER) of 2.95% after pretraining on synthetic data and incorporating a character-based language model for modern English. Compared to other state-of-the-art solutions, our model uses approximately 10–20 times fewer parameters. You can access our shared code on GitHub at: https://github.com/Planet-AI-GmbH/tfaip-hybrid-ctc-s2s.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA) represents a robust mathematical framework that remains underutilized in theoretical chemistry. This study illustrates how TDA offers novel perspectives on the topological characteristics of electron densities and reduced density gradients, specifically by examining relativistic influences on the bonding within the Au4-S-C6H4-S'-Au'4 molecule. While prior investigations using the Quantum Theory of Atoms-In-Molecules [Anderson et al., Chem. Eur. J. 25, 2538, 2019] suggested that relativistic effects created non-covalent interactions between gold and hydrogen atoms based on emerging topological features, our findings indicate these features lack significance due to their low persistence values, which diminish as basis set size increases. Additional analysis of the reduced density gradient further validates the absence of relativity-induced non-covalent interactions in this species. We contend that TDA ought to be incorporated into electronic structure analysis methodologies and serve as a foundation for developing new topology-driven approaches.

Feynman integrals within quantum field theory yield special functions and numbers characterized by transcendental weight. This paper introduces a technique to project a dimensionally-regularised Feynman integral—such as one contributing to a scattering amplitude—onto its maximal weight component. Leveraging insights into the singularity structure of space-time loop integrands, this approach complements standard generalised unitarity methods. We detail the methodology and demonstrate its viability through a proof-of-principle application to the two-loop $gg \to H$ scattering amplitude in the heavy top-quark mass limit, encompassing both planar and non-planar integrals. Additionally, we address potential future applications and examine subtleties concerning evanescent integrand terms.

In Statistical Learning, the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension represents a crucial combinatorial characteristic of classifiers. To our knowledge, no theoretical findings currently address the VC dimension of edited nearest-neighbour (1NN) classifiers utilizing a reference set of fixed size. Existing related results are dispersed throughout the literature with their implications remaining implicit. We gather pertinent findings to establish explicit lower and upper bounds for the VC dimension of 1NN classifiers with a prototype set of fixed size. Additionally, we examine the consequences of these bounds regarding the training set size required to learn such a classifier to a specified accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a novel lower bound for the two-dimensional case, derived from a new geometrical argument.

Code reviews serve as a highly effective technique for assessing defects in source code, yet current methodologies often rely heavily on experts or suffer from inefficiencies. This paper enhances the speed and memory efficiency of our existing code review tool, CRUSO, by introducing a new approach that estimates code defectiveness based on the scores of similar code fragments found across various StackOverflow posts. The primary contributions include i) SOpostsDB, a dataset comprising PVA vectors and StackOverflow post details, and ii) CRUSO-P, a code review assistant leveraging PVA models trained on this database. For any input code, CRUSO-P classifies it as "Likely to be defective," "Unlikely to be defective," or "Unpredictable." The development of CRUSO-P involved processing over 3 million StackOverflow posts and more than 188,200 GitHub source files, with support for C, C#, Java, JavaScript, and Python. In performance tests, CRUSO-P surpassed the original CRUSO with a 97.82% reduction in response time and a 99.15% decrease in storage requirements. Furthermore, when evaluated on C programming code, CRUSO-P achieved a peak mean accuracy of 99.6%, representing a 5.6% improvement over previous methods.

To gain deeper insights into how humans navigate during multi-stop shopping trips, we examine motion data from grocery store shoppers. Our findings reveal patterns consistent with a noisy decision-making process regarding the sequence of item retrieval, effectively breaking down a shopping trip into a series of discrete choices about the next item to grab. Specifically, our analysis demonstrates that the probability of swapping the order of any two items is monotonically linked to the entropy of that pair-wise ordering task. Leveraging these insights, we introduce a noisy distance estimation model designed to predict retrieval sequences based on a shopping list. We confirm that this model accurately replicates the observed entropy law both theoretically and practically when simulating real shopping lists. Consequently, our approach offers immediate utility for enhancing simulations of human navigation in retail environments and beyond.

Probabilistic logic programming constitutes a core component of statistical relational artificial intelligence, integrating logical and probabilistic methods to handle uncertainty within relational domains. Nevertheless, the behavior of these statistical representations varies complexly with domain size, making the scaling of inference and learning for large domains a persistent hurdle. Recently, links have been established between domain size dependency, lifted inference, and learning from sampled subpopulations. Researchers have increasingly scrutinized the asymptotic behavior of these representations, focusing on projectivity as the most stringent form of domain-size independence, where query marginals remain entirely unaffected by domain size.

This contribution demonstrates that every probabilistic logic program adhering to the distribution semantics is asymptotically equivalent to an acyclic probabilistic logic program composed solely of determinate clauses over probabilistic facts. Consequently, we establish that any probabilistic logic program inducing a projective family of distributions is universally equivalent to a program within this specific fragment, and we examine the implications for the projective families expressible by such programs.

To enable the application of classical finite model theory results, we propose the abstract distribution semantics, defined as an arbitrary logical theory over probabilistic facts. This framework bridges the gap to the distribution semantics inherent in probabilistic logic programming. In this representation, determinate logic programs map to quantifier-free theories, thereby making asymptotic quantifier elimination results applicable to probabilistic logic programming. This manuscript is currently under review for publication in TPLP.

Reducing query execution time is critically dependent on optimizing execution plans, an area that has been extensively researched for relational databases over the last few decades. Recently, the Resource Description Framework (RDF) has gained prominence for web data publishing, leading to the emergence of federations that combine diverse data models, including RDF and relational databases. A specific instance of these federations is the Semantic Data Lake, where each data source retains its native model while being semantically annotated via ontologies or controlled vocabularies. However, current state-of-the-art query engines for federated processing over Semantic Data Lakes predominantly utilize optimization strategies designed specifically for RDF. This paper introduces heuristic-guided query optimization techniques that consider the physical design of a Data Lake. Implemented on top of Ontario, a SPARQL engine for Semantic Data Lakes, these source-specific heuristics enable the generation of more efficient execution plans by leveraging knowledge regarding relational indexes and normalization. Our results demonstrate that incorporating the physical design of the Data Lake into optimization heuristics significantly accelerates query processing.

Nonreciprocal radiation describes electromagnetic emission where a structure exhibits distinct responses depending on the direction of the incident wave. Contemporary wireless telecommunication requires versatile devices capable of full-duplex nonreciprocal wave processing and amplification, particularly within reflective modes. To achieve this unique and adaptable functionality, we introduce an architecture integrating a series of cascaded radiating patches with nonreciprocal phase shifters, creating an original and efficient apparatus for full-duplex reflective beamsteering. This ultrathin reflective metasurface offers directive and varied radiation beams, significant wave amplification, and steerable beams simply by adjusting the bias of the gradient active nonmagnetic nonreciprocal phase shifters, all while remaining immune to unwanted time harmonics. By delivering these capabilities in the reflective state, the metasurface serves as a notable device for efficient, controllable, and programmable wave engineering.

Quantum theory and relativity propose distinct views of time. To investigate the tension between these frameworks, we examine a quantum adaptation of the standard light-clock used to demonstrate relativistic time dilation. This semiclassical approach integrates features from both theories. We demonstrate that for Gaussian states of the light field, the clock's time remains independent of the initial state. We then compute the difference between two such clocks, where one remains stationary within a gravitational field while the other falls a specific distance. Comparing our findings to those of pointlike observers in general relativity and classical light-clocks reveals both quantitative and qualitative divergences. We observe that the quantum contribution to the clock discrepancy grows with increasing gravitational field strength, leading to a minimum resolution for the falling clock that is separate from the quantum uncertainty inherent in its measurement.

This work presents a general approach to building nonlocal recursion operators for the symmetries of partial differential equations. To illustrate this, the cotangent equation associated with the 3D rdDym equation, $u_{yt} = u_xu_{xy} - u_yu_{xx}$, is examined, where a pair of mutually inverse operators is derived. Furthermore, the discussion provides a rigorous criterion for verifying the hereditary property.

High-level frameworks are essential for the rapid prototyping and efficient development of complex algorithms in spiking neural networks. While such tools have recently appeared for conventional computers, programming neuromorphic hardware remains difficult, often necessitating low-level coding with specific knowledge of the chip's architecture. PeleNet addresses this by simplifying reservoir computing for Intel's Loihi hardware. Built on the NxSDK and written in Python, the framework handles weight matrices, parameters, and probes. Notably, it enables the automatic and efficient distribution of networks across multiple cores and chips, allowing users to bypass technical complexities and focus on experimentation.

We introduce a novel family of quivers to uniformly compute the cluster modular groups for both affine and doubly extended type cluster algebras. Leveraging this unified framework, we establish a natural finite quotient of the cluster complex associated with each such algebra. This construction enables the definition of affine and doubly extended generalized associahedra and facilitates the enumeration of their facets.

Deriving symbolic data from signals is a vibrant research area with extensive applications, particularly within Musical Information Retrieval. This intricate task, which intersects with pitch extraction and instrument identification, has inspired many methods relying on sophisticated signal processing algorithms. Nevertheless, these methods are often specific to certain physical attributes like pitch or octave, failing to support arbitrary vocabularies or general annotations. Furthermore, they are unidirectional: they can convert audio to symbols but cannot reverse the process to generate signals from symbols. This paper introduces a bijective framework for translating between signals and symbols by framing the challenge as a density estimation problem over both domains, treating them as correlated random variables. We employ two distinct variational auto-encoders, one for each domain, whose internal representations are aligned via an additive constraint. This setup enables both models to learn and generate independently while supporting bidirectional inference. We evaluate our approach on pitch, octave, and dynamics, marking a crucial advancement for music transcription and label-constrained audio synthesis. Beyond its versatility, the system is computationally efficient during training and generation, offering various creative applications discussed at the article's conclusion.

Contemporary caches frequently need to manage data volumes that surpass available memory, making hybrid DRAM/SSD solutions increasingly common. In these setups, minimizing writes to the secondary cache is crucial alongside maintaining high hit ratios, as this mitigates write amplification and SSD wear. This paper introduces BiDiFilter, an innovative multilevel caching strategy that regulates item promotion and demotion via a frequency sketch filter. Additionally, it divides the upper cache tier into two distinct zones to ensure both the most recent and most frequently accessed data remain near the user. Through extensive testing on real-world traces against prior multilevel policies, we demonstrate that our approach reduces write operations by approximately tenfold in nearly all scenarios and frequently cuts latency by up to 20%.

This study investigates the continuum states of three particles with short-range interactions subjected to a deformed external one-body field. The analysis employs an equivalent $d$-method, utilizing a non-integer dimension $d$ within a spherical framework that incorporates a dimension-dependent angular momentum barrier. Special attention is given to dimensions near the critical value $d=d_E$ (ranging between two and three), where two-body energies vanish and the Efimov effect becomes possible. A schematic, realistic three-body spherical model based on square wells at long distances is constructed for this dimensional regime, yielding analytic formulas for wave functions, scattering lengths, phase shifts, and elastic scattering cross sections. These procedures and findings are universal, applicable to all short-range potentials and large scattering lengths. The properties and validity of these expressions are examined using the simplest system of three identical bosons. The derived formulas are especially valuable at very low energies, where comprehensive numerical computations are often impractical; however, in energy ranges where numerical methods are feasible, strong agreement with the analytic results is observed. These model predictions can be verified through scattering experiments involving three particles in an equivalent deformed oscillator potential. Notably, for $d<3$, all cross sections approach zero in the zero-energy limit, following a specific power law dependent on $d$.

We examined the spatial distribution of Meissner shielding currents within a flat superconducting ring and provided a quantitative description of magnetic avalanche (dendrite) penetration. By employing a recursive method, we determined the external magnetic field ($H_{ext}$) at which a perforating avalanche, crossing the ring's rim, occurs. The study comprehensively characterizes the staircase relationship between the mean trapped field ($\langle H \rangle$) and the external field ($H_{ext}$). The slope of this staircase is identified as a universal function dependent on the ring's geometry, specifically the ratio of rim width to diameter. Furthermore, the heat generated by each successive penetrating dendrite increases linearly. The presence of flux pinning alters this staircase behavior, resulting in reduced step sizes. Our theoretical findings align well with experimental observations.

Large-scale diffusion-based generative models have revolutionized high-resolution image synthesis conditioned on text. These models iteratively transform random noise into images based on textual prompts. However, we observe a qualitative shift in their synthesis behavior over time: early stages heavily depend on the text prompt to ensure alignment, whereas later stages largely disregard the text conditioning. This indicates that using shared model parameters for the entire generation process is suboptimal. Consequently, unlike prior approaches, we propose training an ensemble of specialized text-to-image diffusion models, each tailored to specific synthesis stages. To ensure training efficiency, we first train a single model and then partition it into stage-specific variants. Our proposed ensemble, named eDiff-I, achieves superior text alignment and outperforms previous large-scale models on standard benchmarks while maintaining inference computation costs and high visual quality. Furthermore, we train the model to leverage diverse conditioning embeddings, including T5 text, CLIP text, and CLIP image embeddings. These different embeddings exhibit distinct behaviors; notably, CLIP image embeddings facilitate an intuitive method for transferring the style of a reference image to the generated output. Finally, we introduce a technique that empowers eDiff-I with a "paint-with-words" capability, allowing users to select specific words in the input text and paint them on a canvas to precisely control the resulting image. The project is accessible at https://deepimagination.cc/eDiff-I/.

We extend the definition of spherical knotoids by incorporating a framing, mirroring the approach used for framed knots, and introduce an additional modification involving a secondary "coframing" to create "biframed" knotoids. We identify topological spaces where ambient isotopy classes correspond bijectively to framed and biframed knotoids, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these concepts enable the generalization of quantum knot invariants to the knotoid context, resulting in the development of general Reshetikhin-Turaev type biframed knotoid invariants.

We propose the notions of symmetry-protected sign problems and symmetry-protected magic to investigate the complexity inherent in symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases of matter. Specifically, a state is defined as possessing a symmetry-protected sign problem or symmetry-protected magic if it cannot be converted into a non-negative real wave function or a stabilizer state, respectively, by any finite-depth quantum circuit utilizing symmetric gates. We demonstrate that states within specific SPT phases exhibit these characteristics due to anomalous symmetry actions at their boundaries. For instance, one-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ SPT states, such as the cluster state, display a symmetry-protected sign problem, whereas two-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ SPT states, like the Levin-Gu state, exhibit symmetry-protected magic. Additionally, we discuss the connection between the symmetry-protected sign problem and the computational wire property found in one-dimensional SPT states. Finally, an appendix presents explicit decorated domain wall models of SPT phases, which may hold independent interest.

Topological insulators represent a category of electronic materials characterized by robust edge states that resist perturbations and disorder. This principle has been effectively translated into photonics through the creation of topologically nontrivial waveguides and lasers. Nevertheless, investigating topological properties within specific photonic setups is currently restricted to static, fabricated samples, lacking the ability to reconfigure the structure dynamically. In this work, we present an all-optical implementation of the orbital Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model within a microcavity exciton-polariton system, where cavity photons hybridize with excitons in a GaAs quantum well. By tailoring nonresonant laser excitation, we generate a zigzag potential for exciton polaritons, enabling the direct measurement of the eigenspectrum and topological edge states within a polariton lattice under nonlinear bosonic condensation. Moreover, leveraging the tunability of this optically induced lattice, we adjust intersite tunneling to achieve a transition from a topological phase to a trivial state. These findings pave the path for investigating topological phase transitions on demand in fully reconfigurable hybrid photonic systems, eliminating the need for complex sample engineering.

Over the past few years, Deep Learning (DL) models have gained prominence for their ability to tackle intricate learning challenges, proving effective across various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications like part-of-speech tagging and machine translation. Disease Named Entity Recognition (Disease-NER), a vital task focused on identifying disease-related entities within text, is the subject of this paper, which introduces and evaluates a DL approach leveraging dictionary data. The model was tested on the NCBI disease corpus and the BC5CDR dataset, utilizing word embeddings derived from both general and biomedical domains to represent inputs. Furthermore, the study assesses two distinct Segment Representation schemes: IOB2 and IOBES. The findings demonstrate that integrating dictionary information, pre-trained and character-based word embeddings, and Conditional Random Fields (CRF) with global scoring significantly enhances the performance of the Disease-NER system.

The characteristics of the disk/jet interaction in quiescent low-mass X-ray binaries (BH LMXBs) containing black holes remain largely unexplored. This study reports the inaugural quasi-simultaneous radio and X-ray observations of MAXI J1348$-$630, a BH LMXB exhibiting a hybrid disk/jet relationship that varies with accretion rate, during its quiescent phase. Utilizing the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Australia Telescope Compact Array, we conducted deep observations. MAXI J1348$-$630 was detected in quiescence for the first time with an X-ray luminosity of $L_{\rm X} = (7.5 \pm 2.9) \times 10^{30} (D/2.2 \ {\rm kpc})^2$ erg s$^{-1}$, representing one of the faintest X-ray luminosities recorded for a quiescent BH LMXB, which may suggest a short orbital period. Additionally, the source was detected in radio with a luminosity of $L_{\rm R} = (4.3 \pm 0.9) \times 10^{26} (D/2.2 \ {\rm kpc})^2$ erg s$^{-1}$. These detections enable us to position MAXI J1348$-$630 on the radio/X-ray diagram during quiescence, revealing that it aligns with the standard (radio-loud) track. This finding robustly confirms that sources with hybrid correlations adhere to the standard track at low luminosities and extend into quiescence, thereby enhancing our understanding of the disk/jet connection in BH LMXBs.

Assuming the critical Allard condition—where an integral 2-varifold $V=\underline{v}(\Sigma,\theta_{\ge 1})$ in the unit ball $B_1$, passing through the original point, exhibits an area $\mu_V(B_1)$ nearly equal to that of a unit disk and possesses a generalized mean curvature with sufficiently small $L^2$ norm—we establish that $\Sigma$ is locally bi-Lipschitz homeomorphic to a flat disk in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Decoherence illustrates how the openness of quantum systems—specifically their interaction with the environment—dampens obvious quantum effects. Einselection explains the emergence of preferred quasi-classical pointer states. Quantum Darwinism extends this framework by proposing that the information gathered by the monitoring environment (which drives decoherence) is proliferated across many copies within the environment, rendering it accessible to observers. This mechanism for the emergence of an objective classical reality from a quantum foundation relies on the indirect acquisition of information: observers utilize the environment as a communication channel rather than performing direct measurements. Consequently, the systems of interest remain unperturbed and can persist unaffected by the information observers extract about them.

Massive vector fields appear across various domains of particle physics, serving as mediators for weak interactions, candidates for dark matter, or as effective representations of photons within a plasma. In this study, we examine vector fields with self-interactions by substituting the standard mass term in the Proca equation with a general potential. We demonstrate that this seemingly innocuous alteration inevitably generates ghost instabilities, identical in nature to those recently found in vector-tensor modified gravity theories, albeit within this simpler, minimally coupled framework. Although it has been proposed that nonperturbative dynamics might evade such instabilities, we refute this by simulating a self-interacting Proca field on a Kerr background. Our results show that while the system initially behaves like a massive field, it succumbs to instabilities in finite time once self-interactions become dominant, driven by superradiant effects. These findings have significant consequences for the formation of condensates involving massive, self-interacting vector bosons, the viability of spin-one bosenovae, vector dark matter models, and effective descriptions of interacting photons in plasmas.

A primary obstacle in gaze-based interaction is distinguishing intentional computer commands from normal eye movements, a phenomenon known as the "Midas touch." This paper introduces EyeTAP (Eye tracking point-and-select by Targeted Acoustic Pulse), a hands-free method designed for point-and-select operations. Evaluation through two user studies, each comprising two experiments with 33 participants, demonstrates that EyeTAP remains robust against ambient audio noise up to 70 dB. Compared to voice recognition, EyeTAP yields faster movement and task completion times while reducing cognitive workload. Additionally, it exhibits a lower error rate than the dwell-time method in ribbon-shaped interface tests. These attributes make EyeTAP suitable for individuals with physical disabilities who cannot perform standard movements. Furthermore, its lack of specific user interface design requirements allows for easy integration into existing systems with minimal changes, positioning EyeTAP as a viable solution to the Midas touch problem.

Let $\ell$ denote a prime number and $F$ represent a global function field of characteristic $\ell$. This work investigates the solutions to Catalan's equation $X^m - Y^n = 1$ within $F$, demonstrating that under specific additional constraints, no non-constant solutions exist in $F$.

We present a novel and natural stationary set preserving forcing, denoted as $\mathbb{P}^{c-c}({\lambda},{\mu})$, which, assuming ${\rm NS}$ is precipitous along with the existence of $H_{\theta}^{\#}$ for a sufficiently large regular ${\theta}$, elevates the second uniform indiscernible $u_2$ past a specified ordinal ${\lambda}$. This forcing exhibits the same capability as those constructed in references [9] and [2]. A primary instrument in our approach involves specific natural open two-player games of independent significance, namely the capturing games $G^{cap}(X)$ and the catching-capturing games $G^{c-c}(X)$. Specifically, these games facilitate the identification of a distinct family of countable elementary submodels $M \prec H_{\theta}$, which serve as side conditions within $\mathbb{P}^{c-c}$, thereby enabling robust control over the forcing mechanism.

We introduce a novel semi-supervised relational VAE model designed to harmonize disentanglement with low-complexity relation modeling across various symbolic characteristics. Our study evaluates how relation-decoder intricacy and latent space organization influence both inductive and transductive transfer learning. The findings reveal a nuanced landscape: imposing structure on semi-supervised representations significantly enhances zero-shot transductive transfer, yet it may offer fewer benefits or even hinder inductive transfer capabilities.

This study investigates whether the accretion of a brown dwarf (BD) by a solar-type main-sequence (MS) star significantly impacts the star's internal structure and surface lithium (Li) abundance. We conducted 3D Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics simulations of BDs with masses of 0.01 and 0.019 solar masses being engulfed by a 1 solar mass MS star of solar composition, examining three distinct scenarios: head-on, grazing, and merger collisions. Our analysis details the interaction dynamics, assessing how the collision type and BD mass influence the ultimate fate of both the sub-stellar object and the host star, specifically regarding system mass loss, angular momentum transfer, and surface Li enrichment. Our results indicate that in most cases, the majority of the BD mass is diluted within the denser regions of the MS star, with only the merger scenario retaining a substantial fraction (40%) of BD material in the outer layers. We observed a marked increase in the host star's surface rotational velocity post-interaction, ranging from 25 km/s for grazing collisions to 50 km/s for mergers. Furthermore, the engulfment caused significant mass loss from the system (1e-4 to 1e-3 solar masses), potentially forming a circumstellar disk-like structure in merger cases. Assuming the convective envelope depth and mass content of the host star remain unchanged, head-on and grazing collisions resulted in only minor changes to surface Li abundance. In contrast, mergers produced substantial Li enhancements by factors of 20 to 30, dependent on the BD mass. These observational signatures may be detectable in host stars if they persist over sufficient time.

The European Spallation Source (ESS) represents the next generation of spallation-based neutron facilities globally. Research at ESS aims to uncover and advance new materials across diverse sectors such as manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, aerospace, engine technology, plastics, energy, telecommunications, transportation, IT, and biotechnology. By delivering an unprecedented neutron flux, the ESS requires its selected reflectometers, ESTIA and FREIA, to meet demanding specifications. Local incident peak rates may reach $10^5$~Hz/mm$^2$. To enable new scientific inquiries, these instruments must achieve a spatial resolution under 1 mm and a scattering level of $10^{-4}$ (peak-to-tail ratio), a performance standard roughly two orders of magnitude superior to current state-of-the-art detectors. The primary objective of this study is to quantify how various detector components contribute to neutron scattering and to demonstrate that the effects on the ESS Multi-Blade detector remain within the required limits. Consequently, multiple configurations of geometry and beam parameters are examined, with particular emphasis on the cathode coating and the thickness of the detector window.

Kemeny's constant represents the expected duration for a random walk to travel from any given vertex $x$ to a randomly selected vertex $y$ within a connected graph, serving as an indicator of the graph's connectivity. While the impact of adding or removing edges on this constant remains largely unclear, this work derives its directional derivative for various graph families by drawing inspiration from the directional derivative of the normalized Laplacian. Furthermore, the study establishes sharp bounds for the directional derivative of an eigenvalue associated with the normalized Laplacian, alongside bounds for the directional derivative of Kemeny's constant itself.

This study evaluates the efficacy of a combined ozone (O3) and ultraviolet (UV) light reactor for the gas-phase oxidation of flue gas pollutants, specifically focusing on sulfur dioxide (SO2) removal. Numerical simulations of a continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR) were conducted, integrating chemical kinetics with the modeling of radiation intensity distribution generated by a UV lamp using five distinct radiation models. The research included a grid convergence study and an optimization of the number of discrete point light sources required for certain radiation models. Additionally, the influence of residence time and reactor dimensions on SO2 removal efficiency was investigated. Overall, the results indicate that an O3-UV reactor operating under optimized conditions is a viable approach for sustainable air cleaning applications.

At a foundational level, the majority of physical equations exhibit time reversibility. This paper introduces a computational integrator designed to maintain this characteristic at the discrete level. Consequently, our simulations can execute forward and backward, retracing the exact same path down to the bit. We accomplish this by deploying theoretically reversible integrators through a combination of fixed and floating-point arithmetic. The primary application of this integrator is to efficiently execute the reverse step in the adjoint method for optimization. Furthermore, it offers utility in differential simulations and machine learning tasks such as backpropagation.

This paper introduces a time-varying parameter (TVP) vector error correction model (VECM) featuring heteroscedastic disturbances, integrating a suite of econometric techniques for dynamic model specification into an automated process. We utilize continuous global-local shrinkage priors to drive the parameter space toward sparsity. Subsequently, we refine the cointegration relationships, autoregressive coefficients, and covariance matrix by minimizing Lasso-type loss functions to achieve genuinely sparse estimates. This two-step methodology mitigates overfitting and lowers parameter estimation uncertainty while delivering time-varying estimates for the count of cointegrating relationships. When applied to European electricity price modeling, our proposed econometric framework demonstrates improved forecast performance compared to a range of established benchmark models.

Accurate determinations of exoplanet radii are essential for comprehending their origins and characteristics. Transit-based radius measurements have now achieved a level of precision necessitating the consideration of stellar surface phenomena. While the impact of starspots is well-documented, our understanding of facular effects remains limited, especially regarding M-dwarfs. Inhomogeneous facular distributions on the stellar surface can introduce significant complications. By applying the eclipse mapping technique to GJ1214 using Ca II H&K lines as indicators, we investigated the spatial distribution of these faculae. To quantify this distribution's uniformity, we defined the Inhomogeneity Factor (IHF), which equals 0% for a homogeneous spread, yields positive values when plage regions align with the planet's transit path, and produces negative values when they are situated outside it. For GJ1214, we calculated an IHF of 7.7 +12.0 -7.7%, indicating a relatively small inhomogeneity. We further evaluate the implications of this finding for the upcoming PLATO and ARIEL space missions.

Drawing inspiration from natural language embeddings, we introduce ASTROMER, a transformer-based model designed to generate light curve representations. Pre-trained in a self-supervised fashion, ASTROMER requires no human-labeled data and was trained on millions of R-band light sequences to optimize its weights. These learned representations are highly adaptable to new surveys through re-training on additional sources. ASTROMER's primary strength lies in its ability to extract light curve embeddings that significantly enhance the performance of downstream models, such as classifiers and regressors. For instance, we utilized ASTROMER embeddings to train two neural classifiers using labeled variable stars from MACHO, OGLE-III, and ATLAS. Across all experiments, classifiers leveraging ASTROMER embeddings surpassed a baseline recurrent neural network trained directly on light curves, particularly when labeled data was scarce. Additionally, employing ASTROMER embeddings reduces computational requirements while delivering state-of-the-art results. We have also released a Python library containing all functionalities discussed, with the main code and pre-trained weights accessible at https://github.com/astromer-science.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) typically model data within a low-dimensional latent space, conventionally assumed to be Euclidean. This standard assumption usually justifies using a standard Gaussian prior for continuous latent variables. However, recent studies indicate that this prior limits model capacity and results in inferior performance. We argue that the Euclidean assumption is the primary cause of this limitation. To address this, we adopt a Riemannian structure for the latent space, offering a more rigorous geometric interpretation of latent codes, and substitute the Gaussian prior with a Riemannian Brownian motion prior. We also introduce an efficient inference method that avoids dependence on the unknown normalizing constant of this prior. Finally, we show that this approach substantially boosts model capacity with just one extra scalar parameter.

In the realm of quantum computing, geometric phase-gates are gaining prominence due to their inherent robustness against disturbances. While the Berry phase, achieved through adiabatic cyclic evolution, facilitates geometric transformations, executing as many quantum gates as possible within the coherence timescale is hindered by systematic errors. This work introduces an accelerated adiabatic quantum gate leveraging the Berry phase, transitionless driving, and dynamical decoupling. This approach successfully balances high fidelity with high speed, even under control noise or imperfections. Furthermore, we optimize the dynamical-decoupling sequence in the time domain, specifically addressing a common Gaussian noise spectrum that follows an inversely quadratic power-law.

This paper examines the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to the two-dimensional commissioning challenge in high-bay storage, a problem that can be framed as an instance of the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP). We evaluate the mlrose library, which offers a TSP optimizer utilizing various heuristic techniques, with a specific focus on its Genetic Algorithm and Hill Climbing methods. We introduce modifications to both algorithms that enhance computed tour lengths by moderately leveraging the inherent structure of the TSP. Notably, these proposed improvements possess a general nature and are not restricted solely to TSP applications.

This paper introduces screen almost semi-invariant (SASI) lightlike submanifolds within indefinite Kaehler manifolds. We derive the necessary and sufficient conditions under which the induced connection becomes a metric connection on these SASI-lightlike submanifolds and provide a concrete example. Furthermore, we establish specific conditions for the integrability of distributions and explore various characterizations.

For any integer $n \geq 2$, we investigate the optimal lower bound $v_{n, n-i}$ for the canonical volume and the optimal upper bound $r_{n,n-i}$ for the canonical stability index of minimal projective $n$-folds of general type that admit canonical fibrations by $i$-folds, where $i \in \{0, 1\}$. While experts already know the cases for $i = 0$ as $v_{n,n}=2$ and $r_{n, n}=n+2$, this article establishes that $v_{n,n-1}=\frac{6}{2n+(n \bmod 3)}$ and $r_{n,n-1}=\frac{1}{3}(5n+ 3 + (n \bmod 3))$. Furthermore, the methodology employed extends to all canonical dimensions $n-i$.

Inspired by the effectiveness of serial dictatorship in social choice theory, we investigate its application to diverse combinatorial optimization challenges. We propose an abstract framework where agents act sequentially according to a specified order. Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. We derive tight bounds on the social welfare achievable with a polynomial number of queries. While these general bounds indicate only a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal welfare, significantly better approximations emerge when valuations originate from specific combinatorial structures. For instance, when valuations correspond to bipartite matchings, directed graph arborescences, or Boolean satisfiability, simple query-efficient algorithms achieve a $2$-approximation. We also address truthfulness concerns, demonstrating how certain algorithms can be made truthful via VCG-like payments. Furthermore, we define and analyze the "price of serial dictatorship," a metric offering an optimistic assessment of the solution quality produced by action sequences in combinatorial optimization.

This research investigates the application of quantum optimal control to execute unitary operations on the $I=9/2$ nuclear spin of \textsuperscript{87}Sr, which resides in a $d=10$ dimensional (qudecimal) Hilbert space. By combining nuclear spin-resonance with a tensor AC-Stark shift and modulating only the phase of a radio-frequency magnetic field, the system is rendered fully controllable. Alkaline earth atoms like \textsuperscript{87}Sr are particularly advantageous for this purpose because of their narrow intercombination lines and substantial hyperfine splitting in excited states. Our numerical analysis examines the quantum speed limit, optimal control parameters, and the fidelity of arbitrary state preparation and complete SU(10) maps, accounting for decoherence caused by optical pumping from the light-shifting laser. Additionally, we explore robust control strategies to reduce dephasing arising from inhomogeneities in the light shift. Results indicate that with an rf-Rabi frequency of $\Omega_\text{rf}$ and 0.5% light-shift inhomogeneity, one can prepare an arbitrary Haar-random state within $T={4.5}\pi/\Omega_\text{rf}$ achieving an average fidelity of $\langle \mathcal{F}_\psi \rangle =0.9992$, and implement an arbitrary Haar-random SU(10) map within $T=24\pi/\Omega_\text{rf}$ with an average fidelity of $\langle \mathcal{F}_U \rangle = 0.9923$.

Although extensive research has examined the discriminatory characteristics of the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's (HOLC) home mortgage risk maps from the late 1930s, few studies have investigated whether these maps still accurately depict racial residential boundaries in their respective cities eighty years later. To fill this gap, this study employs Markov Chain Monte Carlo—a method previously unused in this field—to randomly generate numerous plausible alternative mortgage security maps. The racial evenness of both the original HOLC maps and the generated alternatives is then evaluated using Shannon's entropy. The results demonstrate that the HOLC maps significantly correspond to the precise racial residential boundaries existing in eleven U.S. cities as of 2010. Furthermore, the methodology presented is highly modular and reproducible, facilitating future research to measure various outcome statistics, locations, and time periods.

The study of $\alpha$-clustering structures remains a critical area of research in light nuclei. To distinguish between initial non-clustered and clustered configurations—specifically Woods-Saxon distributions and three-$\alpha$ triangular (or four-$\alpha$ tetrahedral) arrangements in $^{12}$C and $^{16}$O—a Bayesian convolutional neural network (BCNN) was employed. This classifier was trained using data from heavy-ion collisions simulated via the AMPT multi-phase transport model, utilizing charged pion azimuthal angles and transverse momentum distributions as input features. Based on multiple events, the model achieved an overall classification accuracy of $95\%$ for $^{12}$C/$^{16}$O collisions with $^{197}$Au at $\sqrt{S_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. By carefully constructing training samples, deviations in predictions for mixed datasets containing varying proportions of both configurations were kept within $5\%$. Furthermore, applying a straightforward confidence threshold enhanced prediction performance on these mixed sets. These findings suggest that machine-learning techniques hold significant promise for analyzing real experimental data and addressing other challenges in heavy-ion collision physics.

Graph codes are vital to photonic quantum technologies due to their robust protection against qubit loss, a primary source of noise. In this work, we introduce techniques for analyzing and optimizing measurement-based resilience to both qubit loss and computational errors across arbitrary graph codes. Applying these methods, we have identified optimized codes ranging from up to 12 qubits to asymptotically large modular architectures. These advancements offer substantial advantages for diverse photonic applications, as demonstrated by new all-photonic quantum repeater states for communication and high-threshold fusion-based protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

This research concentrates on optimizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for graphic processing units (GPUs) through a direct sparse algorithm, aiming to enhance their efficiency. While the Nvidia cuDnn library currently represents the most effective implementation of deep learning (DL) algorithms for GPUs, and weight pruning combined with quantization remains a primary technique for improving CNN performance, specific trade-offs exist. Pruning is generally categorized into structural and non-structural types; the former facilitates easier acceleration across various hardware but often struggles to match the high sparsity and accuracy levels achievable with the latter. Non-structural pruning, particularly when accompanied by retraining, can yield weight tensors with sparsity rates exceeding 90% in certain deep CNN architectures. This article introduces a novel pruning algorithm capable of attaining high sparsity without compromising accuracy. Subsequently, both linear and non-linear quantization methods are adapted to further minimize computational time and memory footprint. Building upon a previously published work regarding efficient pruning techniques, this paper presents real-world models featuring high sparsity and reduced precision that demonstrate superior performance compared to the CuDnn library.

Neuroscience datasets frequently exhibit hierarchical structures, typically involving neuronal activity recorded across multiple animals, trials, and cells. Consequently, the data points are interdependent, yet conventional statistical methods like Student's t-test often erroneously treat them as independent. Although the hierarchical bootstrap is a well-established and effective solution for analyzing such nested data within the broader statistical community, it remains underutilized in neuroscience despite the prevalence of these datasets. This paper demonstrates the approach's intuitive utility using simulated neural data, revealing that traditional tests can inflate false positive rates to over 45% even when the Type-I error is set at 5%. While aggregating data across non-independent levels can mitigate this issue, it significantly diminishes statistical power. In contrast, the hierarchical bootstrap, when applied sequentially through the hierarchy's levels, maintains the Type-I error rate within the desired bounds while preserving greater statistical power than summarization techniques. The study concludes by validating the method's effectiveness through two real-world applications: analyzing singing behavior in male Bengalese finches (*Lonchura striata var. domestica*) and quantifying optogenetically controlled behavioral changes in flies (*Drosophila melanogaster*).

We present the concept of residual intersections for modules and demonstrate their existence. Our findings reveal that modules with a projective dimension of one possess Cohen-Macaulay residual intersections, thereby fulfilling the associated Artin-Nagata property. Furthermore, we derive a formula for the core of orientable modules under specific homological constraints, which generalizes earlier work by Corso, Polini, and Ulrich regarding the cores of projective one modules. In conclusion, we illustrate various classes of modules that meet our stated assumptions.

This paper reviews general results concerning convex bodies to establish an exact, closed-form parametric equation for the boundary of the Minkowski sum of $k$ ellipsoids within $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Unlike prior approaches that relied on iterative algorithms—where each ellipsoid was sequentially added to an approximate sum of preceding ones—this work introduces direct, one-shot formulas capable of incorporating $k$ ellipsoids simultaneously without intermediate approximations. This advancement reveals a novel degree of freedom within the family of ellipsoidal bounds for such geometric sums. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of these tools by computing the reachable set of a discrete-time dynamical system.

General hyperplane sections of a Fano threefold $Y$ with index 2 and Picard rank 1 yield del Pezzo surfaces, whose Picard group corresponds to a root system. By associating objects within the Kuznetsov component of $Y$ to these roots, we examine their moduli spaces. This investigation employs the stability condition developed by Bayer, Lahoz, Macr\`i, and Stellari, alongside the Abel--Jacobi map. We identify a subvariety within the moduli space that is isomorphic to $Y$ itself, and as a consequence, we establish a (refined) categorical Torelli theorem for general quartic double solids.

The skin effect, originally observed experimentally in one dimension, refers to the physical phenomenon where numerous eigenstates of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian become localized at the boundaries of an open chain. Extending this concept to two and higher dimensions, we present a theorem stating that the skin effect occurs if and only if the periodic-boundary spectrum of the Hamiltonian occupies a finite area within the complex plane. This theorem demonstrates the universality of the effect, as the specified condition is met by nearly all generic non-Hermitian Hamiltonians and remains consistent with all spatial symmetries, unlike in one-dimensional systems. We introduce two novel forms of the skin effect in higher dimensions: the corner-skin effect, where all eigenstates localize at a single corner of the system, and the geometry-dependent-skin effect, where skin modes vanish for specific shapes but emerge in generic polygons. A direct consequence of our theorem is that any non-Hermitian system featuring exceptional points (or lines) in two (or three) dimensions will exhibit the skin effect, rendering this phenomenon experimentally accessible in photonic crystals, Weyl semimetals, and Kondo insulators.

Microservices Architecture (MSA) has garnered substantial interest within the software sector, yet empirical data regarding its design, monitoring, and testing remains scarce. This study seeks to deepen the understanding of industry practices concerning these areas. Employing a mixed-methods approach involving 106 surveys and 6 interviews with practitioners, the research yielded several key insights: (1) the prevailing strategy for decomposing applications combines domain-driven design with business capabilities; (2) more than half of the respondents utilize both architecture evaluation and implementation phases during design; (3) API gateways and Backend for Frontend patterns are the most frequently adopted MSA patterns; (4) monitoring relies heavily on resource usage and load balancing metrics, alongside log management and exception tracking; and (5) unit and end-to-end testing represent the dominant testing strategies. However, the inherent complexity of microservices systems presents significant challenges for design, monitoring, and testing, currently lacking dedicated solutions. Consequently, further research is required to address complexity at the design stage, manage security within these systems, and develop specialized solutions for monitoring and testing challenges.

This study examines the 2-relay multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) Gaussian diamond channel. We demonstrate that a multihopping decode-and-forward protocol with multiple access (MDF-MAC) attains rates within a constant gap of capacity whenever the channel parameter $\Delta$ is positive. Furthermore, we specify the transmit covariance matrices required for each relay during the multiple-access phase of the MDF-MAC protocol. Consistent with prior work on the single-antenna 2-relay Gaussian diamond channel, the parameter $\Delta$ is defined as the difference between the product of the capacities of the source-to-relay links and the product of the capacities of the relay-to-destination links.

This research investigates transfer learning within the framework of functional linear regression, aiming to enhance the estimation and prediction of a target model by utilizing information from associated source models. The connection between source and target models is quantified using the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) norm, which allows the nature of transferred information to be understood through the structural characteristics of these spaces. Two distinct transfer learning algorithms are introduced: the first transfers data from known source tasks, while the second aggregates results from the first algorithm to ensure robustness in scenarios where prior knowledge of useful sources is unavailable. Additionally, we derive optimal convergence rates for the prediction risk of the target model, thereby providing mathematical proof of the statistical benefits of transfer learning. The theoretical examination of this risk also offers insights into the determinants of transfer learning success, specifically identifying the conditions that render source tasks beneficial for the target task. Finally, the efficacy of the proposed algorithms is validated through extensive experiments on synthetic data and a real-world application involving financial data.

We examine a population of two-dimensional oscillators featuring random couplings to investigate their collective behaviors. The coupling strength is randomly quenched, taking one of two values: positive or negative, while the oscillators' spatial movement depends on both phase and position state variables. Our findings indicate that the system undergoes a phase transition from an incoherent state to full synchronization at a specific ratio of positive couplings to the total. This threshold was determined numerically and analytically predicted through linear stability analysis of the synchronized state. Additionally, we discovered that random quenched couplings induce long-term state patterns similar to those seen with constant coupling strengths; specifically, oscillators migrate to locations where the quenched couplings effectively behave as if they were annealed. Furthermore, systems with mixed randomness in quenched couplings exhibit combined deformed patterns that can be understood as the sum of individual annealed averages.

Driven by the rapid advancement of internet technologies and new tools, the volume of online sports videos is growing at an unprecedented rate. To automate the editing and highlight generation of these videos, a critical step involves accurately identifying and pinpointing events within long, untrimmed footage. This technical report introduces a two-stage framework designed to detect both the occurrence and timing of events in soccer broadcasts. Specifically, we fine-tune various action recognition models on soccer datasets to derive high-level semantic features and develop a transformer-based temporal detection module to localize target events. This method achieved state-of-the-art results in both action spotting and replay grounding tasks within the SoccerNet-v2 Challenge, hosted under the CVPR 2021 ActivityNet workshop. Our soccer-specific embedding features are available at https://github.com/baidu-research/vidpress-sports, and we aim to foster further research in soccer video understanding by sharing these resources with the broader community.

We demonstrate that the cross sections for a wide variety of resonant inelastic processes involving excitation exchange—such as spin-exchange, F\"orster resonant, or angular momentum exchange—follow an atypical near-threshold scaling of $E^{\Delta m_{12}}$. In this expression, $E$ represents the collision energy, and $\Delta m_{12}=m_1'+m_2'-m_1-m_2$ denotes the change in the sum of the angular momentum projections of the colliding species ($i=1,\,2$), where $m_i$ and $m_i'$ are the initial and final values. Specifically, for $\Delta m_{12}=0$ transitions, the inelastic cross sections exhibit an unconventional $E^0$ scaling akin to elastic cross sections, with rates that vanish as $T^{\Delta m_{12}+1/2}$. For collisions dominated by even partial waves, such as those between identical bosons in the same internal state, the scaling adjusts to $\sigma_\text{inel}\propto E^{\Delta m_{12} +1}$ when $\Delta m_{12}$ is odd. We provide precise quantum scattering calculations that exemplify these modified threshold laws for resonant spin exchange in ultracold Rb+Rb and O$_2$+O$_2$ collisions. Our findings indicate that the threshold scaling of collision cross sections depends solely on the energetics of the underlying process (whether resonant or exothermic) and not on whether the internal states of the colliding particles change during the collision.

Video super-resolution (VSR) involves reconstructing high-resolution video from its low-resolution counterpart, a field that has garnered significant recent interest. This paper introduces a novel dual dense connection network designed to produce high-quality super-resolution outcomes. We creatively partition input frames into a reference frame, a pre-temporal group, and a post-temporal group to capture information from distinct time periods. This grouping strategy ensures accurate temporal representation without disrupting the sequence of time information. Additionally, we develop a new loss function that improves the model's convergence. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms other advanced models on the Vid4 and SPMCS-11 datasets.

We describe the identification of a new skyrmion phase in the multiferroic insulator Cu2OSeO3 that exists at magnetic fields lower than the equilibrium skyrmion pocket. This state can only be achieved by driving the sample out of equilibrium using near-infrared (NIR) femtosecond laser pulses and cannot be attained through standard field cooling methods. Based on the pronounced wavelength dependence of the photo-creation process and spin dynamics simulations, we conclude that the magnetoelastic effect is the primary mechanism responsible for this phenomenon. This effect causes a transient alteration of magnetic interactions, thereby extending the equilibrium skyrmion pocket to lower magnetic fields. Upon formation, the skyrmions reorganize and maintain stability for extended periods, lasting up to several minutes. These findings hold significant relevance for developing high-efficiency, non-volatile data storage technologies utilizing magnetic skyrmions.

This study employs a relativistic configuration-interaction (CI) framework within a stabilization method to determine the autoionization resonance structure of heliumlike ions. In this approach, the ion is restricted by an impenetrable spherical cavity, where the cavity's dimensions dictate the radial space accessible to electron wavefunctions and electron-electron interactions. By adjusting the cavity size, the resonance position and width are calculated. The method's validity is verified against benchmark data for helium atom resonances. Furthermore, the approach is utilized to analyze the resonance structure of heliumlike uranium ions, necessitating a relativistic treatment. In the strong-confinement regime, this technique offers a means to simulate atomic and ionic properties under extreme pressure conditions. Additionally, a brief discussion highlights an exemplary application of the method for determining the structure of ions situated within a dense plasma environment.

Active Position Estimation (APE) involves localizing one or more targets via one or more sensing platforms. This capability is essential for search and rescue operations, wildlife monitoring, source term estimation, and collaborative mobile robotics. The success of APE relies on factors such as the cooperation level, quantity, degrees of freedom, and data quality of the sensing platforms. APE control laws facilitate active sensing by adhering to either pure-exploitative or pure-explorative criteria: the former reduces uncertainty in position estimation, while the latter directs the platform toward task completion. In this paper, we outline the core components of APE to systematically categorize and critically evaluate existing literature. Furthermore, we introduce a reference framework as a formal method for classifying APE-related solutions. Overall, this survey examines key challenges and outlines future research directions in autonomous perception systems for localization, while also encouraging the advancement of robust active sensing methods for search and tracking applications.

Item response theory (IRT) represents a non-linear generative probabilistic framework designed to identify, measure, and compare latent traits of individuals against their peers within a specific population. Traditional multidimensional IRT methods necessitate a pre-existing factorization of test items, typically achieved through linear exploratory factor analysis, which renders IRT a post-hoc model. We propose bypassing this initial factor analysis step by employing a sparsity-promoting horseshoe prior to conduct factorization directly within the IRT model, ensuring that all training occurs in a single, self-consistent iteration. As a hierarchical Bayesian model, we adapt the WAIC metric for dimensionality selection. Given that IRT models are analogous to probabilistic autoencoders, integrating the generative IRT model with a Bayesian neural network creates a probabilistic autoencoder that yields a scoring algorithm consistent with the interpretable Bayesian framework. While the black-box nature of neural network scoring is advantageous for certain IRT applications, this manuscript demonstrates in-IRT factorization and evaluates various scoring strategies.

Building upon successful data augmentation strategies for sentence and sentence-pair NLP tasks, this study introduces and evaluates similar techniques for named entity recognition, a problem typically framed as token-level sequence labeling. Experimental results on biomedical (i2b2-2010) and materials science (MaSciP) datasets demonstrate that these straightforward augmentation methods enhance the performance of both recurrent and transformer-based architectures, particularly when training data is limited.

This paper introduces TauRieL, a method designed for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) due to its extensive relevance in both theoretical and applied fields. TauRieL employs an actor-critic architecture using standard feedforward networks to derive a policy update vector, $v$. This vector is then leveraged to refine the state transition matrix, which subsequently generates the policy. Additionally, this matrix enables the solver to initialize using precomputed solutions, such as nearest neighbors. Within an online learning framework, TauRieL integrates training and search processes to produce near-optimal results within seconds. The actor-critic neural networks accept raw 2-D inputs to maintain a compact model size, accepting the trade-off of excluding distributed representations found in wider embedding architectures. As a result, TauRieL generates TSP solutions two orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art offline methods, with a maximum performance degradation of 6.1%.

Transfer learning has proven vital and effective across various applications by moving knowledge from related but distinct source domains to a target domain. Online Transfer Learning (OTL) presents a more difficult challenge, as target data arrive sequentially. Most existing OTL approaches directly merge source and target classifiers by dynamically adjusting weights assigned to each. However, these methods largely overlook the reduction of distribution discrepancies between domains. This paper introduces a new OTL framework designed to discover an optimal feature representation that simultaneously minimizes both marginal and conditional distribution discrepancies in an online setting. We address OTL with multiple source domains, utilizing the Hedge strategy to exploit knowledge from these sources. We also examine the theoretical properties of our algorithm and establish an upper bound on the mistake rate.
