Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

Non-randomized treatment effect models are extensively utilized across various disciplines, particularly within social sciences such as political science, psychology, and psychometrics. These models address scenarios where treatment assignment depends on individual characteristics—such as merit-based scholarships or blood-pressure-guided antihypertensive therapy—rather than randomization, which is typical in randomized clinical trials. Existing popular methods for estimating these effects often suffer from suboptimal convergence rates, specifically slower than $\sqrt{n}$. This paper introduces SCENTS (Score Explained Non-Randomized Treatment Systems), a novel model and estimation method capable of achieving $\sqrt{n}$ convergence rates even under general forms of confounding, provided the treatment assignment score can be explained by specific individual features. We demonstrate that the proposed estimator is asymptotically normal and semi-parametrically efficient under normal error assumptions. Furthermore, we extend this framework to high-dimensional covariates by proposing a $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal estimator utilizing a debiasing technique. Our high-dimensional analysis can also be applied to partial linear models involving noisy variables associated with the non-linear component, where noise may be correlated with linear variables. Finally, we apply our method to two real-world datasets, comparing outcomes with prior approaches, and conclude with a discussion on potential future extensions.

Analyzing time series with irregular sampling intervals presents a significant challenge, demanding methodologies that accommodate both gradual and sudden shifts in sampling frequency without creating new biases. Edit distance serves as a robust metric for quantifying differences between time series segments of varying lengths by calculating the transformation cost between them. We demonstrate that these transformation costs typically correlate non-trivially with local sampling rates; consequently, when sampling resolution fluctuates dramatically, this relationship hinders unbiased comparisons across different time periods. We investigate how this phenomenon affects recurrence quantification analysis (RQA), a framework particularly effective for detecting regime shifts in nonlinear time series. To address the resulting bias in RQA metrics, we introduce a constrained randomization method. This strategy relies on generating novel surrogates—specifically sampling rate constrained (SRC) surrogates—that include both new time series data and corresponding time axis adjustments. We validate the efficacy of this approach using both a synthetic dataset and an irregularly sampled speleothem record from Niue island in the central tropical Pacific. Applying this correction scheme reveals a false transition caused exclusively by an abrupt change in sampling rate and simultaneously exposes intervals of diminished seasonal rainfall predictability linked to intensified ENSO and tropical cyclone activity.

Self-supervised methods for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) in semantic segmentation often struggle with generating and selecting high-quality pseudo-labels. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the scale-invariance inherent in semantic segmentation models for self-supervised domain adaptation. Our method relies on the premise that semantic labels should remain consistent regardless of object or scene size within a given context. We demonstrate that this invariance is frequently violated in target domain images, creating an opportunity to transfer labels between patches of varying scales. Specifically, we observe that scaling up target domain images leads to higher entropy in model outputs compared to original-sized images; consequently, we extract scale-invariant examples from the most confident target images. To ensure reliability, we implement a dynamic, class-specific entropy thresholding mechanism to filter out poor pseudo-labels. Additionally, we integrate focal loss to mitigate class imbalance issues common in self-supervised learning. Extensive experiments show that our scale-invariant labeling strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art self-supervised domain adaptation techniques. Notably, using a VGG16-FCN8 baseline, we achieve performance gains of 1.3% and 3.8% for the GTA5-to-Cityscapes and SYNTHIA-to-Cityscapes tasks, respectively.

We present a novel methodology for simulating the evolution of particle clouds surrounding small celestial bodies, such as asteroids and comets. This process necessitates handling diverse temporal and spatial scales with high efficiency, precision, and modularity. To enhance the accuracy and computational speed of these simulations, we developed an N-body modeling package extending the widely used orbital dynamics integrator, Rebound. Currently available as a standalone variant, our code is designed to provide a comprehensive analysis of individual particle trajectories, external forces, and interactions at a resolution often missed by other methods. The resulting tool, Rebound Ejecta Dynamics (RED), is a Python-based implementation requiring no additional dependencies. It integrates key mechanisms influencing particle behavior in low-gravity settings, facilitating straightforward simulations of combined effects. These capabilities include variable size and velocity distributions, solar radiation pressure, ellipsoidal gravitational potentials, binary or triple asteroid systems, and particle-particle interactions. This paper demonstrates RED's capabilities through an application to a small asteroid binary system modeled after the Didymos/Dimorphos pair, the target of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test mission.

This study examines the precursors to superconductivity in BaPb$_{0.75}$Bi$_{0.25}$O$_3$ by employing temperature-dependent resistivity, x-ray diffraction, and photoemission spectroscopy. The material demonstrates superconductivity at approximately 11 K ($T_C$). Our synthesis method is notably more straightforward than those previously reported in literature. Within the temperature range of 10 K to 25 K, which lies above $T_C$, we observed an increase in both orthorhombic and tetragonal strain. Well-screened features detected in the Bi and Pb 4$f_{7/2}$ core levels confirm the sample's metallic character. At 300 K, the compound shows finite intensity at the Fermi level; however, this intensity diminishes as the temperature drops, evolving into a pseudogap. The temperature-dependent spectral density of states indicates a disordered metallic state. Additionally, band structure calculations demonstrate that Pb doping induces a structural transition that closes the band gap at the Fermi level.

This study reports a measurement of the forward-backward asymmetry for pairs of oppositely charged leptons (dimuons and dielectrons) generated via the Drell-Yan process in proton-proton collisions. The analysis utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$ acquired by the CMS detector at the LHC, operating at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The asymmetry is evaluated as a function of lepton pair mass for values exceeding 170 GeV and is contrasted with standard model forecasts. An inclusive measurement covering both decay channels and the entire mass spectrum results in an asymmetry of 0.612 $\pm$ 0.005 (stat) $\pm$ 0.007 (syst). Additionally, to test lepton flavor universality, the difference between dimuon and dielectron asymmetries is determined. No statistically significant discrepancies from standard model predictions are found. These results are employed to constrain the existence of additional gauge bosons; specifically, for a Z' boson within the sequential standard model, the observed (expected) 95% confidence level lower bound on its mass is established at 4.4 (3.7) TeV.

This study presents a search for charged Higgs bosons ($H^\pm$) decaying into top and bottom quarks within all-jet final states. Utilizing 2016 proton-proton collision data from the CMS detector at the LHC, with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV and an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, no significant excess over the predicted background was detected. Model-independent 95% confidence level upper limits on the product of the $H^\pm$ production cross-section and branching ratio were established for two production scenarios. In the associated production mode with a top quark, limits ranging from 21.3 down to 0.007 pb were derived for $H^\pm$ masses between 0.2 and 3 TeV. When combined with results from a search in leptonic final states, these constraints were tightened to 9.25 to 0.005 pb. Additionally, the complementary $s$-channel production of $H^\pm$ was examined for masses from 0.8 to 3 TeV, yielding upper limits of 4.5 to 0.023 pb. These findings are discussed in the context of various minimal supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model.

Achieving the fourth post-Newtonian (4PN) gravitational-wave generation from compact binaries requires expressing the "canonical" multipole moments of the source via "source" and "gauge" moments. While canonical moments characterize wave propagation beyond the source's near zone, the latter two sets encode explicit details of the matter distribution. These descriptions—whether using two sets of canonical moments or six sets of source and gauge moments—are isometric. Consequently, we have constructed the non-linear diffeomorphism connecting them up to the third post-Minkowskian order and provided the specific expression for the 4PN-order canonical mass-type quadrupole moment. This calculation represents one of the final missing components needed to determine the 4PN gravitational-wave phasing of compact binary systems.

Knowledge discovery in databases seeks to extract actionable insights for decision-making. Over the last decade, high utility itemset mining has become a major research area, focusing on identifying patterns within databases that satisfy specific utility objectives. Although numerous algorithms exist for mining high utility items, most suffer from significant execution times and high memory usage. This paper introduces R-Miner, a new algorithm built upon a novel data structure known as residue maps, which directly stores item utility information to facilitate the mining process. Experimental evaluations comparing R-Miner against benchmark algorithms demonstrate that it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in performance.

Minimal Lorentzian surfaces embedded in $\mathbb{R}^4_2$ with a two-dimensional first normal space and satisfying the condition $K^2-\varkappa^2 >0$ (where $K$ is the Gauss curvature and $\varkappa$ is the normal curvature) are designated as minimal Lorentzian surfaces of general type. These surfaces possess canonical parameters; relative to these parameters, they are uniquely determined up to an isometry of $\mathbb{R}^4_2$ by the curvatures $K$ and $\varkappa$, which obey a system of two natural partial differential equations. This paper investigates minimal Lorentzian surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4_2$ and derives a Weierstrass representation in terms of isothermal parameters for any minimal surface having a two-dimensional first normal space. Furthermore, we establish a Weierstrass representation using canonical parameters for any minimal Lorentzian surface of general type and explicitly resolve the associated system of natural PDEs, expressing every solution via four real functions of a single variable.

Adversarial training (AT) serves as a prominent defense strategy for enhancing the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks. Fundamentally, AT relies on min-max optimization (MMO), where the defender minimizes the worst-case training loss against adversarial examples generated by an attacker. However, traditional MMO approaches hinder the scalability of AT. Consequently, methods like Fast-AT (Wong et al., 2020) and similar recent algorithms aim to simplify MMO by substituting the maximization step with a single gradient sign-based attack generation process. While Fast-AT is straightforward to implement, it lacks theoretical foundations and suffers from unsatisfactory empirical results due to robust catastrophic overfitting when facing strong adversaries. This paper re-examines Fast-AT through the lens of bi-level optimization (BLO). We demonstrate that standard Fast-AT is essentially a stochastic gradient approach solving a linearized BLO problem with a sign operation; however, the discrete nature of this sign operation obscures the algorithm's performance dynamics. Drawing inspiration from BLO, we propose and analyze a new family of robust training algorithms called Fast Bi-level AT (Fast-BAT). This method effectively defends against sign-based projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks without relying on gradient sign techniques or explicit robust regularization. Empirical results across various models and datasets show that our approach delivers significant robustness gains over baseline methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/OPTML-Group/Fast-BAT.

Tabular data forms the foundation for many high-impact machine learning applications, ranging from genomics and healthcare to fraud detection. While practitioners traditionally rely on classical techniques like random forests and gradient boosting, recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated performance comparable to these established methods. We introduce a hybrid deep learning framework for tabular data called SAINT, which incorporates attention mechanisms across both rows and columns alongside an improved embedding strategy. Additionally, we propose a novel contrastive self-supervised pre-training technique designed for scenarios with limited labels. On average across various benchmark tasks, SAINT consistently surpasses prior deep learning models and even exceeds the performance of leading gradient boosting libraries, including XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, embedded system designers must efficiently simulate these platforms to facilitate early architecture exploration. Running artificial neural networks on simulated neuromorphic systems via virtual platforms (VPs) is computationally intensive, yet it remains a critical benchmarking step for comparing architectural alternatives. Consequently, leveraging the multicore capabilities of the VP's host hardware is essential for accelerating simulations. This paper introduces a parallel SystemC-based VP tailored for RISC-V multicore platforms that integrate multiple computing-in-memory neuromorphic accelerators. Furthermore, it examines various VP segmentation architectures for integrating these accelerators and demonstrates their performance gains through speedup simulations relative to traditional sequential SystemC execution.

State space models (SSM) are extensively utilized for analyzing and visualizing extensive sequential data. While Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) remains a favored particle-based approach for sampling latent states from intractable posteriors, its performance is heavily dependent on the selection of the proposal distribution. Recently, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) has demonstrated significant success across various practical applications. This paper introduces an HMC-augmented SMC (HSMC) framework designed for the inference and learning of nonlinear SSMs, eliminating the need to manually learn proposals and substantially reducing model complexity. Leveraging the measure-preserving property of HMC, particles generated directly via the transition function can approximate the latent state posterior with arbitrary precision. To better accommodate the local geometry of the latent space, HMC is executed on a Riemannian manifold defined by a positive definite metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed HSMC method enhances SSM implementations based on both Gaussian Processes (GP) and Neural Networks (NN).

The geometry of latent space offers a robust and comprehensive framework for engaging with latent variables in deep generative models. However, current theoretical approaches depend on the decoder being a Gaussian distribution, leveraging its straightforward reparameterization to view the generation process as a random projection of a deterministic manifold. This method fails when applied to decoders that lack such easy reparameterization. In this work, we propose utilizing the Fisher-Rao metric from the space of decoder distributions as a reference metric, which is then pulled back into the latent space. We demonstrate that this allows for the creation of meaningful latent geometries across a broad spectrum of decoder distributions where prior theory was inapplicable, thereby enabling "black box" latent geometries.

The DES-CMASS sample (DMASS) is constructed to optimally merge weak lensing data from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) with redshift-space distortion (RSD) measurements from the BOSS CMASS galaxy sample. This study demonstrates the viability of using DMASS as a proxy for BOSS CMASS within a joint analysis framework for modified gravity. We employ the angular clustering of DMASS galaxies, cosmic shear from DES METACALIBRATION sources, and their cross-correlation as primary data vectors. By jointly fitting these data alongside RSD measurements from BOSS CMASS and Planck data, we derive constraints on modified gravity parameters of $\mu_0 = -0.37^{+0.47}_{-0.45}$ and $\Sigma_0 = 0.078^{+0.078}_{-0.082}$. No significant deviation from General Relativity is detected. Our DMASS-based constraints on modified gravity are 29% tighter for $\mu_0$ and 21% tighter for $\Sigma_0$ compared to those obtained using the DES Year 1 redMaGiC sample with identical external datasets, and they remain comparable to published DES Year 1 results despite utilizing fewer external inputs. This enhanced precision stems primarily from the shared and more tightly constrained galaxy bias parameter in both CMASS and DMASS, which effectively breaks degeneracies with other cosmological parameters. This methodology for optimally integrating photometric and spectroscopic surveys by employing a photometric equivalent to a spectroscopic sample is applicable to future surveys with limited overlap, such as DESI and LSST.

This study investigates the constraints of basic methods in Music Information Retrieval (MIR) for piano transcription by performing a comprehensive analysis of neural network-driven, frame-level transcription. We systematically evaluate various common input representations to identify those best suited for neural architectures. Leveraging recent advancements in training methodologies, novel regularizers, and hyper-parameter optimization, we demonstrate that a straightforward bottom-up, frame-wise approach can produce a piano transcriber that surpasses the current state-of-the-art on the publicly available MAPS dataset, all without relying on complex post-processing. Consequently, we introduce this simplified method as a new baseline for the dataset, providing a foundation for future research to build upon and enhance.

Federated learning represents a distributed learning paradigm, primarily challenged by the non-i.i.d. nature of data across participating clients. This paper extends federated learning to a multi-model environment where multiple unrelated models are trained concurrently. In this setting, each client trains one of $M$ available models at any given time, while the server maintains an averaged version of each model based on client computations. We introduce several strategies for assigning learning tasks to clients over time. The first strategy adapts the well-known FedAvg algorithm to multi-model learning by distributing models to clients in an i.i.d. stochastic fashion. Furthermore, we propose two novel client selection policies for the multi-model federated setting that base their decisions on the current local losses of each client-model pair. We evaluate these policies using both synthetic and real-world data tasks and analyze their performance. Our key finding is that the proposed multi-model policies achieve performance that is equal to or superior to single-model training via FedAvg.

This paper investigates degenerate Bell numbers and polynomials, which represent degenerate forms of the classical Bell numbers and polynomials. We establish several new identities and properties concerning these numbers and polynomials that are linked to degenerate Stirling numbers of both kinds.

Detecting the global 21-cm signal from the Cosmic Dawn (CD) and Epoch of Reionization (EoR) is severely hindered by foreground emissions that are 2 to 5 orders of magnitude stronger than the target signal. A robust approach to isolating the signal involves fitting a physics-driven parametric forward model to the data using Bayesian methods, provided there is adequate knowledge of the instrument and sky. Previous work established that dividing the sky into $N$ regions and scaling a base map with distinct uniform spectral indices per region can generate a sufficiently accurate foreground model. Using the Radio Experiment for the Analysis of Cosmic Hydrogen (REACH) as a reference instrument, we demonstrate that uncorrected amplitude errors in the low-frequency radio maps used for the base model prevent the recovery of the 21-cm signal; specifically, the resulting bias scales with both the error amplitude and the correlation length of the base-map errors. We propose an improved foreground model that addresses these measurement uncertainties by fitting for a monopole offset and a collection of spatially varying scale factors representing the ratio of true to modeled sky temperatures, with the number of factors selected via Bayesian evidence comparison. Our simulations using a smooth conical log spiral antenna show that this flexible model can handle various foreground error scenarios, enabling the unbiased detection of the sky-averaged 21-cm signal.

An analysis of exam scores from an introductory economics course at a Taiwanese business school from 2008 to 2019 yielded three key findings. First, there was no statistically significant gender gap in performance. Second, a student's major was significantly correlated with their scores, suggesting it reflects pre-college academic ability. Third, these exam scores served as strong indicators of future academic success.

This work investigates traversing vector flows $v$ on smooth, compact manifolds $X$ possessing a boundary. Given a compact manifold $\hat X$ with a traversing vector field $\hat v$ that is {\sf convex} relative to $\partial\hat X$, we examine submersions or embeddings $\alpha: X \to \hat X$ where $\dim X = \dim \hat X$, and the image of the boundary $\alpha(\partial X)$ avoids pre-selected tangency patterns $\Theta$ with respect to $\hat v$-trajectories. Specifically, for every $\hat v$-trajectory $\hat\gamma$, we constrain the number of intersections with $\alpha(\partial X)$ to be an even integer $d$. We define $(\hat X, \hat v)$ as a {\sf convex pseudo-envelop or envelop} for the pair $(X, v)$, where the vector field $v = \alpha^\dagger(\hat v)$ represents the transfer of $\hat v$ to $X$ via $\alpha$.

For a fixed $(\hat X, \hat v)$, we establish an equivalence relation among convex pseudo-envelops or envelops $\alpha: (X, v) \to (\hat X, \hat v)$, termed a {\sf quasitopy}. This concept bridges the gap between bordisms of pseudo-envelops and their pseudo-isotopies. In analyzing the quasitopies $\mathcal{QT}_d(Y, \mathbf c\Theta)$, the spaces $\mathcal P_d^{\mathbf c\Theta}$ of real univariate polynomials of degree $d$ with real divisors avoiding the combinatorial types of the closed poset $\Theta$ assume the role traditionally held by Grassmannians.

We calculate the quasitopies of convex envelops avoiding $\Theta$-tangency patterns using homotopy-theoretical terms involving $(\hat X, \hat v)$ and $\mathcal P_d^{\mathbf c\Theta}$. Furthermore, we define characteristic classes for pseudo-envelops and demonstrate that these classes remain invariant under quasitopy equivalence. Finally, we prove that the quasitopies $\mathcal{QT}_d(Y, \mathbf c\Theta)$ frequently stabilize as $d$ approaches infinity.

The generalization of machine learning models relies intricately on the interplay between data, the model architecture, and the learning algorithm. We investigate typical behaviors by analyzing train and test performance alongside the generalization gap, defined as the mean difference between them across various dataset samples. We derive a formula for this gap as a function of the covariance between the model parameter distribution and training loss, and another expression for average test performance, demonstrating that test generalization depends solely on the data-averaged parameter distribution and data-averaged loss. Furthermore, we establish that for a broad class of parameter distributions, a modified generalization gap remains non-negative. By focusing specifically on parameter distributions generated by stochastic gradient descent (SGD), incorporating certain approximations and modeling assumptions, we predict how the generalization gap and performance metrics vary with respect to SGD noise. Finally, we validate these predictions empirically on the Cifar10 classification task using a ResNet architecture.

Sampling from the stationary distribution of a Markov chain is a widely applied problem across numerous disciplines, where the duration required for convergence is termed the classical mixing time. This article explores analog quantum algorithms designed to address this issue. We present an algorithm that, given a Markov chain, enables sampling from its stationary distribution in a time proportional to the sum of the square roots of the classical mixing time and the classical hitting time. This approach utilizes interpolated quantum walks, relying on Hamiltonian evolution alongside von Neumann measurements.

Additionally, there is a distinct concept of quantum mixing: sampling from the time-averaged limiting distribution of quantum walks. In this context, quantum mixing time is defined as the duration needed to approximate this limiting distribution. We previously established an upper bound for this time on Erdős-Renyi random graphs [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 050501 (2020)] and now expand upon those results. We offer an intuitive explanation of the advanced random matrix theory tools employed, specifically highlighting the necessity of macroscopic, mesoscopic, and microscopic eigenvalue statistics. Furthermore, we present numerical simulations that validate our analytical conclusions and generalize this mixing framework from simple graphs to any ergodic, reversible Markov chain.

Previous research on the out-of-domain performance of Question Answering (QA) systems has predominantly concentrated on broad domains, such as news or Wikipedia, often overlooking the significance of subdomains defined by the internal features of QA datasets. This paper broadens the definition of "out-of-domain" by partitioning QA examples into distinct subdomains based on internal attributes like question type, text length, and answer position. We subsequently evaluate the performance of QA systems trained on data from these varied subdomains. The experimental findings reveal that system performance can drop substantially when training and testing data originate from different subdomains. These outcomes challenge the generalizability of current QA systems across multiple subdomains and highlight the necessity of addressing biases stemming from the internal characteristics of QA datasets.

Text is commonly represented using Unicode formats, specifically UTF-8 and UTF-16. UTF-8 has gained widespread popularity, particularly in web technologies like XML, HTML, JSON, and programming languages such as Rust, Go, Swift, and Ruby. Conversely, UTF-16 remains the standard in Java, .NET environments, and operating systems like Windows. Software often requires converting text between these two formats. Although modern disks offer bandwidths exceeding 5 GiB/s, traditional transcoding methods for non-ASCII text operate at only a fraction of a gigabyte per second. We demonstrate that Unicode text can be validated and transcoded at gigabyte-per-second speeds on current x64 and ARM systems without compromising safety. Our open-source library achieves performance up to ten times faster than the widely used ICU library for non-ASCII strings and is even more efficient for ASCII strings.

This study tackles the challenge of calibrating sensor array gains and phases blindly using ambient noise, aiming to simplify the setup by eliminating complex procedures. We demonstrate that calculating the sample covariance matrix within a diffuse field allows for the recovery of complex gains. Our approach formulates a non-convex least-squares problem utilizing both sample and model covariances. To solve this, we employ low-rank matrix approximation, leading to the development of two efficient proximal algorithms. The first algorithm addresses a convex-relaxed version of the problem to ensure a global minimum, while the second directly tackles the original non-convex formulation. Through numerical and experimental evaluations across various sensing configurations, we assess the algorithms' performance. Results indicate that calibration efficiency is heavily influenced by measurement correlation, with higher accuracy achieved when the field is spatially over-sampled.

The emergence of two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals magnets has created new avenues for investigating magnetism in quantum materials and developing advanced spintronic technologies. In this study, we employ a multiscale modeling framework integrating first-principles calculations with a Heisenberg model parameterized via ab-initio methods to reveal strong magnetoelastic coupling in a free-standing CrTe$_2$ monolayer. We show that distinct crystal phases of CrTe$_2$ induce non-collinear magnetism driven by magnetic frustration and the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). Furthermore, using atomistic spin dynamics, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the intricate magnetic characteristics of this 2D material under various structural distortions resembling charge density waves.

The development of the quantum internet suggests that intricate network topologies could facilitate efficient communication and improve resilience against failures. Nevertheless, concerns regarding complexity persist, including potential constraints on end-to-end transmission capacity. These challenges necessitate model systems capable of investigating the feasibility and impact of complex structures on quantum communication protocols. This study introduces a theoretical framework for complex quantum communication networks based on a lattice of spins, where entangled spin clusters within interacting quantum systems function as links between specific spin regions. Specifically, we demonstrate that ground state Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger clusters in the two-dimensional random transverse Ising model can serve as these communication links, yielding quantum networks with complexity akin to the classical internet. Consequently, our work offers an accessible generative model to advance research into the characteristics of the emerging quantum internet.

A finite subset of Euclidean space is defined as an $s$-distance set if it contains exactly $s$ distinct Euclidean distances. The primary challenge in this field is determining the maximum size of such sets, a problem that has been resolved only for small values of $s$ and low dimensions. Specifically, for $s=2$, Lison\v{e}k (1997) provided a classification for all dimensions up to $7$, utilizing computer assistance alongside graph representation theory. This paper extends that theoretical framework to pseudo-Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{p,q}$, introducing the concept of an $s$-indefinite-distance set based on the norm $|| \boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y} ||=(x_1-y_1)^2 +\cdots +(x_p -y_p)^2-(x_{p+1}-y_{p+1})^2-\cdots -(x_{p+q}-y_{p+q})^2$ rather than the standard Euclidean distance. We develop a representation theory for symmetric matrices within the context of $s$-indefinite-distance sets, which either encompasses or enhances existing results for Euclidean $s$-distance sets when $s$ is large. Furthermore, we classify the largest possible $2$-indefinite-distance sets for small dimensions.

We created two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis methods to identify wide separation binary asteroids within wide-field surveys. These techniques were subsequently applied to Pan-STARRS1 images of main belt asteroids ranging from 4 to 60 km in diameter. Since Johnston (2019) reports fewer than 10 known binaries in this size category with separations exceeding 10% of the primary's Hill radius, finding additional wide binaries is essential for determining the limits of binary stability and refining our understanding of asteroid masses. Our analysis involved two steps: first, comparing the major axis orientation of an asteroid's elliptical PSF against its non-sidereal sky rate, and second, contrasting the one-dimensional median profile (generated by collapsing the image along the direction of motion) with that of nearby field stars. We flagged results that significantly deviated from expected single-asteroid measurements, and the targets with the highest number of flags were selected as binary candidates for confirmation using high-acuity imaging.

This paper introduces a deep learning method for probabilistically forecasting macroeconomic and financial time series. By capturing intricate patterns within data-rich environments, our approach supports decision-making processes that rely on understanding the uncertainty surrounding numerous economic outcomes. It is particularly valuable for agents dealing with asymmetric loss functions dependent on non-Gaussian, non-linear variables. We demonstrate the method's efficacy on two distinct datasets where machine learning identifies underlying patterns. First, we generate macroeconomic fan charts incorporating information from high-dimensional data. Second, we highlight improvements in predicting stock return distributions, which are characterized by heavy tails, asymmetry, and a low signal-to-noise ratio.

This paper presents an analytical study of holographic superconductors within the framework of four-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (EGB) gravity. This recent formulation of four-dimensional EGB gravity involves rescaling the Gauss-Bonnet coupling constant as $\alpha\rightarrow \frac{\alpha}{d-4}$ and taking the limit $d\rightarrow 4$, which predicts several novel features. To examine the impact of curvature corrections on $(2+1)$-dimensional superconductors, we analyzed the system using $3+1$-dimensional EGB gravity. Employing the Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue method, we investigated the critical temperature and condensation operator values within this framework, specifically outside the probe limit. Our analytical findings successfully reproduce the corresponding numerical results.

By superimposing multiple plane waves, one can generate helicity lattices where optical helicity changes periodically in space. This study introduces an inverse design approach to construct arbitrary helicity configurations by positioning a digital object composed of dielectric inclusions within a three-dimensional environment. We utilize this method to create structures that replicate two-dimensional lattices inside a 3D volume using merely a single input plane wave. Furthermore, to showcase the versatility and capability of our technique, we extend beyond standard regular lattices to propose designs capable of forming arbitrary images with spatially varying helicity, all driven by a single plane wave.

Programmable hardware has enabled numerous innovative solutions, and the 5G Core (5GC) is well-positioned to leverage this approach by offloading specific tasks to the dataplane. This study presents a P4-based architecture designed for traffic identification and chaining on the Netronome Agilo SmartNIC. Deployed between the RAN and the UPF (User Plane Function), the system identifies incoming RAN traffic and constructs SRv6 chains based on control-plane-defined rules, with all identification and segment list generation occurring entirely within the SmartNIC. A minimalist Proof-of-Concept (PoC) was implemented and assessed, demonstrating the system's ability to establish service function chains transparently and efficiently.

Grasping the intricacies of small-scale convection and storm development is vital for accurately modeling large-scale planetary dynamics. Currently, atmospheric researchers rely on high-resolution simulations that resolve individual storms to capture kilometer-scale weather phenomena. However, the sheer volume of data generated by these simulations makes them difficult to interpret using traditional methods. This study adopts a data-driven strategy by jointly encoding spatial arrays of vertical wind speeds, temperature, and water vapor as three distinct "channels" within a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework. This proposed "multi-channel VAE" yields more robust and interpretable latent representations compared to previous efforts that analyzed vertical velocities in isolation. By clustering and analyzing the VAE's latent space, the research identifies weather patterns and their geographical distributions in a fully unsupervised manner. Ultimately, this approach demonstrates that VAEs are essential tools for extracting key weather and climate characteristics from high-dimensional simulation data.

We introduce a novel correlation technique for determining F-corona intensity distributions, grounded in the analysis of temporal changes in total and polarized visible light (VL) imagery. By examining one-month variation profiles of brightness obtained via the Large Angle Spectrometric COronagraph (LASCO-C2), we identified regions where total and polarized signals exhibit strong correlation. Under the assumption that the F-corona remains relatively stable over a one-month period, we calculated its intensity in these high-correlation zones and reconstructed corresponding intensity maps for both solar-minimum and solar-maximum phases. Systematic uncertainties were assessed through specific simulations. A comparison between these F-corona images and those derived via inversion techniques revealed that the correlation method yields a smoother intensity distribution. Furthermore, F-corona images computed for successive months demonstrated no significant variations. Lastly, we highlight that this approach is applicable to future high-cadence VL observations planned for the Metis/Solar Orbiter coronagraph.

Current WLAN scheduling depends exclusively on collision and success outcomes at the station level. To enhance traffic differentiation within dense WLAN environments, this paper introduces CSMA/ECA-DR, a distributed reservation mechanism for the CSMA/ECA MAC protocol that enables stations to cooperatively boost network performance. Furthermore, the Contention Window (CW) is dynamically adjusted based on real-time estimates of active network contenders. Simulation studies in dense scenarios with differentiated traffic confirm that CSMA/ECA-DR significantly improves WLAN efficiency for traffic differentiation, even when dealing with a large number of contenders.

This study catalogs 734 ultracool dwarfs with spectral types ranging from M6 to later, including one L0 object. Among this group, 625 were observed spectroscopically for the first time. All targets lie within 360~pc and have a *Gaia* G-band magnitude brighter than approximately 19.2 mag. Analysis of their spectra and stellar parameters ($T_{\text{eff}}$, $\log g$, and [Fe/H]) derived using the LAMOST pipeline reveals a cool, red nature with metallicities consistent with Galactic thin-disk stars. Additionally, 77 members exhibit lithium absorption at 6708 Å, signaling their youth and substellar classification. Kinematic data from LAMOST radial velocities, combined with proper motions and parallaxes from *Gaia* EDR3, confirm that most targets belong to the thin disk. Stellar ages were estimated by correlating velocity dispersion with population averages. Finally, we identified 35 binary systems, six of which were newly reported.

Traditionally, forecasting infectious diseases for active epidemics has focused on communicating numerical targets for cases, deaths, and hospitalizations across one to four-week horizons. Although predicting these specific numbers is valuable for assessing disease burden, we contend that conveying the future trajectory—or the shape of the epidemic curve, such as whether cases will plateau or surge—is equally important. To ensure this communicated information is useful, it is essential to evaluate how accurately the predicted shape aligns with the actual observed shape. Rather than framing this as a classification task selecting one of $n$ shapes, we propose transforming numerical forecasts into a "shapelet" space. In this framework, each dimension quantifies the similarity between the forecast and a specific reference shape (a shapelet). We demonstrate that this mapping preserves the intuitive notion of shape similarity, ensuring that similar shapes are represented closely together. Our approach effectively captures trends in COVID-19 case and death time-series data. Using this representation, we establish metrics for evaluating shape accuracy and measuring agreement among multiple models. Furthermore, we define a shapelet-space ensemble as the mean of individual models' representations, which we show can accurately forecast future epidemic trends for COVID-19. Additionally, we find that the degree of agreement between models serves as a strong indicator of forecast reliability.

This study examines acoustic cues for modeling turn-taking in dyadic spoken dialogues. Prior research indicates that speaker intentions, such as asking questions or providing backchannels, significantly influence turn-taking behavior and serve as effective predictors for turn transitions. However, these intentions are not easily accessible to automated systems during real-time operation, hindering their utility for anticipating turn changes. Consequently, we introduce a multi-task neural approach that simultaneously predicts turn transitions and speaker intentions. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating the auxiliary task of predicting speaker intentions enhances turn-transition prediction performance in spoken dialogues, all without requiring additional input features at run-time.

Theia represents a new class of "hybrid" optical neutrino detectors offering a robust physics agenda. This article offers a concise summary of its underlying concepts and potential scientific discoveries. Comprehensive information is available in the Theia white paper [1].

Discovering causal relationships from purely observational categorical data remains a persistent and difficult challenge. Unlike methods designed for continuous variables, most existing approaches for categorical data only determine the Markov equivalence class, leaving the direction of certain causal links ambiguous. This paper introduces an identifiable ordinal causal discovery technique that leverages inherent ordinal information found in many practical applications to uniquely reconstruct the causal structure. Although designed for ordinal data, the method can also be applied to non-ordinal data through discretization. Empirical evaluations using both real-world and synthetic datasets show that combining this ordinal approach with straightforward score-and-search algorithms yields favorable and robust results compared to state-of-the-art alternatives for both ordinal categorical and non-categorical data. An accompanying R package, OrdCD, is freely accessible via CRAN and at https://web.stat.tamu.edu/~yni/files/OrdCD_1.0.0.tar.gz.

Solution-processed amorphous silicon holds great promise for semiconductor applications, yet its fabrication typically introduces a high density of defects. These imperfections can be mitigated through treatment with hydrogen radicals. This study introduces an optimized hydrogenation protocol designed to achieve the highest performance in solar cells based on solution-processed amorphous silicon. We analyzed the quantity and bonding nature of incorporated hydrogen using infrared absorption and hydrogen effusion techniques. The treatment not only substantially increases total hydrogen content but also significantly boosts the proportion of hydrogen in the specific bonding configuration beneficial for electronic properties, though this effect is primarily confined to the surface. Electron spin resonance and photothermal deflection spectroscopy confirmed a marked reduction in defect density. Electrically, the ratio of photoconductivity to dark conductivity improved by nearly two orders of magnitude. Consequently, solar cell devices utilizing this material as the absorber layer exhibit greatly enhanced performance, with efficiency increasing by a factor of three.

An injective, information-preserving function can map a semantic network (a directed, labeled network) to a directed network (a directed, unlabeled network), where edge labels are encoded as topological features. Similarly, an injective function exists that transforms a directed network into an undirected network (an undirected, unlabeled network), with edge directionality represented as topological features. By composing these functions, an injective mapping from a semantic network to an undirected network is established. Consequently, aside from spatial limitations, semantic networks possess no modeling capabilities that cannot be achieved by either directed or undirected network representations. This concept will be demonstrated through two proofs: one illustrating the function composition described above, and another providing a simpler proof via an undirected binary encoding of the semantic network.

We introduce DietNeRF, a 3D neural scene representation capable of being estimated from a limited number of images. Standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve a continuous volumetric representation of a scene via multi-view consistency and render novel viewpoints through ray casting. Although NeRF excels at reconstructing geometry and fine details when provided with numerous images—up to 100 for difficult 360-degree scenes—it frequently converges to degenerate solutions when only a few input views are available. To enhance few-shot performance, we propose DietNeRF, which incorporates an auxiliary semantic consistency loss designed to promote realistic renderings at unseen poses. DietNeRF is trained per scene to (1) accurately render the provided input views from their original poses and (2) align high-level semantic attributes across various, random viewpoints. This semantic loss enables supervision of DietNeRF from arbitrary poses by leveraging pre-trained visual encoders like CLIP, a Vision Transformer trained on hundreds of millions of diverse, single-view 2D photographs collected from the web with natural language supervision. Experimental results demonstrate that DietNeRF improves the perceptual quality of few-shot view synthesis when trained from scratch, can render novel views using as few as one observed image when pre-trained on a multi-view dataset, and generates plausible completions for entirely unobserved regions.

Drawing upon and reusing datasets from an external digital marketing agency, this study investigates the role of targeted advertising in perpetuating broader systems of racial discrimination. Centered on a case study of ads for educational services in New York City, the research analyzes data visualizations and trend mappings of targeted demographics alongside corresponding U.S. Census data for specific zip codes. We synthesize and reflect on these findings to examine how online platforms systematically and differentially direct advertising based on race; the concrete harms and risks stemming from an internet traffic architecture built on discrimination; and finally, innovative frameworks and methodologies for auditing such systems amidst opaque, black-boxed processes that hinder transparency and accountability.

The intricate real-world applications of cyber-physical systems necessitate multi-objective controller synthesis, which involves determining an optimal controller that satisfies multiple, potentially conflicting, criteria. While human decision-makers often define the relative weight of these objectives, inherent uncertainty exists in these preferences, stemming from factors such as artifacts introduced by various preference elicitation techniques. This paper formalizes the concept of uncertain human preferences and introduces a novel method to address this uncertainty within multi-objective controller synthesis for Markov decision processes (MDPs). Grounded in mixed-integer linear programming, our approach generates an optimally permissive multi-strategy that adheres to uncertain human preferences regarding a multi-objective property. Experimental evaluations across numerous large-scale case studies demonstrate that the proposed method is both feasible and scalable, accommodating different MDP sizes and levels of preference uncertainty. Furthermore, an online user study confirms the quality and advantages of the synthesized controllers.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm for automated performance testing that leverages an online variant of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to optimize test generation. The primary goal is to create a test suite that maximizes the detection of performance defects within a specified budget. This is accomplished by employing a GAN to both generate tests and forecast their results, with the model training continuously during the generation and execution phases. Notably, the approach requires no pre-existing training data or system model. We present an initial evaluation of the algorithm using a sample test system and compare its outcomes against alternative methods. We regard this algorithm as a proof of concept and hope it encourages further research into applying GANs for test generation.

This paper examines transitions between low-density and high-density states in bistable plasma-condensate systems, incorporating anisotropy in adatom transfer between adjacent layers caused by the electric field near the substrate. We develop a generalized one-layer model under the assumption that the electric field strength undergoes both periodic oscillations and multiplicative fluctuations. By analyzing the homogeneous system, we evaluate the mean passage time. In the regime of weak fluctuations, we demonstrate that varying the frequency of periodic driving optimizes the mean passage time within the non-adiabatic limit. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of noise-induced effects, specifically asynchronization and acceleration in the transition dynamics.

Data-driven extrapolation necessitates defining a functional model tailored to available data to ensure reliable predictions of unknown dynamics. Given that data can be scattered, this approach prioritizes meshfree kernel models. Specifically, the proposed numerical method employs Variably Scaled Kernels (VSKs) to execute a feature augmentation strategy grounded in discrete data. Addressing potential data uncertainty and the goal of modeling dynamic behavior, a regularized solution via ridge regression is sought. Focusing on polyharmonic splines, the study examines their implementation within the VSK framework and establishes error bounds in Beppo-Levi spaces. The method's performance is evaluated on functions typical of Laplace transform inversion, with comparisons to Support Vector Regression (SVR) demonstrating its effectiveness, particularly as it avoids the need to train complex architectural structures.

The binary neutron star merger GW170817 and its subsequent multi-messenger detections provide robust evidence for two phenomena: the expansion of merger ejecta at significant velocities and the propagation of a relativistic jet through this ejecta. Unlike systems such as collapsars and active galactic nuclei, the non-negligible expansion speed of the ejecta fundamentally alters the motion of the jet head. This study introduces an analytic model for jet propagation within an expanding medium, highlighting a novel term in the equations for breakout time and velocity. Concurrently, we conducted over one hundred 2D numerical simulations, utilizing high-resolution numerical relativity data to prepare the BNS merger ejecta. Our analytic predictions align well with numerical results across a broad parameter space. Applying this model to GW170817 yields two key constraints: the central engine's isotropic luminosity ($L_{iso,0} \sim 3\times10^{49}-2.5\times10^{52}$ erg s$^{-1}$) and the delay between merger and engine activation ($t_0-t_m < 1.3$ s). These findings suggest that the seemingly faint short gamma-ray burst (sGRB) 170817A would resemble typical sGRBs if viewed on-axis, given the implied engine power.

This study investigates time-reversal (T) asymmetries in the decays $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda V$ (where $V = \phi, \rho^0, \omega, K^{*0}$) by analyzing spin correlations. We derive T-odd eigenstates with specific angular momenta and extract T-odd spin correlations from the complex phases of helicity amplitudes. Angular distributions for the process $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda(\to p \pi^-)V(\to PP')$, with $P^{(\prime)}$ representing pseudoscalar mesons, are presented alongside their corresponding spin correlations. Due to $s$-quark helicity conservation within the $\Lambda$, the $\Lambda$ polarization asymmetries are predicted to be near $-1$. Since the Standard Model (SM) decay $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda \phi$ involves only a single weak phase from the CKM product $V_{tb}V_{ts}^*$, both true T and CP asymmetries are suppressed, offering a pristine environment to test the SM and probe new physics. Under the factorization approach, SM helicity amplitudes share a common complex phase, eliminating T-violating effects; however, the observed branching ratio $Br(\Lambda_b \to \Lambda \phi) = (5.18\pm 1.29 )\times 10^{-6}$ indicates that nonfactorizable contributions or new physics are significant. By modeling these nonfactorizable effects using an effective color number, we compute branching ratios and direct CP asymmetries, and we further examine potential T-violating signatures arising from new physics.

This paper examines the necessary and sufficient conditions for central configurations composed of two twisted regular polygons (an N-regular and an L-regular polygon). Although our goal is to extend findings regarding symmetrical central configurations of two twisted N-regular polygons, we will demonstrate that the general setting yields no additional central configurations beyond those already identified in specific, more restricted cases.

Current image generation networks predominantly depend on spatial convolutions and, optionally, self-attention mechanisms to synthesize images progressively from coarse to fine details. In this work, we introduce a novel architecture where the color value of each pixel is calculated independently based on a random latent vector and the pixel's coordinates, eliminating any spatial convolutions or operations that transfer information across pixels during synthesis. We evaluate the modeling capabilities of these generators under adversarial training conditions and find that they achieve generation quality comparable to state-of-the-art convolutional models. Additionally, we explore several distinctive properties inherent to this new architecture.

A sequential effect algebra, defined as an effect algebra equipped with a sequential product $\circ$ possessing specific physical attributes, serves as a crucial framework for investigating quantum measurement theory. In 2005, Gudder posed the question: for elements $a, b$ in such an algebra where $a \bot b$ and $a \circ b \bot a \circ b$, does the inequality $2(a \circ b) \leq a^2 \oplus b^2$ necessarily hold? This paper provides a counterexample, thereby demonstrating that the answer to Gudder's problem is negative.

We report on archival data regarding Main-belt asteroid (248370) 2005 QN173 (also known as 433P), a recently identified active asteroid, showing that it exhibited activity near perihelion during a previous orbit in addition to its known outburst. This second episode of activity was identified in an image taken on July 22, 2016, using the Dark Energy Camera on the 4-meter Blanco telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile. To date, (248370) 2005 QN173 is the eighth active asteroid confirmed to display recurrent activity near perihelion. Our analysis indicates that this object belongs to the subset of Main-Belt Comets, characterized by activity driven by sublimation while orbiting within the Main Asteroid Belt. We employed a detection method called "wedge photometry," which can identify tails in solar system object imagery and measure their alignment with computed anti-solar and anti-motion vectors. Additionally, we provide a catalog and image gallery of these archival observations. The object will soon become unobservable as it passes behind the Sun from Earth's perspective; when it reappears visibility in late 2022, it will be more than 3 au from the Sun. Our results suggest that (248370) 2005 QN173 is most active within 2.7 au (0.3 au from perihelion), so we urge the scientific community to observe and study this unique object before December 2021.

Knowledge distillation (KD) offers an efficient strategy for transferring expertise from a large "teacher" model to a compact "student" model. Conventional KD techniques, however, depend heavily on abundant labeled data and access to a teacher's internal parameters (white-box), conditions that are frequently unmet in practical scenarios. In many real-world cases, distillation occurs remotely where data access is limited and the teacher's weights remain hidden due to privacy or security constraints. To address these limitations, we introduce a black-box few-shot KD framework capable of training a student using minimal unlabeled data and an inaccessible teacher. Our core approach involves expanding the training dataset by synthesizing diverse out-of-distribution images via MixUp and a conditional variational auto-encoder; the teacher then generates labels for these synthetic samples to guide student training. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art few-shot and zero-shot KD approaches on image classification benchmarks. The source code and models can be accessed at: https://github.com/nphdang/FS-BBT

Although transfer learning (TL) methods—known for boosting performance and shortening training times by leveraging knowledge from differently distributed data—are prevalent in computer vision (CV) and natural language processing (NLP), they remain underutilized in radio frequency machine learning (RFML). This study systematically investigates RF TL behavior by analyzing how specific training domains and tasks, defined by transmitter/receiver hardware and channel conditions, influence TL performance within an automatic modulation classification (AMC) scenario. By conducting extensive experiments on meticulously designed synthetic datasets featuring diverse signal types, signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), and frequency offsets (FOs), the research establishes general guidelines for optimizing RF TL for domain adaptation and sequential learning. Aligning with trends observed in other modalities, the findings indicate that RF TL efficacy is strongly correlated with the similarity between source and target domains or tasks. Furthermore, the study examines the effects of channel environments, hardware discrepancies, and task difficulty on performance, while comparing outcomes achieved through head re-training versus model fine-tuning.

SU Lyn is a binary system consisting of a red giant and a white dwarf. Despite its known brightness and variability at X-ray wavelengths, the optical counterpart initially appeared as a solitary red giant lacking prominent emission lines. Due to the absence of optical characteristics typical of interacting systems, it was categorized as a hidden symbiotic star. This study presents findings from optical monitoring of the system. Although SU Lyn exhibited no significant photometric variability, spectroscopic data revealed complex dynamics, including strong fluctuations in emission lines, P Cygni profiles, shifting emission environments, and variable reddening. Both X-ray and optical data suggest that the components interacted only briefly within the last twelve years of observation. For the first time, we demonstrate that SU Lyn mimicked a classical symbiotic star during periods of high X-ray brightness but remained hidden subsequently. Additionally, we examine the current evolutionary stage of the red giant and speculate on the system's future evolution, proposing that SU Lyn may serve as a progenitor for a persistent, classical symbiotic system.

Structure from Motion (SfM) facilitates scene reconstruction from casual multi-view camera captures, while Novel View Synthesis (NVS) enables rendering these scenes from unseen angles. Both tasks face significant difficulties with casual captures of dynamic environments: SfM typically yields noisy, spatio-temporally sparse point clouds, leading to NVS results that lack consistency across space and time. To address these challenges, we integrate SfM and NVS into a unified framework. For the SfM component, we recover stable camera poses and relax the need for temporally consistent points, instead reconstructing a sparse, noisy point cloud for each individual timestep. For the NVS component, we introduce a variational diffusion model applied to depths and colors, which robustly handles noise by enforcing spatio-temporal consistency through per-pixel reprojection weights derived from input views. Collectively, this deferred approach generates novel views for dynamic scenes without demanding difficult spatio-temporal reconstruction consistency or training complex models on large datasets. We validate our algorithm on real-world dynamic scenes, comparing it against both classic and recent learning-based baselines.

This paper examines a specific class of verifiable disclosure games in which the sender's utility is independent of the state, and the receiver's best response relies solely on the expected state. Messages are verifiable, meaning they can be imprecise but must remain factually accurate. I determine the sender's most favored equilibrium and investigate scenarios where commitment power yields no advantage. I establish criteria for when an information design result constitutes an equilibrium outcome in these games and provide straightforward sufficient conditions under which the sender gains nothing from commitment. These findings aid in defining the sender's preferred equilibria and payoff ranges within this game class. Finally, I apply these concepts to analyze voter influence and sales strategies involving quality disclosure.

This study investigates the contrarian voter model for opinion dynamics within a society subjected to stochastic noise and external oscillating propaganda. Population agents, each holding either a favorable or unfavorable opinion, interact via imitation or anti-alignment dynamics. Specifically, an agent adopts a neighbor's opinion with a time-dependent probability $p(t)$ or the opposite opinion with probability $1-p(t)$. The imitation probability $p(t)$ is governed by social temperature $T$ and modulated by a periodic field representing external propaganda, encouraging alignment with the field. Simulations on complete graphs and lattices reveal diverse behaviors as $T$ changes: consensus at $T=0$, bimodal distribution for $T<T_c$, field-synchronized oscillations for $T>T_c$, and complete disorder for $T \gg 1$. In complete graphs, the critical temperature scales with population size $N$ as $T_c \simeq 2/\ln N$. Furthermore, residence time distributions in the bimodal phase decay approximately as $t_r^{-3/2}$. Within the oscillatory regime, a stochastic resonance-like effect occurs at a specific temperature $T^*$. Mean-field analysis indicates that opinion oscillation amplitude peaks at an intermediate temperature and exhibits a phase lag relative to the field that diminishes as $T$ increases.

We investigate nonclassical correlations arising from measurements on two spatial radiation modes. These correlations cannot be replicated by statistical mixtures of coherent states or, more broadly, by non-negative phase-space functions describing quantum states and measurements. We contend that nonclassical correlations are inherently linked to Bell nonlocality, with the former representing a broader category of quantum correlations. It is established that both local realistic and noncontextual models map to non-negative solutions of a linear equation system governing the joint probability distributions of all observables. We show that nonclassical correlations correspond to a specific solution within this system, which can exhibit negative values even when local realism remains unviolated. By adapting Bell inequalities, we can test for these correlations. Furthermore, our methodology yields a formulation of Bell inequalities suitable for continuous variables. These findings are demonstrated using two-mode squeezed vacuum states and hybrid entangled states (Schrödinger-Cat states), where one mode is examined via balanced homodyne detection and the other via unbalanced homodyne detection.

Semiring provenance effectively details the specific combinations of atomic facts underlying query results. Specifically, interpreting polynomials or formal power series within general provenance semirings offers precise accounts of successful query evaluation strategies. Although database provenance analysis has traditionally been restricted to negation-free query languages, a recent methodology extends this capability to model checking problems involving logics with complete negation. This extension relies algebraically on novel quotient semirings constructed from dual-indeterminate polynomials or power series. To date, this approach has primarily been applied to first-order logic and the positive fragment of least fixed-point logic. A significant gap remained in adequately handling fixed-point calculi that allow arbitrary interleaving of least and greatest fixed points. We demonstrate that a suitable framework for analyzing full fixed-point logics is established by semirings that are (1) fully continuous, (2) absorptive, and (3) chain-positive. Full continuity ensures that provenance values for both least and greatest fixed points are well-defined. Absorptive semirings create a symmetry between these two types of computations, ensuring that provenance values for greatest fixed points remain informative. Chain-positivity ensures truth-preserving interpretations, assigning non-zero values to all true formulae. Furthermore, we identify semirings of generalized absorptive polynomials and prove universal properties establishing them as the most general appropriate semirings for LFP. Finally, we illustrate the utility of provenance interpretations in these semirings by connecting them to provenance values derived from plays and strategies in associated model-checking games.

This paper investigates the geometry of $\mathcal{Q}$-conic arrangements within the complex projective plane, which are composed of smooth conics and possess specific quasi-homogeneous singularities. We demonstrate that no such $\mathcal{Q}$-conic arrangements are free and establish combinatorial restrictions governing their weak combinatorics.

Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) seeks to enable machines to infer human subjective emotions from audio alone, yet extracting and leveraging deep audio features remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces an end-to-end SER system that utilizes multi-level acoustic information through a newly designed co-attention module. Specifically, we extract diverse acoustic features—MFCCs, spectrograms, and high-level representations derived from CNN, BiLSTM, and wav2vec2—which serve as multimodal inputs fused via the proposed co-attention mechanism. Evaluated on the IEMOCAP dataset using two distinct speaker-independent cross-validation strategies, our model demonstrates competitive performance. The source code is publicly available on GitHub.

Data races represent one of the most prevalent bugs in concurrent programming. Traditionally, detecting these races relies on dynamic analysis, which examines program executions rather than source code. While extensive research has defined various dynamic race notions that are efficiently detectable when parameters like the thread count are small, the fine-grained complexity of these definitions has remained unclear, preventing a clear characterization of the trade-offs between precision and efficiency. This work establishes fine-grained separations among several popular dynamic race concepts. Given an execution trace containing $N$ events, $T$ threads, and $L$ locks, our primary findings are as follows. First, we demonstrate that happens-before (HB) races can be detected in $O(N\cdot \min(T, L))$ time, which improves upon the standard $O(N\cdot T)$ bound when $L$ is significantly smaller than $T$. Furthermore, we prove that reporting an HB race involving a read is difficult for 2-orthogonal vectors (2-OV), providing the first rigorous proof of the conjectured quadratic lower bound for detecting HB races. Second, we show that synchronization-preserving races are hard to detect using OV-3, resulting in a cubic lower bound when $T=\Omega(N)$, thereby establishing a complexity gap between these races and the less expressive HB races. Third, we prove that lock-cover races are hard for 2-OV, yielding a quadratic lower bound even when $T=2$ and $L$ grows faster than $\log N$. In contrast, the similar lock-set race notion is detectable in $O(N\cdot L)$ time, creating a complexity separation between the two. Additionally, we show that when $L=\Theta(N)$, lock-set races become hitting-set (HS)-hard, also incurring a quadratic lower bound for sufficiently complex inputs.

Since John Vidale introduced the original numerical algorithm for solving the isotropic eikonal equation in 1988, the field has seen significant advancements aimed at enhancing solution accuracy, integrating surface topography, incorporating complex physics such as anisotropy and attenuation, and accelerating computations through multi-CPU and GPU architectures. However, existing methods lack a mechanism to transfer insights gained from solving one problem to the next, and they often fail when confronting complex variations of the eikonal equation, necessitating approximate solutions. To address these limitations holistically, we propose an alternative approach that simplifies the inclusion of topography, accommodates any level of physical complexity, leverages the computational power of multiple CPUs and GPUs, and enables knowledge transfer between problems. We develop an algorithm grounded in the emerging paradigm of physics-informed neural networks to solve diverse forms of the eikonal equation. By utilizing transfer learning and surrogate modeling, we demonstrate how prior solutions can accelerate computations. Additionally, we introduce a two-stage optimization scheme to streamline training in scenarios involving sharp heterogeneities within the velocity model. Our approach also illustrates how integrating additional physics and features becomes significantly more straightforward compared to conventional methods, which historically required years or decades to achieve similar progress. Ultimately, this methodology not only simplifies the implementation of eikonal solvers but also accelerates the pace of future advancements.

Using the vector meson dominance model within the hidden local symmetry framework, this study examines the Dalitz decay ${\eta}^{\prime} \to V e^{+}e^{-}$. The results indicate that the partial width ${\Gamma}({\eta}^{\prime} \to {\omega}e^{+}e^{-})$ is approximately 40 eV, corresponding to a branching ratio ${\cal B}({\eta}^{\prime} \to {\omega}e^{+}e^{-})$ of roughly $2{\times}10^{-4}$. Furthermore, the rates for the ${\rho}$ channel are estimated to be about ten times those of the ${\omega}$ channel, i.e., ${\Gamma}({\eta}^{\prime} \to {\rho}e^{+}e^{-}) \approx 10{\Gamma}({\eta}^{\prime} \to {\omega}e^{+}e^{-})$ and ${\cal B}({\eta}^{\prime} \to {\rho}e^{+}e^{-}) \approx 10{\cal B}({\eta}^{\prime} \to {\omega}e^{+}e^{-})$. The peak of the dilepton mass distribution occurs at $m_{e^{+}e^{-}} \approx 1.33$ MeV. These decay processes are expected to be observable once high-statistics ${\eta}^{\prime}$ experiments become available.

This work investigates the computational complexity of $c$-Colored $P_\ell$ Deletion and $c$-Colored $C_\ell$ Deletion. In these problems, the objective is to eliminate all induced $c$-colored paths or cycles of length $\ell$ by removing at most $k$ edges from a $c$-edge-colored graph, where a structure is considered $c$-colored if it utilizes edges of all $c$ distinct colors. We demonstrate that both problems are NP-hard for every non-trivial pair of parameters $c$ and $\ell$. Subsequently, we examine their parameterized complexity by generalizing neighborhood diversity to edge-colored graphs, proving that both problems are fixed-parameter tractable with respect to this measure. Furthermore, we establish hardness results to delineate the boundaries of parameterization by the solution size $k$. Finally, focusing on bicolored graphs, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for a specific instance of $2$-Colored $P_4$ Deletion.

This extended abstract outlines prior work from the CamFort project, which created an external unit-of-measure type system designed for Fortran code to assist scientists. Our method guides programmers in introducing type annotations into existing code, thereby facilitating the adoption of such systems on legacy projects. Aligned with the themes of the HATRA workshop, this discussion focuses on the human aspects of the tool. CamFort is open-source and accessible online at no cost.

As neural-network-driven QA models grow in depth and complexity, there is an increasing need for robust frameworks capable of accessing the rationale behind their predictions. Existing methods for gaining insights into model operations either rely on adversarial datasets or require models with built-in explicit explanation components; both approaches are time-consuming and difficult to adapt to existing models or new datasets. This study employs `Integrated Gradients` to extract rationale for current state-of-the-art models in Reading Comprehension-based Question Answering (RCQA). Through a detailed analysis comparing these extracted rationales with human-generated ones, we observe that while 40-80% of the extracted words align with human rationale (precision), the extracted rationale contains only 6-19% of the human rationale (recall).

To explain the coincidence between current dark matter and dark energy densities, we propose a unified framework where dark energy is modeled as a homogeneous scalar field $\phi$ governed by a non-canonical $k$-essence Lagrangian with a constant potential. In this scenario, dark matter particles experience velocity diffusion within the background medium of the $k$-essence field, causing energy to transfer from the dark matter fluid to the dark energy fluid. This energy exchange manifests as a source term in the continuity equations for both fluids, characterized by a diffusion coefficient that quantifies the average energy transfer per unit time. Utilizing the time evolution of the FRW spacetime scale factor, along with the energy density and pressure of the dark fluid derived from Supernova Ia data, we establish constraints on the diffusion parameter. For a constant potential, we derive the temporal dynamics of the homogeneous $k$-essence field $\phi$ across various diffusion parameter values. These dynamics can be expressed as $\phi(t/t_0) = \phi_0 + \varepsilon_1 (t/t_0 - 1) + \varepsilon_2 (t/t_0 -1)^2$, where $t_0$ represents the present epoch. The coefficients $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$ are determined as linear functions of the diffusion parameter.

This report serves as a review of fundamental concepts in the theory of prequantizing a symplectic manifold for my Master's reading project, including a presentation of the classic proof that a symplectic manifold is prequantizable if and only if its symplectic form is integral.

To characterize and measure fluctuations in plasticity and failure within additively manufactured metals caused by microstructural imperfections, we established an uncertainty quantification framework utilizing pseudo marginal likelihood and embedded variability approaches. This method incorporates both porosity visible in computed tomography scans of the raw material and the sub-threshold distribution of voids via a physically grounded model. Model calibration reveals that the sub-threshold defect population primarily governs yield and failure behavior. Furthermore, the technique enables the quantification of material parameter distributions linked to manufacturing-induced microstructural variability, facilitating assessments of material quality and process control.

This paper presents supplementary findings concerning the setting, model, and estimators outlined in Auerbach (2019a). Section 1 examines the large sample properties of the estimators introduced in Section 2 of Auerbach (2019a). Section 2 explores extensions to the model, while Section 3 applies these methods to estimate network peer effects. Finally, Section 4 displays the outcomes of various simulations.

This paper presents Choice Trees (ctrees), a monad designed within Coq to model programs that are nondeterministic, recursive, and impure. Drawing inspiration from Xia et al.'s itrees, this new structure embeds computations into coinductive trees featuring three node types: external events and two forms of nondeterministic branching. Although this design appears redundant, it enables a shallow embedding of denotational models with internal choice in the style of ccs, while simultaneously recovering an inductive LTS perspective on computation. CTrees leverage a comprehensive suite of existing bisimulation and refinement tools, allowing the authors to establish a robust equational theory. The work links ctrees to the itrees framework by demonstrating how a monad morphism embedding ctrees into itrees facilitates the implementation of nondeterministic effects. Finally, the paper illustrates the practical value of ctrees through two case studies modeling concurrency semantics: ccs and cooperative multithreading.

The CDF II Collaboration has recently reported a precise measurement of the $W$ boson mass that deviates from the Standard Model prediction by $7\sigma$.
