Applying a perpendicular electric field of ${\cal E}= \pm 0.5$~V/{\AA} induces substantial modifications to the exchange constants. We demonstrate that the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in this heterostructure is primarily governed by nearest-neighbor interactions, producing quantitative agreement between methods (i) and (ii). Moreover, we show that the DMI is highly tunable through strain, stacking, and electric fields, achieving magnitudes comparable to those at ferromagnetic/heavy metal (FM/HM) interfaces. This high tunability stems from geometrical changes and hybridization effects at the interface. While the electric-field-induced DMI calculated via method (iii) qualitatively matches the more accurate \textit{ab initio} results of method (ii), it overestimates the field effect by approximately 50%. Additionally, the magnetocrystalline anisotropy energy can be significantly altered by applying either compressive or tensile strain to the Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$/germanene system.

Accurately identifying and classifying the thickness of mechanically exfoliated graphene flakes is crucial for advancing nanomanufacturing and developing next-generation devices that surpass the limitations of Moore's Law. Currently, this process relies on manual inspection of optical microscope images, whereas existing machine learning approaches struggle to handle the varying backgrounds inevitably encountered in experimental settings. This paper introduces a deep learning solution designed to automatically detect and categorize the thickness of exfoliated graphene flakes on Si/SiO2 substrates, regardless of optical settings or background colors. The proposed approach utilizes a hierarchical deep convolutional neural network that retains knowledge from previously learned images while adapting to new data. Trained on diverse datasets, the model classifies flakes into monolayer (1L), bi-layer (2L), tri-layer (3L), four-to-six-layer (4-6L), seven-to-ten-layer (7-10L), and bulk categories. Compared to current methods, this deep learning framework demonstrates superior accuracy, efficiency, and robustness against variations in image background and resolution. Experimental results indicate a classification accuracy of up to 99%, offering significant potential for scaling up the manufacturing and characterization of graphene for advanced materials and devices.

"Monkey see, monkey do" is a longstanding proverb describing naive imitation that lacks a deep grasp of a system's internal workings. Specifically, if the demonstrator possesses information inaccessible to the imitator—such as distinct sensors—even a flawless model of the perceived environment may result in suboptimal outcomes when attempting to replicate the demonstrated behavior. While causal imitation learning has been explored in literature to address scenarios where the demonstrator and imitator differ (Zhang et al., 2020), current methods are restricted to single-stage decision-making. This study examines causal imitation learning within sequential contexts, where the imitator must generate multiple decisions per episode. We introduce a graphical criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for assessing the feasibility of causal imitation, outlining conditions under which an imitator can match a demonstrator's performance despite capability disparities. Furthermore, we present an efficient algorithm to determine imitability and validate our theoretical findings through simulations.

Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) stands as a leading candidate for dark matter, gaining significant attention due to its ability to resolve numerous astrophysical issues, especially those related to small-scale structures. This paper examines results from two prior simulations of cluster-sized halos within the SIDM framework and proposes a novel density profile function for galaxy clusters that accurately reproduces these simulation outcomes. Leveraging this profile, we derive the velocity dispersion profile and establish a relationship between cluster mass and concentration. Using these relations, we analyze two key scaling relations: mass-velocity dispersion and mass-temperature. Our findings indicate that under the SIDM model, halos are more massive than predicted by the standard non-interacting model for any given temperature. Furthermore, we investigate the mass-temperature relation in a hybrid interacting model, which combines SIDM with a dark sector theory where particle mass is defined by its interaction with dark energy. This super-interacting dark sector (SIDS) model modifies the mass-temperature relation to yield results consistent with non-interacting models. Finally, we present quantitative expressions describing the constants of this interacting model in terms of the dark matter particle's cross-section per unit mass.

Optimization tasks involving the minimization of a convex function combined with a composite function are prevalent across many disciplines. The generalized Levenberg--Marquardt (LM) method, alternatively called the prox-linear method, was originally designed to address these challenges by iteratively solving strongly convex subproblems augmented with a damping term. This research introduces a novel generalized LM approach tailored for problems featuring smooth composite functions. The proposed method offers three key theoretical assurances: bounds on iteration and oracle complexity, as well as local convergence under a H\"olderian growth condition. Notably, the local convergence analysis includes quadratic convergence under a quadratic growth condition, marking the first extension of classical least-squares results to general smooth composite functions. Furthermore, this work presents the first LM algorithm to simultaneously achieve an oracle complexity bound and local quadratic convergence under standard assumptions. These advancements result from precisely managing the damping parameter and utilizing the accelerated proximal gradient method with a specific termination criterion to solve subproblems. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the method's effectiveness in practical scenarios, such as neural network classification and nonnegative matrix factorization.

This study focuses on the robust approximation of multiphase mean curvature flows, potentially featuring highly contrasted mobilities, utilizing a variational phase field method. While the scenario of harmonically additive mobilities was recently handled via a specific metric defining the gradient flow of the phase field energy, we extend this framework to arbitrary nonnegative mobilities by decomposing them into sums of harmonically additive components. We validate the method's consistency through an analysis of the sharp interface limit, where a formal phase field expansion demonstrates second-order accuracy. Additionally, we introduce a straightforward numerical scheme to solve the proposed model and provide numerical experiments in two and three dimensions. These results highlight the approach's efficacy, particularly in simulating flows where certain phases exhibit zero mobility.

To fully comprehend the behavior of quantum error correction codes (QECC) under noise, explicit coding maps must be derived. However, the immense computational effort required to obtain these maps has kept them relatively obscure, even for the widely studied five-qubit code—the smallest perfect code capable of correcting generic single-qubit errors. By performing direct yet intricate calculations, we derive the explicit process matrix for the coding maps of the five-qubit code when subjected to a unital error channel. This matrix enables an exact analysis of the code's performance. We demonstrate that the code can correct generic errors; specifically, under repeated self-concatenation of the coding map, the code makes no assumptions about the error model other than its weakness, effectively transforming sufficiently small error channels into the identity channel. We further examine recent coherent error models (non-diagonal channels) and numerically establish a lower bound on the convergence threshold for the code. Additionally, we analytically determine how the code influences the average gate infidelity and diamond distance of error channels, deriving explicit formulas for both pre- and post-error scenarios to analyze logical error rates. Our results refine the upper bounds on the diamond distance of the noise channel following error correction, improving upon previous literature.

The challenge of obtaining identical physical observables from different current components, specifically the minus current, has long persisted within the light-front quark model (LFQM), even when calculating two-point functions like meson decay constants. By incorporating all current components, including the minus component, we demonstrate that pseudoscalar and vector meson decay constants are uniquely determined at the level of one-body current matrix elements, adhering to the Bakamjian-Thomas construction. Regardless of the specific current components, polarization vectors, or reference frames used, these decay constants remain uniquely defined within the non-interacting constituent quark and antiquark basis, provided that constituent interactions are incorporated into the meson mass operator in the LFQM.

The phenomenon of neutron-nucleus interaction varying with temperature is recognized as Doppler broadening of cross-sections. This established effect arises from the thermal motion of target nuclei during neutron-nucleus collisions, and its rapid calculation is essential for various nuclear applications. Existing methods for computing these Doppler effects primarily rely on numerically solving Solbrig's kernel equation, a formalism derived from the hypothesis of a free gas atom distribution. This paper investigates a novel non-linear methodology utilizing deep learning techniques. Deep neural networks are trained on both synthetic and experimental datasets to serve as an alternative to traditional Doppler Broadening (DB) calculations. Furthermore, the study explores the application of physically informed neural networks, which are physically regularized to ensure their outputs satisfy a partial differential equation inferred from Solbrig's kernel. The efficacy of this learning process is demonstrated by calculating fission, capture, and scattering cross-sections for $^{235}U$ across an energy spectrum ranging from thermal levels to 2250 eV.

This study investigates the implementation of a distributed power method in a parallel framework. Conventional distributed approaches typically update eigenvectors sequentially, presenting two significant drawbacks: first, computing the $h$th eigenvector requires waiting for the completion of the preceding $(h-1)$ eigenvectors, resulting in delays in obtaining all eigenvalues; second, each power iteration incurs information exchange costs among neighboring nodes, which becomes prohibitive as the number of nodes or eigenvectors increases. To address these issues, we propose a parallel distributed power method that computes all eigenvectors simultaneously during each iteration, thereby maximizing information exchange within a single communication round. We focus specifically on distributed power methods for both eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) and singular value decomposition (SVD), utilizing a gossip algorithm to facilitate the distributed process. Our analysis demonstrates that, under identical conditions, the communication cost of this gossip-based parallel approach is reduced to $1/H$ of that required by the sequential method, where $H$ represents the target number of eigenvectors, while maintaining comparable convergence times and error performance.

We propose a policy evaluation algorithm for Markov Decision Processes that demonstrates superior empirical convergence rates. By tracking the Projected Bellman Error and functioning as a true gradient-based method, it distinguishes itself from both the TD($\lambda$) family and residual algorithms, which also rely on tracking the Projected Bellman Error. Furthermore, empirical results indicate that our algorithm converges significantly faster than GTD2, another class designed to track the Projected Bellman Error. When integrated into DQN and DDPG frameworks, the proposed method yields comparable performance in both experimental settings.

We investigate a conservative system comprising two nonlinear coupled oscillators. Because the system's eigenmodes are nonlinearly coupled, one can induce parametric amplification in the other, a phenomenon known as autoparametric resonance. This amplification involves two distinct time scales: a rapid one associated with the forcing and a slow one corresponding to the forced mode, making a multiscale expansion appropriate for deriving amplitude equations that describe the slow dynamics. We first review parametric resonance in a dissipationless system, specifically the parametrically forced Duffing oscillator, focusing on the energy transfer between the source and the oscillator that drives the parametric forcing. We observe that energy conservation holds when averaging occurs on the slow time scale relevant to parametric amplification, as indicated by a constant of motion within the amplitude equation. Next, we examine a dimer situated in a periodic potential well, representing a conservative yet non-integrable system. When the dimer's energy confines it to neighboring potential wells, we derive coupled nonlinear differential equations for the amplitudes of the eigenmodes (representing center-of-mass and relative motions). We identify two constants of motion, proving that these amplitude equations are integrable. We establish the criteria for the autoparametric amplification of relative motion by center-of-mass motion and characterize the system's phase portraits. Conversely, in the limit where the dimer slides along the external potential such that center-of-mass motion is essentially translational, we compute the amplitude equation for the relative motion. In this scenario as well, we demonstrate the autoparametric amplification of the dimer particles' relative motions. In both instances, comparing numerical integration of the full system with our asymptotic analysis reveals excellent agreement.

Previous research indicates that integrating bootstrap imputation with tree-based machine learning for variable selection yields performance comparable to fully observed data under Missing At Random (MAR) conditions, though this approach is computationally intensive for large datasets. We introduce RR-BART, an inference-driven method that combines Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) with Rubin's rule to aggregate variable importance estimates and variances from multiply imputed datasets. Through a representative simulation study comparing RR-BART against bootstrap-based techniques, we evaluate its practical performance. Additionally, we apply the method to a case study examining risk factors for metabolic syndrome incidence over three years in middle-aged women using data from the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN). The simulations demonstrate that RR-BART effectively recovers prediction and variable selection accuracy akin to fully observed data, even in complex scenarios involving nonlinearity, nonadditivity, and high missingness rates. Specifically, RR-BART matches the optimal performance of bootstrap methods when using the best selection threshold, exhibits superior capability in detecting discrete predictors, and delivers significant computational efficiency. In the SWAN analysis, RR-BART identified a set of biologically justified risk factors that had previously been overlooked, thereby contributing new insights to the literature.

Although traditional High-Performance Computing (HPC) adequately supports most workflows, a new cohort of researchers now demands sophisticated, scalable, on-demand, and self-service compute infrastructure within a cloud-like setting. Additionally, many require secure environments to process or store sensitive and controlled-access data at high capacity.

To address the needs of these modern users, the Minnesota Supercomputing Institute developed and implemented Stratus, a locally hosted cloud environment built on the OpenStack platform and supported by Ceph storage. This subscription-based service augments existing HPC systems by fulfilling specific unmet user requirements: a) immediate access to compute resources, b) support for long-running jobs (exceeding 30 days), c) container-based computing via Docker, and d) robust security measures to meet controlled-access data mandates.

This document offers a detailed examination of Stratus's design, specifically focusing on security and adherence to the NIH's controlled-access data policy. The narrative highlights lessons learned from integrating OpenStack and Ceph into a "walled garden" architecture and how these technologies shaped the security framework. Various Stratus capabilities, such as tiered secure storage featuring a controlled-access data "cache," fault-tolerant live migrations, and comprehensive two-factor authentication, rely on recent advancements in OpenStack and Ceph.

We introduce a compact, fibre-coupled single photon source that integrates an InAsP semiconductor quantum dot inside an InP photonic nanowire waveguide, utilizing gradient-index (GRIN) lenses. This GRIN lens assembly captures photons near the nanowire tip and couples them directly into a single-mode optical fibre, delivering a stable, high-brightness source of fibre-coupled single photons. Through pulsed excitation, we achieve on-demand operation with 98.5% single photon purity at saturation; the device features a source-fibre collection efficiency of 35% and an overall single photon collection efficiency of 10%. Furthermore, we demonstrate "plug and play" functionality by leveraging room temperature photoluminescence from the InP nanowire to facilitate alignment at room temperature.

Over recent years, there has been a surge in interest regarding the use of drone-mounted aerial base stations to augment ground cellular networks. By exploiting reconfigurable air-to-ground channels, these aerial stations can improve user access links by hovering in positions that maximize line-of-sight connectivity. This paper introduces an analytical framework for the three-dimensional deployment of a coordinated fleet of drone relays. The framework aims to optimize network performance specifically regarding user throughput fairness, quantified via the $\alpha$-fairness metric. Since the resulting optimization problem is formulated as an intractable mixed-integer non-convex program, we developed an extremal-optimization-based algorithm named Parallelized Alpha-fair Drone Deployment. This algorithm solves the problem online within low-degree polynomial time. We validate our approach through numerical simulations based on the real-world topology of a dense urban environment. Furthermore, we examine the benefits of integrating drone relays into existing networks and evaluate various resource scheduling strategies across both static and dynamic scenarios, accommodating increasingly larger and denser crowds.

Building large-scale discrete frameworks, such as trusses and space frames, using additive robotics is becoming increasingly appealing due to the potential gains in efficiency, safety, and design flexibility. However, manually programming complex robots, like seven-degree-of-freedom manipulators, to execute these tasks is often prohibitively difficult or impossible for humans. Specifically, the construction sequence must maintain structural integrity, such as stiffness, at every stage while enabling the robot to manipulate components within the evolving structure without violating geometric constraints, such as avoiding collisions with already built parts. This paper introduces a novel, automated planning method capable of simultaneously determining a valid construction sequence and a corresponding robot motion plan that meets these criteria. The proposed approach is versatile across various additive construction processes and is specifically demonstrated here for spatial extrusion and discrete bar assembly. We validate the method's efficacy through several simulated and real-world tasks, including the deployment of our algorithm on a human-scale physical prototype to assemble a complex double tangent bar system for the first time.

This report details our named-entity recognition system presented at the VLSP 2018 evaluation campaign. We framed the task as a sequence labeling problem utilizing the BIO encoding scheme. Our approach employed a feature-based model that integrates word and word-shape features, Brown-cluster-based features, and word-embedding-based features. We also evaluated various methods for handling nested entities within the dataset. Our results demonstrate that employing a joint-tag model, which combines entity tags across all levels for training the sequence labeling model, enhances the accuracy of nested named-entity recognition.

The relative index theorem is established for general complete, coercive first-order elliptic operators defined on measured manifolds at infinity. This work generalizes earlier findings by Gromov-Lawson regarding generalized Dirac operators and those by Bär-Ballmann concerning Dirac-type operators. By examining the problem through the lens of boundary value problems, the proof utilizes the graphical decomposition of elliptically regular boundary conditions for such operators, as developed by Bär and Bandara. Additionally, the study demonstrates the splitting and decomposition principles alongside the Phi-relative index theorem as foundational steps leading to the main relative index theorem.

Writing style can inadvertently expose sensitive author characteristics, such as race or age, potentially resulting in privacy breaches and bias within both human and algorithmic decision-making processes. For instance, the stylistic elements in job applications may disclose protected candidate attributes, leading to unfair hiring outcomes whether the process is automated or manual. To address this, we introduce a VAE-based framework that employs style transfer to automatically rephrase text, thereby obscuring stylistic features. Our approach defines "obfuscated style" flexibly through two distinct strategies: (1) a minimal concept that blends styles observed during training, and (2) a maximal concept that integrates stylistic traits from all sensitive attributes to create a union of styles. While our framework has broad applications, we highlight its success in enhancing the fairness of downstream classifiers. Furthermore, we present an extensive analysis of style pooling's impact on fluency, semantic consistency, and attribute removal across two and three-domain obfuscation scenarios.

Let $G$ be a connected unimodular group endowed with a Haar measure $\mu_G$ (which is both left and right invariant), and assume $A$ and $B$ are nonempty compact subsets of $G$. Kemperman established the inequality $\mu_G(AB) \geq \min\{\mu_G(A)+\mu_G(B),\mu_G(G)\}$. Our primary contribution identifies the precise conditions under which equality occurs, thereby resolving a query posed by Kemperman in 1964. Furthermore, we characterize the connected, compact structures $G$, $A$, and $B$ that almost achieve this equality, deriving quantitative bounds with optimal exponents. This work effectively functions as a $(3k-4)$-theorem for this context and validates the connected case of conjectures proposed by Griesmer and Tao. Additionally, we apply these findings to derive a measure expansion gap result for connected compact simple Lie groups. The methodology relies on analyzing the geometry of minimally and nearly minimally expanding set pairs, linking these insights to a specific pseudometric, and constructing continuous group homomorphisms to either $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ based on this pseudometric.

In La2-xSrxCuO4, suppressing superconductivity with high magnetic fields establishes a striped antiferromagnetic (AFM) order as the magnetic ground state across the entire pseudogap regime, persisting until the doping level p*. This state exhibits glass-like freezing, as evidenced by 139La NMR measurements of the spin-lattice relaxation rate 1/T1. This study provides a quantitative analysis of 1/T1 data for hole dopings between p=x=0.12 and 0.171, utilizing a modified Bloembergen-Purcell-Pound (BPP) theory that accounts for statistical parameter distributions due to strong spatial inhomogeneity. We find that spin fluctuations slow down near the onset of static charge order, and the magnetic field effect generally resembles strengthening stripe order as doping approaches p=0.12. However, our detailed analysis reveals a significant deviation from typical field-induced magnetic transitions. The continuous increase in fluctuating moment amplitude with higher magnetic fields suggests a nearly-critical state in the zero-field limit, potentially involving very weak quasi-static moments confined within small regions such as vortex cores. Furthermore, the nucleation of spin order within these vortex cores quantitatively explains both the magnitude and doping dependence of the field scale governing bulk spin freezing. The correlation time of the fluctuating moment exhibits an exponential dependence on B/T across the studied range. This accounts for the observed timescale variations in experiments, clarifying why AFM moments can be treated as static over extensive ranges of temperature and field in transport studies. Consequently, these findings establish the high-field magnetic ground state up to p* as a crucial component in discussions regarding potential quantum criticality.

Classifying hate speech has long been a persistent challenge in natural language processing. Despite the existence of many detection methods, they often fail to identify implicit hateful statements. Creating datasets to support the classification of implicit hate speech presents significant hurdles, including linguistic nuances, inconsistent definitions of hate speech, and the laborious nature of data annotation. These issues have resulted in a scarcity of training and testing data, causing high variance when parameter-heavy transformer models are applied. This paper investigates various optimization and regularization strategies and introduces a novel RoBERTa-based model that achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Circular Synthetic Aperture Sonars (CSAS) acquire multiple scene observations to generate high-resolution imagery. Resolution in CSAS can be modeled as the convolution of a scene's point scattering distribution with a system-specific Point Spread Function (PSF), which induces a fixed level of blur based on the transmitted waveform's bandwidth. While deconvolution theoretically reverses this blur to recover the scattering distribution, it remains an ill-posed, noise-sensitive inverse problem. We introduce a self-supervised pipeline called SINR that utilizes an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) to deconvolve CSAS images without requiring training data. By comparing SINR against existing methods, we demonstrate its superior performance. Furthermore, while prior approaches assume a spatially invariant PSF—often leading to suboptimal results—we provide theoretical and methodological frameworks to handle spatially varying PSFs. Our results on both simulated and real acoustic data confirm that accounting for PSF variation enables SINR to achieve state-of-the-art deconvolution performance. We also release the associated code to facilitate research reproducibility.

This study determines the short-time asymptotic behavior of the sub-Riemannian heat content within a smoothly bounded domain in the first Heisenberg group. Our derived asymptotic formula extends the findings of van den Berg-Le Gall and van den Berg-Gilkey into the sub-Riemannian setting, explicitly expressing the initial coefficients of the sub-Riemannian heat content through the horizontal perimeter and the total horizontal mean curvature of the boundary. The proof employs probabilistic methods, utilizing a characterization of heat content via Brownian motion.

This study introduces Trans10K-v2, an enhanced fine-grained dataset for transparent object segmentation that builds upon Trans10K-v1, the pioneering large-scale dataset in this domain. While the original version was restricted to only two categories, Trans10K-v2 offers significant improvements: it includes 11 fine-grained categories of transparent objects frequently found in domestic settings, enhancing its practical utility for real-world applications, and it presents greater challenges for state-of-the-art segmentation techniques. Additionally, we propose Trans2Seg, a novel transformer-based segmentation pipeline. Its transformer encoder leverages a global receptive field, offering superior performance compared to the local receptive fields of pure CNN architectures. Furthermore, by reframing semantic segmentation as a dictionary look-up task, the Trans2Seg decoder utilizes learnable prototypes as queries, with each prototype capturing the statistical properties of a specific category across the entire dataset. Benchmarking against over 20 recent semantic segmentation methods reveals that Trans2Seg significantly surpasses all CNN-based approaches, demonstrating the algorithm's potential to effectively address transparent object segmentation.

We examine a specific family of infinite-dimensional representations of $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$, denoted as $L_n(p)$, which are determined by a positive integer $p$ and correspond to the lowest component of the $p$-fold tensor product of the metaplectic representation of $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$. By utilizing the embedding $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2np) \supset \mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$, we develop a novel polynomial basis for $L_n(p)$. The vectors in this basis are indexed by semi-standard Young tableaux and take the form of Clifford algebra-valued polynomials with integer coefficients in $np$ variables. Leveraging the combinatorial attributes of these tableau vectors, we establish their validity as a basis. Furthermore, calculating the matrix elements of a set of $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2n)$ generators acting on these basis vectors involves additional combinatorial analysis, including the effect of a Young subgroup on the horizontal strips of the tableaux.

Automating the extraction of information from form-like documents at scale is urgently needed to streamline business workflows across diverse sectors such as healthcare, insurance, and finance. The primary obstacle is the vast variability in document layouts, necessitating solutions that can generalize to unseen structures and languages. Achieving this requires a comprehensive understanding of both visual cues and textual content, a non-trivial task. Although natural language processing and computer vision fields are beginning to address this, there remains a lack of focus on data efficiency and the ability to generalize across various document types and languages. This paper demonstrates that using a straightforward transfer learning approach from a structurally distinct, larger labeled corpus to a small target dataset (approximately 50 documents) can improve F1 scores by up to 27 points compared to training solely on the small corpus. Furthermore, we present a simple multi-domain transfer learning method currently in production, which achieves an additional 8-point F1 improvement. We argue that data efficiency is essential for scaling information extraction systems to handle hundreds of document types, and that learning robust representations is key to this success.

Existing multi-person pose estimation techniques usually handle joint localization and association as distinct steps, a process that is convenient yet inefficient due to redundant computation and time consumption. In contrast, this paper introduces PoseDet (Estimating Pose by Detection), a new framework that simultaneously localizes and associates body joints to achieve faster inference. We also propose a keypoint-aware pose embedding to represent objects based on their keypoint locations. This embedding integrates both semantic and geometric information, enabling the efficient extraction of discriminative and informative features. Within PoseDet, this embedding facilitates candidate classification and joint localization, resulting in robust predictions across diverse poses. This streamlined framework delivers unmatched speed and competitive accuracy on the COCO benchmark compared to state-of-the-art approaches, while extensive experiments on the CrowdPose benchmark demonstrate its robustness in crowded environments. The source code is publicly available.

Drift theory serves as an intuitive framework for analyzing random processes, facilitating the conversion of expected stepwise changes into expected first-hitting times. Although widely adopted in the study of randomized search heuristics, it remains underutilized in other domains despite its potential to address numerous research questions framed as first-hitting time problems. This work outlines the most practical drift theorems and illustrates their application across diverse randomized processes, such as the coupon collector problem, winning streaks, vertex cover approximation, and a random sorting algorithm. Furthermore, we address processes lacking expected stepwise changes by presenting applicable drift theorems for such scenarios. These tools are employed to analyze the gambler's ruin process, a coloring algorithm, a 2-SAT algorithm, and an unbiased version of the Moran process. Finally, we introduce a tight theorem for processes within finite state spaces, applying it to the Moran process. Our objective is to empower researchers to utilize drift theory for deriving accessible proofs and to present it as a straightforward method for analyzing random processes.

This paper investigates Cauchy-Riemann (CR) submanifolds within Lorentzian Concircular Structure ($LCS^n$), Lorentzian Para-Sasakian (LP)-cosymplectic, $S$, and Generalized Kenmotsu (GKM) manifolds. It explores findings related to distributions, structure vector fields, totally geodesic submanifolds, and leaves. Specifically, it establishes results on totally umbilical contact CR-submanifolds where the anti-invariant distribution exhibits certain properties. Furthermore, the study examines D-totally geodesic CR-submanifolds, contact CR-submanifolds, D-perp-totally geodesic CR-submanifolds, and $\xi$-horizontal CR-submanifolds with integrable distributions (where $D$ denotes the distribution and $\xi$ the structure vector field). Additional proofs cover D-umbilic CR-submanifolds, mixed totally geodesic CR-submanifolds, foliate $\xi$-horizontal mixed totally geodesic CR-submanifolds, leaves of the distribution, totally geodesic leaves, and CR-products. The work concludes with examples of CR-submanifolds in $(LCS)^n$-manifolds and a GKM manifold.

The most effective method to expand the Standard Model of particle physics to account for the observed B anomalies is the leptoquark hypothesis, which proposes a color-triplet, weak-singlet boson with an electric charge of $Q=+\frac{2}{3}$. We highlight that SU(15) grand unification, featuring a scalar leptoquark in the adjoint representation, offers a natural explanation for the violation of lepton flavour universality. Additionally, we briefly address biquarks and bileptons.

Decomposing galaxies into bulge, disk, and bar components is crucial for addressing several scientific questions. By measuring the structural parameters of these parts, researchers can constrain models of galaxy assembly, including both violent and secular processes, as well as recurrent bar formation and dissolution. This approach also aids in quantifying the fraction and characteristics of bulgeless galaxies—systems lacking a classical bulge or possessing only a minor disky-pseudobulge—thereby challenging formation paradigms that assume nearly all disk galaxies host a central classical bulge. We present a proof of concept and preliminary findings from our ongoing three-component (bulge-disk-bar) decomposition of near-infrared (NIR) images across three complementary samples spanning various epochs and environments (both field and cluster). Unlike earlier studies that typically modeled only a two-component bulge-disk structure, we utilize GALFIT to fit three distinct components: a bulge, a disk, and a bar. We demonstrate that including the bar component is essential, as it can significantly reduce the bulge-to-total luminosity ratio (B/T) by a factor of two or more in many cases, effectively shifting a galaxy's Hubble classification from early to late type.

We demonstrate experimentally that quantum interference can be generated within an integrated quantum architecture consisting of an arch-shaped short quantum wire (or quantum point contact, QPC) containing 1D electrons and a reflector that creates an electronic cavity. When the coupling between the QPC and the cavity is adjusted, fine oscillations appear in the quasi-1D regime of the arch QPC. These oscillations arise from interference between 1D states and a state resembling a Fabry-Perot mode, which is suppressed by a transverse magnetic field of approximately 60mT. By tuning the reflector, we observe a resistance peak consistent with Fano resonance behavior. We propose this as a notable instance of Fano resonance in an open system, representing interference near Ohmic contacts caused by a directly propagating, reflected discrete path interacting with the continuum states of the cavity via multiple scattering. Notably, the Fano factor exhibits oscillatory behavior, peaking at each fine oscillation, thereby confirming the coupling between discrete and continuum states. These findings suggest that such a straightforward quantum device can serve as a fundamental building block for constructing more complex integrated quantum circuits, with potential applications spanning quantum information processing to the exploration of fundamental complex quantum systems.

While quantum computing offers transformative potential for information processing, novel tools are essential to translate program logic into the physical instructions that quantum hardware requires. This work introduces a specialized adaptation of the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) embedded within a quantum compiler, designed specifically to facilitate program execution verification. We first illustrate how MLIR facilitates quantum circuit transformations to optimize performance on quantum devices, followed by a demonstration of compiler-based transformations utilizing "mirror circuits." Our findings show that inserting these mirror circuits during compilation allows for the assessment of hardware performance by evaluating circuit accuracy across various superconducting and ion-trap platforms. Consequently, our results confirm MLIR as a robust and efficient framework for gathering hardware-specific diagnostics through the automated transformation of quantum circuits.

This paper introduces algorithms designed to align Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) graph components with English sentence spans. By integrating unsupervised learning with heuristics, our method combines the strengths of prior AMR aligners. Unlike previous models, our unsupervised approach is more responsive to graph substructures and eliminates the need for a separate syntactic parse. Our strategy addresses a broader range of AMR substructures, resulting in improved coverage of both nodes and edges alongside greater accuracy. We will make our LEAMR datasets and aligner publicly available to support research in AMR parsing, generation, and evaluation.

Although data-driven single-view techniques have advanced significantly in modeling 3D dressed humans, they are severely limited by depth ambiguities and occlusions inherent to single inputs. This paper addresses these challenges by leveraging a small number of input views and exploring optimal strategies to utilize information from them. We present a data-driven, end-to-end framework that reconstructs an implicit 3D representation of clothed humans from sparse camera perspectives. Our method incorporates three core components: a spatially consistent reconstruction module enabling arbitrary person placement within input views using a perspective camera model; an attention-based fusion layer designed to aggregate visual data across multiple viewpoints; and a mechanism for encoding local 3D patterns within a multi-view context. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods on standard datasets, both quantitatively and qualitatively. To validate spatial consistency, we apply the method to dynamic scenes. Furthermore, testing on real-world data captured by a multi-camera setup shows that our technique achieves results comparable to multi-view stereo while requiring significantly fewer views.

Standard image classification deep neural networks usually combine a convolutional feature extractor with a fully connected classifier, representing labels as one-hot vectors that assume uniform dissimilarity across all classes. This approach overlooks the inherent visual similarities and hierarchical structures among classes; therefore, explicitly learning this latent hierarchy could yield significant insights. We introduce an alternative architecture termed the Latent Hierarchy (LH) Classifier, paired with an end-to-end learned Class2Str mapping designed to uncover these class hierarchies. Our results demonstrate that replacing the classifier in top-performing models on CIFAR and ImageNet datasets with the LH classifier maintains accuracy while drastically reducing the parameter count. Unlike prior work such as HDCNN, which only supports two hierarchy levels, our method learns hierarchies of arbitrary depth and achieves improved accuracy on ImageNet. Furthermore, we confirm that the learned hierarchy successfully clusters visually similar classes together.

Refactoring involves modifying a system's design to improve future adaptability and understanding without changing its behavior. Since preserving behavior is central to this process, numerous studies utilizing formal verification, language transformation, and dynamic analysis have been developed to track refactoring operations and their effects on program semantics. However, no existing research comprehensively examines the behavior preservation strategies available for each specific refactoring operation. The objective of this paper is to identify these behavior preservation approaches found in the literature. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic mapping study that captures and classifies existing approaches based on criteria such as methodology, applicability, and the level of automation. The results show that various preservation strategies have been proposed, ranging from formalisms and techniques to automatic safety tools and manual source code analysis. Finally, our taxonomy highlights that certain refactoring operations remain under-researched regarding behavior preservation, while our classification suggests that combining multiple strategies can more effectively detect violations of program semantics.

Handling missing data in time series is a critical challenge. Current approaches often struggle with irregular sampling or suffer significant performance drops when data is sparse. This study redefines time series as permutation-equivariant sets and introduces NRTSI, a new imputation model that avoids recurrent architectures. By leveraging this formulation, we develop a rigorous and efficient hierarchical imputation process. Furthermore, NRTSI is capable of directly processing irregularly sampled sequences, generating multiple-mode stochastic imputations, and accommodating partially observed dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate that NRTSI attains state-of-the-art accuracy across various time series imputation benchmarks.

Socialbots are software-controlled accounts on social media platforms that operate autonomously by mimicking human behavior to influence public opinion or disseminate targeted misinformation. Because these bots threaten the integrity of social ecosystems, they are widely regarded as harmful, prompting various computational initiatives to automatically identify them. However, to our knowledge, the adversarial capabilities of socialbots have not yet been explored. This raises the critical question: "Can adversaries controlling socialbots leverage AI techniques to their benefit?" We demonstrate that adversaries can indeed exploit computational learning mechanisms, such as reinforcement learning (RL), to enhance socialbot influence while evading detection. We formulate adversarial socialbot learning as a cooperative game involving two hierarchical RL agents: one agent designs a sequence of activities to avoid detection, while the other maximizes network influence by strategically connecting with specific users. Our policy networks, trained on extensive synthetic graphs, outperform baseline models on unseen real-world graphs, achieving up to an 18% increase in network influence and up to a 40% improvement in undetectability even under a strong bot detector with 90% accuracy. Furthermore, during inference, our approach maintains linear complexity, remaining independent of network structure and news virality. These characteristics make our method a practical adversarial attack suitable for deployment in real-life scenarios.

Building upon recent developments in random tensor theory, this paper investigates a rank-$r$ asymmetric spiked tensor model defined as $\sum_{i=1}^r \beta_i A_i + W$, where $\beta_i\geq 0$ and the $A_i$'s represent rank-one tensors satisfying $\langle A_i, A_j \rangle\in [0, 1]$ for $i\neq j$. Based on this framework, we conduct an asymptotic analysis of Hotelling-type tensor deflation within the large-dimensional regime. Our study specifically delineates the singular values and alignments at every stage of the deflation process for asymptotically large tensor dimensions. These findings enable the construction of consistent estimators for various underlying parameters, including the signal-to-noise ratios $\beta_i$ and the alignments between distinct signal components $\langle A_i, A_j \rangle$.

Lithography simulation, a critical component of physical verification, relies heavily on advanced optical and resist models, where the resist model translates aerial image simulations into final printed patterns. Although learning-based approaches for resist modeling have proven effective, they require extensive datasets. Furthermore, manufactured data generated for a specific lithography setup is limited to training a single model, resulting in poor data efficiency. Given the intricacies of manufacturing, acquiring sufficient data for high accuracy is prohibitively expensive in both time and cost, a challenge that intensifies during technology node transitions when the design space is extensively explored. This paper introduces a novel resist modeling framework for contact layers that leverages data from legacy technology nodes and employs active data selection for target nodes, thereby minimizing the data burden on the target lithography configuration. By integrating transfer learning and active learning, our framework achieves competitive accuracy, reducing the required training data by 3 to 10 times while maintaining performance comparable to current state-of-the-art methods.

We examine a one-dimensional Rabi-Hubbard-type system where a quantum dot (qdot) is placed between each cavity. These qdots facilitate photon transmission between adjacent cavities while simultaneously introducing non-linear effects. Specifically, we analyze three-level qdots in a $\Lambda$ configuration, where the left and right legs couple only to their respective neighboring cavities. This non-commuting interaction gives rise to two highly entangled, incompressible phases separated by a second-order quantum phase transition. In this context, qdot degrees of freedom function as a dynamical lattice for photons, and a Peierls instability breaks a second $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, resulting in dimerization of both entanglement and photon number. Additionally, we identify a normal insulating phase and a superfluid phase characterized as a quantum many-body superradiant state. Within the superradiant phase, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking occurs, and the phase transition belongs to the universality class of the transverse field Ising model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific limit of this model can be interpreted as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory.

We investigate many-body chaos within a (2+1)D relativistic scalar field theory at elevated temperatures using the classical statistical approximation, a framework that encompasses both the quantum critical regime and the thermal transition from order to disorder. By calculating out-of-time ordered correlation functions (OTOCs), we observe that the corresponding Lyapunov exponent scales linearly with temperature during the quantum critical phase and follows an algebraic approach to the non-interacting limit based on a fluctuation parameter. Furthermore, OTOCs exhibit ballistic spreading across all regimes, including at the thermal phase transition where the butterfly velocity reaches its maximum. This study advances our comprehension of the connection between classical and quantum many-body chaos, and the methodology employed here is applicable to other field theories where classical modes dominate at long wavelengths.

We introduce straightforward conditions guaranteeing that a strongly elliptic operator $L$ generates an analytic semigroup on Hölder spaces over any complete manifold with bounded geometry. This result is achieved by demonstrating the equivalent property that $L$ is "sectorial," a criterion defining the resolvent $(\lambda I - L)^{-1}$'s decay as $\lambda$ moves away from the Hölder spectrum of $L$. As an intermediate step, we establish the resolvent's existence for sufficiently large $\lambda$ and employ a geometric microlocal adaptation of semiclassical pseudodifferential calculus on this broad class of manifolds. The derived properties of $L$ and $e^{-tL}$ subsequently enable the proof of well-posedness for a wide range of nonlinear flows. We demonstrate this application by proving well-posedness on Hölder spaces for the flow linked to the ambient obstruction tensor on complete manifolds of bounded geometry.

Given a quotient $A$ of the graded polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\cdots,x_m]\otimes\Lambda[y_1,\cdots,y_n]$ where the ideal is generated by monomials having leading coefficients equal to 1, we have constructed a space $X_A$ such that $A$ is isomorphic to the cohomology of $X_A$ with torsion elements excluded.

The ALICE experiment investigated femtoscopic correlations for $K^0_{\rm S}K^0_{\rm S}$ and $K^0_{\rm S}K^\pm$ pairs in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ and $13$ TeV. By fitting models assuming Gaussian source size distributions to the measured two-particle correlation functions, source parameters were derived for both pair types at these energies. The analysis for $K^0_{\rm S}K^0_{\rm S}$ incorporated quantum statistics and strong final-state interactions mediated by the $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ resonances, whereas the $K^0_{\rm S}K^\pm$ analysis considered only the final-state interaction via the $a_0$ resonance. The extracted source parameters were compared with previously published data from $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV collisions, revealing consistency across different pair combinations. Furthermore, the observation that $K^0_{\rm S}K^0_{\rm S}$ correlations are significantly stronger than $K^0_{\rm S}K^\pm$ correlations supports the hypothesis that the $a_0$ resonance is a tetraquark state composed of $(q_1,\overline{q_2}, s, \overline{s})$, where $q_1$ and $q_2$ represent $u$ or $d$ quarks.

We have calculated and compared the vacuum effective potential and phase diagram of the three-flavor (2+1) quark-meson model using an extended mean-field approximation (e-MFA), where model parameters are determined via various renormalization prescriptions that account for quark one-loop vacuum fluctuations. When the vacuum one-loop divergence is regularized using the minimal subtraction scheme and parameters are fixed by the scalar and pseudo-scalar meson curvature masses, the quark-meson model with the vacuum term (QMVT) proves inconsistent; this is because curvature masses are defined by evaluating self-energy at zero momentum. This study represents the first application of a consistent on-shell parameter fixing scheme to the three-flavor quark-meson (QM) model. In this renormalized quark-meson (RQM) framework, the physical (pole) masses of the $\pi, K, \eta$, and $\eta^{\prime}$ pseudo-scalar mesons, along with the scalar $\sigma$ meson, the pion decay constant, and the kaon decay constant, are related to the running mass parameter and couplings through both on-shell and minimal subtraction renormalization schemes. For the RQM and QMVT models, the normalized vacuum effective potential plots in the nonstrange direction are identical when $m_\sigma = 658.8$ MeV. Similarly, the nonstrange direction order parameter temperature variations and phase diagrams for the RQM and PQMVT models coincide when the $\sigma$ mass is reduced by 10 MeV to $m_\sigma = 648$ MeV. This agreement occurs because variations in the normalized vacuum effective potential along the nonstrange direction are partially driven by changes in the strange direction.

While multiplicative error models (MEMs) are standard for real-valued time series, their reliance on multiplication prevents direct application to discrete count data, as this operation fails to maintain integer values. To address this, we introduce a multiplicative operator specifically designed for counts, alongside several concrete implementations, to construct Multiplicative Error Models for counts (CMEMs). When these CMEMs incorporate a linear conditional mean, they align closely with integer-valued generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (INGARCH) models and can serve as a semi-parametric extension. We establish key stochastic properties for various INGARCH-CMEM variants and develop corresponding estimation methods, including quasi-maximum likelihood and weighted least squares. Finally, the efficacy and practical utility of these models are validated through simulations and two real-world case studies.

Over the last two decades, various crises, including the 2008 financial meltdown and its lingering effects, have destabilized global economies and social welfare, eroding trust in Western societal stability. This study seeks to identify and demonstrate the root causes of such instability and potential societal collapse. To this end, we introduce a simplified, low-dimensional model featuring two interconnected agent classes: "labourers" and "administrators," drawing inspiration from Joseph Tainter's theory on the collapse of complex societies. The model numerically simulates societal complexity, quantified by the proportion of administrators, which influences the productivity of energy-producing labourers. Our findings indicate that the probability of collapse rises as societal complexity continuously expands in response to external stresses mirroring the problems societies must address. We also present an analytical approximation of the system's primary dynamics that aligns closely with numerical results, enabling precise identification of tipping points beyond which collapse occurs. The administration's capacity to enhance labour productivity emerges as the most critical factor for extending societal survival, a resilience further supported by a baseline level of social connectivity. Additionally, we demonstrate that stochastic transitions between the labour force and administration—representing social mobility—can significantly prolong the society's lifespan. Ultimately, this research enhances the understanding of socio-ecological collapse by highlighting its potential direct connection to escalating complexity in response to external shocks, driven by a self-reinforcing feedback loop.

Data poisoning represents an adversarial situation in which an adversary supplies a meticulously designed series of samples to an online model to undermine its learning process. We present the Lethean Attack, an innovative data poisoning method designed to trigger catastrophic forgetting within online models. This attack is specifically deployed within Test-Time Training, a contemporary online learning framework intended to maintain generalization despite distribution shifts. We provide the theoretical basis for this approach and empirically evaluate it against other sample sequences that naturally cause forgetting. Our findings indicate that through the use of Lethean attacks, an adversary can reduce a test-time training model's accuracy to the level of random guessing using a brief sequence of samples.

This paper investigates the evaluation of MSO queries containing free variables on trees using enumeration algorithms. Building on prior research that achieved linear-time preprocessing and output-delay linear in the size of each result (constant delay for free first-order variables), we extend these capabilities to handle relabelings, a specific type of tree update that modifies node labels. Our primary contribution demonstrates that it is possible to enumerate answers to MSO queries on trees with linear preprocessing and delay proportional to each answer, even while supporting node relabelings in logarithmic time. To achieve this, we adapt the circuit-based enumeration framework from our previous work and devise methods to maintain its indexing under relabeling operations. Furthermore, we illustrate how enumeration under relabelings can be utilized to evaluate practical query languages, including those involving aggregates, group-by operations, and parameterized queries.

The energy eigenvalue equations for a particle confined within a square well are solved to yield exact solutions expressed as power series, alongside accurate analytical approximations. These findings are applied to quantum well physics, with specific focus on ultra-thin metallic films, as well as resonant cavities, heterojunction lasers, and phenomena involving revivals and super-revivals.

This study introduces a self-improving artificial intelligence system designed to boost the safety of reinforcement learning (RL) agents in autonomous driving (AD) by leveraging black-box verification techniques. While RL methods have gained significant traction in AD recently, their efficacy relies heavily on the diversity of training data; a scarcity of safety-critical scenarios during training often results in poor generalization in real-world settings. We present a new framework that utilizes black-box verification to identify deficiencies in the training set. Upon discovering failure scenarios, the RL agent's training is restarted to specifically address these previously unsafe conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach effectively uncovers safety failures in RL-based adaptive cruise control (ACC) systems and substantially decreases vehicle collisions through iterative application.

Quantum routing, defined as the entanglement of an input signal across multiple output paths, will play a pivotal role in future quantum networks. Given the noisy quantum devices currently in development, implementing such routing in emerging networks is a distinct possibility, necessitating quantum error correction tailored for the arbitrary noise encountered during the routing process. This study presents a combined circuit design for quantum routing and error correction, achieving the first implementation of this system on a real-world noisy quantum device. Assuming statistical knowledge of the channel, we experimentally confirm the quantum nature of the error-corrected routing by quantifying path-entanglement via quantum state tomography and calculating the success probability. The deployed error correction is deemed successful as it enhances routing performance. These experiments demonstrate, for the first time, the feasibility of error-corrected quantum routing in near-term noisy quantum hardware, while our detailed findings establish a benchmark for quantum routing across all current quantum devices.

We introduce a novel interconnection framework for infinite-dimensional port-Hamiltonian systems, allowing the coupling of ports with varying spatial dimensions through integration over excess dimensions. To demonstrate practical applicability, we apply this framework to an actively cooled gas turbine blade model. Furthermore, we verify that the interconnection relation remains robust under finite element discretization, thereby guaranteeing its suitability for real-world applications.

Since quantum effects are not observed on cosmological scales, Loop Quantum Cosmology (LQC) must accommodate semi-classical quantum states of spacetime geometry to accurately represent reality. These states require being sharply peaked around a single classical geometry with minimal quantum fluctuations, a property generally attributed to Gaussian states based on their behavior in ordinary quantum mechanics. In this study, we derive exact closed-form expressions for the fluctuations of Gaussian states in LQC and their lower bounds defined by the Robertson-Schrödinger inequality. Contrary to standard quantum mechanics, we demonstrate that in spatially flat, homogeneous, and isotropic LQC, fluctuations for Gaussian states diverge as state variance increases—a phenomenon also observed in related models sharing the same kinematic Hilbert space and canonical observables. However, if the holonomy length scales with a volume regularization parameter, these fluctuations can be arbitrarily suppressed by increasing the fiducial volume, thereby offering analytic control over the divergence. Furthermore, we establish that Gaussian states in LQC typically fail to minimize uncertainty, leading to the conjecture that no such minimal-uncertainty states exist. The work underscores the critical importance of the assumed condition where holonomy length scales with volume; violating this condition results in operator closure pathologies and other unusual algebraic characteristics within the theory.

This study derives a system of partial differential equations designed to calculate the complete stress field from a known strain field, even when the plastic component of the material's constitutive behavior is unknown. These equations extend earlier formulations that were restricted to scenarios where elastic strain could be ignored. Although the model assumes isotropic constitutive relations, it imposes minimal other constraints, allowing direct application to problems involving finite deformations, non-linear elasticity and plasticity, compressible and rate-dependent materials, various yield surface geometries, and diverse hardening laws. Unlike previous linear hyperbolic equations, the new system is non-linear and evolves over time. This approach enables the determination of the stress field (and consequently the constitutive equation) for arbitrary geometries and loading conditions whenever the full-field strain is available. This generalization addresses a critical challenge in elasto-plastic stress computation: the coexistence of elastic unloading in some material regions and significant plastic deformation in others. While this mixed behavior previously limited the utility of existing methods, it is now fully resolved. To demonstrate the technique, a two-dimensional case study of necking in a uniaxial tensile specimen is analyzed. The governing equations are solved numerically using a finite volume algorithm detailed in related work. Validation against the forward problem solution confirms the accuracy of the results within numerical error margins, proving that this approach offers unique capabilities, including the first theoretically exact solution to this well-established problem.

This study analytically extends the theory of cosmic-ray acceleration via cyclotron autoresonance to encompass any polarization state, utilizing a two-parameter model for the radiation field. The rigorously derived equations are applied to examine the dynamics of hydrogen, helium, iron, and nickel nuclides under extreme astrophysical conditions. Both single-particle calculations and many-particle simulations demonstrate that these species can achieve ZeV energies ($1 ~ZeV = 10^{21}$ eV) through interactions with superintense radiation featuring wavelengths of 1 and 10 $\mu$m, as well as 50 pm, alongside magnetic fields ranging from mega- to gigatesla. The discussion includes scenarios involving radiation intensities between $10^{32}$ and $10^{42}$ W/m$^2$.

This paper examines an infeasible interior-point method for linear optimization that employs a full-Newton step. The proposed approach applies an algebraic equivalent transformation to the centering equation defining the central path. We demonstrate that the method identifies an $\varepsilon$-optimal solution to the problem within polynomial time.

A correctly specified and appropriately decomposed $U(2)$ flavour symmetry establishes precise quantitative connections between quark mass ratios and CKM mixing angles. Simultaneously, the inherent distinction within $U(2)$ between the third family and the first two families of quarks and leptons could account for anomalies in charged and neutral current semi-leptonic $B$-decays, similar to those preliminarily detected in current flavour studies. We demonstrate the feasibility of this scenario through the exchange of a $(3,1)_{2/3}$ vector leptoquark in two distinct $U(2)$-models, which exhibit markedly different levels of Lepton Flavour Universality violation that are anticipated to be measurable in upcoming experiments.

This study conducts an experimental analysis of pattern formation and evolution in bilayered tubular organs, utilizing swelling deformation of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) to provide a comprehensive comparison with theoretical and finite element models. To establish a twin model for simulation, the shear modulus of an incompressible neo-Hookean material is determined through uni-axial tensile and pure shear tests. Five bilayered tubes, varying in material or geometric parameters, were fabricated and subjected to swelling experiments within a specific setup that ensures plane-strain deformation. These experiments revealed various surface patterns and mode transitions, including creases, wrinkles, period-doubling profiles, and transitions between wrinkles and creases or period-doubling states, alongside interfacial wrinkling. For validation, a buckling analysis based on finite elasticity using the Stroh formulation was performed, complemented by finite element analysis to track the evolution of surface instabilities. Results demonstrate strong agreement between experimental observations and both theoretical predictions and finite element simulations. Specifically, the study finds that creasing can occur instead of wrinkling when both layers possess similar mechanical properties. This work offers new experimental insights into pattern formation in tubular structures, and the alignment between experimental, theoretical, and simulation outcomes provides robust evidence that phenomenological growth models effectively explain the mechanisms behind complex surface morphology in tubular tissues.

This paper explores a deep learning strategy for speech denoising utilizing an efficient ensemble of specialized neural networks. By partitioning the denoising task into non-overlapping subproblems and incorporating a classifier, we enhance performance while simultaneously lowering computational complexity. Specifically, the proposed architecture employs a gating network that routes noisy speech signals to the most suitable specialist network, selecting based on either the degree of speech degradation or the speaker's gender. Experimental results compare a baseline recurrent network against an ensemble of similarly designed, smaller recurrent networks managed by an auxiliary gating mechanism. Trained on stochastically generated batches from a large corpus of noisy speech, the model learns to estimate a time-frequency masking matrix using the magnitude spectrogram of the input mixture. While both the baseline and specialist networks are trained to predict the ideal ratio mask, the gating network is dedicated to subproblem classification. Our findings indicate that a fine-tuned ensemble network surpasses the denoising capabilities of a generalist network while utilizing fewer parameters.

Jupiter's atmosphere is characterized by numerous jet streams deeply connected to its three-dimensional circulation. Since the planet lacks a solid lower boundary, various theories have proposed how meridional circulation penetrates its interior. By synthesizing data from multiple Juno mission instruments, we demonstrate the presence of mid-latitude meridional circulation cells driven by turbulence, analogous to Earth's Ferrel cells. Unlike Earth, which hosts only one such cell per hemisphere, Jupiter's greater size and rapid rotation allow for multiple cells. These cells create distinct upwelling and downwelling zones, clearly visible in Juno's microwave data across latitudes 60°S to 60°N. The identification of these cells is further validated by successfully replicating ammonia observations using a simplified model. This research resolves a decades-old mystery concerning Jupiter's sub-cloud dynamics and provides evidence for eight cells in each hemisphere.

This study examines the mean number of limit cycles emerging from a randomly perturbed linear center, where the perturbation involves random bivariate polynomials with independent coefficients. Through classical perturbation theory applied to the Poincaré first return map, this inquiry simplifies to analyzing the real roots of a random univariate polynomial, $\displaystyle f_n(x) = \sum_{m=0}^n c_m \xi_m x^m$. In this formulation, the coefficients $\xi_m$ are independent with zero mean and unit variance, while $c_m$ scales as $m^{-1/2}$. This polynomial falls within the class of {\it generalized Kac polynomials} at the critical threshold. We derive asymptotic estimates for the expected number of real zeros to resolve the question regarding bifurcating limit cycles, and we also establish the precise order of the mean number of real roots in the subcritical regime.

We examine the effect of adding an arbitrary node to a finite, undirected, unweighted graph $G$ on the Perron eigenvalue of its non-backtracking matrix. We establish an interlacing-type theorem demonstrating that this eigenvalue does not decrease following such an addition. Additionally, our approach yields rigorous bounds for the magnitude of the eigenvalue's change, representing the first fully proven bounds of this kind. These findings rely on the assumption that the non-backtracking matrix is diagonalizable; while practical observations suggest this condition holds for many graph families, determining necessary and sufficient conditions for it remains an open problem.

Persistence within the spatial environment is a fundamental capability for robots, making positional knowledge a critical component of spatial cognition. This thesis introduces foundational techniques for qualitative spatial representation and reasoning, reviews various existing calculi, and summarizes their features and applications. A novel calculus is proposed for representing and reasoning about qualitative spatial orientation and distances, capable of supporting arbitrary levels of granularity regarding ternary point relations. The study demonstrates methods to enhance the complexity of composition and provides an implementation that illustrates the calculus's capabilities. Finally, the new approach is compared with existing qualitative spatial calculi for positional information, and potential avenues for future research are identified.

Ellingsen et al. recently introduced the concept of multiplicative differential, which inspired the construction of power functions exhibiting low c-differential uniformity. Building on this foundation, Wang et al. [27] defined the c-differential spectrum for power functions. This paper explores specific properties of that spectrum and utilizes them to analyze the c-differential spectra of various power functions, ultimately deriving a new class of APcN functions.

We introduce version 4.0 of the hfbtho code, which addresses the nuclear Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov problem using a deformed harmonic oscillator basis within cylindrical coordinates. This updated version incorporates the restoration of rotational, particle number, and reflection symmetries. Notably, the restoration of rotational symmetry operates without relying on bases that are closed under rotation. Additionally, the SeaLL1 functional has been integrated, and the calculation of the Coulomb potential has been enhanced. The code has also undergone refactoring to streamline maintenance and support future advancements.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in \mathbb{C}: |z|<1\}$ denote the unit disk. For $0<\alpha<1$, define $f_{\alpha}(z)=z/(1-z^\alpha)$ for $z \in \mathbb{D}$. We examine the class $\mathcal{F}$ consisting of analytic functions $f_{\alpha}$ that satisfy $\Re \left(1+zf"_{\alpha}(z)/f'_{\alpha}(z)\right) > \beta$ for $0<\beta<1$. This paper establishes the region of variability for $\log f'_{\alpha}(z_0)$ at a fixed point $z_{0} \in \mathbb{D}$ as $f$ ranges over the subclass ${\mathcal F}(\lambda):=\{f_{\alpha} \in \mathcal{F}: f_{\alpha}(0)=0, f'_{\alpha}(0)=1 \, \mbox{and} \, f"_{\alpha}(0)=2\lambda (1-\beta) \,\,\, \mbox{for} \,\, 0\leq \lambda \leq 1\}$.

For a linear code $C$ defined over length $n$, dimension $k$, and minimum distance $d$, it is beneficial for the ratio $kd/n$ to be substantial. Over an arbitrary field $\mathbb{F}$, we present a new yet straightforward method to generate a recursively defined sequence of $\mathbb{F}$-linear codes $C_1, C_2, C_3, \dots$ with parameters $[n_i, k_i, d_i]$, where the value $k_id_i/n_i$ increases rapidly, satisfying $k_id_i/n_i>\sqrt{k_i}-1>2i-1$. A similar instance of rapid growth occurs within a specific subsequence of Reed-Muller codes, where $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_2$ and $k_i d_i/n_i$ behaves asymptotically as $3n_i^{c}/\sqrt{\pi\log_2(n_i)}$, with $c=\log_2(3/2)\approx 0.585$.

We introduce a warm-start strategy utilizing upfront clustering of demonstrations within feature space to enhance the Expectation Maximization (EM) framework for Multiple-Intent Inverse Reinforcement Learning (MI-IRL). This approach aims to derive a reward function ensemble capable of rationalizing demonstrations with diverse but unlabeled intents. Theoretical analysis indicates that this warm-start method yields a near-optimal reward ensemble, contingent upon mild separation conditions among behavior modes. Additionally, we propose an MI-IRL performance metric that extends the Expected Value Difference measure to evaluate learned rewards against a ground-truth ensemble. By employing a min-cost flow formulation, this metric elegantly resolves the challenge of pairing learned and true rewards while remaining computationally efficient. To facilitate rigorous algorithmic assessment, we also establish a dedicated MI-IRL benchmark problem. Experiments on this benchmark reveal that the proposed warm-start strategy prevents convergence to low-quality local minima, thereby significantly enhancing behavior clustering. Extensive sensitivity analyses confirm that the quality of learned reward ensembles improves across various configurations, even when theoretical assumptions are not strictly met. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our methods by identifying distinct driving styles within a large-scale real-world dataset of driver GPS trajectories.

The emergence of switches featuring programmable dataplanes has facilitated the swift creation of novel network capabilities and served as a foundation for accelerating diverse application-level tasks. Nevertheless, legacy switch hardware lacks the design considerations necessary for application acceleration, forcing applications that rely on operations or data types absent from standard network protocols to utilize costly workarounds. Prominent examples include distributed machine learning training and distributed query processing, which involve floating-point data. This paper introduces FPISA, a floating-point representation optimized for efficient operation within programmable switches. We initially implemented FPISA on an Intel Tofino switch but identified constraints that negatively affected both throughput and accuracy. To overcome these issues, we proposed hardware modifications grounded in the open-source Banzai switch architecture, which were synthesized using a 15-nm standard-cell library to validate their practicality. Subsequently, we leveraged FPISA to build accelerators for machine learning training and query processing, evaluating their performance via emulation on a switch incorporating our enhancements. Our results demonstrate that FPISA enables distributed training to reduce CPU core requirements by 25–75% and achieve up to 85.9% higher throughput in CPU-constrained settings compared to SwitchML. Furthermore, for distributed query processing involving floating-point data, FPISA delivers up to 2.7x improved throughput over Spark.

Let $f$ be a function mapping an $n$-dimensional vector space over $GF(p)$ to $GF(p)$. When $p=2$, Bernasconi et al. demonstrated a correspondence between specific attributes of $f$ (such as being bent) and those of its associated Cayley graph. Similarly, but earlier, Dillon proved that for $p=2$, $f$ is bent if and only if the "level curves" of $f$ possess particular combinatorial characteristics. This work seeks to develop an analogous theory for $p > 2$ by employing the combinatorial notion of a weighted partial difference set. Specifically, we aim to identify which Cayley graph properties of $f$ can be described via function-theoretic traits of $f$, and which function-theoretic properties of $f$ align with the combinatorial nature of its "level curves" (the inverse image of $f$). Although natural extensions of the Bernasconi and Dillon correspondences do not hold universally, extensive computations have enabled a classification for certain small cases. Our primary hypothesis is stated in Conjecture 67.

This paper presents O-metric spaces, a new generalization of metric-type spaces that categorizes nearly all metric types into upward and downward O-metrics. The study outlines various topologies derived from O-metrics and examines convergence, sequential continuity, first countability, and T$_2$ separation. Since the topology of an O-metric space can be generated by an upward O-metric, the analysis focuses primarily on upward O-metric spaces. The paper also proves a theorem regarding the existence and uniqueness of fixed points for certain contractive-like mappings, linking these findings to established fixed point results.
