Furthermore, applications are provided for estimating distances, establishing polygon inequalities, and optimizing entries in infinite symmetric matrices.

This research addresses set discovery, a task where the objective is to identify a specific set from a collection given only a few example tuples. A key challenge lies in the fact that these examples may not uniquely define the target set, potentially yielding a vast number of candidates. We concentrate on an interactive approach where users examine additional tuples from candidate sets to accept or reject them as members of the desired set, aiming to reach the correct set with minimal interaction. This scenario is modeled as an optimization problem involving the construction of a decision tree that guides the search process, minimizing the number of user queries required. We introduce a general algorithm capable of finding an optimal solution, along with two variants that trade off solution quality for computational efficiency. Additionally, we present a novel pruning technique that safely narrows the search space without generating false negatives. Through extensive experiments on both real and synthetic data, comparing our methods against existing literature, we demonstrate that our pruning strategy accelerates search algorithms by 2 to 5 orders of magnitude.

The determinants of second-rank tensors prove valuable for constructing generally invariant terms, exemplified by the volume element in gravitational actions. In this work, we expand the action for matter fields by introducing an arbitrary function $f(D)$, where $D$ represents the ratio of the determinant of the energy-momentum tensor to that of the metric ($D=|\textbf{det}.T|/|\textbf{det}.g|$). We derive the corresponding gravitational field equations and analyze the nonlinear contributions arising from the determinant, particularly the inverse energy-momentum tensor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such extensions necessitate a nonzero stress-energy tensor for the vacuum. We propose a scale-free model defined by $f(D)=\lambda D^{1/4}$ and illustrate how expanding the action around the vacuum stress-energy yields familiar invariant terms involving the trace of the energy-momentum tensor. By assigning specific values to the dimensionless constant $\lambda$, we investigate the hydrostatic equilibrium equations for neutron stars. Our findings reveal that for $\lambda \sim -10^{-2}$, deviations from General Relativity in mass-radius relations—which are sensitive to the equation of state—are significant. Additionally, we confirm that applying this model to the early radiation era leaves predictions regarding primordial nucleosynthesis unaffected. Ultimately, this novel form of gravity-matter coupling suggests a rich phenomenology within gravitational physics.

We examine the wave function of a tensor model within the canonical framework, specifically focusing on cases where the argument assumes Lie group invariant values or those in close proximity. Numerical results indicate the existence of two distinct phases, termed the classical and quantum phases. In the classical phase, fluctuations are suppressed, giving rise to configurations that represent discretized classical geometric spaces invariant under Lie group symmetries. This phenomenon is explicitly verified for the emergence of $S^n$ ($n=1,2,3$) under $SO(n+1)$ symmetries by analyzing both topological and geometric (Laplacian) characteristics of these configurations. The transition between phases manifests as a splitting or merging of variable distributions, analogous to the shift between one-cut and two-cut solutions in matrix models; however, the underlying mechanisms differ, obscuring a direct resemblance. Furthermore, we interpret this transition as a form of replica symmetry breaking and conduct various preliminary investigations into the properties of these phases and the transition itself for the specified argument values.

Certain special functions hold significant importance in applied statistics and probability. For instance, the cumulative central beta distribution is represented by the incomplete beta function. This paper examines the inversion of the central Student's-$t$ distribution, which serves as a specific instance of the central beta distribution. Inverting this distribution is valuable for hypothesis testing and for generating random samples following the corresponding probability density function. A key component of our analysis will be a novel asymptotic representation expressed via the complementary error function. We demonstrate that this representation also facilitates the calculation of the distribution function. Furthermore, we validate the performance of all derived approximations through numerical examples.

Plasma functions as an ionized gas that reacts collectively to internal or external disturbances. Adding micron-sized solid dust grains to this environment enhances its complexity; these grains develop significant surface negative charges and display collective dynamics akin to the surrounding plasma. Notably, the unique characteristics of this charged dust grain medium (dusty plasma) make it an ideal model system for investigating complex phenomena at a microscopic scale. This perspective paper emphasizes the utility of dusty plasma experiments as educational tools for both undergraduate and graduate physics curricula. By conducting these experiments, students can gain profound insights into fundamental physical principles while mastering advanced data analysis methodologies. The discussion further explores how a single laboratory device dedicated to dusty plasma research can significantly facilitate the learning process for students at various academic levels.

The Metaverse represents the evolution of the Internet, envisioning a persistent, immersive virtual environment where individuals can reside, study, work, and socialize. Yet, current technological limitations fail to ensure the high visual fidelity and ultra-low latency required for a seamless user experience. Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) addresses this by deploying proximal edge servers to handle latency-sensitive, computation-heavy tasks such as video analysis and image processing. By processing vast amounts of data at the source, MEC drastically cuts latency to achieve near real-time performance. This paper proposes integrating key enablers—5G and 6G wireless communications, blockchain, digital twins, and artificial intelligence—into the MEC framework to support the Metaverse. We further explore specific research challenges and applications within this MEC-driven ecosystem. Finally, through a real-world case study focused on maximizing user utility, we aim to provide deep insights into practical scenarios and identify promising future research directions.

Although $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ techniques offer robustness against worst-case perturbations, they frequently suffer a significant decline in nominal performance when faced with conventional stochastic disturbances. While this inherent compromise between robustness and nominal performance is acknowledged, it lacks a precise quantitative characterization. To address this gap, we adapt the widely adopted concept of adversarial training from machine learning to develop a class of controllers optimized for disturbances that combine both stochastic and worst-case elements. Our analysis reveals that an optimal stationary controller exists for this problem, featuring a straightforward analytic structure closely aligned with suboptimal $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ solutions. Furthermore, we present a quantitative assessment of the performance-robustness tradeoff, where system-theoretic attributes like controllability and stability emerge in an interpretable way. This framework offers practitioners actionable guidance on calibrating the level of robustness based on prior system knowledge. Finally, we empirically verify our findings by benchmarking our controller against standard baselines and visualizing the resulting tradeoff curves.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a prevalent method for deriving compact, informative representations from high-dimensional complex data. In numerous computer vision applications, such as image classification, these approaches have outperformed supervised learning methods, achieving state-of-the-art results. This study explores the potential of applying SSL to learn precise state representations within game environments and evaluates the extent of this capability. To this end, we gathered frame sequences and corresponding internal state data from three distinct 3D games: VizDoom, the CARLA racing simulator, and the Google Research Football Environment. We trained image encoders using three established SSL algorithms on raw frames alone, then sought to reconstruct the game's internal variables from these learned representations. Across all three environments, our results demonstrate a significantly stronger correlation between SSL-derived representations and the actual game state compared to pre-trained baselines like ImageNet. These findings indicate that SSL-based visual encoders can generate general, task-agnostic, yet highly informative game representations using solely pixel data. Such representations serve as a foundation for enhancing downstream learning tasks in gaming, including gameplay, content generation, and player modeling.

This note introduces a significant enhancement to the computational complexity regarding the Erd\H{o}s-Szekeres partitioning problem and provides a review of recent advancements in dynamic \textsf{LIS}.

Let $\Bbb F_q$ denote a finite field containing $q$ elements, and let $n$ be a positive integer where $rad(n)$ represents the product of its distinct prime divisors. Previous research by Martinez, Vergara, and Oliveira (2015) and Wu, Yue, and Fan (2018) established the irreducible factorization and a counting formula for $x^n-1$ over $\Bbb F_q$ under the condition that the order of $q$ modulo $rad(n)$ is either 1 or a prime. This paper extends these results by explicitly decomposing $x^n-1$ into irreducible factors within $\Bbb F_q[x]$ and determining the number of such factors when the order of $q$ modulo $rad(n)$ equals the product of two primes.

Moiré superlattices within twisted two-dimensional materials have sparked significant interest as a means to engineer quantum properties. Nevertheless, these patterns are extremely sensitive to interlayer atomic alignment, and existing assembly methods struggle with imprecise average twist angles, spatial variations in local angles, and distortions caused by random strain. We present a novel approach to modulating moiré patterns in both hetero- and homo-bilayers by applying in-plane bending to monolayer ribbons via an atomic force microscope tip. This method enables continuous adjustment of twist angles while enhancing homogeneity and minimizing random strain, thereby producing moiré patterns with highly tunable wavelengths and exceptionally low disorder. These findings establish a foundation for in-depth investigations of ultra-low disorder moiré systems and the development of precise strain-engineered devices.

Consider a compact metric space $X$ with finite topological dimension. Let $C^{0}(X)$ denote the space of continuous functions on $X$, and let $H^{\alpha}(X)$ represent the space of $\alpha$-Hölder continuous functions for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, where $H^{1}(X)$ corresponds to Lipschitz continuous functions. The inclusion hierarchy is given by:
$$H^{1}(X)\subset H^{\beta}(X) \subset H^{\alpha}(X) \subset C^{0}(X),\quad\text{ for }0<\alpha<\beta<1.$$
It is established that any $\phi \in H^{1}(X)$ possesses a metric mean dimension of zero. Conversely, if $X$ is a finite-dimensional compact manifold, a residual subset of $C^{0}(X)$ consists of functions with positive metric mean dimension. This paper demonstrates that for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$, there exists a function $\phi \in H^{\alpha}([0,1])$ exhibiting positive metric mean dimension.

This work integrates strong negation into the theory of computable functionals TCF—a widely recognized extension of Plotkin's PCF and Gödel's system $\mathbf{T}$—by concurrently defining the strong negation $A^{\mathbf{N}}$ for any formula $A$ and the strong negation $P^{\mathbf{N}}$ for any predicate $P$ within TCF. As a specific instance of the latter definition, we derive strong negations for both inductive and coinductive predicates in TCF. We establish suitable formulations of the principle of explosion (ex falso quodlibet) and double negation elimination tailored to strong negation within this framework, and we investigate "tight" formulas in TCF, which are those implied by the weak negation of their strong negation. Through various case studies and examples, we demonstrate the naturalness of our strong negation definition in TCF and validate its suitability as a formal system for a significant portion of Bishop-style constructive mathematics.

This paper examines the full engineering lifecycle of trustworthy Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, which are intended to provide critical systems with sophisticated analytics and decision-making capabilities. Beginning with foundational ML principles, we outline the essential factors that establish trust, focusing on design aspects such as domain definition, data engineering, algorithm design, implementation, evaluation, and deployment. These components are structured into a unified framework specifically for creating trusted ML systems.

While feedback and outflows linked to the quasar phase are anticipated to be critical in shutting down star formation in the most massive galaxies, observational data on the molecular outflow phase—which dominates mass and momentum removal and depletes immediate star formation fuel—is scarce in high-redshift QSO hosts. Massive quiescent galaxies at z ~ 4 are expected to have ceased star formation by z ~ 5 after experiencing their peak growth at z > 6. This study presents two ALMA detections of molecular outflows, identified via blue-shifted absorption in the OH 119-micron doublet, within a sample of three infrared-luminous QSO hosts at z > 6: J2310+1855, P183+05, and P036+03. Additionally, OH 119-micron emission was detected in P183+03 and tentatively in P036+03. Applying assumptions similar to those used for high-redshift Dusty Star-Forming Galaxy outflows, we determined that these QSOs drive molecular outflows with comparable mass outflow rates and energies, with the exception of J2310+1855, which exhibits significantly lower outflow energy flux. We found no evidence requiring additional AGN input to drive the outflow in J2310+1855; however, an AGN contribution in P183+05 cannot be ruled out if a significant AGN contribution to the far-infrared luminosity ($L_{FIR}$) is assumed or if the outflow covering fraction is high (greater than 53%), though literature suggests the latter is unlikely. Observed differences in the blue-shifted absorption spectral properties may instead stem from the QSO hosts' more compact dust continua, which limit observations to lower altitudes and more central regions of the outflows.

Chemical reactions occurring within small droplets are widely studied to expedite new material discovery, enhance efficiency and specificity in catalytic biphasic conversions, and support high-throughput analytics. This study examines the local reaction rates of gas-evolution processes inside femtoliter droplets fixed on a solid surface. We measured the growth rate of hydrogen microbubbles (with radii exceeding 500 nm) generated by these reactions using online high-resolution confocal microscopy. Our findings indicate that bubbles grew more rapidly in smaller droplets and at locations near the three-phase boundary within the same droplet. These observations held true for both pure and binary reacting droplets across substrates with varying wettability. A theoretical model incorporating diffusion, chemical reaction, and bubble growth under steady-state conditions predicted that the concentration of reactants diffusing from the surroundings depends on droplet size and bubble position, aligning well with experimental data. Consequently, our results demonstrate that reaction rates within reacting microdroplets can be spatially non-uniform, suggesting significant implications for defining the chemical properties and applications of such droplets.

Self-healing slip pulses represent a key spatiotemporal failure mechanism in frictional systems, characterized as propagating solitonic structures with a distinct length scale. This study numerically establishes a range of steady-state slip pulse solutions across both generic and realistic rate-and-state frictional interfaces that separate large, deformable contacting bodies. These nonlinear interfaces display a non-monotonic relationship between frictional strength and slip velocity, featuring a local minimum. As the driving stress approaches this local minimum from above, the resulting solutions demonstrate diverging lengths and propagation velocities dominated by strong inertial effects, while their nature shifts when the stress moves away from this point. An approximate scaling theory quantitatively accounts for these phenomena. Furthermore, the derived pulse solutions reveal significant spatially extended dissipation that exceeds edge-localized dissipation (the effective fracture energy), alongside an unconventional edge singularity. The implications of these results for existing observations are examined.

We introduce a new approach for calculating $p$-values by applying nested sampling (NS) to the sampling space, differing from its traditional application in Bayesian parameter space estimation. While the computational expense of NS grows as $\log^2{1/p}$, this represents a significant improvement over the $1/p$ scaling typical of Monte Carlo (MC) simulations. In both a toy model and a simplified resonance search, we demonstrate that for significances exceeding approximately $4\sigma$, NS achieves results with orders of magnitude fewer simulations than standard MC methods. This efficiency is especially critical for high-energy physics, where a $5\sigma$ threshold is required for discovery claims. Finally, we discuss emerging links between Bayesian and frequentist computational techniques and suggest ways to optimize NS implementations for enhanced performance in this context.

This study investigates the factors that complicate the recognition of specific classes defined by intersections. The primary focus is on unit grid intersection graphs (UGIGs), which represent intersections of unit-length axis-aligned segments; grid intersection graphs (GIGs), defined similarly but without the unit-length constraint; and string graphs, which are formed by arc-connected curves in a plane. We demonstrate that recognizing these graph classes is NP-hard, even when restricted to graphs with arbitrarily large girth (the length of the shortest cycle). Furthermore, we establish that recognition remains computationally difficult even for graphs with bounded degrees (specifically 4, 5, or 8, depending on the class). Additionally, for UGIGs, we provide structural insights regarding the size of feasible representations.

Scattering amplitudes serve as a fertile ground for uncovering new concepts in Quantum Field Theory (QFT) while holding significant phenomenological value for generating precise predictions regarding particle collider observables and, more recently, gravitational wave signals. This review chapter surveys recent advancements in reformulating QFT using mathematical and geometric constructs such as polytopes, associahedra, Grassmannians, and the amplituhedron. Within this innovative framework, traditional principles like locality and unitarity emerge as derived outcomes rather than foundational building blocks, potentially offering solutions to longstanding QFT questions that have remained unresolved for decades. The discussion begins with an introduction to positive geometry, followed by an examination of the associahedron—a simple yet physically significant geometric example—and its connection to tree-level scattering amplitudes in bi-adjoint $\phi^3$ theory. The second focus is the amplituhedron construction applied to scattering amplitudes in planar maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory.

Word segmentation serves as the foundational step for all Vietnamese language processing tasks. This paper reviews state-of-the-art methods and systems for segmenting Vietnamese words. To provide a comprehensive overview spanning from corpus construction to toolkit development, we examine the corpus building process, segmentation approaches, and existing tools for processing Vietnamese sentences. Furthermore, this study highlights the motivations behind creating corpora and implementing machine learning techniques to enhance segmentation accuracy. Based on our observations, the research also reports specific achievements and limitations found in current Vietnamese word segmentation systems.

Efficiently exciting quantum sources like quantum dots or single molecules typically demands high numerical aperture (NA) optics, a requirement that often conflicts with the constraints of cryogenic or ultrafast environments. We introduce a 3.2 µm wide parabolic mirror with a 0.8 µm focal length, created through direct laser writing on CdSe/CdS colloidal quantum dots. This device focuses excitation light into a sub-wavelength spot and collimates emitted photons into a narrow beam. Manufactured using in-situ volumetric optical lithography, the mirror can be precisely aligned to individual emitters and is adaptable to various geometries beyond the paraboloid shape. As a compact solid-state transducer bridging the far-field and the emitter, this technology holds significant promise for objective-free quantum applications.

From a Bayesian standpoint, the category of conditional probabilities—which serves as a variant of the Kleisli category for the Giry monad, featuring measurable spaces as objects and Markov kernels as arrows—offers a robust framework for conceptualizing and analyzing various facets of machine learning. By applying categorical techniques, we develop models for both parametric and nonparametric Bayesian reasoning within function spaces, thereby establishing a foundation for supervised learning. Specifically, stochastic processes act as arrows into these function spaces, functioning as prior probabilities. Consequently, the resulting inference maps can frequently be derived analytically within this symmetric monoidal weakly closed category. Furthermore, we illustrate how general stochastic processes can be understood through functor categories and present the Kalman filter as a representative example of the hidden Markov model.

Functional Data Analysis is an increasingly significant area within statistics. Although numerous studies have yielded fundamental insights, the development of valid and efficient prediction sets remains largely unaddressed. Most existing methods depend heavily on strong distributional assumptions (such as Gaussianity), dimension reduction, or asymptotic reasoning. This work introduces a novel nonparametric approach grounded in Conformal Prediction, utilizing a new class of nonconformity measures to generate predictors that produce closed-form, finite-sample valid or exact prediction sets with minimal distributional constraints. Furthermore, the resulting prediction sets are structured as bands, a critical feature for functional data that facilitates visualization and interpretation. The proposed method is rapid and scalable, avoids functional dimension reduction, and permits users to select appropriate nonconformity measures for specific problems while guaranteeing valid bands. Within this framework, we present a specific measure that yields prediction bands asymptotically as efficient as those with constant width.

Continual learning focuses on acquiring new tasks over time while retaining knowledge of prior ones, a challenge often addressed with limited or no access to historical data. Existing solutions typically employ complex strategies such as memory replay, knowledge distillation, model regularization, and dynamic network expansion, which incur retraining costs at every step, demand specific memory allocations, and rely on design choices tailored to particular settings. This study demonstrates that a frozen CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) model achieves remarkable continual learning performance without any fine-tuning, enabling zero-shot evaluation. We assessed CLIP across diverse scenarios—including class-incremental, domain-incremental, and task-agnostic incremental learning—using five standard benchmarks (ImageNet-100 & 1K, CORe50, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet). Without additional enhancements, CLIP surpassed state-of-the-art continual learning methods in most configurations. Furthermore, we investigated performance variations by adjusting text inputs through simple prompt templates. To our knowledge, this is the first report of CLIP's zero-shot capabilities within a continual learning framework. We recommend this robust yet deceptively simple baseline as a standard for future continual learning comparisons.

CTCV J2056-3014 is a nearby cataclysmic variable located approximately 853 light-years away, characterized by an orbital period of roughly 1.76 hours. Recent X-ray observations identify it as an unusual accretion-powered intermediate polar featuring a rapidly spinning white dwarf (WD) with a spin period of 29.6 seconds. Given its low X-ray luminosity and modest accretion rate per unit area, the accretion shock likely does not form near the WD surface; consequently, the maximum shock temperature cannot be used to estimate the WD mass, which would otherwise be inferred as approximately 0.46 $M_\odot$. This study investigates the stability of this fast-rotating WD using a modern equation of state (EoS) that incorporates electron-ion, electron-electron, and ion-ion interactions. We calculate the mass density thresholds for pycnonuclear fusion and examine how microscopic stability and rapid rotation influence the structure of WDs composed of helium, carbon, oxygen, and neon. Our analysis establishes a minimum mass of 0.56 $M_\odot$ and a maximum mass of roughly 1.38 $M_\odot$ for CTCV J2056-3014. If the object's mass approaches the lower limit, its equatorial radius, expanded by rapid rotation, would be approximately $10^4$ km—significantly larger than the ~7,000 km radius of a nonrotating average-mass WD ($0.6\, M_\odot$). Furthermore, variations in stellar matter temperature and composition were found to have a negligible impact on the calculated minimum mass.

As Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) become increasingly widespread, ensuring their coexistence and mitigating interference has emerged as a critical challenge. To address this, the study proposes two-hop relay-assisted cooperative communications utilizing opportunistic relaying (OR) to enhance WBAN coexistence. The access protocols for both intra-WBAN and inter-WBAN scenarios employ appropriate Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) schemes. To replicate real-world WBAN conditions, the research utilizes extensive on-body and inter-body channel measurements under "everyday" usage scenarios. Furthermore, a realistic inter-WBAN channel model is simulated to analyze how body shadowing and hub placement impact WBAN performance in fostering coexistence. Comparisons with single-link communications reveal that opportunistic relaying significantly improves the Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR), outage probability, and Level Crossing Rate (LCR) regarding outages; however, the Average Outage Duration (AOD) remains unchanged. Additionally, a lognormal distribution provides a superior fit for received SINR when channel coherence time is short, whereas a Nakagami-m distribution is more appropriate for stable channels. Based on these estimated SINR distributions, theoretical calculations for outage probability, LCR, and AOD align closely with empirical results.

A continuous linear operator $L$ on the space of entire functions $\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{C})$ is defined as an extended $\lambda$-eigenoperator of the differentiation operator $D$ if it satisfies the commutation relation $DL = \lambda LD$. This paper provides a complete characterization of the conditions under which such an operator is supercyclic, possesses a hypercyclic subspace, or contains a supercyclic subspace.

Singing Voice Conversion (SVC) represents a promising method for enhancing human-computer interaction by enabling computers to generate high-fidelity and expressive singing voices. This paper introduces DiffSVC, an SVC framework built upon denoising diffusion probabilistic models. The system utilizes phonetic posteriorgrams (PPGs) as content features and employs a denoising module that accepts distorted mel spectrograms generated during the diffusion/forward process, along with their corresponding step information, to predict the added Gaussian noise. To facilitate this denoising process, the model also incorporates auxiliary inputs comprising PPGs, fundamental frequency features, and loudness features. Experimental results demonstrate that DiffSVC achieves superior performance in terms of naturalness and voice similarity compared to current state-of-the-art SVC methods.

This paper introduces the concept of $n$-L-dendriform algebras, which represent a dendrification of $n$-pre-Lie algebras via $\mathcal{O}$-operators. We explore the representation theory of $n$-pre-Lie algebras and offer several associated constructions. Additionally, we define the phase space of an $n$-Lie algebra, demonstrating that such a phase space exists if and only if the $n$-Lie algebra is sub-adjacent to an $n$-pre-Lie algebra. Finally, we outline a method for constructing $(n + 1)$-pre-Lie algebras starting from $n$-pre-Lie algebras endowed with a generalized trace function.

Although extensive research exists on detecting lexical semantic change, few methods extend beyond standard benchmark evaluations. This paper advocates shifting the focus from mere detection to discovery, specifically identifying novel word senses emerging over time across the entire vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both token-based and type-based approaches on recently published German data, we demonstrate that these models can effectively uncover words undergoing meaning shifts. Additionally, we present an almost fully automated framework for both discovery and evaluation.

Unlike public exchanges such as the NYSE, Over-the-Counter (OTC) trading relies on broker-dealers to ensure price stability and market liquidity. This study employs machine learning to model and forecast the trading strategies of OTC dealers in the US corporate bond market. By constructing daily transaction sequences for each dealer across a specific vocabulary of bonds, we utilize this historical activity to anticipate future trading choices. We evaluate various neural network architectures and introduce the Pointwise-Product ReZero (PPRZ) Transformer, demonstrating its superior performance. Our findings indicate that individual-specific historical data yields the highest accuracy for highly active dealers, whereas collective models outperform for those with lower activity levels. Additionally, clustering dealers based on behavioral similarities enhances predictive capability, and overall accuracy fluctuates depending on the activity levels of both the specific bond and the dealer.

How does online popularity develop? Does success require immediate viral traction, or can it be cultivated through consistent, disciplined effort? What other temporal indicators reveal the trajectory of online content? To address these inquiries, we employ a comprehensive temporal analysis of how popular online content evolves. We introduce dipm-SC, a multi-dimensional shape-based time-series clustering algorithm enhanced with a heuristic for determining the optimal cluster count. First, we verify the algorithm's accuracy using synthetic data derived from standard time-series models. Next, we demonstrate that dipm-SC effectively identifies distinct patterns of popularity behavior within a real-world Twitter dataset. By clustering multi-dimensional popularity time-series alongside other domain-specific metrics, we reveal two primary temporal patterns: bursty and steady growth. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the specific manner in which popularity is accumulated over time does not significantly influence the total cumulative popularity achieved.

In recent years, knowledge graphs (KGs) have become increasingly prevalent across diverse fields to facilitate applications such as question answering and recommendations. A common challenge when merging knowledge from multiple KGs is identifying which subgraphs correspond to the same real-world entity. Lately, embedding techniques have been employed for entity alignment, learning vector-space representations that maintain entity similarity within the original KGs. Numerous supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised approaches have been developed, leveraging both factual (attribute-based) and structural (relation-based) entity information. However, the literature lacks a quantitative evaluation of these methods' strengths and weaknesses in real-world KGs based on various performance metrics and KG characteristics. This study presents the first meta-level analysis of popular embedding methods for entity alignment, utilizing a statistically rigorous methodology. Our findings reveal statistically significant correlations between different embedding methods and various KG meta-features, allowing us to rank these methods effectively across all real-world KGs in our testbed. Finally, we examine key trade-offs regarding the effectiveness and efficiency of these methods.

We demonstrate that a one-dimensional tight-binding chain, consisting of both interacting and non-interacting atomic sites, can display multiple mobility edges at distinct carrier energy levels when subjected to an external electric field. Employing a mean-field Hartree-Fock approximation, we numerically determine two-terminal transport properties via the Green's function formalism. Our study examines various configurations of interacting and non-interacting atoms within the chain. These findings could assist in the design of mesoscale switching devices.

We propose the existence of novel $k_\perp$-dependent functions. Unlike the established Boer-Mulders function, these new functions relate to the collective alignment of quark spins. Additionally, they exhibit sensitivity to the transverse motion of partons within hadrons, which is connected to their spin alignment, and arise from interactions represented by the relevant correlators.

Although simple models are generally favored over complex ones, excessive simplification can result in incorrect conclusions. The traditional method involves beginning with a basic model, evaluating its limitations through residual diagnostics, and then incrementally increasing complexity to achieve a superior fit. In contrast, this work demonstrates transformation analysis as an alternative strategy for model selection. Rather than building up from simplicity, this approach employs step-wise complexity reduction to uncover models that are both simpler and more interpretable. Using body mass index distributions in Switzerland as a case study, the analysis examines how factors like sex, age, smoking, and other lifestyle choices influence BMI via transformation models. The primary goal was to balance model fit with interpretability, with particular attention paid to the relationships between transformation models of varying complexity. The models span a spectrum from established methods, such as normal linear regression with constant variance, to innovative, highly flexible approaches like transformation trees and forests.

The detailed analysis covers how incident incoherent electromagnetic radiation, such as sunlight, excites molecules and contrasts this with the effects of coherent light sources like lasers. Particular emphasis is placed on the quantum coherences generated by incoherent radiation, which are significant for transport mechanisms in both natural and technological contexts. The discussion addresses both equilibrium and steady-state scenarios, utilizing three illustrative examples—simple models, calcium excitation under polarized light, and retinal isomerization within rhodopsin—to reveal the fundamental qualitative characteristics of these established coherences.

Collisionless physics plays a dominant role in governing the transport of fusion-generated alpha particles within three-dimensional equilibrium states. In stellarators, various transport pathways are identified, including stochastic diffusion arising from class transitions, ripple trapping, and banana drift-convective orbits. By analyzing guiding center dynamics across six quasihelical and quasiaxisymmetric equilibria, we classify the resulting trapping states and transport mechanisms. Beyond standard banana drift convection and ripple transport, we detect significant non-conservation of the parallel adiabatic invariant, which can lead to losses via diffusive banana tip motion. Additionally, numerous lost trajectories exhibit transitions between trapping classes over extended timescales, displaying either periodic or irregular patterns. We explore potential optimization strategies for each identified transport mechanism and compare fast ion losses against metrics indicating the prevalence of specific phenomena such as banana-drift convection, transitioning orbits, and wide orbit widths. The results indicate that quasihelical configurations offer inherent protection against ripple-trapping and diffusive banana tip motion, thereby reducing prompt losses.

We re-examine the orbital period decay in binary systems caused by gravitational wave emission within modified gravity frameworks where the coupling $G_{gw}$ between matter and on-shell gravitons may deviate from the Newton constant $G_N$. Leveraging the most accurate orbital parameters from the Double Pulsar, we restrict the ratio $G_{gw}/G_N$ to a precision of $10^{-4}$, thereby enhancing the current limit on this parameter by two orders of magnitude.

This paper introduces a methodology for quantifying how program evaluations narrow disparities between demographic groups, such as those defined by gender or race. We begin by demonstrating that the decrease in inter-group disparities can be expressed as the difference in conditional average treatment effects (CATE) across each group. Subsequently, employing a Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder-style decomposition, we analyze how these CATEs break down into unexplained variations in CATEs regarding other observables versus compositional differences across those same observables (e.g., endowments). Finally, we utilize this framework to examine the effects of Medicare on Americans' access to health insurance.

Recent years have seen intense efforts to establish lower bounds for homogeneous depth-4 arithmetic circuits, achieving results that nearly imply $\textsf{VP} \neq \textsf{VNP}$. It remains an open question whether these methods can extend beyond homogeneity. This paper advances that inquiry by examining depth-4 circuits with low algebraic rank, a natural generalization of the homogeneous case. A depth-4 circuit represents an $N$-variate, degree-$n$ polynomial $P$ as $P = \sum_{i = 1}^T Q_{i1}\cdot Q_{i2}\cdot \cdots \cdot Q_{it}$, where each $Q_{ij}$ is expressed via its monomial expansion. While homogeneity requires that $\sum_{j} \operatorname{deg}(Q_{ij}) = n$ for all $i$, we investigate a broader constraint where the algebraic rank of the set $\{Q_{i1}, Q_{i2}, \ldots ,Q_{it}\}$ is bounded by a parameter $k$. Notably, when $k = n$, these circuits encompass the homogeneous class, as this implies $t \leq n$ and consequently $k \leq n$.

We analyze lower bounds and polynomial identity tests for these circuits, yielding several key findings. First, we demonstrate an $\exp{(\Omega(\sqrt{n}\log N))}$ lower bound for an explicit family of $N$-variate, degree-$n$ polynomials when $k \leq n$. Second, we present quasipolynomial hitting sets under the condition that both the degree of each $Q_{ij}$ and the parameter $k$ are bounded by $\operatorname{poly}(\log n)$. A pivotal technical component of our proofs, potentially of independent value, establishes that over fields of characteristic zero, every polynomial in a given set can be expressed as a function of the polynomials in a transcendence basis of that set, up to a translation. By integrating this result with techniques involving shifted partial derivatives, we derive our final conclusions.

Substantial advancements across various material classes are anticipated if large, experimentally sourced datasets containing atomic identities and 3D coordinates become widely available. Techniques like atom probe tomography (APT), which routinely produce datasets with millions of atoms, represent a critical step toward this objective. Nevertheless, current APT instruments often yield noisy and sparse data that reveal elemental composition while obscuring atomic arrangements, thereby restricting their utility for materials discovery. Applying a materials fingerprinting process—a machine learning algorithm integrated with topological data analysis—offers a pathway to extract previously unattainable structural insights from APT data. As a proof of concept, this fingerprinting method was applied to high-entropy alloy APT datasets featuring both body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) structures. By assigning a topological descriptor to the local atomic configuration around an arbitrary atom, the system successfully characterized the lattice type as either BCC or FCC with near-perfect accuracy, overcoming inherent data noise. This successful fingerprint identification marks a vital initial step in developing algorithms capable of deriving more detailed information, such as chemical ordering, from existing datasets of complex materials.

Robot-assisted surgical procedures often involve planning and controlling manipulator movements that interact with highly deformable objects. This study introduces a realistic, time-constrained simulator utilizing Position-based Dynamics (PBD) to emulate brain deformation caused by catheter insertion, thereby aiding pre-operative path planning and intra-operative guidance in keyhole surgeries. To enhance the probability of success, the model incorporates uncertainties related to deformation models, sensor noise, and unpredictable actuation. Initial PBD deformation parameters were set on a parallelepiped-shaped simulated phantom to establish a viable baseline for brain white matter, subsequently calibrated by comparing displacement results against data from catheter insertion tests on a composite hydrogel phantom. Recognizing the distinct behaviors of gray matter structures, these parameters were further refined to create a generalized human brain model, with average structural displacements validated against existing literature. The simulator's numerical approach differs from current literature and has demonstrated a close alignment with real brain deformations through validation using in-vivo animal trial data, achieving a mean mismatch of 4.73$\pm$2.15%. Due to its stability, accuracy, and real-time capabilities, this model is well-suited for establishing a dynamic environment for keyhole navigation (KN) path planning, pre-operative planning, and intra-operative guidance.

Using input-output time-domain data from a complex simulator, this study introduces a constructive method to derive a reduced-order linear, bilinear, or quadratic time-invariant dynamical model that accurately replicates underlying phenomena. Grounded in linear dynamical systems and approximation theory, the method sequentially employs the versatile and scalable interpolatory Pencil and Loewner frameworks, alongside a linear least squares problem utilizing raw data and reduced internal variables. Unlike intrusive techniques, it requires no prior knowledge of the operator. Furthermore, compared to traditional non-intrusive operator inference methods, it eliminates the necessity of measuring internal variables of the original full-order model, thereby expanding its applicability beyond standard approaches. The proposed rationale is successfully demonstrated through a large eddy simulation of pollutant dispersion over an airport area, which involves multi-scale and multi-physics dynamical phenomena. Although the resulting low-complexity model is simple, it delivers satisfactory predictions of the pollutant plume pattern while offering significantly faster simulation speeds.

The defining event of 2020 was the emergence of the Coronavirus Disease (Covid-19), a lethal pathogen that compromises the respiratory system so severely that patients often require ventilator support. By June 21, 2020, the virus had reached 12,929,306 confirmed cases and caused 569,738 deaths across 216 countries, territories, and areas. The pandemic's unprecedented scale forced nations to grapple with both preventive and curative strategies. The infamous lockdowns implemented to curb transmission drastically disrupted social routines, causing a surge in demand for online services. As the virus spread, so did misinformation and fake news circulating through social media, where virality often outweighs truth. With much of the population confined to their homes for extended periods, the risk of being harmed by toxic online disinformation became significant. For instance, various myths surrounding Covid-19, if unaddressed, could lead to catastrophic consequences and undermine efforts to combat the virus.

While scientists actively work on identifying treatments, there is increasing focus on fighting the associated harmful "infodemic." In response, researchers have begun curating and documenting various Covid-19 datasets. Consistent with existing studies, we present an extensive collection of curated data to aid in the fight against the pandemic, particularly regarding misinformation. This collection includes three categories of Twitter data, information on standard practices from credible sources, and a chronicle of global situation reports. We also explain how to access the hydrated versions of this data and propose research problems that can be addressed using it.

Adversarial attacks continue to pose a major challenge for neural networks. Although recent studies indicate that adversarial perturbations predominantly consist of high-frequency components, the underlying reasons for this remain unclear. Drawing inspiration from theoretical research on linear full-width convolutional models, we propose that the local (bounded-width) convolutions standard in current networks create an implicit bias toward learning high-frequency features, thereby contributing to the prevalence of high-frequency adversarial examples. To validate this hypothesis, we examined how various linear and nonlinear architectural choices influence the implicit bias of learned features and adversarial perturbations across both spatial and frequency domains. Our findings reveal that high-frequency adversarial perturbations are critically reliant on the convolution operation, as the spatially constrained nature of local convolutions induces a bias toward high frequencies. This phenomenon is explained by the Fourier Uncertainty Principle, which dictates that a filter limited in the spatial domain cannot simultaneously be limited in the frequency domain. Additionally, employing larger kernel sizes or eliminating convolutions entirely (e.g., through Vision Transformers) substantially mitigates this high-frequency bias, though it does not fully eliminate overall vulnerability to attacks. Looking ahead, our research underscores that comprehending and regulating the implicit biases inherent in architectures will be crucial for achieving robustness against adversarial attacks.

The COVID-19 recession risks widespread housing instability that could derail economic recovery. Although unprecedented federal interventions paused court-ordered evictions, uncertainties persist regarding whether these measures sufficiently address the complex dynamics of landlord-tenant relationships, such as mounting arrears, limited unit availability, and scarce affordable housing options. A system dynamics model examines the intricate feedback loops influencing decision-making by tenants and landlords in the low-income rental market both before and after pandemic-era protections were enacted. These feedback loops reveal the tradeoffs faced by low-income households amid scarcity and uncertainty. Simulations indicate that the eviction moratorium successfully reduced evictions by 51% prior to its expiration in late 2021; however, rates of rental arrears, overcrowding, and homelessness remained elevated. While federal emergency rental assistance helped maintain low eviction numbers, its impact on alleviating housing insecurity and homelessness was modest, suggesting that faster fund allocation would significantly enhance effectiveness. Ultimately, failing to resolve underlying financial hardships and the shortage of affordable housing will hinder the nation's recovery from the pandemic.

George Boros and Victor Moll's seminal work, *Irresistible Integrals*, appropriately features an appendix on "The Revolutionary WZ Method," offering a concise introduction to the celebrated Wilf–Zeilberger technique for definite summation. Ironically, the book lacks a similarly titled appendix for "The Revolutionary AZ Method," which would have provided an excellent summary of the Almkvist–Zeilberger method for definite integration. While this oversight is forgivable, it certainly needs correction, as the remarkable AZ framework deserves broader recognition. To address this, we will present a series of case studies that conclude with a playful yet excessive integral-based proof demonstrating the irrationality of $e$.

Within formal concept analysis, the set of protoconcepts for any context constitutes a fully contextual double Boolean algebra (dBa), whereas semiconcepts form a pure dBa. This article investigates topological representations of dBas, with specific attention to fully contextual and pure variants. The study introduces a context on topological spaces (CTS), focusing on a specialized subclass termed CTSCR, where both the defining relation and its converse are continuous relative to the underlying topologies. It is demonstrated that the clopen object-oriented protoconcepts of a CTSCR generate a fully contextual dBa, while their semiconcept counterparts yield a pure dBa. The paper further proves that every dBa can be quasi-embedded into the dBa of clopen object-oriented protoconcepts of a specific CTSCR; this quasi-embedding becomes a standard embedding for contextual dBas and an isomorphism for fully contextual ones. Additionally, pure dBas are shown to be isomorphic to the algebra of clopen object-oriented semiconcepts of the CTSCR. The work also addresses representations for finite dBas and Boolean algebras. By abstracting the properties of CTSCR, the concept of Stone contexts is defined. The resulting category, Scxt, comprises Stone contexts and CTSCR-homeomorphisms, exhibiting a correspondence between dBa isomorphisms and these homeomorphisms. This relationship drives the second part of the article, which explores the categorical duality of dBas. Categories PDBA and FCDBA are defined for pure and fully contextual dBas along with their isomorphisms. It is established that PDBA is equivalent to FCDBA, and both are dually equivalent to Scxt.

Contrastive divergence (CD) serves as a promising inference technique for high-dimensional distributions with intractable normalizing constants, yet its theoretical underpinnings remain somewhat unstable. This document introduces a framework to elucidate CD inference, specifying the conditions under which it succeeds, and offers multiple justifications for its moment conditions, notably by casting them as a variational approximation. The text discusses inference algorithms, applying them to social network data via exponential-family random graph models (ERGM). Furthermore, the framework offers guidance on constructing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) kernels that yield effective CD inference, revealing that these kernels differ significantly from those typically employed to achieve rapid global mixing.

We present two characterizations of Jacobians associated with curves possessing an involution with fixed points, situated within the context of two specific instances of Welter's trisecant conjecture. Geometrically, each characterization asserts that these Jacobians are precisely those that contain a shifted Abelian subvariety, the image of which under the Kummer map is orthogonal to a clearly defined vector.

Temporal ontology and reasoning are typically grounded in two established approaches: point-based and interval-based frameworks. Conventionally, interval-based reasoning treats points as a specific instance of duration-less intervals. However, a recent study by Balbiani, Goranko, and Sciavicco introduced an explicit two-sorted point-interval framework where time instants and time periods hold equal status, enabling a flexible shift between these perspectives within formal discourse. This paper examines two-sorted first-order languages built on the same principle, incorporating relations between points, between intervals, and across sorts, as originally explored by Reich and others. We provide complete classifications of sub-languages based on relative expressive power, identifying the specific number and types of intrinsically distinct extensions of two-sorted first-order logic augmented with one or more such relations. This methodology resolves the classical debate regarding whether points must be included in interval-based semantics. Part II of this work addresses scenarios involving all dense and all unbounded linearly ordered sets.

In federated learning (FL) environments, such as wireless networks, communication overhead between clients and the central server often acts as a bottleneck. To mitigate this, communication compression has emerged as a prevalent strategy. This paper specifically investigates biased gradient compression within non-convex FL scenarios. While error feedback (EF) is a standard approach in distributed learning to counteract the drawbacks of biased compression, we examine a compressed FL framework utilizing EF, termed Fed-EF. We introduce two specific variants, Fed-EF-SGD and Fed-EF-AMS, contingent on the global model optimizer used. Our generic theoretical analysis reveals that applying biased compression directly in FL results in a non-vanishing bias affecting the convergence rate; however, Fed-EF successfully matches the convergence rate of full-precision FL methods under data heterogeneity while achieving linear speedup. Additionally, we present a novel analysis of EF under partial client participation, a critical FL scenario. We demonstrate that partial participation introduces an extra slowdown factor in the Fed-EF convergence rate due to a "stale error compensation" effect, a finding supported by numerical studies on the impact of stale error accumulation on norm convergence. Furthermore, we show that integrating two-way compression into Fed-EF does not alter these convergence outcomes. In summary, this work offers a comprehensive theoretical examination of error feedback in federated non-convex optimization. Our analysis of partial participation also highlights theoretical limitations of the EF mechanism and suggests potential avenues for future enhancements.

Simulating geometrically resolved rigid particles within a fluid requires coupling algorithms to exchange momentum bidirectionally between the two phases. This study employs a parallel Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) featuring adaptive grid refinement to enhance numerical efficiency, utilizing the momentum exchange technique for particle coupling. When applied in its basic form, this coupling can become unstable if the particles are less dense than the fluid; however, stability is restored through a virtual mass correction specifically tailored for LBM. The proposed approach is evaluated across a broad range of physically significant regimes, independently varying the density ratio between the body and the fluid, as well as the relative scales of inertial and viscous forces. Investigations into a single rising particle reveal periodic and chaotic motion regimes, consistent with prior literature. Furthermore, the new method is rigorously benchmarked against existing experimental and numerical data. This comparison not only validates the coupled LBM framework but also yields novel physical insights for specific parameter configurations.

The efficacy of large-scale clinical trials is often compromised by poor recruitment, follow-up, and adherence. External pilot studies assess these metrics and apply pre-defined decision rules to evaluate whether a definitive trial is viable. However, there is limited methodological guidance on selecting these decision rules or determining the appropriate sample size for pilots. This paper introduces a hypothesis testing framework for assessing the feasibility of a definitive trial using external pilot data to guide progression decisions. Feasibility is quantified by the anticipated power of the planned trial, dependent on recruitment, follow-up, and adherence rates. Based on this metric, we formulate testable hypotheses, propose a specific test statistic, and derive methods to calculate error rates for a common two-arm parallel group design with a normally distributed primary endpoint. We apply this methodology to re-design the TIGA-CUB external pilot trial, which compared psychotherapy against treatment as usual for children with conduct disorders. Furthermore, we extend the approach to utilize pilot data for estimating the primary endpoint's standard deviation and integrate this estimate into the final progression decision.

Gravitational-wave detectors comprise intricate and delicate ensembles of advanced instruments that are influenced by both mechanical and electronic systems as well as the surrounding environment. Consequently, it is crucial to classify and mitigate noise by leveraging data from numerous auxiliary channels associated with these devices and their surroundings to detect gravitational-wave signals. This approach enhances the signal-to-noise ratio and diminishes false alarms triggered by coincident loud events. Therefore, establishing coherent relationships among complex channels is vital. This study introduces a method for identifying both linear and non-linear couplings between related channels using correlation coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's applicability to practical challenges within gravitational-wave detectors, including noise generated by lightning strikes, air compressor vibrations, and wind effects.

Within the unified model of active galactic nuclei (AGN), a dusty torus intercepts and reprocesses a portion of the intrinsic luminosity emitted at longer wavelengths. Consequently, after accounting for radiative transfer effects, the torus's covering factor ($f_c$)—representing the fraction of the sky obscured as viewed from the central engine—can be approximated by the ratio of infrared to bolometric luminosities ($f_c = L_{\rm torus}/L_{\rm Bol}$). However, uncertainties in calculating $L_{\rm Bol}$ complicate this estimation, particularly for nearby AGN where the spectral energy distribution (SED) peaks in the ultraviolet. In this study, we determine $f_c$ for a sample of 51 X-ray/optically selected type~1 AGN by deriving their bolometric luminosities using a self-consistent, energy-conserving model that accounts for the unobservable far-UV region via multi-frequency data from SDSS, \textit{XMM-Newton}, \textit{WISE}, 2MASS, and UKIDSS. We find a mean covering factor of $f_c \sim 0.30$ with a dispersion of 0.17. Analysis of sample correlations alongside simulations indicates that $f_c$ exhibits a stronger anti-correlation with $\lambda_{\rm Edd}$ than with $L_{\rm Bol}$. This suggests that large-scale variations in torus geometry are driven by Eddington-dependent accretion flows rather than a receding torus whose inner sublimation radius is set solely by central heating. Additionally, we observe no significant differences in the $f_c$ distribution between radio-loud sources and Narrow Line Seyfert~1 galaxies (NLS1s), although these sub-samples are limited in size.

Understanding cooperation among agents relies heavily on game theory, particularly the widely studied Prisoner's Dilemma within complex networks. While prior research has examined how cooperation emerges, the specific impact of memory on its evolution remains unclear. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of cooperation dynamics involving agents equipped with memory. By simulating the evolutionary Prisoner's Dilemma across random, scale-free, and degree-correlated networks, we demonstrate that assortativity enhances cooperation as the temptation to defect rises. Additionally, our findings indicate that incorporating memory diminishes the influence of network structure. These results advance our comprehension of how network topology and player memory jointly shape cooperative behavior.

Predicting trends is a critical challenge across various scientific fields. This study specifically addresses trend prediction within complex networks, aiming to forecast which nodes will become the most popular in the future. While existing methods have successfully utilized recent and cumulative node degrees based on preferential attachment mechanisms in real-world systems, we introduce a novel temporal-based predictor (TBP) that incorporates more granular details regarding network evolution. The TBP estimates future trends by calculating node strength in a weighted network where link weights follow an exponential aging function. Validated using three time-series datasets, our results demonstrate that the TBP achieves high accuracy in identifying future popular nodes. Notably, it effectively uncovers objects that were previously obscure but are poised to gain significant popularity. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of how the decay rate in the exponential aging process influences these outcomes.

We define split Malcev-Poisson-Jordan algebras as the natural generalization of split Malcev Poisson algebras and split (non-commutative) Poisson algebras. We demonstrate that any split Malcev-Poisson-Jordan algebra $P$ decomposes into a direct sum $P = \oplus_{j \in J}I_j$, where each $I_j$ is a non-zero ideal of $P$, such that for distinct indices $j_1 \neq j_2$, the conditions $[I_{j_1},I_{j_2}] = 0$ and $I_{j_1} \circ I_{j_2} = 0$ hold. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we establish that this decomposition is determined by the family of $P$'s simple ideals.

We show that a simple feedforward neural network can simultaneously and sensitively identify two successive phase transitions linked to the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase in q-state clock models by examining the weights connecting the hidden and output layers. This approach requires only raw spatial spin configurations generated via Monte-Carlo thermalization at specific temperatures for training. Unlike most supervised machine learning methods, it does not rely on prior knowledge of transition temperatures, phase counts, or order parameters, nor does it need preprocessed data such as vortex configurations, spin orientation histograms, or correlation functions. For the eight-state clock model on a square lattice, the network determined the transition temperatures to be $T_2/J = 0.921$ (paramagnetic-to-BKT) and $T_1/J = 0.410$ (BKT-to-ferromagnetic), both of which align closely with results from previous numerical studies.

This study introduces a framework to measure a nation's digital investigative capacity and saturation, specifically to guide future expansion strategies. It highlights the critical role of external international partners, noting that they can negatively impact the return on investment if not properly managed. The research concludes that when addressing digital crime, expanding national capacity must account for international partners, as they may serve as a limiting factor or bottleneck for investigation requests.

A common method for proving theorems in modal logic involves translating them into predicate calculus and applying standard resolution-based provers. However, this strategy has often been deemed impractical due to the excessive length of the generated formulas and the inability to demonstrate that modal formulas are non-theorems. This paper establishes the practical viability of the relational translation method. By employing a state-of-the-art first-order logic theorem prover, we successfully verified numerous benchmark theorems drawn from the modal logic literature. Furthermore, we established the invalidity of propositional modal and temporal logic formulas by utilizing model generators or satisfiability testers for classical logic. Our analysis revealed that many satisfiable formulas correspond to extremely small models. Finally, we compare several distinct approaches.

Recent advancements in 4D-Particle Tracking Velocimetry (4D-PTV) have consistently yielded more precise Lagrangian particle trajectories. This paper proposes a novel Track Initialisation technique designed to complement 4D-PTV by leveraging the local temporal and spatial coherence of neighboring trajectories. The introduced Lagrangian Coherent Track Initialisation (LCTI) method utilizes physics-based Finite Time Lyapunov Exponents (FTLE) to construct tracks that are coherent across four frames. Specifically, it employs FTLE to identify the boundaries (ridges) of Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCS) among adjacent trajectories, thereby distinguishing clusters of coherent motion. To validate this approach, an open-access synthetic dataset comprising both Lagrangian and Eulerian data was generated from 3D Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of a smooth cylinder wake at a Reynolds number of 3900; this dataset is publicly available. Evaluation of the LCTI method across three key parameters—temporal scale, particle density, and noise ratio—demonstrated robust performance in identifying true tracks compared to recent initialization algorithms, with sensitivity regarding untracked and erroneous tracks also analyzed. Furthermore, the study addresses the method's applicability within 4D-PTV schemes for high-density particle flows in the context of the Lagrangian Particle Tracking challenge. Finally, the LCTI behavior was assessed using a real-world jet impingement experiment, confirming its reliability as a tracking tool for complex flow dynamics, particularly in scenarios involving high particle concentrations.

Determining the configuration of line defects within a Quantum Field Theory under a specific duality is generally a challenging task. This work serves as the second installment in a series dedicated to resolving this issue through the lens of 3d $\mathcal{N}=4$ mirror symmetry. In a previous publication [arxiv:2103.01243], the author introduced a general method for building vortex defects and determining their mirror counterparts in quiver gauge theories extending beyond $A$-type, illustrating this with examples of $D$-type and affine $D$-type quivers. The current paper utilizes this established prescription to generate a family of vortex defects, modeled as coupled 3d-1d systems, for quiver gauge theories that exceed the $ADE$ classification. Our investigation specifically targets quiver gauge theories containing unitary gauge nodes linked by edge multiplicities greater than one, meaning two nodes can be connected by multiple bifundamental hypermultiplets. Such theories emerge as 3d mirrors of specific Argyres-Douglas theories compactified on a circle. Certain instances of these quiver gauge theories possess a pair of 3d mirrors that are related by an infrared duality, a topic recently explored in [arxiv:2109.07493]. For a concrete case where such a pair of 3d mirrors exists, we examine how the vortex defects constructed via our method correspond to Wilson defects in each of the mirror theories.

This paper introduces BESSIE (Behavior and Epidemic Simulator for Synthetic Information Environments), an open-source, agent-based tool designed to model epidemics similar to COVID-19. BESSIE utilizes a synthetic population where every individual possesses demographic characteristics, household affiliations, and a seven-day baseline schedule of activities and visits. Disease transmission occurs through contacts formed by joint visits to shared locations. The model features a plugin-based, programmable behavioral framework; based on tracked dynamics and observables, agents autonomously decide on actions such as mask-wearing, social distancing, or staying home to avoid specific activities. These plugins are implemented in Python. To our knowledge, BESSIE is the only simulator offering this specific combination of features, particularly as open software. To demonstrate BESSIE's capabilities, we present a COVID-relevant example using a synthetic population of Charlottesville, Virginia. Both the Python plugin modules and the example population are publicly available. The Python implementation, compatible with systems ranging from laptops to clusters, is released under the Apache 2.0 license, while the accompanying example population is provided under the CC BY 4.0 license.

Recent attention has focused on landmark-based robot self-localization as a highly compressive, domain-invariant method for visual place recognition (VPR) across varying conditions such as time, weather, and season. However, for passive observers like manually controlled robots, this task can be ill-posed because many viewpoints fail to offer effective landmark visibility. This study addresses active self-localization by an active observer, introducing a novel reinforcement learning (RL) framework for next-best-view (NBV) planning. The key contributions are: (1) SIMBAD-based VPR, which formulates landmark-based compact scene description as similarity-based pattern recognition and extends it with deep learning; (2) VPR-to-NBV knowledge transfer, which mitigates RL uncertainty in active self-localization by leveraging VPR's state recognition capabilities for NBV planning; and (3) NNQL-based NBV, which treats VPR as an experience database using nearest-neighbor Q-learning approximation. This approach yields an extremely compact data structure that merges both VPR and NBV into a single incremental inverted index. Experiments on the public NCLT dataset confirm the method's effectiveness.

Highly charged ions (HCIs) represent a leading prospect for next-generation atomic clocks, primarily due to their compact electron configurations that effectively mitigate common environmental noise affecting quantum oscillators. We introduce and implement an experimental approach focused on multiple charge states of a single element, designed to maximize the availability of candidate clock transitions. Applying this strategy, we identified four consecutive charge states of nickel HCIs that provide up to six optical transitions. Using the compact Shanghai-Wuhan Electron Beam Ion Trap, we successfully demonstrated the production of these ions at low energy. Employing a new calibration technique, we measured the wavelengths of four magnetic-dipole ($M$1) and one electric-quadrupole ($E$2) clock transitions with ppm-level accuracy; notably, two of these spectral lines were observed and characterized for the first time under controlled laboratory conditions. Our results represent an order-of-magnitude improvement in wavelength accuracy compared to previous determinations, a precision essential for narrowing the search range for extremely narrow spectral lines. Furthermore, we calculated the frequencies and quality factors of these transitions and assessed their sensitivity to potential variations in the fine structure constant $\alpha$ for fundamental physics research. We conclude that all six nickel HCI transitions possess inherent immunity to typical quantum oscillator perturbations, with one transition projected to achieve a fractional frequency uncertainty as low as $10^{-19}$.

This study applies the reconstruction of unitary symmetry \cite{TFD}, achieved through a non-linear dynamical mapping of the Hilbert space of action amplitudes $C^N$ to the projective Hilbert space $CP(N-1)$ \cite{Le1}, to the quantum dynamics of elementary vacuum excitations. In this framework, the "vacuum manifold of virtual action states" is modeled by $CP(N-1)$, with its tangent vectors serving as local dynamical variables (LDV's) that characterize "matter." The conservation laws governing these LDV's reflect the self-conservation of "material particles" during continuous evolution, which is mathematically expressed as affine parallel transport consistent with the Fubini-Study metric; this process generates an "affine gauge potential" as the solution to specific partial differential equations. Consequently, quantum dynamics are embedded within a dynamical space-time, where state-dependent coordinates emerge from the encoding of quantum measurement results via qubit spinors. These spinor components undergo Lorentz transformations termed "quantum boosts" and "quantum rotations." Thus, within the context of super-relativity, the objective nature of quantum measurement is intrinsically linked to the structure of this dynamical space-time, which supersedes the traditional concept of an "observer."

Cybersecurity vulnerabilities expose surveillance systems to video forgery attacks, where legitimate live feeds are manipulated to hide illicit human behavior. Conventional video forensics methods can identify and pinpoint these forgeries within individual frames through spatial-temporal analysis, yet they are too computationally intensive for real-time verification of live streams. Recent approaches leverage time-series correlations between camera and wireless signals to detect replayed videos via event-level timing, but they fail to perform fine-grained detection and localization at the frame level. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Secure-Pose, a novel cross-modal system designed for detecting and localizing forgeries in live surveillance footage using nearby WiFi signals. We observe that simultaneous camera and WiFi data share common semantic information regarding human activity, which becomes decoupled when video frames are forged. Secure-Pose extracts effective human pose features from synchronized multi-modal inputs to identify and localize tampering under both inter-frame and intra-frame attack scenarios. Implemented using a commercial camera and two Intel 5300 NICs, the system was evaluated in real-world settings, achieving a detection accuracy of 95.1% and successfully localizing tampered objects across various forgery types.

Recent research has significantly advanced intelligent traffic management systems, particularly those utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for license plate reading, which serves as a foundational component for automation. To enhance algorithmic performance, the research community increasingly demands high-quality datasets. There is a specific gap in available data for nations employing unique characters, such as Morocco's Arabic script on license plates. This study introduces a labeled, open dataset of Moroccan vehicle plates covering cars, trucks, and motorcycles. Manually collected, the dataset comprises 705 distinct images annotated for both plate segmentation and matriculation number recognition. Additionally, we demonstrate that data augmentation techniques can expand this collection into training sets containing thousands of images for various machine learning and AI applications. We present and evaluate several models trained on this data and release it as an open-access resource to foster innovation in OCR, image processing, and the management of heterogeneous vehicles for traffic control and broader transportation applications.

Navigating uncontrolled intersections presents a primary challenge for autonomous vehicles. Recognizing nuanced variations in the hidden characteristics of other drivers offers substantial advantages in these settings. We introduce an unsupervised approach to infer driver attributes, such as driving styles, based on observed vehicle trajectories. By employing a variational autoencoder combined with recurrent neural networks, we generate a latent representation of these traits without relying on ground truth labels. Subsequently, we utilize this trait representation to develop a navigation policy for an autonomous vehicle approaching a T-intersection via deep reinforcement learning. This framework allows the vehicle to adapt its maneuvers to drivers with diverse traits, thereby enhancing both safety and efficiency. Our method shows promising results and surpasses current state-of-the-art baselines specifically within the T-intersection scenario.

The "Predicting Generalization in Deep Learning (PGDL)" competition established a platform for the rigorous analysis of deep learning model generalization and to advance the understanding and explanation of these systems. This report details the submission by user \emph{smeznar}, which secured eighth place. The proposed methodology involves developing simple metrics and identifying their optimal combination through automatic testing on the provided dataset, thereby investigating how various properties of input neural network architectures can be leveraged to predict generalization performance.

Although deep neural networks demonstrate resilience against minor label noise, their capacity to memorize noisy labels under high noise rates remains unresolved. Leading algorithms for this challenge typically follow a two-stage pipeline: first, an unsupervised phase classifies samples as clean or noisy, and second, a semi-supervised phase minimizes empirical vicinal risk (EVR) using a labeled subset of clean samples and an unlabeled subset of noisy ones. This paper posits that the generalization performance of such two-stage methods hinges on the accuracy of the unsupervised classifier and the training set size utilized for EVR minimization. We empirically verify these hypotheses and introduce LongReMix, a novel two-stage noisy-label training algorithm. Evaluated on benchmarks including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, WebVision, Clothing1M, and Food101-N, LongReMix demonstrates superior generalization compared to existing methods, especially in scenarios with high label noise, achieving state-of-the-art results across most datasets. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/filipe-research/LongReMix.

Bosonic codes provide noise resilience for quantum information processing, where additive Gaussian noise is a prevalent challenge. A longstanding open problem in this domain is designing a concatenated code that reaches the hashing bound for this specific noise channel.
