TIGER operates in a trigger-less mode, continuously streaming over-threshold data to an FPGA-based readout module known as the GEM Read Out Card, which constructs event packets upon receiving a trigger. Two of the three layers have been operational in Beijing since January 2020 under remote control. Due to the pandemic, integration efforts proceeded using a small-scale prototype. Recently, a test beam was conducted at CERN utilizing the final electronics configuration. This presentation will outline the overall status of the CGEM-IT project, with a specific emphasis on results derived from the test beam data acquisition.

The paper provides a novel characterization of internal groupoids that remains valid even without assuming the existence of finite limits and exists as a full subcategory within the category of involutive-2-links (morphisms endowed with a pair of interlinked involutions). This finding underscores that, despite internal groupoids being internal categories with an involution, they are equivalently representable as tri-graphs with an involution. Furthermore, this tri-graph structure can be reduced to a more streamlined form consisting of a single morphism with two interlinked involutions. This perspective stands in sharp contrast to the traditional approach of viewing groupoids as reflexive graphs equipped with a multiplicative inverse structure.

This study utilizes Pad\'e approximants to investigate the analytic structure of the four-dimensional $SU(2)$ Landau-gauge gluon and ghost propagators within the infrared domain. These model-independent approximants function as fitting tools for lattice data, with uncertainties from the fitting process carefully propagated, including all relevant correlations. Analysis of the gluon-propagator data confirms a pair of complex poles located at $p_{\rm pole}^2 = \left[(-0.37 \,\pm\, 0.05_{\rm stat}\,\pm\, 0.08_{\rm sys}) \pm i\,(0.66\, \pm\, 0.03_{\rm stat}\, \pm\, 0.02_{\rm sys})\right]\, \mathrm{GeV}^2$, where the initial uncertainty is statistical and the subsequent one is systematic. While previous studies hinted at these poles, our findings, bolstered by model independence and rigorous error handling, establish them on a more solid foundation. Regarding the ghost propagator, the Pad\'e approximants reveal a single pole at $p^2 = 0$, consistent with expectations, and also suggest a branch cut along the negative real axis of $p^2$. This finding is supported by D-Log Pad\'e approximants, which are more appropriate for functions containing branch cuts and are applied here for the first time. However, due to specific characteristics and limited statistics in the gluon-propagator dataset, our analysis cannot definitively determine the presence of a branch cut in the gluon case.

We present the identification of KMT-2020-BLG-0414Lb, a microlensing planet with a mass ratio $q_2$ between $0.9$ and $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ (equivalent to $3$ to $4$ Earth masses at the $1\sigma$ level), marking the lowest mass-ratio planet discovered to date. Alongside two other recent findings ($4 \lesssim q/q_\oplus \lesssim 6$), this system populates the previously vacant lower region of the triangular $(\log s, \log q)$ diagram, where $s$ denotes the planet-host separation relative to the angular Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E}$. Consequently, these results challenge the existence or magnitude of the previously hypothesized break in the mass-ratio function intended to explain the scarcity of very low-$q$ planets. Given the event's extreme magnification ($A_{\rm max}\sim 1450$) of the underlying single-lens event, the light curve also revealed a second companion with $q_3 \sim 0.05$ and $|\log s_3| \sim 1$, placing it roughly a factor of ten closer to or farther from the host in projection. Utilizing measurements of the microlens parallax $\pi_{\rm E}$ and the angular Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E}$, we derived estimates for the masses of the host, planet, and second companion as $(M_1, M_2, M_3) \sim (0.3M_{\odot}, 1.0M_{\oplus}, 17M_{J})$, along with their projected separations, $(a_{\perp,2}, a_{\perp,3}) \sim (1.5, 0.15~{\rm or}~15)$~au, and a system distance of $D_{\rm L} \sim 1$ kpc. The lens likely accounts for most or all of the blended light ($I \sim 19.3$), enabling immediate investigation through high-resolution photometric and spectroscopic observations to further elucidate the system's nature. This planet was detected through a new initiative focused on high-cadence follow-up of high-magnification events. Notably, the successful detection of this planet, despite significant challenges posed by the pandemic which caused the shutdown of two KMT sites and OGLE, demonstrates the program's considerable potential utility.

Using Dark Energy Survey Science Verification data, we identify a promising candidate for a distant supercluster located at a redshift of approximately 1.1. By analyzing smoothed semi-3D galaxy density maps across various photometric redshift slices, we pinpoint the most significant overdense region, which exhibits a $3\sigma$ overdensity spanning roughly 160 Mpc at $z \sim 1.1$. This scale far exceeds that of typical galaxy clusters, which measure only several Mpc. Since the supercluster's sky projection is non-circular, we designate the point of maximum overdensity as the center for quantitative analysis. Mass estimates derived from two different methods yield a value of $1.37\substack{+1.31 \\ -0.79} \times 10^{17} M_{\odot}$, representing a mass more than an order of magnitude greater than regular clusters. Excluding protosuperclusters identified via emission-line galaxies, this object represents the most distant supercluster to date defined by regular galaxies. Spectroscopic confirmation would render this structure highly significant for cosmological studies, prompting a discussion of its potential implications for $\Lambda$CDM cosmology.

Microflares are recognized as significant contributors to the energy input shaping the active solar corona. To examine the low atmosphere's response to these events, we performed ALMA observations at 3 mm on March 19, 2017, coordinated with data from IRIS and Hinode. During this period, the Hinode X-ray telescope captured a soft X-ray loop-type microflare (active-region transient brightening) with high temporal resolution. A brightening loop footpoint was situated within the narrow fields of view of ALMA, the IRIS slit-jaw imager, and the Hinode spectro-polarimeter. While counterparts to the microflare were detected at the footpoint in Si IV and ALMA images, they were less distinct in C II and Mg II k images. The impulsive time profiles of these features exhibit the Neupert effect relative to soft X-ray intensity evolution. The thermal energy magnitude measured by ALMA was approximately 100 times lower than that measured in the corona. These findings suggest that impulsive counterparts can be observed in the transition region and upper chromosphere, where plasma is heated by impinging non-thermal particles. However, our energy assessment indicates a deficit of accelerated particles reaching the footpoints for certain soft X-ray microflares. The footpoint counterparts comprise multiple brightening kernels, all located in weak (void) magnetic areas formed by a patchy distribution of strong magnetic flux at the photospheric level. These kernels offer a conceptual model where transient energy release occurs at various locations along the sheaths of magnetic flux bundles in the corona.

We report updated measurements of the Hubble parameter and the parameter $\Xi_0$, which characterizes modified gravitational wave propagation, derived from the third gravitational wave transient catalog (GWTC-3). These results utilize correlations with galaxy catalogs and data on the source-frame mass distribution of binary black holes. The analysis of the latter yields the most stringent constraint on $\Xi_0$ to date: $\Xi_0 = 1.2^{+0.7}_{-0.7}$ assuming a flat prior, and $\Xi_0 = 1.0^{+0.4}_{-0.8}$ with a prior uniform in $\log\Xi_0$ (representing the maximum posterior and $68\%$ HDI). The determination of $H_0$ is primarily driven by the bright siren event GW170817, producing a value of $H_0 = 67^{+9}_{-6} \, \rm km \, s^{-1} \, Mpc$ when combined with the galaxy catalog.

The POLAR instrument, a compact space-borne detector launched aboard the Chinese space laboratory Tiangong-2 (TG-2) on September 15, 2016, was originally designed to measure the polarization of hard X-rays from Gamma-Ray Bursts within the 50-500 keV energy range. After activation several days post-launch, the detector generated tens of gigabytes of raw data daily, which were transmitted to Earth. Prior to launch, a comprehensive software pipeline was developed to rapidly pre-process both engineering and science raw data, producing high-level scientific products suitable for subsequent analysis. Following the successful launch and activation of POLAR, this pipeline has been effectively utilized by the POLAR Science Data Center at the Institute of High Energy Physics (IHEP). This paper provides a detailed overview of the pipeline and highlights several core algorithms integral to its operation.

We present a neural stack architecture featuring a differentiable, parameterized stack operator that approximates push and pop operations to explicitly model a stack. We demonstrate the stability of this architecture, showing that regardless of the number of operations, the neural stack's state remains closely aligned with that of a discrete stack. By integrating this neural stack with a recurrent neural network, we develop a neural network Pushdown Automaton (nnPDA) and prove that an nnPDA with finite or bounded neurons and time can simulate any Pushdown Automaton. Furthermore, we extend this framework to propose a neural state Turing Machine (nnTM). We establish that a differentiable nnTM with bounded neurons can simulate a Turing Machine in real-time. Similar to the neural stack, these architectures are also stable. Finally, we extend our findings to show that a differentiable nnTM is equivalent to a Universal Turing Machine and can simulate any Turing Machine using only seven neurons with finite or bounded precision. This research establishes a new theoretical upper bound on the computational power of bounded-precision RNNs enhanced with memory.

We present a classification of supersymmetric warped product dS4 solutions within D=11 supergravity. The corresponding Killing spinors correspond to two potential stabilizer groups, SU(3) and G_2. We demonstrate that no solutions satisfy the Killing spinor equations when the stabilizer is G_2. Conversely, for the SU(3) stabilizer scenario, all supersymmetry-imposed constraints on the 4-form flux and the internal manifold's geometry are fully expressed using SU(3) invariant spinor bilinears.

We investigate Feynman checkers, a fundamental model of electron dynamics proposed by R. Feynman, where a checker traverses a grid and turns are tallied; this system is also recognized as a one-dimensional quantum walk. Within this framework, we establish novel number-theoretic findings, such as the alternating signs of the real and imaginary components of the electron wave function within a designated region. Furthermore, all our results can be formulated using Young diagrams, specifically by comparing the quantities of diagrams containing an odd versus an even number of steps.

Cartan resolved the local equivalence problem for generic 2-plane fields on 5-manifolds and established the corresponding fundamental curvature invariant. When these fields, known as $(2,3,5)$-distributions, are defined by a single function $F(q)$, the condition for the curvature invariant to vanish corresponds to a sixth-order nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE). An and Nurowski demonstrated that this sixth-order ODE is the Legendre transform of a seventh-order nonlinear ODE previously identified by Dunajski and Sokolov. This work shows that the sixth-order equation can be simplified into a third-order nonlinear ODE representing a generalized Chazy equation. Similarly, the seventh-order equation reduces to another generalized Chazy equation, where its Chazy parameter is the reciprocal of the first. Solving these related generalized Chazy equations yields further examples of flat $(2,3,5)$-distributions that do not conform to the form $F(q)=q^m$. Additionally, we present four-dimensional metrics of split signature whose twistor distributions, constructed via the An-Nurowski method, possess split $G_2$ symmetry groups.

Achieving photorealistic telepresence demands both high-fidelity body modeling and accurate driving to generate dynamically synthesized visuals that are virtually indistinguishable from reality. This work introduces an end-to-end framework designed to tackle two primary hurdles in modeling and animating full-body avatars of real individuals. First, it addresses the difficulty of driving avatars while maintaining fidelity to intricate details and dynamics that global low-dimensional parameterizations, such as body pose, fail to capture. Our method enables the animation of clothed avatars, including wrinkles and movements beyond the scope of the training data, mirroring a real performer's actions. Unlike traditional global state representations or non-parametric screen-space techniques, we propose texel-aligned features—a localized representation that simultaneously exploits the structural prior of skeleton-based parametric models and observed sparse image signals. Second, we address the challenge of creating temporally coherent clothed avatars, which usually necessitates precise surface tracking. To overcome this, we introduce a novel volumetric avatar representation by extending mixtures of volumetric primitives to articulated objects. By explicitly integrating articulation, our approach naturally generalizes to unseen poses. Additionally, we implement localized viewpoint conditioning, which significantly enhances the generalization of view-dependent appearance. This volumetric representation eliminates the need for high-quality mesh tracking as a prerequisite and delivers substantial quality improvements over mesh-based alternatives. Experimental results carefully evaluate our design choices, demonstrating the method's effectiveness and showing superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches in demanding driving scenarios.

This work employs exponential asymptotics to analyze travelling waves within woodpile systems, modeled as singularly perturbed granular chains featuring zero precompression and a small mass ratio. Due to the systems' strong nonlinearity, no closed-form analytic expression exists for the leading-order solution; instead, a hybrid numerical-analytic approach yields an approximate leading-order result. We demonstrate that travelling waves in these nonlinear woodpile configurations typically manifest as "nanoptera"—waves possessing exponentially small yet non-decaying oscillatory tails that emerge upon crossing a Stokes curve. Specifically, we show that travelling waves in the zero precompression regime involve two Stokes curves, resulting in two distinct sets of tailing oscillations. By explicitly calculating the behavior of these oscillations, we identify specific system configurations where they completely cancel out, yielding solitary wave behavior. Furthermore, we examine the evolution of travelling waves as precompression increases, revealing a critical threshold above which the two Stokes curves merge into one. Consequently, the cancellation of tailing oscillations ceases, a finding that aligns with prior research indicating that such cancellation does not occur in chains subjected to strong precompression.

We investigate encodings from CSP to asynchronous CCS with name passing and matching, which corresponds to the asynchronous pi-calculus. In this process, we examine two distinct approaches to translating CSP's multi-way synchronisation into CCS's two-way synchronisation. Both encodings meet Gorla's criteria except for compositionality, as each relies on an additional top-level context. Drawing on the work of Parrow and Sj\"odin, the first encoding employs a central coordinator and establishes a variant of weak bisimilarity between source terms and their translations. The second encoding is decentralised, offering greater efficiency, but guarantees only a form of coupled similarity between the source terms and their translations.

Two-dimensional dilaton gravity models, such as the Jackiw--Teitelboim model and its variations, are specific instances of Poisson sigma models. Since diffeomorphisms of the target space can transform one Poisson sigma model into another, we suggest leveraging these transformations to align asymptotic conditions, boundary actions, and asymptotic symmetries across different dilaton gravity frameworks. As an illustration, we apply the asymptotic conditions found in Jackiw--Teitelboim gravity to formulate an asymptotic problem exhibiting Virasoro symmetry within a specific set of asymptotically Rindler models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of dilaton gravity pairs and explore potential avenues for generalization.

Recent years have seen a resurgence in studying dislocation behavior within crystals characterized by significant atomic-scale disorder, a feature common in compositionally complex single-phase alloys. This behavior is frequently analyzed using the elastic manifold pinning model for disordered systems. This work examines necessary modifications to that framework when addressing extended dislocations that dissociate into widely separated partials. We show that stacking faults introduce an additional stress scale, which must be compared against the pinning stress from elastic manifold theory to determine if partials are pinned individually or the entire dislocation is pinned. For weakly interacting partial dislocations, we identify multiple metastable states below the depinning threshold and examine how stacking fault width evolves under load. Furthermore, we explore how geometrical constraints influence dislocation-solute interactions and amplify pinning stress. Finally, we validate our theoretical predictions against atomistic and discrete (partial) dislocation dynamics (D(P)DD) simulation results.

Although LED panels in virtual production environments offer vibrant imagery with extensive color gamuts, their narrow-band red, green, and blue spectra cause problematic color shifts when utilized as lighting sources. This study introduces an enhanced color calibration workflow for virtual production stages that resolves these rendering issues while maintaining accurate in-camera background hues. We achieve this by optimizing linear color correction transforms for: 1) the LED pixels captured within the camera's field of view, 2) the out-of-view pixels illuminating the subjects, and 3) the recorded pixel values as a post-processing step. Consequently, footage captured in RGB LED virtual production environments displays more faithful skin tones and costume colors while simultaneously reproducing the intended in-camera background colors.

Optical imaging polarimetry observations of the hydrogen-poor superluminous supernova SN 2020znr were performed at three post-maximum light epochs (approximately +34, +288, and +289 days). Following corrections for instrumental and interstellar polarization, the results consistently indicate null polarization. Light curve modeling using a magnetar spin-down framework reveals that SN 2020znr possesses magnetar and ejecta parameters comparable to other superluminous supernovae. However, when compared to SN 2017egm and SN 2015bn—two hydrogen-poor SLSNe that exhibit increasing polarization after peak brightness—the best-fit values suggest SN 2020znr has a higher ejecta mass. This increased mass likely obstructs optical polarimetry from probing the geometry of the inner ejecta. Consequently, integrating spectroscopy and light curve analysis for Type I SLSNe offers a promising method for categorizing the polarization characteristics of these transients, provided that future efforts expand the existing sample by acquiring new early- and late-time polarimetry measurements.

Introduced by Google in 2008, the Android platform serves as an operating system for mobile devices, supported by an SDK that offers extensive programming resources, examples, and documentation. Given that smartphone applications frequently handle sensitive personal data, ensuring reliability has become a critical concern, necessitating tools and methods to verify correct application behavior. This paper demonstrates how the Event-B method can be employed to reason about and verify Android app designs, as well as to document implementation choices. Our methodology involves modeling an app's core functionality in Event-B and utilizing the generated Proof Obligations to analyze both the design and implementation. While not proposing a new technique, we substantiate that heavyweight Formal Methods using Event-B can effectively support the development of correct Android applications. We illustrate this through a case study where we modeled WhatsApp's core features in Event-B, encoding them across three machine refinements that cover basic operations (such as chatting, deleting, and forwarding content, and managing chat sessions), chat status tracking, and implementation specifics. Finally, we report on and discuss the challenges encountered during the design and implementation of these core functionalities.

To broaden the accessibility of magnetic field studies in stellar astronomy, I introduce MOOGStokes, an updated version of the one-dimensional LTE radiative transfer code MOOG that integrates a Stokes vector approach for polarized radiation within magnetic environments. MOOGStokes consists of three complementary programs designed to generate disk-averaged emergent spectra for stars possessing magnetic fields. The first component, a pre-processing script named CounterPoint, determines wavelength shifts and polarizations for Zeeman-sensitive line components based on a specified magnetic field strength. The second component, a MOOG driver called SynStokes (derived from the original Synth driver), utilizes the catalog of Zeeman-shifted absorption lines alongside MOOG's existing capabilities to synthesize emergent spectra at various points across the stellar disk, factoring in both stellar and magnetic field geometry. The final component, a post-processing script named DiskoBall, computes the disk-averaged spectrum by weighting individual emergent spectra according to limb darkening and projected area while applying Doppler broadening effects. Collectively, the MOOGStokes package enables users to synthesize emergent spectra for stars with magnetic fields within a familiar computational environment. MOOGStokes generates disk-averaged spectra for all Stokes vectors (I, Q, U, and V), normalized by the continuum. It demonstrates strong agreement with INVERS10, a well-established polarized radiative transfer code used for studying stellar magnetic fields, and also aligns with the scalar version of MOOG in the non-magnetic limit.

Achieving Shannon's capacity demands signal shaping, but doing so at ultra-high speeds remains difficult. Probabilistic shaping typically relies on arithmetic coding to achieve the desired distribution, while geometric shaping necessitates look-up tables for constellation storage. This paper introduces a four-dimensional amplitude coding (4D-AC) geometric shaper architecture. By utilizing simple logic circuits and two standard quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) modulators, the proposed design generates geometrically shaped 4D formats in real time. Specifically, the 4D-AC technique is applied to create approximations of two recently developed 4D orthant symmetric modulation formats with spectral efficiencies of 6 bit/4D-sym and 7 bit/4D-sym. Numerical simulations indicate that these approximations incur losses of less than 0.05 dB relative to the baseline formats.

We examine two key limitations in quantum computing: restricted memory capacity and noise resulting from heat dissipation. To address both, we explore "on-the-go erasure," a method that clears quantum registers once they are no longer required by an algorithm; this process frees auxiliary qubits and aids in parallelizing computations. Our analysis determines the minimal thermodynamic cost of erasure in these contexts, utilizing findings on the Landauer erasure of entangled quantum registers. For algorithms addressing the Abelian hidden subgroup problem, we identify optimal on-the-go erasure protocols. We conclude that a trade-off exists: possessing sufficient partial information to implement efficient on-the-go erasure allows one to instead simplify the algorithm, thereby reducing the initial qubit count required for execution. We present explicit protocols for both strategies.

Visual grounding identifies specific regions, such as bounding boxes or segments, within an image that align with provided referring expressions. This study tackles the challenge of segmenting images based on these expressions, a task previously limited to fully-supervised frameworks. While fully-supervised methods demand costly pixel-level annotations that hinder scalability, we propose a novel weakly-supervised task. We introduce Text Grounded Semantic SEGmentation (TSEG), a transformer-based approach that learns segmentation masks directly from image-level referring expressions without requiring pixel-level labels. By calculating patch-text similarities and utilizing a new multi-label patch assignment mechanism to guide the classification objective during training, TSEG effectively segments image areas matching natural language descriptions. Experimental results on the challenging PhraseCut and RefCOCO datasets demonstrate the method's promise for weakly-supervised referring expression segmentation. Furthermore, TSEG exhibits competitive performance in a zero-shot setting for semantic segmentation on the Pascal VOC dataset.

We investigate the challenge of identifying planted solutions within random satisfiability formulas. By applying the framework of hypothesis testing from statistical analysis, we characterize the minimax optimal rates for detection. Our approach depends on analyzing the count of satisfying assignments, for which we establish novel findings. Furthermore, we tackle algorithmic concerns by presenting a computationally efficient test that achieves optimal statistical performance. Finally, we contrast this outcome with the average-case hypothesis regarding the difficulty of refuting satisfiability in random formulas.

Since the neutral hydrogen Lyman-alpha (Lya) line represents the brightest emission feature in the solar spectrum, identifying irradiance spikes caused by solar flares at this wavelength is difficult against the intense background. Prior research on major flares indicates that even extreme events produce only a few percent increase in Lya above the background. This study employed a superposed-epoch analysis on approximately 8,500 flares exceeding B1 class to quantify their impact on solar EUV irradiance. By using the peak of 1-8A X-ray emission as a reference time, time series data for 3,123 B-class and 4,972 C-class flares from the GOES-15 EUV Sensor were averaged to suppress background noise and isolate the flare signal. Aggregating these weaker events revealed a 0.1–0.3% enhancement in solar Lya irradiance. In contrast, applying the same method to 453 M-class and 31 X-class flares yielded a 1–4% increase in Lya emission. Additionally, flares were averaged based on their heliographic angle to assess center-to-limb variations. Results showed that for every GOES class, the relative Lya enhancement at peak intensity decreased for flares near the solar limb, likely due to line opacity and foreshortening of footpoints. One notable event, a C6.6 flare, displayed an anomalously high 7% increase in Lya, possibly linked to a failed filament eruption; such magnitudes have previously been observed only in a limited number of X-class flares.

During the big data era, graph computing has become essential for extracting hidden value from real-world graphs across diverse applications like social networks, knowledge graphs, web search, and recommendation systems. However, random memory access patterns lead to poor cache utilization, and irregular degree distributions cause significant load imbalance. As a core component for many complex algorithms, Breadth-First Search (BFS) is frequently employed. This paper introduces a preprocessing strategy utilizing the Reverse Cuthill-McKee (RCM) algorithm to enhance data locality and optimize load balancing for BFS operations. Additionally, we accelerate computations on RCM-reordered data through SIMD execution. We assessed the performance of this approach using Kronecker graphs from the Graph500 benchmark alongside real-world datasets. Our BFS implementation on RCM-reordered data achieved 326.48 MTEPS/W on an ARMv8 system, securing the 2nd position on the June 2020 Green Graph500 list, trailing only the GPU-accelerated solution.

The interaction between magnetic impurities and vortices in topological superconductors holds fundamental significance for the development of quantum computing. However, the impurity-pinned vortex state has remained elusive due to the complex interplay of multiple degrees of freedom, including Majorana zero modes (MZMs), Caroli de Gennes Matricon (CdGM) states, and bulk electron states forming Cooper pairs. In this study, we provide an accurate solution to this problem utilizing a generalized mapping scheme combined with the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method. We identify distinct in-gap states separate from the conventional Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states. This novel in-gap physics arises from three primary mechanisms: (i) the coupling between impurities and bulk states creates a competition between Kondo screening and Cooper pairing, driving a singlet-doublet quantum phase transition; (ii) the interaction between impurities and CdGM states introduces an effective Zeeman splitting to the doublet; and (iii) the coupling between impurities and MZMs transforms the singlet-doublet transition into a crossover. Collectively, these mechanisms generate a unique spin-resolved local density of states. Notably, despite the presence of MZMs, a robust nearly zero-energy peak emerges with comparable magnitude but opposite spin polarization relative to the MZM. These findings reveal new emergent physical phenomena and provide valuable insights for interpreting puzzling experimental observations.

Magnetic skyrmions represent promising prospects for energy-efficient computing because of their mobility, detectability, and non-volatility. Although a recent approach grounded in reversible computing allows for large-scale circuits using directly cascaded skyrmion logic gates, this method is constrained by the high energy costs and manufacturing complexities linked to using notches for skyrmion synchronization. To address these limitations, we introduce a synchronization strategy for skyrmion logic based on modulating voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy (VCMA). Beyond validating the principles of VCMA synchronization through micromagnetic simulations, we analyze how anisotropy barrier height, skyrmion velocity, and current density influence skyrmion dynamics. Additional micromagnetic findings confirm the viability of cascaded logic circuits where VCMA synchronizers facilitate clocking and pipelining, thereby outlining a practical route to developing large-scale, energy-efficient computing systems utilizing magnetic skyrmions.

Discrete Fracture Networks (DFNs) represent intricate three-dimensional geometries formed by the intersection of planar polygonal fractures, serving as a framework for simulating fluid flow in fractured media. Although these structures are well-suited for Domain Decomposition (DD) approaches, research applying DD methods to DFNs remains limited. This paper presents a theoretical investigation into the application of Optimized Schwarz Methods (OSMs) to DFNs. Notably, we demonstrate that OSMs achieve weak scalability—converging to a specified tolerance within an iteration count independent of the number of fractures—provided specific domain decomposition assumptions hold. This work aligns with the growing interest in the weak scalability of DD methods, particularly following recent findings that established such scalability for certain geometric configurations even in the absence of coarse spaces. While the analysis relies on simplifying assumptions that may not always hold in practical scenarios, it offers valuable heuristics for reducing computational costs in realistic applications. Furthermore, we highlight that the proposed methodology can be readily extended to examine other classical DD techniques used in DFNs.

This paper examines the forward dynamical properties of nonautonomous lattice systems. Initially, we establish a collection of sets $\{\mathcal{A}_\varepsilon(\sigma)\}_{\sigma\in \Sigma}$ situated within an arbitrarily small vicinity of a global attractor associated with the skew-product flow of a general nonautonomous lattice system. These sets are forward invariant and uniformly attract any bounded subset of the phase space over time. Additionally, subject to specific conditions, we define another family of sets $\{\mathcal{B}_\varepsilon(\sigma)\}_{\sigma\in \Sigma}$ that ensures the uniform forward exponential attraction of bounded subsets within the phase space. To demonstrate the practical utility of these theoretical findings, we conduct a detailed analysis of the discrete Gray-Scott model, showcasing how our abstract results can be applied to specific lattice systems.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) function as intricate dynamical systems that can sustain activity independently of external inputs. Their long-term free-running behavior—characterized by fixed points, periodic oscillations, or chaos—is governed by the statistical properties of synaptic weights, specifically the density of active connections ($d$) and the excitatory-inhibitory balance ($b$). While these intrinsic dynamics are well understood, it remains unclear which regime best supports information processing when external signals are introduced. To address this, we quantify information import using average correlations ($C$) and mutual information ($I$) between input vectors and subsequent system states, analyzing how these metrics vary with network density and balance. Surprisingly, the resulting phase diagrams for both $C(b,d)$ and $I(b,d)$ show strong consistency, suggesting a fundamental connection between dynamical systems theory and information processing in complex networks. Maximal information import does not occur at the traditionally favored "edge of chaos" for computation; instead, it peaks in the low-density chaotic regime and at the boundary between chaotic and fixed-point dynamics. Furthermore, we identify a novel resonance phenomenon termed "Import Resonance" (IR), where information import exhibits a peak dependent on the coupling strength between the RNN and its input. This complements the known "Recurrence Resonance" (RR), where correlations and mutual information between successive states peak at specific noise amplitudes. Both IR and RR offer strategies for optimizing information processing in artificial neural networks and may be equally significant in biological neural systems.

When randomized trial data are unavailable, researchers frequently rely on observational data to infer causality regarding treatment effects on time-to-event outcomes, often focusing on treatment-specific survival curves representing the entire study population. Provided that specific causal conditions are met, such as the observation of all confounders linking treatment and outcome, these survival curves can be identified through covariate-adjusted survival functions. Various estimators for this function have been developed, including those based on outcome regression, inverse probability weighting, and doubly robust approaches. This article introduces a new cross-fitted doubly robust estimator that integrates data-adaptive (e.g., machine learning) methods for estimating conditional survival functions. We define conditions on nuisance estimators that ensure our proposed method is both consistent and asymptotically linear, holding true both pointwise and uniformly over time. Additionally, we present a novel ensemble learner designed to combine multiple candidate estimators for conditional survival. Importantly, our approach and findings apply to events occurring in discrete, continuous, or mixed timeframes. We evaluate the practical utility of these methods through numerical simulations and an application analyzing the impact of surgical treatment on mortality in parotid carcinoma patients to prevent metastases.

Because data frequently resides in disparate sources, integration is essential to establish a comprehensive perspective necessary for extracting value and knowledge. A pivotal component of this integration process is schema matching, which seeks to identify semantic equivalences between schema elements. To minimize the manual labor associated with this task, numerous automatic solutions for determining schema correspondences have been developed. This paper introduces a novel, end-to-end schema matching methodology grounded in neural embeddings. The core concept involves a two-stage process: first matching tables, then matching attributes, utilizing embeddings at both the table and individual attribute levels. Our findings demonstrate that this approach reliably identifies correspondences robustly, outperforming traditional methods by detecting non-trivial matches.

We present a novel approach to efficiently generate text-to-image models using a pre-trained CLIP and StyleGAN. This method facilitates text-driven sampling with an existing generative model, eliminating the need for external data or fine-tuning. The technique involves training a diffusion model conditioned on CLIP embeddings to sample latent vectors from a pre-trained StyleGAN, a process we term clip2latent. By exploiting the alignment between CLIP's image and text embeddings, we circumvent the requirement for text-labeled data to train the conditional diffusion model. Our results demonstrate that clip2latent enables the creation of high-resolution (1024x1024 pixels) images from text prompts with rapid sampling, superior image quality, and minimal computational and data demands for training. Furthermore, leveraging the well-established StyleGAN architecture without additional fine-tuning allows for the direct application of existing techniques to control and modify generated images, thereby introducing an extra layer of control to our text-to-image pipeline.

We investigate the existence and properties of the exotic Fulde-Ferrel-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) phase in a one-dimensional Fermi gas subject to attractive Hubbard interactions, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and a Zeeman field. Our findings indicate that a robust FFLO phase emerges under attractive on-site interactions and a Zeeman field, while the introduction of SOC suppresses FFLO order but enhances pair formation. Without SOC, tuning the Zeeman field $h$ reveals four distinct phases: Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS), FFLO, multi-mode pairing, and fully polarized states, with quantum transitions between them being discontinuous with respect to $h$. Conversely, when SOC is present, the transition from the BCS to the FFLO phase becomes continuous. We provide a comprehensive phase diagram for this model, both with and without SOC, at quarter electron filling, and specifically analyze the impact of SOC on the FFLO phase.

Continual Learning explores the capacity to acquire sequential tasks without compromising performance on prior ones, with a primary emphasis on incremental classification. We argue that continual object detection warrants significant research attention due to its extensive utility in robotics and autonomous driving. This domain presents greater complexity than standard classification because it must handle unknown classes that emerge as new categories in subsequent tasks, leading to annotation gaps and conflicts with background labels. This review examines current strategies designed to address class-incremental object detection. Our key contributions include: (1) a concise, systematic overview of methods solving traditional incremental object detection problems; (2) a thorough evaluation of existing approaches using a novel metric to standardize the quantification of stability and plasticity; and (3) an analysis of prevailing trends in continual object detection alongside a discussion of potential future research avenues.

Accurately estimating channels is a pivotal operation in digital communications, significantly influencing overall system performance. This paper presents a new technique for MIMO channel estimation utilizing score-based generative models. The proposed method employs a deep neural network trained to approximate the gradient of the log-prior distribution for wireless channels across high-dimensional spaces, subsequently applying this model to solve the estimation problem through posterior sampling. By training a score-based model on channel data generated by the CDL-D model with two distinct antenna spacings, we demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive performance both within and outside the training distribution relative to generative adversarial networks (GANs) and compressed sensing (CS). Specifically, when evaluated on CDL-D channels at $\lambda/2$ antenna spacing, the method reduces channel estimation error by at least $5$ dB compared to in-distribution GAN approaches. Furthermore, when tested on unseen CDL-C channels without fine-tuning, the technique yields up to $3$ dB gains in end-to-end coded performance over CS methods and incurs a mere $0.5$ dB degradation relative to ideal channel knowledge.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated remarkable empirical progress across numerous semi-supervised node classification tasks. However, training GCNs on large-scale graphs often encounters significant computational and memory constraints. One promising solution involves sampling-based approaches, which select a subset of nodes at each layer. While recent studies have empirically validated the efficacy of these sampling methods, they currently lack theoretical convergence guarantees under realistic conditions and fail to fully utilize the information contained in evolving parameters during optimization. This paper introduces and analyzes a general doubly variance reduction framework capable of accelerating any sampling method within memory limitations. The core motivation for this schema stems from a rigorous analysis of sampling variance, revealing that it can be decomposed into node embedding approximation variance (zeroth-order) during forward propagation and layerwise-gradient variance (first-order) during backward propagation. We provide a theoretical convergence analysis demonstrating that the proposed schema achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ convergence rate. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical findings by integrating the schema into various sampling methods and applying them to diverse large-scale real-world graphs.

Although Transformers facilitate attention across all token pairs, the quadratic computational and memory costs associated with these connections suggest that many are superfluous. This study investigates which specific connections can be eliminated through sparsification. We conduct ablation experiments to evaluate various sparsification strategies, comparing masks derived from syntax, lexical similarity, and token position against random connections to identify patterns that minimize performance degradation. Our findings indicate that for three standard fine-tuning tasks, achieving at least 78% sparsity in later transformer layers has negligible impact on performance, whereas applying sparsity across the entire network significantly harms it. Furthermore, by varying the sparsity levels for three previously supported patterns, we determine that connections to neighboring tokens are the most critical. Finally, we treat sparsity as a learnable parameter, proposing an algorithm that optimizes the density of neighboring connections. This approach offers fine-grained control over the accuracy-sparsity trade-off while nearly matching the performance of current methods.

This study investigates the connection between Eulerian and Lagrangian frameworks for modeling vector-borne disease dynamics in discrete spaces. The Eulerian method explicitly tracks host movement via rates defined by a graph Laplacian matrix ($L$), whereas the Lagrangian method considers only the proportion of time individuals spend in other patches using a mixing matrix ($P$). We define a relationship between these models based on $L$ and $P$, stating they are consistent if, for a specific $P$, an $L$ exists such that their respective residence times align. We derive a sufficient condition for this consistency and analyze disease metrics, including the basic reproduction number and final outbreak size, under both consistent and inconsistent scenarios. In two-patch systems, we note that consistent values for the reproduction number and outbreak size can sometimes appear even when the models are inconsistent. Nevertheless, our proposed relationship reveals situations where the final outbreak sizes predicted by the two approaches can differ substantially.

In this study, we investigate the thermoelectric characteristics of the topological semimetal CoSi within the 300–800 K range using a combination of experimental data and density functional theory (DFT). CoSi was prepared via arc melting, with Rietveld refinement yielding lattice parameters of a = b = c = 4.445 Å. The measured Seebeck coefficient (S) exhibits non-monotonic behavior across the temperature range, starting at approximately -81 μV/K at room temperature. The magnitude of S rises to about -93 μV/K at 560 K before declining to roughly -84 μV/K at 800 K, confirming dominant n-type behavior throughout. Electrical conductivity ($\sigma$) and thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) display monotonic decreasing and increasing trends, respectively; at 300 K and 800 K, $\sigma$ values are approximately $5.2 \times 10^5$ and $3.6 \times 10^5$ $\Omega^{-1}m^{-1}$, while $\kappa$ values are around 12.1 and 14.2 W/m-K. The thermal conductivity follows a temperature dependence of $\kappa \propto T^{0.16}$. Boltzmann transport theory based on DFT was employed to interpret these trends, revealing that multi-band electron and hole pockets primarily govern the temperature-dependent transport. Specifically, the reduction in $|S|$ above 560 K and the change in $\sigma$'s slope near 450 K are attributed to thermally excited carriers from hole pockets. Calculations of the temperature-dependent relaxation time indicate a scaling of $1/T^{0.35}$. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the DFT-derived electronic band structure provides a reliable estimate of CoSi's transport coefficients in the high-temperature regime of 300–800 K.

Egocentric videos record human activities from a first-person viewpoint, offering rich multimodal data. However, existing localization techniques typically rely on third-person footage and utilize only visual cues. This study investigates the efficacy of audiovisual context for action detection in egocentric settings and proposes a straightforward yet effective method called Observing, Watching, and Listening (OWL). OWL exploits both audio and visual information and their temporal context to enhance egocentric temporal action localization (TAL). Our approach is evaluated on two large-scale datasets, EPIC-Kitchens and HOMAGE. Comprehensive experiments highlight the significance of audiovisual temporal context, achieving improvements in localization performance (mAP) of +2.23% and +3.35% over visual-only models on these respective datasets.

Interactive segmentation has recently gained significant interest for specialized applications requiring expert input to boost performance. This study introduces a new interactive segmentation framework in which user click sizes are dynamically adjusted according to the current segmentation mask. These clicked areas generate a weight map that serves as a novel weighted loss function for a deep neural network. To assess this loss function, we utilize an Interactive U-Net (IU-Net) model that relies on both foreground and background clicks as its primary interaction method. The model is trained and validated on the BCV dataset and tested on spleen and colon cancer CT images from the MSD dataset. Results demonstrate that our weighted loss function significantly outperforms the standard U-Net, with dynamic user click sizes increasing overall accuracy by 5.60% and 10.39%, respectively, using only a single user interaction.

Although Active Learning (AL) has been investigated in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), only a limited number of studies address scenarios with restricted annotation budgets, such as when only a small number of sentences can be translated. These conditions are particularly difficult, often arising in endangered languages with scarce human annotators or under strict cost constraints for labeling. While AL proves beneficial with abundant data, it falls short of building high-quality translation systems in low-resource environments. This work introduces a cost-effective training procedure to enhance NMT model performance using a minimal set of annotated sentences and dictionary entries. Our approach utilizes monolingual data with self-supervised objectives and a small, inexpensive dictionary to provide additional supervision for initializing the NMT model before applying AL. We demonstrate that integrating these knowledge sources is crucial for effectively leveraging AL strategies and maximizing gains in low-resource settings. Furthermore, we present a novel AL strategy inspired by domain adaptation for NMT, proving its effectiveness under tight budget constraints. We propose a new hybrid data-driven method that selects sentences diverse from the labeled data while being most similar to unlabeled data. Finally, our results show that initializing the NMT model and employing our AL strategy can yield improvements of up to 13 BLEU points over conventional AL methods.

This study introduces a domain-informed neural network architecture tailored for experimental particle physics, specifically applying it to dark matter research via particle interaction localization within time-projection chambers (TPCs). Although multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) are currently dominant for TPC reconstruction, their black-box nature fails to incorporate prior scientific knowledge. This paper re-evaluates neural approaches by embedding domain-specific information regarding signal characteristics and detector geometry directly into the feature encoding and output layers of a multilayer neural network. The proposed Domain-informed Neural Network (DiNN) restricts the receptive fields of neurons in initial encoding layers to reflect the spatially localized nature of TPC signals. This design, akin to emerging graph neural networks where early-layer neurons connect only to a limited subset of subsequent neurons, drastically reduces the total parameter count compared to standard MLPs. Furthermore, the output layers are adjusted using two geometric transformations to ensure localization predictions remain within the detector's interior. Ultimately, the DiNN achieves 60% fewer parameters than an MLP while maintaining comparable localization performance, offering a scalable framework for future architectures that can integrate additional domain knowledge.

In our prior work, we proposed a deep learning neural network designed to identify extremely shallow periodic planetary transits amidst red noise, though that feasibility study did not offer details about the detected events. This current paper addresses that gap by presenting a neural network capable of tagging specific samples obtained during transits. This task is analogous to "semantic segmentation" in computer vision, where the semantic context of each pixel in an image is identified, a process frequently executed by deep neural networks. Our approach leverages novel deep learning concepts, including U-Nets, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and adversarial loss. The resulting segmentation will facilitate further analysis of light curves confirmed to contain transits. This methodology for detecting and analyzing very shallow transits is expected to be pivotal for future space-based surveys like PLATO, which specifically target the challenging detection of long-period, shallow transits. Additionally, our segmentation network expands the expanding toolkit of deep learning applications in exoplanet research, shifting the focus from merely vetting transits to their initial detection.

We investigate a non-supersymmetric SO(10) Grand Unified Theory characterized by an intermediate symmetry breaking scale at very high energies. In this framework, both gauge coupling unification and Yukawa coupling unification are achieved through appropriate threshold corrections and matching conditions. For the gauge unification analysis, we examine specific symmetry breaking patterns involving the intermediate groups ${\rm SU(4)_C \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R}$ (Pati-Salam) and ${\rm SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R\times U(1)_{B-L}}$ (minimal left-right symmetry). These scenarios assume an additional global U(1) Peccei--Quinn symmetry and a Standard Model sector augmented by a second Higgs doublet at the electroweak scale. We derive the necessary conditions and approximate analytical solutions for two-loop gauge coupling unification, alongside discussing constraints imposed by proton decay on the high scale. Focusing on the Pati-Salam intermediate breaking pattern, we further enforce the unification of third-generation fermion Yukawa couplings at the high scale, also at the two-loop level. Within this context, Yukawa unification establishes a relationship between fermion couplings to the 10- and 126-dimensional scalar representations of the SO(10) group. We analyze one such viable relation, which arises in an ${\rm E_6}$ model where these two scalar fields constitute a single multiplet. Incorporating phenomenological requirements, such as the absence of tree-level flavor changing neutral currents, we derive constraints on the low-energy model parameters, specifically targeting the ratio of the vacuum expectation values of the two Higgs doublets, $\tan\beta$.

Graph representation learning facilitates the use of conventional machine learning techniques and analytical tools on graph structures. A core strategy in this field involves substituting discrete, unordered graph nodes with real-valued vectors. These vector embeddings map nodes into a high-dimensional space, thereby encoding the discrete relationships inherent in the original data. Typically, graphs model interactions among real-world entities, where nodes often hold significant meta-information about those entities. Although embeddings are potent machine learning instruments, they frequently fail to retain these node-specific attributes. This work addresses that limitation by proposing the learning of discrete node embeddings where the vector coordinates are themselves graph nodes. This approach enables the creation of interpretable machine learning algorithms for graphs, ensuring that all original node attributes are preserved. We introduce COLOGNE, a framework for coordinated local graph neighborhood sampling, where each node is represented by a fixed set of graph nodes along with their attributes. These individual samples are coordinated to maintain the similarity between node neighborhoods, and we develop scalable algorithms for various similarity definitions, accompanied by theoretical proofs. Finally, experiments on benchmark graphs assess the quality of these embeddings and illustrate their utility in training interpretable machine learning models for graph data.

In kernel regression (KR), the selection of the kernel serves as the main hyperparameter. While most theoretical frameworks assume the kernel is predetermined and independent of the training data, research under this assumption identifies the prior covariance of the target function as the optimal kernel. This note examines a scenario where the kernel can be adjusted after observing the training data, demonstrating that choosing the kernel based on the posterior distribution of the target function yields optimal results in this context. Additionally, the discussion explores the relationship between this approach and the perspective of deep neural networks as learners of data-dependent kernels.

The study employed high-harmonic-generation laser-based time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy to examine photo-induced changes in the band structure of samarium monosulfide (SmS), a rare-earth semiconductor. Researchers detected a nonlinear shift in Sm 4f multiplets, consisting of two distinct phenomena. The first involved a shift toward higher binding energy attributed to a substantial surface photovoltage (SPV) effect of roughly 93 meV, a magnitude similar to the bulk band gap, yet exhibiting a relaxation time exceeding 0.1 ms. The second was an ultrafast shift to lower binding energy, opposing the SPV direction, which indicated a rapid valence transition from divalent to trivalent Sm ions upon photo-excitation. This latter shift measured approximately 58 meV, aligning with the energy gap reduction observed when transitioning from ambient pressure to the boundary between the black insulator and golden metallic phases under pressure. These findings imply that while the photo-induced valence transition can reach the phase boundary, additional mechanisms are required to achieve the golden metallic state.

Causal abstraction offers a framework explaining how multiple causal models can depict the same system at varying levels of granularity. While current theoretical approaches restrict the analysis of abstract models to "hard" interventions—where causal variables are fixed to constant values—this work extends causal abstraction to accommodate "soft" interventions. These soft interventions assign potentially non-constant functions to variables without introducing new causal links. Specifically, we (i) extend the concept of $\tau$-abstraction by Beckers and Halpern (2019) to apply to soft interventions, (ii) introduce an additional definition of soft abstraction to ensure a unique mapping $\omega$ between them, and (iii) demonstrate that our constructive definition of soft abstraction ensures the intervention map $\omega$ possesses a specific and necessary explicit structure.

Emphasis Selection is a recently introduced task dedicated to selecting words for emphasis within short sentences. Unlike traditional approaches that rely solely on sequential information and overlook structural details and word relationships, this paper presents a novel framework incorporating sentence structure through a sentence structure graph and word relationships via a word similarity graph. The sentence structure graph is constructed from the sentence's parse tree, while the word similarity graph enables nodes to exchange information with neighbors based on the premise that similar words are frequently emphasized together. Graph neural networks are utilized to learn representations for nodes across both graphs, with experimental results confirming that the proposed framework achieves superior performance.

This paper introduces algorithms designed to compute the reduced Gröbner basis for the vanishing ideal of a finite point set within the context of ideal interpolation. In this framework, ideal interpolation is characterized by a linear projector with a polynomial ideal as its kernel. We convert interpolation condition functionals into formal power series using Taylor expansion, subsequently deriving the reduced Gröbner basis through Gaussian elimination applied to these series. The proposed algorithm achieves polynomial time complexity and demonstrates superior performance compared to the MMM algorithm in scenarios involving both single-point and multi-point ideal interpolation.

Natural Language Generation (NLG) serves as a crucial module in task-oriented dialogue systems, transforming structured meaning representations (MR) into natural language. In large-scale conversational environments featuring hundreds of intents and thousands of slots, both template-based and model-based methods struggle to scale. Recently, neural NLG techniques have begun utilizing transfer learning to achieve promising outcomes in few-shot scenarios. This paper introduces AUGNLG, an innovative data augmentation strategy that integrates a self-trained neural retrieval model with a few-shot NLU model to automatically generate MR-to-Text pairs from open-domain sources. On the FewShotWOZ dataset, the proposed system achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, as measured by both BLEU scores and Slot Error Rate. Additionally, we validate these improvements on the FewShotSGD dataset and offer a thorough analysis of the system's key components. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/XinnuoXu/AugNLG.

Turbulence within the intracluster medium (ICM), driven by processes like mergers, accretion, and active galactic nucleus feedback, influences its dynamics. While X-ray surface brightness fluctuations have previously been utilized to constrain this turbulence, this study employs simulations to explore the relationship between gas density and turbulent velocity fluctuations, specifically examining the impact of ICM stratification. Using the cosmological code ENZO, we analyzed a sample of galaxy clusters to investigate turbulence generated by hierarchical accretion. By applying a fixed scale filtering technique to separate laminar from turbulent flows, we identified a correlation between the root mean square of density and velocity fluctuations in dynamically perturbed clusters, though the slope differed from earlier reports. We also examined the Richardson number, a metric for the ratio of turbulence to buoyancy, which showed a strong dependence on the filtering scale. Contrary to findings from recent, more idealized simulations, we failed to detect a significant link between the Richardson number and logarithmic density fluctuations. Our results highlight a pronounced effect from radial accretion, which appears to be the primary driver of gas fluctuations. The pervasive radial bias in ICM dynamics indicates that assumptions of homogeneity and isotropy are not always valid, even when turbulent spectra adhere to Kolmogorov scaling. Finally, we observed that the slopes of the velocity and density spectra remain independent of the cluster-centric radius.

The decays $B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi$ and $B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ are investigated using generalized QCD factorization, incorporating all leading-order $\alphas$ corrections. We highlight that the ratio of the computed widths, $\Gamma (B_s^0\to J/\psi f_0(980), f_0(980)\to \pi^+\pi^-)/ \Gamma(B_s^0 \to J/\psi \phi,\phi\to K^+K^-)$, strongly suggests that $S$-wave contributions from the daughter pions or kaons of the $f_0(980)$ resonance must be accounted for when extracting the $B_s-\bar{B}_s$ mixing angle, $-2\beta_s$, from $B_s^0 \to \phi J/\psi$ decay amplitudes.

Although financial networks assist firms in mitigating risk, they also facilitate the transmission of financial shocks. Current models of these networks suffer from several constraints, typically relying on static structures with simple geometries (such as rings) or assuming conditional independence among connections. In contrast, we introduce a novel framework in which the network evolves from interactions among heterogeneous firms seeking to maximize utility. In this model, edges represent contractual agreements between firm pairs, with edge weights reflecting contract sizes. We demonstrate that a unique "stable network" almost invariably exists, where every edge weight is determined by the collective beliefs of all firms. Moreover, firms can converge on this stable network through iterative pairwise negotiations. However, when beliefs shift, the resulting stable network changes accordingly. Under realistic conditions, regulators cannot determine the specific altered beliefs that drove these network modifications. Additionally, while each firm can leverage its view of the network to update its own beliefs—such as identifying outlier firms with beliefs diverging from their peers—it cannot pinpoint the exact nature of the deviation, as heightened risk-seeking behavior is indistinguishable from increased expected profits. Consequently, even trivial news can resolve this ambiguity, precipitating substantial shifts within the network.
This paper determines the total, equitable, and neighborhood sum distinguishing total chromatic numbers for various classes of circulant graphs.

Atmospheric models for stars, substellar objects, and planets rely heavily on input opacities, with discrepancies between current state-of-the-art models largely stemming from incomplete or obsolete atomic and molecular line lists. This study introduces a database of pre-calculated absorption cross-sections for all isotopologues of critical molecules in late-type stellar, brown dwarf, and planetary atmospheres, specifically MgH, AlH, CaH, TiH, CrH, FeH, SiO, TiO, VO, and H2O. These computed opacities span pressure ranges from 10$^{-6}$ to 3000 bar and temperature ranges from 75 to 4000 K, covering spectral intervals of 0.25–330 $\mu$m where data availability permits; collision theory is applied to address gaps in pressure-broadening information. Additionally, we investigate how varying absorption cross-sections derived from different line lists impact Ultra-Hot Jupiter and M-dwarf atmospheres. Utilizing 1-D self-consistent radiative-convective equilibrium models, we demonstrate substantial variations in the theoretical spectra and thermal structures of substellar atmospheres. Specifically, for a 2000 K Ultra-Hot Jupiter, transmission and thermal emission spectra show variations of up to 320 and 80 ppm, respectively, while a 3000 K M-dwarf exhibits spectral differences as large as 125%. The most pronounced discrepancies are attributed to the selection of TiO line lists, particularly below 1 $\mu$m. In summary, we provide (1) a comprehensive database of molecular absorption cross-sections and (2) a quantification of biases introduced by line list differences in characterizing substellar and exoplanet atmospheres, underscoring the necessity of accurate and complete opacities for high-precision spectroscopy and photometry.

This work investigates high-dimensional multiple packing within Euclidean space. As a natural extension of sphere packing, multiple packing is characterized by a set $\mathcal{C}$ of points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ where every location in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is covered by at most $L-1$ balls of radius $\sqrt{nN}$ centered at points in $\mathcal{C}$, given parameters $N>0$ and $L\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge2}$. Leveraging established links to coding theory, these structures serve as the Euclidean counterpart to list-decodable codes, which are extensively researched over finite fields. In this study, we establish the current best lower bounds for the optimal density of list-decodable infinite constellations with a fixed $L$, specifically under the stricter framework of average-radius multiple packing. Our approach utilizes techniques from high-dimensional geometry and large deviation theory.

Scene understanding remains a critical yet difficult challenge within computer vision. While scene graphs have gained significant traction for their robust semantic capabilities in defining the visual structure of images, constructing accurate scene graphs for image retrieval, generation, and multi-modal tasks remains problematic. Traditional annotation interfaces are cumbersome for manual labeling, whereas existing automatic generation methods based on deep neural networks often produce redundant information while missing fine-grained details. To address these issues, we introduce SGDraw, an interactive scene graph drawing interface that leverages an object-oriented representation to facilitate user-driven creation and editing. This object-oriented model treats objects, their attributes, and inter-object relationships as cohesive structural units. SGDraw serves as a web-based tool designed for both annotating and generating scene graphs to support various scene understanding applications. Through comparative analysis with conventional tools and dedicated user experience studies, we demonstrated that SGDraw enables the creation of scene graphs with greater detail and higher accuracy compared to traditional bounding box annotations. Consequently, we posit that SGDraw offers significant utility for diverse vision tasks, including image retrieval and generation.

Recent advances in digitizing Whole Slide Images (WSIs) have facilitated the application of deep learning for automated disease diagnosis. However, WSIs pose distinct computational and algorithmic hurdles: their gigapixel dimensions (approximately 100,000 pixels) render them unsuitable for direct training of deep neural networks, and the scarcity of detailed annotations, due to the time-consuming nature of expert labeling, often limits training to slide-level labels. Multiple-Instance Learning (MIL) frameworks have emerged as a solution to these issues. Existing state-of-the-art methods typically employ a decoupled architecture, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to encode patches followed by a separate aggregation module for slide-level prediction; in this setup, the aggregation process does not influence the representations learned by the CNN. We introduce Cluster-to-Conquer (C2C), an end-to-end framework that partitions WSI patches into $k$ clusters, selects $k'$ patches from each cluster for training, and employs an adaptive attention mechanism for slide-level prediction. We demonstrate that clustering WSIs enhances model training by exposing the network to diverse discriminative features within patches. Furthermore, we regularize the clustering process by applying a KL-divergence loss between the attention weights of patches within a cluster and a uniform distribution. The framework is optimized end-to-end using slide-level cross-entropy, patch-level cross-entropy, and KL-divergence losses (Implementation: https://github.com/YashSharma/C2C).

We examine the ground-state characteristics of the material-relevant honeycomb Kitaev-$\Gamma$ model by employing both classical and quantum simulation techniques. The classical framework displays a complex network of highly ordered spin double helices, characterized by $18$ distinct helical axes, spontaneous periodic anisotropy, and a chirality pattern governed by ${\rm sgn}(\Gamma)$. Using infinite PEPS simulations on clusters of up to $36$ sites, we detect signatures of this many-body order within the quantum spin-$1/2$ system. These results offer a novel viewpoint on the Kitaev-$\Gamma$ model and expand our understanding of Kitaev magnetism.

The electrostatic characteristics of p-type nanowires (NWs) fabricated from InSb and GaSb are investigated, with particular attention to their gate capacitance, and benchmarked against conventional p-MOS semiconductors like Si and Ge. To ensure an accurate modeling of the Valence Band and charge dynamics under varying gate biases, a self-consistent kp simulator was developed. The analysis evaluates the specific contributions of insulator, centroid, and quantum capacitances, revealing that the latter two are highly sensitive to the semiconductor material. The study confirms that GaSb and InSb NWs exhibit intrinsic electrostatic performance comparable to Ge and Si, positioning these III-Sb compounds as promising candidates for next-generation technological nodes.

While a strong magnetic field is a common characteristic of many degenerate stars, their origins and evolutionary paths remain poorly understood. New data from volume-limited surveys suggest that no single mechanism explains the magnetic properties of all stars. We demonstrate that high-mass white dwarfs, likely formed through mergers, frequently possess extremely strong magnetic fields that emerge immediately upon entering the cooling phase; these may result from a dynamo active during the merger process. In contrast, lower-mass white dwarfs, typically products of single-star evolution, are rarely magnetic at birth, with detectable fields appearing weakly and gradually in only about 25% of cases. This may indicate that internal fields generated in earlier stages slowly migrate to the surface. Furthermore, both the frequency and intensity of these fields increase over time, eventually matching those of highly massive stars, especially after core crystallization begins—an effect that could drive a dynamo mechanism analogous to Earth's internal one.

Accurately understanding and quantifying uncertainty in black-box Neural Networks (NNs) is essential for their deployment in real-world domains like healthcare. While recent studies utilizing both Bayesian and non-Bayesian techniques have demonstrated how to model unified predictive uncertainty for NNs, decomposing this uncertainty allows for the disentanglement of granular heteroscedasticity sources, offering deeper insights into underlying causes. We introduce a conceptually straightforward non-Bayesian method, the deep split ensemble, which employs a multivariate Gaussian mixture model to separate predictive uncertainties. In this approach, NNs are trained on clusters of input features to generate uncertainty estimates specific to each cluster. We assess our method across multiple benchmark regression datasets, comparing it against unified uncertainty approaches. Extensive analyses, including dataset shifts and empirical rules, confirm that our models are inherently well-calibrated. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's applicability in a multi-modal context using a benchmark Alzheimer's dataset, illustrating how deep split ensembles can reveal hidden modality-specific biases. Due to the minimal modifications required for NN architecture and training, along with the high flexibility in grouping features into clusters, the approach is highly deployable and practical. The source code can be found at https://github.com/wazeerzulfikar/deep-split-ensembles.

Waiting times frequently occur in business processes during transitions between activities. Therefore, examining the root causes of these delays can assist analysts in pinpointing opportunities to shorten overall cycle times. This paper introduces a process mining method designed to break down waiting times observed at each activity transition into distinct direct causes and assess how each cause affects process efficiency. Empirical evaluation confirms that the approach successfully identifies various direct causes of waiting, and its practical utility is validated through an application to a real-world process.

The high instantaneous luminosity at CERN's Large Hadron Collider results in multiple proton-proton collisions occurring simultaneously or in adjacent bunch crossings, a phenomenon known as pileup. To address the noise generated by these pileup particles and enhance the accuracy of key physics observables, advanced mitigation algorithms are employed. This research implements a semi-supervised graph neural network designed to identify and remove pileup-induced noise at the particle level. The network is initially trained on charged particles with known labels derived from detector measurements in either data or simulation, before being applied to neutral particles lacking such labels. This semi-supervised method eliminates the reliance on simulation ground truth, enabling direct training on experimental data. Results indicate that this approach consistently outperforms widely used domain algorithms and achieves performance comparable to fully supervised training utilizing simulation truth. As the first application of semi-supervised learning to pileup mitigation, this study establishes a new pathway for fully data-driven machine learning approaches in this field.

Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) encompasses two primary subtasks: intent detection (ID) and slot filling (SF). Current research in this field generally follows two paths: one that jointly addresses both subtasks to enhance prediction accuracy, and another that prioritizes the domain-adaptation capabilities of individual subtasks. This paper seeks to unite these approaches by introducing a method that is both joint and domain-adaptive for SLU. We define SLU as a constrained generation task, leveraging a dynamic vocabulary constructed from domain-specific ontologies. Experiments conducted on the ASMixed and MTOD datasets demonstrate that our model achieves performance competitive with prior state-of-the-art joint models. Furthermore, the results indicate that our joint framework can be effectively adapted to new domains.
These represent the open issues addressed at the 13th International Symposium on Orthogonal Polynomials, Special Functions and Applications (OPSFA13), held in Gaithersburg, Maryland, on June 4, 2015.

We focus on learning representations from both labeled and unlabeled datasets. Drawing inspiration from the recent achievements of self-supervised learning (SSL), we propose a non-contrastive approach capable of incorporating auxiliary information. This extra knowledge can originate from annotated labels in supervised scenarios or from an SSL model trained on a different modality within an SSL framework. Our core concept involves extending the mean-shift algorithm by restricting the search space for nearest neighbors, thereby yielding semantically more refined representations. Specifically, our technique adjusts an instance's embedding to move closer to its nearest neighbors within this knowledge-constrained search space. By utilizing this non-contrastive loss function, we demonstrate that supervised pretraining on ImageNet-1k yields superior transfer performance compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we show that our approach exhibits robustness against label noise. Finally, we prove that noisy cross-modal constraints can be effectively leveraged to train self-supervised video models.

A defining feature of infectious disease propagation is the capacity to exploit efficient transmission routes within contact networks, thereby maximizing infection rates among target populations. This study develops methods to localize infections and reduce transmission by analyzing disease pathways in human proximity graphs. Experimental findings indicate that while contact tracing slows disease spread at low visibility rates, halting an epidemic requires high visibility (at least 60%) into the proximity graph combined with isolating half the population.
