Scientific workflows are ubiquitous across various domains and have facilitated numerous major discoveries over the last few decades. However, many of these workflows require substantial computational power, storage, and communication capabilities, necessitating execution on diverse large-scale platforms ranging from extensive cloud environments to emerging exascale high-performance computing (HPC) systems. To manage these executions, specialized software infrastructure is required. Consequently, Workflow Management Systems (WMSs) have been created to offer convenient, efficient, and portable abstractions for workflow creation and execution. Despite the value of these initiatives, the landscape is now fragmented by hundreds of independent WMSs, many of which are obsolete. This proliferation of seemingly similar yet incompatible systems creates significant entry barriers, leading many organizations to develop custom solutions instead of leveraging existing tools. This fragmentation adversely affects users, developers, and researchers alike. In response, the "Workflows Community Summit" was conducted online on January 13, 2021, with the primary objective of assessing the state of the art and pinpointing critical research challenges within the community. Preceding the summit, a survey of stakeholders—including both WMS developers and workflow users—identified key issues that were distilled into six broad themes for focused discussions led by community volunteers. This report compiles and structures the extensive information shared by participants before, during, and after the summit.

We employ the $GW$ + EDMFT approach to determine the correlated electronic structure of stacked $1T$-TaS$_2$ bilayers. The semi-infinite uncorrelated system's behavior varies by surface termination, manifesting as either a band insulator or a metallic surface state. For realistic onsite and intersite interaction strengths, a Mott gap emerges within the surface state, yet it remains narrower than the gap induced by the bilayer configuration. These findings align with recent scanning tunneling spectroscopy data across various terminating layers, as well as our own photoemission results, which reveal the coexistence of spatial regions exhibiting distinct gaps in the electronic spectrum.

Accurately measuring facial expressiveness is essential for analyzing human emotional behavior on a large scale. However, unlike the well-studied field of discrete expressions, methods for quantifying expressiveness at the video frame level remain largely unexplored. This paper introduces an algorithm that generates a bounded, continuous expressiveness score by integrating multimodal facial features, including action units (AUs), landmarks, head pose, and gaze. The algorithm places greater emphasis on AUs exhibiting high intensity and significant temporal variation. Capable of calculating expressiveness in terms of discrete expressions, this approach supports tasks such as facial behavior tracking and contextual subjectivity quantification. Evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in capturing temporal dynamics and overall expressiveness, measuring subjective differences within context, and yielding valuable insights.

Software Engineering researchers are increasingly employing Natural Language Processing (NLP) to automate the assessment of Software Vulnerabilities (SVs) by analyzing descriptions found in public repositories. However, current NLP-based methods struggle with concept drift, primarily due to the inadequate handling of new or out-of-vocabulary terms when evaluating unseen vulnerabilities over time. To address this, we propose a systematic approach that integrates both character and word features for automated SV assessment. This method predicts seven specific Vulnerability Characteristics (VCs). From a pool of eight NLP representations and six established Machine Learning models, the optimal configuration for each VC is identified using a customized time-based cross-validation technique. We validated this approach through large-scale experiments involving over 100,000 SVs from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Our results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively mitigates concept drift in NVD descriptions spanning 2000 to 2018, even without model retraining, and performs competitively against existing word-only methods. Furthermore, we explore strategies for constructing compact, concept-drift-aware models with reduced feature sets and provide recommendations regarding classifier selection and NLP representations for SV assessment.

Automatically interpreting image content is a critical practical challenge, particularly in e-commerce and social media where pictures must be automatically categorized. Currently, the standard method involves fine-tuning pre-trained image models with domain-specific data. However, organizations also gather collaborative signals regarding user interactions with online content, such as views, ratings, or tags, which are typically utilized for item recommendation by deriving latent user and item representations. This work demonstrates that such collaborative information can enhance the classification of new images. Specifically, we introduce a multitask learning framework in which the auxiliary task involves reconstructing collaborative latent item representations. Experiments conducted on datasets from e-commerce and social media platforms reveal that incorporating these collaborative signals significantly boosts image classification performance, achieving improvements of up to 9.1%.

We present Token Merging (ToMe), an uncomplicated approach to boost the throughput of current Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures without requiring retraining. ToMe employs a general, lightweight matching algorithm to progressively merge similar tokens within a transformer; this method is as rapid as pruning yet achieves higher accuracy. When applied directly, ToMe doubles the throughput of state-of-the-art ViT-L @ 512 and ViT-H @ 518 models on images and increases ViT-L video throughput by 2.2x, with only a 0.2–0.3% reduction in accuracy. Additionally, ToMe can be seamlessly integrated during training, enhancing training speeds by up to 2x for MAE fine-tuning on video. Incorporating ToMe into training further reduces accuracy loss, resulting in 2x throughput for ViT-B on audio tasks with merely a 0.4% drop in mAP. Qualitatively, our analysis shows that ToMe successfully consolidates object parts into single tokens, even across multiple video frames. In summary, ToMe offers accuracy and speed performance that rival state-of-the-art solutions for images, video, and audio.

This study employs density-functional theory (DFT) to investigate the structural, electronic, and bonding characteristics of germanium (Ge)-doped vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$). The primary objective is to elucidate the experimentally observed rise in the metal-insulator transition temperature upon Ge doping and to assess the extent to which conventional DFT can capture the underlying physics and chemistry. Using a supercell approach, we simulated doping at various concentrations and spatial arrangements of Ge atoms within the VO$_2$ lattice. Our findings indicate that introducing Ge atoms significantly disrupts the high-symmetry metallic rutile phase, triggering structural distortions that partially mimic the dimerization found in the experimental insulating phase. Consequently, this work offers a potential explanation for the elevated transition temperature under Ge doping and encourages further research into the interplay between structural and electronic transitions in VO$_2$.

The TRSM is a novel physics framework that augments the Standard Model's scalar sector with two extra CP-even scalars. This extension generates a wide range of intriguing signatures, several of which remain uninvestigated by LHC experiments. I will also address the possibility of examining the hhh final state within this model.

Abstraction is a critical component of intelligence that allows agents to build resilient representations for efficient decision-making. Over the past decade, deep networks have demonstrated efficacy by generating increasingly complex abstractions; however, because these abstractions are spread across numerous neurons, reusing learned skills remains computationally expensive. Prior approaches either imposed designer biases by forcing abstraction formation or relied on extensive neural units without adequately addressing how to extract high-level features that better capture source tasks. To circumvent both designer bias and excessive resource consumption, we propose leveraging neural response dynamics to create compact representations for skill transfer. Specifically, we evaluate two competing strategies: (1) the maximum information compression principle and (2) the concept that abstract events produce slowly varying signals. These methods are applied to neural signals generated during task execution. In our simulations, we utilize either Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or Slow Feature Analysis (SFA) on data from the final hidden layer of a deep network performing a source task, subsequently employing these features for transferring skills to a new target task. We assess the generalization performance of these methods against baselines involving full-layer output transfer and no transfer. Our findings indicate that SFA units yield the most successful skill transfer. Both SFA and PCA require fewer resources than standard skill transfer, with many resulting units exhibiting localized responses that reflect relationships between end-effectors, obstacles, and goals. Furthermore, SFA units associated with the lowest eigenvalues resemble symbolic representations that strongly correlate with high-level features like joint angles, potentially serving as precursors to fully symbolic systems.

Employing the MPI-AMRVAC relativistic MHD code alongside post-processing radiative transfer simulations, we examine how magnetic field configurations and the transverse stratification of an over-pressured jet affect its morphology, the dynamics of moving shocks, and the resulting radio light curves. Initially, we assess various large-scale magnetic fields and their impact on standing shocks and the stratified jet structure. Subsequently, we analyze the interaction between moving shock waves and these standing shocks. We generate synthetic synchrotron maps and radio light curves, analyzing variability at 1 and 15.3 GHz across multiple viewing angles. Finally, we compare our simulated light curves with radio flares from the blazar 3C 273 observed via OVRO and VLBA within the MOJAVE survey (2008–2019). Our findings indicate that in a structured, over-pressured relativistic jet, large-scale magnetic fields alter standing shock properties and cause the jet to open. As moving shocks carrying overdensities from the jet base cross these standing shocks, they trigger highly luminous radio flares. Observing the temporal structure of these flares from different angles probes varying optical depths within the jet. At 1 GHz and small viewing angles, self-absorption by the moving shock becomes significant, causing a flux drop after the shock interacts with the brightest standing knot. A slight asymmetry in the simulated flare shapes arises from remnant emission of the shocked standing shocks. The characteristics of these simulated flares and the correlation between light curve peaks and the crossing of moving and standing shocks support this scenario as an explanation for the observed radio flares of 3C 273.

This paper introduces a novel data augmentation technique for action recognition that leverages instance segmentation. While numerous data augmentation approaches exist for image recognition, few are specifically designed for action recognition tasks. Our proposed method, ObjectMix, isolates object regions from two distinct videos via instance segmentation and merges them to generate synthetic videos. Evaluations on the UCF101 and HMDB51 datasets confirm the method's efficacy and demonstrate its superiority over the prior approach, VideoMix.

This study introduces a new linear prediction coding (LPC) based data augmentation technique tailored for low- and zero-resource dialect automatic speech recognition (ASR) in children. The augmentation process involves perturbing formant peaks within the LPC spectrum during both analysis and reconstruction phases. The method was assessed using two new children's speech datasets: one featuring California English from the Southern California region, and the other comprising a blend of Southern American English and African American English from Atlanta, Georgia. The approach was tested by training both HMM-DNN and end-to-end systems to verify model robustness. Results indicate that the algorithm enhances ASR performance, particularly for zero-resource dialect tasks involving children, outperforming standard augmentation strategies like VTLP, Speed Perturbation, and SpecAugment.

As decentralized optimization gains traction across fields like robotics, sensor networks, control systems, and machine learning, concerns regarding privacy have also intensified. Current privacy-preserving methods typically integrate decentralized optimization with external mechanisms such as differential privacy or homomorphic encryption, often at the cost of reduced accuracy or significant computational and communication burdens. In contrast, we introduce an algorithm that is inherently privacy-preserving by leveraging the robustness of decentralized optimization against uncertainties in its dynamics. Specifically, we propose a general decentralized optimization framework demonstrating that privacy can be achieved by introducing randomness into optimization parameters. We establish that this added randomness does not compromise optimization accuracy and prove that the algorithm converges $R$-linearly when the global objective function is smooth and strongly convex. Furthermore, we rigorously demonstrate that the algorithm prevents other nodes from inferring a specific node's gradient, with numerical simulations validating these theoretical findings.

This study reports the inaugural search for signatures of brane-world extra-dimensional dark matter (DM) in the very-high-energy gamma-ray regime, utilizing observations of the Segue 1 dwarf spheroidal galaxy with the MAGIC telescope system. Branons, which emerge as new degrees of freedom in flexible brane-world models, represent weakly interacting massive particles and viable candidates for dark matter. Ground-based gamma-ray observatories like MAGIC can indirectly identify branon DM within the multi-TeV mass range by detecting secondary products resulting from DM annihilation into Standard Model particles. Lacking a detected signal, we constrain the branon DM parameter space through a binned likelihood analysis of nearly 160 hours of deep exposure on Segue 1 obtained by the MAGIC telescopes. Our most restrictive upper limit on the thermally-averaged annihilation cross-section, established at the 95% confidence level, is approximately $\langle \sigma v \rangle \simeq 1.4 \times 10^{-23}~\text{cm}^{3}\text{s}^{-1}$ for a branon mass of roughly $0.7~\text{TeV}$.

This paper tackles a convolutive blind source separation (BSS) challenge by introducing an extended FastMNMF framework that incorporates prior information for the joint diagonalization of the spatial covariance matrix model. Although FastMNMF was recently developed as a rapid multichannel nonnegative matrix factorization technique under the assumption that multiple source spatial covariance matrices can be jointly diagonalized, it failed to enhance source-separation performance, and the physical significance of its joint-diagonalization mechanism remained ambiguous. To address these limitations, we first demonstrate the strong connection between the joint-diagonalization process and the demixing system employed in independent low-rank matrix analysis (ILRMA). Building on this insight, we propose a regularized FastMNMF approach supported by ILRMA and establish parameter update rules with guaranteed convergence. Experimental results from BSS tasks indicate that the proposed method achieves superior source-separation accuracy compared to conventional FastMNMF while maintaining nearly identical computational efficiency.

Accelerating battery formation rates can substantially reduce the costs of manufacturing lithium-ion batteries. However, implementing these faster protocols in real-world production is difficult because there is a shortage of affordable, quick diagnostic metrics capable of predicting effects on long-term battery lifespan. This study identifies cell resistance measured at low states of charge as a viable early-life diagnostic indicator for evaluating new formation strategies. Our findings demonstrate that this metric correlates with cycle life and enhances the precision of data-driven models for forecasting battery longevity. The signal can be captured at the conclusion of the manufacturing line within seconds and does not necessitate specialized testing hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the physical link between this resistance reading and the amount of lithium consumed during formation, proposing that the signal could serve as a universal tool for assessing any manufacturing process adjustments that influence total lithium usage.

The Latent Block Model (LBM) serves as a model-based approach for clustering both the $d$ columns and $n$ rows of a data matrix simultaneously. While parameter estimation within the LBM is complex and multifaceted, various estimation strategies have been developed and are empirically well-understood; however, theoretical assurances regarding their asymptotic behavior remain scarce, with most existing results restricted to binary data. This work establishes theoretical guarantees for valued settings. Under mild constraints on the parameter space and within an asymptotic regime where $\log(d)/n$ and $\log(n)/d$ converge to zero as $n$ and $d$ grow infinitely large, we demonstrate that: (1) the maximum-likelihood estimate of the complete model (with known labels) is consistent, and (2) the log-likelihood ratios are equivalent between the complete and observed (with unknown labels) models. This equivalence enables the transfer of asymptotic consistency, along with asymptotic normality under mild conditions, to the maximum likelihood estimate for the observed model. Furthermore, the variational estimator is also shown to be consistent and, under identical conditions, asymptotically normal.

We conducted a chemodynamical study of 11,562 metal-rich, high-eccentricity halo-like main-sequence stars, collectively known as the Splash or Splashed Disk, drawn from SDSS and LAMOST datasets. By dividing these stars into a low-[$\alpha$/Fe] population (LAP) and a high-[$\alpha$/Fe] population (HAP) based on their kinematics and chemical compositions, we identified distinct properties suggesting different origins. Our detailed analysis of orbital inclinations indicates that the HAP consists primarily (~90%) of heated disk stars, with a minor component (~10%) of in situ stars from a starburst event likely triggered by the Milky Way's interaction with the Gaia Sausage/Enceladus (GSE) or other early mergers. Conversely, the LAP is composed of roughly equal parts accreted GSE stars and stars formed during a GSE-induced starburst. These results imply that the Splash stars in our sample originated through at least three distinct mechanisms: accretion, disk heating, and merger-induced starbursts.

We introduce a precise and efficient solver for atmospheric dynamics simulations capable of non-conforming mesh refinement. The governing equations are the conservative Euler equations for compressible flows. The numerical approach utilizes an $h$-adaptive Discontinuous Galerkin spatial discretization combined with a second-order Additive Runge Kutta IMEX time discretization method, specifically optimized for low Mach number regimes. Implemented within the $deal.II$ library, the solver leverages its mesh refinement features to improve computational efficiency. Numerical experiments utilizing standard benchmarks for atmospheric dynamics validate the characteristics and benefits of this proposed method.

End-to-end (E2E) artificial intelligence (AI) workflows encompass multiple phases, such as data preprocessing, ingestion, model definition and training, hyperparameter tuning, deployment, inference, postprocessing, and subsequent downstream analyses. Achieving an efficient E2E workflow necessitates optimizing nearly every stage of the pipeline. Intel Xeon processors, equipped with substantial memory and AI acceleration features like Intel Deep Learning Boost, are ideally suited for executing multiple training and inference instances in parallel while maintaining a low total cost of ownership (TCO). To demonstrate performance on Xeon hardware, we implemented comprehensive optimization strategies alongside software and hardware acceleration across various E2E pipelines spanning Computer Vision, NLP, and Recommendation systems. These efforts yielded performance gains ranging from 1.8x to 81.7x across different pipelines. This paper details the specific optimization strategies employed to achieve these results on Intel Xeon processors using a set of eight distinct E2E pipelines.

This brief note aims to provide heuristic reasoning regarding the unconventional fractional Laplacian operator. It is intended to broaden the perspective of readers aspiring to cultivate an interest in research within this field.

Addressing the persistent challenge of enhancing imitation learning's generalization with limited demonstrations in reinforcement learning (RL) is crucial. Current issues include narrow, biased data distributions from poor demonstrations, difficulties in learning from non-Markovian human experts, and the hindrance of performance improvement due to over-reliance on sub-optimal trajectories. To resolve these challenges, we introduce TD3fG, an algorithm designed to facilitate a smooth transition from expert-based learning to experience-based learning. Demonstrating robust performance in the MUJOCO environment even with scarce and sub-optimal data, our approach employs behavior cloning to train a network as a reference action generator, utilizing it within both the loss function and exploration noise. This innovation enables agents to extract prior knowledge from demonstrations while mitigating the adverse effects of poor Markovian properties. Comparative results show that TD3fG outperforms both BC+ fine-tuning and DDPGfD, particularly in scenarios with limited demonstrations. The name TD3fG stands for "TD3 from a generator."

The measured foliations at infinity for a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifold correspond to the horizontal measured foliations derived from the Schwarzian derivatives of the uniformization maps linked to the boundary components at infinity. For a pair of measured foliations $(\mathsf{F}_{+},\mathsf{F}_{-})$ that fill a closed hyperbolic surface $S$, we demonstrate that for sufficiently small $t>0$, the scaled foliations $t\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $t\mathsf{F}_{-}$ can be uniquely realized as the measured foliations at infinity of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifold homeomorphic to $S\times\mathbb{R}$. This manifold resides in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the Fuchsian locus. This finding parallels a theorem by Bonahon, which establishes that a quasi-Fuchsian manifold near the Fuchsian locus is uniquely determined by the data of filling measured bending laminations on the boundary of its convex core. Additionally, we provide an interpretation of this result within the framework of half-pipe geometry.

This study investigates a novel approach to achieving controlled, spin-dependent transport within a two-terminal bridge configuration. The setup features a magnetic quantum ring directly connected to a magnetic quantum wire, with an in-plane electric field applied perpendicular to the wire's axis. By adjusting the external electric field under a finite bias voltage—without altering any intrinsic system parameters—spin currents can be effectively regulated. At specific field intensities, a significant level of spin polarization is attained, allowing the system to function as an externally controlled spin-polarized device. Furthermore, a comprehensive comparison of spin current magnitudes derived from various bridge configurations is included to ensure the investigation stands as a self-contained study.

This study introduces novel mathematical and computational frameworks for modeling portfolio return distributions. By integrating advanced computational geometry and spline theory, we derive analytical formulas and efficient algorithms to calculate probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, and the $k$-th moments. Our implementation successfully processes portfolios containing up to 10,000 assets and computes moments of order $k$ up to 40 within seconds, effectively addressing real-world complexities. We specifically address the prevalent long-only investment strategy, characterized by non-negative weights that sum to unity, while maintaining a framework that is easily adaptable to broader contexts. Our approach utilizes a geometric representation of the stock market, defining the investment set as a simplex polytope, where the cumulative distribution function serves as a portfolio score representing the proportion of portfolios with returns below a specific threshold. We present closed-form analytic expressions for the first four moments of the cross-sectional return distribution alongside a new algorithm for determining all higher-order moments, demonstrating that the first four moments directly map to the underlying asset return moments. Furthermore, our solutions are fully general, encompassing the special case of equal asset returns often omitted in prior research. Finally, we apply our portfolio score to develop new performance metrics and asset management strategies, revealing that score-based optimal portfolios exhibit lower concentration and significantly reduced ranking risk compared to traditional mean-variance portfolios.

This paper introduces a dataset designed for natural language understanding and inference tasks. It comprises logical puzzles in natural language drawn from three specific domains: comparison puzzles, knights and knaves, and zebra puzzles. For each puzzle, we include the complete set of atomic questions derivable from the text's relations and entities. Alongside every question, we provide the correct answer—categorized as entailment, contradiction, or ambiguity—which has been validated using theorem provers. High-quality puzzles exhibit two key characteristics: (i) every piece of information is essential, and (ii) no extraneous details are included. These attributes render such puzzles particularly suitable for machine comprehension tasks.

Large Doppler spreads represent a primary obstacle in high-speed mobile communications, making the precise estimation of the Maximum Doppler Spread (MDS) critical for enhancing communication link performance. This paper derives both data-aided (DA) and non-data-aided (NDA) Cramer-Rao lower bounds (CRLBs) and maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) for MDS within multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) frequency-selective fading channels. Additionally, a low-complexity NDA moment-based estimator (MBE) is introduced. This proposed NDA-MBE utilizes the second- and fourth-order moments of the received signal to estimate the normalized squared autocorrelation function of the fading channel. Subsequently, the MDS estimation task is modeled as a non-linear regression problem, solved using a least-squares curve-fitting optimization method to obtain the MDS estimate. Notably, this study presents the first investigation into DA and NDA MDS estimation specifically for MIMO frequency-selective fading channels. Simulation results indicate that the performance of the derived NDA-MLE closely approaches the NDA-CRLB, even with relatively small observation windows. Furthermore, the NDA-MBE's significantly reduced complexity yields a low normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) across a broad spectrum of MDS values, provided the observation window is sufficiently large.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for the early identification of heart conditions, yet the automatic analysis of heart sounds for detecting abnormalities is hindered by additive noise and sensor-specific degradation. This study proposes methods to tackle cardiac abnormality detection in the presence of both distortion types. Initially, we mathematically evaluate the impact of additive and convolutional noise on short-term filterbank features and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) layers. Guided by this analysis, we introduce a hybrid approach combining linear and logarithmic spectrogram-image features. These 2D representations are fed into a Residual CNN (ResNet) for detecting heart sound anomalies. Validation was conducted using an open-access dataset of noisy heart sounds recorded by various stethoscope sensors. The proposed method outperforms conventional techniques, achieving an AUC of 91.36%, an F-1 score of 84.09%, and a Macc of 85.08%. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates superior mean accuracy across diverse source domains, including variations in stethoscope types and noise levels, confirming its robustness under different recording conditions. By effectively mitigating the effects of background noise and sensor variability in phonocardiogram (PCG) classification, this combination of linear and logarithmic features with a ResNet classifier facilitates the development of computer-aided cardiac auscultation systems capable of operating in noisy environments using low-cost stethoscopes.

Utilizing non-contrast CT (NCCT) for quantifying cardiac structures may enhance cardiovascular risk assessment. However, manually creating reference standards to train a fully convolutional network (FCN) for automatic NCCT segmentation is practically unfeasible, and models trained on coronary CT angiography (CCTA) fail to generalize to NCCT data. Consequently, we propose training an FCN using virtual non-contrast (VNC) images generated by a dual-layer detector CT scanner, paired with a reference standard derived from perfectly aligned CCTA images.

Finding Moore-Penrose inverses for the incidence, Laplacian, and signless Laplacian matrices of graph families has remained an open challenge, with the notable exceptions of trees and unicyclic graphs. Given that inverse formulas for odd and even unicyclic graphs differ significantly, this study focuses on wheel graphs, which are constructed from either odd or even cycles. This article resolves the open problem specifically for wheel graphs and establishes an intriguing link to the inverses of circulant matrices.

Archaeological literature is expanding quickly, but access to this data was previously limited to metadata searches. To address this, we developed a text retrieval engine for a massive collection of approximately 658 million words of archaeological text. Given the importance of domain-specific entities like locations, time periods, and artifacts in archaeological information retrieval, we created a named entity recognition (NER) model to annotate the entire corpus. This paper introduces ArcheoBERTje, a BERT model pre-trained specifically on Dutch archaeological texts. We evaluated its performance against both a generic multilingual model and a generic Dutch model on a NER task. Additionally, we explored ensemble techniques that combine multiple BERT models and the integration of a domain thesaurus with the best-performing BERT model using Conditional Random Fields (CRF). Our findings show that ArcheoBERTje significantly outperforms both the multilingual and generic Dutch models, exhibiting lower variance across runs and achieving an average F1 score of 0.735. It also surpasses ensemble methods that combine the three models. Furthermore, augmenting ArcheoBERTje's predictions with explicit domain knowledge from a theasaurs did not improve the F1 score. Through quantitative and qualitative analysis of vocabulary and outputs across the full collection, we offer insights into the effects of domain-specific fine-tuning. Our results suggest that for highly specialized domains like archaeology, pre-training on domain-specific data yields a significantly larger improvement in NER quality than previously observed in other fields, rendering the addition of external domain knowledge from a thesaurus unnecessary.

The energy budget for gravitational waves generated by cosmological first-order phase transitions relies on the thermal plasma's sound speed within the phases surrounding the bubble wall. Utilizing a real-singlet augmented Standard Model capable of supporting a strong two-step electroweak phase transition, we calculate higher-order corrections to both pressure and sound speed. Our results are compared against lower-order approximations for the sound speed and energy budget to assess their influence on the gravitational wave signal. We observe that deviations of the sound speed from $c_s^2 = 1/3$ are amplified by up to $\mathcal O(5\%)$ in our higher-order analysis, leading to a suppression of the energy budget by as much as $\mathcal O(50\%)$ relative to approximations that assume $c_s^2 = 1/3$. This effect is particularly pronounced in hybrid and detonation scenarios. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to include multiple inert scalars and a reduced number of fermion families to simulate hypothetical dark sector phase transitions. In such modified field configurations, the sound speed can experience substantial suppression, potentially altering the gravitational wave amplitude by an order of magnitude.

The spinel-structured CuIr$_{2}$S$_{4}$ exhibits an unusual orbitally driven three-dimensional Peierls-like transition between insulating and metallic states. Its low-temperature symmetry-broken insulating phase is particularly notable for hosting a metastable, irradiation-induced disordered state with weak conductivity. This study employs all-optical ultrafast multi-pulse time-resolved spectroscopy to investigate the effects of intense femtosecond optical pulses. We demonstrate that above a specific excitation fluence threshold, the structural coherence of the low-T broken symmetry state is strongly disrupted within a sub-picosecond window, creating a structurally inhomogeneous transient state that lasts for several tens of picoseconds before relaxing into the low-T disordered weakly conducting state. In contrast, the electronic order exhibits transient gap filling at a significantly lower fluence threshold. The findings suggest that the photoinduced transition to the high-T metallic phase follows first-order nucleation kinetics; this mechanism inhibits a complete ultrafast structural transition even when the absorbed energy far exceeds the equilibrium enthalpy difference required for the high-T metallic phase. Conversely, the dynamically decoupled electronic order is suppressed on a sub-picosecond timescale through an independent photoinduced Mott transition.

This study addresses the minimization of a nonlinear function subject to nonlinear equality constraints using a sequential quadratic programming (SQP) approach, specifically under conditions where only noisy evaluations of the objective and constraint functions are available. To ensure stability, the classical SQP method is adapted by modifying the standard Armijo line search to account for the known noise level within the functions. Theoretical analysis establishes conditions under which the algorithm's iterates converge to a neighborhood of the solution, defined by the noise magnitude and problem conditioning, assuming the SQP procedure does not utilize regularization or trust regions. Numerical results demonstrate that this relaxed line search enhances the practical performance of the method on problems featuring uniformly distributed noise. A significant application of this research lies in derivative-free optimization, particularly when finite differences are used to approximate gradients.

This paper examines the impact of Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) in both IPv4 and IPv6 through mathematical, logical, and graphical models. We developed a mathematical framework to simulate PMTUD operations by analyzing packet transmission, specifically calculating the time required to send a single packet from source to destination in an IPv6 network with PMTUD enabled and an IPv4 network with the DF bit set. Our analysis reveals that communication time increases as the MTU of intermediate nodes varies. Consequently, we formulated a model to determine network communication delay, establishing an asymptotic lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ and an upper bound of $\Theta(n^2)$ for time taken using PMTUD. We observed that packet drop frequency adheres to Bernoulli trials, allowing us to define a success probability that is notably higher for the initial 2% of nodes along the path. Furthermore, we identified that $^{n}C_{a}$ distinct combinations of packet drop frequencies without repetition can occur for a specific drop rate. The relationship between the summation of these combinations (acting as coefficients in the time wastage equation) and their frequencies produces symmetric graphs, revealing underlying mathematical and statistical structures to quantify time wastage and its behavior. This approach also facilitates the measurement of relative maximum, minimum, and average time wastage, while enabling the calculation of the probability for these relative values given a specific packet drop frequency and path node count.

This phenomenological study investigates the CP properties of the top quark Yukawa coupling by analyzing $t\bar{t}h$ events at the 13 TeV LHC, specifically focusing on the $h\rightarrow b\bar b$ decay and the dilepton channel of $t\bar{t}$. Signal generation covered pure CP-even, pure CP-odd, and mixed-CP coupling scenarios, alongside standard model backgrounds. The research examined angular distributions and asymmetries, identifying them as effective probes of the coupling's CP nature even after applying detector simulations and full event reconstruction via kinematic fitting. Furthermore, expected limits on the $t\bar{t}h$ production cross-section times branching ratio were derived for various top quark Yukawa CP-mixing angles across different LHC integrated luminosities.

Cosmic-ray antiprotons serve as a valuable diagnostic instrument for investigating astroparticle physics processes within the Galaxy. Although the majority of observed antiprotons align with a secondary origin, some investigations have indicated a subdominant primary component in the AMS-02 dataset. This proceedings article re-examines this excess by accounting for systematic uncertainties that may influence the signal. Key among these are previously unknown correlations in the AMS-02 systematics, primarily linked to cosmic-ray absorption cross-sections within the detector. We calculate these correlations through a meticulous reassessment of nuclear scattering data, employing Glauber-Gribov theory to establish necessary redundancy for a comprehensive global fit. Incorporating these correlated errors substantially alters the signal's significance; notably, the analysis becomes more responsive to diffusion models at low rigidities. When extending the diffusion model minimally beyond a single power law, the global significance falls below 1$\sigma$, casting serious doubt on the reliability of the original finding.

This study examines the population of "wandering" black holes—those physically displaced from their host halo centers—within the Romulus cosmological simulations. Distinct from most existing simulations, Romulus seeds black holes based on local gas conditions and allows them to evolve dynamically rather than fixing them at halo centers. By tracking these objects, we generate robust predictions regarding this offset population. Our results indicate that the number of wandering black holes scales approximately linearly with halo mass, suggesting thousands exist within galaxy cluster halos. Locally, these wanderers constitute about 10% of the total local black hole mass budget after accounting for seed masses. However, at higher redshifts ($z \gtrsim 4$), wandering black holes both outnumber and outshine their central supermassive counterparts. We find that most wanderers retain seed-like masses and originate from the centers of previously disrupted satellite galaxies. Although most lack a resolved stellar counterpart, those that do are located farther out at larger fractions of the virial radius. Conversely, more luminous wanderers tend to reside at smaller radii within more massive halos, often aligning closer to the host's mid-plane or associated with stellar overdensities. Ultimately, this analysis reveals that current censuses of supermassive black holes are incomplete, indicating a significant population of off-center wanderers likely remains undetected.

We both experimentally and theoretically investigate the temporal rotation and radial twist occurring in the interference pattern formed between a vortex beam and its conjugate counterpart. To quantitatively analyze these phenomena, we intentionally introduce controlled variations in frequency or wavefront curvature to the conjugate beam using a movable Mach-Zehnder interferometer. We systematically examine how physical parameters—including topological charge, frequency difference, and wavefront curvature difference—affect both the temporal rotation and radial twist. Furthermore, we determine the rotation velocity ($\Omega$) and twist coefficient ($\alpha$) to characterize the extent of these effects. Theoretical models describing the interference of vortex beams show strong agreement with our experimental findings. This study is valuable for elucidating the detailed structure of such interference patterns and for manipulating matter using superimposed vortex beams.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is rapidly achieving significant success across diverse domains, ranging from simple pendulum control to managing complex data centers, by enabling agents to learn optimal behaviors through environmental interaction. Nevertheless, the performance and reliability of RL-based inference models for decision-making are heavily dependent on selecting appropriate hyperparameters. Identifying these optimal settings is a tedious, iterative, and computationally intensive task. Unlike other neural network architectures, deep RL has seen limited hyperparameter tuning due to its algorithmic complexity and reliance on simulation environments. To address this, we introduce a distributed variable-length genetic algorithm framework designed to systematically optimize hyperparameters for various RL tasks. This evolutionary approach enhances training efficiency and architectural robustness. We validate the scalability of our method across a spectrum of problems, from basic gym environments to complex real-world scenarios, comparing our results against Bayesian optimization. Our findings demonstrate that increasing the number of generations yields optimal solutions that demand fewer training episodes and are computationally efficient, all while maintaining high deployment robustness. These results are crucial for advancing deep RL controllers for practical, real-world applications.

In 1980, J. Powell conjectured that five specific elements are sufficient to generate the Goeritz group for any Heegaard splitting of $S^3$, building upon Goeritz's earlier findings for genus $2$ cases. This paper demonstrates that Powell's conjecture holds true for genus $3$ splittings and outlines a framework for determining its validity in higher genus scenarios.

Since traditional searches for supersymmetry have yielded no compelling evidence for new physics, the CMS experiment is developing specialized searches focused on more challenging and specific supersymmetric scenarios. This contribution outlines three such recent analyses utilizing 13 TeV proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a search for heavy gluinos decaying via a heavy next-to-lightest neutralino into final states featuring boosted Z bosons and missing transverse momentum; a search for compressed supersymmetry characterized by soft taus; and a search for compressed, long-lived charginos within hadronic final states marked by disappearing tracks.

Classical light field rendering excels at synthesizing novel views with high-fidelity view-dependent phenomena like reflections, refractions, and translucency, yet it demands dense scene sampling. In contrast, geometric reconstruction techniques function with sparse views but fail to accurately capture non-Lambertian effects. We propose a unified model that leverages the advantages of both approaches while addressing their respective drawbacks. By utilizing a four-dimensional light field representation, our model achieves precise modeling of view-dependent characteristics. Simultaneously, it implicitly infers scene geometry from sparse inputs by enforcing geometric constraints throughout training and inference. Specifically, we present a two-stage transformer architecture that first aggregates features along epipolar lines and subsequently combines them along reference views to determine target ray colors. Experimental results on various forward-facing and 360-degree datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios exhibiting significant view-dependent variations.

This study focuses on Spatial Variability Aware Neural Networks (SVANNs) to develop mathematical and computational models that offer comparative physical interpretations, thereby enhancing transparency through attributes like simulability, decomposability, and algorithmic clarity. Addressing this issue is critical for applications requiring reusability, debugging, and legal explainability. However, challenges such as high parameter counts, loose generalization bounds, overfitting risks, and noise sensitivity hinder interpretability. Existing post-hoc interpretation methods, whether model-specific or model-agnostic, are limited because they often neglect physical constraints (e.g., mass balance) and properties (e.g., the second law of geography). To address this, the work introduces novel comparative approaches for interpreting SVANNs based on geographically heterogeneous features, evaluated through a wetland mapping case study. These findings demonstrate that the proposed physical interpretation improves SVANN transparency while highlighting the trade-off between interpretability and performance metrics like the F1-score. Additionally, the study describes an interpretation framework utilizing geographically heterogeneous processes modeled as partial differential equations (PDEs).

This study provides a theoretical analysis of electromagnetic wave emission resulting from electron transitions between spin subbands within a ferromagnet. We examine various mechanisms driving these spin-flip transitions, including those induced by the wave's magnetic field and those arising from Rashba spin-orbit interaction. While these two mechanisms operate in homogeneously magnetized ferromagnets, additional mechanisms emerge in non-collinear magnetic media: one involves the dependence of the exchange interaction constant on conduction electron quasimomentum, and the other is intrinsic to any non-collinear configuration. We investigate these processes specifically within a non-collinear ferromagnet exhibiting a helicoidal magnetization distribution. Using realistic parameters, we calculate transition probabilities for each mechanism and compare their effectiveness. Furthermore, we estimate the resulting radiation power and the threshold current within a simplified model where spin injection occurs via a spin-polarized electric current passing through a tunnel barrier.

In Phys. Rev. D 103, L111303 (2021), we presented an enhanced calculation of the nuclear spin-independent parity-violating electric dipole transition amplitude ($E1_{PV}$) for the $6s ~ ^2S_{1/2} - 7s ~ ^2S_{1/2}$ transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster (RCC) theory. Recently, B. M. Roberts and J. S. M. Ginges questioned our determination of the Core contribution to $E1_{PV}$ in a Comment. While their results differ from ours, our findings align with previous studies that explicitly calculated this contribution. In our response, we provided a detailed justification for our evaluation of the Core contribution. We highlighted that, unlike sum-over-states approaches, our work treats the Main, Core, and Tail contributions equally. Additionally, we addressed their concerns regarding our approximate treatment of QED corrections, noting that while this was not the primary objective, it was included for completeness. Ultimately, the conclusions of our paper remain valid even if our estimated QED contribution to $E1_{PV}$ is substituted with earlier estimates.

This study examines Calderón's inverse boundary value problem for specific classes of nonlinear Helmholtz Schrödinger and Maxwell equations within a bounded domain in $\R^n$. The primary approach involves the higher-order linearization of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map associated with these equations. Building on the methodology in \cite{DKSU}, we establish local uniqueness for the linearized partial data Calderón inverse problem. Furthermore, by utilizing Runge approximation properties and the unique continuation principle, these results are extended to global contexts. As practical applications, we demonstrate the simultaneous recovery of unknown cavities or boundaries alongside coefficients.

This research investigates energy transfer via exact resonances in surface gravity waves within a finite periodic spatial domain. Utilizing a kinematic model that simulates active wave mode generation in a discrete wavenumber space $\mathcal{S}_R$, we explore the feasibility of both direct and inverse energy cascades. Specifically, we initialize a region of excitation that iteratively distributes energy to modes within $\mathcal{S}_R$ through exact resonances. At each step, new modes are activated via scale resonances (creating modes of different lengths), followed by the analysis of two boundary conditions for angle resonances (transferring energy at identical length scales): a lower bound excluding angle resonances and an upper bound where all modes sharing the length of active modes are excited. This approach is crucial for performing computations over large domains $\mathcal{S}_R$ with a maximum wavenumber $R\sim 10^3$. Our findings indicate that energy cascades toward the boundaries of $\mathcal{S}_R$ occur in both direct and inverse scenarios provided the initial excited region is sufficiently large; otherwise, the system enters a frozen turbulence state. A sharp transition between these regimes is observed, particularly in the direct cascade. By analyzing the structure of resonant quartets, we clarify the mechanisms driving this abrupt transition and the function of angular energy transfer within the cascades.

This study examines the structure of a specific class of two-loop massive vacuum Feynman integrals. These integrals are characterized by a linear relationship among their three propagator masses, $m_1+m_2=m_3$, which aligns with the zeros of the corresponding Källén function. Beyond their utility in thermal field theory, these integrals can be transformed into one-loop three-point functions featuring collinear external momenta, a property that justifies the designation "collinear" masses. We derive a closed-form solution for these integrals, demonstrating that they invariably factorize into products of one-loop integrals for all integer-valued propagator powers.

We examine $n$ identical Kuramoto oscillators connected via an Erdős–Rényi (ER) random graph, where each pair of oscillators is bidirectionally coupled with unit strength independently with probability $0 \leq p \leq 1$. A network is defined as globally synchronizing if the oscillators converge to an all-in-phase state for almost all initial conditions. The question arises whether there exists a critical threshold for $p$ such that global synchrony becomes highly probable above it but extremely unlikely below it. It is conjectured that such a threshold exists near the connectivity limit, approximately $p \sim \log(n)/n$ for large $n$. Ling, Xu, and Bandeira made initial strides by proving that if $p \gg \log(n)/n^{1/3}$, ER networks of Kuramoto oscillators are globally synchronizing with high probability as $n \to \infty$. This work improves upon that finding by demonstrating that $p \gg \log^2(n)/n$ is sufficient. Our bounds are explicit; for instance, a random network with $n = 10^6$ and $p > 0.01117$ has a probability exceeding 99.9996% of being globally synchronizing.

Spin lasers, driven by spin-polarized carriers, are defined by their threshold characteristics marking the beginning of stimulated emission. While conventional lasers utilizing unpolarized carriers exhibit a single threshold, spin lasers are anticipated to display two distinct thresholds. As laser technology advances with miniaturization and the integration of novel two-dimensional materials, it remains uncertain whether the standard spin laser model—assuming negligible spontaneous emission and linear optical gain—remains applicable, or even how to accurately determine lasing thresholds in these contexts. This study employs a rate-equation framework that incorporates significant spontaneous emission and nonlinear optical gain to address these uncertainties. We offer a clear analytical approach to investigate the resulting threshold dynamics, highlight deviations from previous research, and provide guidance for developing spin lasers as a versatile spintronics platform extending beyond magnetoresistance applications.

Recent years have seen extensive research into online user privacy and tracking, driven by data protection laws in the EU and USA, including the GDPR, ePrivacy Regulation, and CCPA. Studies have uncovered novel tracking and PII leakage techniques used by first and third parties globally, along with the intensity of such surveillance. However, most previous research has scaled by focusing solely on website homepages, neglecting deeper analysis of tracking on topical subpages. Furthermore, the majority of these studies have centered on Global North markets like the EU and USA, leaving large regions like India—which represents 20% of the global population and lacks explicit privacy legislation—largely unstudied.

To address these gaps, we investigate the following questions: Is tracking on Indian news website subpages distinct from their homepages? Do third-party trackers target specific topics, and how does this preference correlate with content similarity? To answer these, we propose a novel method for automatically extracting and categorizing Indian news subpages based on URL details. We analyze these subpages in comparison to homepages regarding cookie injection intensity, third-party embeddedness, and types. Our findings reveal differential tracking between subpages and homepages, as well as a preferential attachment of third-party trackers to specific topics. Additionally, we observe that embedded third parties often track specific subpages simultaneously, suggesting active user profiling.

Photosynthetic light reactions and mitochondrial energy production occur within specialized membranes rich in redox-active lipids. The in-plane charge transfer along these membranes is thought to rely on the diffusion of redox lipids and protein mobility. Employing a membrane-on-a-chip approach, we demonstrate that model redox-active membranes can sustain surprisingly high (milliampere) currents, exhibiting specific resistivity characteristic of semiconductors. Our findings indicate that charge transfer in cell walls housing electron transfer chains is facilitated by self-assembling molecular redox-wires, which couple redox proteins through simultaneous in-plane electron and proton hopping. This discovery fundamentally reshapes our understanding of lipid membrane function, with broad implications: it suggests that conductive membranes may have been precursors to the evolution of complex biological redox systems, and that electrochemical membrane degradation could be a key factor in mitochondrial aging. Additionally, these self-assembling organic two-dimensional conductors possess technologically valuable properties, enabling the design of adaptive and self-assembling bio-electronic devices.

This chapter examines the mechanisms behind the formation of comets and planetesimals. We begin by outlining the physics of dust grain growth within planet-forming disks, specifically focusing on how gas-dust interactions facilitate this process. Subsequently, we explore various planetesimal formation models, detailing their formation mechanisms and resulting structural characteristics. Our analysis centers on comparing two primary paradigms: the gravitational collapse of particle overdensities (arising from diverse mechanisms) and the accumulation of particles into planetesimals through collisional and gravitational coagulation. Finally, we evaluate the predictions of these models against data from the Rosetta and New Horizons missions, as well as observations of distant Kuiper Belt Objects.

Linde et al. (2021), after a comprehensive simulation study of three equivalence assessment methods (frequentist "TOST," Bayesian "HDI-ROPE," and the Bayes factor interval null procedure), advised researchers to prioritize the Bayes factor interval null approach for quantifying equivalence evidence. We replicated their entire simulation study, however, by calibrating all procedures to share an identical predetermined maximum Type I error rate. Our findings indicate that under this calibration, the Bayes factor, HDI-ROPE, and frequentist equivalence tests exhibit nearly identical Type II error rates. Consequently, claims suggesting that frequentist methods are empirically superior or inferior to Bayesian methods appear highly questionable. Once a researcher selects a foundational principle for addressing a specific problem, the corresponding method naturally follows. Given that these procedures can largely be reverse-engineered from one another, attempting to favor one approach over another based solely on empirical performance seems futile.

This research examines the ability of Cyclic Redundancy Checks (CRCs) to identify both random and burst errors. Throughout the history of computing, scholars have prioritized these error detection codes, leading to their widespread implementation in global communication protocols. Found in nearly every device, both in hardware and software, CRCs are essential for maintaining the efficiency of digital communication systems and identifying erroneous packets. Given the significant rise in data generation and transmission over the past two decades, the likelihood of encountering errors has increased accordingly. Consequently, it is vital to evaluate the tools and methodologies used to safeguard digital communication integrity, ensuring they can manage higher information frequencies. In this study, we investigate the necessity of enhancing error-detection code capabilities to accommodate larger data volumes by assessing the error detection properties of CRCs within a constrained domain.

We present a method for rapidly generating conditional phase shifts and entanglement between two qubits coupled to a shared thermal bath. By employing dynamical decoupling, our approach remains effective even under strong qubit-environment interactions, and it requires no direct coupling between the two qubits.

Ensuring the full realization of autonomous systems requires safe navigation through intricate urban settings, making the prediction of future locations for vulnerable road users like pedestrians and cyclists a critical area of recent research. Although prior studies have focused on modeling interactions with both static obstacles and dynamic human agents, this work addresses a significant gap in trajectory prediction by introducing SafeCritic. This model integrates generative adversarial networks to produce multiple realistic trajectories with reinforcement learning to ensure safety. The Discriminator assesses generated candidates for consistency with observed inputs, while the environmentally aware Critic prunes trajectories that risk collision or violate environmental constraints. An auto-encoding loss is employed to stabilize training and prevent mode collapse. Experiments on two large-scale datasets demonstrate considerable improvements over state-of-the-art methods, and the results confirm that the Critic can effectively classify trajectory safety.

Drawing on the exceptional learning and predictive capabilities of deep neural networks (DNNs), this work employs a specialized DNN framework called model-driven deep unfolding to enhance reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted millimeter wave (mmWave) single-input multiple-output (SIMO) systems. The study targets uplink cascaded channel estimation, assuming fixed base station combining vectors and RIS phase shift matrices to gather observations. To improve estimation accuracy while minimizing training burden, the approach exploits the inherent sparsity of mmWave channels within the deep unfolding architecture. Verification shows that this proposed deep unfolding network surpasses the least squares (LS) method, achieving superior performance with reduced online computational complexity and lower training overhead.

This work introduces novel relationships among Feynman integrals, demonstrating that these integrals obey functional equations linking those with varying scalar invariants and masses. A methodology is proposed to derive such relations, with specific derivations provided for one-loop propagator and vertex-type integrals. It is established that a propagator-type integral can be expressed as the sum of two integrals featuring altered scalar invariants and a single massless propagator. Similarly, a vertex-type integral can be represented as a summation over vertex integrals where all but one propagator are massless, and one external momentum squared equals zero. Furthermore, it is shown that these functional equations facilitate the analytic continuation of Feynman integrals across different kinematic domains.

Discrete time crystals are periodically driven quantum many-body systems that exhibit broken discrete-time translational symmetry, forming a non-equilibrium steady state characterized by the self-organization of quantum particle motion. To date, observations of this discrete time-crystalline order have been restricted to magneto-optical experiments; notably, it has never been detected in transport experiments involving systems connected to external electrodes. In this work, we demonstrate that both discrete time crystals and quasi-crystals persist across a broad range of environments defined by single-particle gain and loss resulting from system-electrode coupling, over experimentally relevant timescales. Leveraging dynamical symmetries, we analytically determine the conditions required to observe time-crystalline behavior in a periodically driven open Fermi-Hubbard chain linked to electrodes. Remarkably, the presence of a spin-polarized transport current serves as a direct indicator of time-crystalline behavior. These results are experimentally verifiable using current technologies, including quantum-dot arrays and fermionic ultra-cold atoms in optical lattices.

This study investigates unconditionally non-oscillatory, high-order implicit time-marching techniques utilizing time limiters. Our primary contribution is the development of the Limited-DIRK3 (L-DIRK3) scheme, a high-resolution method designed for conservation laws and convection-diffusion equations within the method-of-lines framework. This approach is compatible with various high-order spatial discretizations, including the 5th order WENO scheme. While strongly S-stable DIRK3 schemes exist, they are not Strongly Stable Preserving (SSP) and can generate significant oscillations when large time steps are employed. To address this instability, the L-DIRK3 scheme applies local time limiters (citing K. Duraisamy, J.D. Baeder, and J.-G. Liu), which locally reduce temporal accuracy to first order in regions where the solution lacks smoothness. This strategy ensures local satisfaction of monotonicity conditions while maintaining high-order accuracy across the majority of the solution domain. To facilitate application to systems of equations, we introduce a novel and straightforward construction for time limiters that permits flexible selection of reference quantities with minimal computational overhead. Furthermore, this work extends time-limiter methodologies to multidimensional problems and convection-diffusion equations. Numerical experiments involving scalar and system equations in one and two dimensions demonstrate the scheme's high resolution and enhanced stability under large time steps. Additionally, the results suggest that time-limiter schemes offer a versatile and efficient means to improve the stability of arbitrary DIRK methods.

In set theory lacking the Axiom of Choice, we examine the hierarchy of weak choice principles by analyzing the Erdős–Dushnik–Miller theorem applied to uncountable vertex sets. Furthermore, we enhance several findings by Brunner and address a query posed by Lajos Soukup.

Despite their widespread industrial application, conventional task-oriented dialogue systems face three primary limitations: (i) the complexity of building ontologies such as intents and slots, (ii) limited controllability and interpretability, and (iii) a heavy reliance on annotated data. This paper introduces the concept of Dialogue Action as a more straightforward representation for utterances, using it to develop a tree-structured TaskFlow that serves as the core component of a task-oriented chatbot. We present a framework capable of automatically generating TaskFlows from large-scale conversational datasets and deploying them online. Experimental results from real-world after-sales customer service scenarios demonstrate that TaskFlow effectively addresses key requirements while significantly reducing the burden on developers.

The $AV_3Sb_5$ family of kagome metals, characterized by a distinctive structural motif, hosts fascinating phenomena including chiral charge order and superconductivity. CsV$_3Sb_5$ stands out due to its double superconducting dome within the temperature-pressure range where charge order persists, though the microscopic cause of this anomaly remains unresolved. To investigate this, we integrated high-pressure, low-temperature muon spin relaxation experiments with first-principles calculations. Our observations reveal a pressure-induced threefold increase in superfluid density that mirrors the double-peak behavior of the superconducting critical temperature. This creates three distinct regions in the phase diagram, each defined by unique slopes in the linear relationship between superfluid density and critical temperature. We attribute these findings to an evolution in the charge order pattern: transitioning from a superimposed tri-hexagonal Star-of-David phase at low pressures (inside the first dome) to a staggered tri-hexagonal phase at intermediate pressures (between the domes). These results indicate a shift in the nature of the charge-ordered state across the CsV$_3Sb_5$ phase diagram, accompanied by varying levels of competition with superconductivity.

Despite significant research interest in analog semantic communication, digital semantic communication systems remain underexplored. This paper introduces VQ-DeepSC, a deep learning-driven vector quantized framework designed for image transmission. We propose a convolutional neural network (CNN) transceiver capable of extracting multi-scale semantic features, utilizing multi-scale embedding spaces to quantize these features for compatibility with digital communication channels. Additionally, we enhance received image quality through adversarial training by incorporating a PatchGAN discriminator. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed VQ-DeepSC system surpasses conventional image transmission methods in SSIM performance.

We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the induction and co-induction functors on linear representation categories to be naturally isomorphic, given a morphism of small groupoids with an injective object map. Such a morphism is defined as a Frobenius morphism of groupoids. Consequently, an extension by a subgroupoid qualifies as Frobenius if and only if every orbit in the (left or right) pull-back biset fibers is finite. These findings generalize and refine the classical Frobenius reciprocity formulas for finite groups and characterize Frobenius extensions of algebras possessing sufficient orthogonal idempotents.
This is a dynamic document outlining the meta-theory, implementation, and instantiations of Gillian, a multi-language symbolic analysis platform.
This paper presents a formula for determining the maximum count of non-intersecting diagonals of any length that can be placed within n × n square grids, given that n is a multiple of l+1.

Hierarchical text classification offers numerous practical applications, yet annotating extensive document collections is expensive. To mitigate this, practitioners often employ semi-supervised or weakly supervised techniques, such as dataless classification. This paper introduces a path cost-sensitive learning algorithm designed to exploit structural information while leveraging both unlabeled and weakly labeled data. By utilizing a generative model to capitalize on vast amounts of unlabeled data and integrating path constraints into the learning process, the method incorporates the hierarchical structure of classes. The approach combines posterior probabilities from unlabeled and weakly labeled data with path-dependent scores. By imposing structure-sensitive costs to ensure classification consistency with the class hierarchy and avoiding the need to reconstruct feature vectors for various structures, the method achieves significant computational savings compared to structural output learning. Experiments on two hierarchical text classification benchmarks demonstrate that this approach is both effective and efficient for handling semi-supervised and weakly supervised hierarchical text classification tasks.

3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is a cornerstone of autonomous driving. To enhance model generalization across various sensors and environments, several recent Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) methods have been developed for point cloud data. Building on image domain research demonstrating that sample mixing can reduce domain shift, we introduce Compositional Semantic Mix (CoSMix), a novel sample mixing technique specifically designed for point cloud UDA. CoSMix utilizes a two-branch symmetric network capable of simultaneously processing labelled synthetic source data and unlabelled real-world target point clouds. Each branch operates on a single domain by incorporating selected data segments from the opposing domain, leveraging semantic information derived from source labels and target pseudo-labels. Evaluations on two large-scale datasets demonstrate that CoSMix significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The implementation code can be accessed at https://github.com/saltoricristiano/cosmix-uda.

This paper introduces an impulse response identification framework that leverages internal positivity information regarding the system. Drawing on the realization theory of positive systems, which defines criteria for the existence of a positive realization for specific transfer functions, we translate these transfer function requirements into conditions governing the shape and structure of impulse responses in positive systems. By applying these conditions, the impulse response estimation task is modeled as a constrained optimization problem within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space featuring a stable kernel, where constraints encode the internal positivity data. Although the original optimization problem is infinite-dimensional with infinite constraints, we derive an equivalent finite-dimensional convex optimization problem formulated as a convex quadratic program. This reformulation renders the approach amenable to numerical simulation and practical deployment. Finally, a Monte Carlo study assesses the benefits of integrating internal positivity side-information, and the method's efficacy is validated using data from a heating system experiment.

Graph learning research has primarily focused on two inductive biases for graph-inspired architectures. First, high-order interactions and message passing are effective for homophilous graphs, as utilized by GCNs and GATs, but these models struggle to scale to large real-world datasets. Second, shallow or node-level models that rely on ego features and adjacency embeddings perform well on heterophilous graphs. This paper introduces GLINKX, a new scalable shallow method capable of handling both homophilous and heterophilous graphs. GLINKX integrates (i) novel monophilous label propagation, (ii) ego/node features, (iii) knowledge graph embeddings for positional encoding, (iv) node-level training, and (v) low-dimensional message passing. We formally derive new error bounds to validate the model's components and demonstrate its efficacy across various homophilous and heterophilous datasets through experiments.

The Transformer architecture demonstrates its effectiveness as an end-to-end framework for constructing expression trees from online handwritten gestures representing glyph strokes. Specifically, the attention mechanism effectively encodes, learns, and enforces the syntax of these expressions, generating latent representations that are accurately decoded into precise mathematical expression trees. This approach exhibits robustness against ablated inputs and previously unseen glyphs. Notably, for the first time, the encoder processes spatio-temporal data tokens that can form an infinitely large vocabulary, opening applications beyond simple online gesture recognition. The study introduces a new supervised dataset of online handwriting gestures to facilitate training on generic handwriting recognition tasks and proposes a novel metric for evaluating the syntactic correctness of resulting expression trees. Furthermore, a compact Transformer model optimized for edge inference was successfully trained, achieving an average normalized Levenshtein accuracy of 94%, which corresponds to valid postfix RPN tree representations in 94% of predictions.

The Environmental Microorganism Data Set Fifth Version (EMDS-5) is a microscopic image collection comprising original Environmental Microorganism (EM) images alongside two Ground Truth (GT) sets: one for single objects and another for multi-objects. The dataset encompasses 21 distinct EM types, with each type containing 20 original images, 20 single-object GT images, and 20 multi-object GT images. EMDS-5 is designed to assess capabilities in image preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction, classification, and retrieval. To validate the dataset's effectiveness, representative algorithms and performance metrics were selected for each function. The preprocessing phase includes image denoising and edge detection; denoising employs nine filters against 13 noise types, while edge detection utilizes six operators. Evaluation for these tasks relies on the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Mean Structural Similarity (MSSIM). Segmentation covers both single and multi-object scenarios, using six methods for the former and k-means and U-net for the latter. Feature extraction involves deriving nine attributes from the images, tested via a Support Vector Machine classifier. For classification, VGG16 features are used to evaluate various classifiers. Retrieval testing includes texture-based and deep learning-based approaches, where feature vectors are extracted from the final layers of two deep learning networks, with Mean Average Precision (mAP) serving as the evaluation metric.

New high-intensity muon beamlines are currently under construction globally, paving the way for novel physics investigations involving muons. These facilities will enable the measurement of transverse positron polarization from polarized $\mu^+$ decays, providing a test of the Standard Model. Additionally, they will probe the Mu-to-$\bar{\text{Mu}}$ transition, a phenomenon of interest in theories beyond the Standard Model. Observing this transition in the near future would be highly significant, as it would suggest the existence of an approximate discrete symmetry within the lepton sector. If the Mu-to-$\bar{\text{Mu}}$ transition operator is present, a new muon decay operator may arise, potentially interfering with the Standard Model operator to alter the transverse positron polarization in $\mu^+$ decay. This paper explores the connection between the Mu-to-$\bar{\text{Mu}}$ transition and the correction to transverse positron polarization, demonstrating that they are linked in the neutral flavor gauge boson model. Furthermore, we examine various mechanisms capable of generating the Mu-to-$\bar{\text{Mu}}$ transition, including an inert $SU(2)_L$ doublet, an $SU(2)_L$ triplet within the type-II seesaw framework, a dilepton gauge boson, and a left-right model. A non-zero value for one of the transverse polarization directions, $P_{\rm T_2}$, would signal a violation of time-reversal invariance; however, experimental limits on the electron electric dipole moment could impose strict constraints on $P_{\rm T_2}$ depending on the specific model considered.

Because robots and humans operate within a shared environment, physical human-robot collaboration demands rigorous safety assurances. This letter introduces a new control framework designed to manage safety-critical position-based constraints during physical human-robot interaction. The methodology combines admittance control, exponential control barrier functions (ECBFs), and quadratic programming (QP) to ensure compliant force interaction while maintaining safety guarantees. Specifically, the admittance control formulation is recast as a second-order nonlinear system where interaction forces serve as the control input. A virtual force feedback, generated in real-time via the ECBFs-QP framework, acts as a compensator for external human forces within the admittance control scheme. Consequently, the proposed adaptive admittance control scheme derives a safe trajectory for a low-level controller to follow. The key innovation of this approach is its ability to allow the robot to respond to human forces with natural fluidity, ensuring no safety constraints are violated, even if external human forces momentarily attempt to breach them. Simulation studies on a two-link planar robot manipulator demonstrate the effectiveness of this method.
