Multiple scattering of waves in three-dimensional random media can potentially induce a disorder-driven phase transition from diffusion to localization, as proposed by Anderson in 1958 and further developed by Abrahams et al. in 1979. In his 1985 paper, "The question of classical localization: A theory of white paint?", P.W. Anderson hypothesized that light localization might be observable in TiO$_2$ samples. Our previous work asserted the detection of localization effects in such materials by analyzing photon time-of-flight (ToF) distributions (Störzer et al. 2006) and transmission profiles (Sperling et al. 2013). However, this study provides a rigorous examination of the long-time tails of ToF distributions and the asymptotic behavior of transmission profile widths across various turbidities and in very thin samples, which challenges the localization interpretation. Additionally, we present new data supporting an alternative, consistent explanation based on a fluorescence process. An adapted diffusion model incorporating an exponential fluorescence decay successfully reproduces the observed ToF distribution shapes and transmission profile widths. These findings cast doubt on the feasibility of achieving a strong localization regime with visible light in polydisperse TiO$_2$ "white paint," given that the disorder parameter in such materials is difficult to increase further.

Learning-based navigation systems are prevalent in autonomous applications like robotics, unmanned vehicles, and drones, prompting the development of specialized hardware accelerators to enhance performance and energy efficiency. Nevertheless, hardware systems face rising risks of transient and permanent faults that can severely compromise safety. While traditional redundancy-based protection methods are difficult to implement in resource-constrained edge environments, this paper experimentally assesses the resilience of navigation systems across various algorithms, fault models, and data types used in both reinforcement learning training and inference. Additionally, we introduce two efficient fault mitigation techniques that improve the success rate by 2x and enhance flight quality by 39% in learning-based navigation systems.

Accuracy-efficiency trade-offs are a central challenge in fields like law and public health, where established policies guide decision-making under uncertainty. Although computer science frequently analyzes these trade-offs, their governance implications remain largely unexplored. By adapting risk assessment practices from the United States, we argue that governing computer systems requires a similar reckoning with these balances, particularly within distributed machine learning. This focus is urgent because such high-stakes, safety-critical systems—exemplified by autonomous vehicles—demand rigorous oversight. Our analysis first outlines how these trade-offs manifest in distributed machine learning, then identifies discrepancies between current US risk standards and the specific needs of these systems. Finally, we propose actionable steps to ensure accountability when theoretical risks materialize as real-world accidents, concluding with a discussion on how these mechanisms foster governance that is transparent, just, and aligned with public values.

This study examines the application of batch normalization within neural architecture search (NAS). While Frankle et al. demonstrated that training only batch normalization layers yields nontrivial performance, and Chen et al. reported that this approach accelerates one-shot NAS supernet training by over tenfold, no prior work has explained why this method identifies high-performing architectures so efficiently or how it differs from standard training of all parameters. We first demonstrate theoretically that networks trained exclusively on batch normalization converge to the neural tangent kernel regime, exhibiting identical training dynamics to those where all parameters are trained, thereby validating the claim of reduced training time. Subsequently, our empirical analysis reveals that the "train-BN-only" strategy favors convolutional operators over others, creating an unfair competitive environment because only convolutions are coupled with batch normalization. Consequently, search algorithms tend to bias toward convolution-heavy models. To address this bias, we introduce fairness into the search space by attaching a batch normalization layer to every operator. However, we find that the performance predictor proposed by Chen et al. fails in this modified context. In response, we develop a novel composite performance metric that evaluates networks based on expressivity, trainability, and uncertainty, leveraging the theoretical properties of batch normalization. Finally, we validate our methodology across multiple NAS benchmarks (NAS-Bench101 and NAS-Bench-201) and search spaces, including DARTS and MobileNet.

Recent progress in path-based explainable recommendation systems has garnered significant interest due to the abundant information available in knowledge graphs. However, most current approaches rely solely on static knowledge graphs, neglecting dynamic user-item evolutions, which results in explanations that are often inaccurate and unconvincing. While some studies acknowledge that modeling temporal sequential behavior can enhance both performance and explainability, they typically either focus exclusively on sequential interactions within a path or treat this modeling independently from the recommendation mechanism itself. To address these gaps, this paper introduces TMER-RL, a novel Temporal Meta-path Guided Explainable Recommendation framework leveraging Reinforcement Learning. TMER-RL employs attention mechanisms to model dynamic user-item evolutions on dynamic knowledge graphs by constructing reinforcement item-item paths between consecutive items. Unlike existing methods that depend on heavy recurrent neural networks for temporal modeling, our approach utilizes simple yet effective neural networks to capture historical item features and path-based context for predicting the next purchased item. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that TMER achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to recent strong baselines.

This paper analytically and numerically investigates the intriguing interference effect known as quantum collapse and revival within a simple model featuring a slightly anharmonic Hamiltonian. The study utilizes a displaced harmonic oscillator ground state as the initial wave-function and provides a detailed discussion of potential experimental implementations involving cold atoms.

The IEC 61850 standard is widely adopted in Smart Grid (SG) applications primarily because it effectively resolves communication, interoperability, and migration challenges. Although IEC 61850 currently focuses on internal substation communication, there is a growing need to extend its application to distributed SG environments, such as Home Energy Management Systems (HEMS) and Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) communication, which may involve distributed substations or SG components. Existing IEC 61850-based systems impose strict timing constraints on communication; the conventional solution involves allocating static link bandwidth, which can result in over-provisioning. This paper introduces the Substation Cognitive Communication Resource Management (IC2RM) framework, designed to manage bandwidth allocation for IEC messages through a cognitive provisioning approach and SDN/OpenFlow for deployment. By dynamically assigning bandwidth to IEC messages, IC2RM optimizes connections between SG substations and related systems, potentially lowering operational expenditures (OPEX).

This paper outlines the key findings and results from SemEval-2020 Task 10, titled "Emphasis Selection for Written Text in Visual Media." The shared task aimed to develop automatic methods for selecting text candidates for emphasis to facilitate automated design assistance during the authoring process. The primary focus was on short text instances, ranging from social media posts to inspirational quotes, where participants were required to model emphasis using plain text without additional user context or design constraints. The task attracted 197 participants in its initial phase, with a total of 31 teams submitting results. The top-ranked submission achieved a Matchm score of 0.823. System analysis revealed that BERT and RoBERTa were the most frequently used pre-trained models, and part-of-speech tagging was identified as the most beneficial feature. Comprehensive results are available on the task's official website.

Current state-of-the-art document dewarping methods rely on predicting 3D information, which often leads to errors when processing documents with irregular distortions or significant depth variations. This paper introduces FDRNet, a Fourier Document Restoration Network designed to restore diverse distortions and enhance document recognition through a more reliable and streamlined approach. By targeting high-frequency components in the Fourier domain—where most structural details reside and visual degradation is minimal—FDRNet effectively dewarps documents using a flexible Thin-Plate Spline transformation. This method handles various deformations without needing deformation annotations during training. Consequently, FDRNet can learn from a limited set of simply labeled images, accurately dewarping documents with complex geometric distortions and recognizing the restored text. To support further research, we have developed a benchmark dataset comprising over one thousand camera-captured documents featuring diverse geometric and photometric distortions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FDRNet significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both dewarping and text recognition tasks. Furthermore, FDRNet requires only a small amount of simple training data and is easy to deploy.

The CLICTD is a monolithic silicon pixel sensor built using a modified 180 nm CMOS imaging process, featuring a high-resistivity epitaxial layer and a compact collection electrode. It employs an innovative sub-pixel segmentation strategy designed to achieve rapid charge collection and superior spatial resolution. Developed to meet the tracking detector specifications for the proposed future Compact Linear Collider (CLIC), the sensor targets a temporal resolution in the few-nanosecond range and a spatial resolution under 7 microns. This paper presents beam test results, highlighting recent investigations into assemblies of varying thicknesses (as thin as 50 microns to reduce material budget) and measurements involving inclined particle tracks.

This study details the computation of next-to-leading order QCD corrections for Higgs boson production and decay in association with top quarks. We focus on the leptonic top quark decay channel at the LHC ($\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV), resulting in the hadronic process $pp\to e^+\nu_e\, \mu^-\bar{\nu}_\mu \, b\bar{b}\,H\, (H\to X)$. The calculation incorporates all resonant and non-resonant Feynman diagrams, along with interferences and off-shell effects for both the top quark and $W$ gauge boson; however, Higgs boson decays are treated using the narrow-width approximation. We analyze Higgs decays into $b\bar{b}$, $\tau^+\tau^-$, $\gamma\gamma$, and $e^+e^-e^+e^-$. Numerical findings are presented at both integrated and differential fiducial levels across various factorization and renormalization scale settings and parton distribution function (PDF) sets. We investigate primary theoretical uncertainties arising from neglected higher-order perturbative terms and different PDF parametrizations. Additionally, we assess the magnitude of off-shell effects by comparing our results to calculations performed strictly within the narrow-width approximation. Finally, we examine the influence of the bottom-quark parton density.

This paper presents an alternative proof of the asymptotic stability of solitons for nonlinear Schrödinger equations that possess internal modes. The key innovation involves employing "refined profiles," previously created by the authors for analyzing small bound states. This new approach allows us to bypass the use of normal forms and enables the tracking of functions within the Fermi Golden Rule hypothesis.

Quantum technologies, which leverage unique quantum physics phenomena like objective randomness, superposition, and entanglement, have revolutionized how information is distributed and processed. The rapid advancements in this field over recent decades have created an urgent demand for new educational initiatives and young professionals. In this context, we introduce a strategic card game that allows players to interact with the fundamental components of a quantum computer. During gameplay, participants begin at the lowest quantum state, use cards to "program" the system, and strive to reach the highest possible quantum state. Through this process, they gain hands-on experience with quantum characteristics such as superposition, interference, and entanglement. By incorporating high-dimensional quantum states—systems capable of exceeding two possible values—and offering various multi-player modes, the game facilitates the comprehension of complex quantum state operations and serves as an accessible introduction to quantum computational tasks for students. Consequently, it is a valuable tool for classroom settings designed to enhance conceptual understanding, spark interest, and boost motivation. Ultimately, this game supports the broader effort to gamify quantum physics education, with a specific emphasis on the counter-intuitive principles underlying quantum computing.

Neural language models have advanced to a point where their generated text is nearly indistinguishable from human writing. While this capability offers significant value across various applications, it also enables malicious uses that threaten the integrity of academic publishing. To counter this risk, we introduce two datasets containing artificially created research content: one fully synthetic and another based on partial text substitution. The entirely synthetic dataset consists of content generated by the GPT-2 model following brief prompts derived from original papers. The hybrid dataset is formed by replacing specific sentences within abstracts with those generated by the Arxiv-NLP model. We assess the quality of these datasets by comparing the generated outputs to aligned original texts using fluency metrics like BLEU and ROUGE; the more natural the artificial texts appear, the harder they are to detect and the more effective the benchmark becomes. Additionally, we measure the difficulty of distinguishing between original and generated text by employing state-of-the-art classification models.

This study extends the Hidden Markov Model to accommodate Markovian observations, where the one-step transition probabilities of the observation sequence are conditioned on the underlying hidden Markov chain. An Expectation-Maximization variant of the Baum-Welch algorithm is introduced to estimate the transition probabilities for both the hidden and observation chains, as well as the initial joint distribution of hidden states and observations. From these calculations, a filtering recursion is derived to track the hidden state. Additionally, a dynamic programming approach analogous to the Viterbi algorithm is formulated to identify the most probable sequence of hidden states corresponding to a given observation sequence.

We present a comparison of the matter bispectrum calculated via various perturbation theory approaches at next-to-leading order against results from an extensive suite of $N$-body simulations. Using a $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test, we evaluate the accuracy of these models across different simulation volumes. Our findings indicate that Effective Field Theory (EFT) models offer the broadest applicability, while standard perturbation theory has the narrowest; `classical' resummed methods fall in between. However, the improvement provided by EFT is smaller than previously reported. We demonstrate that the estimated accuracy range of EFT predictions is significantly sensitive to the method used to fit counterterm amplitudes. For the volumes typical of galaxy redshift surveys, our results suggest it is beneficial to constrain three EFT bispectrum counterterms to zero and determine the fourth from the power spectrum. Additionally, we observe substantial variability in the estimated reach between different simulation realizations. Consequently, we conclude that defining a definitive accuracy range for models with free parameters is challenging. Finally, we address systematic effects arising from the $N$-body technique by either applying scale- and shape-dependent bias or increasing statistical error bars as commonly practiced. We find that the latter method artificially expands the reach of EFT models because of the presence of tunable parameters.

This research investigates a chance-constrained variation of the cooperative aerial-ground vehicle routing problem. In this scenario, an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) with restricted battery life and an Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV), capable of serving as a mobile charging hub, must collaborate to execute a mission, such as monitoring specific locations. Because of the UAV's limited power, the two units occasionally must abandon their primary tasks to meet and recharge. Departing from previous studies that assumed deterministic conditions, this work tackles the uncertainty inherent in the UAV's energy consumption. The objective is to determine the optimal rendezvous policy that minimizes the UAV's expected travel time while ensuring the probability of a battery failure remains below a specified threshold. We model this as a Chance Constrained Markov Decision Process (CCMDP). To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural CCMDP-based formulation for UAV-UGV routing under power uncertainty. We employ a Linear Programming (LP) method to solve the problem optimally and validate our approach using an Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) mission scenario.

Silicate rock weathering at planetary surfaces sequesters atmospheric CO$_2$ for long-term storage within the planet, acting as a critical negative feedback mechanism in the carbonate-silicate cycle that stabilizes climates on Earth and potentially on temperate exoplanets. By applying thermodynamic principles to calculate weathering rates based on surface rock types, this study establishes upper limits for climate regulation. The modeling reveals that the weathering of mineral assemblages within a rock is more significant than that of individual minerals. Using a fluid-transport controlled method that integrates chemical kinetics and thermodynamics, we simulated rates for three rock types inspired by Earth's continental and oceanic crust and upper mantle. Our findings indicate that thermodynamic weathering rates for continental crust-like lithologies are one to two orders of magnitude lower than those for oceanic crust-like lithologies. We demonstrate that as CO$_2$ partial pressure drops or surface temperatures rise, thermodynamics becomes the dominant control over weathering rather than kinetics. While kinetically and thermodynamically limited regimes vary by lithology, supply-limited weathering remains independent of it. Consequently, our results suggest that the temperature sensitivity of thermodynamically limited silicate weathering could trigger a positive feedback in the carbon cycle, causing weathering rates to decline as surface temperatures increase.

This paper presents a systematic investigation of $SU(2)$ flavor amplitude sum rules, focusing specifically on $U$-spin. The analysis uncovers a complex mathematical framework inherent in these sum rules, enabling the creation of an algorithm to derive all $U$-spin amplitude sum rules to any order of symmetry breaking. This innovative methodology eliminates the need for explicit calculation of Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and facilitates a straightforward diagrammatic understanding. Additionally, we provide several examples illustrating how this new method applies to experimentally accessible systems.

The ZX-calculus, along with the ZXH-calculus variant discussed in this paper, serves as a formal diagrammatic language for qubit quantum computing. We demonstrate its capability to describe SU(2) representation theory. To do so, we first review Yutsis diagrams—a standard graphical calculus in quantum chemistry and gravity that encapsulates key aspects of SU(2) theory. Next, we detail how these diagrams embed within Penrose's binor calculus and subsequently unify both systems under the ZXH-diagram framework. This process reveals that the SU(2) invariance of Wigner symbols is trivially provable within ZXH-calculus. Furthermore, we provide methods for explicitly calculating 3jm, 4jm, and 6j symbols using diagrams. While it has long been believed that quantum gravity should align closely with quantum information theory, this paper establishes an exact connection by expressing loop quantum gravity (LQG) spin-networks in the ZX-diagrammatic language of quantum computation.

Achieving speaker transfer in text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis—specifically applying speech characteristics from one group to another that lack them—is a persistent challenge. A key obstacle is that models capable of high-quality transfer often suffer from stability issues, rendering them unsuitable for critical, user-facing applications. This study shows that robust TTS systems can be developed by training on data generated by a less stable but high-quality transfer model. Specifically, a CHiVE-BERT monolingual TTS system was trained using outputs from a Tacotron model designed for accent transfer. Although some quality degradation is expected with this method, experimental results indicate that models trained on such synthetic data can successfully produce high-quality audio with effective accent transfer while maintaining speaker traits like speaking style.

We investigate the root distribution of the polynomial sequence $\{P_n(z)\}_{n=0}^{\infty}$, defined by the rational generating function $$ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} P_n(z)t^n= \frac{1}{1+ B(z)t^\ell +A(z)t^k} $$ for the specific cases $(k,\ell)=(3,2)$ and $(4,3)$, where $A(z)$ and $B(z)$ are arbitrary polynomials with complex coefficients. We demonstrate that the zeros of $P_n(z)$ satisfying $A(z)B(z)\neq 0$ are situated on a real algebraic curve, which we provide an explicit description for.

We investigate the relationship between the energy cost of bit reset and the duration of the protocol. Since bit reset must occur within a finite timeframe, it incurs an additional energy penalty beyond the quasistatic work cost established by Landauer. This excess energy dissipates as heat, imposing a fundamental constraint on the operating speed of irreversible computing systems. We develop a hardware-agnostic expression for this limit using stochastic process theory. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form lower bound for the work penalty as a function of the protocol's time duration and the associated bit reset error. This result applies to both discrete and continuous systems, provided the master equation adheres to detailed balance.

We performed three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of common envelope evolution (CEE) involving a neutron star (NS) or black hole (BH) within a red supergiant (RSG) envelope. Our findings indicate that jets launched by the NS/BH during CEE transfer angular momentum to the envelope that is aligned with the jets' orientation. Specifically, when jets are perpendicular to the orbital plane (aligned with the orbital angular momentum), they deposit angular momentum in the same direction; conversely, if the jet axis is inclined relative to the orbital angular momentum, the deposited angular momentum is likewise tilted. Such misaligned jets may occur if the NS/BH possesses a close companion upon entering the RSG envelope. Note that our simulations did not account for spiralling-in and covered only three orbits: the first representing the rapid plunge-in phase, and the third representing the slow, self-regulated phase. We observed that significant angular momentum deposition occurs exclusively during the plunge-in phase. Consequently, a post-CEE core-collapse supernova may result in two NS/BH systems that are either bound or unbound, with spins potentially misaligned relative to the orbital angular momentum. These results reinforce earlier assertions that CEE in inclined triple-star systems can lead to spin-orbit misalignment in NS/BH-NS/BH binaries.

This study presents speckle interferometric data from 2020 collected at the 4.1 m Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope (SOAR), combined with previously unpublished records, yielding a total of 1,735 measurements involving 1,288 resolved pairs and 1,177 unresolved targets for 1,177 distinct objects. For the first time, we identified 59 new pairs or subsystems within known binary systems, primarily among nearby dwarf stars. This effort extends our long-term speckle initiative, which focuses on tracking the orbital dynamics of close binaries, including high-order hierarchical systems and Hipparcos pairs within the solar neighborhood. Additionally, we report on observations of 892 members of young moving groups and associations, among which we resolved 103 new pairs.

This study examines strong-field gravitational lensing caused by a rotating Simpson-Visser black hole, which features an extra parameter ($0 \leq l/2M \leq 1$) alongside mass ($M$) and spin ($a$). The rotating Simpson-Visser metric encompasses four distinct regimes: (i) a Schwarzschild metric when $l/2M = a/2M = 0$ ($M 
eq 0$); (ii) a Kerr metric when $l/2M = 0$, $|a/2M| < 0.5$, and $M 
eq 0$; (iii) a rotating regular black hole when $|a/2M| < 0.5$, $M 
eq 0$, and $0 < l/2M < 0.5 + \sqrt{(0.5)^2 - (a/2M)^2}$; and (iv) a traversable wormhole when $|a/2M| > 0.5$ and $l/2M 
eq 0$. Our results indicate a reduction in both the deflection angle ($\alpha_D$) and the flux ratio between the first image and subsequent images ($r_{mag}$). Conversely, the angular position ($	heta_1$) rises more gradually, the photon sphere radius ($x_m$) shrinks more rapidly, and the angular separation ($s$) expands more quickly, exhibiting behaviors comparable to those of the Kerr black hole. Applying this formalism to supermassive black holes reveals that rotating Simpson-Visser black holes can theoretically be distinguished from Kerr black holes through gravitational lensing. For $0 < l/2M < 0.6$ (with $a/2M = 0.45$), the deviations in lensing observables ($\Delta	heta_1$ and $\Delta s$) for Sgr A* and M87 fall within the ranges $0.0422	ext{--}0.11658~\mu$as and $0.031709	ext{--}0.08758~\mu$as, respectively, while $|\Delta r_{mag}|$ ranges from $0.2037$ to $0.95668$. However, distinguishing between the two remains challenging because these discrepancies are on the order of microarcseconds, likely beyond the resolution of current Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) observations. Furthermore, we derive a two-dimensional lens equation and a strong-field deflection angle formula, focusing on trajectories near the equatorial plane.

We address the challenge of adapting patrolling strategies efficiently within a dynamic environment where the Defender's movement patterns and the criticality of protected targets shift unpredictably. The Defender must immediately transition to a new, optimized strategy tailored to the altered conditions without interrupting the current patrol, ensuring this new strategy is calculated rapidly under any circumstances. Because switching strategies can inadvertently introduce security vulnerabilities that undermine existing protection, our approach incorporates mechanisms to detect and mitigate these risks. The performance of our framework is validated through experimental evaluation.

The CDMSlite experiment, utilizing a germanium target with a low ionization threshold, successfully detected minute recoil energies, thereby probing a novel region of parameter space defined by charge, mass, and velocity for Lightly Ionizing Particles (LIPs). We present the first direct-detection constraints derived via the optimum interval method for the vertical flux of cosmogenic LIPs carrying an electric charge below $e/(3\times10^5)$, establishing the most stringent limits to date for charges $\leq e/160$. These constraints reach a minimum vertical intensity of $1.36\times10^{-7}$\,cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$sr$^{-1}$ at a charge of $e/160$. Spanning LIP masses from 5\,MeV/$c^2$ to 100\,TeV/$c^2$ and $\beta\gamma$ values from 0.1 to $10^6$, these findings mark the first-ever exclusion of non-relativistic LIPs with $\beta\gamma$ as low as 0.1.

While sign language is a primary communication tool for the deaf and mute, it demands significant dedication to master, involving intricate hand gestures, body postures, and facial expressions. Existing Sign Language Recognition (SLR) systems typically rely on deep neural networks to extract features but often overfit due to scarce and noisy datasets. Recently, skeleton-based action recognition has gained traction for its invariance to subjects and backgrounds, yet skeleton-based SLR remains underdeveloped due to a lack of hand annotations. Although some studies have utilized offline hand pose trackers combined with recurrent neural networks to extract keypoints, these methods have yet to surpass RGB-based approaches. To address this, we introduce SAM-SLR-v2, a novel Skeleton Aware Multi-modal Framework incorporating a Global Ensemble Model (GEM) designed for isolated SLR. This framework learns and fuses multi-modal features to enhance recognition accuracy. Specifically, we employ a Sign Language Graph Convolution Network (SL-GCN) to capture the dynamics of skeleton keypoints and a Separable Spatial-Temporal Convolution Network (SSTCN) to leverage skeleton features. These skeleton-based predictions are integrated with RGB and depth modalities through a proposed late-fusion GEM to provide comprehensive global information and ensure reliable SLR outcomes. Experiments across three isolated SLR datasets confirm that our SAM-SLR-v2 framework is highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art performance with substantial improvements. The source code is available at https://github.com/jackyjsy/SAM-SLR-v2.

Prior research has predominantly examined the fairness of image captioning systems through the ambiguous concept of "bias." In contrast, we introduce a suite of methods designed to quantify five distinct categories of representational harm, along with the measurements derived from two leading image captioning datasets using a state-of-the-art system. Our objective was not to audit the system itself, but rather to create normatively grounded measurement techniques that facilitate reflection on the associated complexities. We propose multiple techniques for each harm category, arguing that this approach better captures the multifaceted nature of these harms and thereby enhances the collective validity of the results. Throughout, we examine the assumptions underpinning our methodology and identify instances where they fail to hold.

This work investigates celestial chiral algebras within celestial holography, employing the light-cone gauge formalism for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravity, alongside an exploration of a deformation of the gravitational theory. The $w_{1+\infty}$ algebra, recently identified in self-dual gravity, originates from the soft expansion of an area-preserving diffeomorphism algebra; this algebra functions as the kinematic algebra in the colour-kinematics duality and facilitates the double copy relation between the self-dual theories. A $W_{1+\infty}$ deformation of this structure emerges from a Moyal deformation of self-dual gravity, which is interpreted as a constrained chiral higher-spin gravity featuring a field tower of higher-spin components entirely determined by the graviton. Across these frameworks, the chiral structure of the operator-product expansion manifests the colour-kinematics duality: the implicit "left algebra" corresponds to the self-dual kinematic algebra, while the "right algebra" supplies the structure constants of the operator-product expansion, thereby guaranteeing its associativity. In the context of a scattering amplitudes-based Ward conjecture, the left algebra ensures the classical integrability of these theories, specifically by enforcing the vanishing of tree-level amplitudes through the double copy mechanism.

Automatically generating radiology reports holds the potential to significantly enhance current diagnostic radiology practices. This automation offers a dual benefit: it alleviates the substantial workload of report writing for radiologists while simultaneously serving as a reminder of detected abnormalities, thereby reducing the risks of misdiagnosis and missed diagnoses. However, implementing this task remains a formidable challenge for data-driven neural networks due to significant biases present in both visual and textual data. To address this, we introduce the Posterior-and-Prior Knowledge Exploring-and-Distilling (PPKED) approach, which mimics the radiologist workflow of first identifying abnormal regions and assigning disease tags, and subsequently leveraging extensive medical knowledge and professional experience to draft reports. Consequently, PPKED comprises three core modules: the Posterior Knowledge Explorer (PoKE), the Prior Knowledge Explorer (PrKE), and the Multi-domain Knowledge Distiller (MKD). Specifically, PoKE investigates posterior knowledge to provide explicit visual regions of abnormality, mitigating visual data bias. Meanwhile, PrKE explores prior knowledge derived from medical knowledge graphs and historical radiology reports to counteract textual data bias. Finally, the MKD distills this extracted knowledge to produce the final reports. Evaluated on the MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray datasets, our method demonstrates superior performance compared to previous state-of-the-art models.

As data volumes expand across various applications, analyzing large datasets has become increasingly critical. Frameworks like Apache Hadoop, Apache AsterixDB, and Apache Spark were developed to address this need. Traditional cluster-based big data systems primarily prioritize high performance, typically defined by minimizing end-to-end latency or execution time. However, the growing adoption of data analytics has necessitated improvements over these conventional methods, specifically calling for more interactive and adaptive processing, particularly for long-running jobs. The value of early insights during iterative data wrangling has further spurred a result-aware approach to big data analytics. This dissertation is driven by the need for such enhancements and the insights gained from the Texera project, a collaborative analytics service currently being developed at UC Irvine. The research is structured into three main components. First, it details the design of the Amber engine, which acts as the backend processing framework for Texera. Second, it introduces Reshape, an adaptive and result-aware framework for handling data skew; Reshape employs rapid control messages to execute iterative skew mitigation across diverse operators, with an analysis of how these techniques impact user-facing results. Third, it presents Maestro, a result-aware workflow scheduling framework that determines execution strategies on computing clusters to make informed, result-conscious decisions. Collectively, this work enhances the data analytics lifecycle by integrating interactivity, adaptivity, and result-awareness.

This study maps the 2+1 Dirac-Moshinsky oscillator (2+1 DMO) interacting with an external isospin field onto the Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM), which characterizes the coupling between two two-level systems and a single-mode quantum field. The analysis derives both time-dependent wave functions and density matrices for two distinct scenarios: one utilizing number states and the other employing coherent states as initial conditions. The research investigates how the detuning parameter and coherence angle influence entanglement and population inversion. Results indicate that the coherent state provides a superior description of both entanglement and population inversion compared to the number state.

This study evaluates a workforce training initiative compared to cash transfers for underemployed youth in Rwanda. Three and a half years post-intervention, the training program improved productive time allocation and asset accumulation, whereas cash transfers significantly boosted productive assets, livestock value, savings, and subjective well-being. Both interventions substantially impacted entrepreneurship; however, despite increases in labor, sales, and profits, the implied wage rates within these enterprises remained low. Our findings indicate that access to credit is a primary obstacle to self-employment, suggesting that more profound structural reforms are necessary for entrepreneurship to serve as an effective route out of poverty.

This study examines a West Nile virus (WNv) model incorporating nonlocal diffusion to represent long-range dispersal, a free boundary to depict the spreading front, and seasonal succession to reflect warm and cold cycles. The research first establishes the model's well-posedness and then analyzes its long-term dynamics based on the generalized eigenvalues of the associated linear operator. For the spatial-independent model with seasonal effects, these eigenvalues are computed to reveal new properties, while for the nonlocal seasonal model, they are analyzed qualitatively. Building on this, the authors develop specific indices for the free boundary scenario to determine whether the virus will spread or vanish. These criteria extend existing findings for both nonlocal diffusion and free boundary cases separately. Furthermore, the generalized eigenvalues indicate a positive correlation between the length of the warm season and infection risk. A time-dependent index for the nonlocal free boundary problem serves as the determinant for spreading versus vanishing. Additionally, the initial infection length, the initial infection scale, and the virus's capacity to invade new areas significantly influence the solution's long-term behavior.

Current state-of-the-art systems for emotion classification and intensity prediction, which rely primarily on non-contextualized word embeddings, fail to adequately process adjective phrases such as "a little bit surprised," "completely shocked," or "not stunned at all." Motivated by this limitation, we investigate the differences among these embeddings regarding their ability to manage such expressions. We contend that intensifiers accompanying emotion words require specialized handling—a practice already established in sentiment polarity classification but overlooked in finer-grained emotion prediction. To address this, we examine various components of a post-processing pipeline designed to enhance the word representations of these phrases. This approach involves expanding semantic spaces at both the phrase and sub-word levels, followed by retrofitting to emotion lexica. We assess the efficacy of these steps using A La Carte and Bag-of-Substrings extensions built upon pretrained GloVe, Word2vec, and fastText embeddings, evaluated against a crowd-sourced corpus of intensity-labeled tweets containing our target phrases. Our results indicate that fastText-based models do not benefit from processing these specific phrases. Conversely, for Word2vec embeddings, our proposed post-processing pipeline yields performance improvements of up to 8% on a novel dataset heavily populated with intensifiers.

The existence and nature of the many-body localization (MBL) phase within random many-body quantum systems have been a subject of active debate. In dimensions $d>1$, there is general agreement that the MBL phase is susceptible to rare thermal inclusions, which can trigger an avalanche leading to full thermalization. This note investigates the potential for MBL in quasiperiodic systems with $d>1$. We contend that (i) the MBL phase remains stable under sufficiently strong quasiperiodic modulations when $d = 2$, and (ii) the threat of an avalanche significantly restricts the finite-size scaling characteristics of the MBL transition. Furthermore, we propose a construction suggesting that MBL becomes unstable for $d \geq 3$.

To acquire high-quality, high-resolution (HR) magnetic resonance (MR) images, we introduce IREM, a new image reconstruction network. Trained on various low-resolution (LR) MR images, IREM achieves reconstruction at any desired up-sampling rate. Our approach models the target HR image as an implicit continuous function of 3D spatial coordinates, treating thick-slice LR images as sparse, discrete samples of this function. Consequently, the super-resolution (SR) task involves learning this continuous volumetric function from limited observations using a fully-connected neural network enhanced with Fourier feature positional encoding. By minimizing the discrepancy between network predictions and acquired LR image intensities across each imaging plane, IREM learns to represent a continuous model of the observed tissue anatomy. Experimental results demonstrate that IREM effectively captures high-frequency image features. In real-world data collection, IREM reduces scan times while delivering high-quality HR MR imaging, characterized by improved signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and preserved local image details.

This paper examines the scattering dynamics within a two-field $(1+1)$-dimensional model featuring multiple topological solutions: (i) a high-rest-mass solution defined by a nested defect (a lump embedded within a kink), and (ii) four lower-rest-mass, degenerate solutions characterized by a kink within a kink. We focus on symmetric kink-antikink scattering involving the higher-rest-mass configurations with identical initial velocity magnitudes. The scattering results exhibit diverse behaviors, including pair annihilation, radiation jet emission, the formation of oscillating pulses, and transitions between topological sectors. Our findings indicate that topological sector transitions are favored, with only two of the four possible sectors serving as outcomes. Furthermore, despite energy degeneracy, the final state distribution in phase space is asymmetric due to vibrational states; this phenomenon likely represents a general effect applicable to other phenomenologically significant two-field models.

This study addresses unsupervised Video Object Segmentation (VOS), a task that derives visual correspondence—representing pixel-level feature similarity—from unlabeled video sequences. Existing approaches primarily rely on contrastive learning, optimizing features either at the image or pixel level. Image-level optimization, such as using spatially pooled ResNet features, captures robust high-level semantics but remains sub-optimal because pixel-level features are optimized implicitly. Conversely, pixel-level optimization is more explicit yet proves sensitive to training data quality and lacks robustness against object deformation. To unify these two optimization levels, we introduce In-aNd-Out (INO), a purely generative learning framework leveraging naturally designed class and patch tokens within a Vision Transformer (ViT). For image-level optimization, we implement "out-generative learning" by encouraging the imagination of out-views from local to global perspectives on class tokens, thereby enhancing high-level semantic capture. For pixel-level optimization, we employ "in-generative learning" through in-view masked image modeling on patch tokens, which restores corrupted image regions by inferring fine-grained structures. Furthermore, to better capture temporal dynamics, we enforce inter-frame consistency across both feature and affinity matrix levels. Extensive evaluations on the DAVIS-2017 and YouTube-VOS 2018 validation sets demonstrate that INO significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/pansanity666/INO_VOS

Contemporary unmanned technologies enable their deployment across nearly every sector, including radiation monitoring. Since the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, drones have been utilized to assess radiation levels in affected areas, making the refinement of such devices a critical area of focus. Our research group has developed a concept for a gamma radiation detector module tailored for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). This design utilizes a matrix of upgraded silicon photomultipliers constructed from silicon structures featuring deep pixel photodiodes of the MLPD type. Current experimental prototypes demonstrate superior performance in key metrics, such as high ionizing radiation detection efficiency. Additionally, the modules' low vibration sensitivity and minimal power consumption allow for seamless integration into compact, unmanned radiation monitoring systems.

Large-scale structures have been confirmed in the spatial arrangement of optical galaxies out to a redshift of approximately 1. However, the connection between dust-obscured, star-forming galaxies detected at millimetre wavelengths and the cosmic dark matter filaments predicted by cosmological hydrodynamical simulations remains an active area of research. Utilizing the NIKA2 dual-band millimetre camera, we conducted simultaneous observations of a ~90 arcminute² field toward the star GJ526 in the 1.15-mm and 2.0-mm continuum bands. Our goal was to investigate five sources previously identified ten years ago by the MAMBO camera at 1.2 mm that appeared quasi-aligned. We conclude that these sources are not circumstellar debris clumps around GJ526, as initially suggested, but are instead distant, dust-obscured star-forming galaxies, also known as sub-millimetre galaxies (SMGs). The new NIKA2 map at 1.15 mm reveals seven SMGs projected along a filament-like structure spanning the entire observed field. Additionally, we demonstrate that NIKA2 data, combined with supplemental Herschel photometry, align with a spectral energy distribution (SED) model for these sources assuming a common redshift of 2.5 and standard dust parameters for SMGs. Consequently, we propose that these SMGs may reside within a filament of the distant cosmic web. The candidate filament extends at least 4 comoving megaparsecs (cMpc) across the map, with source separations ranging from 0.25 to 1.25 cMpc at this redshift, consistent with cosmological simulation expectations. Nevertheless, definitive confirmation of this hypothesis regarding SMGs embedded in a dark matter filament requires further observations to determine precise spectroscopic redshifts.

Beam loss represents a critical challenge in high-intensity accelerators, necessitating significant effort during both design and operation to suppress it to acceptable levels. As accelerators advance in power, the implications of beam loss grow increasingly severe. H- ion beam linacs, exemplified by the facility at the Oak Ridge Spallation Neutron Source, exhibit a greater variety of loss mechanisms compared to H+ (proton) linacs, such as the one planned for the European Spallation Neutron Source. Distinctive loss mechanisms for H- beams include residual gas stripping, H+ capture and acceleration, field stripping, black-body radiation, and the recently identified intra-beam stripping. Conversely, beam halo formation and transients during ion source or RF power cycling are loss mechanisms shared by both H+ and H- accelerators. Machine protection systems are essential for constraining beam loss.

Doctrines serve as categorical frameworks ideal for examining diverse logics within a unified setting, specifically the 2-category Dtn. Within this structure, modal interior operators are defined as specific adjoints. This work demonstrates that these operators can be derived both from comonads and from adjunctions in Dtn, comparing the two methods. Furthermore, we quantify the information lost when transitioning from either a comonad or an adjunction to a modal interior operator. This research builds upon foundational contributions by John Power.

Advanced gravitational-wave detectors, which rely on high-precision interferometry, necessitate sophisticated seismic isolation systems to separate the apparatus from ambient ground vibrations. The integration of enhanced inertial sensors for active isolation could significantly boost the sensitivity of current and upcoming detectors, particularly in the frequency band below 30 Hz, thus expanding the scope of observable astrophysical phenomena. This study introduces a vertical inertial sensor designed to measure the relative displacement between a seismically isolated platform and a test mass suspended via a blade spring. Utilizing an interferometric readout scheme ensures minimal sensing noise and maintains a broad dynamic range through fringe-counting techniques. The projected sensitivity aligns with leading interferometric inertial sensors, achieving $10^{-10}\,\text{m}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ at 100 mHz and $10^{-12}\,\text{m}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ at 1 Hz. Comparative analysis indicates that this sensor offers a sensitivity gain of approximately two orders of magnitude over commercial L-4C geophones at 10 mHz and 100 mHz, and one order of magnitude at 1 Hz. Below 10 Hz, thermal noise within the suspension of the inertial test mass is anticipated to be the primary limiting factor. Additionally, the study quantifies and addresses other performance constraints, including tilt-to-vertical coupling resulting from imperfect leveling and nonlinearities inherent to the interferometric readout.

Aortic regurgitation, a form of valvular heart disease, significantly impacts cardiovascular hemodynamics, necessitating metrics based on blood flow to detect its onset and assess its severity. While four-dimensional (4D) flow magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows for the non-invasive acquisition of these metrics, its accuracy is heavily reliant on spatial resolution, which is often compromised by the technique's inherent limitations and the complex nature of aortic regurgitation flow. To overcome this, researchers converted computational fluid dynamics simulations into synthetic 4D flow MRI data to train various neural networks. These networks successfully produced super-resolution, full-field phase images with a four-fold upscaling, yielding reduced velocity errors, high structural similarity scores, and enhanced learning capabilities compared to prior studies. Validation using two distinct sets of in-vivo 4D flow MRI data confirmed the method's effectiveness in de-noising flow images. Consequently, this approach offers a promising avenue for the comprehensive, non-invasive analysis of aortic regurgitation hemodynamics.

Analogies have long served as a cornerstone of creative problem-solving in science and technology. With scientific publications growing exponentially, there is an increasing potential to discover diverse solutions to current challenges. However, unlocking this potential demands a search mechanism capable of navigating vast corpora beyond superficial matches and basic keywords. This study introduces the first end-to-end system for analogical search within scientific literature, evaluating its efficacy using real problems provided by scientists. By employing a human-in-the-loop AI system as a probe, we demonstrate that the tool fosters creative ideation, with success dependent on an intermediate level of problem abstraction matching (neither too high nor too low). Furthermore, we present a fully automated AI search engine that attains comparable accuracy to the human-assisted approach. Finally, we outline design principles for automated analogical inspiration engines aimed at accelerating scientific innovation.

Continuously observing measurement devices possess an intrinsic reality independent of the states that trigger their sensors, a concept known as the Principle of Instrument Autonomy. While this principle is inherent to the mathematical definition of an instrument, traditional analyses of continuous observation have predominantly focused on state dynamics rather than the instruments themselves. Consequently, it is often overlooked that instruments operating for finite durations undergo their own stochastic evolution, which occurs prior to the Born rule and Schrödinger equation governing the measured system. This article reviews the two most prominent continuously observing instruments—the Srinivas-Davies photodetector and the Goetsch-Graham-Wiseman heterodyne detector—with a specific focus on their autonomous evolution, clarified through the recently developed Kraus-operator distribution function. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the heterodyne instrument's evolution offers a complete alternative to the original concept of energy quantization, effectively replacing standard notions of a state's *temperature* and *energy* with the *time* and *positivity* of the *instrument*.

We introduce a technique for determining hyperfine vectors between a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center and a surrounding environment of interacting nuclear spins. Our approach facilitates the creation of tunable electron-nuclear coupling Hamiltonians while minimizing undesired inter-nuclear interactions. This allows for the individual addressing and control of each nucleus, enabling the reconstruction of specific hyperfine vectors. Consequently, the three-dimensional structure of spin ensembles and spins within biomolecules can be identified without needing to alter the orientation of applied magnetic fields. We illustrate this capability through examples, including the full reconstruction of an interacting spin cluster in diamond and the three-dimensional imaging of all nuclear spins in a biomolecule.

The orthorhombic Pnma GeS-structured SnSe monolayer represents a significant two-dimensional indirect band gap material at room temperature. Utilizing first-principles density functional theory, we conducted systematic investigations into the electronic and magnetic characteristics of SnSe monolayers doped with X atoms (where X = Ga, In, As, or Sb). Electronic structure calculations reveal that Ga doping preserves the semiconducting nature of the system, whereas In doping renders the SnSe monolayer half-metallic. Both As- and Sb-doped variants exhibit n-type semiconductor behavior. Furthermore, all examined substitutional doping scenarios induce magnetic ground states, each possessing a magnetic moment of 1 μB. Additionally, formation energy calculations confirm the thermodynamic stability of these four doped configurations. These findings offer a promising pathway for leveraging doped SnSe monolayers in future 2D photoelectronic and magnetic semiconductor applications.

The memorization capability of deep neural networks (DNNs) is a critical component in contemporary label noise learning techniques. To leverage this, model-prediction-based approaches have become popular, utilizing early-stage DNN outputs to rectify noisy labels. However, we note that these models often err during prediction, leading to suboptimal performance. In contrast, features generated in the early learning phase demonstrate superior robustness. Motivated by this finding, we introduce a novel feature embedding-based approach for handling label noise in deep learning, named LabEl NoiseDilution (LEND). Specifically, we first construct a similarity matrix using current embedded features to identify the local structure of the training data. Subsequently, the erroneous supervision signals from mislabeled instances are suppressed by neighboring correctly labeled ones—a process termed label noise dilution—which is ensured by the intrinsic robustness of feature embeddings. Finally, a robust classifier is trained using this data with diluted labels. We validate the efficacy of LEND through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world noisy datasets, comparing it against several state-of-the-art robust learning methods.

Accurately estimating bone age from hand radiographs is crucial for diagnosing endocrine disorders and assessing the growth status of children. However, current automatic methods often fail to account for the gap between training and test data, resulting in reduced generalization capabilities. To address this, we introduce Adversarial Regression Learning Network (ARLNet) for bone age estimation. Our approach begins by extracting bone features using a fine-tuned Inception V3 network and employing a regression percentage loss for training. To bridge the discrepancy between training and test datasets, we implement adversarial regression loss and feature reconstruction loss. These mechanisms ensure seamless transition between training and test data while maintaining invariant features from both sources. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

Model-based methods offer a promising avenue for enhancing reinforcement learning sample efficiency by conducting numerous explorations and evaluations within learned models, thereby conserving real-world samples. However, significant model errors can render sequential steps difficult to assess accurately, thus restricting the model's effective use. To address this limitation, we propose substituting multi-step actions with multi-step plans in model-based RL. Our approach utilizes multi-step plan value estimation to evaluate the expected discounted return from executing a sequence of action plans from a given state, while the policy is updated by directly calculating the multi-step policy gradient through this estimation. The resulting algorithm, MPPVE (Model-based Planning Policy Learning with Multi-step Plan Value Estimation), demonstrates superior utilization of the learned model and achieves higher sample efficiency compared to current state-of-the-art model-based RL techniques.

This work examines global 1- and $(d-2)$-form symmetries within gauge theories defined by disconnected groups that incorporate charge conjugation. We demonstrate that for pure gauge theories, the associated 1-form symmetries are non-invertible. Furthermore, the disconnected nature of these gauge groups ensures the presence of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ global $(d-2)$-form symmetry. We suggest String Theory realizations for theories based on such groups. Notably, these embeddings invariably include twist vortices that break the $(d-2)$-form global symmetry, aligning with the conjecture that global symmetries are absent in Quantum Gravity.

Following the approach outlined in [G. Groenewald, M.A. Kaashoek, A.C.M. Ran, Wiener-Hopf indices of unitary functions on the unit circle in terms of realizations and related results on Toeplitz operators. Indag. Math. 28 (2017) 694--710], our objective is to explicitly determine the Wiener-Hopf indices for a rational $m \times m$ matrix function $R(z)$ that possesses no poles or zeros on the unit circle $\mathbb{T}$. Unlike the aforementioned paper, however, $R(z)$ is not required to be unitary on $\mathbb{T}$. Instead, by employing a Douglas-Shapiro-Shields type factorization, we demonstrate that $R(z)$ decomposes into $R(z)=\Xi(z)\Psi(z)$, where $\Xi(z)$ and $\Psi(z)$ are rational $m \times m$ matrix functions, $\Xi(z)$ is unitary on the unit circle, and $\Psi(z)$ is an invertible outer function. Moreover, the unitarity of $\Xi(z)$ on the unit circle enables the factorization $\Xi(z) =V(z)W^*(z)$, where $V(z)$ and $W(z)$ are rational bi-inner $m \times m$ matrix functions. This decomposition facilitates the resolution of the Wiener-Hopf indices problem. Finally, deriving explicit formulas for $V(z)$ and $W(z)$ necessitates additional realization properties of $\Xi(z)$, which are detailed in the final two sections.

We examine higher-dimensional effective field theory (EFT) operators involving fermionic dark matter (DM) interacting with Standard Model (SM) leptons up to dimension six. By analyzing all such operators under the assumption of thermal freeze-out, we determine the allowed parameter space for dark matter mass ($m_\chi$) and the new physics (NP) scale ($\Lambda$), incorporating one-loop direct detection constraints from the XENON1T experiment. The model's viable parameter space is further tested at the proposed International Linear Collider (ILC) through monophoton signatures for both Dirac and Majorana DM scenarios, subject to a center-of-mass energy limit of $\sqrt{s} = 1$ TeV. In this regime, pair production allows probing DM masses up to $m_\chi < \frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}$, while the EFT framework remains valid only when $\Lambda > \sqrt{s}$.

A temporal-probabilistic (TP) join with negation determines, at every time point, the likelihood that a tuple from a positive relation ${\bf p}$ matches no tuple in a negative relation ${\bf n}$ under a specific join condition $\theta$. Consequently, TP outer and anti joins mirror the behavior of their relational counterparts, even when input tuples from ${\bf p}$ and ${\bf n}$ possess non-zero probabilities of being true and false, respectively. To compute these joins, we propose generalized lineage-aware temporal windows, a mechanism that links output intervals to the lineages of all valid matching tuples from each input relation. These windows from two TP relations are categorized into three disjoint sets based on how attributes, lineage expressions, and intervals are generated. By computing all windows incrementally, we demonstrate that pipelined execution enables the direct integration of this method into PostgreSQL. This approach reduces the redundancies common in interval calculations of prior methods, a claim substantiated by extensive experiments using real-world datasets.

Content-based retrieval for remote sensing (RS) images fundamentally relies on understanding image similarity. Recently, deep metric learning has become a popular approach in this field by mapping semantic relationships into an embedding space. A standard technique for constructing this space involves selecting triplets consisting of a reference image (anchor), a similar image (positive), and a dissimilar image (negative). However, generating these triplets is particularly challenging for multi-label RS retrieval, where images carry multiple class annotations. To solve this, we introduce a new triplet sampling method tailored for multi-label RS CBIR within a deep neural network (DNN) framework. Our approach identifies a concise set of highly representative and informative triplets through a two-step process. First, an iterative algorithm selects a diverse set of anchors from the current mini-batch based on their distribution in the embedding space. Second, for each anchor, we select specific positive and negative images by evaluating their relevancy, hardness, and diversity using a novel strategy. Experiments on two multi-label benchmark datasets demonstrate that prioritizing informative triplets within DNNs yields two key benefits: it reduces training computational complexity without compromising performance, and it accelerates learning speed by enabling faster convergence due to the quality of the selected triplets. The source code for our proposed method is publicly accessible at https://git.tu-berlin.de/rsim/image-retrieval-from-triplets.

The varying requirements of different summarization tasks, coupled with their expensive annotation processes, have created a pressing demand for few-shot summarization. Despite the growing number of available tasks and datasets, existing few-shot summarization training methods fail to leverage potentially transferable knowledge across heterogeneous data sources. To address this, we introduce \textsc{UniSumm}, a unified few-shot summarization model pre-trained on multiple tasks and capable of achieving top performance on any few-shot dataset through prefix-tuning. Additionally, guided by principles of diversity and robustness, we have compiled and released a new benchmark called \textsc{SummZoo} to better evaluate few-shot summarization systems. This benchmark features eight diverse summarization tasks, each with multiple few-shot sample sets, spanning both monologue and dialogue domains. Experimental results and ablation studies demonstrate that \textsc{UniSumm} significantly outperforms strong baseline systems across all \textsc{SummZoo} tasks under both automatic and human evaluation metrics. Our code and benchmark are available at \url{https://github.com/microsoft/UniSumm}.

The swift advancement of computing technology has enabled wearable devices, such as smartphones and wristbands, to readily collect health-related data on activities, sleep, and sports. Smart healthcare has seen significant progress by training machine learning models on vast amounts of user data. Nevertheless, two major obstacles remain: first, data often resides in isolated silos, hindering aggregation while threatening privacy; second, cloud-trained models struggle to offer personalization. To address these issues, this paper introduces FedHealth, the inaugural federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and subsequently constructs personalized models through transfer learning, ensuring accurate and tailored healthcare solutions without sacrificing privacy or security. Experimental results indicate that FedHealth outperforms traditional methods with a 5.3% boost in accuracy for wearable activity recognition. Furthermore, the framework is general and extensible, holding potential for diverse healthcare applications.

The Riesz Theorem defines a link between $\sigma$-additive regular Borel measures and linear positive functionals. This paper explores an idempotent counterpart to this relationship, connecting possibility capacities with functionals that maintain the maximum and t-norm operations via t-normed integrals.

Computational ghost imaging typically involves breaking an image into patterns that are weighted by their overlap with the target scene, a process managed by computers. In this study, we show that this computational integration can instead be executed directly by the human eye. By applying this human-based ghost imaging method, we assessed the eye's temporal response, determining an image persistence time of approximately 20 ms, followed by an additional 20 ms of exponential decay. These findings align with prior research but now offer the potential for a more precise characterization of visual stimuli and serve as a novel experimental tool for investigating visual perception.

We generalize existing analytic findings on Yang-Mills connections to $\Omega$-Yang-Mills connections defined on an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, where $\Omega$ represents a smooth $(n-4)$-form that need not be closed. This framework encompasses $\Omega$-anti-self-dual connections and Hermitian-Yang-Mills connections across various complex manifolds. Leveraging a pivotal observation, we establish a weak compactness property for the moduli space of smooth $\Omega$-Yang-Mills connections characterized by uniformly $L^2$-bounded curvature; this result is further refined specifically for Hermitian-Yang-Mills connections on general complex manifolds. Additionally, we prove a removable singularity theorem for singular $\Omega$-Yang-Mills connections on trivial bundles exhibiting small energy concentration. Applying these findings, we demonstrate a method to compactify the moduli space of smooth Hermitian-Yang-Mills connections on unitary bundles over a specific category of balanced manifolds of Hodge-Riemann type, which includes metrics derived from multipolarizations and Kähler metrics. Notably, when considering multipolarizations on a projective algebraic manifold, the compactification of smooth irreducible Hermitian-Yang-Mills connections with a fixed determinant, modulo gauge transformations, acquires a complex structure grounded in algebro-geometric principles.

This study introduces two new Volume-of-Solid (VoS) formulations designed for pore-scale micro-continuum simulations of mineral dissolution. The conventional VoS-psi approach employs a diffuse interface localization function ($\psi$) to maintain stability and constrain reactive surface diffusion, though its accuracy heavily relies on the specific choice of this function. Our first proposed method, iVoS, localizes reactions at the fluid-solid interface using the divergence of a reactive flux, thereby eliminating the need for a localization function. The second method, VoS-psi', utilizes a localization function with an adjustable parameter optimized to globally conserve reactive surface area. Both novel approaches were validated against experimental data, numerical simulations using an Arbitrary Eulerian-Lagrangian (ALE) interface tracking method, and the traditional VoS-psi technique. All implementations were developed within the GeoChemFoam reactive transport toolbox and tested across three benchmark scenarios involving both synthetic and real pore geometries: (1) calcite post dissolution via acid injection in a microchannel compared with experiments, (2) dissolution in a 2D polydisperse disc micromodel across various regimes, and (3) dissolution in Ketton carbonate rock compared with *in-situ* micro-CT results. Findings indicate that iVoS achieves high accuracy, aligning closely with both experimental observations and ALE simulations, whereas VoS-psi produces inaccuracies that are largely resolved by the VoS-psi' formulation. Furthermore, the VoS methods demonstrate significantly superior computational efficiency compared to the ALE method, achieving speed-ups ranging from 2 to 12 times.

We report continuum observations from the Very Large Array at C, X, and Q bands, alongside 1.3 mm continuum and CO(2-1) data obtained with the Submillimeter Array, all directed toward the high-mass protostellar candidate ISOSS J23053+5953 SMM2. Compact cm-scale continuum emission was identified near the SMM2 core center, exhibiting a spectral index of 0.24 across 3.6 to 6 cm and a radio luminosity of 1.3 mJy kpc$^2$. Thermal dust emission at 1.3 mm suggests a core mass of 45.8 Msun for SMM2. CO(2-1) observations uncover a large, massive molecular outflow centered on SMM2, characterized by a highly collimated, fast component (> 50 km/s relative to the cloud's systemic velocity) accompanied by a broader, lower-velocity part. Derived outflow mass (45.2 Msun) and momentum rate (6 x 10$^{-3}$ Msun km/s/yr) from the CO emission align with those typical of outflows driven by high-mass young stellar objects, with a dynamical timescale ranging from 1.5 to 7.2 x 10$^4$ years. Additionally, the ratio of C18O to thermal dust emission indicates a CO depletion factor of approximately 20, potentially caused by CO freeze-out onto dust grains. Our results support earlier findings that ISOSS J23053+5953 SMM2 is an emerging high-mass protostar in an early evolutionary stage, featuring an ionized jet and a fast, highly collimated, massive outflow.

An unattainable control architecture led to adverse effects on a UAV. The noise affecting performance was characterized using stochastic techniques, and a corrective term was added to an external controller. Our results indicate that the unconventional nature of the sonar noise issue may necessitate the creation of a novel methodology.

This study investigates whether E-mode polarization data from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can validate four temperature anomalies: the absence of large-scale correlations, the quadrupole-octupole (Q-O) alignment, point-parity asymmetry, and hemispherical power asymmetry. By employing CMB simulations that incorporate noise levels matching those of the Planck satellite, the Cosmology Large Angular Scale Surveyor (CLASS), and the LiteBIRD satellite, we assess how both existing and upcoming observations constrain these irregularities. Our results show that the correlation coefficients ($\rho$) between temperature and E-mode estimators remain below 0.1, with the exception of point-parity asymmetry ($\rho=0.17$ in cosmic-variance-limited simulations), thereby confirming that E-mode data offer a largely independent verification of these anomalies. Relative to Planck's SMICA component-separated data, the anticipated LiteBIRD survey would decrease errors in E-mode anomaly estimators by approximately 26 for the lack of large-scale correlation, by roughly 3 for both hemispherical power asymmetry and point-parity asymmetry, and by at least 100 for Q-O alignment, despite the latter being limited by significant cosmic variance. CLASS yields intermediate improvements compared to these extremes.

This paper categorizes various portfolio optimization techniques that incorporate higher moments like skewness and kurtosis, offering practitioners in hedge funds a clear view of the field's diverse paradigms and approaches. It reviews several methods grounded in different frameworks, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, while outlining the pros and cons of each. Keywords: multi-objective optimization, portfolio optimization, scalarization, utility.

Verifying array-manipulating programs automatically is difficult, primarily because it often requires inferring inductive quantified loop invariants that may not even be expressible in first-order logic. This paper introduces a novel verification approach based on induction over the user-defined rank of program states, serving as an alternative to traditional loop invariants. Our method, termed inductive rank reduction, operates in two stages. First, we simplify the verification task by proving program correctness for input arrays with a length of B or less, treating the array length as the state's rank. Second, we utilize a squeezing function $g$ that maps a program state $\sigma$ containing an array longer than B to a state $g(\sigma)$ with an array of length B-1 or less. We demonstrate that if $g$ meets specific natural conditions, any specification violation on $\sigma$ implies a corresponding violation on $g(\sigma)$. Consequently, the program's correctness for arrays of arbitrary length is established through induction. To automate this technique for array programs where execution time scales with input array length, we (i) use symbolic execution for the initial step, (ii) verify the required conditions for $g$ using Z3, and (iii) employ a heuristic procedure to synthesize $g$. We have implemented this approach and successfully applied it to various array-manipulating programs, including a bidirectional summation program whose loop invariant is not first-order expressible, yet whose specification remains quantifier-free.

In a prior study (Hermundstad et al., 2014), we demonstrated that under sampling constraints, the efficient coding principle gives rise to a "variance is salience" hypothesis, which explains visual sensitivity to binary image statistics. In this work, leveraging extensive new psychophysical data and image analysis, we reveal that this hypothesis accurately predicts visual sensitivity to a broad range of grayscale image statistics with remarkable precision, while also delineating its boundaries. We constructed a 66-dimensional space of local grayscale light-intensity correlations and assessed the relevance of each dimension within natural scenes. The "variance is salience" hypothesis posits that two-point correlations are the most salient and forecasts their relative salience. We validated these predictions through a texture-segregation task employing synthetic, non-natural textures. Consistent with the hypothesis, correlations of order higher than two showed no salience, and the predicted thresholds for over 300 second-order correlations aligned closely with psychophysical thresholds, exhibiting a median fractional error below 0.13.

Answering natural language questions over RDF data has garnered significant attention recently, especially within the QALD benchmark series. This task involves translating natural language inquiries into executable formats like SPARQL to retrieve answers from a knowledge base. Existing systems are typically limited to monolingual inputs and depend on hard-coded rules for interpretation and query generation. We introduce the first multilingual QALD pipeline that utilizes a model trained on data to map natural language questions into a logical form via probabilistic inference. Specifically, our method learns to convert universal syntactic dependency structures into a language-independent logical form using DUDES (Dependency-based Underspecified Discourse Representation Structures), which are subsequently deterministically transformed into SPARQL queries. Our model employs factor graphs that leverage features derived from dependency graphs and semantic representations. We utilize approximate inference techniques, particularly Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods and Sample Rank, to update parameters based on a ranking objective. Our primary focus is bridging the lexical gap through a novel integration of machine translation and word embedding techniques. As a proof of concept, we evaluate our approach on the QALD-6 datasets for English, German, and Spanish.

Most machine learning (ML) approaches presume that training data originates from the target population, yet practitioners frequently encounter dataset shift in real-world scenarios, which can degrade model performance if unaddressed. When the specific nature of the shift is known—such as covariate or label shift—transfer learning techniques can enhance predictive accuracy. However, existing detection methods are limited to identifying specific shift types or lack the ability to formally test for their existence. We present a unified, general framework that identifies various shift types, quantifies their magnitude, and offers strategies to improve prediction methods. This approach is applicable to all data formats (tabular, image, text) and supports both classification and regression tasks. Furthermore, it employs formal hypothesis tests to control false positives. We demonstrate the framework's practical utility using both synthetic and real datasets, including a case study where the framework provided insights that directly boosted a supervised model's predictive power. The associated package for dataset shift detection is available at https://github.com/felipemaiapolo/detectshift.

This paper introduces a method for investigating normalization strategies in cases where termination is asymptotic, meaning it is reached as a limit rather than within a finite number of steps. Such asymptotic termination arises in various contexts, including effectful and specifically probabilistic computation—where limits represent distributions over potential outputs—as well as infinitary lambda-calculi, where limits take the form of infinitary normal forms like Böhm trees. As a specific application, we derive a result of independent significance: a normalization theorem for the probabilistic lambda-calculus under Call-by-Value evaluation, which also applies uniformly to Call-by-Name evaluation.
