Our conservative analytical estimates are notably optimistic, indicating that the protocol is well-suited for long-range entanglement generation both within and between near-term quantum computing devices.

This study introduces a low-overhead beam management strategy for near-field millimeter-wave multi-antenna systems utilizing Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RISs). We develop a new variable-width hierarchical phase-shift codebook applicable to both near-field and far-field RIS scenarios and propose a rapid alignment algorithm for optimizing RIS phase shifts and transceiver beamformers. Performance evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed method when compared against multiple benchmark schemes.

It is commonly assumed that stochastic processes can be approximated by a fluid limit (also known as a "mean field" or "hydrodynamic limit") as a scale parameter grows large. A frequent technique, termed the "fixed point approximation," involves estimating the stationary behavior of the stochastic process using the stationary points of the fluid limit. However, this approach is generally flawed because the stationary behavior of a fluid limit is not always defined solely by its stationary points. We demonstrate that the fixed point approximation remains valid when the stochastic process is reversible. Specifically, we assume that the process converges in distribution (and thus in probability) to the fluid limit at any fixed time, an assumption that is quite weak and applicable to a broad range of models, including many mean field and interaction systems. We prove that the reversibility of the stochastic process ensures that any limit point of its stationary distribution is concentrated on the stationary points of the fluid limit. Consequently, if the fluid limit possesses a unique stationary point, it serves as an approximation for the stationary distribution of the stochastic process.

The primary goal of this study is to introduce a method for creating an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Language Assessment (LA) tool designed to detect language deficits linked to dementia in elderly individuals. Since Machine Learning (ML) classifiers form the core of our proposed framework, we examine various binary classifiers to ensure the resulting tool achieves high sensitivity and specificity. Furthermore, we evaluate the reliability and validity of our approach by analyzing how different language tasks, feature sets, and recording media influence the performance of these ML classifiers.

Art installed in public areas significantly influences individuals' sense of belonging, as urban public art signals which cultures and interests are prioritized. This paper introduces a graph matching method incorporating local constraints to create a curatorial tool for selecting public art that fosters inclusivity. We construct a cost matrix based on Schelling's segregation model and solve the resulting optimization problem using projected gradient descent to generate a soft assignment matrix. The study also explores regularization terms to establish curatorial limits. This optimization framework assigns artworks to public venues and walls while minimizing "in-group" preferences by adhering to minimum representation and exposure standards. Leveraging existing research, we define a fairness metric to evaluate our algorithmic results. Finally, using Tufts University as a case study, we evaluate the method's efficacy and examine potential drawbacks regarding both curation and equity.

IHP fabricated a monolithic silicon pixel detector prototype using the 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS SG13G2 process. The ASIC features a hexagonal pixel matrix with a pitch of roughly 100 $\mu$m. Calibration of three analog pixels was performed in the lab using radioactive sources, followed by testing in an 180 GeV/c pion beamline at CERN's SPS. Measurements at the optimal operating point—150 $\mu$A preamplifier bias current and 160 V sensor bias voltage—yielded a detection efficiency of $\left(99.9^{+0.1}_{-0.2}\right)$% and a time resolution of $(36.4 \pm 0.8)$ps. Additional characterization was conducted at reduced bias voltages and preamplifier currents.

Detecting when residents are away from home is an emerging area within smart home technology, a capability that proves vital in various situations, including caring for elderly individuals living alone, managing dementia patients, and adhering to home quarantine protocols. While most existing research relies on intrusive methods like pressure/door sensors or cameras—requiring specific installation modifications—to identify outings, this study investigates appliance electrical usage as a non-intrusive alternative. By utilizing energy consumption data derived from power disaggregation, a non-invasive sensing technique, we address the lack of available datasets containing both energy metrics and ground truth for absence detection. Consequently, artificial outing events were generated within the UK-DALE dataset, a standard resource for Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), to facilitate evaluation. After testing several machine learning algorithms on this synthetic data, benchmark results confirm that detecting home absence through appliance power consumption is a feasible approach.

The study examines fermion superpartners, specifically neutralinos and charginos, within the economical supersymmetric 3-3-1 framework. By enforcing R parity, their masses and eigenstates are determined. Assuming a Bino-like composition for dark matter, its mass density is computed. Cosmological dark matter density constraints limit the lightest neutralino mass to a range of 20–100 GeV and the lightest slepton mass to a range of 60–130 GeV.

Automated tools are commonly employed within social coding repositories to handle repetitive tasks inherent to distributed software development. Recently, GitHub launched GitHub Actions, a feature designed to facilitate automated workflows for repository maintainers. Gaining insight into and forecasting the impacts of adopting such technologies is crucial for effective planning and management. This study examines how projects utilize GitHub Actions, the topics discussed by communities regarding them, and shifts in activity metrics following their implementation. The findings reveal that a significant portion of projects (nearly 30% of the sample) have adopted GitHub Actions, with developers often seeking assistance. Additionally, the data suggests that adopting GitHub Actions results in increased pull request (PR) rejections, heightened communication within accepted PRs but reduced communication in rejected ones, a decrease in commits for accepted PRs versus an increase for rejected ones, and longer durations required to accept PRs. Similar trends were observed for Utility Actions, though Code Quality Actions showed fewer rejected PRs. These results hold particular significance for practitioners, offering critical considerations when integrating GitHub Actions into their projects.

This paper introduces VisualEnv, a novel tool designed to construct visual environments for reinforcement learning. Developed by combining the open-source modeling and rendering software Blender with the Python-based OpenAI Gym module for generating simulation environment models, VisualEmp enables users to design custom environments featuring photorealistic rendering and seamless Python integration. The framework is outlined and evaluated through a series of example problems that demonstrate its capabilities in training reinforcement learning agents.

This work investigates Safe Policy Improvement (SPI) within the offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework under specific constraints. The scenario involves a dataset gathered from a known baseline policy and multiple reward signals that generate distinct optimization objectives. We introduce an SPI formulation tailored to this setting, which incorporates user preferences for balancing trade-offs among these rewards while guaranteeing that the new policy matches or exceeds the baseline's performance on every individual objective. Building upon conventional SPI approaches, we propose a novel method grounded in Safe Policy Iteration with Baseline Bootstrapping (SPIBB, Laroche et al., 2019), offering high-probability performance guarantees in the actual environment. We validate the efficacy of our approach on a synthetic grid-world safety task and in a real-world critical care application focused on learning policies for administering IV fluids and vasopressors to treat sepsis.

This study examines the mechanism for producing asymmetric leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), highlighting its significance for establishing robust constraints on leptoquark parameters and accurately identifying these promising sources of new physics. The defining characteristic of this process, which sets it apart from standard leptoquark pair production, is that the two leptoquarks generated in proton-proton collisions via $t$-channel lepton exchange are not charge conjugates; consequently, the term "asymmetric leptoquark pair production" is applied. We detail the necessary conditions for this mechanism to function and list all viable combinations of leptoquark multiplets capable of producing it. Furthermore, we conduct several phenomenological analyses within various simple scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model to illustrate how to correctly incorporate asymmetric pair production into the reinterpretation of current experimental data, thereby yielding precise constraints on the parameter space.

Deep learning models are extensively utilized for anomaly detection in surveillance footage, typically functioning by reconstructing normal video sequences and flagging anomalies based on reconstruction errors. However, current methods face two primary limitations: first, they process individual identities' movements in isolation, neglecting inter-identity interactions that can also signal anomalies; second, they rely on rigid architectures with fixed structures across varying scenes, hindering scene comprehension. To overcome these issues, this paper introduces the Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Neural Network (HSTGCNN). This model comprises multiple branches representing different levels of graph abstraction: low-level graphs capture local body postures of individuals, while high-level graphs encode person trajectories and their mutual interactions. We further propose a mechanism to dynamically weight these branches based on scene suitability, thereby enhancing single-level graph performance and facilitating scene understanding for anomaly detection. Specifically, high-level graphs are prioritized in low-resolution videos to track movement speed and direction, whereas low-level graphs are favored in high-resolution videos to analyze human skeletons. Experimental evaluations across four benchmark datasets (UCSD Pedestrian, ShanghaiTech, CUHK Avenue, and IITB-Corridor) demonstrate that HSTGCNN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models while utilizing substantially fewer learnable parameters.

Linking relations is crucial for facilitating question answering over knowledge bases. Despite numerous attempts to enhance relation linking, current state-of-the-art methods fall short of optimal performance, thereby hindering overall end-to-end question answering capabilities. This paper introduces a novel approach that frames relation linking as a generative task, leveraging pre-trained sequence-to-sequence models. We augment these models by integrating structured data from the target knowledge base to better capture its nuances. Furthermore, the model is trained to produce a structured output of argument-relation pairs, which supports a knowledge validation process. Experiments conducted on four datasets from DBpedia and Wikidata demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing systems. Notably, this improvement is achieved using a simpler model that is easily adaptable to various knowledge bases.

We investigate elastic manifolds incorporating self-repelling terms to estimate their effective radius. This system is modeled by a self-repelling vector-valued Gaussian free field defined on the domain $[-N,N]^d\cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ with Neumann boundary conditions, taking values in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our primary finding shows that for two dimensions ($d=2$), the effective radius $R_N$ scales approximately as $N$. For dimensions $d\geq 3$, we establish a comparable lower bound for $R_N$ alongside an upper bound of order $N^{d/2}$. These results indicate that self-repelling elastic manifolds experience significant stretching across all dimensions.

This study investigates the double copy relationship between anyons in gauge theory and gravity. By employing on-shell amplitude methods, we develop little group covariant spinor-helicity variables for massive spinning particles; combined with locality and unitarity, these allow us to determine long-range tree-level scattering amplitudes for anyons. We find that classical gauge theory anyon solutions map to their gravitational analogues through a non-trivial double copy mechanism. Notably, we demonstrate that the massless double copy encodes the topological structure of three-dimensional curved spacetime via a non-trivial mixing of the topological graviton and the dilaton. Furthermore, we derive the celebrated Aharonov-Bohm phase directly from the constructed on-shell amplitudes, showing that it also exhibits a straightforward double copy relation to its gravitational counterpart.

This study quantitatively investigates the hypothesis that solar eruptions, specifically coronal mass ejections (CMEs), are necessary to release magnetic helicity and prevent its excessive buildup within each hemisphere. Through a parametric simulation of flux rope ejections starting from nearly marginally stable force-free states, we systematically varied the guide and strapping field ratios along with the flux rope twist to determine different self- and mutual helicity proportions and trigger either torus or helical kink instabilities. Our findings reveal that the amount of shed helicity spans a wide spectrum, ranging from a small to a dominant fraction of the initial helicity. Specifically, self-helicity is almost entirely or fully expelled, whereas mutual helicity—which constitutes the majority of the initial helicity—is only partially released. Configurations that are torus-unstable with subcritical twist and no guide field can shed approximately two-thirds of the initial helicity, whereas highly twisted, kink-unstable configurations release only about one-quarter. Additionally, the study identifies stable force-free flux rope equilibria with a total flux-normalized helicity reaching 0.25, characterized by a self-to-total helicity ratio of 0.32 and a flux rope to external poloidal flux ratio of 0.94. These numerical results confirm the conjecture that CMEs facilitate helicity shedding and offer the first detailed analysis of its parametric dependencies. Significantly, both self- and mutual helicity are substantially reduced, decreasing the total initial helicity by roughly 40% to 65% under typical source region conditions.

Recent studies have highlighted the efficacy of mmWave radar for object detection in low-visibility conditions, positioning it as a prime solution for autonomous navigation. This paper presents Radar to Point Cloud (R2P), a deep learning framework that transforms rough, sparse, and noisy 3D point clouds—derived from inconsistent 2D depth images generated by raw mmWave radar sensors—into smooth, dense, and highly accurate representations with fine geometric details. The R2P architecture employs two sequential encoder-decoder blocks to extract essential features from multi-viewpoint radar inputs, ensuring internal consistency and precise shape reconstruction. We integrate R2P as the second stage of our recently developed 3DRIMR (3D Reconstruction and Imaging via mmWave Radar) system. Experimental results demonstrate that R2P significantly outperforms established methods, including PointNet, PCN, and the baseline 3DRIMR design.

We compute Wilson loops at the leading order of perturbation theory for triangular contours composed of circular arcs. By appropriately disentangling the relationships between the metrical and conformal parameters of these contours, our results align precisely with the structure anticipated by the anomalous conformal Ward identity. In the general 4D scenario, the conformal remainder function relies on three cusp angles and three torsion angles. We examine the constraints these angles must satisfy due to the requirement of contour closure, extending this discussion to cases in 3D and 2D.

We introduce a novel, efficient, and broadly applicable approach to calculate the Hofstadter spectrum for isolated narrow bands. This technique is effective for both trivial and topological narrow bands by mapping zero $\mathbf{B}$-field hybrid Wannier states—which are localized along one axis and Bloch-extended along another—onto a representation of the magnetic translation group within the Landau gauge. Utilizing this method, we determine, for the first time, the Hofstadter spectrum for exact single-particle charged excitations in the strong coupling limit of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene at the charge neutrality point and at $|\nu|=2$. These calculations extend down to low magnetic fields where the flux through the moiré unit cell is merely $\sim 1/25$ of the electronic flux quantum (approximately 1 T) at the first magic angle. The resulting spectra offer a pathway to explore the Landau quantization of quasiparticles, even when their dispersion arises from interactions.

We compute the leading- and next-to-leading-logarithmic electroweak corrections to the charm-top-quark contribution within the effective $|\Delta S| = 2$ Lagrangian, which is pertinent to the parameter $\epsilon_K$. Our results indicate that these corrections induce a $-0.5\%$ adjustment to the associated Wilson coefficient. Additionally, our calculation eliminates an inherent ambiguity in the standard-model prediction for $\epsilon_K$ by establishing a precise renormalization scheme for the electroweak input parameters.

We demonstrate that deciding if a closed three-manifold possesses an elliptic structure is solvable in NP, and identifying the homeomorphism type of such a manifold falls within the FNP complexity class. These findings stem from a key result: for any lens space M (excluding RP³ and prism manifolds) with a triangulation T, there exists a loop within the one-skeleton of the 86th iterated barycentric subdivision of T such that the simplicial neighborhood of this loop forms a Heegaard solid torus for M.

Analyzing physiological processes over time typically involves spectrometric or gene expression data characterized by a limited number of time points but a vast array of variables. This analysis presents significant challenges, with only a handful of existing methods available. Information can be encoded either as time-independent classical expression differences at a single point or as full expression profiles over time. Currently, available approaches are restricted to unsupervised and semi-supervised environments, where predictive variables can only be identified using wrapper or post-processing techniques; this is further complicated by the scarcity of samples in such studies. We introduce a supervised learning framework called Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), which learns a supervised mapping of temporal sequences onto a low-dimensional grid. This approach employs a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to handle the time domain and utilizes relevance learning to pinpoint the most predictive feature dimensions over time. The resulting mapping facilitates the visualization of temporal sequences and enables the prediction of classes for new sequences. By using relevance learning, we identify discriminating masses or gene expressions while pruning dimensions that are irrelevant to the classification task or primarily represent noise, thereby creating a highly efficient learning system for temporal data. Results demonstrate that combining simultaneous supervised learning with metric adaptation significantly enhances prediction accuracy for both synthetic and real-world data compared to standard techniques. Furthermore, the discriminating features identified by our relevance learning method perform comparably to those found by alternative approaches. Finally, our method allows for the visualization of data on a low-dimensional grid, effectively highlighting the underlying temporal structure.

The paper establishes the author's "Eight Levels Theorem," introduces a novel explicit expansion method for the Lucas-Lehmer primality test regarding Mersenne primes, and provides a new criterion for determining Mersenne compositeness. Additionally, the work demonstrates four new combinatorial identities.

This study establishes time-uniform bounds for solutions within a specific category of thermo-diffusive systems, encompassing both classical and fractional diffusion models. In the context of classical diffusion, the nonlinear terms are permitted to grow exponentially, whereas in the fractional diffusion scenario, they must exhibit slightly sub-exponential growth. The underlying proofs utilize the approach developed by Herrero, Lacey, and Velazquez.

Although research on Ethiopic scripts exists, previous studies have omitted Geez numbers for various reasons. This paper introduces a method for recognizing offline handwritten and machine-printed Geez numbers using a feed-forward back-propagation artificial neural network. Data collection involved gathering diverse Geez character images from Google and instructing three individuals to write the numbers with a pencil, resulting in a total dataset of 560 characters. Of these, 460 were allocated for training and 100 for testing, achieving an overall classification accuracy of approximately 89.88%.

Prescriptive process monitoring utilizes historical data to recommend runtime actions that prevent adverse case outcomes or enhance process performance. A core component of such methods is the intervention policy, a decision mechanism that dictates whether and when to act on an active case. Prior research in this domain relies on policies that evaluate only the current state of a case, neglecting the tradeoff between intervening immediately amidst predictive uncertainty versus postponing action to a future state. Additionally, these earlier approaches assume unlimited resource availability for interventions. This paper bridges these gaps by proposing a method that filters and ranks ongoing cases based on prediction scores, uncertainty levels, and the causal impact of interventions, triggering actions to maximize a gain function within resource constraints. Evaluated on a real-world event log, the proposed approach demonstrates superior total gain compared to existing baselines.

Nitrogen is a vital component of life's chemical foundations. Titan, Saturn's largest moon, features a thick atmosphere rich in molecular nitrogen and methane, providing a unique natural laboratory to study how this element integrates into carbon chains via atmospheric chemistry. A persistent brownish haze forms in this atmosphere and settles on the surface as a nitrogen-rich solid that may harbor prebiotic molecules. The primary goal of this research is to address the limited understanding of nitrogen incorporation into organic chains by simulating Titan's upper atmosphere. Using a combination of experimental work and theoretical modeling, the study demonstrates that the abundant N₂⁺ ion, generated at high altitudes by extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) solar radiation, can synthesize nitrogen-rich organic compounds. The results reveal the unexpected formation of CH₃N₂⁺ and CH₂N₂⁺ diazo-ions when a nitrogen-methane gas mixture is exposed to EUV radiation. Theoretical analysis indicates that these diazo-ions primarily arise from the reaction between N₂⁺ ions and CH₃ radicals. With a nitrogen-to-carbon ratio of two, these small, nitrogen-dense ions represent a crucial missing link in explaining Titan's high organic nitrogen content. Furthermore, this work underscores the significance of ion-radical reactions—a rarely explored area—thereby opening new avenues in astrochemistry.

This study recreates and enhances the binary classification approach for particles introduced by Roe et al. (2005) in "Boosted decision trees as an alternative to artificial neural networks for particle identification." The particles involved are tau neutrinos, classified as background, and electronic neutrinos, which constitute our signal. While the original work favored boosted decision trees due to their ease of tuning and performance at that time, we have opted for a deep neural network, which offers superior speed and potential for better results. We demonstrate that applying modern techniques allows us to surpass the original findings, achieving improvements in both accuracy and training efficiency.

The newly identified family of AV$_3$Sb$_5$ (where A = K, Rb, Cs) kagome metals exhibits a distinctive blend of nontrivial band topology, superconductivity, and electron correlation signatures indicated by competing charge density wave (CDW) order. While the mechanisms driving the CDW instability in these materials and its link to the emerging large anomalous Hall response remain poorly understood, this study investigates the CDW's effect on the electronic structure using quantum oscillation measurements on single crystals of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$. Our findings offer direct proof that the CDW triggers a significant reconstruction of Fermi surface pockets tied to vanadium orbitals and the kagome lattice. Combined with density functional theory simulations, we identified split oscillation frequencies arising from these reconstructed pockets, which consist of vanadium-derived states and Dirac-like bands. Additionally, complementary diffraction data confirms that the CDW instability displays correlated phasing between adjacent V$_3$Sb$_5$ planes. These results yield crucial insights into the fundamental CDW instability in AV$_3$Sb$_5$ kagome metals and validate minimal models attributing CDW order to the vanadium-based kagome lattice.

A sandpile torsor algorithm functions as a mapping that links every planar graph embedding to a free transitive action of its sandpile group on its spanning trees. We introduce a consistency requirement, mandating that such an algorithm remain invariant under specific contraction and deletion operations. Our results establish that the rotor-routing sandpile torsor algorithm (which is equivalent to the Bernardi algorithm) satisfies this consistency. Moreover, we identify exactly three additional consistent algorithms, all sharing the same structural properties as rotor-routing, thereby confirming a conjecture by Klivans. Additionally, we extend the definition of sandpile torsor algorithms to regular matroids and propose a corresponding consistency framework. We hypothesize that the Backman-Baker-Yuen algorithm is consistent within this context and conjecture that only three other consistent algorithms exist for regular matroids, each possessing the same underlying structure.

The challenge of deriving hydrodynamics from the Boltzmann equation and associated dissipative systems is framed as identifying slow invariant manifolds within the space of distributions. We examine specific instances where these hydrodynamic manifolds have been derived analytically, either through the summation of the Chapman–Enskog asymptotic expansion or by directly solving the invariance equation. These model cases, including both linear and nonlinear Grad's moment systems, are analyzed in detail to inform expectations regarding the Boltzmann equation. Specifically, we highlight the dispersive dominance and the saturation of the dissipation rate in exact hydrodynamics within the short-wave limit, as well as viscosity modifications under high flow velocity divergence, as significant barriers to solving Hilbert's 6th Problem. Moreover, we review the derivation of an approximate hydrodynamic manifold for the Boltzmann equation via Newton's iteration without relying on smallness parameters, comparing these results to exact solutions. We also discuss projecting the Boltzmann equation onto an approximate hydrodynamic invariant manifold using entropy principles. Finally, we propose a set of hypotheses outlining open questions and defining the boundaries for future exact derivations or proofs concerning hydrodynamic manifolds in the context of the Boltzmann equation.

The electronic and magnetic properties of the newly suggested cuprate Cu$_2$F$_5$, including parameters for the Heisenberg exchange interaction, were investigated. DFT+U calculations reveal that this compound consists of copper ions with $d^9$ and $d^8$ electronic configurations. We identified a highly stable antiferromagnetic order characterized by strong exchange interaction anisotropy, leading to distinctive 2D magnetism: within the (100)-plane, the exchange coupling between S=1 and S=1/2 Cu ions is nearly as strong as that between two S=1 ions. In contrast, the interplane magnetic interaction is approximately five times weaker than the in-plane coupling.

This study examines the processes $pp\to \{W, W'\} \to l\nu$ and $pp\to \{\gamma, Z, Z'\} \to l^+l^-$ (with $l=e,\mu$) within the framework of gauge-Higgs unification (GHU) models based on the $SU(3)_C\times SO(5)\times U(1)_X$ symmetry, where $W'$ and $Z'$ represent Kaluza-Klein (KK) excited states of the electroweak gauge bosons. Utilizing experimental data from the Large Hadron Collider, constraints are established regarding the KK mass scale and the Aharonov-Bohm phase. Specifically, within a GUT-inspired GHU model, the KK mass scale can be probed up to 18 TeV for an integrated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$ and up to 22 TeV for 3000 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=14$ TeV.

This study details the analysis of plasmonic metal-insulator-metal (MIM) waveguides by utilizing their complete modal structure. The methodology is valid across all frequencies, spanning the visible and near-infrared spectra, and accommodates various dimensions, including nanoscale metallic features. Specifically, we apply this framework to investigate waveguide junctions. We demonstrate that the full modal spectrum of MIM waveguides—which includes real and complex discrete eigenvalues alongside a continuous spectrum—constitutes a complete basis set. These modes are derived using techniques adapted from Sturm-Liouville and generalized eigenvalue problems. We establish that incorporating every component of the spectrum is essential for achieving a complete set of basis vectors when employing the mode-matching technique to describe scattering in MIM waveguides. Our numerical comparison between the mode-matching formulation and finite-difference frequency-domain analysis reveals excellent agreement regarding modal scattering at symmetric MIM junctions. Additionally, we highlight mathematical parallels between the underlying structure of MIM waveguides and PT-symmetric quantum mechanical pseudo-Hermitian Hamiltonians. The diverse array of modes supported by MIM waveguides serves as a canonical benchmark for comparing more complex geometries. While our work includes results from the microwave regime, it also extends to waveguides involving real metals at infrared and optical frequencies.

Recent advancements in the precision of Lattice QCD calculations for key quantities in flavour physics have necessitated the incorporation of isospin-breaking effects, specifically electromagnetic corrections. These corrections are essential for maximizing the utility of this enhanced precision in determining fundamental Standard Model parameters, such as CKM matrix elements, and in identifying experimental deviations that could indicate new physics. In collaboration with colleagues from Rome, we have established and implemented a framework to include isospin-breaking corrections in leptonic decays $P\to\ell\bar\nu_\ell(\gamma)$, where $P$ denotes a pseudoscalar meson and $\ell$ a charged lepton. The following sections review both the theoretical framework and numerical results. Additionally, we present the current status of our efforts to extend this framework to semileptonic decays $P_1\to P_2\ell\bar\nu_\ell(\gamma)$, where $P_{1,2}$ represent pseudoscalar mesons.

This study presents the inaugural direct examination of how the perceived credibility of an auction format influences bidding strategies and final results. Through a series of laboratory experiments, we assigned a human subject to the role of seller, who retained the auction revenue and, contingent on the experimental treatment, possessed the authority to manipulate the outcome. Our findings indicate that in the non-credible version of the second-price auction, the vast majority of bids fall between the theoretical predictions of the first-price and credible second-price auctions. Although sellers in this non-credible setting frequently violate auction rules to overcharge the winner, they generally fail to maximize revenue. We attribute these outcomes to behavioral factors: bidders hold incorrect beliefs, while sellers exhibit an aversion to breaking rules, a hypothesis supported by revealed preference tests.

Minimum-phase finite impulse response (FIR) filters are extensively utilized in practice, prompting significant research into their design. Nevertheless, a notable discrepancy exists between current best practices and established theoretical principles, particularly regarding Chebyshev filters. This paper demonstrates that such a mismatch can be elucidated by analyzing the time-domain factorization of an appropriate extended matrix. This analysis indicates that the definition of a factorable linear phase filter requires revision. Furthermore, time-domain factorization analysis suggests initial values that facilitate rapid and precise convergence in iterative design algorithms for minimum-phase FIR filters. Numerical results confirm that adhering to these well-established theoretical principles significantly enhances filter tap accuracy.

This paper establishes that the well-established linear inequality technique for rational Chebyshev approximation is fundamentally equivalent to applying the bisection method within quasiconvex optimization. While this connection may not be unexpected, it effectively bridges rational and generalized rational Chebyshev approximation with contemporary advances in quasiconvex function theory, thereby providing enhanced theoretical and computational resources for solving these problems. Specifically, this insight enables a direct extension of the linear inequality method to generalized rational approximation as defined by Loeb (the ratio of two linear forms). A second major contribution involves expanding the linear inequality method to a wider range of Chebyshev approximation problems where the objective functions retain quasiconvexity. In this expanded class, inequalities need not be linear; it suffices that each inequality defines a convex set, shifting the computational focus to solving the associated convex feasibility problems. Consequently, we propose a more systematic and general framework for addressing Chebyshev approximation, specifically targeting problems where the approximations are quasilinear with respect to their parameters, which serve as the decision variables in the optimization.

A critical step in deciphering the mechanistic foundations of the central dogma involves quantitatively characterizing the dynamics of nucleic-acid-bound molecular motors within living cells, where a crowded cytoplasm and competing processes can significantly influence their speed and reliability. To capture these dynamics, we introduce a novel method called lag-time analysis for measuring *in vivo* behavior. This approach utilizes exponential growth as a timing mechanism to resolve dynamics in asynchronous cultures, thereby avoiding the challenges and artifacts linked to synchronization or fluorescent labeling. While lag-time analysis is broadly applicable to quantitative *in vivo* dynamics, we concentrate on a key application: characterizing replication dynamics. To validate this method, we analyzed replication in three distinct species and various mutants. We present the first quantitative, locus-specific measurements of fork velocity in kilobases per second and replisome-pause durations, with some precision reaching the level of seconds. Our data reveal that fork velocity varies by locus and time, even in wild-type cells. Beyond characterizing known phenomena, we identify brief, locus-specific pauses at rDNA in wild-type cells for the first time and observe temporal oscillations in fork velocity across three highly divergent bacterial species. In addition to offering new insights into replication as demonstrated here, lag-time analysis holds significant potential to provide quantitative understanding of other vital cellular processes.

Recent discoveries have highlighted striking parallels between many Type IIn supernovae and the enigmatic SN 2009ip, the nature of which remains debated. This study examines ten years of data on SN 2011fh, an interacting transient spectroscopically and photometrically akin to SN 2009ip. SN 2011fh exhibited an initial brightening event with a peak magnitude of $M_r \sim -16$, followed by a more luminous outburst reaching $M_r \sim -18$ in August 2011. Throughout its evolution, its spectra were characterized by narrow to intermediate Balmer emission lines and P Cygni profiles, signaling fast-moving material at approximately $6400 \ \textrm{km s}^{-1}$. HST/WFC3 observations from October 2016 detected a bright source with $M_{F814W} \approx -13.3$ mag, suggesting either continued ejecta-circumstellar material interaction or an eruptive phase occurring five years after the 2011 outburst. Photometry of the surrounding stellar cluster indicates a progenitor age of roughly 4.5 Myr; single-star evolution models estimate a mass of $\sim 60 \ \textrm{M}_\odot$, while binary system considerations allow for a mass range of $35 - 80 \ \textrm{M}_\odot$. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the progenitor exceeded the classical Eddington limit significantly in the months prior to the 2011 outburst, pointing to strong super-Eddington winds as a likely mass-loss mechanism. These results support a model of an energetic outburst originating from a young, massive star, potentially a luminous blue variable.

This study investigates the proper twice epi-differentiability of a specific class of non-amenable functions, defined as the composition of a piecewise twice differentiable (PWTD) function with a parabolically semidifferentiable mapping. These composite structures are prevalent in various optimization contexts, including major constrained and composite problems, disjunctive programs, and issues involving low-rank or sparsity. To accomplish this, we first establish the appropriate twice epi-differentiability, parabolic epi-differentiability, and regularity of PWTD functions, subsequently deriving upper and lower bounds for the second subderivatives of these composites via a chain rule for their parabolic subderivatives. Utilizing these bounds, we characterize parabolic regularity and second subderivatives to demonstrate proper twice epi-differentiability for several popular function classes, such as compositions of PWTD outer functions with twice differentiable inner mappings, regularized functions promoting group sparsity, and indicator functions of the $q$-order cone where $q > 1$.

Recent research has empirically explored various techniques for training stochastic neural networks on classification tasks by optimizing a PAC-Bayesian bound through stochastic gradient descent. However, most of these approaches require substituting the misclassification error with a surrogate loss, creating a discrepancy between the optimization goal and the true generalization bound. This paper introduces a new training algorithm that optimizes the PAC-Bayesian bound directly without depending on any surrogate loss. Empirical findings demonstrate that this method surpasses existing PAC-Bayesian training techniques.

This article demonstrates that for any commutative ring $C$ with unity, every Jordan derivation defined on the upper triangular matrix algebra $T_n(C)$ is an inner derivation. Furthermore, we generalize this finding to Jordan derivations on the full matrix algebra $M_n(C)$.

Training graph neural networks (GNNs) is notably time-consuming due to the difficulty hardware faces in accelerating sparse graph-based operations. While prior research has reduced time complexity by trading off computational precision through sampling-based approximation—successfully speeding up dense matrix operations like convolution and linear layers with minimal accuracy loss—sparse matrices present distinct hurdles. Unlike dense matrices, sparse matrices utilize irregular data formats where rows and columns vary in non-zero entry counts, creating two unique challenges: first, the inability to directly control the efficiency of approximated sparse operations since computation only occurs on non-zero entries; and second, the inefficiency of sub-sampling sparse matrices caused by their irregular structure. To overcome these issues, we introduce a strategy to balance accuracy and efficiency by optimizing resource allocation across layers and epochs. Specifically, we tailor computation resources to various sparse operations while constraining total usage within a defined budget to address the first challenge. For the second, we mitigate epoch-wise sampling overhead by caching previously sampled sparse matrices. Additionally, we propose a switching mechanism to enhance the generalization of GNNs trained with approximated operations. This approach, termed Randomized Sparse Computation (RSC), is the first to demonstrate the viability of training GNNs using approximate operations. Practically, RSC achieves up to an $11.6\times$ speedup for individual sparse operations and a $1.6\times$ reduction in end-to-end wall-clock time, all with negligible accuracy degradation.

An analytical formula has been established to determine the lower bound of the average population ($\overset{\_\_}{\rho _{0}}$) of $\mu =0$ hyperfine components in the ground state of spin-1 condensates subjected to a magnetic field, with the derivation rigorously maintaining total magnetization $M$ conservation. Numerical examples demonstrate the utility of this expression, revealing that within a broad range of parameters outlined in the study, the lower bound closely approximates the actual $\overset{\_\_}{\rho _{0}}$. Consequently, in this domain, $\overset{\_\_}{\rho _{0}}$ can be accurately calculated directly using the derived analytical formula.

Although the current description of accelerated cosmology is moderately successful, the early evolution of the universe remains a significant challenge for humanity. Our proposed solution involves a novel class of symmetric teleparallel gravity known as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ mediates gravitational interactions, potentially addressing several unresolved issues. To investigate the universe's early stages, we assume an anisotropic locally rotationally symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I spacetime and derive the corresponding field equations. Our analysis of the energy density, equation of state, and skewness parameter reveals that the models exhibit anisotropic spatial geometry during the early universe, likely driven by an anisotropic fluid. However, as time progresses, inflation and the diminishing anisotropy of the fluid cause the universe to transition toward isotropy.

Rotating Rayleigh--Bénard convection serves as a widely used model for investigating the interaction between buoyancy-driven forces and Coriolis effects, a dynamic interplay crucial to numerous geophysical and astrophysical phenomena. These systems are characterized by extreme parameter values, specifically high Rayleigh numbers ($Ra$) indicating strong thermal forcing and low Ekman numbers ($E$), which scale inversely with rotation speed. Such conditions establish a dominant geostrophic balance where pressure gradients counteract Coriolis forces. However, the so-called geostrophic regime of rotating convection is challenging to probe via laboratory experiments or numerical simulations due to the simultaneous requirements of achieving large $Ra$ and small $E$. In this study, we employ stereoscopic particle image velocimetry to measure flow within a large-scale rotating convection apparatus, focusing on the horizontal plane at mid-height to explore the complex phenomenology of this regime. We determine horizontal length scales by analyzing spatial correlations of vertical velocity and vertical vorticity, successfully reproducing characteristics of convective Taylor columns and plumes typical of the geostrophic regime. Furthermore, we observe that at elevated Rayleigh numbers, the flow organizes into a quadrupolar vortex structure emerging from the plume state within this horizontal plane.

While the core principle of reinforcement learning (RL) involves agents striving to maximize the total cumulative reward, active inference—an evolving framework in cognitive and computational neuroscience—suggests that agents act to maximize evidence for a biased generative model. This study demonstrates how active inference concepts can enhance traditional RL methods by (i) naturally balancing exploration and exploitation and (ii) offering a more adaptable definition of reward. Drawing inspiration from active inference, we created and implemented a new decision-making objective called the free energy of the expected future. Our results show that this algorithm effectively manages the exploration-exploitation trade-off, delivering robust performance across various difficult RL benchmarks, including those characterized by sparse, well-shaped, or absent rewards.

Neural personalized recommendation systems are integral to diverse datacenter workloads such as search, social networking, and entertainment. Current state-of-the-art architectures rely on massive embedding tables containing billions of parameters, which demand substantial memory resources. While high-performance DRAM incurs significant infrastructure costs, conventional SSDs provide an order of magnitude more capacity at the expense of higher read latency and reduced bandwidth, thereby hindering inference speed. RecSSD addresses this by implementing a near-data processing SSD memory system specifically tailored for neural recommendation inference, achieving a 2X reduction in end-to-end latency compared to commercial-off-the-shelf SSDs across eight industry-standard models.

Over the last few decades, theoretical developments regarding scoring rules have expanded their application in probabilistic forecasting. Specifically, within meteorological forecasting, statistical postprocessing is crucial for enhancing predictions generated by deterministic physical models. Many leading statistical postprocessing methods rely on distributional regression evaluated using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). However, existing theoretical analyses of CRPS evaluation have been limited to unconditional frameworks (excluding covariates) and infinite sample sizes. This work extends those findings by examining the convergence rates of distributional regression methods with respect to the CRPS. We identify the optimal minimax convergence rate for specific distribution classes and demonstrate that both k-nearest neighbor and kernel methods achieve this optimal rate.

This article focuses on a project connecting Gopakumar-Vafa invariants with quantum K-invariants on Calabi-Yau threefolds, presenting findings in genus zero that include both recent and upcoming research.

We present the direct observation of a new modulated flux striped domain phase in a YBCO crystal with minimal twin defects. These domains originate from instabilities in the vortex structure occurring within a narrow range of tilted magnetic fields at small angles relative to the in-plane direction. By comparing experimental data with theoretically derived vortex phase diagrams, we conclude that these stripe domains arise from a first-order phase transition of the vortex structure. The dimensions of domains containing vortices of specific orientations are governed by the equilibrium between the energy of the vortex stray field and the positive energy of the domain boundaries. Our findings validate the existence of the kinked vortex chain phase in an anisotropic high-temperature superconductor and demonstrate a sharp transition in this phase's state, leading to the formation of regular vortex domains.
The paper investigates maximal estimates for Schrödinger means and the almost everywhere convergence of sequences comprising these means.

We examine both theoretically and experimentally the evaporation of liquid disks under natural convection driven by density gradients between the vapor and ambient gas. Drawing an analogy between thermal convection above a heated disk and our system, we establish scaling laws to characterize the evaporation rate. This local rate is influenced by the gas-phase boundary layer, resulting in a total evaporation rate composed of multiple scaling contributions that mirror the boundary layer's structure. Our theoretical predictions are validated against experiments conducted with water in a humidity-controlled environment.

Reactor neutrino experiments are essential for expanding our understanding of neutrinos. Accurate measurements of the reactor electron antineutrino flux and its spectral evolution serve as critical inputs for refining knowledge regarding neutrino mass and mixing, reactor nuclear physics, and the search for physics beyond the Standard Model. This study reports the evolution of flux and spectrum as a function of reactor isotopic composition, expressed through the inverse-beta-decay (IBD) yield at the Daya Bay experiment using 1958 days of data and reduced systematic uncertainties. The results are compared against two theoretical predictions: the Huber-Mueller model, which relies on the conversion method, and the SM2018 model, based on the summation method. The measured average flux and spectrum, along with their variation relative to the ²³⁹Pu fraction, contradict the Huber-Mueller model's predictions. Conversely, while the SM2018 model aligns with the average flux and its evolution, it fails to accurately describe the energy spectrum. Adjusting the predicted IBD spectrum for ²³⁹Pu does not enhance agreement with the data for either model. However, better consistency with the measurements can be achieved by either modifying the predicted spectrum from ²³⁵U or adjusting the predicted spectra for ²³⁵U, ²³⁸U, ²³⁹Pu, and ²⁴¹Pu simultaneously.

This paper demonstrates that the final quarter of the 20th century marks the golden age of mathematical finance. During this era, the collaboration between eminent economists and an exceptional generation of probabilists—many hailing from Paul André Meyer's Strasbourg School—laid the groundwork for the field. These scholars formulated the two fundamental theorems of arbitrage theory, derived closed-form solutions for options, and developed primary modeling frameworks.

This paper examines statistical decision-making in the context of dynamic treatment assignment, where interventions are allocated sequentially to individuals across multiple stages. In such policies, the impact of a treatment at any given stage often varies depending on prior treatments, historical outcomes, and observed covariates. The study focuses on estimating an optimal dynamic treatment rule that determines the best intervention for each individual based on their unique history. An empirical welfare maximization framework is proposed to estimate this rule using panel data from experimental or quasi-experimental settings. Two distinct estimation strategies are introduced: one utilizes backward induction to solve the assignment problem stage-by-stage, while the other addresses the entire dynamic assignment problem simultaneously across all stages. The authors derive finite-sample upper bounds for the worst-case average welfare regret associated with these methods and demonstrate $n^{-1/2}$-minimax convergence rates. Furthermore, the simultaneous estimation approach is adapted to accommodate intertemporal budget or capacity constraints.

Sound-soft fractal screens possess the ability to scatter acoustic waves despite having zero surface measure. To address these scattering challenges, we present what seems to be the inaugural application of the boundary element method (BEM) where every basis function is defined over a fractal set. Unlike traditional approaches, the matrix integration within this BEM framework relies on a non-integer order Hausdorff measure instead of the standard Lebesgue surface measure. Leveraging recent advancements in function spaces on fractals, we establish the convergence of the Galerkin formulation for this "Hausdorff BEM" in acoustic scattering within $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ ($n=1,2$), provided the scatterer—a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^n\times\{0\}$—is a $d$-set with Hausdorff dimension $d \in (n-1,n]$. For fractals arising as attractors of iterated function systems, we demonstrate convergence rates and superconvergence for smooth antilinear functionals, contingent upon natural regularity conditions of the solution to the underlying boundary integral equation. Furthermore, we introduce numerical quadrature routines for implementing the Hausdorff BEM, accompanied by a fully discrete convergence analysis that utilizes numerical integration estimates and inverse inequalities on fractals to bound discrete condition numbers. Finally, numerical experiments validate the sharpness of our theoretical findings and solution regularity assumptions, including specific cases of scattering in $\mathbb{R}^2$ by Cantor sets and in $\mathbb{R}^3$ by Cantor dusts.

This study investigates the joint allocation of wireless and computing resources within mobile edge computing (MEC) frameworks featuring multiple access points, where users may simultaneously connect to several points and leverage the processing power of multiple servers. The objective is to minimize total transmission energy subject to response time limits, a problem proven to be non-convex. Following an analysis of the computational complexity regarding specific system parameters, an Iterative Resource Allocation algorithm is introduced, which converges to a local optimum. The efficacy of this joint allocation strategy is assessed by benchmarking it against lower and upper bounds derived from less and more flexible multi-cell MEC architectures. Findings indicate that allowing free selection of the access point is essential for achieving optimal system performance.

We report 168 arcmin² spectral images of the Sgr B2 complex acquired using Herschel/SPIRE-FTS, revealing widespread emission from CO (up to the J=12-11 transition), H₂O, [CI] at 492 and 809 GHz, and [NII] at 205 μm. Additionally, we provide maps of SiO, N₂H⁺, HCN, and HCO⁺ derived from IRAM30m observations. The surrounding cloud environment accounts for the majority of the luminosity in the far-infrared (80%), H₂O 752 GHz (60%), mid-J CO (91%), and [CI] (93%) bands. Notably, the region exhibits highly extended [NII] emission, which spatially aligns with 24 and 70 μm dust emission. These FIR luminosities suggest a radiation field strength of G₀ ~ 10³. The extended [CI] emission originates from a pervasive neutral gas component with a density of n_H ~ 10³ cm⁻³. Elevated cosmic-ray (CR) fluxes drive high ionization rates, heating the gas to Tk ~ 40-60 K. Conversely, mid-J CO emission arises from a similarly extended but more pressurized gas component (P_th ~ 10⁷ K cm⁻³). Specific areas characterized by enhanced SiO emission and high CO-to-FIR intensity ratios (>10⁻³) display mid-J CO profiles consistent with shock models. A key distinction from quiescent star-forming clouds in the Galactic disk is the extended distribution of SiO and N₂H⁺ in Sgr B2. This is attributed to cloud-scale shocks caused by cloud-cloud collisions and stellar feedback, as well as significantly higher CR ionization rates (>10⁻¹⁵ s⁻¹) that produce excess H₃⁺ and N₂H⁺. Consequently, Sgr B2 represents a more extreme environment than typical star-forming regions in the Galaxy. When used as a template for extragalactic comparisons, Sgr B2 resembles ultra-luminous infrared galaxies like Arp 220 more than pure starburst galaxies such as M82, particularly regarding a "deficit" in [CI]/FIR and [NII]/FIR intensity ratios. However, the extended cloud environment, rather than the dense cores, serves as the more appropriate template for galaxies where telescopes cannot resolve such large-scale structures.

Can neural networks acquire goal-directed behaviors through brain-like strategies that integrate current organism states with the outcomes of future actions? Recent studies indicate that recurrent neural networks trained on goal-oriented tasks can develop representations similar to those in the brain's entorhinal cortex, such as grid cells. This study investigates the evolution of internal dynamics within these networks and compares them to experimental data. We find that when a recurrent network learns environmental structure purely through sensory prediction, an attractor-based landscape emerges in its representation, mirroring the structure and function of hippocampal place cells. Furthermore, we extend the predictive objective to include Q-learning for reward-based tasks where actions depend on delayed cues. Similar to rodent hippocampus recordings during identical tasks, this training paradigm induces nonlocal neural activity to sweep forward in space at decision points, anticipating the path to a reward. Additionally, choice and cue-selective neurons emerge within the network, further aligning with experimental observations. Collectively, these findings suggest that integrating unsupervised predictive learning of environmental structure with reinforcement learning facilitates the formation of hippocampus-like representations that encompass both spatial and task-relevant information.

The growing popularity of microblogging platforms, such as Twitter, has spurred increased adoption of content annotation techniques like hashtags. These tags serve as a mechanism for users to organize, categorize, and enhance the visibility of their posts. Although the concept is straightforward, practical implementation often proves difficult, resulting in sporadic usage. This paper explores various methods for recommending hashtags as new posts are drafted to promote broader adoption. However, hashtag recommendation faces significant hurdles, including handling massive streams of noisy, short-text data. We will examine preprocessing techniques to mitigate data noise and identify an effective recommendation approach grounded in popular classification algorithms.

Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides host tightly bound bright excitons at degenerate valleys, where strong Coulomb exchange interactions couple the valley pseudospin to the exciton's momentum. When positioned on a periodically structured dielectric substrate, spatial variations in the Coulomb interaction generate exciton Bloch states, creating a real-space valley pseudospin texture within a mesoscopic supercell. Our findings reveal that this spatial valley texture in the exciton Bloch function is locked to the propagation direction, facilitating the nano-optical excitation of directional exciton flow via valley selection rules. The lateral directionality of the injected exciton current is governed by the excitation's circular polarization, whereas the angular directionality is determined by the excitation location, forming a vortex pattern across the supercell. This phenomenon mirrors chiral light-matter interactions in nano-photonics, with the guided electromagnetic wave substituted by a valley-orbit coupled exciton Bloch wave in a uniform monolayer, suggesting new excitonic devices capable of non-reciprocal functionalities.

Singlet exciton fission involves the spin-allowed creation of two triplet electronic excited states from a single singlet state. While intramolecular singlet fission has been hypothesized to occur in individual carotenoid molecules within protein complexes—specifically when the conjugated backbone adopts an out-of-plane twist—this hypothesis has only been proposed for systems containing multiple carotenoids and bacteriochlorophylls in close proximity. To test this hypothesis using a 'minimal' one-carotenoid system with twisted carotenoids, we investigated the orange carotenoid protein (OCP). OCP exists in two distinct conformations: the orange form (OCPo), where the bound carotenoid is twisted, and the red form (OCPr), where it is planar. To facilitate room-temperature spectroscopy of canthaxanthin-bound OCPo and OCPr without inducing photoconversion via lasers, we trapped the samples in trehalose glass. Through transient absorption spectroscopy, we found no evidence of long-lived triplet generation via intramolecular singlet fission, even though the canthaxanthin molecule in OCPo exhibits a twisted configuration.

We introduce a novel and practical framework for perceiving traffic scenes using roadside cameras, designed to support infrastructure-assisted autonomous driving through a complete perception pipeline. This pipeline encompasses object detection, localization, tracking, and multi-camera information fusion. Distinguishing itself from prior vision-based systems that depend on depth offsets or 3D annotations during training, our approach utilizes a modular decoupling architecture and a landmark-based 3D localization technique. This design effectively separates detection from localization, enabling models to be trained efficiently using solely 2D annotations. The framework is compatible with both optical and thermal cameras, regardless of whether they employ pinhole or fish-eye lenses. Deployed at a two-lane roundabout on Ellsworth Rd. and State St. in Ann Arbor, MI, USA, the system delivers round-the-clock, real-time traffic flow monitoring and high-precision vehicle trajectory extraction. Furthermore, the entire system operates efficiently on a low-power edge computing device, achieving an end-to-end latency of under 20ms.

Cell membranes feature proteins and lipids arranged into nanodomains of diverse sizes, shapes, and compositions that execute specific roles. Although biologically critical, the precise morphology of these domains remains elusive. Their minute scale renders them difficult to detect via conventional microscopy, and currently, no unified theoretical framework exists to describe their structuring and geometry. In this study, we combine analytical calculations with Monte Carlo simulations—grounded in a model linking membrane composition to shape—to demonstrate that higher protein concentrations induce the elongation of membrane nanodomains. These findings are validated by Single Particle Tracking experiments on HIV receptors within engineered living cells, where receptor expression levels were precisely controlled. These results underscore that protein abundance can regulate nanodomain shape and, consequently, their biological activity. Furthermore, this meso-patterning mechanism holds broader relevance for various soft-matter systems, as it depends on fundamental physical principles.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies with measured total luminosities for the two fine-structure transitions of neutral atomic carbon ($^{3}P_1 \rightarrow ^{3}P_{0}$ and $^{3}P_2 \rightarrow ^{3}P_{1}$), determining that their average excitation conditions are strongly subthermal. This conclusion was drawn from modeling the CI(2-1)/(1-0) ratios ($R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$) using exact solutions for a 3-level system, without relying on specific assumptions regarding the kinematic state of the associated $\rm H_2$ gas or its line formation mechanism. This non-LTE excitation likely explains the recent findings by Valentino et al. (2020) regarding a curious clustering of gas temperatures near $\sim$25 K when derived under LTE assumptions—a clustering that shows no correlation with actual gas temperatures. Consequently, non-LTE excitation in the interstellar medium complicates simple estimates of molecular gas temperatures and introduces uncertainty into CI-based mass calculations, particularly when utilizing the J=2-1 line. Nevertheless, the $R^{(ci)}_{21/10} = \rm F(n, T_{k})$ ratio offers significant value for combined CO/CI spectral energy distribution (SLED) and dust spectral energy distribution (SED) models, remaining independent of assumptions inherent in CO radiative transfer models, such as the LVG approximation. Finally, we hypothesize that the coexistence of low $R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$ ratios ($\leq 1$) and high dust temperatures ($\rm T_{dust}$) in certain extreme starbursts signals the presence of massive, low-density molecular winds and/or circumgalactic gas reservoirs. If confirmed through imaging observations, this metric could serve as a useful indicator for identifying such reservoirs in galaxies.

Let $I$ and $J$ be square-free monomial ideals in a polynomial algebra over a field, where the generators have degrees at least 1 and 2, respectively, and assume $I$ strictly contains $J$. In most cases where $I$ consists of exactly one variable alongside other generators of degree at least 2, the Stanley Conjecture is valid: if the Stanley depth of the quotient $I/J$ does not exceed 2, then the usual depth of $I/J$ also does not exceed 2.

It is widely acknowledged that determining the existence of a strongly polynomial-time simplex algorithm for linear programs (LPs) remains the most difficult open problem in optimization and discrete geometry. This paper provides an affirmative solution to this question by employing the parameter analysis method we previously introduced (arXiv:2006.08104). We demonstrate that a simplex algorithm exists where the count of pivoting steps is bounded by the number of variables in the LP problem.

Point clouds and RGB images serve as two primary perceptional inputs for autonomous driving; while point clouds offer precise object localization, RGB images provide denser and more semantically rich data. Although AutoAlign recently introduced a learnable approach to fuse these modalities for 3D object detection, it incurs high computational costs due to global-wise attention mechanisms. To address this, we propose the Cross-Domain DeformCAFA module, which utilizes sparse learnable sampling points for cross-modal relational modeling. This design enhances robustness against calibration errors and significantly accelerates feature aggregation across modalities. Additionally, to mitigate the challenges of complex ground-truth augmentation in multi-modal settings, we introduce a simple yet effective cross-modal augmentation strategy based on convex combinations of image patches guided by depth information. Furthermore, our novel image-level dropout training scheme enables dynamic inference. Consequently, we present AutoAlignV2, a faster and more powerful multi-modal 3D detection framework built upon AutoAlign. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes benchmark validate its effectiveness and efficiency. Notably, our best model achieves a 72.4 NDS score on the nuScenes test leaderboard, establishing a new state-of-the-art among all published multi-modal 3D object detectors. The code is available at https://github.com/zehuichen123/AutoAlignV2.

We examine surveys of molecular cloud structures utilizing tracers that span from CO $J = 1-0$ and $^{13}$CO $J = 1-0$ to dust emission and NH$_3$ observations. Both the mean virial parameter and the proportion of mass contained within bound structures vary depending on the structural identification method. Generally, as the effective density, surface density, mass, and galactic distance of the structures increase, the virial parameter decreases while the fraction of bound mass rises. In the most comprehensive Galactic surveys based on CO $J = 1-0$, only 0.19 of the mass resides in bound structures, whereas surveys of other galaxies using CO $J = 2-1$ indicate a fraction of 0.35. These findings significantly mitigate the long-standing issue of slow star formation. When considering only clouds identified as bound and assuming they collapse in a free-fall time at their mean density, a complete survey of the Galaxy predicts a star formation rate of 46 solar masses per year; this is 6.5 times lower than the rate calculated if all clouds were assumed to be bound.

This study investigates the challenges associated with annotating transcribed spoken Dutch-Frisian code-switching utterances according to Universal Dependencies standards. Leveraging data from the FAME! corpus, which includes both audio and transcriptions, the research highlights unique difficulties beyond standard annotation tasks. These include the low-resource status of Frisian, the informal context of the data, code-switching phenomena, and irregular sentence segmentation. To begin, two annotators processed 150 randomly selected utterances across three rounds of 50 items each, with disagreements being discussed and resolved after every stage. This iterative process resulted in a performance gain of 7.8 points in UAS and 10.5 points in LAS between the initial and final rounds. The paper concentrates on the specific issues encountered during the annotation of this transcribed speech corpus and proposes several solutions to address them.

Driven by the potential for strain to tune graphene's electronic properties, we numerically investigate the semimetal-to-Mott insulator transition on a uniaxial honeycomb lattice using Determinant Quantum Monte Carlo. Since our simulations employ the half-filled repulsive Hubbard model, the sign problem is avoided. We characterize electronic transport through temperature-dependent DC conductivity. Results indicate that metallic behavior is suppressed under strain. Notably, finite-size scaling analysis reveals the emergence of a novel antiferromagnetic phase near $U\sim U_{c}$. Consequently, we construct a phase diagram reflecting the interplay between interactions and strain, which could broaden the applications of strain engineering in graphene.

The most efficient computation sequence within a computational graph can be modeled using algebraic expressions. While computational graphs and algebraic expressions share strong connections yet exhibit notable distinctions, this study examines their relationship and differences to clarify how they can be converted into one another. By identifying various multiplication relationships in algebraic expressions and their corresponding elimination dependencies within line-graphs, we derive a theoretical upper bound on the efficiency of face elimination.

We introduce a randomized Local Computation Algorithm (LCA) for the Maximal Independent Set (MIS) problem that achieves a query complexity of $poly(\Delta) \cdot \log n$. Specifically, the algorithm determines with high probability whether each node belongs to the resulting MIS by performing $poly(\Delta) \cdot \log n$ queries to the graph's adjacency lists. These computations can be executed simultaneously and independently for various nodes, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum degree and $n$ the total number of nodes. This approach addresses a significant open issue in the fields of local computations and sublinear algorithms, a challenge originally attributed to Rubinfeld.

Quasiparticle poisoning—the erratic generation and annihilation of quasiparticles—frequently impairs the operation of superconducting devices. This study presents electrostatic manipulation of such poisoning through single-electron tunneling across a static barrier into a Coulomb island within an InAs/Al hybrid nanowire. Utilizing high-bandwidth charge sensing, we tracked the island's charge occupancy during Coulomb blockade peaks, where tunneling rates peak, and valleys, where they vanish. We observed that adjusting electrostatic gates altered on-peak tunneling rates by two orders of magnitude, even with a constant normal-state barrier resistance; this phenomenon is linked to the gate-dependent modulation of the induced superconducting gap's magnitude and softness on the island, a finding supported by independent density-of-states measurements. Additionally, the study examines how tunneling rates vary with temperature and magnetic fields.

We address the challenge of determining an $N$-point arrangement on the sphere $S^d\subset \RR^{d+1}$ that minimizes the absolute maximum value of its total potential across $S^d$. The potential generated by a point ${\bf y}$ within a configuration at a point ${\bf x}\in S^d$ is defined as $f\(\left|{\bf x}-{\bf y}\right|^2\)$, where $f$ is continuous on $[0,4]$ and completely monotone on $(0,4]$, with $\left|{\bf x}-{\bf y}\right|$ representing the Euclidean distance between ${\bf x}$ and ${\bf y}$. We demonstrate that any sharp point configuration $\OL\omega_N$ on $S^d$, provided it is either antipodal or constitutes a spherical design of even strength, solves this optimization problem. Furthermore, we establish that for any such configuration $\OL\omega_N$, the absolute maximum of its potential over $S^d$ occurs at points belonging to $\OL\omega_N$ itself.

We extend the derivation of the Wallis formula for $\pi$ by employing a variational approach to calculate the spectrum of the Hydrogen atom. This method yields infinite product representations for specific combinations of gamma functions, encompassing irrational values like $\sqrt{2}$ and various nested radicals. Additionally, we establish Euler's reflection formula for the reciprocals of positive even integers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Bohr's correspondence principle enables the derivation of these product formulas and the reflection formula independently of the limit definition of the gamma function.

Intuitively sound arguments involving intensionality often elude first-order logic, even when augmented with modal and epistemic operators. Previous efforts to adequately address intensionality within logic and language have been plagued by both philosophical and technical challenges. Bealer's approach to this issue relies on an ontological commitment to a Theory of Properties, Propositions, and Relations (PRP). At its foundation, the PRP theory distinguishes between two conceptions: an objective one linked to modality and necessary equivalence, and a mental (intentional) one connected to concepts and the demand for non-circular definitions. Drawing on the work of Russell, Church, and Quine, Bealer introduces two distinct intensional logics, T1 and T2, which correspond to these respective conceptions. Both logics extend first-order language with an intensional abstraction operator. In T1, necessitation can be defined, and its axioms entail S5 modal logic. These logics possess unique features and desirable attributes that differentiate them from higher-order approaches. Bealer develops a non-Tarskian algebraic semantic framework, separate from possible worlds semantics and its associated ontological commitments, providing two classes of models for which both T1 and T2 are sound and complete. Additional strengths include the ability to handle quantifying-in and various substitution puzzles, the absence of artificial type restrictions, adherence to a Russellian semantics, and satisfaction of Davidson's learnability requirement. Bealer presents his logic as the foundation for a broader philosophical project rooted in logicism, as detailed in his book *Quality and Concept* (1982). This paper serves as an elementary introduction to Bealer's theory.

The transport capacity of a communication network is defined by the shift from free-flow to congestion. This study introduces a dynamic routing strategy for complex networks utilizing hierarchical bypass selection. Reinforcement learning agents, positioned at nodes with high betweenness centrality, execute routing decisions. Because their bypass options are degenerate, the learning processes of these agents remain independent. However, through interactions driven by underlying traffic dynamics, the agents cooperate spontaneously, generating coherent actions. Consequently, even a small number of agents significantly enhances transport capacity, as demonstrated in real-world Internet networks at both the router and autonomous system levels. Furthermore, this strategy proves resilient against link removals.

We examine a system of equations in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ($d\geq2$) describing the evolution of isothermal, viscous, compressible fluids of Korteweg type, which serves as a model for phase transitions. When the sound speed is zero ($P'(\rho^{\ast})=0$), the linearized system exhibits a \textit{purely} parabolic structure, allowing us to prove the global-in-time existence and Gevrey analyticity of strong solutions within hybrid Besov spaces of $L^p$-type. Specifically, if the full viscosity coefficient and capillary coefficient satisfy $\bar{\nu}^2\geq4\bar{\kappa}$, acoustic waves are absent in these compressible fluids. Under this condition, the existing $L^2$ bounds on the low-frequency components of density and velocity can be extended to the general $L^p$ case for $1\leq p\leq d$ when $d\geq2$. The proof primarily depends on novel nonlinear Besov (-Gevrey) estimates regarding the product and composition of functions.

Multilingual sequence-to-sequence pretrained language models (Seq2Seq PLMs), such as mBART, typically undergo self-supervised pretraining on a broad spectrum of monolingual corpora (e.g., 25 languages from CommonCrawl), whereas downstream cross-lingual tasks usually rely on a narrower bilingual subset (e.g., English-German). This creates a mismatch in both domain and cross-lingual learning objectives between the pretraining and fine-tuning phases. To address these gaps, we augment the standard pretrain-finetune framework with an additional code-switching restoration task. In the first stage, this self-supervised task serves as a pretext to help the models acquire in-domain alignment knowledge. The second stage involves standard fine-tuning on downstream datasets. Experimental results across Natural Language Generation (12 bilingual translation tasks, 30 zero-shot translation tasks, and 2 cross-lingual summarization tasks) and Natural Language Understanding (7 cross-lingual natural language inference tasks) demonstrate that our model consistently outperforms the strong baseline mBART using standard fine-tuning. Analyses reveal that this approach reduces the Euclidean distance between cross-lingual sentence representations and enhances model generalization with minimal computational overhead. The code is available at: https://github.com/zanchangtong/CSR4mBART.

The electrocardiogram (ECG) stands as a ubiquitous diagnostic instrument in healthcare, essential for identifying cardiovascular conditions. Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective approach for detecting abnormalities within ECG signals.
