We introduce two novel heuristic stopping rules, Quant and QuantCI, which leverage model-based estimation techniques derived from survey research. When compared against a spectrum of existing heuristics, our proposed methods demonstrate superior accuracy in meeting varied recall targets while significantly lowering review costs.

Cosmic rays, consisting of protons and other atomic nuclei, are thought to reach petaelectronvolt (PeV) energies and higher within our Galaxy at astrophysical accelerators known as 'PeVatrons.' A defining trait of such PeVatrons is expected to be a hard gamma-ray spectrum extending past 100 teraelectronvolts (TeV) without a cutoff; however, no currently identified source displays this spectrum, likely due to low maximum acceleration energies or insufficient detector sensitivity near 100 TeV. This study reports the detection of gamma-ray emission from the supernova remnant G106.3+2.7 exceeding 10 TeV. The findings provide flux measurements up to and beyond 100 TeV and suggest that the very-high-energy gamma-ray emission above 10 TeV is strongly correlated with a nearby molecular cloud rather than the pulsar PSR J2229+6114. Concerning the emission mechanism in G106.3+2.7, this spatial correlation supports a hadronic origin driven by neutral pion ($\pi^0$) decay from accelerated relativistic protons, as opposed to a leptonic origin involving inverse-Compton scattering by relativistic electrons. Additionally, the authors note that establishing an X-ray flux upper limit on the synchrotron spectrum would offer crucial data to definitively confirm the hadronic acceleration scenario at this source.

Mutation serves as a vital mechanism for evolution to navigate protein functional landscapes. Although we can experimentally induce mutations at will, connecting specific sequence changes to system-wide responses remains challenging. This study introduces a framework based on measuring system free energy changes to associate individual mutations in an allosteric transcriptional repressor with the parameters controlling its response. We observe that the energetic impacts of these mutations fall into distinct categories, each exhibiting characteristic curves relative to inducer concentration. Using the well-defined *E. coli* LacI repressor, we experimentally validated these diagnostic predictions by examining mutations within both the DNA binding and inducer binding domains. Our results indicate that the gene expression shifts caused by point mutations can be modeled by adjusting only a specific subset of parameters describing the affected domain of the wild-type protein. These parameters appear functionally insulated: mutations in the DNA binding domain affect solely DNA affinity, while those in the inducer binding domain alter only allosteric parameters. Modifying these subsets tunes the system's free energy in alignment with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that induction profiles and free energies for pairwise double mutants can be quantitatively predicted based on data from single mutants, offering a method to identify and measure epistatic interactions.

We describe a spin filtration mechanism within an antiferromagnetic helix system, which inherently possesses zero net magnetization. While conventional understanding dictates that such systems cannot generate spin-polarized currents from unpolarized electron beams, applying an electric field perpendicular to the helix axis induces a significant energy separation between up and down spin channels, resulting in high spin polarization. To the best of our knowledge, this specific approach has not been previously documented. Using a tight-binding model to represent the antiferromagnetic helix, we calculate spin filtration efficiency by evaluating spin-selective currents via the Landauer-Büttiker formalism. Our analysis highlights the critical influence of geometrical configuration on spin channel separation, specifically investigating the impacts of both short-range and long-range electron hoppings under an applied electric field. We observe that filtration performance enhances as the electron hopping range increases. Furthermore, the phase of spin polarization can be selectively tuned by adjusting the electric field's strength and direction, as well as by modifying the physical parameters defining the antiferromagnetic helix. Finally, we examine the role of dephasing to enhance the system's realism and ensure the study is self-contained. Our findings suggest a novel pathway for achieving conformation-dependent spin polarization through extended electron hopping, a concept that may be extended to various other intriguing antiferromagnetic systems.

We introduce Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF), an object-centric neural scene representation that separates a scene into distinct objects ("things") and background ("stuff"). Each object is defined by an oriented 3D bounding box and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that accepts position, orientation, and time as inputs to generate density and radiance. The background is modeled by a comparable MLP that also produces semantic labels. Because these object-specific MLPs are instance-based, they are more compact and efficient than prior object-aware methods, yet they still benefit from category-specific priors through meta-learned initialization. Our framework constructs a panoptic radiance field for any scene using only color images. We employ standard algorithms to estimate camera poses, track objects, and generate 2D semantic segmentations. Subsequently, we jointly optimize the MLP parameters and bounding box coordinates using analysis-by-synthesis, leveraging self-supervision from color data and pseudo-supervision from the predicted segmentations. Experiments on real-world dynamic scenes demonstrate that our model effectively supports various applications, including novel view synthesis, 2D panoptic segmentation, 3D scene editing, and multi-view depth prediction.

For an essentially small hereditary abelian category $\mathcal{A}$, we introduce a novel algebra $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta}(\mathcal{A})$, termed the $\Delta$-Hall algebra of $\mathcal{A}$. The foundation of this algebra consists of the isomorphism classes of objects within $\mathcal{A}$, while the $\Delta$-Hall numbers enumerate specific three-cycles of exact sequences in the category. We demonstrate that the $\Delta$-Hall algebra $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta}(\mathcal{A})$ is isomorphic to the 1-periodic derived Hall algebra of $\mathcal{A}$. Through appropriate extensions and twisting operations, one can derive the $\imath$Hall algebra and the semi-derived Hall algebra associated with $\mathcal{A}$. When applied to the nilpotent representation category $\mathcal{A}={\rm rep^{nil}}(\mathbf{k} Q)$ for an arbitrary quiver $Q$ devoid of loops, the $\Delta$-Hall algebra (respectively, its extended variant) yields a new realization of the $\imath$quantum group (respectively, the universal $\imath$quantum group) linked to $Q$.

This research investigates a k-wise independent relaxation of the standard G(N,p) random graph model. In this framework, N labeled vertices remain fixed, and each edge is selected with probability p, but the constraint is relaxed so that only any subset of k edges must be independent. This approach is valuable for modeling scenarios where only k-wise independence is valid or when dealing with massive graphs where generating standard G(N,p) instances is computationally infeasible, necessitating the use of more efficient, random-like distributions. However, since many established G(N,p) properties are global in nature, it remains uncertain whether they persist under k-wise independence. We examine these properties by determining the necessary upper and lower bounds on k to preserve key characteristics of G(N,p) graphs, including connectivity, Hamiltonicity, connectivity-number, clique-number, chromatic-number, and the emergence of fixed subgraphs. Our findings indicate that for a broad range of p values, these properties are maintained either by a constant k or by k = poly(log(N)). This implies that graphs with N vertices exhibiting random-like behavior can be generated using a seed of size poly(log(N)). The proofs integrate combinatorial, probabilistic, and spectral methodologies.

The $n$-simplex equation ($n$-SE), originally proposed by A. B. Zamolodchikov as a generalization of the Yang--Baxter equation (which corresponds to the $2$-simplex case), is the focus of this paper. We propose several methods for constructing $n$-SE solutions, categorize various solution types, and define an operation that, under specific conditions, generates a solution for the $(n+m+k)$-SE from solutions of the $(n+k)$-SE and $(m+k)$-SE. Additionally, we examine the tropicalization of rational solutions and outline a pathway to extend this concept. We demonstrate that if a group $G$ is an extension of $H$ by $K$, solutions of the $n$-SE on $G$ can be derived from solutions on $H$ and $K$, and we identify solutions of the parametric Yang-Baxter equation on $H$ with parameters in $K$. Furthermore, to investigate $3$-simplex equations, we introduce algebraic systems featuring ternary operations and provide examples that yield $3$-SE solutions, ultimately determining all elementary verbal solutions of the $3$-SE on free groups.

The correspondence between Renyi holographic dark energy (RHDE) is examined within the framework of higher-dimensional Kaluza-Klein (KK) cosmology, analyzing both interacting and non-interacting scenarios. Results indicate that the non-interacting model inherently accounts for the late-time acceleration of the universe, a feature that standard four-dimensional Holographic Dark Energy models lack without invoking interactions. While the interacting model also yields late-time acceleration, it fails to match the observed present-day value of the deceleration parameter. The study evaluates the evolution of key cosmological parameters and applies two diagnostic tools—the state-finder and $Om$ diagnostics—to the non-interacting model, which is currently favored by recent observational data. Additionally, the classical stability of these cosmological models is discussed.

Lenstra defined the concept of a Euclidean ideal class, and we establish its existence within abelian quartic fields. As a direct consequence, we demonstrate that every biquadratic field possessing a class number of two contains a Euclidean ideal class. Furthermore, we show that Euclidean ideal classes exist in specific cubic and quadratic extensions.

The backbending phenomenon in $^{48}$Cr has been studied using the newly developed Projected Configuration Interaction (PCI) method, which directly links deformed intrinsic states to shell model (SM) wavefunctions. Two prior explanations—(i) $K=0$ band crossing and (ii) $K=2$ band crossing—were re-examined with PCI, revealing that both can effectively replicate the observed experimental backbending. The PCI wavefunctions corresponding to the $K=0$ and $K=2$ band crossing scenarios exhibit significant overlap. Consequently, it is concluded that no unique intrinsic states are associated with the yrast states following backbending in $^{48}$Cr.

The "double descent" phenomenon characterizes model generalization across under- and over-parameterized regimes. Existing theoretical insights, largely grounded in linear and kernel regression with informal neural network analogues via the Neural Tangent Kernel, fail to fully capture the mechanisms driving double descent in finite-width neural networks, often neglecting critical factors like loss function selection. To address these gaps, we employ influence functions to formulate expressions for population loss and its lower bound under minimal assumptions regarding parametric model structure. Our derived bounds are closely tied to the Hessian spectrum at the optimum and demonstrate double descent behavior at the interpolation threshold. Furthermore, our analysis explores the impact of the loss function on this phenomenon, revealing significant properties of neural networks and their Hessian spectra near the interpolation limit.

We propose an iterative quantum protocol designed to tackle optimization problems characterized by glassy energy landscapes. This method relies on periodic cycling around the tricritical point of the many-body localization transition, guaranteeing that every iteration yields a non-negligible probability of locating a lower local energy minimum. A crucial component involves customizing the cycle parameters based on the currently achieved optimal state, referred to as the "reference" state, and resetting them upon discovering a deeper minimum. We demonstrate that, provided the location of the tricritical point is known, the algorithm can approach the absolute minimum with arbitrary precision within polynomial time.

High-resolution observations of edge-on proto-planetary disks, utilizing molecular species with varying critical densities and formation routes, provide a means to map the vertical chemical and physical architectures of these disks. Through an analysis of sub-arcsecond ALMA archival data for the edge-on Flying Saucer disk (2MASS J16281370-2431391), we characterize the vertical and radial distribution of CN emitting regions relative to those of $^{12}$CO and CS, and model the physical conditions driving CN emission. Our results show that the scale heights of the $^{12}$CO (2-1), CN (2-1), and CS J=5-4 emitting layers diminish above the midplane, indicating that these molecules trace strata of increasing density and decreasing temperature. Specifically, beyond 100 au from the central star, CN emission originates primarily from intermediate layers, whereas in the inner disk, it arises from regions closer to the midplane. Using RADEX non-LTE modeling of the three brightest CN hyperfine lines, we examined the physical conditions within CN-emitting zones, determining ranges for excitation temperature and column density. Near the midplane, where hydrogen densities ($n_{H_2}$) reach $\sim 10^7$ cm$^{-3}$ at low kinetic temperatures ($\sim 12$ K), CN is found to be thermalized; conversely, sub-thermal, non-LTE conditions prevail in higher (intermediate) disk layers. Finally, we explore how the specific spatial location and excitation environment of CN emission in the Flying Saucer disk relate to CN production mechanisms, which are governed radially and vertically by the extent of disk flaring irradiation by X-rays and UV photons from the central star.

Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) systems hold significant promise for biometric applications in logical access control and authentication; however, their compromise carries severe consequences. Preliminary work presented a comparative analysis of state-of-the-art spoof detection methods based on wavelets and MFCCs, citing Novoselov et al. (2016) and Alam et al. (2016a). Results from the ASVspoof 2015 challenge validated the preference for wavelet-based features over MFCCs. Conversely, experiments on the ASVspoof 2019 database revealed the limitations of traditional handcrafted features, highlighting the necessity of advancing toward end-to-end deep neural networks. Using Sincnet as a baseline, we developed two end-to-end models, WSTnet and CWTnet, by substituting the Sinc layer with Wavelet Scattering and Continuous Wavelet Transform layers, respectively. On the ASVspoof 2019 dataset involving modern spoofing attacks, the fusion model demonstrated a 62% relative improvement over traditional handcrafted models and a 17% improvement over the Sincnet baseline. However, the initial scale distribution and count in CWTnet were suboptimal for the task. To address this, the CWT layer was replaced with a Wavelet Deconvolution (WD) layer (Khan and Yener, 2018) in the CWTnet architecture. This WD layer computes the Discrete-Continuous Wavelet Transform similarly to CWTnet but optimizes scale parameters via back-propagation. The resulting WDnet model achieved a 26% relative improvement over CWTnet and a 7% improvement over Sincnet on the ASVspoof 2019 dataset. These gains indicate that WDnet extracts more generalized features than CWTnet by focusing exclusively on the most critical and relevant frequency regions.

Autoregressive models are extensively applied in image and audio generation, yet their sampling mechanisms lack flexibility for interruptions and cannot adjust to real-time computational constraints. This limitation hinders the practical deployment of advanced autoregressive models, which rely on slow, sequential sampling that scales linearly with data dimensions. To overcome this, we introduce a novel family of autoregressive models capable of anytime sampling. Drawing inspiration from Principal Component Analysis, we construct a structured latent space where dimensions are ranked by their significance for reconstruction. By applying an autoregressive model within this space, we balance sample quality against computational efficiency by halting generation prior to decoding into the original data space. Our experiments across various image and audio generation tasks show that sample quality degrades smoothly as the computational budget decreases. Specifically, the method incurs negligible quality loss (as measured by FID) when utilizing only 60% to 80% of the latent dimensions for image data. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Newbeeer/Anytime-Auto-Regressive-Model.

The Mandelstam-Tamm quantum speed limit establishes an upper bound on the evolution rate of closed systems in pure states. This paper derives multiple extensions of this limit for closed systems in mixed states, comparing their strengths and evaluating their tightness. The most prevalent extension stems from Uhlmann's energy dispersion estimate. By rigorously analyzing the geometry underlying this estimate, we demonstrate that the Bures metric—or equivalently, quantum Fisher information—rarely yields tight extensions. This insight prompts an investigation into whether a single tightest general extension exists for the Mandelstam-Tamm limit. Employing a geometric framework akin to Uhlmann's, we prove that such a tightest extension does exist. Furthermore, we establish that tight evolutions in mixed states are typically driven by time-dependent Hamiltonians, a distinction that contrasts with the behavior observed in pure state systems.

This paper introduces a novel framework for locating global minima, termed "optimization by cut." During each iteration, the method samples points from the feasible region and evaluates the objective function at these locations. Utilizing these observations, it excises a subregion unlikely to harbor a global minimum. This process repeats, refining the feasible region with each step until the remaining area is sufficiently small. Provided that a global minimum is retained within the feasible region at every iteration, it can be pinpointed with arbitrary precision. Notably, this framework is surprisingly efficient despite its simplicity and is applicable to black-box functions, as it requires neither specific structural properties nor derivative information. Evaluations on benchmark functions demonstrate that the proposed framework can identify a global minimum with considerable speed.

This study introduces a new approach to calculating the twist-3 gluon fragmentation function's impact on hyperon polarization in proton-proton collisions. By utilizing a covariant gauge and fully leveraging the Ward-Takahashi identities prior to the collinear expansion, the method establishes a reliable framework for deriving the general cross-section formula. Furthermore, it offers a transparent explanation for why ghost-like terms do not appear in the leading-order twist-3 cross section with respect to the QCD coupling constant.

This paper addresses questions regarding the methodology found in certain Brazilian mid-level textbooks concerning stationary sound waves in tubes. Beyond ranking these textbooks against specific criteria, we offer recommendations for further exploration of the subject. These suggestions include incorporating GIFs and animations, as well as utilizing two experiments that enable the visualization of pressure and air displacement profiles across various harmonic vibration modes.

The TREC Video Retrieval Evaluation (TRECVID) is a TREC-style initiative focused on video analysis and retrieval, designed to advance research and development in extracting and retrieving information from digital video through open, metrics-driven assessment. Over the past two decades, this effort has enhanced the understanding of effective system processing and established reliable methods for benchmarking performance. Funded by NIST and other U.S. government agencies, the project also benefits from substantial contributions of time and effort from numerous global organizations and individuals. TRECVID 2020 continued four existing tasks while introducing two new ones, resulting in a total of six challenges completed by 29 teams from various international research institutions: 1. Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS), 2. Instance Search (INS), 3. Disaster Scene Description and Indexing (DSDI), 4. Video to Text Description (VTT), 5. Activities in Extended Video (ActEV), and 6. Video Summarization (VSUM). This paper serves as an introduction to the evaluation framework, tasks, data, and metrics employed in the campaign.

While recent neural Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems excel with abundant data, adapting them to new speakers or languages under low-resource constraints remains challenging. This study demonstrates that minimal adjustments to a Tacotron architecture enable the transfer of an existing TTS model to new speakers—whether from the same or a different language—using as little as 20 minutes of training data. To achieve this, we present a base multi-lingual Tacotron featuring language-agnostic inputs and illustrate how speaker adaptation can be performed across various scenarios without relying on pre-trained speaker encoders or code-switching methods. Finally, we assess the performance of the adapted model through both subjective and objective evaluations.

Image harmonization aims to modify the foreground of a composite image so it aligns with the background, resulting in a more realistic and cohesive result. Training deep learning models for this task demands extensive data, yet obtaining paired composite images with corresponding ground-truth harmonized versions is exceptionally challenging. Consequently, current approaches attempt to adjust foreground appearance in real images to synthesize composites; however, these adjustments often fail to accurately mimic natural illumination shifts. This work introduces a novel transitive method for dataset construction. Specifically, leveraging existing datasets that include recorded illumination data, we first transform the foreground of a real image to a standard lighting condition and then re-render it under a different illumination setting, combining this modified foreground with the original background to create a synthetic composite. This process yields the ccHarmony dataset, named after the color checker (cc), which is accessible at https://github.com/bcmi/Image-Harmonization-Dataset-ccHarmony.

This study introduces the gMOSS (Galaxies of Medium-band One-meter Schmidt telescope Survey) catalog, which comprises approximately 19,000 galaxies observed across 20 filters—consisting of four broadband SDSS filters and 16 medium-band filters. The observations covered a 2.386 $\mathrm{deg^2}$ area within the central region of the HS47.5-22 field using the 1-m Schmidt telescope at the Byurakan Astrophysical Observatory. The catalog represents a complete, flux-limited sample of galaxies with an $r$-band SDSS magnitude limit of $\le$ 22.5 AB. Spectral energy distributions (SEDs) were derived for each object using photometric data from the 16 medium-band filters and the $u$ SDSS filter, facilitating subsequent analysis. Galaxy classification and photometric redshift estimation were performed via spectral template matching using the ZEBRA software, achieving a redshift accuracy of $\sigma_\mathrm{{NMAD}} < 0.0043$. Furthermore, stellar population properties, including rest-frame $(u - r)_{\mathrm{res}}$ colour, stellar mass, extinction, and mass-weighted age, were determined using the CIGALE SED-fitting code with precisions of $0.16 \pm 0.07$ mag, $0.14 \pm 0.04$ dex, $0.27 \pm 0.1$ mag, and $0.08 \pm 0.04$ dex, respectively. By employing a dust-corrected colour-mass diagram, the full sample was separated into red and blue galaxy populations to examine dependencies between stellar mass and age; results indicate that throughout cosmic time, red sequence galaxies are consistently older and more massive than blue cloud galaxies. Additionally, the star formation history of a complete subsample selected within the redshift range $0.015 \le z \le 0.05$ and stellar mass $\log M > 8.3$ [M$_\odot$] reveals an increase in the Star Formation Rate Density (SFRD) up to $z \sim 3$, aligning with findings from previous studies.

Knowledge graph embedding (KGE) is essential for artificial intelligence and supports various downstream tasks like recommendation and question answering. Although numerous KGE approaches have been developed recently, most existing methods overlook semantic similarities among related entities and entity-relation pairs across different triples because they optimize each triple independently using scoring functions. To solve this, we introduce a simple and efficient contrastive learning framework for tensor decomposition-based KGE. This approach reduces the semantic distance between related entities and entity-relation couples in distinct triples, thereby enhancing KGE performance. We assessed our method on three standard datasets: WN18RR, FB15k-237, and YAGO3-10. Our approach achieves new state-of-the-art results, attaining 51.2% MRR and 46.8% Hits@1 on WN18RR, 37.8% MRR and 28.6% Hits@1 on FB15k-237, and 59.1% MRR and 51.8% Hits@1 on YAGO3-10.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) serves as a machine learning approach ideal for addressing complex, high-dimensional control challenges. This research introduces a real-time DRL-based control system designed to manage long-term voltage stability issues. The study explores the feasibility of utilizing demand response (DR) and energy storage systems (ESS) as control mechanisms to maintain system stability. Performance assessments were conducted on a modified Nordic32 test system. Results indicate that the DRL controller rapidly develops an effective policy capable of managing the uncertainties associated with DR and ESS integration. When compared against a rule-based load shedding strategy, the DRL approach demonstrated significantly faster stabilization and reduced load curtailment. Furthermore, testing on load and disturbance scenarios absent from the training dataset confirmed the controller's robustness and strong generalization capabilities.

A Voronoi diagram is a fundamental geometric construct that divides space into regions linked to a specific set of sites, ensuring every point within a region is nearer to its associated site than to any others. Although extensively researched in Euclidean contexts, these diagrams also hold significant interest in hyperbolic space, where multiple algorithms exist for various hyperbolic models. However, the polar-coordinate model, despite gaining traction in network science, has previously been overlooked. Its geometric complexity, compared to other models, has hindered the creation of efficient algorithms, even though Voronoi diagrams could greatly benefit this field. This paper introduces an algorithm for natively computing Voronoi diagrams within the polar-coordinate model of the hyperbolic plane. Drawing inspiration from Fortune's sweep line algorithm for Euclidean diagrams, we define the hyperbolic equivalents of its core concepts, implement necessary adaptations for geometric differences, and demonstrate that the algorithm correctly produces the Voronoi diagram in $O(n \log n)$ time.

**Context.** Recent years have seen an increase in the identification of streamers—asymmetric material flows originating outside a star's natal core and directed toward its protostellar disk. Their influence on mass accretion, especially beyond the Class 0 stage, remains uncertain. **Aims.** This study examines the gas kinematics surrounding Per-emb-50, a Class I source within the dense star-forming region NGC 1333, with the objective of tracing mass infall from the envelope down to the disk. **Results.** We identify a streamer feeding material into Per-emb-50 via H$_2$CO and C$^{18}$O emission. The streamer's characteristics align well with analytic models of gas falling along a streamline while conserving angular momentum, observable in both the image plane and line-of-sight velocities. With a mean infall rate of $1.3 \times 10^{ -6}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{ -1}$, the streamer supplies mass 5 to 10 times greater than the protostar's current accretion rate. Additionally, SO and SO$_2$ emissions indicate asymmetric infall motions in the inner envelope beyond the streamer, with SO$_2$ potentially signaling the impact zone of the incoming material. **Conclusions.** The streamer provides enough mass to maintain the protostellar accretion rate and may trigger an accretion burst, accounting for the source's elevated luminosity compared to other Class I objects. These findings underscore the significance of late-stage infall in protostellar evolution, suggesting that streamers can deliver substantial mass for accretion even after the Class 0 phase.

Recent years have seen the study of implicit regularization in neural networks (NNs) become a focal point of deep learning theory, yet this concept remains ill-defined and poorly understood. This work attempts to provide a rigorous mathematical definition and analysis of implicit regularization. Crucially, we investigate the limitations of the prevailing approach that seeks to characterize implicit regularization using data-independent functions. We introduce two dynamical mechanisms—the Two-point and One-point Overlapping mechanisms—to construct classes of one-hidden-neuron NNs that provably cannot be fully described by any or all data-independent functions. These findings underscore the significant data-dependency inherent in implicit regularization generally, motivating future detailed investigations into this phenomenon within neural networks.

Server breaches are an unfortunate reality of the modern Internet, yet they pose a particularly severe threat to deep neural network (DNN) models. A leaked model grants attackers "white-box" access to craft adversarial examples, a scenario for which no practical robust defenses currently exist. For practitioners who have invested years and millions of dollars into proprietary DNNs, such as those in medical imaging, this appears to be an impending catastrophe.

This paper addresses the challenge of post-breach recovery for DNNs. We introduce Neo, a novel system that generates new versions of leaked models and employs an inference-time filter to identify and eliminate adversarial examples derived from previously compromised models. By introducing hidden distributions, Neo creates slightly offset classification surfaces across different model versions and detects when attacks overfit to the specific leaked model used in their generation. Our results demonstrate that across various tasks and attack methodologies, Neo can filter out attacks from leaked models with very high accuracy. Furthermore, it offers strong protection, enabling the recovery of 7 to 10 breaches even against attackers who repeatedly compromise the server. While performance drops slightly against a range of powerful adaptive attacks, Neo proves to be a promising complement to existing DNN defenses in real-world applications.

We develop an algebra of generalized functions, denoted as $^*\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and establish an embedding of the space of Schwartz distributions, $\mathcal{D}^\prime(\mathbb{R}^d)$, into this algebra. This construction offers a solution to the problem of multiplying Schwartz distributions that advances upon J.F. Colombeau's approach. As an application, we demonstrate the existence of a weak delta-like solution to the Hopf equation within $^*\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, a solution absent from the classical theory of partial differential equations. Furthermore, our findings refine a comparable result by M. Radyna, which was derived using perturbation theory.

We introduce a rapid technique with statistical assurances for learning exponential family density models where the natural parameter resides in a potentially infinite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By fitting the log-density derivative, known as the score, our method circumvents the necessity of calculating a normalization constant. This approach enhances the computational speed of a previous solution through the use of a low-rank, Nyström-inspired approximation. The new method maintains the consistency and convergence rates of the full-rank counterpart (precise in Fisher distance and nearly so in other metrics) while offering guarantees regarding reductions in cost and storage. We assess the method through experiments on density estimation and the development of an adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler. In contrast to an existing score learning approach based on denoising autoencoders, our estimator demonstrates superior data efficiency in score estimation, faster execution, and a reduced parameter count that allows for principled and interpretable tuning, all accompanied by statistical guarantees.

Regularisation techniques are essential for addressing ill-posed inverse problems. This paper concentrates on discrete unfolding derived from counting experiments, although the underlying formalism is broadly applicable. We evaluate the results by assessing the consistency between measurements and the unfolded output, as well as the posterior response matrix. Following a review of fundamental concepts, we introduce a new regularisation method utilizing a discrete-valued penalty function and benchmark it against a standard cutoff-regularisation. Unlike traditional approaches, this discrete-valued penalty stabilizes the solution without requiring a case-specific regularisation parameter. Toy studies demonstrate its high performance. Furthermore, uncertainties are addressed using a bootstrap method, as the discontinuities in the penalty function preclude the use of derivative-based error propagation.

Insufficient repeatability and generalizability pose major obstacles to the ongoing advancement of Natural Language Processing. The increasing complexity of language models and learning algorithms has rendered standard conference paper lengths inadequate for providing the technical depth necessary for replication. Using Target Dependent Sentiment Analysis as an example, we demonstrate that recent studies frequently fail to release code or specify learning method settings with sufficient detail, resulting in poor comparability and generalizability across training, testing, and validation datasets. To address these issues and facilitate rigorous comparative evaluations, we conducted the first reproduction studies of three complementary method groups and performed a large-scale mass evaluation across six distinct English datasets. Based on our findings, we advise that future replication efforts must include diverse datasets alongside thorough documentation and code release to reduce barriers to reproducibility. We have made our code available via a GitHub model zoo, complete with Jupyter Notebooks and comprehensive documentation, and we urge other researchers to adopt similar practices by submitting anonymized GitHub repositories with their papers.

Under the assumptions of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) and the Ramanujan-Petersson conjecture, we establish explicit bounds for $L(1,f)$ across a broad spectrum of $L$-functions $L(s,f)$, encompassing those associated with automorphic cuspidal forms on $GL(n)$. This approach extends the research conducted by Lamzouri, Li, and Soundararajan. Additionally, our primary findings refine the classical estimates provided by Littlewood:
\[(1+o(1))\left(\frac{12e^{\gamma}}{\pi^2}\log\log C(f)\right)^{-d} \leq
|L(1,f)|\leq (1+o(1))\Big(2e^{\gamma}\log\log C(f)\Big)^d,\]
where $C(f)$ represents the analytic conductor of $L(s,f)$.

As data-driven deep neural networks, recognized as universal function approximators, have become dominant in computer vision research, traditional hand-crafted image processing techniques have largely been abandoned. This paper demonstrates that a well-designed classical algorithm can surpass neural network-based approaches in the task of depth completion. The proposed method is straightforward, computationally efficient, and operates on a CPU using only fundamental image processing operations to complete depth for sparse LIDAR data. Evaluated on the challenging KITTI depth completion benchmark, our approach achieved the top ranking among all published methods on the KITTI test server at the time of submission. Additionally, the algorithm is data-independent, meaning it requires no training data to function. The Python implementation will be made publicly available at https://github.com/kujason/ip_basic.

Intersections involving vehicle turns and interactions with vulnerable road users (VRUs), such as pedestrians and cyclists, represent some of the most difficult environments for accurately recognizing road user behavior in automated systems. This paper introduces a deep conditional generative model designed to detect such interactions. The objective is to automatically analyze extensive video data regarding the continuity of road users' actions, a critical task for intelligent transportation systems like self-driving cars and traffic safety controls that rely on understanding human locomotion. We trained a Conditional Variational Auto-Encoder utilizing Gaussian latent variables to encode road user behavior and generate diverse, probabilistic predictions of interactions. The model ingests data on road user type, position, and motion—automatically extracted via a deep learning object detector and optical flow from video—alongside frame-wise probabilities that capture the dynamics between turning vehicles and involved VRUs. The model's effectiveness was validated using real-world datasets from two distinct intersections. It achieved an F1-score exceeding 0.96 at a busy right-turn intersection in Germany and 0.89 at a busy left-turn intersection in Japan.

This paper presents a novel homotopy function designed to trace solution trajectories using a modified homotopy continuation method for solving linear complementarity problems (LCPs). While previous researchers have developed homotopy functions directly from the original problem formulation, our approach derives the function from the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the associated quadratic programming problem. This strategy expands the applicability of the method to a broader class of LCPs and addresses the constraints found in other existing homotopy techniques. We demonstrate that the resulting homotopy path is smooth and bounded, featuring a positive tangent direction. Furthermore, various numerical examples are provided to validate the algorithm's effectiveness and highlight its superiority over other established iterative methods.

We introduce a unitary quantum control method designed to generate a highly monochromatic ion beam from a Paul trap. This protocol can be implemented by applying voltages in the range of Volts to segmented electrodes, a strategy that reduces the sensitivity to voltage fluctuations found in earlier designs and results in a low-dispersion ion beam. Furthermore, our approach eliminates the requirement for sympathetic cooling, thereby removing the necessity of introducing additional species into the trap—such as the primary ion and a cooling agent like $^{40}$Ca$^+$—which in turn increases the repetition rate of the launch process. The scheme relies on an invariant operator that is linear in position and momentum, allowing precise control over the mean extraction energy and the spread of outgoing momentum. Additionally, we propose a sequential operation to adjust the beam's transversal characteristics prior to ejection, aiming to reduce the impact spot size and enhance the lateral resolution of the implantation.
We provide an explicit integral formula for the Dunkl kernel related to the $A_2$ root system with parameter $k>0$, utilizing recent findings from [1].

Optical lattices and spin-orbit coupling serve as standard experimental methods for tailoring dispersion. We demonstrate self-interfering dynamics within a noninteracting Bose-Einstein condensate when such engineered dispersion is applied. This self-interference arises from the simultaneous occupation of positive and negative effective mass regimes within the modified dispersion relation. We elucidate the physical mechanism behind this phenomenon using the Wigner distribution function of the self-interfering wave packet and provide a detailed characterization of the resulting interference pattern.

A generalized Stiefel manifold represents the collection of orthonormal frames within a vector space equipped with a non-degenerate bilinear or Hermitian form. This article determines the isometry group of these manifolds, at least up to connected components, in an explicit manner. The approach involves analyzing a natural non-associative algebra, denoted as $\mathfrak{m}$, which corresponds to the affine structure of the Stiefel manifold; by explicitly calculating the automorphism group $Aut(\mathfrak{m})$, the isometry group is subsequently derived.

This study initially examines a flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe containing two scalar fields governed by a single potential, effectively modeling a combination of quintessence and K-essence. Using the Hamiltonian formalism, we derive both classical and quantum solutions for this setup. The second model also features a flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe with two scalar fields, but it incorporates two distinct potentials alongside standard kinetic energy and a mixed term characteristic of the chiral field approach. For this second scenario, setting the coefficient of the mixed momentum term to zero allows for the analysis of two distinct cases: a quintom-like scenario ($m^{12}_{+}$) and a quintessence-like scenario ($m^{12}_{-}$). Classical and quantum solutions are provided for both of these cases.

Existing reserve procurement methods overlook the stochastic variability of reserve asset availability, thereby constraining both the volume and variety of reserve offers. This study introduces a reliability-conscious probabilistic framework that enables renewable generators to submit reserve capacity bids incorporating specific reliability characteristics. Within this model, offers exhibiting lower reliability are assigned correspondingly lower prices. The originally non-convex market clearing challenge is approximated through a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) reformulation. By facilitating the participation of restricted reserve providers, this probabilistic procurement strategy enhances market liquidity and holds the potential to reduce procurement costs within power systems characterized by high penetrations of variable renewable energy.

This report details a search for supersymmetric particle pair production characterized by events containing two oppositely charged leptons (electrons or muons) and missing transverse momentum. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC during the 2016 run. No significant excess beyond the predicted Standard Model background is observed. These findings are interpreted within various simplified models involving chargino and top squark pair production, under the assumptions of $R$-parity conservation and a neutralino as the lightest supersymmetric particle. In scenarios where the chargino decays via sleptons with a mass equal to the average of the chargino and neutralino masses, 95% confidence level exclusion limits are established for chargino and neutralino masses up to 800 GeV and 320 GeV, respectively. For top squark production, the study targets models with a small mass splitting between the top squark and the lightest neutralino; specifically, when the top squark decays into an off-shell top quark and a neutralino, the limits reach 420 GeV and 360 GeV for the top squark and neutralino masses, respectively.

**Objectives.** Our goal is to automatically produce artificial leaf images using sophisticated Deep Learning (DL) methods to establish a training dataset for AI-driven modern crop management. Since these applications demand vast amounts of data, and while leaf images themselves are not rare, gathering and labeling them is extremely labor-intensive. Although data augmentation via simple transformations of existing samples can mitigate scarcity, the resulting data lacks sufficient richness, necessitating alternative solutions. **Methods.** We adopt a Deep Learning generative model strategy, proposing a Leaf-to-Leaf Translation (L2L) workflow divided into two stages. First, a residual variational autoencoder creates synthetic leaf skeletons—including profiles and veins—derived from binarized skeletons of real leaves. Second, we utilize a Pix2pix framework employing conditional generative adversarial networks to transfer coloration to the leaf blades while maintaining the original shape and venation patterns. **Results.** The L2L method produces synthetic leaf images with a realistic visual appearance. We evaluate performance both qualitatively and quantitatively; the latter involves a Deep Learning-based anomaly detection approach to measure how closely synthetic leaves resemble real samples. **Conclusions.** Generative DL techniques offer a promising new paradigm for supplying low-cost, meaningful synthetic data for computer-aided applications. The proposed L2L approach advances this objective by generating synthetic samples that exhibit significant qualitative and quantitative similarity to real leaves.

Enhancing the quality of few-shot facial animation from landmarks enables new applications, such as ultra-low bandwidth video chat compression with high realism. However, significant challenges remain for real-world deployment. Specifically, existing methods struggle to render profile views without distortion while operating under low computational constraints. We address this critical issue by introducing "Frontalizer," a multi-frame embedding designed to improve profile view rendering. Beyond this core enhancement, we investigate conditioning latent code generation alongside landmarks to better capture facial expressions. Our dense models achieve a 22% boost in perceptual quality and a 73% reduction in landmark error compared to the first-order baseline on a subset of DFDC videos featuring head movements. When adapted for mobile architectures, our models surpass previous state-of-the-art results—improving perceptual quality by over 16% and reducing landmark error by more than 47% across two datasets—while running in real-time on an iPhone 8 with minimal bandwidth requirements.

Lowering the operating temperature of a Silicon Photo-Multiplier (SiPM) reduces its dark noise, making cryogenic conditions a viable option for low-noise applications. The TAO detector exemplifies this, necessitating operation near $T\approx -50~^\circ$C, where a significant study previously reported a drastic decline in Photon Detection Efficiency (PDE) around this threshold. This paper investigates the performance of SiPM samples from Hamamatsu and AdvanSID (FBK) across a wide temperature spectrum, revealing no substantial differences in PDE between the two.

Although Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is rapidly expanding into diverse fields, its application to deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) remains limited. Given that RL is becoming ubiquitous in critical and public-facing systems, there is an urgent need for methods that enhance its interpretability and understandability. This research introduces a novel method for explaining cooperative strategies in multi-agent RL by utilizing Shapley values—a game theory concept within XAI that effectively elucidates the decision-making rationales of machine learning algorithms. By testing standard assumptions of this technique across two socially challenging, cooperation-focused multi-agent environments, the study argues that Shapley values are highly relevant for assessing individual player contributions in cooperative multi-agent RL scenarios. To mitigate the method's high computational overhead, the authors approximate Shapley values using Monte Carlo sampling. Experiments conducted on Multiagent Particle and Sequential Social Dilemmas demonstrate that Shapley values successfully estimate each agent's contribution. These findings suggest broader implications beyond gaming, including applications in economics, non-discriminatory decision-making, ethical AI, and policy formulation under fairness constraints. However, the results also highlight a limitation: while Shapley values provide general explanations of a model, they cannot account for specific episodes or justify individual agent actions. Future research must address these critical gaps.

We demonstrate that the affine cone associated with a general primitively polarized K3 surface of genus $g$ admits a smooth deformation precisely when $g \le 10$ or $g = 12$. Additionally, we present various instances of singularities exhibiting unique characteristics, including cases where the affine cone is smoothable despite the projective cone not being so.

Author profiling involves characterizing individuals based on key attributes like gender, age, and language. This paper introduces an RNN with Attention (RNNwA) model designed to predict a Twitter user's gender from their tweets. The model leverages both word-level and tweet-level attention mechanisms to determine relevant features. It is further enhanced by integrating LSA-reduced n-gram features with the neural representations of the user. The proposed models were evaluated across three languages: English, Spanish, and Arabic. The improved RNNwA + n-gram variant achieves state-of-the-art results for English and competitive performance for Spanish and Arabic.

This research investigates the ruin problem for an insurer operating two business lines, life and non-life, which allocates its reserves to a risky asset governed by geometric Brownian motion. We establish the smoothness of the ruin probability with respect to initial capital and derive the corresponding classical integro-differential equation. Specifically, when jumps follow an exponential distribution, the survival probability satisfies a fourth-order ordinary differential equation. Asymptotic analysis of this equation demonstrates that the ruin probability approaches zero at a rate consistent with previously examined models featuring one-sided jumps.

We introduce the initial subexponential-time parameterized algorithms addressing various cut and cycle-hitting problems on $H$-minor free graphs. Specifically, our findings include:
1. Algorithms running in $2^{O(\sqrt{k}\log k)} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time for Edge Bipartization and Odd Cycle Transversal.
2. A $2^{O(\sqrt{k}\log^4 k)} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time algorithm for Edge Multiway Cut, alongside a $2^{O(r \sqrt{k} \log k)} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time algorithm for Vertex Multiway Cut, where $r$ denotes the number of terminals.
3. A $2^{O((r+\sqrt{k})\log^4 (rk))} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time algorithm for Edge Multicut and a $2^{O((\sqrt{rk}+r) \log (rk))} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time algorithm for Vertex Multicut, with $r$ representing the number of terminal pairs.
4. A $2^{O(\sqrt{k} \log g \log^4 k)} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time algorithm for Group Feedback Edge Set and a $2^{O(g \sqrt{k}\log(gk))} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ time algorithm for Group Feedback Vertex Set, where $g$ indicates the group size.
5. Furthermore, our method yields $n^{O(\sqrt{k})}$ time algorithms for all the aforementioned issues, except for $n^{O(r+\sqrt{k})}$ time for Edge/Vertex Multicut and $(ng)^{O(\sqrt{k})}$ time for Group Feedback Edge/Vertex Set.

These outcomes stem from a novel decomposition theorem applicable to graphs of bounded genus, or more broadly, $h$-almost-embeddable graphs for any fixed constant $h$. Specifically, for an $h$-almost-embeddable graph $G$ and any natural number $p$, we demonstrate the existence of disjoint vertex sets $Z_1,\dots,Z_p \subseteq V(G)$ such that for each $i \in \{1,\dots,p\}$ and every subset $Z'\subseteq Z_i$, the treewidth of the graph $G/(Z_i\backslash Z')$ is bounded by $O(p+|Z'|)$. The graph $G/(Z_i\backslash Z')$ is formed by contracting all edges whose endpoints lie within $Z_i \backslash Z'$.

Recent breakthroughs in establishing stable dipolar Bose systems and innovative box trap designs have sparked significant interest. However, theoretical investigations into dipolar bosons at finite temperatures (T) remain scarce. Driven by this gap, we examine two-dimensional dipolar bosons at any tilt angle, $\theta$, employing the finite-T random phase approximation. Our analysis demonstrates that a thorough comprehension of phases and instabilities at non-zero T requires simultaneously accounting for dipole strength, density, temperature, and $\theta$. We identify that the system resides in a homogeneous, non-condensed state that experiences a collapse transition at high $\theta$ and a finite momentum instability indicative of a striped phase at high dipolar strength; these behaviors differ notably from the T=0 scenario. Specifically, at T=0, Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) occurs only at critical dipolar strength and critical density. Our predictions regarding polar molecule systems, specifically $^{41}K^{87}Rb$ and $^{166}Er$, offer opportunities to validate these findings. Furthermore, our methodology is likely applicable to a wide range of systems characterized by long-range, anisotropic interactions.

We re-express the concept of uncertainty regarding pairs of unitary operators through the framework of guessing games, establishing an entropic uncertainty relation for them. Furthermore, we demonstrate that distinguishable operators are compatible, whereas maximal incompatibility among unitary operators can be linked to bases within certain subspaces of mutually unbiased operators.

This study examines the elastic scattering of both longitudinal and transverse neutrinos off spinless nuclei, incorporating the effects of fermion charge, magnetic, anapole, and electric dipole moments alongside their weak neutral currents. The compound structure of the neutrino-nucleus interaction cross-section is established, and the invariance of the process under C- and P-operations is analyzed with respect to polarization-type dependencies.

Given the exponential growth of social media's influence, it is crucial to address its detrimental effects, such as societal division and incitement to violence. This paper details our team's system description for the ComMA@ICON shared task, which involves classifying sentence aggression levels and detecting gender or communal biases—three factors capable of causing major social issues. As team Hypers, we developed an approach leveraging various pretrained models combined with Attention and mean pooling techniques. Our results achieved a Rank 3 with a 0.223 Instance F1 score on Bengali, Rank 2 with a 0.322 Instance F1 score on the Multi-lingual set, Rank 4 with a 0.129 Instance F1 score on Meitei, and Rank 5 with a 0.336 Instance F1 score on Hindi. The source code and pretrained models for this work are available here.

This paper introduces findings on local dynamic bifurcations concerning invariant sets within nonlinear evolution equations. Specifically, we demonstrate that when the trivial solution constitutes an isolated invariant set at the critical parameter value $\lambda=\lambda_0$, two outcomes are possible: either there exists a one-sided neighborhood $I^-$ around $\lambda_0$ where the system bifurcates from the trivial solution into an isolated, nonempty, compact invariant set $K_\lambda$ that excludes zero ($0\not\in K_\lambda$) for each $\lambda\in I^-$, or there exists a one-sided neighborhood $I^+$ around $\lambda_0$ where the system experiences attractor bifurcation from $(0,\lambda_0)$ for $\lambda\in I^+$. Furthermore, we provide a revised formulation of the attractor bifurcation theorem and apply these findings to the classical Swift-Hohenberg equation to illustrate their use on a specific evolution equation.

We present a polynomial-time pseudo-approximation algorithm for min-sum clustering that accommodates both scenarios with and without outliers, permitting the exclusion of an arbitrarily small constant fraction of points. For example, we demonstrate the ability to cluster 98% of the input data with a cost no more than a constant factor times the optimal cost for clustering 99% of the data. More broadly, we provide a bicriteria approximation guarantee: for any $\eps > 0$, any instance of $n$ points, and any integer $n' \le n$, our algorithm computes a clustering of at least $(1-\eps)n'$ points in polynomial time with a cost bounded by a constant factor relative to the optimal cost for $n'$ points. This approximation factor scales with $1/\eps$. These results hold for points in real space using squared Euclidean distance as well as for points in arbitrary metric spaces, where the number of clusters and dimensionality (if applicable) are part of the input rather than fixed constants.

We address the challenge of obtaining an approximate solution for $\ell_1$ regression with a limited number of observed labels. Provided with an $n \times d$ matrix $X$ containing unlabeled data, we select a small subset of $m \ll n$ rows to observe their labels and produce an estimate $\widehat{\beta}$ that achieves an error within a $(1 + \varepsilon)$ factor of the optimum. Our results demonstrate that sampling $X$ based on Lewis weights and returning the empirical minimizer achieves success with probability $1-\delta$ when $m > O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2} d \log \frac{d}{\varepsilon \delta})$. This performance mirrors leverage score sampling for $\ell_2$ regression but features an exponentially superior dependence on $\delta$. Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound of $\Omega(\frac{d}{\varepsilon^2} + (d + \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}) \log\frac{1}{\delta})$.

We introduce an extrinsic Bayesian optimization (eBO) framework designed for general optimization tasks on manifolds. Standard Bayesian optimization methods utilize Gaussian processes to create a surrogate model of the objective function and determine an acquisition function to measure uncertainty within that model. This acquisition function, which estimates the likelihood of improvement using the Gaussian process kernel, directs the search strategy during optimization. A primary challenge in adapting Bayesian optimization to manifolds is the difficulty of developing valid covariance kernels for Gaussian processes in these general settings. Our solution involves using extrinsic Gaussian processes: we first embed the manifold into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space through equivariant mappings and subsequently construct a valid covariance kernel on the embedded image. This approach yields efficient and scalable algorithms for optimizing over complex manifolds. We validate the effectiveness of our eBO framework through simulations and real-world data analysis, applying it to diverse optimization problems across manifolds such as the sphere, the Grassmannian, and the manifold of positive definite matrices.
We demonstrate that the threshold for the existence of a rainbow copy of a power of a Hamilton cycle in a randomly edge-colored $G_{n,p}$ aligns precisely with the uncolored threshold.

This paper demonstrates that retrocausality emerges naturally from quantum mechanics, offering a consistent explanation for quantum measurement that aligns with macroscopic realism. We examine a measurement $\hat{x}$ on a system initially in a superposition of eigenstates $|x_{j}\rangle$, modeling the process through amplification. By establishing a path-integral theorem, we prove an equivalence between the quantum probability distribution $Q(x,p,t)$ and simultaneous stochastic equations describing amplitudes $x(t)$ and $p(t)$ evolving forward and backward in time, respectively, which are connected at the initial-time boundary. Consequently, a Deutsch-like 'causal consistency' and Born's rule arise naturally. A notable characteristic is the vacuum noise linked to the eigenstate; unlike the eigenvalue, this noise remains unamplified and unmeasurable, stemming from precise fluctuations defined by past and future boundary conditions. Our findings support macroscopic realism: for macroscopic superpositions, the outcome of the measurement $\hat{x}$ is deemed determined before the measurement begins. This creates hybrid relations involving both macro-causality and micro-retrocausality, compatible with other realism models. Our results indicate that wave function 'collapse' occurs via amplification: the distribution $Q_{j}(x,p,0)$ for the initial 'state' postselected on outcome $x_{j}$ is not a quantum state but converges toward the eigenstate $|x_{j}\rangle$ in cases of macroscopic superposition. The full irreversible collapse is simulated through coupling to a meter. Finally, we address Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen and Bell correlations.

This work introduces the TCFHs for every AdS background within 11-dimensional supergravity and investigates the characteristics of the linked connections. Consequently, we show that all Killing spinor bilinears adhere to a generalized form of the conformal Killing-Yano equations relative to the TCFH connection. Furthermore, we examine the hidden symmetries of spinning particle probes moving through these spacetimes. We provide multiple examples of these hidden symmetries for probes situated on maximally supersymmetric AdS backgrounds, as well as on certain AdS geometries that emerge as the near-horizon limits of intersecting M-branes.

This study extends our prior analysis of two-body hadronic parity violation from operators involving one derivative to those with three derivatives, utilizing a combined framework of pionless effective field theory (EFT$_{\pi\!}$) and the large-$N_c$ expansion, where $N_c$ represents the number of colors in quantum chromodynamics (QCD). In the context of elastic scattering, these operators facilitate $S$-$P$ and $P$-$D$ wave transitions, with the $S$-$P$ sector characterized by five operators and their associated low-energy coefficients (LECs), and the $P$-$D$ sector by six such operators and LECs. We demonstrate that the large-$N_c$ approach organizes these contributions hierarchically into leading and next-to-leading orders. Furthermore, we identify relationships between EFT$_{\pi\!}$ LECs that arise within the large-$N_c$ expansion and examine the dependence of these coefficients on the renormalization scale. This analysis serves to complement lattice QCD computations and assist in prioritizing future experiments designed to probe parity violation.

This paper primarily aims to define network synchronizability for cluster synchronization (CS), mirroring the approach Barahona and Pecora used for complete synchronization. However, this problem proves significantly more intricate. We differentiate between networks with and without intertwined clusters, as well as between scenarios where the master stability function is negative within bounded or unbounded argument ranges. First, we establish a synchronizability definition for individual clusters and then seek to extend it to the whole network. In CS, the stability of a cluster's synchronous solution can be independent of others, leading to distinct synchronization ranges (isolated CS). For every pair of clusters, we categorize three distinct situations: Matryoshka Cluster Synchronization (where one cluster's stability range is contained within another's), Partially Disjoint Cluster Synchronization (where stability ranges partially overlap), and Complete Disjoint Cluster Synchronization (where stability ranges do not overlap).

Manganese is primarily created during Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) events. Because manganese production depends on entropy during explosive thermonuclear burning, models of SN Ia involving near-Chandrasekhar-mass white dwarfs (WDs) predict manganese-to-iron ratios that are significantly higher than those from explosions of sub-Chandrasekhar-mass WDs. Among existing supernova models, only those featuring near-Chandrasekhar-mass WDs yield a [Mn/Fe] ratio greater than 0.0. The study's objective is to determine the relative proportions of near-Chandrasekhar-mass versus sub-Chandrasekhar-mass WD progenitors in the Galaxy by analyzing yields from competing SN Ia scenarios. To achieve this, the researchers extracted manganese yields from three-dimensional thermonuclear simulations covering various initial conditions and progenitor channels. They then modeled the chemical evolution of manganese in the Solar neighborhood, varying the assumed fractions of these explosion types. The results indicate that, due to the entropy dependence of freeze-out yields from nuclear statistical equilibrium, [Mn/Fe] is highly sensitive to the exploding WD's mass, with near-Chandrasekhar-mass WDs generating substantially higher ratios. Among potential nucleosynthetic sources, only thermonuclear incineration of near-Chandrasekhar-mass WDs predicts solar or super-solar [Mn/Fe]. Consequently, chemical evolution calculations show that observed [Mn/Fe] levels in the Solar neighborhood for [Fe/H] > 0.0 cannot be explained without including near-Chandrasekhar-mass SN Ia primaries. Assuming that 50% of all SNe Ia originate from the explosive burning of near-Chandrasekhar-mass WDs provides a strong match to observational data.

The James Webb Space Telescope's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) represents a pioneering multi-object spectrograph in orbit, featuring approximately 250,000 adjustable micro-shutters alongside integral field unit and fixed slit capabilities. Central to its operation is the NIRSpec grating wheel assembly, a cryogenic unit containing six dispersion gratings, a prism, and a mirror. Due to the wheel's limited angular positioning repeatability, the light beam experiences minor yet quantifiable shifts on the focal plane, rendering a static light-path prediction impossible. To mitigate this, two magneto-resistive position sensors track the tip and tilt displacements of the selected grating wheel assembly element during each rotation. Calibrating these sensors is vital for the model-based strategy employed in NIRSpec for tasks including calibration, spectral extraction, and target placement within the micro-shutters. This paper details the progression of GWA sensor performance and calibration as the system transitions from ground-based testing to the space environment.

Bayesian experimental design (BED) seeks to optimize experiment setups to extract maximum information from data, typically by maximizing the mutual information (MI) between observations and model parameters. When analytical MI expressions are unavailable, as is common with implicit models featuring intractable data distributions, recent methods have utilized neural networks to estimate a lower bound of the MI, optimized via gradient ascent. However, the approach by Kleinegesse et al. (2020) necessitates a pathwise sampling path to compute gradients with respect to design variables, a requirement that is often unattainable for implicit models. To address this, we introduce a hybrid gradient method that integrates recent variational MI estimators with evolution strategies (ES) and black-box stochastic gradient ascent (SGA) to maximize the MI lower bound. This enables a unified, scalable design procedure for implicit models that bypasses the need for sampling path gradients. Empirical results indicate that our method substantially enhances the scalability of BED for implicit models within high-dimensional design spaces.

This study initially aims to automatically detect pancreatitis in CT scan images. Unlike traditional object recognition tasks, identifying pancreatitis is difficult due to the fine-grained and non-rigid variability of the affected local regions. To address this, we introduce a customized Region-Manipulated Fusion Network (RMFN) designed to capture the essential characteristics of local lesions for pancreatitis detection. Specifically, a novel region-manipulation scheme within RMFN is proposed to emphasize imperceptible lesion areas while suppressing non-lesion regions by continuously aggregating multi-scale local information onto feature maps. This scheme can be flexibly integrated into existing neural networks, such as AlexNet and VGG. To assess the method's performance, a real-world CT image database containing pancreatitis cases was collected from hospitals. Experimental results on this dataset effectively demonstrate the proposed method's efficacy in recognizing pancreatitis.

QCD splittings represent some of the most foundational theoretical concepts investigated at the LHC. We demonstrate that these can be analyzed systematically using invertible neural networks, which leverage sub-jet data to derive fundamental parameters from jet samples. This methodology extends LEP's measurements of QCD Casimirs into a comprehensive test of QCD characteristics grounded in low-level jet observables. Beginning with a toy model, we examine in detail the impact of the complete shower process, hadronization, and detector effects.

This report presents a real-time 2D object detection system tailored for realistic autonomous driving scenarios, built upon a newly designed YOLO model known as YOLOX. On the Argoverse-HD dataset, our system attained a streaming AP of 41.0, outperforming the second-place entry by margins of 7.8 and 6.1 on the detection-only and fully tracked tracks, respectively. Additionally, when accelerated with TensorRT, the model delivers 30FPS inference speeds even at high-resolution input sizes, such as 1440-2304. The corresponding code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/Megvii-BaseDetection/YOLOX.

This study examines a SEIRD epidemic model for a population divided into two groups exhibiting asymmetric interactions. By specifying two distinct sets of parameters, we estimate the distance between solutions for the second group based on the distance observed in the first group. Additionally, we analyze the final epidemic size for each group. Our findings are illustrated through the application of the model to the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York County, USA, as well as in the Brazilian cities of Petrolina and Juazeiro.

This article investigates bounded solutions of Euler-type equations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ that lack integrability as $|x| \rightarrow +\infty$. It is well-established that such solutions do not yield unique solutions to initial value problems, despite satisfying strong smoothness requirements. This situation stands in contrast to well-posedness results derived via the Leray projection operator. The apparent contradiction is resolved by recognizing that employing the Leray projector necessitates an additional condition on the behavior of solutions at infinity; we demonstrate that this condition is both necessary and sufficient. Consequently, we establish a complete well-posedness theorem for the Euler equations within the space $C^0_T(B^1_{\infty, 1})$. Furthermore, we extend the methodologies developed for the Euler system to other hydrodynamic frameworks, including the Navier-Stokes equations and magnetohydrodynamics.

Classical multi-core platforms struggle to meet the escalating computational demands and strict timing constraints of hard real-time systems, such as autonomous driving and image processing. To address this, Heterogeneous Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) platforms are well-suited for accelerating real-time workloads by utilizing application-specific cores like GPUs, DSPs, and ASICs. Furthermore, these platforms offer greater design flexibility, allowing specific functionalities to be implemented across various compute elements. Recently, the HPC-DAG (Heterogeneous Parallel Directed Acyclic Graph) task model was introduced to represent real-time workload execution on such heterogeneous systems. This model captures ISA diversity and hardware accelerator traits, including the lack of preemption or expensive preemption costs, alternative implementation options, and online conditional execution. This paper presents a scheduling approach using Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to allocate and schedule HPC-DAG tasks across a set of heterogeneous cores. Our design effectively manages resource heterogeneity and online execution costs while accelerating the solution process by progressively exploring the design space.

This study introduces a new longitudinal, multimodal dataset comprising physiological and behavioral information gathered directly from clinical staff within a hospital environment. The research aims to evaluate the efficacy of readily available wearable and environmental sensors for tracking individual-specific metrics—such as job performance, social interactions, and well-being—over time in natural work settings. Data were collected from 212 participants using Internet-of-Things Bluetooth hubs, various wearable devices (including wristbands, biometric garments, smartphones, and audio recorders), and a comprehensive set of surveys designed to measure personality traits, behavioral states, performance, and well-being longitudinally. Beyond its standard utility, we anticipate diverse research avenues and applications for this dataset, such as multi-modal and multi-task behavioral modeling, biometric authentication, and the development of privacy-aware and privacy-preserving machine learning techniques.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptive (UDA) person re-identification (ReID) focuses on transferring a model trained on a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. While many successful UDA-ReID methods alternate between clustering-based pseudo-label generation and representation learning, their offline interaction often allows noisy pseudo-labels to significantly degrade model performance. To address this, we introduce the Group-aware Label Transfer (GLT) algorithm, which facilitates online interaction and mutual enhancement between pseudo-label prediction and representation learning. Specifically, GLT employs a label transfer mechanism that simultaneously trains the model using pseudo-labels and refines them via an online clustering approach. By framing online label refinement as an optimal transport problem, the method minimizes the cost of assigning M samples to N pseudo-labels. Furthermore, we incorporate a group-aware strategy to assign implicit attribute group IDs to samples. This combination effectively corrects noisy pseudo-labels in real-time and narrows the search space for target identities. Experimental results on Market1501$\to$DukeMTMC (82.0\%) and DukeMTMC$\to$Market1501 (92.2\%) demonstrate the efficacy of GLT, significantly narrowing the performance gap between unsupervised and supervised ReID.

We examine a two-dimensional square lattice formed by straight nonlinear waveguides, where a specific set of central layers is tilted relative to the remainder of the structure. This arrangement creates a periodically modulated line defect within the lattice plane. In the linear regime, the system supports line defect modes, with the total number of such modes matching the count of tilted layers. When nonlinearity is introduced, branches of defect solitons traveling along the defect line emerge via bifurcation from each linear defect mode. Depending on the effective dispersion dictated by the Floquet spectrum of the underlying system, these bifurcating solitons may manifest as either bright or dark types. The dynamics and stability of these solitons are investigated through numerical analysis.

This study proposes flavorful and chiral vector bosons with a mass scale of approximately $1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ to explain current flavor anomalies observed in $K$ and $B$ meson systems, including the CP-violating Kaon decay parameter ($\epsilon'/\epsilon$) and lepton-flavor universality violations in $B$ decays ($R_{K^{(*)}}$ and $R_{D^{(*)}}$). However, if these composite vector bosons are significantly heavier than $1\,\mathrm{TeV}$, it becomes challenging to simultaneously resolve the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly and satisfy constraints from $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing. While both anomalies can be individually accommodated within the $1\sigma$ confidence level, the relevant parameter space requires further investigation by the NA62 and KOTO experiments, alongside direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider.

Current Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) approaches typically employ graph augmentations in two ways: either by randomly corrupting the anchor graph, which risks losing semantic details, or by leveraging domain knowledge to retain salient features, which hampers generalization across different domains. Adopting an invariance perspective on GCL, we contend that effective augmentations must preserve the salient semantics of anchor graphs essential for instance discrimination. Consequently, we link GCL with invariant rationale discovery and introduce a novel framework called Rationale-aware Graph Contrastive Learning (RGCL). Specifically, RGCL operates without supervision signals; it utilizes a rationale generator to identify salient features regarding graph instance discrimination as the rationale, subsequently constructing rationale-aware views for contrastive learning. This rationale-aware pre-training strategy equips the backbone model with robust representation capabilities, thereby enhancing performance on downstream tasks after fine-tuning. Experiments on the MNIST-Superpixel and MUTAG datasets, supported by visual analysis of the discovered rationales, demonstrate that the rationale generator effectively captures salient features (such as distinguishing semantic nodes). Furthermore, state-of-the-art results on biochemical molecule and social network benchmarks confirm the efficacy of rationale-aware views for contrastive learning. The project code is accessible at https://github.com/lsh0520/RGCL.

Beyond its extensive application in clinical settings, biological age (BA) serves a critical role in legal medicine by estimating unknown chronological age (CA) when identification documents are unavailable. While existing automatic age estimation methods typically predict point estimates, these can be misleading without quantifying predictive uncertainty. Our multi-factorial method for age estimation using MRI data employs Variational Inference to calculate the uncertainty of a Bayesian CNN model.
