By distinguishing between model uncertainty and data uncertainty, we interpret the latter as biological variation—representing the range of possible chronological ages for individuals who share the same biological age.

Modern astronomical surveys generate vast datasets that serve as ideal environments for testing machine learning applications. It is crucial to assess current tools to identify the most effective methods for deriving scientific insights from observational data. This study investigates the use of clustering algorithms to segregate stellar populations with unique chemical signatures. Since star clusters represent the most chemically homogeneous groups in the Galaxy, any viable method for distinguishing stellar populations must first be capable of separating individual clusters. We evaluated eight clustering algorithms paired with four dimensionality reduction techniques to automatically identify stellar clusters based on the chemical abundances of 13 elements. Our dataset comprises 18 stellar clusters containing a total of 453 stars. Statistical analyses reveal that certain cluster pairs are indistinguishable using Apache Point Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) chemical data; however, for the majority of clusters, we successfully achieved automatic membership assignment with metric scores comparable to prior research. The confusion rates observed in our automatically selected clusters align with statistical findings that confirm it is impossible to perfectly differentiate every cluster. These results establish a fundamental limit on the feasibility of blindly identifying stars born in the same cluster using only chemical abundances. We conclude that several of the tested algorithms can effectively identify stellar populations with similar ages and chemical distributions within the APOGEE data. Given that some clusters are chemically indistinguishable, this study supports the strategy of expanding weak chemical tagging to include families of clusters rather than focusing on individual ones.

Although autonomous driving began as an academic pursuit, it has attracted unprecedented corporate investment over the past ten years. Despite this, current autonomous vehicles primarily operate within ideal conditions, leaving challenging lighting environments—such as night, sunrise, and sunset—as unsolved problems. In these scenarios, conventional cameras struggle with low-light performance and high dynamic range requirements. To tackle these issues, we introduce DSEC, a novel dataset designed to capture such demanding illumination conditions while providing extensive sensory information. DSEC features data from a wide-baseline stereo configuration comprising two color frame cameras and two high-resolution monochrome event cameras. Furthermore, the dataset includes LiDAR scans and RTK GPS measurements, all hardware-synchronized with the camera feeds. A key distinguishing aspect of DSEC is its integration of high-resolution event cameras, which have gained traction for their superior temporal resolution and dynamic range capabilities. However, because these cameras are relatively new, datasets for driving scenarios utilizing them are scarce. This work presents the first large-scale, high-resolution stereo dataset incorporating event cameras. The collection consists of 53 sequences recorded across diverse lighting conditions and offers ground truth disparity, facilitating the development and assessment of event-based stereo algorithms.

The discrepancy in total widths between the $B_c^+$ and $B^+$ mesons has been determined using 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of data from the LHCb experiment, gathered during 7 and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC. By analyzing the time-dependent evolution of $B_c^+ \rightarrow J/\psi \pi^+$ and $B^+\rightarrow J/\psi K^+$ decays, the width difference is found to be
$$ \Delta\Gamma \equiv \Gamma_{B_c^+} - \Gamma_{B^+} = 4.46 \pm 0.14 \pm 0.07 \, \text{mm}^{-1}\text{c}, $$
with the first error representing statistical uncertainty and the second systematic uncertainty. Utilizing the established lifetime of the $B^+$ meson allows for a precise determination of the $B_c^+$ lifetime:
$$ \tau_{B_c^+} = 513.4 \pm 11.0 \pm 5.7 \, \text{fs}, $$
where the initial uncertainty is statistical and the subsequent one is systematic.

The prevailing approach to spatiotemporal action detection involves classifying actions using spatiotemporal features extracted by 2D or 3D Convolutional Networks. However, we contend that many actions are defined by their context, including relevant actors and objects within the video. Consequently, we propose an architecture leveraging self-attention and Graph Convolutional Networks to model contextual cues, such as interactions between actors and between actors and objects, thereby enhancing video-based action detection. This work focuses on a weakly-supervised setting, minimizing the need for action bounding box annotations. Our model improves explainability by visualizing learned context through attention maps, even for actions and objects not seen during training. We assess the model's ability to highlight relevant context using a quantitative metric based on the recall of objects identified by attention maps. The system utilizes a 3D convolutional RGB stream and avoids the computational cost of optical flow. Evaluated on the DALY dataset, which features human-object interaction actions, our experimental results demonstrate that this contextualized method surpasses baseline action detection approaches by over 2 points in Video-mAP. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/micts/acgcn}.

Time-Frequency (TF) domain signal representation is highly beneficial for various applications, such as radar imaging and inverse synthetic aperture radar, as it enables the identification of signal components within a mixed time-frequency plane. Established tools like the Wigner-Ville Distribution (WVD), Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), and their variants are commonly employed for this purpose. The primary objective of any TF representation tool is to provide high-resolution visualization that allows for clear identification of signal features. A widely adopted technique is the reassignment process, which mitigates cross-terms by shifting smoothed WVD values from their original positions to the center of gravity of their respective regions. This article introduces a novel reassignment approach utilizing a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN). By training a CGAN to execute the reassignment task, the proposed method demonstrates, through illustrative examples, the generation of high-resolution TF representations that outperform existing reassignment techniques.

Competing risks data featuring discrete lifetimes frequently arise in practical applications, yet existing literature addressing this specific scenario remains scarce. This study introduces a non-parametric test utilizing U-statistics to evaluate the independence between time to failure and the cause of failure for competing risks data where the lifetime is a discrete random variable. The asymptotic distribution of the proposed test statistic is derived, and an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study is performed to evaluate its finite sample performance. Furthermore, the adaptability of the testing procedure is demonstrated through real-world datasets concerning oral cancer patients and pregnancies exposed to drugs.

The ASACUSA experiment at CERN's Antiproton Decelerator aims to determine the ground state hyperfine splitting of antihydrogen to investigate potential violations of CPT invariance. Its hodoscope detector comprises two layers of 32 plastic scintillator bars, each equipped with two serially connected silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) at the ends. Two supplementary layers originally used scintillator fibers for position resolution along the beam axis; these are now being replaced by scintillating tiles mounted on the existing bars, also read out via SiPMs. When an antihydrogen antiproton annihilates at the hodoscope's center, it generates particles—predominantly pions—that traverse the detector layers, creating detectable signals. During the previous data collection period at CERN, the hodoscope operated successfully. Waveform digitizers combined with software constant fraction discrimination provided the necessary time resolution to distinguish between external particles and those produced internally. However, this readout method suffered from a slow speed. This limitation was overcome by a two-order-of-magnitude improvement achieved by removing the digitizers and substituting them with Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) that process digital time-over-threshold (ToT) signals using leading edge discrimination.

This paper tackles the challenging problem of comparing and classifying 3D human motion sequences. The difficulty arises from the non-linear dynamics of human movement and the temporal variations in surface parametrization. To address this, we propose embedding 3D shape sequences into an infinite-dimensional varifold space equipped with an inner product defined by a positive definite kernel. Our method consists of two key steps: first, representing surfaces as varifolds, which yields metrics that are invariant to parametrization and equivariant to rigid motions; second, representing shape sequences via Gram matrices constructed from their infinite-dimensional Hankel matrices. Consequently, comparing two 3D human motion sequences is framed as comparing their respective Gram-Hankel matrices. Extensive experiments on the CVSSP3D and Dyna datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods for 3D human motion retrieval. The experimental code is available at https://github.com/CRISTAL-3DSAM/HumanComparisonVarifolds.

This study introduces a learning-driven nonlinear $H^\infty$ control framework designed to ensure system performance despite learned dynamics and disturbance estimates. Gaussian Process (GP) regression is employed to refine the nominal system dynamics and generate disturbance estimates using data collected from system interactions. Subsequently, a soft-constrained differential game addressing disturbance attenuation in nonlinear $H^\infty$ control is formulated to derive the controller. This differential game is resolved using the continuous-time min-max Game-Theoretic Differential Dynamic Programming (GT-DDP) algorithm. Simulation studies on a quadcopter illustrate the algorithm's effectiveness in managing external disturbances.

Urban logistics have undergone a paradigm shift in recent years, driven by surging demand for instant, real-time mobility and delivery. This trend presents significant hurdles for logistics providers, as stochastic dynamic vehicle routing problems (SDVRPs) necessitate anticipatory, real-time routing decisions. Identifying efficient actions within this combinatorial space is already a formidable mixed-integer programming (MIP) challenge familiar to operations researchers. This difficulty is compounded by the need to evaluate these actions against future uncertainty and dynamism, a scenario ideally suited for reinforcement learning (RL), a domain well-established in computer science. While solving SDVRPs requires collaboration between these two fields, our findings reveal that such synergy is currently virtually absent. Both communities tend to leverage their individual strengths in isolation, overlooking opportunities for enhancement. This survey paper underscores the untapped potential for research originating from both disciplines, identifies existing barriers in SDVRPs, and directs attention toward collaborative strategies to overcome them.

The goal of image outpainting involves extending an image's current borders and creating new areas based on existing content. While earlier approaches utilized Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to produce realistic images, the absence of explicit semantic representation often results in blurry or anomalous pixels, particularly when outpainting complex regions containing diverse objects. To address this, our work splits the outpainting process into two phases. First, a GAN is trained to expand regions within the semantic segmentation domain rather than the image domain. Second, a separate GAN generates realistic images using these expanded semantic structures. This two-stage design allows the initial model to focus on low-frequency semantic cues such as object sizes and classes, while the second model concentrates on high-frequency details like color and texture. Consequently, our approach manages semantic information more effectively, leading to superior performance in complex scenarios. We assessed the framework across multiple datasets through both quantitative and qualitative analysis. Experimental results confirm that our method produces logical extended semantic layouts and images, surpassing current state-of-the-art models.

This paper introduces the inaugural discrete-time realization of a Rydberg quantum walk within multi-dimensional spatial environments, designed to simulate various classes of topological insulators. By leveraging distance-selective exchange interactions among Rydberg-excited atoms in an atomic array featuring dual lattice constants, the proposed configuration supports both coined and coin-less discrete-time quantum walk (DTQW) models. Complex coupling tessellations are achieved through a global laser that specifically targets sites within the anti-blockade region. Furthermore, long-range interactions enable the design of distinct topologically ordered periodic boundary conditions. By restricting the Rydberg population to two excitations, the system can sustain coherent quantum walks across hundreds of lattice sites and steps using existing technology. These capabilities are expected to enhance the quantum machine's efficiency in executing search algorithms on topologically ordered databases and expand the spectrum of simulatable topological insulators.

This work presents computer code designed to solve Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (HFB) equations using the gradient method, driven by the requirement for efficient and robust tools to compute configurations needed for HFB extensions like the generator coordinate method. The software architecture separates Hamiltonian-specific components from those generic to the gradient approach, enabling complete flexibility in selecting symmetries for HFB solutions. It calculates ground states for both even and odd particle numbers, a decision dictated by the input data. The code's application is demonstrated on $sd$-shell nuclei utilizing the USDB shell-model Hamiltonian.

Investigating gamma-ray burst (GRB) spectra through statistical methods can yield crucial insights into their underlying physics. The Fermi GBM catalog provides estimated GRB parameters—including peak energy, spectral indices, and intensity—derived from fitting the gamma-ray spectral energy distribution (SED) across the total emission (fluence) and the peak flux interval. By employing contingency tables, we examined the correlation between the models that best fit these two time intervals. Our analysis demonstrated a sequential ordering of spectra ranging from power law to Comptonized, then to smoothly broken power law, and finally to the Band model. This finding was corroborated by a correspondence analysis (CA) of the categorical spectral variables for both peak flux and fluence intervals. Furthermore, a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was conducted to identify relationships between spectral categories and model-independent physical data. The LDA results indicated highly significant physical distinctions among the spectral types, a trend that was more pronounced in peak flux spectra than in fluence spectra. We attribute this discrepancy to temporal spectral evolution during the outburst, a hypothesis supported by observed differences in low-energy spectral indices and peak energies between the two intervals. Additionally, our findings confirm that synchrotron radiation plays a significant role in GBM spectra. The mean low-energy spectral index approaches the canonical value of $\alpha = -2/3$ during the peak flux but shifts to approximately -0.9 for fluence spectra. We interpret this shift as evidence that cooling effects are relevant primarily for the fluence spectra.

This study examines the design of optimal routing paths within an Internet of Things (IoT) environment involving moving vehicles. Our model accounts for jammers that can disrupt wireless node communication, degrading Quality of Service (QoS), while also enforcing transmit power limits on battery-powered nodes to conserve energy. We introduce a three-step algorithm to achieve reliable and energy-efficient routing. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that leveraging moving vehicles can significantly reduce total energy consumption. Additionally, we analyze how factors such as path loss, maximum transmit power constraints, and QoS requirements influence the optimal routing design and energy usage.

It is a well-established fact that for a hyperelliptic curve of genus $g$, the symmetric products of $g$ points are described via their Abel-Jacobi images using the hyperelliptic sigma function, a relationship known as the Jacobi inversion formulae. Matsutani and Previato naturally extended these formulae to broader algebraic curves of the form $y^r=f(x)$, which represent specific instances of $(n,s)$ curves, and subsequently identified new vanishing characteristics of the sigma function for such curves. This paper further generalizes the formulae to telescopic curves introduced by Miura, which encompass $(n,s)$ curves as special cases, and establishes new vanishing properties of the sigma function for telescopic curves.

Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) models have proven effective in deep learning-based speech applications, especially when data is scarce. However, their performance heavily relies on the alignment between the SSL training domains and the target data. In contrast, hand-crafted spectral feature (SF) extractors, such as log Mel-filterbanks, are non-learnable components that may offer greater robustness to domain shifts. This study investigates the hypothesis that integrating non-learnable SF extractors with SSL models is a viable strategy for low-resource speech tasks. We introduce a learnable and interpretable framework for fusing SF and SSL representations. Experimental results on three low-resource datasets demonstrate that this framework significantly outperforms both baseline and standalone SSL models in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Speech Translation (ST). Furthermore, we developed a mixture-of-experts model to combine these approaches. This model indicates that when there is a domain mismatch between the SSL training set and the target language data, the contribution of SSL models compared to conventional SF extractors is minimal.

Let $E$ be a complete Hausdorff locally convex space defined over $\mathbb{C}_{p}$. Suppose $A$ belongs to $\mathcal{L}(E)$ and the inverse $(I-\lambda A)^{-1}$ is analytic within its domain. This paper establishes a necessary and sufficient condition on the resolvent of $A$ that ensures the sequence $(A^{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is equi-continuous.

Contemporary deep learning models have transformed computer vision, yet a major limitation of most is their heavy reliance on extensive labeled datasets for effective generalization. Recent advances in few-shot learning seek to mitigate this issue. This paper introduces a novel, lightweight CNN architecture designed for 1-shot image segmentation, inspired by successful semantic segmentation frameworks and adapted specifically for the 1-shot context. We trained the model using four meta-learning algorithms proven effective in image classification. On the selected dataset, our proposed architecture achieves a 70% reduction in parameter count compared to the benchmark while delivering equal or superior mean Intersection over Union (IoU) scores across all four meta-learning methods.

Serverless platforms are fundamentally constrained by the tradeoff between container startup latency and the use of provisioned concurrency, a challenge intensified by the necessity of remote container initialization. This paper introduces MITOSIS, an OS primitive that enables rapid remote forking through a deep integration of the kernel and RDMA. By utilizing RDMA's high-speed remote read features and facilitating partial state migration across serverless containers, MITOSIS narrows the performance divide between local and remote initialization. Notably, it is the first system to spawn over 10,000 new containers from a single instance across multiple machines in under a second, while efficiently transferring the pre-materialized states of the parent container. Implemented on Linux and integrated with the popular serverless platform FN, MITOSIS achieves an 89% reduction in function tail latency during real-world load spikes with significantly reduced memory overhead. Furthermore, for stateful serverless workflows, it accelerates execution time by 86%.

This paper investigates the $p$-adic $L$-functions and (strict) Selmer groups over $\mathbb{Q}_{\infty}$, the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, associated with $p$-adic weight one cusp forms $f$. These forms arise from the $p$-stabilization of weight one Eisenstein series, provided that a specific Eisenstein component of the $p$-ordinary universal cuspidal Hecke algebra satisfies the Gorenstein condition. As an application, we calculate the Iwasawa invariants for ordinary modular forms of weight $k \geq 2$ sharing the same residual Galois representation as $f$, which is reducible and non-$p$-distinguished in this context. By combining these findings with Kato's result \cite[Theorem~17.4.2]{kato04}, we establish the Iwasawa main conjecture for such forms. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples that adhere to the Gorenstein hypothesis. A key analytical advancement is the ability, under the Gorenstein assumption, to define the $p$-adic $L$-functions of weight one forms $f$ as elements within the one-dimensional Iwasawa algebra, following the Greenberg--Vatsal approach. This definition utilizes the Mazur--Kitagawa two-variable $p$-adic $L$-function and allows for explicit computation through local explicit reciprocity laws. On the algebraic side, we determine the (strict) Selmer groups of $f$ over $\mathbb{Q}_{\infty}$ by leveraging the Galois representations of $f$ analyzed in \cite{BDP}.

We demonstrate the existence and finiteness of physical (Sinai-Ruelle-Bowen) measures for a class of $C^k$ ($k>1$) partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms featuring circle center leaves, where these measures' basins encompass a subset of full Lebesgue measure within the ambient manifold. These conditions apply to an open and dense subset of all $C^k$ partially hyperbolic skew-products defined on compact circle bundles. Our approach synthesizes concepts from the theory of Gibbs states for diffeomorphisms with predominantly contracting center directions and recent advancements in cocycle theory over hyperbolic systems, leveraging geometric characteristics of invariant foliations such as absolute continuity. While recent findings indicate that absolute continuity of the center foliation is typically a rigid property in volume-preserving systems, we establish that this rigidity does not hold in the dissipative context, where absolute continuity can instead be robust.

This paper addresses the core challenge of clock synchronization within synchronous multi-agent systems where agents begin with arbitrary clock values that must eventually align. Unlike prior approaches that relied on static networks with strict connectivity requirements and global knowledge, we introduce solutions for time-varying topologies that function without strong connectivity or any global network information. First, focusing on unbounded clocks, we propose a self-stabilizing $MinMax$ algorithm effective whenever, within any sufficiently long bounded interval, a "root" agent exists that can indirectly reach all others. These networks are highly dynamic as roots change arbitrarily, and the duration required for such rootedness remains unknown to the agents. Second, we present a finite-state algorithm for synchronizing periodic clocks in dynamic networks that achieve strong connectivity over bounded periods, again without requiring agents to know this time bound. Notably, this algorithm unifies various previously distinct methods designed for static networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strong connectivity is unnecessary; the algorithm succeeds even if the network is merely rooted over bounded periods with a stable set of roots. Finally, we analyze the time and space complexities of these algorithms and explore how initial timing data can lead to more efficient solutions.

The widespread integration of printed circuit boards (PCBs) into contemporary electronic systems and embedded devices has elevated their integrity to a critical security priority. To achieve cost efficiencies, modern PCB design and fabrication are frequently outsourced to global suppliers, creating numerous security vulnerabilities within the fragmented supply chain. Furthermore, the escalating complexity of PCB architectures provides ample opportunities for covert board-level attacks at various stages of a PCB's lifecycle, endangering a vast array of electronic devices. This paper introduces PDNPulse, a power delivery network (PDN)-based framework for detecting PCB anomalies capable of identifying a broad range of malicious board-level modifications. PDNPulse exploits the inevitable impact of PCB alterations on PDN characteristics, regardless of how minor they are. By analyzing shifts in the PDN impedance profile and employing Frechet distance-based anomaly detection algorithms, PDNPulse effectively distinguishes malicious modifications. Through extensive experiments involving seven commercial-off-the-shelf PCBs with varying design scales, threat models, and seven distinct anomaly types, the study demonstrates that PDNPulse establishes a robust security asymmetry between attackers and defenders.

This study presents inter-order formulas for both partial and complete moments of a Student $t$ distribution with $n$ degrees of freedom. We demonstrate that the partial moment of order $n - j$ regarding any real value $m$ can be formulated using the partial moment of order $j - 1$, where $j \in \{1,\dots, n \}$. Additionally, closed-form expressions for complete moments are derived. The analysis further examines $L_p$-quantiles, a category of generalized quantiles defined via an asymmetric $p$-power loss function. Leveraging these findings, we establish that for a Student $t$ distribution, the $L_{n-j+1}$-quantile and the $L_j$-quantile are identical at any confidence level $\tau$ within the interval $(0, 1)$.

This study addresses an optimization problem characterized by uncertain constraint coefficients, modeled using possibility theory. Specifically, a joint possibility distribution over potential realizations of these coefficients, termed scenarios, is defined. This distribution generates a necessity measure within the scenario set, which subsequently defines an ambiguity set of probability distributions. A distributionally robust approach is employed to transform these imprecise constraints into deterministic equivalents by evaluating the left-hand side of each constraint using a risk measure relative to the worst-case probability distribution within the set. The Conditional Value at Risk serves as the chosen risk measure, offering a generalization of both the strict robust and expected value approaches frequently found in existing literature. Furthermore, the paper outlines a general framework for solving this class of problems and identifies specific cases that admit polynomial-time solutions.

The microstructure of Ni in three dimensions, recorded following five annealing cycles, was contrasted with grain growth simulations employing the threshold dynamics method, which considered capillarity as the sole driving force. By comparing individual grains, researchers pinpointed the origins of discrepancies between experimental data and simulations. The most notable divergence involved the smallest grains, which simulations predicted would shrink and vanish more rapidly than observed experimentally. This premature loss of small grains introduced errors regarding the neighbor counts of surviving grains, revealing a correlation between mistakes in simulated grain volumes and inaccuracies in near-neighbor numbers. Although anisotropic grain boundary properties likely contribute to these differences, the observed size-dependent nature of the errors suggests that incorporating a size-dependent factor into the model for grain boundary migration kinetics may be essential.

Audio segmentation and sound event detection are pivotal areas within machine listening, focusing on identifying acoustic categories and their temporal limits. These technologies support applications such as audio indexing, content analysis, speech recognition, and music information retrieval. While recent studies predominantly utilize a segmentation-by-classification method—dividing audio into frames for individual classification—this paper introduces a novel technique named You Only Hear Once (YOHO), inspired by the Computer Vision algorithm of the same name. Unlike frame-based classification, YOHO frames boundary detection as a regression problem by employing separate output neurons to identify class presence and simultaneously predict start and end points. Experimental results show that YOHO improves the F-measure by 1% to 6% compared to the state-of-the-art Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network across various datasets. Furthermore, due to its end-to-end architecture and reduced number of prediction neurons, YOHO achieves inference speeds at least six times faster than traditional segmentation-by-classification. Additionally, directly predicting acoustic boundaries eliminates the need for extensive post-processing, resulting in a sevenfold speedup in smoothing operations.

We re-examine Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) constraints regarding primordial magnetic fields and turbulent motions, specifically considering how turbulent sources decay between their generation and the BBN epoch. This consideration results in higher predicted estimates for the gravitational wave (GW) signal than earlier projections. Furthermore, we evaluate detection possibilities using space-based interferometers for GWs produced near the electroweak energy scale, as well as pulsar timing arrays and astrometric missions for GWs originating around the quantum chromodynamics energy scale.

Quantum many-body states within the BCS-BEC crossover regime have remained a subject of enduring fascination. We present direct spectroscopic confirmation of this crossover occurring in real space, utilizing spatially resolved scanning tunneling spectroscopy on a FeSe monolayer thin film. This transition is induced by a shift in the band structure relative to the Fermi level. Furthermore, theoretical calculations employing a two-band model qualitatively match the measured spectra across the entire crossover range. Additionally, the observed Zeeman splitting of quasi-particle states aligns with the properties of a condensate. Our findings establish a foundation for investigating exotic BCS-BEC crossover states in two-dimensional crystalline materials at the atomic scale.

A theoretical framework is constructed to examine how gas expansion resulting from heat release impacts unsteady diffusion flames within a pipe flow where reactant mixing is governed by Taylor dispersion. This work extends an existing thermo-diffusive model. Initially, it is demonstrated that for times exceeding radial diffusion scales, the pressure gradient caused by gas expansion is negligible compared to the dominant flow-driving pressure gradient, implying minimal corrections to the background velocity profile. Subsequently, corrections to velocity components, alongside leading-order mixing variables such as concentration, temperature, and density, are calculated for a Burke-Schumann flame. Because the effective Taylor diffusion coefficients depend on gas density, the study reveals both quantitative and qualitative deviations between the predictions of this expanded model and the original thermo-diffusive model.

The severe reduction in outlier detection capabilities caused by stacking Gaussian Processes, especially when paired with non-zero mean functions, leads to artificially low non-parametric variance in areas with sparse training data. To address this, we introduce a hybrid kernel rooted in Varifold theory that functions across both Euclidean and Wasserstein spaces. We argue that explicitly incorporating variance into the calculation of Wasserstein-2 distances is crucial for preserving the identification of outliers throughout the hierarchical structure. Our approach demonstrates superior performance on medium to large-scale datasets and significantly enhances out-of-distribution detection on both synthetic and real-world data.

Achieving scientific breakthroughs on complex issues requires machine learning (ML) to process vast, varied datasets at scale. Nevertheless, strict data governance rules like GDPR and ethical considerations make aggregating personal or sensitive information difficult, driving the adoption of alternative approaches such as distributed ML (DML). Methods like Federated Learning (FL) enable data owners to keep control over their information and train models locally, avoiding data sharing; these are frequently labeled as "privacy-preserving." However, we argue that this terminology is misleading and highlight the dangers of depending on protocols lacking formal privacy definitions. Furthermore, we offer guidance and illustrative examples on how to enhance these algorithms to ensure governance, security, privacy, and verifiability, tailored for a general ML audience without requiring prior knowledge of formal privacy methodologies.

This study introduces a straightforward, universal parametrization scheme for the Hubble parameter tailored to scalar field dark energy models. Our method unifies quintessence and phantom scalar fields within a single analytical framework, allowing for the derivation of cosmological parameters that remain independent of the specific scalar field type. Additionally, we derive a general condition for phantom barrier crossing. To validate this approach, we employ a well-behaved parametrization of the normalized Hubble parameter and constrain various cosmological parameters using extensive observational datasets, including CMB, Supernovae, and BAO data. The results indicate that the current value of the dark energy equation of state lies within the phantom regime. A notable finding is that despite the present phantom nature of the equation of state, a phantom crossing occurred in the recent past. Furthermore, a Bayesian model comparison between the proposed model and the $\Lambda CDM$ model reveals that the data favors our proposed model over the standard $\Lambda CDM$ framework.

Using paraphrasing tools to hide plagiarized content poses a serious risk to academic integrity. To improve the detection of machine-generated rewrites, this study assesses five pre-trained word embedding models paired with machine learning classifiers and advanced neural language models. The research analyzes paraphrased preprints, theses, and Wikipedia articles created using various configurations of SpinBot and SpinnerChief. The most effective approach, Longformer, attained an average F1 score of 80.99%, outperforming human evaluators who scored 78.4% for SpinBot and 65.6% for SpinnerChief cases. These results demonstrate that automated classification can overcome the limitations of established text-matching platforms like Turnitin and PlagScan. To support further investigation, all datasets, code, and two web applications illustrating these contributions are publicly accessible.

The ability to understand the generalization and robustness of machine learning models depends heavily on defining a suitable metric within the data space, a task that becomes especially difficult when dealing with non-Euclidean data like graphs. To address this, we introduce the Tree Mover's Distance (TMD), a pseudometric designed for attributed graphs, and investigate its connection to generalization. By utilizing a hierarchical optimal transport framework, TMD accounts for both the local distribution of node attributes and the distribution of local computation trees—factors known to critically influence graph neural network (GNN) learning. First, we demonstrate that TMD effectively captures properties pertinent to graph classification, as a basic TMD-SVM model performs comparably to standard GNNs. Second, we establish a relationship between TMD and the generalization of GNNs facing distribution shifts, showing that TMD strongly correlates with the magnitude of performance degradation under such conditions.

Recent research has examined the unsigned degenerate r-Stirling numbers of the first kind and the degenerate r-Stirling numbers of the second kind, which represent degenerate forms of the standard unsigned r-Stirling numbers of the first kind and r-Stirling numbers of the second kind, respectively. This paper aims to establish certain identities concerning these special numbers by utilizing their respective inverse relations.

This paper introduces a generalized Lucas matrix, defined as a recursive structure of higher order linked to generalized Fibonacci sequences, and demonstrates numerous unique properties beyond standard matrix algebra. Furthermore, we propose a modified public key cryptography system that utilizes these matrices as keys within an Affine cipher and key agreement protocol, incorporating terms from generalized Lucas sequences under residue operations. Unlike traditional methods requiring the exchange of entire key matrices, this scheme necessitates the transmission of only a pair of numerical parameters, thereby significantly reducing both time and space complexity for key distribution while offering an extensive key space.

Matter's ground state might be strange quark matter (SQM) rather than hadronic matter, allowing for a stable sequence of SQM objects ranging from stars to dwarfs and planets. Under this hypothesis, a strange dwarf possesses a mass comparable to a standard white dwarf but contains an exceptionally dense SQM core (approximately $\sim \rm 4\times10^{14}\,g\,cm^{-3}$), resulting in a significantly reduced radius. This study investigates strange dwarfs within the observed population of "white dwarfs" by analyzing deviations in their mass-radius relationship. Seven candidates were identified with masses between $\sim 0.02$ and $0.12\,M_{\odot}$ and radii confined to roughly 9,000–15,000 km. These objects are LSPM J0815+1633, LP 240-30, BD+20 5125B, LP 462-12, WD J1257+5428, 2MASS J13453297+4200437, and SDSS J085557.46+053524.5. Relative to white dwarfs of equivalent mass, these candidates exhibit distinctly smaller radii, prompting a call for further observations using large radio, infrared, and optical telescopes.

Recent research has predominantly focused on editing face images by utilizing the latent space of pre-trained GANs. However, extending these methods to videos remains underexplored due to three main challenges: a lack of temporal consistency, computational slowness when processing video sequences, and an inability to precisely capture facial motion and expression details. To address these issues, we introduce a new network designed to encode face videos into the StyleGAN latent space for semantic manipulation. Leveraging a vision transformer architecture, our model repurposes the high-resolution segment of the latent vector to ensure temporal coherence. Furthermore, to capture nuanced facial movements and expressions, we develop specialized losses incorporating sparse facial landmarks and dense 3D face meshes. Our approach has been rigorously evaluated and successfully applied to diverse face video editing tasks. Notably, we present a novel framework for controlling pose and expression within a 3D coordinate system. Both qualitative and quantitative assessments demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses existing single-image techniques while achieving real-time performance at 66 frames per second.

In 2001, V. Levenshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, which examines a scenario where an identical sequence from a specific set is sent through several channels, with the decoder observing the resulting distinct outputs. Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed the maximum overlap between two metric balls of radius $r$, provided their centers are separated by at least distance $d$. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations using Hamming distance. Within this framework, we define a Cayley graph and calculate the precise value of the largest intersection of two metric balls under Hamming distance for the cases where $r=4$ and $d\geqslant 5$, as well as when $d=2r$.

This paper explores first- and second-order methods for solving continuous optimization problems in machine learning. For first-order approaches, we introduce a framework transitioning from deterministic or semi-deterministic to stochastic quadratic regularization, utilizing the two-phase structure of stochastic optimization to create a new algorithm featuring adaptive sampling and step sizes. Regarding second-order methods, we present a novel stochastic damped L-BFGS technique that outperforms existing algorithms in the highly nonconvex landscape of deep learning. Both proposed algorithms are tested on standard deep learning benchmarks and demonstrate promising results.

This study examines the polaronic characteristics of a single impurity embedded in a weakly interacting bosonic medium trapped within a one-dimensional double-well potential, utilizing an exact diagonalization method. Our findings indicate that strengthening the impurity-bath coupling causes the residue to vanish, marking the polaron orthogonality catastrophe. In the strongly interacting regime, we derive the asymptotic configurations of the ground state wave function via Schmidt decomposition, which elucidates the observed orthogonality catastrophe. We demonstrate that three distinct residue behaviors emerge relative to the impurity-bath coupling, contingent upon the repulsion of the Bose gas. These regimes are defined by two critical values of bosonic repulsion and stem from the interplay between intra- and interband impurity excitations. Furthermore, these regimes are distinctly identifiable in the corresponding species reduced density matrices, which reveal phase separation at either the one- or two-body level. We also highlight how interspecies mass imbalance influences impurity excitation processes, resulting in a shift of the residue regions. Ultimately, our results clarify the interaction between intra- and interband excitation mechanisms for polaron formation in multiwell traps and for engineering specific polaron entangled states, thereby motivating their exploration in current experimental setups.

This paper extends the recently examined Stochastic Matching problem to better represent key applications such as kidney exchange and others. Previous research on Stochastic Matching assumed a graph $G = (V, E)$ where each edge appears independently with probability $p_e$, aiming to find a degree-bounded subgraph $Q$ whose expected maximum matching approximates that of the realized subgraph. However, this earlier model failed to address vertex dropouts, a critical factor in scenarios like kidney exchange (where donors or patients withdraw) and online platforms (where profiles may be fraudulent). Consequently, we investigate a generalized Stochastic Matching framework where both vertices and edges are realized independently with probabilities $p_v$ and $p_e$, respectively, offering a more accurate fit for these applications. We present the first algorithms and analysis for this generalization, demonstrating strong approximation ratios. Specifically, we prove that a natural algorithm achieves an approximation factor of at least $0.6568$ for unweighted graphs and $1/2 + \epsilon$ for weighted graphs (where $\epsilon > 0$ is a constant). Furthermore, by utilizing edge degree constrained subgraphs (EDCS), we enhance the result for unweighted graphs to $2/3$.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge established a novel dataset to benchmark contemporary image copy detection techniques, attracting 200 participants. This study provides both qualitative and quantitative evaluations of the leading entries, revealing that the most challenging transformations include severe cropping, concealment within unrelated images, and local pixel perturbations. The primary algorithmic strategies employed by the top performers encompass training with robust augmentations, self-supervised learning, score normalization, explicit overlay detection, and a workflow involving global descriptor matching followed by pairwise image comparison.

This study presents CUTS (Contrastive and Unsupervised Training for Segmentation), the inaugural fully unsupervised deep learning framework designed for medical image segmentation. This approach unlocks the potential of the vast majority of unlabeled imaging data. Segmenting medical images into regions of interest is vital for enhancing patient diagnoses and quantitative research. However, segmentation is often hindered by a scarcity of labeled data, as obtaining expert annotations for new datasets or tasks is costly, labor-intensive, and prone to inter-annotator inconsistency. To address this, we employ self-supervision utilizing pixel-centered patches derived directly from the images. Our unsupervised methodology relies on a training objective that integrates both contrastive learning and autoencoding. Unlike previous contrastive learning methods for medical segmentation, which focused on image-level training or used such techniques merely as pre-training steps requiring subsequent supervised fine-tuning, our framework operates entirely unsupervised at the pixel-centered patch level. We achieve this by incorporating novel augmentations, a patch reconstruction loss, and a new pixel clustering and identification framework. The model demonstrates improved performance on several key medical imaging tasks, validated by held-out expert annotations for segmenting geographic atrophy (GA) regions in retinal images.

The problem of determinant maximization provides a unified framework for modeling challenges across various disciplines, including statistics \cite{pukelsheim2006optimal}, convex geometry \cite{Khachiyan1996}, fair allocations\linebreak \cite{anari2016nash}, combinatorics \cite{AnariGV18}, spectral graph theory \cite{nikolov2019proportional}, network design, and random processes \cite{kulesza2012determinantal}. In such instances, given a set of vectors $U=\{v_1,\ldots, v_n\} \subset \RR^d$, the objective is to select a subset $S\subseteq U$ that maximizes the determinant of the matrix $\sum_{i\in S} v_i v_i^\top$. Typically, the chosen subset $S$ must adhere to additional combinatorial constraints, such as a cardinality limit ($|S|\leq k$) or a matroid constraint (where $S$ forms a basis of a matroid defined on the vectors). This paper presents a deterministic algorithm running in polynomial time that achieves an $r^{O(r)}$-approximation for any matroid with rank $r\leq d$. This result surpasses prior approaches, which offered $e^{O(r^2)}$-approximations using $e^{O(r)}$-approximate \emph{estimation} methods \cite{NikolovS16,anari2017generalization,AnariGV18,madan2020maximizing} for $r\leq d$. Previous methods relied on convex relaxations and their connections to stable and strongly log-concave polynomials. Conversely, our approach leverages combinatorial techniques for matroid intersection, iteratively enhancing solutions by identifying \emph{alternating negative cycles} within the \emph{exchange graph} defined by the matroids. Although the $\det(.)$ function is non-linear, we demonstrate that applying suitable linear approximations at each iteration is sufficient to derive the improved algorithm.

Dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) are among the most dark matter-dominated systems in the universe. Typically, their dynamical masses are estimated based on stellar kinematics assuming a state of equilibrium. However, as satellites of massive galaxies like the Milky Way, these objects are subject to tidal forces. This study examines the consequences of the equilibrium assumption by modeling the Sculptor dSph using tailored $N$-body simulations. These simulations follow observationally motivated orbits within the Milky Way's gravitational field, calibrated to match the observed spectroscopic and photometric data of Sculptor's stars. Our results indicate that while the tidal field does not directly affect the stellar component, it strips approximately 30% to 60% of the mass from the more extended dark matter halo. Consequently, given the latest measurements of Sculptor's proper motion, the system appears unaffected by tides, making stellar kinematics a reliable indicator of its internal dynamics. In simulations consistent with observed Sculptor properties, the dark-to-luminous mass ratio is approximately 6 within the stellar half-light radius ($\approx 0.3$ kpc) and exceeds 50 within the maximum analyzed radius ($\approx 1.5^\circ \approx 2$ kpc).

Adapting a trained Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model to new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting of previous tasks, thereby restricting the model's capacity for continual learning and expansion to new speakers, dialects, or languages. Focusing on End-to-End ASR, this paper introduces a straightforward yet effective approach to mitigate catastrophic forgetting: weight averaging. By averaging the parameters of the adapted model with the previous one, the method maintains high performance on both old and new tasks. Performance can be further enhanced by incorporating a knowledge distillation loss during the adaptation process. We demonstrate the method's efficacy on both monolingual and multilingual ASR tasks, where it significantly outperforms all baselines, even in its simplest configuration.

While existing deep learning approaches for musical instrument recognition typically rely on abundant data for specific classes, this study leverages hierarchical relationships within a few-shot learning framework to classify a broader range of instruments using only a few examples at inference. By applying a hierarchical loss function to prototypical networks and aggregating prototypes in a manner that reflects a predefined instrument taxonomy, we achieve these results without modifying the network architecture, allowing for easy addition or removal of hierarchy levels. Compared to non-hierarchical few-shot baselines, our approach yields a substantial improvement in classification accuracy and significantly reduces the severity of errors on instrument classes not seen during training.

This paper examines recent progress regarding the restoration of QCD chiral symmetry at finite temperature using Effective Theories. We derive $U(3)$ Ward Identities linking pseudoscalar susceptibilities to quark condensates, which elucidate the behavior of lattice meson screening masses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that unitarized interactions and the thermally generated $f_0(500)$ state are crucial for characterizing the transition via the scalar susceptibility.

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission by NASA aims to enhance our knowledge of hot Jupiters by delivering a magnitude-limited, all-sky sample of transiting candidates ideal for population analysis. Creating this dataset necessitates verifying hundreds of potential planets via supplementary follow-up studies. This work introduces twenty confirmed hot Jupiters identified through TESS data and validated using photometric, spectroscopic, and imaging techniques organized by the TESS Follow-up Observing Program (TFOP). All twenty planets orbit relatively bright FGK stars ($10.9 < G < 13.0$) with periods under 7 days. While most share a mass similar to Jupiter, four are lighter than Saturn. TOI-3976 b, the sample's longest-period planet at 6.6 days, may possess a moderate eccentricity ($e = 0.18\pm0.06$), whereas the remaining targets appear to follow circular orbits. Additionally, the projected stellar obliquity of TOI-1937A b—a hot Jupiter with a 22.4-hour orbital period—was measured via the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect, revealing a well-aligned orbit with the star's spin axis ($|\lambda| = 4.0\pm3.5^\circ$). Although we explored whether TOI-1937 belongs to the NGC 2516 open cluster, the evidence remained inconclusive. These discoveries contribute to a broader initiative to construct a comprehensive hot Jupiter sample for future demographic and detailed characterization research.

This study focuses on deriving fundamental characteristics of hyperbolic valued metric spaces. Additionally, we formulate the Banach contraction principle within the context of hyperbolic metrics. Furthermore, we define a hyperbolic valued metric on the set of all continuous hyperbolic valued functions and demonstrate several associated theorems.

Web search and large-scale web analytics depend on processing web archives stored in a standardized, efficient format. Since its 2008 introduction, the IIPC's Web ARCive (WARC) format has become the industry standard. Functioning as a collection of individually compressed HTTP request and response records, it enables constant-time random access to diverse web data using readily available open-source parsers in various programming languages, with WARCIO serving as the de-facto standard for Python. However, when handling web archives at the terabyte or petabyte scale, even minor inefficiencies in these tools accumulate rapidly, leading to wasted compute time ranging from hours to weeks. By examining the fundamental components of WARCIO and identifying its performance bottlenecks, we developed FastWARC, a high-performance WARC processing library for Python implemented in C++/Cython. This new library achieves performance gains of 1.6 to 8 times compared to existing solutions.

Mayall II (G1) represents one of the brightest globular clusters within M31. In this study, we estimate its age and mass by aligning multicolor photometry with theoretical stellar population synthesis models. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset that includes far- and near-ultraviolet GALEX observations, broad-band UBVRI measurements, and infrared JHK_s data from 2MASS, we generated the most detailed spectral energy distribution for G1 to date, covering wavelengths from 1538 to 20,000 Å. Comparing this distribution against various simple stellar population (SSP) models indicates a mean age consistent with G1 being one of M31's earliest constituents, having formed approximately 1.7 billion years after the Big Bang. Regardless of the specific SSP model or stellar initial mass function used, the derived mass estimates (around $10^7 M_\odot$) suggest G1 is among the most massive globular clusters in the Local Group. However, we hypothesize that this unusually high mass implies G1 might not be a true globular cluster. Additionally, we estimate that G1 likely contains an average of $(1.65\pm0.63)\times10^2$ far-ultraviolet-luminous, hot extreme horizontal-branch stars, contingent on the chosen SSP model. More broadly, we demonstrate that extensive multi-passband photometry combined with SSP analysis can yield age determinations for old stellar populations with accuracy comparable to integrated spectroscopy or resolved stellar photometry, assuming certain free parameters are independently constrained.

The Electron Ion Collider (EIC) mandates that absolute helion (${}^3\text{He}$, $h$) beam polarization be measured with systematic uncertainties below $\sigma^\text{syst}_P/P\lesssim1\%$. This study explores using the Polarized Atomic Hydrogen Gas Jet Target (HJET)—currently employed at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider to achieve $\sim0.5\%$ accuracy in absolute proton polarization—to measure the polarization of a $\sim$100 GeV/n helion beam. Key challenges in adapting the HJET method for this purpose include: (i) the need for high-precision knowledge of the ratio between $p^\uparrow{h}$ and $h^\uparrow{p}$ analyzing powers, $A_\text{N}^{ph}(t)/A_\text{N}^{hp}(t)$; (ii) the risk of ${}^3\text{He}$ beam breakup; and (iii) compatibility with a 10 ns bunch spacing. Preliminary analysis suggests these obstacles can be surmounted, enabling the HJET to measure the helion beam's absolute polarization with the necessary accuracy.

This paper presents a Nivat-like characterization for weighted alternating automata (WAFA) over commutative semirings. We demonstrate that WAFA can be defined as the concatenation of weighted finite tree automata (WFTA) and a particular class of tree homomorphisms. Furthermore, we establish that the series recognized by these automata are closed under inverse homomorphisms but not under homomorphisms themselves. Additionally, we provide a logical characterization utilizing weighted MSO logic for trees and explore the significant relationship between WAFA and polynomial automata. Leveraging existing results for polynomial automata, we prove that the ZERONESS problem for WAFA with rational number weights is decidable.

This research examines diffusion processes halted or reflected at a domain's boundary, where the generator consists of a primary component that degenerates orthogonally to the boundary and a minor non-degenerate perturbation. The dynamics of these processes govern the stabilization of solutions to associated parabolic equations featuring a small parameter, giving rise to metastability effects where asymptotic behavior varies with the time scale as the perturbation diminishes. The study addresses initial-boundary value problems under both Dirichlet and Neumann conditions, and additionally investigates periodic homogenization for operators exhibiting degeneration.

Let $K$ denote a $p$-adically closed field and let $G$ be a group interpretable within $K$. We demonstrate that if $G$ is definably semisimple (meaning it possesses no definable infinite normal abelian subgroups), then there exists a finite normal subgroup $H$ such that the quotient $G/H$ is definably isomorphic to a $K$-linear group. This conclusion also holds for models of $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbb{Q}_p^{an})$.

Virtual development and prototyping have become essential components of automated driving systems (ADS), supported by numerous software tools. Among these, IPG Automotive's CarMaker is a widely adopted solution within both the scientific community and the automotive industry, offering extensive capabilities for modeling vehicles, drivers, control systems, sensors, and environmental conditions. Since realistic environment perception is crucial for developing highly automated vehicle guidance functions, precise detection of longitudinal and lateral paths is required to identify relevant traffic elements and plan trajectories. To address this, a lane sensor model was created to efficiently detect lanes within the CarMaker simulation environment. Specifically, the Advanced Lane Detection Model (ALDM) has been optimized for computational efficiency, enabling accurate lateral and longitudinal vehicle guidance.

Using the kinetic energy driven superconductivity framework, the electromagnetic response of cuprate superconductors is investigated via the linear response method. By evaluating the response function kernel under a specular reflection model for a purely transverse vector potential, the study calculates the local magnetic field distribution, magnetic penetration depth, and superfluid density. Results indicate that at low temperatures, the magnetic field profile exhibits exponential decay near the surface, while the penetration depth scales linearly with temperature, aside from significant deviations observed at extremely low temperatures. Furthermore, the superfluid density is observed to decline linearly as doping concentration decreases in the underdoped region. Finally, the issue of gauge invariance is resolved by proposing and discussing an approximation for the dressed current vertex that adheres to local charge conservation.

This paper introduces $lc$-homology, a scaled homology theory for metric spaces that allows any metric space to be viewed as "locally contractible." We verify that $lc$-homology fulfills all Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms except the exactness axiom, while its corresponding $lc$-cohomology satisfies all cohomology axioms. This theory relaxes the smooth manifold constraints on compact metric spaces, enabling the entropy conjecture to hold for the first $lc$-homology group.

A software architect transforms system requirements into a suitable architecture through an optimization process. However, determining which quality enhancements to prioritize—such as security versus reliability—remains a challenge. Furthermore, in software product lines, it is unclear whether a minor improvement across multiple products should take precedence over a significant improvement for a single product. Although existing optimization methods address various stages of the process, none systematically guide architects in deriving an optimal architecture from initial requirements. This work introduces an end-to-end approach for generating an optimal architecture for individual products and an optimal family of architectures for product lines. We validate this approach through a case study optimizing five industry-grade products within a real-world product line architecture, where 359 potential combinations of ten distinct quality efforts were evaluated and prioritized.

This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the lowest-order constraint variational (LOCV) method with the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. Our findings reveal that without a magnetic field, the energy per particle remains symmetric with respect to the spin polarization parameter, indicating that spontaneous phase transitions to a ferromagnetic state do not occur in nuclear matter. However, when magnetic fields reach $B\gtrsim 10^{18}\ G$, this symmetry is broken, and the energy exhibits a minimum at a positive spin polarization parameter. Additionally, we observed that the magnetic field's influence on energy is more pronounced at low densities, where the spin polarization parameter demonstrates greater sensitivity to the magnetic field.

A significant emerging trend in additive manufacturing involves utilizing optimization algorithms to automatically design industrial components like wings, rudders, and beams. Known as topology optimization, this process determines the optimal material distribution within a 3D grid to satisfy specific physical parameters. While designers leverage these automated systems to analyze how physical constraints influence the final product's characteristics, this understanding remains difficult to achieve due to the vast design space and the potential for minor parameter adjustments to yield drastically different outcomes. To overcome these hurdles, we propose a visualization-based method for exploring design solutions. Our novel approach centers on summarizing the ensemble of solutions by automatically selecting representative examples and expressing the full set of results as combinations thereof. These examples establish a meaningful parameterization of the design space, enabling exploration via standard high-dimensional visualization techniques. We present evaluations of our subset selection methodology and demonstrate that the overall approach effectively meets the requirements of expert designers.

We explore recent approaches in metric space theory and the opportunities they offer, with a particular emphasis on generalizations of Lyapunov exponents first introduced in the context of dynamical systems and differential equations. These extensions are now found across diverse fields, including topology, group theory, probability theory, operator theory, and deep learning.

Numerous COVID-19 survivors experienced lingering symptoms such as fatigue, delirium, and headaches, though the long-term health implications of these conditions remain uncertain. To enable timely intervention and treatment, there is a critical need for a system to monitor the health status of these individuals. Given the shortage of personnel available for direct patient follow-up, we propose a novel machine learning-powered smart chatbot solution designed to collect personalized information, effectively creating a digital diary. This article outlines the design framework and components of our prototype.

The necessity for analyzing streaming data exists across numerous applications, with a key research focus being the mining of sequential patterns within these streams. Existing research typically identifies patterns based on their presence in individual transactions, often neglecting the sequences of itemsets and their repeated occurrences. However, examining patterns across a window of itemset streams, including their multiple instances, offers enhanced capabilities to detect essential pattern characteristics and inter-relationships that current presence-based methods miss. This paper investigates this novel sequential pattern mining challenge and introduces a specialized miner equipped with innovative strategies to efficiently prune the search space. Experimental results on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Since numerous relations span across sentence boundaries, there has been a growing focus on document-level relation extraction (DocRE). DocRE involves synthesizing information both within and across sentences to capture intricate interactions between entity mentions. Although most current methods rely on a pipeline that takes entities as input, jointly learning entity and relation extraction can enhance performance and efficiency through shared parameters and training steps. This paper introduces seq2rel, a sequence-to-sequence framework that end-to-end learns the DocRE subtasks—entity extraction, coreference resolution, and relation extraction—replacing the traditional pipeline of specialized components. By employing a technique called "entity hinting," we evaluate our method against existing pipeline-based approaches on several prominent biomedical datasets, achieving superior performance in some cases. Furthermore, we provide the first end-to-end results on these datasets for future benchmarking and demonstrate that our end-to-end model outperforms pipeline-based alternatives. Our code, data, and trained models are accessible at {\url{https://github.com/johngiorgi/seq2rel}}, along with an online demo at {\url{https://share.streamlit.io/johngiorgi/seq2rel/main/demo.py}}.

Digital pathology offers a promising avenue for deploying fully convolutional networks (FCNs) in tasks like the semantic segmentation of whole slide images (WSIs). Nevertheless, conventional FCNs struggle with multi-resolution challenges stemming from the pyramidal structure of WSIs, creating a need for networks capable of learning and integrating information across various levels. This paper introduces two innovative multi-resolution architectures built upon the widely used U-Net framework, which are assessed using a benchmark dataset for binary semantic segmentation of WSIs. The proposed methods surpass standard U-Net performance, exhibiting enhanced learning and generalization abilities.

This study evaluates contributions from a two-Higgs doublet model with additional Yukawa couplings to the electric dipole moments (EDMs) of charged leptons, with a specific emphasis on the muon and tau. Given that upcoming experiments—such as Muon g-2, J-PARC, PSI, and Belle II—are projected to improve sensitivity by multiple orders of magnitude within the next decade, our analysis assumes extra Yukawa couplings have strengths comparable to the Standard Model and exotic scalars exist in the sub-TeV regime. Under these conditions, we determine that the EDMs of the muon and tau can be amplified to levels exceeding those of new physics scenarios scaled by lepton mass. This enhancement is primarily driven by the flavor-conserving extra top coupling, $\rho_{tt}$, through established two-loop diagrams. Furthermore, if the muon $g-2$ anomaly originates from a one-loop process mediated by a singly enhanced lepton flavor-violating $\rho_{\tau\mu}$ coupling, this could also generate a significant muon EDM detectable by future experiments.

Ensuring privacy and communication efficiency remains a significant challenge in federated neural network training, with their integration still being an unresolved issue. This study presents a unified approach that merges highly compressed communication with differential privacy (DP). We adapt a Relative Entropy Coding (REC) technique for the federated context. By making a slight adjustment to REC, we derive a provably differentially private algorithm called DP-REC and demonstrate methods for calculating its privacy bounds. Experimental results indicate that DP-REC substantially lowers communication overhead while achieving privacy protection levels comparable to current state-of-the-art solutions.

Observations of external galaxies are mapped onto the two-dimensional sky plane. Deriving the three-dimensional intrinsic density distribution of a galaxy from this 2D image is difficult, particularly for barred galaxies, yet it is essential for building galactic dynamical models. This study introduces a method for deprojecting barred galaxies, validated against mock images derived from an N-body simulation featuring a peanut-shaped bar. The approach decomposes a galaxy image into a disk and a bulge (which includes the bar); after subtracting the disk component, a barred bulge remains. We apply a multi-Gaussian expansion (MGE) fit to each part, deprojecting them individually by treating the disk as axisymmetric and the barred bulge as triaxial. Constraints are applied to the barred bulge, requiring it to align with the disk plane and maintain a disk-like thickness in outer regions. The final 3D density distribution is constructed by merging the deprojected barred bulge and disk. While our model generally recovers the 3D density of the disk and inner barred bulge, it does not perfectly replicate the peanut-shaped structure. Using identical initial conditions, we integrated orbits within both our model-inferred potential and the true potential (by freezing the N-body simulation). Results show that 85% of these orbits exhibit similar morphologies in both potentials, and our model successfully supports orbits that produce a boxy/peanut-shaped structure and an elongated bar comparable to those in the true potential.

The derivation of the relationship between the quasielastic excitation function and the capture cross section is presented. It is demonstrated that quasielastic data serve as a valuable method for determining capture cross sections and the angular momenta of captured systems in the reactions $^{16}$O+$^{144,154}$Sm, $^{208}$Pb, $^{20}$Ne+$^{208}$Pb, and $^{32}$S+$^{90,96}$Zr at energies near and exceeding the Coulomb barrier.

While Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) feedback is essential in galaxy simulations to control star formation, it also induces downstream impacts on the dark matter distribution within halos and the stellar kinematics of central galaxies. By comparing Numerical Investigation of a Hundred Astrophysical Objects (NIHAO) simulations that include and exclude AGN physics, we examine how AGN influences dark matter profiles and central stellar rotation. Specifically, we analyze the effects of AGN on the concentration-halo mass ($c-M$) relation and the stellar spin parameter ($\lambda_R$). Our findings indicate that AGN physics is vital for lowering the central density of massive galaxies ($\gtrsim 10^{12}$ M$_\odot$) to align with observations from the Spitzer Photometry & Accurate Rotation Curves (SPARC) sample. Furthermore, AGN feedback plays a critical role in replicating the observed dichotomy between slow and fast rotators identified by the ATLAS$^{3\text{D}}$ survey; without the suppression of star formation driven by AGN, the number of fast rotators would significantly surpass observational limits. This study demonstrates that multiple secondary effects underscore the necessity of AGN feedback in galaxy formation, providing avenues to constrain its implementation in numerical models.

We investigate the fluctuations driving pairing in the $d$-wave superconducting phase of the two-dimensional Hubbard model at intermediate coupling using cluster dynamical mean-field theory with a numerically exact quantum impurity solver. By examining how momentum- and frequency-dependent fluctuations induce $d$-wave superconductivity across various representations, we establish antiferromagnetic fluctuations as the pairing mechanism responsible for superconductivity in both underdoped and overdoped regimes. However, within the intermediate coupling regime, the dominant magnetic fluctuations can differ substantially from those predicted by conventional spin-fluctuation theory.

We introduce Poly-GAN, a new conditional GAN framework inspired by the challenge of Fashion Synthesis, which involves automatically draping garments onto human models in arbitrary poses. Designed to accept multiple conditioning inputs, Poly-GAN is versatile enough to handle various tasks such as image alignment, stitching, and inpainting. While existing approaches typically rely on a three-stage pipeline involving separate networks for alignment, stitching, and refinement, Poly-GAN is the first to employ a unified architecture to execute all three functions simultaneously. Our proposed design enforces conditioning throughout every layer of the encoder and implements skip connections from coarse encoder layers to their corresponding decoder layers. This system enables the spatial transformation of garments according to the model's RGB skeleton at any pose, supports stitching regardless of garment orientation, and performs inpainting on garment masks containing irregular holes. On the DeepFashion dataset, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of Structural Similarity Index and Inception Score metrics.

We present N-ImageNet, a large-scale dataset designed for robust, fine-grained object recognition using event cameras. This dataset was gathered using programmable hardware where an event camera systematically moves around a monitor displaying ImageNet images. With its extensive number of classes and samples, N-ImageNet serves as a rigorous benchmark for event-based object recognition. Our empirical results demonstrate that pretraining on N-ImageNet enhances the performance of event-based classifiers and enables them to learn effectively from limited labeled data. Furthermore, we introduce several N-ImageNet variants to evaluate classifier robustness across diverse camera trajectories and challenging lighting conditions, while proposing a new event representation to mitigate performance degradation. To our knowledge, this is the first quantitative study of how various environmental factors impact event-based object recognition algorithms. We anticipate that N-ImageNet and its variants will provide valuable guidance for the practical deployment of event-based object recognition systems in real-world scenarios.

Dense video captioning involves identifying interesting events within untrimmed videos and generating textual descriptions for each. While previous approaches have relied exclusively on visual data, neglecting the audio track, sound and speech are crucial cues for human understanding of an environment. This paper introduces a novel dense video captioning method capable of integrating any number of modalities for event description. Specifically, we demonstrate how incorporating audio and speech can enhance dense video captioning models. We employ an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system to generate temporally aligned text transcripts, treating them as a distinct input alongside video frames and the audio track. We frame the captioning task as a machine translation problem and leverage the recently developed Transformer architecture to transform multi-modal inputs into textual descriptions. Our model's performance is evaluated on the ActivityNet Captions dataset. Ablation studies reveal a significant contribution from audio and speech components, indicating that these modalities provide substantial complementary information to video frames. Additionally, we offer a detailed analysis of the ActivityNet Caption results using category tags from the original YouTube videos. The code is publicly available at github.com/v-iashin/MDVC.

The current standard for document ranking involves a two-stage approach: an initial retrieval using classical information retrieval methods, followed by a neural re-ranking model. The highest performance is attained when transformer-based models, such as BERT, serve as the re-rankers. For the MS MARCO document re-ranking task, we utilize Longformer, a BERT-like model designed for long documents. The full code required for training this model is available at: https://github.com/isekulic/longformer-marco

This paper demonstrates that the permeability of both porous materials and bubbly fluids represent limiting cases of a complexified two-fluid model originally proposed in Lipton_Avellaneda_1990. We define the inclusion fluid's viscosity as $z\mu_1$ and the hosting fluid's viscosity as $\mu_1\in \mathbb{R}^+$, where $z\in\mathbb{C}$. The proof is established by constructing solutions for both large and small $|z|$ through an iterative process combined with analytic continuation. Furthermore, we show that for a fixed microstructure, the permeabilities of these three scenarios share the same integral representation formula (IRF) given in Equation (99), albeit with different values for the contrast parameter $s:=1/(z-1)$. This holds true provided $s$ lies outside the interval $[-\frac{2E_2^2}{1+2E_2^2},-\frac{1}{1+2E_1^2}]$, where $E_1$ and $E_2$ are positive extension constants determined solely by the geometry of the periodic pore space.

Let $\Omega$ be a smooth, bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N\ge2$, and let $\Omega_\epsilon$ denote $\Omega$ excluding the ball $B(P,\epsilon)$ centered at an interior point $P$ with radius $\epsilon$. This paper determines the count, position, and non-degeneracy of critical points of the Robin function within $\Omega_\epsilon$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. We demonstrate that the location of $P$ is pivotal for the existence and multiplicity of these critical points.
