The method's effectiveness is validated through various synthetic and real-world examples. Most significantly, by gating out nuisance input variables, our approach yields superior extracted representations compared to other linear, non-linear, and sparse CCA-based models.

We have made available a fresh set of stellar limb-darkening coefficients (LDCs) and intensity profiles, calculated using quadratic, power-2, and claret-4 laws across Kepler, U, B, V, and R passbands, derived from STAGGER model atmospheres. These datasets are accessible for download via Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.5593162). We evaluated the ExoTETHyS-computed LDCs against previously published values generated from identical atmospheric models by employing the "SPAM" technique, which utilizes synthetic light curves to determine LDCs that best match exoplanetary transit photometry. Our findings confirm that ExoTETHyS accomplishes the same goal with a significantly more streamlined algorithm.

Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) is an off-policy actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm grounded in entropy regularization. By maximizing the balance between expected return and policy entropy (randomness), SAC has achieved state-of-the-art results on various continuous-control benchmarks, surpassing both earlier off-policy and on-policy methods. The algorithm operates off-policy by uniformly sampling data from a replay buffer to update the parameters of its policy and value function networks. To enhance SAC's sample efficiency and performance, we propose specific modifications. Our improved approach first introduces a novel prioritization scheme to select superior samples from the experience replay buffer. Secondly, we train the policy and value function networks using a combination of this prioritized off-policy data and the most recent on-policy data. Comparative evaluations against vanilla SAC and recent SAC variants demonstrate that our method outperforms these benchmarks. Furthermore, our approach exhibits greater stability and sample efficiency when tested across multiple continuous control tasks within MuJoCo environments.

Workplace accidents remain a severe issue resulting in significant fatalities, injuries, and economic damage, with climate change and global warming exacerbating risks for industrial workers. To mitigate these casualties, it is essential to proactively identify hazardous environments by monitoring Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) usage and recognizing unsafe behaviors. Consequently, we introduce an industrial monitoring platform designed to detect PPE compliance and classify unsafe activities within group settings involving multiple humans and objects over extended durations. This method represents the first approach to analyzing prolonged interactions among multiple people or objects by integrating pose estimation with PPE detection into a unified system. Furthermore, we provide the inaugural open-source dataset featuring industrial workplace videos annotated with action classifications and PPE detections. The proposed solution is practical and effective, as it can be deployed using existing surveillance cameras within industrial facilities.

This research investigates the global existence, boundedness, and convergence of nonnegative classical solutions for a Neumann initial-boundary value problem associated with a cross-diffusive SIS epidemic model featuring a power-law infection mechanism that generalizes the standard mass action approach. We establish the global existence and boundedness of these solutions within specific parameter regimes and identify both threshold and non-threshold long-term dynamics for globally bounded solutions. These results substantially enhance and broaden prior related investigations.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) involves training from a static dataset, where most existing algorithms constrain or regularize the policy to avoid errors caused by out-of-distribution actions. Adapting standard RL methods for offline use typically adds complexity, introducing new hyperparameters and auxiliary components like generative models. This paper proposes a deep RL approach that requires minimal modifications to achieve state-of-the-art performance. By simply incorporating a behavior cloning term into the policy update of an online RL algorithm and normalizing the data, we create a straightforward baseline that is easy to implement and tune. Furthermore, this method reduces overall runtime by more than half by eliminating the computational overhead inherent in previous techniques.

A core challenge in computer animation involves generating purposeful and realistic human motion from a comprehensive library of motion capture data. To address this, we employ data-driven generative models known as Motion VAEs, specifically autoregressive conditional variational autoencoders. Within these models, the latent variables establish the action space, dictating how movements evolve temporally. This action space serves as the foundation for planning or control algorithms to synthesize target motions. Notably, we apply deep reinforcement learning to train controllers capable of executing goal-oriented movements. We validate the method's efficacy across various tasks, assess key system-design decisions, and outline the existing constraints of Motion VAEs.

If primordial black holes (PBHs) account for over 10% of the dark matter density, their current energy density matches that of baryons. This cosmic coincidence may suggest a shared origin for the formation of PBHs and the universe's baryon asymmetry. Baryogenesis could be initiated by a rapid shift in the inflaton's rolling rate from slow-roll to (nearly) ultraslow-roll phases, generating significant curvature perturbations that lead to PBH formation within single-field inflationary models. We demonstrate that the constraints required for baryogenesis push the PBH contribution to dark matter, alongside the predicted mass range, the frequency window of the resulting stochastic gravitational wave background, and the associated cosmic microwave background tensor-to-scalar ratio amplitude, into potentially observable ranges.

Flexible building blocks used to construct mechanical metamaterials can display a wide array of remarkable mechanical behaviors, including negative elastic constants, shape transformations, programmability, and memory. Historically, however, energy dissipation in these flexible structures has been largely neglected, often leading researchers to carefully select constitutive materials specifically to minimize dissipative effects. This approach is increasingly inadequate in dynamic loading scenarios where dissipation cannot be ignored. This review demonstrates that the interaction between mechanical instabilities and viscoelasticity is pivotal and can be exploited to achieve novel functionalities. First, we illustrate how this interplay is essential for comprehending the dynamic behavior of flexible dissipative metamaterials that rely on buckling and snapping mechanisms. Furthermore, we explore the new possibilities offered by spatially patterning viscoelastic properties to design metamaterials with characteristics that vary according to the loading rate.

This research explores the use of deep learning for timbre transfer, aiming to convert the timbre of a source audio to that of a target audio with minimal quality degradation. The methodology integrates Variational Autoencoders with Generative Adversarial Networks to create meaningful source representations and generate realistic target audio. The system is evaluated on the Flickr 8k Audio dataset for speaker vocal timbre transfer and the URMP dataset for instrument musical timbre transfer. Various iterations of the approach are trained and assessed using SSIM (Structural Similarity Index) and FAD (Fréchet Audio Distance) to compare generalization performance. Results indicate that a many-to-many architecture outperforms a one-to-one approach in reconstructive capabilities, and that a basic residual block design is more effective than a bottleneck design for enriching latent space content information. Additionally, the study finds that choosing between a variational autoencoder and a vanilla autoencoder for the cyclic loss component does not significantly affect the model's reconstructive or adversarial translation performance.

Maintaining entangled states is crucial for quantum applications, yet environmental energy dissipation often hinders this preservation. Consequently, engineering the environment surrounding quantum bits is essential, as it directly influences the system's final state. This study introduces a concurrence measure to evaluate entanglement between two qubits coupled to a rolled-up epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) waveguide reservoir composed of alternating metal and dielectric layers. Numerical results indicate that this proposed reservoir can sustain qubit entanglement at the cutoff wavelength by facilitating enhanced energy transfer. Furthermore, this unique ENZ waveguide structure offers potential for diverse quantum technologies, including quantum communication, information processing, and single-photon generation. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this novel design can be manufactured using affordable self-rolling fabrication techniques.

String theory stands as the leading contender for a unified theory of everything, yet it requires ten dimensions for mathematical consistency. To derive four-dimensional physics, the remaining six dimensions must be compactified into a small manifold, a process known as string compactification. This review examines various compactification methods, demonstrating that without flux, the resulting manifold must be Calabi-Yau. We further analyze compactifications involving flux through the lens of generalized complex geometry. The discussion then extends to applications in cosmology, including the swampland program and related cosmological models. Additionally, we explore non-relativistic string theories and their toroidal compactifications before concluding with an overview of outstanding questions in the field.

In 2016, as outlined in our work "Intrinsic mirror symmetry and punctured invariants," we constructed and established the consistency of a canonical wall structure. This process begins with a log Calabi-Yau pair $(X,D)$ to generate a wall structure, as defined by Gross-Hacking-Siebert. In essence, this canonical wall structure serves as a data framework encoding an algebro-geometric counterpart to counts of Maslov index zero disks, where these enumerative invariants are formulated using the punctured invariants introduced by Abramovich-Chen-Gross-Siebert. The paper presents two primary theorems: first, we demonstrate that the canonical wall structure is consistent, thereby yielding a mirror family; second, we show that this resulting mirror family aligns with the intrinsic mirror constructed in our aforementioned paper. Although the current framework is more specialized than the one in the earlier paper, it provides a more granular description of the mirror.

We introduce various classes of constraints on Feynman integral discontinuities that extend beyond the Steinmann relations. These constraints stem from a geometric approach to the Landau equations, as proposed by Pham, where Feynman integral singularities map to critical points of transformations between on-shell spaces. To derive our findings, we examine components of Picard-Lefschetz theory, which link the homotopy characteristics of complexified external momentum spaces to the homology of the combined space of on-shell internal and external momenta. A key insight from this analysis concerns the compatibility of Landau singularities—specifically, whether the Landau equations for two distinct singularities can be satisfied at the same time. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, sequential discontinuities relative to non-compatible Landau singularities must be zero. While we provide rigorous proofs only for Feynman integrals with generic masses in this work, the geometric and algebraic perspectives developed here are expected to aid in analyzing more general Feynman integrals.

This article introduces Tensorflow Meter (TFMeter), an extension of the Tensorflow Playground designed as an interactive tool for visually constructing various neural network architectures. Beyond the capabilities of the original Playground, TFMeter displays information-theoretic metrics throughout the network's construction, training, and testing phases. Consequently, every architectural modification alters at least one metric, fostering deeper engineering intuition regarding what different structures can learn. These metrics are sourced from existing literature. This demo outlines our web application, accessible at http://tfmeter.icsi.berkeley.edu/, and posits that while the original Playground builds intuition about neural networks, our extension educates users on specific measurements, ultimately aiming to enhance experimental design and reproducibility in the field.

We present Probabilistic Embeddings using Laplacian Priors (PELP), a model designed to integrate graph-based side-information into static word embeddings. Theoretically, PELP unifies various existing embedding techniques, generalizing approaches for graph-enhanced, group, dynamic, and cross-lingual static embeddings. It allows for the straightforward combination of these methods in any configuration. Empirical results demonstrate that PELP matches the performance of these previous models when treated as special cases. Additionally, we showcase its flexibility through an application comparing political sociolects over time and provide a TensorFlow implementation to support flexible estimation across different settings.

Quantum computing promises substantial performance gains over classical systems for various computational tasks, with ion chains confined in linear Paul traps emerging as a leading candidate due to their extended coherence times and precise control capabilities. This study details the development of a compact, five-qubit universal quantum computer utilizing $^{88}\text{Sr}^{+}$ ions within an RF trap. Fundamental operations—such as initialization, quantum logic, and readout—are executed with high fidelity. A universal gate set, consisting of selective single- and two-qubit gates driven by narrow-linewidth lasers, enables the implementation of any unitary transformation on the register. The paper outlines the primary experimental apparatus and elaborates on distinctive features, specifically the deployment of robust entangling gates and the creation of a quantum coherent feedback loop via EMCCD camera acquisition, a critical component for future quantum error correction efforts.

The Fock-Schwinger proper-time approach is employed to obtain the effective action within a field theory where chiral $U(3)\times U(3)$ symmetry is explicitly broken by the non-equal masses of heavy particles. The resulting one-loop effective action is expressed as an expansion in inverse powers of these heavy masses, with the first two Seeley-DeWitt coefficients calculated explicitly. This robust method provides a valuable pathway for investigating explicit flavor symmetry breaking effects in effective field theories.

This study examines the secrecy performance of an underlay cognitive small-cell radio network characterized by unreliable backhaul connections. In this setup, secondary small-cell transmitters link to a macro base station via wireless backhaul, while sharing spectrum with a primary network under a strict constraint to maintain the primary network's desired outage probability. We introduce an optimal transmitter selection (OTS) scheme to facilitate information transfer to the destination within the small-cell network and derive a closed-form expression for the secrecy outage probability. Our findings indicate that system performance improves by increasing both the primary transmitter's power and the number of small-cell transmitters, while backhaul reliability for the secondary network and the primary network's outage requirements significantly influence overall system behavior.

Recent years have seen extensive research into Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR); however, to the best of our knowledge, few studies specifically target compressed images. The presence of complex compression artifacts impedes progress in this area, despite its significant practical value. To address this challenge, we introduce CISRNet, a network designed with a two-stage coarse-to-fine learning framework optimized for Compressed Image Super-Resolution. Specifically, CISRNet comprises two subnetworks: a coarse network utilizing recursive learning and a refinement network employing residual learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that with careful design choices, CISRNet outperforms competing Single-Image Super-Resolution methods in Compressed Image Super-Resolution tasks.

This work investigates multiple groupcasting over broadcast channels (BC). Specifically, an inner bound is derived for the $K$-receiver discrete memoryless (DM) BC concerning a diamond message set comprising four groupcast messages: one intended for all receivers, one for all but two, and two others each desired by all but one of those two receivers. This bound relies on rate-splitting and superposition coding, presented explicitly here as a union of four-dimensional polytopes across various coding distributions. When applied to the combination network—a specific class of three-layer (two-hop) broadcast networks defined by $2^K-1$ noiseless links of finite or arbitrary capacity between a source and intermediate nodes—our top-down methodology yields an explicit inner bound as a single polytope through a unique coding distribution. The resulting inequalities fall within the class of generalized cut-set outer bounds recently established by Salimi et al. for broadcast networks. Consequently, we determine the capacity region of the general $K$-user combination network for the diamond message set in explicit form. This achievement highlights the robustness of our DM BC inner bound by: (a) revealing a previously unknown capacity region for the combination network and (b) potentially capturing numerous combinatorial characteristics of the $K$-receiver DM BC capacity region itself. Furthermore, we enhance this inner bound by incorporating binning, expressing the updated bound explicitly as a union over coding distributions of four-dimensional polytopes in terms of message rates.

The Lambert W(x) function and its potential uses in physics are introduced, along with a C++ numerical implementation that utilizes Halley's and Fritsch's iterations. These iterations are initialized using approximations derived from branch-point expansions, asymptotic series, rational fits, and continued-logarithm recursion.

Likelihood-free Bayesian inference methods are widely used for calibrating complex stochastic models when the data likelihood is intractable; however, their heavy reliance on repeated simulations makes them impractical when simulation costs are moderate or high. To mitigate this computational burden without sacrificing accuracy, a multifidelity approach—originally developed for approximate Bayesian computation—leverages information from computationally inexpensive approximate models to supplement the target model. This work extends multifidelity techniques to the general likelihood-free Bayesian inference framework. We derive analytical results for optimally allocating computational resources across different fidelity levels and implement these findings in practice. Furthermore, we present an adaptive multifidelity algorithm that learns inter-model relationships to dynamically adjust resource allocation, demonstrating that it yields posterior estimates with near-optimal efficiency.

In an $n$-dimensional space-time defined by the line element $(dx_0^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} dx_i^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}$, general relativity offers a comprehensive geometric framework for gravity, yet it fails to account for the remaining fundamental forces: electromagnetism, the weak interaction, and the strong interaction. These forces are instead described by quantum field theory (QFT), which distinguishes between two particle classes: Fermions with half-integer spin and Bosons with integer spin that serve as force carriers. To date, no Fermions have been observed with fractional spins other than $\pm\frac{1}{2}$. This article introduces a parametric coordinate system within the tangent space of Minkowski space, demonstrating that these coordinates can be assigned a tensor weight of $\frac{1}{2}$. Furthermore, in a generalized space where the line element is $(dx_0^p - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} dx_i^p)^{\frac{1}{p}}$, a similar parametric system can be defined with a tensor weight of $\frac{1}{p}$. We establish eight distinct sets of such coordinates, analyze their transformation properties under various gauge transformations, and illustrate how they can represent different Fermions.

Within the metric formalism, Noether symmetry analysis for $F(R)$ gravity in a vacuum or with pressureless dust uniquely determines $F(R)\propto R^{3/2}$ and the conserved current $\frac{d}{dt} (a\sqrt R)$ in a Robertson-Walker spacetime. Conversely, Roshan et al. (Phys. Lett. B668, 238, 2008) asserted that Palatini $F(\Re)$ theory allows for $F(\Re)\propto \Re^{s}$ with an arbitrary constant $s$ during the matter era of a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe. However, this claim is flawed because the associated conserved current generally fails to satisfy the field equations. This work demonstrates that Noether symmetry in Palatini gravity instead requires $F(\Re)\propto\Re^{3/2}$ alongside the conserved current $\Sigma_{0} {a}[\frac{\dot a}{a}+ \frac{\dot\Phi}{2\Phi}]$, thereby refuting the earlier assertion.

Irreversible entropy production (IEP) is a critical factor in quantum thermodynamic processes. This study explores the geometrical limits of IEP within nonequilibrium thermodynamics by analyzing a system interacting with a squeezed thermal bath, subject to both dissipation and dephasing. Our findings indicate that the geometrical bounds of IEP shift in opposing directions under these two conditions: dephasing tightens the lower and upper bounds, whereas dissipation achieves the same effect. Nevertheless, leveraging the benefits of squeezing effects allows for the reduction of both the critical time required for IEP itself and the time needed for the bounds to reach equilibrium, under either dissipation or dephasing. Furthermore, these squeezing effects lead to smaller IEP values, which quantify the degree of thermodynamic irreversibility. Consequently, the nonequilibrium nature of the squeezed thermal bath causes the system-bath interaction energy to significantly impact IEP, thereby tightening its bounds. These results remain consistent with the second law of thermodynamics, as they treat bath squeezing as a usable resource capable of enhancing the performance of quantum thermodynamic devices.
We examine a geometric method for constructing specific finite-index subgroups within Aut(F2).

Managing and analyzing massive datasets is difficult because of the significant storage and computational expenses involved. To mitigate these costs, subsampling algorithms are commonly employed to reduce data volume and alleviate computational strain. However, current subsampling techniques primarily address data with numerical covariates. Since datasets featuring categorical covariates are prevalent across many fields, there is a lack of established subsampling strategies for such data. This paper introduces a balanced subsampling method specifically designed for categorical covariates. By ensuring a combinatorial balance among covariate values, the resulting subsample offers three key advantages: first, it is nonsingular, enabling the estimation of all parameters in ANOVA regression; second, it yields optimal parameter estimates by minimizing the generalized variance; and third, models trained on this subsample produce robust predictions by minimizing the worst-case error. Extensive simulations and a real-world application demonstrate the superiority of this balanced subsampling approach compared to existing data reduction methods.

Building upon Reshetikhin and Turaev's invariant, Costantino, Geer, and Patureau-Mirand developed $3$-manifold invariants within the framework of relative $G$-modular categories, encompassing both semisimple and non-semisimple ribbon tensor categories. This paper adopts their approach to derive a $3$-manifold invariant from Viro's $\mathfrak{gl}(1\vert 1)$-Alexander polynomial. Using the lens spaces $L(7, 1)$ and $L(7, 2)$ as test cases, we demonstrate that this invariant can differentiate between homotopy equivalent manifolds.

A recent study [arXiv:1805.05217] evaluates the performance of a D-Wave 2000Q system against two variants of the coherent Ising machine (CIM). This commentary identifies specific analytical errors that cast doubt on several of the paper's conclusions.

Although recent advances in marked temporal point processes (MTPP) have facilitated precise modeling of real-world continuous-time event sequences (CTESs), the task of retrieving these sequences remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce NEUROSEQRET, a framework designed to retrieve and rank relevant CTESs from extensive corpora based on a query sequence. The method begins by applying a trainable unwarping function to the query, enabling fair comparison with corpus sequences even when they possess differing attributes. Subsequently, both the unwarped query and corpus sequences are processed by MTPP-guided neural relevance models; we present two model variants that balance accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we propose an optimization framework for learning binary sequence embeddings from relevance scores, which supports locality-sensitive hashing to significantly accelerate the retrieval of top-K results. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that NEUROSEQRET outperforms existing baselines in accuracy and validates the effectiveness of our hashing mechanism.

This paper provides a concise overview of current endeavors to globally examine charge radii and associated indicators using covariant density functional theory (CDFT). By employing major classes of covariant energy density functionals (CEDFs), the study establishes the global precision of CDFT in describing both experimental absolute and differential charge radii, complementing this with an analysis of theoretical statistical and systematic uncertainties. The work presents new findings regarding the accuracy of differential charge radii for deformed actinides and light superheavy nuclei, assessing the influence of octupole deformation on their reproduction. Additionally, novel mechanisms driving odd-even staggering in charge radii are explored, followed by an examination of how self-consistency effects contribute to the accurate modeling of differential charge radii.

Braneworld models serve as compelling theoretical and phenomenological tools for investigating physics beyond the standard model in cosmology and particle physics. This study examines braneworld scenarios where gravitational dynamics are dictated by teleparallel $f(T)$ gravity. Specifically, we highlight a codimension-two axisymmetric configuration, referred to as a string-like brane. Similar to five-dimensional domain-wall models, the $f(T)$ modification of gravity induces a phase transition within the perfect fluid source, thereby facilitating a brane-splitting mechanism. Moreover, torsion alters gravitational perturbations by generating new potential wells within the brane core. These wells create a massless mode that is more tightly localized around ring structures, while simultaneously maintaining a stable, gapless tower of massive non-localizable modes in the bulk.

Metamaterials exhibit unique static and dynamic properties, such as negative effective mass density, dynamic stiffness, and Poisson's ratio, arising from their geometric design instead of their chemical makeup. While this geometry can be conceptualized as the material's phase—typically fixed after fabrication—experimental progress in reconfigurable metamaterials has been hindered by manufacturing difficulties, the destructive effects of re-programming, and inherent non-linearities. By integrating analytical, numerical, and experimental approaches, we employ tunable, self-assembled, nonlinear magnetic lattices to achieve metamaterials with reversible phase transitions. These structures consist of free-floating disks containing embedded permanent magnets, held within magnetic constraints. We leverage the non-destructive adjustability of these magnetic boundaries to develop a series of re-programmable metamaterials for controlling sound wave propagation. Additionally, we demonstrate a robust, real-time tunable wave filter operating at ultra-low frequencies. These results promise to broaden the scope of metamaterials toward functional and tunable devices.

We present a finite analogue of free probability and establish a connection between recent findings involving polynomial convolutions and established free probability theory. A key method employed is a novel transformation that simplifies calculations within this new framework by reducing them to those involving classically independent random variables. Following this, we investigate the concept of finite freeness and its consequences. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of this theory by deriving finite versions of several prominent free distributions and proving their corresponding limit laws directly. Through this process, we uncover valuable insights into convolution behavior in traditional free probability that are often obscured when the convolved operators are not finite. This version includes the original 2016 preprint along with an additional section (Section 5.2) in which we apply finite freeness to establish majorization relations for specific convolutions.

At separations where short-range chemical forces become negligible, van der Waals (vdW) interactions dominate the forces between neutral objects. This dispersive coupling arises from the interplay between material geometry and response properties. This study examines vdW interactions among standard and Dirac materials in one, two, and three dimensions using the Random Phase Approximation (RPA), which incorporates collective excitations driven by the electronic Coulomb potential. We derive a comprehensive understanding of scaling laws and functional characteristics for systems exhibiting both parabolic energy dispersion (standard materials) and crossing linear bands (Dirac materials). Furthermore, by comparing quantum mechanical and thermal limits, we discuss the emergence of thermal fluctuations in vdW forces, demonstrating that these effects become significantly pronounced at smaller scales in reduced dimensions.

Empirical research in software engineering frequently relies on open-source contributors or industry partnerships, yet it rarely employs financial incentives—such as cash or vouchers—to motivate participants, a common practice in fields like economics and psychology. Although the current SIGSOFT Empirical Standards allow for payouts related to survey completion, they do not endorse compensation for simulating real-world conditions or fostering realistic behavior during experiments. Consequently, there remains a gap in understanding the efficacy of financial incentives within software engineering studies. To address this, we propose a survey followed by a controlled laboratory experiment. Specifically, we will utilize the survey data to design up to four distinct payoff functions (mappings of performance or choices to monetary rewards) for a code-review task: (1) a scheme preferred by employees, (2) one currently used in practice, (3) a performance-independent scheme, and (4) one mimicking an open-source environment. Using a between-subject design, we aim to investigate how these varying schemes influence participant performance. Our findings will clarify the impact of financial incentives on developers in both experimental and real-world contexts, offering guidance for researchers in designing studies and organizations in compensating their developers.

Illuminating sensing and measurement processes with quantum light states can enhance performance in harsh environments characterized by noise, loss, and dephasing. While prior studies demonstrated only slight reductions in the measurements required for specific precision levels, this study compares three distinct illumination strategies for estimating relative phase within a noisy, lossy interferometer. By incorporating common phase fluctuations into the noise model, we demonstrate that employing an entangled probe yields a precision advantage in parameter estimation that scales with the count of entangled modes. Consequently, this research establishes a theoretical basis for utilizing highly multimode entangled light states to address practical measurement challenges under experimentally difficult conditions.

The increasing fragility of neural networks has sparked significant interest in adversarial robustness within machine learning. We introduce FIRE, a novel Fisher-Rao regularization technique applied to categorical cross-entropy loss, grounded in an information-geometric approach that utilizes geodesic distance between softmax outputs derived from natural and perturbed inputs. Leveraging the information-geometric characteristics of softmax distributions, we provide an explicit formulation of the Fisher-Rao Distance (FRD) for both binary and multiclass scenarios, highlighting key properties and their relationship to conventional regularization metrics. Additionally, within a simple linear and Gaussian framework, we demonstrate that FIRE can achieve all Pareto-optimal points in the accuracy-robustness trade-off, a capability that other state-of-the-art methods lack. Empirical evaluations on standard datasets using classifiers trained with this loss function reveal simultaneous improvements of up to 1% in both clean and robust performance, while reducing training time by 20% compared to top-performing alternatives.

In the contemporary era, a vast array of digital media, including articles, videos, movies, and e-books, is readily available for consumption. This abundance often overwhelms users, making it difficult to determine what to view next. To leverage this confusion and boost user engagement—and ultimately revenue—digital media providers employ recommendation systems to address information overload. While traditional systems rely on either collaborative filtering (based on user interactions) or content-based filtering (using metadata), and newer hybrid models combine both, this paper focuses exclusively on an enhanced content-based approach. We develop a synthetic movie recommendation system that integrates a ranking algorithm utilizing three specific content similarity metrics: metadata similarity, visual content analysis, and user review sentiment. Specifically, the system applies text vectorization and cosine similarity for metadata, employs a pre-trained VGG19 model with K-means clustering for visual features, and compares sentiments from reviews. This methodology enables the system to suggest movies that share a similar "feel."

We investigate a modified Bose-Hubbard model featuring two cavities with on-site Kerr interactions, subjected to two-photon driving and correlated dissipation. By deriving an exact solution for the steady state of this driven-dissipative interacting system, we demonstrate that it enables the preparation and stabilization of pure entangled non-Gaussian states, specifically entangled cat states. In contrast to prior proposals for dissipative stabilization of such states, our method relies solely on a linear coupling to a single engineered reservoir, eliminating the need for nonlinear couplings to multiple reservoirs. Furthermore, this scheme falls within the capabilities of current state-of-the-art circuit QED experiments.

Existing quantum systems face substantial constraints when handling the high dimensionality and vast datasets characteristic of high-energy physics. This study investigates feature and data prototype selection strategies to address these issues. Through a grid search, quantum machine learning models were developed and evaluated against classical shallow learning methods, utilizing both reduced and full datasets. Results indicate that quantum algorithms achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, even when processing large-scale data.

Thermalization in many-body systems arises from intricate interactions between subsystems and their surroundings. This work establishes the theoretical basis for actively managing local thermal states in arbitrary non-reciprocal systems near equilibrium. Specifically, we outline methods to (i) guide specific components to follow a predetermined trajectory during relaxation (addressing the thermal targeting problem), (ii) isolate certain elements from the rest of the system, or (iii) synchronize their evolutionary dynamics. Furthermore, we derive the necessary conditions for subsystems to relax toward a minimal temperature with minimal energy expenditure or to reach a specified temperature in the shortest possible time. Finally, we illustrate these concepts through representative examples involving radiative heat exchange.

Strategic planning typically depends on non-scientific methods to predict future technologies and market leaders. In contrast, we have developed a rapid quantitative framework with minimal computational demands to identify key technologies and companies within specific sectors using adaptable methodologies applicable across all industries. Leveraging patent data from the US Patent and Trademark Office, we initially assign a value to individual patents through automated machine learning. Subsequently, we utilize network science to analyze the interactions and evolution of companies and patent clusters (representing technologies), generating rankings for both groups that identify significant or emerging network nodes via five distinct network centrality metrics. We demonstrate this system through a case study focused on the cybersecurity sector. The resulting analysis yields valuable insights, such as identifying (i) emerging technologies characterized by rising average patent values and cluster sizes, (ii) the most influential entities within the field, and (iii) promising startups possessing a limited number of highly impactful patents. Additionally, supplementary analysis offers evidence of diminishing marginal returns on research and development in larger cybersecurity firms.

In this thought-provoking book, Richard Healey offers a novel interpretation of quantum theory grounded in pragmatist philosophy. Healey positions this approach as an alternative to realist theories—such as Bohmian mechanics, spontaneous collapse models, and the many-worlds interpretation, which attempt to describe the nature of the quantum world and fundamental physical laws—and non-realist interpretations like quantum Bayesianism, which frame quantum theory as a description of agents' subjective epistemic states. The core of Healey's proposal is to view quantum theory not as a depiction of the physical world, but as a collection of authoritative and objectively valid prescriptions guiding agent behavior. The book thoroughly develops and defends this concept, featuring engaging discussions on various philosophical topics including representation, probability, explanation, causation, objectivity, meaning, and fundamentality. Situated at the crossroads of physics and philosophy, the work is structured in two parts: Part I examines foundational quantum questions through the lens of the prescriptive interpretation, while Part II explores the philosophical implications of this view. Written to be largely accessible to non-specialists, this brief review will concentrate on two key questions: (1) How does Healey's concept function? and (2) What grounds exist for believing in it?

We explore both theoretically and numerically the mechanisms driving soliton ejection, which is triggered by the scattering of bright solitons off modulated reflectionless potential wells. These wells enable the controlled release of solitons at remarkably high velocities. Initially, we outline the scattering configuration and define soliton ejection based on various system parameters. Subsequently, we develop a theoretical framework that uncovers the fundamental physics of this ejection. This model relies on the exchange of energy and norm between the incoming soliton and a stable trapped mode, which represents an exact solution to the governing nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Notably, even stationary solitons can produce high-speed ejection, as a portion of the nonlinear interaction energy converts into the translational kinetic energy of the ejected soliton. Our findings indicate that ejection invariably occurs when the incident soliton's norm exceeds that of the trapped mode, provided their energies are nearly equal. Upon trapping the incident soliton, the surplus norm results in an ejected soliton alongside a minor amount of radiation, both sharing translational kinetic energy. We observed that multi-node trapped modes with greater binding energy yield higher ejection speeds. Furthermore, simultaneous ejection of two solitons was achieved through scattering from both sides of the potential, resulting in ejection speeds nearly double those of single soliton events. The outcome and velocity of the ejection are highly sensitive to the relative phase between the two incoming solitons, suggesting a potential application for soliton phase interferometry.

Kidney cancer ranks among the most prevalent malignancies, with surgical intervention being a standard treatment. However, the complexity of regional anatomy makes this procedure particularly difficult. Accurate organ delineation is crucial for enhancing both surgical planning and execution. This study introduces an ensemble of two fully convolutional networks designed to segment the kidney, tumor, veins, and arteries. While SegResNet demonstrated superior performance in tumor segmentation, nnU-Net offered more precise delineation of the kidneys, arteries, and veins. Consequently, our proposed approach integrates these two architectures and further enhances results through mixup augmentation.

We introduce a family of alchemical perturbation potentials designed to compute hydration free energies for small to medium-sized molecules through a single, concerted coupling step, replacing the standard two-step sequence typically used for Lennard-Jones and electrostatic interactions. These potentials utilize a softplus function applied to solute-solvent interaction energy to concentrate sampling near entropic bottlenecks within the alchemical pathway. Furthermore, we provide a general framework for optimizing the parameters of such potentials, employing the $\lambda$-function formalism and a maximum-likelihood estimation procedure developed previously to prevent multi-modal distributions of coupling energy along the path. A new soft-core function is also presented, which acts on the total solute-solvent interaction energy rather than individual atomic pair potentials, a distinction critical to this outcome. Since this soft-core formulation avoids the need to modify core force and energy routines, it can be readily integrated into existing molecular dynamics simulation software. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by estimating hydration free energies for water droplets containing compounds of diverse sizes and complexities, showing that convergence is achieved rapidly in each instance. This research establishes a foundation for developing more streamlined algorithms for estimating free energies of molecular binding with explicit solvation.

Consider a subfield $F$ within the algebraic closure of a finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$ where $p \neq 2$. Let $R$ be any ring satisfying the condition $F[t] \subset R \subsetneq F(t)$. For a classical Chevalley group $G$ of adjoint type defined over $R$, we demonstrate that the group $G(R)$ possesses the $R_{\infty}$-property.

This paper examines findings regarding the automatic verification of parameterized programs that lack identities, defined as systems comprising an arbitrary number of components, each executing the identical finite-state program. We analyze the complexity involved in determining whether any component can reach an unsafe state. This note is intended for a general audience of theoretical computer scientists.

We present a novel proof of a Tauberian Theorem concerning the complex Laplace transform, employing the theories of measure and functions of bounded variation, thereby deriving a straightforward demonstration of the Prime Number Theorem.

Given the widespread adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), often viewed as black boxes, understanding their behavior is essential across various domains of human life. Leveraging advances in Explainable Artificial Intelligence, this paper introduces Auto DeepVis, a novel approach to analyze catastrophic forgetting within continual learning. Following this investigation, we propose "critical freezing," a new strategy to address this forgetting phenomenon. Rigorous experiments on a captioning model illustrate the mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting, specifically identifying which components degrade or change. Our evaluation demonstrates that critical freezing outperforms baselines on both prior and subsequent tasks, validating the utility of our analytical method. Furthermore, our techniques offer an explainable and supplementary solution to existing methods, contributing to the complete elimination of catastrophic forgetting in lifelong learning.

This paper investigates the metaphor of Science as a generator of clear depictions of our surroundings, grounded in the epistemological framework of Objective Cognitive Constructivism. These vivid representations are transmitted through exact scientific hypotheses, which are subsequently encoded via mathematical equations. Additionally, the article outlines how this knowledge is generated through an iterative cycle of development, refinement, and strengthening, culminating in the emergence of eigen-solutions defined by four fundamental attributes: precision, stability, separability, and composability. Finally, the text examines the function of ontology and metaphysics within the scientific production process and analyzes the extent to which the resulting knowledge can be deemed objective.

We introduce a new framework designed for explainable labeling and interpretation of medical images. While these images traditionally require expert interpretation accompanied by detailed textual reports, our approach differs from previous methods that merely generate reports from images or images from reports. Instead, we utilize a cyclic Generative Adversarial Network (CycleGAN) to create congruent image-report pairs. This ensures that the generated report accurately explains the medical image, while the image reconstructed from the report visually resembles the original. Our primary goal is to produce trustworthy and faithful explanations for chest x-ray diagnostic models by directing users toward similar cases to support diagnostic decisions. Beyond facilitating transparent labeling and interpretation, our method achieves labeling performance comparable to prior approaches, including state-of-the-art results in certain areas, as demonstrated by experiments on the Indiana Chest X-ray dataset.

We investigate the dynamic cognitive hierarchy (CH) framework introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022) within the context of multi-stage games characterized by incomplete information. In this setting, participants simultaneously deduce the payoff-relevant types and sophistication levels of their opponents as the game history evolves. For a specific class of two-person dirty faces games, we provide a complete characterization of the dynamic CH solution, which forecasts that players at lower levels of sophistication will identify their face types in later periods compared to higher-level players. Furthermore, we re-examine experimental data from the dirty faces game collected by Bayer and Chan (2007), demonstrating that the dynamic CH solution offers a superior explanation of the data relative to the static CH model.

We outline recent findings and unresolved issues regarding causality within General Relativity. The notion of a singularity is deeply linked to the emergence of future trapped surfaces and inner event horizons. This overview briefly covers the Hawking-Penrose singularity theorems and addresses open challenges related to the future Cauchy development (domain of dependence), breakdown criteria, and energy conditions necessary for horizon stability. A central inquiry concerns whether regions violating causality, which give rise to Cauchy horizons, can exist. Furthermore, we pose several questions regarding the visibility and stability of closed trapped surfaces originating from future null infinity, establishing imprisonment conditions. Additionally, we offer a novel viewpoint on causal boundaries and spacelike conformal boundary extensions applicable to time-oriented Lorentzian manifolds and more exotic scenarios.

We introduce a novel experimental and theoretical framework that integrates a broadband superluminescent diode (SLED/SLD) with rapid learning algorithms to enhance both speed and precision in optimizing one-dimensional optical dipole potentials generated by a Digital Micromirror Device (DMD). To assess the setup and analyze potential speckle patterns caused by coherence, we contrast the superluminescent diode with a single-mode laser by examining their interference characteristics. Utilizing Machine Learning (ML) techniques, we train a physics-inspired model serving as a digital twin of the optical system, capable of predicting apparatus behavior, including inherent imperfections. By implementing an Iterative Learning Control (ILC) algorithm, we achieve an optimization speed for optical potentials approximately ten times faster than heuristic methods. Furthermore, we evaluate both iterative model-based offline optimization and experimental feedback-based online optimization. Our approach offers a new pathway for rapid optimization of optical potentials, which is essential for the dynamic manipulation of ultracold gases.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA) merges algebraic topology and data science to offer compact, noise-resistant depictions of intricate structures. In contrast, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) acquire millions of parameters through architectural transformations, yielding high-dimensional internal representations that are challenging to interpret. As DNNs permeate various societal sectors, there is a growing consensus that mathematical techniques are essential for helping analysts and researchers comprehend how a model's internal states connect to its final classifications. This paper leverages advanced TDA methods to investigate the interpretability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) employed in image classification. We examine two prevalent TDA strategies for modeling hidden-layer activations as high-dimensional point clouds, offering experimental proof that these point clouds encapsulate significant structural details of the model's processing. First, we illustrate how a persistent homology-based distance metric can quantify meaningful distinctions between layers, contextualizing these findings within existing representational similarity metrics for neural network interpretability. Second, we demonstrate that mapper graphs can yield semantic insights into how models arrange hierarchical class knowledge across layers. These findings underscore TDA as a valuable instrument for deep learning practitioners to reveal the latent structures within their models.

Compositional generalization describes a model's ability to handle novel input combinations formed from elements seen during training. As generalization is crucial for language and problem-solving, this concept has sparked extensive analysis across various tasks, yet research on math word problems (MWPs) remains scarce. This manuscript investigates compositional generalization within MWP solving. We begin by introducing a data splitting strategy to generate compositional splits from existing MWP datasets and synthesize new data to isolate compositional effects. To enhance compositional generalization in MWP solving, we propose an iterative data augmentation technique that incorporates diverse compositional variations into the training set, making it compatible with various MWP approaches. In our evaluation, we tested multiple methods and observed significant performance drops on the benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our proposed data augmentation method substantially improves the compositional generalization of standard MWP models. The code is accessible at https://github.com/demoleiwang/CGMWP.

Knowledge representation learning (KRL) has recently become the leading method for processing queries on knowledge graphs (KGs) by embedding both graph entities and queries into a latent space, positioning answer entities near the query. However, despite extensive research, most existing studies are limited to homogeneous KGs or KG completion tasks, leaving the challenge of answering complex logical queries across multi-view KGs unresolved. To address this, we introduce ROMA, a new KRL framework designed for logical query answering over multi-view KGs. ROMA differs significantly from prior approaches in four key ways: (i) it represents a multi-view KG as a collection of overlaying sub-KGs, one for each view, thereby encompassing various KG types such as temporal graphs; (ii) it handles complex logical queries with diverse relation and view constraints, including those with intricate topologies or spanning multiple views; (iii) it scales effectively to large KGs containing millions of facts and fine-grained views comprising dozens of perspectives; and (iv) it generalizes to query structures and KG views that were not observed during training. Comprehensive empirical evaluations on real-world KGs demonstrate that ROMA significantly outperforms alternative methods.

Reinforcement learning has proven to be a versatile and powerful method for mastering continuous control tasks, including robotic object manipulation. However, in robotics, real-world data collection is expensive, making sample efficiency a critical bottleneck for acquiring new skills. While world models have been shown to enhance sample efficiency in game environments—particularly with rich visual inputs—this project investigates their application to deformable robotic manipulation, specifically focusing on learning to fold cloth in simulation. We evaluated the impact of world models on sample efficiency by comparing RGB image inputs against a feature space that leverages built-in structural keypoints, a common strategy in robot skill learning. Our experiments assessed how these different observation types affected both task performance and learning efficiency with and without the world model. Results indicated that using keypoints boosted the best model's performance by 50%, and generally, utilizing reduced feature spaces (whether learned or constructed) improved both task outcomes and sample efficiency. Furthermore, incorporating a state transition predictor (MDN-RNN) into the world models yielded no significant impact on task performance.

Nonstationary functional time series frequently possess valuable information within their frequency-domain properties, which are defined by the time-varying power spectrum. While practitioners often partition frequencies into bands to create low-dimensional summaries of power, standard bands are typically established via manual inspection and may fail to adequately capture spectral power. This article introduces a framework for adaptive frequency band estimation tailored to nonstationary functional time series, designed to optimally summarize their time-varying dynamics. We present a scan statistic and search algorithm for detecting frequency-domain changes, establish the theoretical foundations of this approach, and provide a computationally efficient implementation. The method's validity is supported by extensive simulation studies and an application to electroencephalogram data from participants alternating between eyes-open and eyes-closed states.

We present new evidence supporting the binary progenitor theory for long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Binary-driven hypernovae (BdHNe) involve a carbon-oxygen core (CO$_{\rm core}$) and a neutron star (NS) companion. In systems with orbital periods of approximately 5 minutes, the collapse of the CO$_{\rm core}$ produces the BdHN I subclass, defined by three key features: 1) an energetic supernova marked by an "SN-rise"; 2) the formation of a black hole (BH) from the collapsing NS via accretion, which generates GeV emission following a luminosity law $L_{\rm GeV} = A_{\rm GeV}\,t^{-\alpha_{\rm GeV}}$ in certain cases; and 3) the birth of a new neutron star ($\nu$NS) from the supernova, driving an X-ray afterglow with $L_X = A_{\rm X}\,t^{-\alpha_{\rm X}}$ that is observed in all BdHN I events. We analyzed 378 sources, focusing on four prototypes (GRBs 130427A, 160509A, 180720B, and 190114C) to determine their spectral properties, luminosity, SN-rise duration, X-ray parameters ($A_X$, $\alpha_X=1.48\pm 0.32$), and the time evolution of the $\nu$NS spin. By combining time-resolved spectral analysis, 3D simulations, and observations of GeV emission presence or absence in 54 sources within the Fermi-LAT boresight, we inferred $A_{\rm GeV}$ and $\alpha_{\rm GeV}=1.19 \pm 0.04$, as well as the BdHN I morphology. Among the 54 sources, 25 exhibited integrated and time-varying GeV emission, while 29 showed no GeV signal but displayed X/gamma-ray flares previously interpreted as emission along the binary plane. The ratio of 25 to 54 suggests that GeV radiation is confined to a cone with a half-opening angle of roughly $60^{\circ}$ relative to the orbital plane's normal. Furthermore, we derived BH masses ranging from $2.3$ to $8.9~M_\odot$ and spins between $0.27$ and $0.87$ by modeling GeV emission via BH energy extraction, with the observed time evolution confirming the validity of the BH mass-energy formula.

We investigate the classical two-dimensional $\mathrm{RP^2}$ and Heisenberg models employing the Tensor-Network Renormalization (TNR) approach. Determining the phase diagrams for these systems has proven difficult and contentious due to extensive correlation lengths at low temperatures. The finite-size spectrum of the transfer matrix derived via TNR aids in identifying the conformal field theory (CFT) associated with potential critical points. Our findings reveal that the ultraviolet fixed points for the Heisenberg model and the ferromagnetic $\mathrm{RP^2}$ model at zero temperature align with a CFT possessing a central charge of $c=2$, consistent with two independent Nambu-Goldstone modes. Conversely, the ultraviolet fixed point for the antiferromagnetic Lebwohl-Lasher model—a variant of $\mathrm{RP^2}$—appears to exhibit a higher central charge, matching the $c=4$ value predicted by effective SO(5) symmetry. At temperatures above zero, the spectral convergence remains poor for both the Heisenberg and ferromagnetic $\mathrm{RP^2}$ models, and no suitable CFT candidate matches the observed spectrum, which suggests an effective central charge of approximately $c \sim 1.9$. These observations imply that both models maintain a single disordered phase at finite temperatures, despite the ferromagnetic $\mathrm{RP^2}$ model displaying a pronounced crossover at the temperature associated with the reported dissociation of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ vortices.

This study examines various mathematical models developed during the current pandemic to tackle key public health concerns regarding epidemic dynamics and their origins. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic.

We derive enhanced spectral projection estimates for manifolds with non-positive curvature, achieving sharp bounds for broad spectral windows in general tori. These findings surpass those in our earlier work [6], supported by significantly streamlined arguments. We leverage pointwise estimates inherent in Berard's research [2] more directly, bypassing the weak-type spaces previously employed in [6] and [22]. Furthermore, we refine and bolster our bilinear approaches by utilizing microlocal $L^2\to L^{q_c}$ Kakeya-Nikodym estimates while omitting the $L^2\to L^2$ estimates found in prior studies. This methodology enables new results for negatively curved manifolds and yields additional sharp estimates for tori. Additionally, we introduce novel and improved techniques for two-dimensional manifolds of non-positive curvature.

The 2015 Paris Agreement established targets to eliminate CO2 emissions from the energy sector by 2050 and limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Achieving these goals necessitates a transition to CO2-free power generation utilizing variable renewable sources. While weather-dependent variability has historically been the primary criticism of renewables, Power-to-X systems—which convert surplus electricity into storable energy forms—offer a vital solution to mitigate this fluctuation. However, these systems must be carefully scheduled to ensure they operate using low-carbon inputs. This paper presents a straightforward, intuitive graphical method for scheduling Power-to-X plants in the day-ahead market to simultaneously minimize electricity costs and carbon emissions. A simulation based on historical price and CO2 intensity data from four countries reveals that extending the scheduling horizon generally reduces both costs and emissions, though this benefit lessens as the required annual full-load hours increase. Furthermore, the study confirms a distinct trade-off between price and CO2 optimization, demonstrating that achieving the absolute lowest values for both simultaneously is unattainable.

By applying the Selberg trace formula, we demonstrate that for a hyperbolic 2-orbifold, the Laplacian's spectrum on functions is uniquely determined by, and uniquely determines, specific geometric and spectral data. This data includes the total volume, the aggregate length of the mirror boundary, the count of conepoints of various orders (treating mirror corners as half-conepoints), and the enumeration of primitive closed geodesics by length and orientability class. In this enumeration, boundary geodesics are counted as half orientation-preserving and half orientation-reversing, while imprimitive geodesics are excluded appropriately. Consequently, Laplace-isospectral hyperbolic 2-orbifolds yield equivalent linear representations of Isom(H^2) and remain isospectral under any natural operator.

We establish a connection describing the steepening of blazar gamma-ray spectra across the multi-GeV Fermi band and the TeV range detected by atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes. This spectral index variation arises from two mechanisms: (1) an intrinsic steepening independent of redshift, driven by emission and absorption characteristics within the source, and (2) a redshift-dependent steepening caused by intergalactic pair production interactions between blazar gamma-rays and low-energy photons from the intergalactic background light (IBL). Leveraging this relation alongside robust data on the mean gamma-ray spectral energy distribution (SED) of TeV-selected BL Lacs, the redshift evolution of the IBL can theoretically be determined without relying on stellar evolution models. We subsequently apply this relation to recent Fermi observations of TeV-selected blazars.

Body-centered cubic (bcc) refractory multi-element alloys (RMEA) have been the subject of intense research over the past ten years due to their promise as high-temperature materials. While many of these alloys exhibit exceptional high-temperature strength that defies the standard thermally-activated screw dislocation model, recent studies on Nb-Mo-Ta-W systems suggest that edge dislocations play a more significant role in deformation. This is typically linked to atomic-scale chemical fluctuations and their interactions with dislocation cores during slip. Although this explains some strengthening from chemical complexity, it fails to account for strength across the full thermal spectrum. We propose a novel mechanism that integrates existing theories on lattice strengthening with a thermally-activated component derived directly from the alloy's chemical complexity. This complexity generates unique vacancy formation energy distributions with tails extending into negative values, causing spontaneous, athermal vacancy formation at edge dislocation cores. These vacancies evolve into atomic-sized super-jogs on the dislocation line, serving as additional pinning sites that raise the activation stress required for dislocation motion. Simultaneously, these super-jogs can move diffusively along the glide direction, releasing some of the accumulated stress and mitigating the hardening effect caused by jog-pinning. The interaction between these opposing processes as a function of temperature provides additional strength to edge dislocations at intermediate-to-high temperatures, a finding that aligns remarkably well with experimental data for Nb-Mo-Ta-W and various other RMEA.

While numerical weather prediction has historically relied on physical atmospheric models, the advent of deep learning has sparked growing interest in purely data-driven medium-range forecasting, leading to initial feasibility studies. To advance this field, the WeatherBench benchmark challenge was established. In this work, we developed a deep residual convolutional neural network (ResNet) to forecast geopotential, temperature, and precipitation at a 5.625-degree resolution for up to five days. To mitigate overfitting and enhance forecast accuracy, the model was pretrained on historical climate model outputs before being fine-tuned with reanalysis data. The resulting forecasts surpassed prior WeatherBench submissions and matched the skill of physical baselines at the same resolution. Additionally, we examined the network's prediction mechanisms, finding that they largely align with physical reasoning, and conducted scaling experiments to assess the potential of data-driven methods at higher resolutions.

Despite the relatively recent development of the theory of discrete Painlevé (dP) equations, an increasing number of such equations are emerging in significant applications. Consequently, it is crucial to recognize these equations, classify their types, and understand their placement within the classification framework. H. Sakai introduced a definitive classification scheme for dP equations, employing geometric concepts to define 22 distinct classes. In stark contrast to the theory of ordinary differential Painlevé equations, each class of discrete equations contains infinitely many non-equivalent forms. Therefore, while specific canonical examples exist for each class, no single general form applies to all equations within a given class. The primary goal of this paper is to demonstrate that, alongside the classification itself, Sakai's geometric approach offers a potent tool for analyzing dP equations. We examine a highly complex dP equation representing a simple Schlesinger transformation of a Fuchsian system, showing how it can be identified with a much simpler canonical equation of the same type and providing an explicit coordinate transformation to convert between them. Key methods include the birational representation of the equation's affine Weyl symmetry group and the period map. Although the discussion centers on a specific example, the techniques employed are general and readily adaptable to other cases.

Accurate and regular population estimates are essential for formulating vaccination policies and planning infrastructure. Given that traditional censuses often lack the necessary spatio-temporal granularity for these purposes, methods independent of censuses—leveraging remote sensing and microcensus data—have gained prominence. This study estimates inter-censal population counts in two pilot districts of Mozambique, evaluating the viability of utilizing publicly available datasets to ensure long-term sustainability. Furthermore, we investigate transfer learning techniques applied to existing annotated datasets for predicting building footprints, enhancing these models with additional "dot" annotations from specific regions of interest. Our findings indicate that population predictions yield better results when incorporating footprint areas estimated through this approach compared to relying solely on publicly available features.

Large-scale Federated Learning (FL) networks face significant hurdles due to the substantial costs associated with communication and computation. This issue arises because existing FL frameworks predominantly rely on a star network topology, where all locally trained models converge at a centralized server, such as a cloud server. Consequently, when the user base is extensive and local model sizes are large, the server experiences considerable overhead. To address this, the paper introduces a novel edge network architecture that decentralizes model aggregation, thereby markedly lowering the network's overall aggregation latency. This architecture features a highly efficient in-network computation protocol composed of two key elements. First, an in-network aggregation mechanism offloads the bulk of aggregation computations from the cloud server to edge nodes. Second, a joint optimization problem for routing and resource allocation is formulated to minimize system-wide aggregation latency during each learning round. Since this problem is NP-hard, the authors propose a polynomial-time routing algorithm capable of delivering near-optimal performance with a proven theoretical bound. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed framework can drastically cut network latency by up to 4.6 times. Additionally, compared to conventional baselines, this approach significantly reduces cloud traffic and computational overhead by a factor of K/M, where K represents the number of users and M denotes the number of edge nodes.

Real-time robot motion planning within complex, high-dimensional spaces remains an unsolved challenge. Effective robot control systems rely heavily on motion planning algorithms and their associated collision checkers, yet the latter often consume the majority of computational resources. Current collision detection methods struggle to balance speed and precision, failing to scale effectively in intricate, high-dimensional settings. To address this, we introduce a new space decomposition technique that utilizes K-Means clustering within the Forward Kinematics domain to enhance proxy collision checking. By training individual configuration space models using Fastron—a kernel perceptron algorithm—on these decomposed subspaces, we generate compact models that offer high accuracy, rapid querying capabilities, and improved scalability. This approach, termed Decomposed Fast Perceptron (D-Fastron), was evaluated on the 7-DOF Baxter robot, achieving an average 29-fold increase in collision checking speed and up to a 9.8-fold acceleration in motion planning compared to existing state-of-the-art geometric checkers.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of Le Cam's one-step estimator applied to weak Fractionally AutoRegressive Integrated Moving-Average (FARIMA) models. In these models, noise terms are uncorrelated but may lack independence or martingale difference properties. Under specific regularity conditions, we demonstrate that the one-step estimator is strongly consistent and asymptotically normal, sharing the same asymptotic variance as the least squares estimator. Simulation results indicate that this proposed estimator is computationally more efficient than the least squares approach. Additionally, we suggest an application for generating remotely computed time series indicators.

Building on our prior work, we employ the isomorphisms connecting the $R$-matrix and Drinfeld presentations of quantum affine algebras in types $B$, $C$, and $D$ to characterize finite-dimensional irreducible representations within the $R$-matrix framework. Additionally, we examine the corresponding isomorphisms for Yangians of these types and apply Gauss decomposition to demonstrate an equivalence between the representation descriptions in both the $R$-matrix and Drinfeld formulations of the Yangians.

Online health information frequently presents skewed interpretations of data and offers dubious connections to original studies. This study assessed the viability of a tool designed to link webpages directly to their underlying evidence. Drawing from a pool of 207,538 eligible PubMed articles on vaccination, we analyzed 3,573 unique webpage links sourced from Altmetric to test various matching strategies. We compared simple baseline feature representations and dimensionality reduction techniques against methods enhanced with canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to rank source articles for vaccine-related content discussed online. Key performance metrics included the median rank of the correct source, the percentage of webpages where the correct source ranked first (recall@1), and the percentage ranked within the top 50 candidates (recall@50). Although integrating CCA with baseline methods generally yielded improvements, no CCA-based approach surpassed the baseline method, which successfully ranked the correct source first for over 25% of webpages and within the top 50 for more than half. Ultimately, tools capable of helping users identify evidence-based sources for vaccination-related web content appear feasible and could aid in mitigating bias and the misrepresentation of research in news and social media.

Speakers often reuse linguistic structures in conversation, a behavior driven by the unique information-theoretic advantages of repetition as a cost-efficient communication strategy. This study examines the recurrence of lexicalized constructions—recurring multi-word units—within English open-domain spoken dialogues. We propose that speakers employ construction repetition to reduce information rates, thereby decreasing the total information content of utterances as a dialogue progresses. Using an adaptive neural language model, we performed a quantitative analysis measuring the information content of both individual constructions and their containing utterances. Our results confirm that utilizing constructions lowers utterance information content. This facilitating effect (i) intensifies over the course of a dialogue, (ii) is amplified by repetition, (iii) scales with repetition frequency and density, and (iv) is more pronounced when referential constructions are repeated.

Recent research has explored smoothed sequential learning to address the significant complexity disparity between sequential and batch statistical learning, where Nature is restricted to choosing contexts with a density bounded by $1/\sigma$ relative to a known measure $\mu$. However, for certain function classes, an exponential gap exists between the statistically optimal regret and what can be achieved efficiently. This paper introduces the first computationally efficient algorithm that attains the statistically optimal $\log(T/\sigma)$ regret for realizable $K$-wise linear classification. We further extend these findings to scenarios involving linear classifiers within over-parameterized polynomial feature spaces and to a realizable piecewise-regression setting, provided an appropriate ERM oracle is available. Surprisingly, standard disagreement-based analyses fail to yield regret logarithmic in $1/\sigma$; instead, we propose a new characterization of the geometry of the disagreement region generated by generalized linear classifiers. Additionally, we introduce several technical tools of independent interest, such as a general anti-concentration bound for the determinant of specific matrix averages.

Current observational data still allow a significant mass range for primordial black holes (PBHs) to constitute all dark matter, specifically $\sim [10^{-16},10^{-14}] \cup [10^{-13},10^{-12}] M_\odot$. The formation of these PBHs inevitably produces gravitational waves (GWs) from curvature perturbations that fall within the LISA frequency band. While these scalar induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) are expected to be detectable by LISA even when accounting for second-order local non-Gaussianity ($F_{\rm NL}$), this letter presents a thorough analysis of GWs arising from local-type non-Gaussian curvature perturbations up to the third order, characterized by the parameter $G_{\rm NL}$. Our findings indicate that a log-dependent slope for SIGWs in the infrared region is generally predicted, and the SIGW amplitude can be suppressed by several orders of magnitude. Consequently, a non-detection of SIGWs by LISA does not exclude the scenario where PBHs account for the entirety of dark matter.

This study examines the Cauchy problem for the time-fractional diffusion equation utilizing the generalized Caputo-type differential operator introduced by Kochubei. Initially, employing Fourier analysis, we demonstrate the existence, positivity, and asymptotic behavior of solutions for the source-free equation. Subsequently, leveraging the representation of solutions for inhomogeneous linear ordinary differential equations with the generalized operator, we investigate analogous issues regarding the diffusion equation that includes a source term.

Let $f(z)$ denote a holomorphic cusp form for the full modular group $SL_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$, and let $L(s,f)$ be the associated automorphic $L$-function. This paper establishes the bound \begin{align*} N_{f}(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(\sigma)(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon} \end{align*}, where \begin{align*} A(\sigma)= \begin{cases} \frac{4}{4\sigma-1} &\textup{for}\ \
\frac{21}{22}\leq\sigma \leq 1,\\ \frac{2}{13\sigma-11} &\textup{for}\ \
\frac{17}{18}\leq\sigma\leq \frac{21}{22}, \end{cases} \end{align*} and \begin{align*} N_{f}(\sigma,T):=\sum_{L(\beta+i\gamma,f)=0 \atop
