\sigma\leq\beta\leq1 ,\ 10\leq|\gamma|\leq T}1. \end{align*} For values of $\sigma$ close to 1, this result refines the findings of Ivi\'{c} \cite{I2} and yields an optimal estimate derived from the exhausted Weyl bounds. Furthermore, these specific outcomes cannot be derived from the general theorems presented by Perelli \cite{P}.

Over recent years, the trend of remote work, particularly within the IT industry, has surged, with its popularity peaking following the COVID-19 pandemic. Concurrently, organizations have shifted toward managing projects using agile methodologies, which rely on continuous, small-scale feedback loops driven by effective communication. This survey aims to identify the obstacles of applying these processes in remote environments, with a specific focus on communication impacts. We analyze the critical role communication plays within agile frameworks and explore strategies to mitigate the risks posed by remote settings. Finally, we outline other miscellaneous challenges that companies may face, noting that while they carry potential dangers, they are generally less significant to agile implementation overall.

This note examines isoperimetric-type problems concerning 3-dimensional parallelohedra, defined as convex polyhedra capable of tiling 3-dimensional Euclidean space via translation. The primary finding establishes that, within the class of unit-volume 3-dimensional parallelohedra, the regular truncated octahedron possesses the minimal mean width.

We investigate the uniqueness, $L^2$ continuity, and asymptotic decay as time progresses for Leray solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations featuring a nonlinear exponential damping term $a (e^{b |u|^{\bf 4}}-1)u$, where $a,b>0$.

Substitution schemes serve as a traditional approach to tiling Euclidean space. By permitting multiple scales within these schemes, we present a diverse family of tile partition sequences generated by substitution rules, of which Kakutani's partition of the unit interval is a specific instance. Leveraging our recent findings on path counting in directed weighted graphs, we demonstrate that these partition sequences are uniformly distributed, thereby generalizing Kakutani's initial result. Additionally, we outline specific limiting frequencies tied to these partition sequences, which correspond to the distribution and occupied volume of tiles of particular types.

We investigate the near-critical dynamics of holographic superfluids at finite temperature and chemical potential within the probe limit. This framework enables an analysis of the coupled evolution between the complete complex order parameter and the system's charge density. By employing analytic methods in the bulk, we formulate an effective theory for long-wavelength gapless and pseudo-gapped modes. Our construction aligns with Model F from the Hohenberg and Halperin classification, allowing us to calculate the complex dissipative kinetic transport coefficient using thermodynamic variables and black hole horizon data. Furthermore, we analyze these modes and contend that at finite density, the dispersion relations exhibit discontinuities between the normal and broken phases. Finally, we evaluate our findings against previous numerical studies.

The radio sky at frequencies below approximately 10 MHz remains largely uncharted, representing the final unexplored segment of the astronomical electromagnetic spectrum. Future space missions targeting these ultra-low frequencies (ULF) would greatly benefit from reliable predictions regarding sky brightness distributions at these wavelengths. This study presents a radio sky model extending down to roughly 1 MHz. Beyond discrete HII regions, our model incorporates free-free absorption caused by thermal electrons within the Milky Way's warm ionized medium (WIM). This absorption effect becomes significant at frequencies below 10 MHz and may cause the global radio spectrum to peak around 3 MHz. Our resulting sky map reveals distinctive characteristics at ultra-long wavelengths, notably a darker Galactic plane compared to higher frequencies, as well as pronounced shadows cast by the spiral arms. This model serves as a valuable guide for planning future ultra-long wavelength observations. The Ultralong-wavelength Sky Model with Absorption (ULSA) is available for download at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4454153.

A significant disparity exists between the number of spoken languages and the resources available for their study. Attention predominantly focuses on major languages due to their extensive media presence and speaker populations, leaving less common languages often lacking high-quality corpora. This paper addresses such an imbalance by introducing new evaluation resources for Tatar, a Turkic language primarily spoken in the Tatarstan Republic of Russia. We provide three datasets: Similarity and Relatedness sets containing human-scored word pairs for assessing semantic models, and an Analogies set featuring analogy questions to investigate semantic, syntactic, and morphological dimensions of language modeling. While these datasets mirror the structure of existing English resources, they are not simple translations; instead, they incorporate Tatar-specific nuances and extend beyond the original English versions. Furthermore, we evaluate state-of-the-art word embedding models for both Tatar and English using these new and original datasets, respectively, to report on comparative performance findings.

We evaluated the emergence of fast neutrino flavor instabilities across two advanced three-dimensional core-collapse supernova simulations utilizing a two-moment, three-species neutrino transport framework: one featuring an exploding 9 solar mass progenitor and another with a non-exploding 20 solar mass model. Beyond confirming existing instabilities within the neutrino decoupling and pre-shock zones, we identified flavor instabilities in the post-shock region of the exploding scenario, which appear to be driven by scattering. Conversely, the failure of the heavier model to achieve a successful explosion significantly suppresses fast instabilities in its post-shock region. This suppression results from elevated matter densities behind the stalled or receding shock, leading to high neutrino scattering rates and consequently more isotropic neutrino and antineutrino distributions. Our results indicate that the specific properties of supernova models and the ultimate fate of the explosion profoundly influence the onset of fast instabilities, underscoring the necessity for a broader array of realistic hydrodynamical collapse simulations to reliably predict flavor conversion dynamics.

We investigate wealth rank correlations within a basic macroeconomic framework. To measure the correlation between wealth rankings across different time points, we employ Kendall's $\tau$, Spearman's $\rho$, Goodman--Kruskal's $\gamma$, and the overlap ratio of the lists. Our findings indicate that the dynamics of wealth flow and the rate at which ranking lists reshuffle are determined by model parameters governing wealth exchange rates and growth volatility. Furthermore, we examine the rheology of wealth in real-world data by analyzing lists of the wealthiest individuals in Poland, Germany, the USA, and globally.

In 1987, one of the review's authors introduced the dislocation model for the supersolid state of $^4$He. Since 2007, extensive theoretical and experimental research has provided robust support for this model, confirming the original 1987 hypothesis. These studies have also introduced new concepts, such as superclimb of dislocations and the syringe effect, characterized by giant isochoric compressibility. This paper examines the primary theoretical and experimental accomplishments regarding dislocation-induced supersolidity and outlines the current understanding of the phenomenon.

Although deep reinforcement learning has yielded significant advancements in complex decision-making scenarios, its primary strength—deep neural networks—remains largely opaque. A viable approach to understanding these black-box models involves distilling them into interpretable structures like decision trees, which utilize if-then rules that are straightforward to comprehend and validate. However, conventional model distillation typically functions as a supervised learning task assuming a stationary data distribution, an assumption that fails in reinforcement learning contexts. Consequently, standard policy distillation, which relies on behavior cloning, can introduce minor errors that lead to data distribution shifts. This results in distilled policies with low fidelity and subpar performance. To mitigate this, we propose shifting the distillation objective from behavior cloning to maximizing advantage evaluation. This novel approach aims to maximize approximated cumulative rewards while prioritizing catastrophic behaviors in critical states, thereby mitigating data shift effects. We tested our method across various Gym environments, a commercial fighting game, and a self-driving car simulator. Empirical results indicate that our method maintains higher cumulative rewards compared to behavior cloning and learns a policy more consistent with the original. Furthermore, analysis of the rules extracted from the distilled decision trees demonstrates that the proposed method yields reasonable and robust decisions.

This work investigates the error associated with counting unimodular lattice points within a dilated and translated parallelogram. Leveraging results by Skriganov, we demonstrate that this error is comparable to an ergodic sum involving the discrete geodesic flow on the space of unimodular lattices. Applying techniques from prior research by Fayad and Dolgopyat, we establish that, under appropriate normalization, a specific point process converges in distribution to a Poisson process. Consequently, when the unimodular lattice is drawn from the normalized Haar measure, the ergodic sum converges to a centered Cauchy distribution. Building on these findings, we extend this methodology—encountering greater complexity—to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the error. We prove that, when normalized by $\log(t)$ where $t$ represents the dilation factor, the error also converges in law to a centered Cauchy distribution as $t \to \infty$, provided the lattice and translation vector are random. In forthcoming research, we will address the case of a ball in dimension $d \geq 2$, showing that the error, when normalized by $t^{\frac{d-1}{2}}$ with $t$ as the ball's dilation factor, converges in law as $t \to \infty$, and that the limiting distribution possesses a moment of order 1.

Although natural crystals are limited to three dimensions ($d$), we propose the concept of \emph{projected topological branes} (PTBs). These are lower-dimensional branes situated within higher-dimensional parent topological crystals, formed by applying a geometric cut-and-project method to the Hilbert space of the parent lattice Hamiltonian. Depending on whether the brane's slope is rational or irrational, the system exhibits either a new lattice periodicity or a quasicrystal, the latter leading to topoquasicrystals within the PTB framework. Crucially, these PTBs retain key characteristics of their parent crystals, including bulk-boundary and bulk-dislocation correspondences, as well as topological invariants. We illustrate these findings using two-dimensional parent Chern insulators, demonstrating how they imprint localized endpoints, dislocation modes, and local Chern numbers onto projected one-dimensional (1D) topological branes. Furthermore, by stacking 1D projected Chern insulators, we reveal signatures of three-dimensional Weyl semimetals in $d=2$, specifically Fermi arc surface states and bulk chiral zeroth Landau levels that drive the chiral anomaly. Collectively, PTBs provide a viable pathway to experimentally realize higher-dimensional ($d>3$) topological phases.

Training deep neural networks (DNNs) is inherently time-consuming. Although most current approaches aim to optimize efficiency by overlapping or scheduling computation and communication, this paper advances the field by eliminating both computation and communication through DNN layer freezing. The core insight is that the training progress of internal DNN layers varies significantly, with front layers typically converging much faster than deeper ones. To investigate this, we introduce the concept of "training plasticity" to measure the training progress of individual internal layers. Building on this, we developed KGT, a knowledge-guided DNN training system that leverages semantic knowledge from a reference model to precisely assess each layer's plasticity and safely freeze those that have converged, thereby bypassing their associated backward computation and communication. The reference model is generated dynamically using quantization techniques and executes forward operations asynchronously on available CPUs to keep overhead minimal. Furthermore, KGT utilizes prefetching to cache intermediate outputs of frozen layers, effectively skipping their forward computation. Experimental results on popular vision and language models demonstrate that KGT achieves a 19%–43% training speedup compared to state-of-the-art methods without compromising accuracy.

This study investigates the generation of photon vortices in synchrotron radiation emitted by a spiral-moving electron subjected to a uniform magnetic field along the z-axis, employing Landau quantization. The resulting photon vortex wave functions are identified as eigenstates of the z-component of total angular momentum (zTAM); specifically, in the m-th harmonic radiation, individual photons correspond to eigenstates of zTAM with the value m, a finding that aligns with prior research. Utilizing these derived wave functions, we compute decay widths and energy spectra under the extreme magnetic fields of $10^{12}$ to $10^{13}$ G, characteristic of astrophysical environments like magnetized neutron stars, jets, and black hole accretion disks. These calculations indicate that photon vortices are predominantly produced in such objects. Despite lacking coherence, future detectors leveraging quantum effects may eventually measure these cosmic photon vortices. Additionally, this phenomenon influences stellar nucleosynthesis occurring within strong magnetic fields.

This paper investigates queueing systems operating with delayed information, employing a generalized version of the multinomial logit choice model for the arrival process. While prior research has restricted the multinomial logit model to an exponential functional form, our work extends this to various other forms. Specifically, we calculate the critical delay and examine its relationship with the selected functional form. We demonstrate that these alternative forms can be interpreted as exponential models where the rate parameter is uncertain; notably, the distribution of this rate parameter corresponds to the inverse Laplace-Stieltjes transform of the functional form, provided it exists. Finally, we conduct extensive numerical experiments to validate our theoretical findings.

This study presents ultrasound velocity and magnetostriction measurements for the orthogonal-dimer antiferromagnet SrCu2(BO3)2, extending up to the magnetic saturation field. Beyond known anomalies linked to fractional magnetization plateaus (M/Ms = 1/8, 1/4, 1/3, 2/5, and 1/2), we identified additional high-field anomalies in sound velocity and magnetostriction occurring at 116, 127, and 139 T. Notably, the sound velocity of the c66 acoustic mode exhibits strong dependence on the plateau state, showing a dramatic 50% reduction within the 1/2 plateau. This drop results from a tetragonal-to-orthorhombic instability driven by triplet crystallization into a checkerboard pattern. Both this effect and the high-field anomalies are accurately described by tensor-network calculations (iPEPS) based on the Shastry-Sutherland model. We specifically conclude that the 139 T anomaly marks magnetization saturation, while the anomalies at 116 and 127 T likely correspond to supersolid phases with nearly degenerate energies in this field range.

Grasping the mechanisms behind quenching in low-mass galaxies is fundamental to comprehending galaxy evolution as a whole. Isolated galaxies serve as vital tools for distinguishing between complex internal and external factors that influence star formation. While comparing quenched field and satellite galaxies in the low-mass regime presents significant discovery potential, very few quenched galaxies with stellar masses below $\sim 10^{9} M_{\odot}$ are known beyond the virial radius ($R_{vir}$) of any host halo. Crucially, both simulations and observations indicate the existence of an intermediate population of backsplash galaxies that can complement interpretations of environmental quenching. Unlike field galaxies, backsplash galaxies reside outside a host halo's virial radius, yet their star formation has been significantly affected by prior interactions with more massive systems. This paper reports the discovery of a quenched low-mass galaxy ($M_{\star} \sim 10^{7} M_{\odot}$) located approximately $1 R_{vir}$ in projection from the M81 group. By employing surface brightness fluctuations (SBF), we investigated whether the newly identified galaxy, designated dw0910p7326 and nicknamed "Blobby," is a backsplash galaxy or a more distant field object. The measured SBF distance of $3.21^{+0.15 +0.41}_{-0.15 -0.36}$ Mpc suggests that Blobby likely resides between $1.0 < R/R_{vir} < 2.7$ outside the combined M81–M82 system. Due to its distance and quiescent state, Blobby represents a strong candidate for a backsplash galaxy and may offer insights into the formation and evolution of these intriguing objects.

Horizontal partitioning is a widely adopted method for scaling transactional databases, offering improvements in scalability, high availability, and self-management. However, selecting or designing an optimal partitioning scheme for a specific workload and database often proves challenging. This technical report introduces a fine-grained, hyper-graph-based database partitioning system tailored for transactional workloads. The system accepts a database, workload, node cluster, and partitioning constraints as inputs, producing a lookup table that encodes the final partitioning strategy. By modeling the database partitioning problem as a multi-constraint hyper-graph partitioning task, the system calculates a minimum cut to reduce the total number of distributed transactions within the workload. This approach ensures balanced partition sizes and access workloads while adhering to all imposed constraints. Furthermore, the system is highly interactive, enabling users to define partition constraints, visualize the resulting partitioning effects, and incorporate human expertise and indirect domain knowledge to refine the generated schemes.

We demonstrate that determining whether two Dedekind sums, $S(c,b)$ and $S(d,b)$, are equal is equivalent to determining if a Dedekind sum defined by parameters $b, c, d$ assumes a specific value. Utilizing this finding, we generate infinite sequences of distinct Dedekind sums that are pairwise equal. Furthermore, we establish a theorem specifying the count of Dedekind sums $S(d,b)$, where $1\le d\le b-1$, that can equal a given $S(c,b)$ when $b$ is square-free.

Molecular clouds, characterized by their complex variable-density structures and role as primary sites of star formation, stand as some of the most functionally important yet poorly understood elements of the universe. To decipher their inherent structural intricacies, we utilize high-resolution bitmap-based 3D printing, a method that capitalizes on the human brain's superior capacity to detect patterns hidden within two-dimensional representations. Drawing from a novel suite of nine simulations depicting various physical extremes of the turbulent interstellar medium, our workflow enables the clear visualization of specific features in the 3D-printed models—such as quasi-planar structures—that are often concealed in conventional renderings and animations. Consequently, our bitmap-based 3D printing technique accurately replicates the subtle density gradients within molecular clouds in a tangible, intuitive, and visually striking format. Beyond establishing a foundation for the intuitive analysis of other complex astronomical datasets, these 3D-printed models also function as effective tools for educational initiatives and public outreach.

This work investigates three-dimensional variational models for dislocations under line-tension scaling. We introduce a unified framework capable of handling energies exhibiting subquadratic growth at infinity, alongside various regularization methods for singularities near dislocation lines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior, established through Gamma convergence, remains invariant regardless of the specific energy functional or regularization technique employed.

Fuzzy incidence graphs (FIGs) offer an efficient modeling approach for real-world scenarios that involve additional attributes within vertex-edge relationships. This article investigates various operations on FIGs, specifically analyzing the join, Cartesian product, tensor product, and composition. The research primarily focuses on strong fuzzy incidence graphs (SFIGs), utilizing the concept of strong incidence domination (SID) to examine the strong incidence domination number (SIDN) across these operations. Fundamental properties derived from these operations are explored, along with the determination of bounds for the domination number of the Cartesian and tensor products of two SFIGs. Additionally, the study covers FIGs involving strong joins and compositions, as well as complete fuzzy incidence graphs (CFIGs) and those containing effective pairs.

Over the past ten years, substantial work has focused on lowering the false positive rate in approximate membership checking, resulting in innovations like cuckoo and xor filters, as well as adaptive filters that dynamically adjust to prevent future collisions. This paper introduces a novel class of static filters designed to entirely eliminate false positives for a specific set of negative elements, demonstrating their efficient implementation via xor probing filters. We present multiple constructions of these filters that minimize the associated memory and speed overheads. Extensive evaluations confirm their functionality and reveal that, in many scenarios, the overhead is negligible. Furthermore, we explore various practical applications to highlight the benefits of these filters.

Managing and curating a commercial sound effects library is a labor-intensive process, further complicated by expanding databases and frequent taxonomy revisions. Additionally, the creation of taxonomies and sound retrieval are hindered by inconsistent metadata, a persistent challenge that remains despite the adoption of the new Universal Category System industry standard. To tackle these issues and bypass dataset-specific constraints that impede the effective training of deep learning models, we employ representation learning to develop generalized embeddings. These embeddings serve as a taxonomy-agnostic representation applicable across diverse sound effects libraries. Our findings demonstrate that a dataset-independent yet task-specific representation can effectively resolve data-related challenges such as class imbalance, inconsistent labeling, and limited dataset sizes, surpassing established methods like OpenL3. Furthermore, detailed experimental results highlight the influence of various metric learning strategies and cross-dataset training techniques on the effectiveness of these representations.

We present seven new eclipse observations for the novalike variable 1RXS J064434.5+334451. Combining these findings with all existing data (36 published and 16 unpublished) produces an optimal linear ephemeris of BJD$_\mathrm{ecl} = 2,453,403.7611(2) + 0.269~374~43(2)~\mathrm{E}$. A slightly better fit is achieved using a quadratic ephemeris: BJD$_\mathrm{ecl} = 2,453,403.7598 + 0.269~374~87~\mathrm{E} - 2.0\times10^{-11}~\mathrm{E}^2$, indicating that the orbital period is likely decreasing at a rate of $\dot P \simeq -1.5\times10^{-10}$.

We present a novel, high-performance architecture for parallelism in the Quantum Monte Carlo code QMCPACK. This new design surpasses the prior GPU implementation by more effectively leveraging the hierarchical parallelism of heterogeneous systems. By introducing a "crowds of Monte Carlo walkers" concept and facilitating greater offloading from host CPU threads to the GPU, the updated version achieves higher GPU occupancy. We anticipate that these performance gains will remain consistent across various hardware platforms, thereby enhancing developer productivity and lowering maintenance expenses. Furthermore, scientific output is bolstered by comprehensive fallback capabilities to CPU execution, ensuring optimal performance whether GPU resources are unavailable or less efficient than CPU execution.

Tree-width serves as a vital instrument for solving computational problems on graphs, yet it is often necessary to analyze other entities—such as decorated graphs or algebraic structures—where no equivalent measure currently exists. This paper introduces an abstract counterpart to tree-width that uniformly encompasses various tree-width-like invariants, ranging from standard graph and hypergraph tree-widths to complemented tree-width and novel constructs like the tree-width of modular quotients. This generalization is achieved by formulating a broad theory of categories supporting abstract versions of both tree decompositions and tree-width, which we term pseudo-chordal completions and the triangulation functor, respectively.

This paper introduces a novel tool designed to assist institutions in deploying targeted countermeasures for emergency prevention and response, such as the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, utilizing quantitative and multi-scale data. Implemented as a centralized, single-user web platform, the system leverages Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms to process heterogeneous data and generate risk assessments. At its core, a specialized neural network is trained to identify correlations among key inputs, including environmental factors (meteorological and chemical-physical), human activity (traffic and crowding), pollution levels (specifically particulate matter concentrations), and epidemiological data tracking contagion progression. Developed in the initial project phase, the tool functions both as a predictive Decision Support System (DSS) utilizing real-time measurements and as a simulation environment for adjusting input parameters to minimize risk levels. Consequently, the authors aim to create various scenarios to evaluate different restrictive strategies, allowing for the comparison of their anticipated benefits. This approach facilitates the adoption of measures tailored to specific needs and geographic areas, effectively safeguarding public health while considering the economic and social implications of such decisions.

Question 1.20 in [4] asks whether a compact group $G$, for which the set $\mathcal{N}_k(G) = \{(x_1,\dots,x_{k+1}) \in G^{k+1} \mid [x_1,\dots, x_{k+1}] = 1\}$ possesses positive Haar measure within $G^{k+1}$, necessarily contains an open $k$-step nilpotent subgroup. While the case $k = 1$ has already been established, we provide a positive answer for $k = 2$.

This study investigates the penetration depths of corner states—localized modes found at the corners of two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators—using the Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes model. We demonstrate that by tuning the energy of these corner states toward the edge gap boundary via an on-site potential, the penetration depth along the edge diverges to infinity, whereas the penetration depth into the bulk remains finite. By analytically deriving the corner-state wavefunction in terms of elliptic integrals, we reproduce this anisotropic behavior, confirming that corner states possess two distinct penetration depths with different characteristics. Furthermore, we show that the hybridization of corner states is mediated by their penetration depth through interference effects, as these states exhibit negligible interference with edge or bulk states.

For nearly a century, theoretical physics has focused on infrared divergences within the perturbative expansions of gauge theory amplitudes and cross-sections. As researchers probe higher perturbative orders, new insights continue to surface, driven by the need for increasingly refined understanding in high-precision phenomenological applications. This review offers a pedagogical survey of the topic. We briefly examine early historical findings, present simple low-order examples within perturbative QCD, and outline the essential tools required to generalize these results to all orders. Furthermore, we discuss recent advances in calculating soft anomalous dimensions for multi-particle scattering amplitudes at high orders and introduce the rapidly evolving field of infrared subtraction used to compute differential distributions at colliders.

This paper introduces a general framework designed to reduce disparities in predicted classes regarding secondary attributes such as race and gender. Our approach involves training a multi-objective function that, alongside predicting primary class labels, utilizes a clustering-based heuristic to minimize differences in class label distributions across cluster memberships, operating under the assumption that each cluster corresponds to a unique combination of attribute values. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset demonstrate that this method effectively mitigates cognitive biases in both zero-shot scenarios, where no secondary attribute annotations are available, and few-shot scenarios, where only a limited number of annotations are provided.

Identities succinctly characterize the attributes of mathematical expressions, enabling the creation of more efficient and precise function implementations. Currently, however, discovering these identities relies on manual intervention, demanding significant expertise. We introduce a two-stage synthesis and deduplication pipeline designed to automate this discovery process. The initial synthesis phase utilizes an e-graph to construct a set of rewrite rules, thereby generating candidate identities. Since many of these candidates are redundant, a secondary deduplication phase eliminates them by employing integer linear programming alongside another e-graph. When applied to 61 benchmarks, this approach produces 7,215 candidate identities in the synthesis stage, which the deduplication phase filters down to 125 core identities.

Deep learning models applied to medical imaging have achieved performance comparable to or surpassing human experts on numerous diagnostic tasks, exemplified by the high multi-class classification accuracy seen in the CheXpert competition for chest x-ray pathology detection. Nevertheless, developing and validating these models demands vast image datasets and still results in false predictions, which are identified through human-in-the-loop review. This paper presents a practical method to enhance pre-trained model predictions using Few-Shot Learning (FSL). Following the initial training and validation, a small set of misclassified images is gathered to retrain the model using **Image Triplets**, consisting of a false positive or false negative paired with a true positive and a true negative. This retrained FSL model yields significant performance improvements using only a few epochs and a minimal number of images. Furthermore, FSL facilitates rapid retraining within human-in-the-loop workflows, allowing radiologists to correct mislabeled inferences and enabling swift model updates. We compare the performance of our retrained model against existing medical imaging FSL approaches that typically train and evaluate models simultaneously.

RooFit and RooStats, the statistical modelling toolkits within ROOT, are currently integral to searches and measurements at the Large Hadron Collider and B factories. Although the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC will generate larger datasets that promise higher precision, it will also demand accelerated data processing to maintain stable fitting times. This paper introduces a redesign of RooFit's internal dataflow and a simplification of its interfaces. The new interfaces adopt an STL-like appearance and feel to enhance accessibility from both C++ and Python, thereby improving interoperability and usability without breaking compatibility with existing code. Furthermore, the revamped dataflow optimizes cache locality and data loading, enabling vectorised SIMD computations for batch processing. These improvements reduce the computation time for unbinned likelihoods by a factor of four to sixteen, ensuring that future, larger datasets can be fitted within the same timeframe or more quickly than current capabilities.

When the outer semi-major axis of a triple or multiple star system exceeds 10³ AU, these systems interact significantly with Galactic field stars. Stable configurations consisting of two white dwarfs (WDs) and a low-mass main sequence (MS) star in a wide outer orbit can be destabilized by gravitational encounters with random field stars. These interactions sufficiently increase the eccentricity of the distant third star, allowing it to interact substantially with the inner binary. This triggers multiple binary-single resonant encounters, which can lead to either a collision between the nondegenerate star and a WD or the disruption of the triple system into a compact binary and an ejected third object. The resulting compact binary may be a surviving MS-WD pair, a colliding MS-WD pair, or a double WD system that could inspiral via gravitational wave emission. We compute the collision rates between MS and WD stars and the merger rates of double WDs, while also outlining the prospects for detecting such collisions, which might manifest as sub-luminous supernova events.

Accurate plasma diagnostics are essential for characterizing the physical conditions of gaseous systems, which relies heavily on the proper execution of extinction corrections. However, a logical circularity exists: determining the extinction correction requires knowledge of the target's physical conditions—precisely the parameters diagnostics aim to measure—since extinction levels are typically derived by comparing observed spectra with theoretical models. A solution to this dilemma involves performing extinction correction and plasma diagnostics simultaneously through an iterative process to reach a converged solution. When executed self-consistently, a stable solution can be achieved using only well-calibrated line intensities, provided an extinction law and $R_V$ value are adopted. Despite this, such rigorous numerical analyses remain uncommon. This contribution to the APN 8e conference reviews these complexities and addresses critical issues based on recent experimental findings. It appears that the intricate nature of these problems, driven by their highly numerical character, historically necessitated analytical simplifications to make them solvable before computers were prevalent. Surprisingly, these simplifications persist in current literature even with abundant computational power available. Consequently, the community is urged to abandon the outdated practice of avoiding numerical calculations, which was once a necessary compromise. This shift is particularly vital for spatially-resolved 2-D spectroscopy, which directly contradicts the uniformity assumptions often blindly applied from 1-D spectroscopy.

Although Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent psychiatric condition, establishing an accurate diagnostic method remains challenging. Recently, researchers have leveraged advances in computing and machine learning to classify ADHD using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI). However, most existing studies train models using data from the entire brain. In contrast, this study proposes a novel approach by identifying and utilizing only the essential brain regions for a deep learning classification of ADHD. Utilizing rsfMRI data from the ADHD-200 Global Competition, we employed Leave-One-Site-Out cross-validation to ensure robust integration across multiple sites. Our results demonstrate that training with just 15 key regions of interest (ROIs) yielded an accuracy of 70.6%, surpassing the 68.6% accuracy achieved when using all ROIs. Furthermore, we explored a new architecture based on SCCNN-RNN by testing three modified models: (1) Separate Channel CNN RNN with Attention (ASCRNN), (2) Separate Channel Dilated CNN RNN with Attention (ASDRNN), and (3) Separate Channel CNN Slicing RNN with Attention (ASSRNN). The ASSRNN model achieved a high accuracy of 70.46% using only 13 critical ROIs. These findings indicate that focusing on crucial brain areas for ADHD diagnosis via deep learning produces superior results compared to utilizing the whole brain.

We examine a discrete-time SISI epidemic model where the population size remains constant, implying that the per capita birth and death rates are equal. The model's evolution operator is a non-linear function of seven parameters. By reducing this operator to a quadratic stochastic operator, we establish the uniqueness of its interior fixed point and investigate the asymptotic behavior of its trajectories under specific parameter conditions.

We present the results of a blinded analysis of low-energy electronic-recoil data from the initial science run of the XENONnT dark matter experiment. The incorporation of novel subsystems and a larger 5.9-tonne liquid xenon target lowered the background in the (1, 30) keV search region to $(15.8 \pm 1.3)$ events/(tonne$\times$year$\times$keV), achieving the lowest background level ever recorded in a dark matter detector and reducing it by approximately five times compared to XENON1T. Using an exposure of 1.16 tonne-years, we detected no excess above background and established new, stringent constraints on solar axions, an enhanced neutrino magnetic moment, and bosonic dark matter.

This paper examines how non-perturbative quantum gravitational corrections influence the stability of a quantum-sized AdS black hole. Employing non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, we analyze the black hole's evaporation process between two distinct states, explicitly deriving the quantum work distribution for this transition. Our findings indicate that both the stability of the black hole and its quantum work distribution are altered by these non-perturbative quantum gravitational corrections.

Collections of highly excited Rydberg atoms within an ultracold gas can be driven by a synergy of van-der-Waals forces and resonant dipole-dipole interactions. This motion may induce changes in the collective electronic Rydberg state through non-adiabatic transitions, especially when the system encounters a conical intersection. Focusing on the most experimentally feasible scenario—where Rydberg atoms are initially randomly excited in a three-dimensional bulk gas under blockade conditions—numerical simulations reveal that non-adiabatic transitions frequently occur when originating from the highest-energy repulsive Born-Oppenheimer surface. We describe a method to selectively excite this state via microwave resonance and identify a regime where nearly all collisional ionization of Rydberg atoms results from a preceding non-adiabatic transition. Given that Rydberg ionization is easily detectable, the proposed excitation and measurement scheme makes demonstrating non-adiabatic effects in Rydberg motion experimentally more accessible than in previously studied scenarios.

Let $K$ be a field, whether finite or infinite, with characteristic not equal to 2, and let $UT_n(K)$ denote the algebra of $n\times n$ upper triangular matrices over $K$. By defining a new product $a\circ b = \frac{1}{2}(ab + ba)$ on this set using the standard matrix multiplication, $UT_n$ becomes a Jordan algebra, denoted as $UJ_n(K)$. This paper characterizes the complete set of $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded polynomial identities for $UJ_2$ under any nontrivial $\mathbb{Z}_2$-grading and provides a linear basis for the associated relatively free $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded algebra.

A Majorana fermion is a unique fermionic particle that serves as its own antiparticle, with its behavior governed by the Majorana equation where the spinor field equals its charge-conjugate. In this study, we examined the Shannon entropy of linear Majorana fermions to determine how an external linear potential alters this quantity. We then constructed an ensemble of these particles to analyze the model's thermodynamic characteristics. Ultimately, we demonstrated how both Shannon entropy and thermodynamic properties change under the influence of a linear potential.

The CGHS black hole exhibits a spectrum and temperature equivalent to an accelerated reflecting boundary in flat spacetime, with beta coefficients matching a moving mirror model featuring exponential acceleration relative to laboratory time. In this framework, the black hole's center and event horizon coincide, a feature modeled by a perfectly reflecting regularity condition that redshifts field modes. Beyond calculating energy flux, we identify the parameters corresponding to the black hole mass and cosmological constant within the gravitational analog. By extending the analysis to arbitrary mirror trajectories, we derive the self-force (Lorentz-Abraham-Dirac) and relate both this force and the radiated power (Larmor) to entanglement entropy, suggesting an interpretation of acceleration radiation as information flow. Finally, applying these concepts to the specific CGHS black hole analog via a moving mirror reveals the physics governing information at the horizon as the system approaches thermal equilibrium.

This study critically examines the evaluation of automatic machine translation for user-generated content (UGC), highlighting how its unique characteristics present significant challenges. Our findings indicate that relying on standard metrics to measure average-case performance on UGC test sets fails to provide a reliable assessment of translation quality. Consequently, we propose a new dataset specifically designed for UGC translation evaluation, featuring manually annotated specificities categorized through a fine-grained typology. Leveraging this dataset, we perform multiple experiments to precisely quantify the impact of various UGC specificities on translation quality, achieving a level of detail not previously possible.

This paper introduces a general framework for modeling high entropy alloys as ensembles of randomly sampled, ordered configurations within a specified lattice. By applying statistical mechanics after the fact, the method derives ensemble properties—such as the free energy of mixing and local structure—as functions of composition and temperature. Random sampling is utilized to mitigate the high computational expenses associated with modeling alloys containing many components. This approach also establishes rigorous convergence criteria, allowing for the quantification of noise arising from random sampling and the estimation of the sample count necessary to reduce this noise to acceptable levels. The method is applicable to various scenarios: i) high entropy alloys, where conventional lattice models are computationally prohibitive; ii) "medium" entropy alloys, where both entropy and enthalpy are significant; and iii) alloys exhibiting residual short-range order. Binary through five-component group-IV chalcogenide alloys serve as case studies, demonstrating that the predicted miscibility aligns excellently with experimental data.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as condensed versions of longer phrases and are widely used across different writing formats. Although they help conserve space and reading time, they can hinder comprehension, particularly when an acronym remains undefined or is separated from its definition within lengthy documents. To address this, researchers and software developers have made significant strides in creating systems to identify acronyms and determine their correct meanings. However, no current solution offers a unified, publicly accessible tool capable of handling acronyms across diverse domains. Consequently, we present the first web-based system for acronym identification and disambiguation, supporting various fields such as general, scientific, and biomedical domains. This system is accessible at http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000, with a demonstration video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Additionally, the source code can be found at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

Direct imaging of circumstellar environments to identify Earth-like exoplanets represents a major challenge in contemporary astronomy, currently hindered by evolving non-common path aberrations (NCPA) arising from optics located downstream of the primary wavefront sensor. The self-coherent camera (SCC) functions as an integrated coronagraph and focal-plane wavefront sensor, creating wavefront-encoding Fizeau fringes in the focal plane by introducing a reference hole (RH) into the Lyot stop. This study demonstrates that incorporating a polarizer within the RH and a polarizing beamsplitter downstream of the Lyot stop allows the RH to be positioned immediately adjacent to the pupil. We designate this enhanced configuration as the polarization-encoded self-coherent camera (PESCC). Through both analytical and numerical analyses, we compare the PESCC to the standard SCC, revealing that the former reduces the requirements for focal-plane sampling and spectral resolution by factors of 2 and 3.5, respectively. Numerical simulations further indicate that the PESCC accesses approximately 16 times more photons, enhancing wavefront sensing sensitivity by a factor of roughly 4. Additionally, we demonstrate that the RH point-spread function (PSF) can be calibrated directly from PESCC images without extra measurements, facilitating coherent differential imaging (CDI) as a contrast-improving post-processing step for all observations. Under idealized conditions simulating space-based systems (clear aperture, charge-two vortex coronagraph, perfect deformable mirror, and noise limited only by phase and amplitude aberrations), we show that combining wavefront sensing with CDI achieves a $1\sigma$ raw contrast ranging from $\sim3 \cdot 10^{-11}$ to $8 \cdot 10^{-11}$ between 1 and 18 $\lambda/D$.

We present the inaugural detection of hydroxyl radical (OH) emission within the atmosphere of an extrasolar planet, specifically on the day-side of WASP-33b. This study analyzes high-resolution near-infrared emission spectra obtained via the InfraRed Doppler spectrograph on the 8.2-m Subaru telescope. Using the SysRem de-trending algorithm, we removed telluric and stellar lines before cross-correlating the residuals with OH and H$_{2}$O planetary spectrum templates generated from various line-lists. The accuracy of the OH line-lists was validated by cross-correlating them with the spectrum of GJ 436. Consequently, we identified an OH emission signature at a radial velocity ($K_\mathrm{p}$) of $230.9^{+6.9}_{-7.4}$ km s$^{-1}$ and a systemic velocity ($v_{\mathrm{sys}}$) of $-0.3^{+5.3}_{-5.6}$ km s$^{-1}$, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of 5.4 and a significance of 5.5$\sigma$. Furthermore, we achieved a marginal detection of H$_{2}$O emission in the H-band using the POKAZATEL line-list, with an S/N of 4.0 and significance of 5.2$\sigma$. However, no significant signal was found using the HITEMP 2010 line-list, likely due to discrepancies in line positions and strengths, as well as the incompleteness of that specific dataset. This marginal H$_{2}$O detection aligns with predictions that water is largely thermally dissociated in the upper atmospheres of ultra-hot Jupiters. Thus, alongside CO, OH is anticipated to be one of the most prevalent oxygen-bearing molecules on the day-side of these planets and must be included in atmospheric studies.

Machine learning models are frequently applied in sensitive domains where, alongside predictive accuracy, interpretability is crucial. Understanding a model's predictions is essential for identifying biases and error sources, serving as a foundational requirement for user trust. For complex, opaque state-of-the-art models, post-hoc, model-independent explanation methods are a standard remedy. Widely used techniques like IME, LIME, and SHAP explain individual predictions by perturbing instance features. However, Slack et al. (2020) recently challenged their robustness, demonstrating that inadequate perturbation sampling allows outcomes to be manipulated. This vulnerability could enable malicious actors to deceive inspections and conceal unethical or illegal biases within sensitive models, akin to the Dieselgate scandal. Such exploitation risks eroding public confidence and prompting legal restrictions on machine learning usage. This paper demonstrates that enhanced sampling strategies can prevent such malicious manipulation. The proposed approach utilizes data generators trained on the dataset distribution to create perturbation instances that closely resemble the training data. We find that this improved sampling boosts the robustness of LIME and SHAP, while confirming that the previously untested IME method is already the most robust among the three.
This paper investigates the existence of a random attractor for a stochastic lattice FitzHugh-Nagumo system perturbed by $\alpha$-stable Lévy noises, subject to specific dissipative conditions.

This study investigates the dynamics of one-dimensional quantum gases featuring strongly attractive contact interactions. We identify a specific set of initial states where these attractive forces effectively behave as strong repulsive forces throughout time evolution. Our results generalize theoretical findings regarding the super-Tonks-Girardeau gas to highly nonequilibrium regimes. This new mechanism is demonstrated using the canonical example of domain stability in a two-component Fermi gas. Furthermore, we examine nonlocal interactions and the universality of our conclusions. Finally, we leverage these insights to propose the existence of metastable quantum droplets within the regime of combined strongly attractive contact and attractive dipolar interactions.

We demonstrate a dual equivalence between the category of finitely presented Wajsberg hoops with homomorphisms and a specific subcategory of rational polyhedra featuring Z-maps. Leveraging this duality, we offer a geometric characterization of finitely generated projective and exact Wajsberg hoops. As applications, we examine logical properties within the positive fragment of Lukasiewicz logic. Our findings reveal that although deducibility in this fragment mirrors deducibility among positive formulas in Lukasiewicz logic, this equivalence does not extend to the admissibility of rules. Furthermore, we establish that the unification type of Wajsberg hoops is nullary, whereas the exact unification type is unitary, thereby proving the decidability of admissible rules in the fragment.

We examine banking networks characterized by assets and liabilities, where certain institutions may face insolvency and a central bank must determine which, if any, to rescue. We model these bailouts as an optimization task in which the central bank seeks to maximize a specific objective using its available resources. We demonstrate that, under diverse assumptions and for several intuitive objectives, this optimization problem is NP-hard and, in certain instances, difficult to approximate. Additionally, we show that when a central bank's bailout objective is fixed, banks within the network can negotiate new debt agreements to boost their market value in the event of a rescue, thereby shifting costs onto the central bank.

We present and investigate a realistic model of superconductivity in twisted bilayer WSe$_{2}$, where electron pairing is driven by spin-valley fluctuations within the weak-coupling regime. This framework integrates the complete continuum moiré bandstructure with a short-ranged repulsive interaction representing the Coulomb force projected onto localized Wannier orbitals. Through calculations of spin-valley susceptibility, we detect a Fermi surface nesting feature near half-filling of the uppermost moiré band, which markedly amplifies spin-valley fluctuations. Subsequently, we examine the dominant Kohn-Luttinger pairing instabilities resulting from these fluctuations, demonstrating that the primary instability can give rise to nematic, chiral, and topological superconductivity. Given that our results are asymptotically exact for weak interactions, they offer a robust foundation for future research into superconductivity in twisted transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers.

This paper presents a systematic investigation into the approximation characteristics of the topological and measurable coarse boundary groupoids linked to sequences of finite graphs with bounded degrees. Regarding the topological aspect, we demonstrate that the asymptotic coarse embeddability of such graph sequences into a Hilbert space corresponds precisely to the coarse boundary groupoid being topologically a-T-menable, thereby resolving a query posed by Rufus Willett. From a measure-theoretic perspective, we establish connections between the amenability and a-T-menability of the coarse boundary groupoid and concepts such as hyperfiniteness, property almost-A, and a variant of "almost asymptotic embeddability into Hilbert space." These findings are immediately applicable to graph spaces derived from sofic approximations.

Memory-limited partially observable stochastic control (ML-POSC) refers to the challenge of stochastic optimal control when information is incomplete and memory is constrained. To derive the optimal control function for ML-POSC, one must solve a coupled system comprising a forward Fokker-Planck (FP) equation and a backward Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. This study demonstrates that the HJB-FP system can be interpreted through Pontryagin's minimum principle applied within the probability density function space. Leveraging this interpretation, we introduce the forward-backward sweep method (FBSM)—an algorithm originally derived from Pontryagin's principle—to address ML-POSC. FBSM alternates between computing the forward FP equation and the backward HJB equation. While the convergence of FBSM is typically not assured, it is guaranteed in the context of ML-POSC due to the restricted coupling of the HJB-FP equations, which depends solely on the optimal control function.

High-dimensional generative models are widely utilized for tasks such as image compression, multimedia creation, anomaly detection, and data completion. Current state-of-the-art estimators for natural images typically employ autoregressive methods that decompose the joint pixel distribution into conditionals parameterized by deep neural networks, such as the PixelCNN. However, PixelCNNs are limited to modeling only a single decomposition and generation order, which restricts their ability to leverage extensive observed context in applications like image completion. To enable data generation in arbitrary orders, we present LMConv: a straightforward modification to standard 2D convolution that permits arbitrary masks to be applied to weights at every image location. By using LMConv, we train an ensemble of distribution estimators that share parameters but vary in generation order, resulting in superior performance on whole-image density estimation (2.89 bpd on unconditional CIFAR10) and globally coherent image completions. Our code can be accessed at https://ajayjain.github.io/lmconv.

Addressing society's intricate challenges demands innovative approaches, and utilizing diverse cognitive styles can foster such novelty in software development targeting these issues. An experiment involving 80 software design professionals revealed that female practitioners who exhibited a preference for multiple cognitive styles—specifically both intuition and rationality—generated the most novel software features compared to all other participants.

This research investigates kink-antikink scattering within the sine-Gordon model, specifically when interactions occur with an extra scalar field, $\psi$, residing in its quantum vacuum. Unlike classical scattering scenarios, this quantum setup generates radiation of $\psi$ quanta and allows kink-antikink pairs to form bound states analogous to sine-Gordon breathers. We calculate the radiation rate and identify the parameter ranges that support bound state formation. Notably, even these bound states emit radiation and decay, ultimately transitioning into long-lived oscillons.

Quantum interference stands out as a defining characteristic of quantum physics in low-dimensional systems. While quantum interference in charge transport has long been established, recent discoveries regarding interference-driven thermal properties have opened new avenues for phase-coherent heat control in mesoscopic devices. This study demonstrates that anomalous thermoelectric behaviors and efficient heat rectification can be realized by utilizing the phase-coherent edge states of quantum Hall systems. By analyzing a tunneling configuration involving multiple quantum point contacts, we show that interference pathways effectively disrupt electron-hole symmetry, enabling a thermoelectric charge current to flow in either direction—from hot to cold or vice versa—based on the specific characteristics of the tunnel junction. In alignment with this, we predict an interference-induced heat current and provide an intuitive physical explanation for these findings. Furthermore, we illustrate that heat rectification is achievable by coupling two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, an effect that can be amplified by leveraging the interference properties of the tunnel junction.

We utilize the Dirac-Frenkel variational principle combined with multiple Davydov ansätze to investigate the time-dependent fluorescence spectra of a driven qubit across weak- to strong-coupling regimes with the reservoir, where both the Rabi frequency and spontaneous decay rate are on par with the qubit's transition frequency. Our approach aligns closely with time-local master-equation methods in the weak-coupling limit and provides a versatile means to calculate spectra from bosonic dynamics rather than relying on two-time correlation functions. Although perturbative master equations fail in the strong-coupling regime, our method gains accuracy under specific conditions by employing bosonic coherent states. We demonstrate that counter-rotating coupling between the qubit and reservoir significantly influences photon number dynamics and spectral features under strong driving, even when the coupling is moderately weak. The resulting time-dependent spectra are generally asymmetric, a characteristic stemming from photon number evolution. Furthermore, we find that spectral profiles can deviate drastically from the standard Mollow triplet due to strong dissipation and/or multiphoton processes linked to intense driving. This formalism offers a distinct viewpoint for interpreting time-dependent spectra.

Modern edge devices, including cameras and mobile units, are evolving beyond their traditional functions of sensing and communication to handle advanced computations. This paper investigates collaborative object detection, specifically focusing on a framework where deep features extracted locally from images are sent to the cloud for additional analysis. We analyze how packet loss affects these transmitted features and explore various strategies to reconstruct the missing data. Our theoretical and experimental findings demonstrate that image inpainting techniques utilizing partial differential equations are highly effective for recovering missing features within the latent space. These results establish a new state-of-the-art benchmark for addressing missing data in collaborative object detection.

Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs) serve as digital certificates of uniqueness for assets ranging from art and music to tweets and memes, with significant discussion occurring on social platforms like Twitter. This study seeks to identify the key drivers behind NFT valuation by constructing a novel dataset that connects Twitter profiles with assets on OpenSea, the leading NFT marketplace. The resulting public dataset comprises 245,159 tweets from 17,155 distinct users, directly associating 62,997 OpenSea assets valued at approximately $19 million. Our analysis examines NFT growth trends, profiles the users promoting these assets, and evaluates how Twitter-specific attributes influence NFT virality. Additionally, we employ various machine learning and deep learning models to assess the predictive power of social media versus platform features regarding asset value. Our findings indicate that incorporating social media data improves prediction accuracy by 6% compared to baseline models relying solely on platform data, with user membership list counts, likes, and retweets emerging as critical social indicators.

Diffusion models, formulated as stochastic differential equations in continuous time, have emerged as a highly effective non-adversarial generative approach. Their training typically employs denoising score matching, a technique akin to multi-scale denoising autoencoders. In this work, we extend the denoising score matching framework to facilitate representation learning entirely without supervised data. While GANs and VAEs derive representations by mapping latent codes directly to data samples, our proposed diffusion-based method utilizes a novel formulation of the denoising score matching objective to inherently encode the necessary denoising information. This distinction enables precise manual control over the level of detail captured within the representation. Furthermore, we introduce an approach to learn infinite-dimensional latent codes, yielding state-of-the-art results in semi-supervised image classification. Finally, we evaluate the quality of these learned representations against other techniques, such as standard autoencoders and contrastive learning systems, by assessing their performance on downstream tasks.

This study investigates the controllability of a fluid-structure interaction system involving an incompressible viscous fluid and an elastic structure situated on a portion of the fluid's boundary. To simplify the analysis, the system is linearized, and the wave or plate equation governing the structure is substituted with a heat equation. We demonstrate that the resulting coupled system, consisting of the Stokes equations and a boundary heat equation, is null-controllable. The proof relies on Carleman estimates and interpolation inequalities, with one estimate specifically addressing Ventcel boundary conditions. This research serves as an initial step toward controlling the actual system where the structure is described by the wave or plate equations.

This study utilizes observed high-redshift galaxy surface brightness profiles to identify the most appropriate cosmological model. We compare theoretical predictions of these profiles against observational data within the $\Lambda$CDM and Einstein-de Sitter frameworks to assess how different spacetime geometries influence evolutionary effects, aiming to determine if current data can distinguish between these cosmologies. Building on the relationship between angular diameter distance and surface brightness established by Ellis and Perry (1979), we derived scaling relations using data from the Virgo cluster to generate theoretical predictions for Sersic-profile modeled brightness at redshifts $1.5 \lesssim z \lesssim 2.3$. These predictions were based on a subset of galaxies from Szomoru et al. (2012). By analyzing the discrepancies between theory and observation, we calculated the necessary adjustments in effective radius and surface brightness required for the observed galaxies to match the evolutionary features of the Virgo cluster. Our findings indicate that, given the uncertainties of this specific galaxy subset, neither cosmological model produces theoretical curves that significantly better align with observations than the other; consequently, no clear or detectable difference in galactic evolution emerges between the two models for our sample. Furthermore, we conclude that the Sersic index $n$ does not exert a significant influence on the evolution of these galaxies.

This study theoretically examines various facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion dynamics within spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates. Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-rigid pendulum model that enables a clear discussion of the emergence of antiferromagnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum," alongside phenomena such as large-amplitude pair oscillations and atom-molecule entanglement.

This paper estimates impulse responses using local projections within high-dimensional frameworks. We employ a desparsified (de-biased) lasso to estimate these projections, ensuring that the impulse response parameter of interest remains unpenalized. Under general conditions, we prove the uniform asymptotic normality of our proposed estimator. Furthermore, we evaluate the estimator's small-sample performance via a simulation study and examine two standard applications in macroeconomic research concerning monetary policy and government expenditure.

Investigating $\Delta L=2$ decays is essential for distinguishing between Dirac and Majorana neutrinos. Although neutrinoless nuclear double beta decay offers the most promising avenue for detecting di-electron signals of $\Delta L=2$, searches in di-lepton channels with other flavors face fewer statistical limitations. This work revisits the calculation of $\Delta L=2$ hyperon decays, specifically $B^-_i\to B^+_f\ell^-\ell'^-$, by incorporating hyperon form factors. This approach yields finite results for one-loop long-range mechanisms involving Majorana neutrinos. Furthermore, we examine short-range contributions within two promising frameworks: first, low-scale seesaw models featuring minimal parametrization with two heavy Majorana neutrinos, and second, an alternative scenario where a scalar boson coupled to di-leptons induces $\Delta L=2$ decays, offering additional predictions.

The Berge Conjecture posits that every bridgeless cubic graph possesses five perfect matchings where each edge belongs to at least one of them. This paper demonstrates that the conjecture is valid for two specific classes of cubic graphs: those with a circuit missing exactly one vertex, and bridgeless cubic graphs containing a 2-factor composed of two circuits. The first finding establishes that the Berge Conjecture applies to hypohamiltonian cubic graphs.

Discussions regarding indeterminism in physics center on the potential for an open future, where alternative future events may exist, and the actual occurrence of one is not entirely dictated by current conditions. However, can indeterminism similarly apply to the past, rendering it open? We demonstrate that adhering to the principle of finite information can imply such a possibility. Furthermore, we present a toy model illustrating how the past could be fundamentally indeterminate, while also accounting for the intuitive and observed asymmetry between the past—which can be partially remembered—and the future—which cannot be fully predicted.

We introduce a new and adaptable DNA-storage architecture that establishes hierarchical relationships among objects sharing the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data updates. Unlike previous approaches, our system treats a 20-base-pair PCR primer pair not as a definition for a single object, but as a distinct storage partition managed independently with its own indexing structure. We observe that while the total number of compatible primer pairs is constrained, the internal address space within each partition is virtually limitless. By exploiting the flexibility of this address space, we enable advanced storage semantics, including hierarchical organization and robust, efficient data update mechanisms. Additionally, to maximize the potential of PCR's prefix-based addressing, we developed a method to convert any arbitrary indexing scheme into a PCR-compatible format. This allows primers to be dynamically extended to include specific index segments, thereby narrowing the reaction scope to precisely retrieve individual objects (such as files or directories) within a partition. Our wet lab validation confirms the feasibility of this approach and demonstrates a 140-fold reduction in sequencing costs when retrieving smaller objects from a partition.

Insider threats refer to cyberattacks originating from within an organization's trusted circles. While deep learning for anomaly detection necessitates comprehensive data, insider threat information is often inaccessible due to organizational confidentiality constraints, creating a need for synthetic data to advance threat analysis methods. We introduce SPCAGAN, a generative adversarial network grounded in linear manifold learning that ingests heterogeneous data sources. This model employs a novel loss function to train the generator, enabling it to produce high-quality synthetic data that closely mirrors the original distribution. Additionally, we present a hybrid deep learning model designed for insider threat analysis. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets evaluated our approach regarding data synthesis, anomaly detection, adversarial robustness, and synthetic data quality. Empirical comparisons indicate that GAN-based oversampling is competitive with standard oversampling techniques. Specifically, our SPCAGAN model successfully mitigates mode collapse and converges more rapidly than prior GAN models. The results confirm that our proposed method yields lower errors, higher accuracy, and generates significantly superior synthetic insider threat data compared to existing models.

This work examines the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with initial data $u_0$ belonging to $L^1(\mathbb{R}^3)\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. A unique solution $u$ exists on a maximal time interval $[0,T_{max})$ within the space $C\big([0,T_{max}); L^2(\mathbb{R}^3) \cap L^p(\mathbb{R}^3)\big)$ for all $p>3$. We identify a specific function class $S_{regular}$, characterized by a scaling-invariant norm pair, such that $T_{max}=\infty$ whenever $u_0\in S_{regular}$. Notably, for any $u_0$ in this class and any $p>3$, the $L^p$ norm $\|u_0\|_{L^p}$ can be arbitrarily large. Conversely, an alternative theorem is established: either $T_{max}=\infty$ or $T_{max}$ falls within the interval $(T_l, T_r]$. In this scenario, the possibility of $T_r<T_{max}<\infty$ is eliminated, with explicit formulas provided for $T_l$ and $T_r$. This alternative serves as a regularity criterion amenable to computer verification. If $T_{max}=\infty$, the solution $u$ remains regular for all $(t,x)\in(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}^3$ and exhibits decay as $t\rightarrow\infty$. Furthermore, when $T_{max}\in (T_l,T_r]$, a lower bound for the blow-up rate of $u$ is derived.

This study investigates the $\Xi_b(6227)$ state, assuming a molecular structure, to extract its magnetic moment using light-cone QCD sum rules. The calculated value is $\mu_{\Xi_b}= 0.12 \pm 0.03~\mu_N$. This magnetic moment provides crucial insights into the state's internal composition and shape deformations. Consequently, measuring the magnetic moment of the $\Xi_b(6227)$ at future experimental facilities would significantly aid in determining its quantum numbers and elucidating its inner structure.

The Multiple Tensor-Times-Matrix (Multi-TTM) operation is fundamental to algorithms involving Tucker tensor decomposition, a technique widely applied in multidimensional data analysis. This work establishes communication lower bounds, defining the minimum data movement necessary for parallel Multi-TTM execution. The proof hinges on analytically solving a constrained, nonlinear optimization problem. Furthermore, we introduce a parallel algorithm that arranges processors into a logical grid featuring twice as many modes as the input tensor. By selecting appropriate grid dimensions, the algorithm achieves the established lower bounds, rendering it communication-optimal. Finally, we demonstrate that this approach substantially lowers communication overhead compared to the direct method of executing the computation as a series of individual tensor-times-matrix operations.
This work serves as both an update and an extension of our paper, "Open problems on $\beta\omega$" from the book *Open Problems in Topology*.

The growing global competition in the wine industry is heightening the demand for precise yield predictions in viticulture. Berry counting stands out as a highly promising, non-destructive, and automatable technique for forecasting harvests. This article introduces a method designed to tackle the issue of berries hidden by leaves, thereby improving the accuracy of berry counts and, consequently, harvest estimates. We employ generative adversarial networks (GANs), a deep learning approach that reconstructs probable scenarios behind foliage by leveraging patterns from images of unobstructed berries. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces berry counts that align more closely with manual reference counts than simple scaling factors. Unlike approaches that rely on multiplying counts, our technique better accommodates local conditions by directly utilizing the visual characteristics of visible berries. Additionally, we show that our method can determine specific image regions requiring new berries without needing explicit data about the occluded areas.

This study introduces a video autoencoder designed to learn self-supervised, disentangled representations of 3D geometry and camera orientation from video sequences. Leveraging the temporal consistency found in videos, the approach assumes that the 3D scene structure remains static across consecutive frames. When provided with a video sequence, the model decouples the scene into two components: (i) a temporally coherent deep voxel feature encoding the 3D structure, and (ii) a 3D camera pose trajectory for every frame. These disentangled elements are subsequently recombined to render the original video frames. Notably, the autoencoder can be trained solely using pixel reconstruction loss, eliminating the need for ground truth 3D or pose annotations. Beyond its core function, this representation facilitates various downstream applications such as novel view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and motion-following video generation. The method is evaluated on multiple large-scale natural video datasets, with demonstrated generalization capabilities on out-of-domain images.

LAMOST-MRS-B functions as a sub-project within the LAMOST medium-resolution (R~7500) spectroscopic survey, focusing on the statistical characteristics of binary and exotic stars, such as binary fractions, orbital period distributions, and mass ratios. The initiative originally aimed to observe approximately 30,000 stars with magnitudes between 10 and 14.5 over a five-year period using at least ten visits per target. Initially, plans called for observing 25 plates along the galactic plane in 2018, but observational constraints reduced this to 12 plates in 2019; concurrently, two new plates at high galactic latitudes were introduced to investigate how different environments affect binary properties. Within this project, identified exotic and low-metallicity stars were assigned the highest observation priority, while remaining selected stars were prioritized by brightness to maximize the acquisition of high-quality spectra. A total of 49,129 stellar spectra were obtained in the LAMOST-MRS-B field and released in Data Release 8 (DR8). Among these, 28,828 stars received more than two visits, and 3,375 received more than ten visits, all with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) greater than or equal to 10. The sample predominantly consists of B-, A-, and F-type stars with metallicities ranging from 0.6 to 0.4 dex relative to solar ([Fe/H]). Additionally, the survey identified 347 variable and exotic stars, as well as approximately 250 stars with [Fe/H] below 1 dex. Radial velocities (RVs) were derived using 892,233 spectra, achieving uncertainties of roughly 1 km/s for 95% of late-type stars and 10 km/s for early-type stars. The datasets described in this paper can be accessed at http://www.doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.j00113.00035.

This study investigates spontaneous symmetry breaking within specific nonlinear theories characterized by second-class constraints. By applying Dirac's method, we analyze the constraints and determine the degrees of freedom count, explicitly constructing the associated effective Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that the symplectic structure becomes degenerate on surfaces where the effective Hamiltonian assumes critical values. Specifically, we show that under conditions of spontaneous symmetry breaking—which entail non-trivial vacuum surfaces—second-class constraints act as first-class constraints in certain phase space regions. This behavior results in ill-defined Dirac brackets and alters the number of degrees of freedom. Consequently, these models may exhibit pathologies, such as modes with acausal propagation, with concrete examples of such phenomena detailed below.

This paper examines the Ricci curvature of Ricci solitons. Specifically, we demonstrate that a complete gradient Ricci soliton with non-negative Ricci curvature, which features a non-constant convex potential function with a finite weighted Dirichlet integral and satisfies a specific integral condition, is Ricci flat and isometrically splits a line. Additionally, we established that a gradient Ricci soliton possessing a non-constant concave potential function and bounded Ricci curvature is non-shrinking, implying that its scalar curvature has at most one critical point.

We investigate cases where (rigid) Calabi-Yau manifolds exhibit modularity, with their periods defined by hypergeometric functions.
