Historically, such attacks focused on eliminating traces from a single manipulation rather than a sequence of operations. Furthermore, recent studies indicate that current anti-forensic attacks suffer from limited transferability, meaning they fail to deceive forensic CNNs not involved in their training. This paper introduces a novel anti-forensic framework capable of removing traces left by diverse manipulation techniques. Designed to be transferable, this attack can effectively target unknown forensic CNNs while introducing only minimal, visually imperceptible distortions. Utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN), our generator is capable of processing color images of any dimension. We achieve this transferability through a specialized training strategy and loss function. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method successfully deceives various state-of-the-art forensic CNNs across different levels of attacker knowledge.

Recent findings from the CDF-II collaboration reveal a $7\sigma$ deviation from Standard Model predictions, complemented by a $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy in Fermilab's measurement of the muon magnetic moment. We investigate the interrelations among neutrino masses, dark matter, the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly, and the W-boson mass anomaly within a unified framework utilizing a $Z_4$ extension of the scotogenic model incorporating vector-like leptons (VLL). Neutrino masses arise at the one-loop level, while the inert doublet resolves the W-boson mass anomaly by modifying the oblique parameters $S$, $T$, and $U$. The coupling between the VLL triplet $\psi_T$ and the inert doublet $\eta$ yields a positive contribution to the muon anomalous magnetic moment. Furthermore, the VLL triplet establishes a lepton portal connecting to dark matter ($\eta_R^0$). The model predicts a lower limit of $m_{ee} > 0.025$ eV at $3\sigma$, a value accessible to current $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay experiments. Consistency with the muon anomalous magnetic moment requires $1.3 < y_\psi < 2.8$ and a dark matter candidate mass between $152\text{ GeV}$ and $195\text{ GeV}$. Additionally, constraints imposed by the W-boson mass anomaly narrow the viable dark matter mass range to $154\text{ GeV} < M_{\eta_{R}^{0}} < 174\text{ GeV}$.

Research into cybersecurity for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) has increasingly focused on developing resilient control and estimation methods against novel threats. Notably, False Data Injection Attacks (FDIAs) can evade Bad Data Detection (BDD), severely compromising state estimators and robust controllers even with minimal sparse data corruption. To counter this, $\ell_1$-minimization has been widely adopted to enhance attack-resilient estimator designs, theoretically accommodating up to 50% compromised nodes. To extend resilience beyond this limit, researchers are integrating prior information into resilient observer frameworks, often derived via data-driven machine learning. Current findings indicate a strong positive correlation between the precision of this prior information and the percentage of tolerated attacks. This paper introduces a pruning technique to enhance the precision of such prior information by accounting for the stochastic uncertainty inherent in machine learning models. Subsequently, a weighted $\ell_1$-minimization approach is proposed using the refined prior. Both theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate that this pruning method significantly boosts observer performance, enabling the system to withstand much higher attack percentages even with moderately accurate machine learning models.

A connected graph is defined as belonging to the non-QE class if it lacks a quadratic embedding within a Euclidean space. Among non-QE graphs, those termed "primary" are those that do not contain a non-QE graph as a proper isometrically embedded subgraph. The classification of graphs with six vertices into categories of QE graphs, non-QE graphs, and primary non-QE graphs has been fully established.

Microrobots offer significant potential for tasks such as targeted delivery and microscale mixing; however, existing manufacturing methods are constrained by low throughput and restricted material choices. We present a flexible approach to synthesize microrobots using readily available micro- and nanoparticles. Our method relies on the toposelective attachment of photocatalytic nanoparticles to microparticles, utilizing a multi-functional polymer and a Pickering-wax emulsification process to produce large volumes of photo-responsive Janus particles. The polymer, featuring both silane and nitrocatechol groups, bonds silica microspheres with various metal oxide nanoparticles. The Pickering-wax emulsions shield portions of the microsphere surfaces, facilitating the asymmetric functionalization necessary for self-propulsion. The resulting photocatalytic microrobots exhibit a unique, orientation-dependent 3D active motion under UV light, distinct from previously reported behaviors. By integrating a vast library of heterogeneous photocatalytic nanoparticles with emerging active matter research, this versatile platform establishes a foundation for designer microrobots capable of swimming through a wide range of catalyzed chemical reactions, opening avenues for future applications.

This paper investigates the optimal control of conditional McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations incorporating jumps, hereafter referred to as conditional McKean-Vlasov jump diffusions. To achieve this, we initially establish a stochastic Fokker-Planck equation governing the conditional law of the solution. By integrating this equation with the original state dynamics, we derive a Markovian system comprising both the state and its conditional law. Subsequently, we utilize this framework to formulate a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation for the optimal control of these jump diffusions. We further examine the scenario where the law is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure; in this context, the Fokker-Planck equation simplifies to a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) describing the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the conditional law. Finally, we leverage these findings to provide explicit solutions for two specific problems: the linear-quadratic optimal control of conditional stochastic McKean-Vlasov jump diffusions and the optimization of consumption from a cash flow modeled as a conditional stochastic McKean-Vlasov differential equation with jumps.

This study aims to localize sound sources within visual scenes. While current audio-visual methods utilize contrastive learning by treating matched audio-visual pairs as positives and randomly mismatched ones as negatives, these negative pairs can sometimes contain semantically aligned information. Consequently, such "hard positives" are incorrectly classified as negatives. Our primary contribution demonstrates that these hard positives yield response maps similar to their true counterparts. We address this by integrating the response maps of hard positives directly into the contrastive learning objective. Evaluations on the VGG-SS and SoundNet-Flickr test sets confirm that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We provide predictions for the photon energy spectrum in inclusive $B\to X_s\gamma$ decays, mediated by the electromagnetic penguin operator $O_7$, up to N$^3$LL$'$. Employing soft-collinear effective theory (SCET), we resum singular contributions within the large-photon-energy peak region. In the tail region, these resummed results are matched to fixed-order calculations at N$^3$LO, incorporating known $O_7$ contributions up to $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2)$. We introduce a method to parameterize the currently unknown $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^3)$ nonsingular corrections using theory nuisance parameters, with their variations serving as an estimate of theoretical uncertainty. Additionally, we examine various approaches to handling higher-order cross terms in the matching procedure. A critical component of this analysis is the choice of short-distance scheme for the $b$-quark mass $m_b$. We observe that the 1$S$ mass scheme, previously applied up to two loops, becomes unsuitable at the three-loop level in this context because the scheme operates at a soft scale significantly below $m_b$, a regime for which it was not designed. By adopting the MSR mass scheme with $R\sim 1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ instead, we achieve stable results exhibiting good perturbative convergence up to N$^3$LL$'$.

Entropy serves as a foundational concept across classical and quantum systems, influencing a vast array of theoretical and practical applications within physics and computer science. This study focuses on developing estimates for the Shannon entropy of classical probability distributions and the von Neumann entropy of mixed quantum states, aiming for a multiplicative accuracy factor of $\gamma > 1$. Our primary contributions include:
  $\quad\bullet$ a quantum algorithm requiring $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( n^{\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}}\right)$ queries to produce a $\gamma$-multiplicative approximation of the Shannon entropy $H(\mathbf{p})$ for a distribution $\mathbf{p} = (p_1,\ldots,p_n)$;
  $\quad\bullet$ a quantum algorithm requiring $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( n^{\frac12+\frac{1+\eta}{2\gamma^2}}\right)$ queries to produce a $\gamma$-multiplicative approximation of the von Neumann entropy $S(\rho)$ for a density matrix $\rho\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$.
In both scenarios, we assume the input entropy is bounded away from zero by a parameter $\eta > 0$, as we demonstrate that no polynomial query algorithm can multiplicatively approximate the entropy of distributions with arbitrarily low entropy. Furthermore, we establish $\Omega\left(n^{\frac{1}{3\gamma^2}}\right)$ lower bounds regarding the query complexity for the $\gamma$-multiplicative estimation of both Shannon and von Neumann entropies. Our analysis employs the quantum purified query access model, which accommodates both classical probability distributions and mixed quantum states, representing the most comprehensive input model currently available in the literature.

We establish that the three-dimensional $e_g$ orbital Hubbard model extends to any dimension $d$, with the resulting form uniquely dictated by two conditions: (i) maintaining the two-fold degeneracy of the $e_g$ orbitals, and (ii) transforming the cubic lattice into a hypercubic one. Although the local Coulomb interaction $U$ remains invariant across different bases of orthogonal orbitals, the kinetic energy's structure varies with the basis, achieving maximum symmetry in the complex-orbital basis. In this basis, the model features two distinct hopping channels: one conserving orbital flavor and another that does not. The noninteracting electronic structure comprises two nondegenerate bands of plane-wave real-orbital single-particle states where the orbital character depends on the wave vector. Consequently, each band remains unpolarized at any filling and exhibits a non-Gaussian density of states as $d \to \infty$. The \textit{orbital liquid} phase arises when these two bands are filled to an identical Fermi energy. We analyze the $e_g$ orbital Hubbard model in the $d \to \infty$ limit using the Gutzwiller approximation to treat the on-site Coulomb interaction $U$, thereby calculating the correlation energy for both the orbital liquid and disordered para-orbital states. We find that the orbital liquid constitutes the ground state across the entire $(n,U)$ phase diagram, except near half-filling at large $U$, where ferro-orbital order with real orbitals becomes favorable. This specific behavior at large $U$ near half-filling is unique to $d=\infty$, stemming from the exponential tails in the density of states.

To elucidate the Fermi-surface topology underlying superconductivity in the topological line-nodal compound CaSb₂, which transitions superconductively at approximately 1.8 K, we conducted micro-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Our analysis revealed that a three-dimensional hole pocket at the G point is consistently present across two single-crystalline samples produced under distinct growth conditions. Conversely, the carrier-doping level, inferred from the chemical potential's position, exhibited sensitivity to fabrication specifics. Notably, although theoretical calculations predict a cylindrical electron pocket at the Y(C) point, this feature was absent in one of the samples, even though both specimens displayed superconductivity with comparable transition temperatures. These findings imply that the three-dimensional hole pocket plays a pivotal role in inducing superconductivity in CaSb₂ and suggest the potential to manipulate the topological characteristics of this superconductivity through carrier tuning.

The motivation behind quantifying database inconsistency stems from objectives such as estimating reliability for new datasets and tracking progress in data cleaning. Additionally, researchers aim to assign individual tuples a degree of responsibility for overall inconsistency, enabling the prioritization of tuples during dirt inspection or explanation. Consequently, inconsistency quantification and attribution have been extensively studied in Knowledge Representation and, more recently, in Databases. Drawing from other fields, the conventional mechanism for sharing responsibility is the Shapley value derived from cooperative game theory. This paper presents a systematic analysis of the computational complexity of calculating the Shapley value across common inconsistency measures for functional-dependency (FD) violations. We establish a comprehensive classification of FD sets into tractable and intractable categories regarding Shapley-value computation and further examine the complexity of approximation methods for intractable scenarios.

We present a proof establishing the existence of a minimizer for a segmentation functional defined by level sets and incorporating prior knowledge of target shapes. Demonstrating this existence is crucial as it ensures the convergence of numerical approaches—such as gradient descent methods or PDE solvers—employed to solve the segmentation problem. Furthermore, this result is applicable to numerous other segmentation models to similarly validate the existence of their minimizers.

Deriving parameters for stochastic models from experimental data is a cornerstone of scientific inquiry. This task becomes especially difficult in strongly indeterminate scenarios, where different parameter combinations produce identical observations. Such situations occur frequently, such as determining whether a radio source is nearby and weak or distant and strong, or estimating amplifier gain alongside brain activity in electrophysiology. In this study, we introduce hierarchical neural posterior estimation (HNPE), a new approach to resolving this ambiguity by leveraging auxiliary observations that share global parameters. Our method adapts recent advances in simulation-based inference using normalizing flows to Bayesian hierarchical frameworks. We quantitatively validate our approach on a problem with known analytical solutions and subsequently apply it to invert a prominent non-linear model in computational neuroscience, utilizing both simulated and real EEG datasets.

This research examines the occurrence of significant interval structures—specifically lattices, modular lattices, distributive lattices, and boolean lattices—within the Bruhat and weak orders of Coxeter groups. We compile and extend existing findings regarding principal order ideals, featuring pattern-based characterizations and enumerations for the symmetric group. This leads naturally to a comparable investigation of arbitrary intervals; however, such results offer fewer defining characteristics for the Bruhat order when considered at this level of generality. Conversely, we achieve a complete characterization for intervals originating at rank one in the symmetric group across all four structural types and both posets. Each category admits enumeration, revealing compelling links to Fibonacci and Catalan numbers. The work concludes with proposals for future research, notably an intriguing examination of intervals defined between a permutation and every generator within its support.

Cancer presents as a heterogeneous condition characterized by varied molecular causes and outcomes. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) has made available a vast dataset comprising over 10,000 tumors with RNA-seq gene expression data, which reflects the diverse molecular profiles of these tumors and allows for the identification of differential pathway activations. Deep unsupervised models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAE), can uncover these underlying patterns. This study compares a one-hidden layer VAE against two deeper VAE architectures, finding that increased depth offers only marginal performance gains. The three VAE models were evaluated alongside other dimensionality reduction methods, including Principal Components Analysis (PCA), Independent Components Analysis (ICA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and Denoising Autoencoders for Gene Expression (ADAGE). Performance was assessed in a supervised task predicting gene inactivation across pan-cancer datasets and through latent space analysis of high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) subtypes. While no significant differences were observed among the algorithms in the classification task, the latent spaces generated by VAEs provide valuable biological insights into HGSC subtype biology.

Researchers and industry leaders are increasingly focusing on the Electric Vehicle Routing Problem (EVRP) to facilitate the transition from fuel-dependent transportation to more efficient and eco-friendly electric vehicles. Although the EVRP appears superficially similar to traditional Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs), it presents distinct challenges, including restricted cruising ranges, extended charging durations, and scarce charging infrastructure. While prior studies have primarily addressed logistics scenarios involving homogeneous commercial fleets returning to a central depot after multiple stops, this work tackles a Personal EV Routing Problem. We determine the optimal path for a single vehicle undertaking a long origin-destination journey. Our approach employs multi-objective optimization to simultaneously minimize total travel time and cumulative charging expenses. Furthermore, the formulation integrates real-world factors such as traffic congestion at charging stations, detour distances required to reach these facilities, and fluctuating electricity costs across different locations. Specifically, we formulate a multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) model and derive feasible solutions using the $\epsilon$-constraint method. Additionally, we apply meta-heuristic algorithms, namely Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), to identify the most optimal routes and corresponding objective values. Finally, experiments conducted on multiple self-generated datasets allow for a comparative analysis of the results.

Transformers have recently attracted significant interest in computer vision for their capacity to model long-range dependencies. However, the self-attention mechanism, central to the Transformer architecture, typically incurs quadratic computational complexity relative to the number of tokens. Numerous architectures attempt to mitigate this complexity by restricting self-attention to local regions or by rethinking tokenization. In this paper, we introduce DAE-Former, a novel approach that offers an alternative strategy by efficiently reengineering the self-attention mechanism. Specifically, we reformulate self-attention to simultaneously capture spatial and channel relationships across the entire feature dimension while maintaining computational efficiency. Additionally, we redesign the skip connection by incorporating a cross-attention module to ensure feature reusability and improve localization capabilities. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques on multi-organ cardiac and skin lesion segmentation datasets without relying on pre-trained weights. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/mindflow-institue/DAEFormer.

Neural end-to-end text-to-speech (TTS) systems, utilizing either recurrent architectures like Tacotron or attention-based models such as Transformers to represent speech utterances, have markedly advanced speech synthesis capabilities. Nevertheless, handling varying sentence lengths remains a significant challenge, especially for long sentences where sequence models face limitations in effective context length. We introduce a novel segment-Transformer (s-Transformer) that operates at the segment level, reusing recurrence through cached memories for both the encoder and decoder. This extended memory captures long-range contexts while simplifying encoder-decoder attention to the segment level. Furthermore, we implement a modified relative positional self-attention mechanism to generalize sequence handling beyond lengths potentially unseen during training. Comparisons with the standard Transformer reveal that both achieve identical MOS scores of 4.29 on short sentences, closely matching the 4.32 score of recorded audio; on long sentences, they yield similar results of 4.22 versus 4.2, while the s-Transformer significantly outperforms on extra-long sentences with a 0.2 MOS gain. Due to the time-based updates of cached memory, the s-Transformer produces natural and coherent speech over extended durations.

Coherent diffraction imaging (CDI) is an advanced technique capable of extracting most information from diffraction data. An optimal CDI system should reconstruct a complex-valued object from a single far-field diffraction measurement without relying on prior knowledge of the target. To achieve this ideal, we introduce a family of parameter-robust illumination patterns. Additionally, a direct phase-optimization algorithm is proposed to enhance phase retrieval performance under strong noise conditions. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our approach in handling practical noisy measurements for complex-valued targets.

Many commodity sensors used to track robots and dynamic obstacles exhibit non-Gaussian noise, yet existing methods often assume Gaussian uncertainty to maintain computational efficiency. Conversely, current planners handling non-Gaussian uncertainty fail to utilize specific distributional traits, such as bias, for efficient collision avoidance. This paper bridges that gap by framing reactive collision avoidance as a distribution matching task between collision constraint violations and a Dirac Delta distribution. To ensure rapid reactivity, the approach embeds distributions within Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space and reformulates the matching process as minimizing the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between them. We demonstrate that calculating MMD for a specific control input reduces to simple matrix-matrix operations. Leveraging this efficiency, we developed a straightforward control sampling method for reactive collision avoidance amidst dynamic and uncertain obstacles. Our contributions advance the state of the art in two key areas. First, extensive empirical analysis reveals that our planner can infer distributional bias from sample-level data, guiding the robot toward favorable homotopies; in contrast, Gaussian approximations often miss this bias, steering the robot toward high-risk states. Second, we provide concrete evidence of the proposed distribution matching method's superiority over previous non-parametric and Gaussian-based reactive collision avoidance techniques.

This study investigates a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted massive multi-user MIMO system, accounting for both transceiver hardware impairments (HWIs) and RIS phase noise. Unlike previous works, our RIS phase shift design relies on long-term angle information. Initially, we derive an approximate analytical formula for the uplink achievable rate. Subsequently, we employ a genetic algorithm (GA) to optimize both the sum rate and the minimum data rate. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating HWIs is essential for effective RIS phase shift design.

Detecting lies is a significant concern in daily life due to its influence on human interactions, prompting individuals to scrutinize both verbal statements and visual cues, particularly facial expressions, to assess truthfulness. Although automated lie detection could aid in understanding deceptive behaviors, existing systems remain limited, largely because of insufficient datasets for evaluating performance in realistic settings. This study presents a newly collected, annotated dataset of facial images containing both 2D and 3D data from multiple participants engaged in a card game designed to encourage lying. Leveraging this dataset, we assessed various machine learning-based lie detectors across generalization, person-specific, and cross-domain experiments. Our findings indicate that deep learning models yield the highest accuracy, achieving up to 57% on generalization tasks and 63% for single-participant scenarios. Additionally, we underscore the limitations of deep learning approaches when applied to cross-domain lie detection.

The drive for large-scale quantum computing necessitates two-qubit gate schemes that maximize fidelity while minimizing resource usage. Specifically, the low anharmonicity of superconducting transmons imposes significant constraints on gate design, resulting in complex hardware and control protocols. In this work, we present a resource-efficient method for controlling interactions in strongly-anharmonic fluxonium qubits. By applying an off-resonant drive to non-computational transitions in a pair of capacitively-coupled fluxoniums, we induce a ZZ-interaction through unequal ac-Stark shifts of the computational levels. With adjustable frequency and amplitude, the drive can either cancel the static ZZ-term or amplify it by an order of magnitude, enabling a controlled-phase (CP) gate with any programmable phase shift. Cross-entropy benchmarking of these non-Clifford operations reveals sub-1% error rates, constrained only by incoherent processes. These findings highlight the superior potential of strongly-anharmonic circuits compared to transmons for developing future quantum processors.

Deep learning and artificial intelligence (AI) depend heavily on extensive datasets for training, testing, and validation. Establishing imaging biobanks is essential to acquire these data and their annotations in a standardized manner. Such initiatives must be meticulously designed and executed in accordance with existing standards, guidelines, and legal constraints. However, merely assembling high-quality imaging collections is insufficient for effective AI development, validation, and deployment due to substantial resource requirements; instead, a hybrid approach integrating on-premise and cloud-based AI pipelines is necessary. This chapter assists readers in addressing technical decisions regarding the AI environment by offering a foundational overview of relevant concepts and implementation strategies concerning data storage, cloud utilization, and AI pipeline architecture.

Modeling multi-turn dialogues represents a demanding area within natural language understanding (NLU), seeking to enable machines to comprehend human conversations and thereby establish a robust basis for various downstream applications. Current research typically utilizes pre-trained language models (PrLMs) to process dialogue history as sequential tokens, a method that often fails to adequately capture the temporal dynamics of conversations. To address this limitation, we introduce the Bidirectional Information Decoupling Network (BiDeN), a universal dialogue encoder designed to explicitly integrate both historical and future context. This approach allows for broad generalization across diverse dialogue-related tasks. Empirical evaluations on datasets spanning multiple downstream applications confirm the effectiveness and versatility of our proposed BiDeN.

This paper investigates $k$-Hessian type equations of the form $S_k^{\frac{1}{k}}(D^2u+\mu|D u|I)= f(u)$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition on $f$ regarding the existence and nonexistence of entire admissible subsolutions, effectively extending the Keller-Osserman condition. These existence and nonexistence results are demonstrated across various ranges of the parameter $\mu$, with the standard Hessian equation case ($\mu=0$), as analyzed by Ji and Bao (Proc Amer Math Soc 138: 175--188, 2010), serving as a specific instance. Additionally, we examine the distinctions between the semilinear scenario ($k=1$) and the fully nonlinear scenario ($k\ge 2$).

This study examines distance metrics for conditional distributions, with a specific focus on the Wasserstein metric and its Gaussian variant, the Frechet Inception Distance (FID). We introduce conditional adaptations of these metrics, investigate their interrelationships, and derive a closed-form solution for the conditional FID (CFID). Through numerical experiments evaluating modern conditional generative models, we demonstrate that CFID offers distinct advantages over classical FID and mean squared error (MSE). Unlike FID, CFID effectively detects failures where generated outputs appear realistic but are unrelated to their conditioning inputs. Conversely, compared to MSE, CFID identifies scenarios where a single realistic output is produced despite the existence of a diverse set of equally probable alternatives.

This paper investigates the curvature properties of convex combinations of Riemannian metrics defined by $g(t) = (1-t)g_0 + tg_1$, specifically examining whether such deformations can elevate the curvature of immersed, totally geodesic flat tori. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for $g(t)$ to exhibit average positive $r$-order variation ($r\geq 2$) along the torus and utilize these conditions to analyze paths connecting $g_0$ to established classical deformations.

Traditionally, HEP event selection is viewed as a binary classification task distinguishing between signal and background. However, in distribution fits for particle masses or couplings, signal events are not uniform; the signal differential cross-section exhibits varying sensitivities to the measured parameter across different regions of phase space. This paper outlines a mathematical framework for evaluating and optimizing HEP parameter fits by defining event-level sensitivity and modeling it for Monte Carlo (MC) events via derivatives of their weights with respect to the parameter. Minimizing statistical measurement errors necessitates separating events based on these differing sensitivities, transforming the problem from a dichotomous classification into a non-dichotomous one. Since weight derivatives are unavailable for real data, the proposed practical approach involves training a regressor on MC events to predict these derivatives, which then serves as an optimal partitioning variable for one-dimensional data fits. This CHEP2019 work extends the CHEP2018 study by demonstrating how event-by-event sensitivities enable the exact calculation of the "FIP" ratio—the quotient of Fisher information from an actual analysis versus the theoretical maximum for an ideal detector. Leveraging this metric, the paper explores the connections between FIP and meteorological metrics such as the Brier score and Mean Squared Error (MSE), highlighting the critical role of "sharpness" in both fields. Finally, it argues that HEP distribution fits should be assessed and optimized using probabilistic metrics like FIP or MSE, as ranking metrics (e.g., AUC) or threshold-based metrics (e.g., accuracy) offer limited relevance for these specific applications.

This paper introduces Salient Image Matting (SIM), a framework designed to estimate per-pixel opacity for the most prominent foreground within an image. While trimaps are traditionally essential for handling the semantic diversity in images by guiding the matting process, generating them is typically costly and labor-intensive. The SIM framework addresses the challenge of learning across various semantic categories and salient object types in a fully automatic, end-to-end manner. Specifically, it generates accurate alpha mattes for diverse foreground objects, even when the foreground class, such as a human, appears in contexts significantly different from the training data, using only RGB input. This capability is achieved by utilizing a salient object detection model to create a trimap that guides the matting model with higher-level semantic information. By leveraging extensive coarse annotations and a heuristic trimap generation strategy, the framework trains a network capable of producing trimaps for arbitrary foregrounds. Additionally, a multi-scale fusion architecture is introduced to better capture fine-grained, low-level opacity details. With high-level guidance from the trimap network, SIM requires only a fraction of the expensive matting data needed by other automatic methods while successfully producing alpha mattes for a wide variety of inputs. Experimental results on diverse images demonstrate that the framework outperforms state-of-the-art matting methods without requiring a manually created trimap.

Metric learning-based classifiers are commonly used in few-shot learning to determine image labels by measuring the distance between extracted feature vectors and class representations. However, utilizing global pooling at the end of a feature extractor can result in embeddings that fail to adequately focus on the target class object. This paper introduces a new framework that constructs class representations by extracting features specifically from class-relevant image regions. Given only a few exemplar images with image-level labels, the proposed approach first identifies class objects by spatially decomposing the similarity between images and their class prototypes. Enhanced class representations are then derived from these localization outcomes. Additionally, we introduce a loss function to improve the discriminative power of the refined features. Our method achieves superior performance compared to baseline few-shot models on the miniImageNet and tieredImageNet benchmarks.

Determining star formation rates (SFRs) in high-redshift galaxies via their rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) continuum is often compromised by dust obscuration. While previous research relied on 850 μm submillimeter emission to estimate intrinsic SFRs for UV-selected galaxies, those findings were limited by low sensitivity and coarse resolution (~15''). This study instead employs ultra-deep 1.4 GHz observations from the Very Large Array, achieving resolutions of approximately 1''–2'', to measure intrinsic SFRs. We conducted stacking analyses on radio images centered on roughly 3,500 Lyman break galaxies (LBGs) at z~4, selected from the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey-North and South fields using Hubble Space Telescope/Advanced Camera for Surveys data. The resulting stacked radio flux is minimal (0.08±0.15 μJy), indicating a mean SFR of 6±11 M☉/yr. This value aligns closely with the uncorrected mean UV SFR of 5 M☉/yr, suggesting that z~4 LBGs experience negligible dust extinction. These low SFR and extinction levels corroborate earlier conclusions that z~4 LBGs are generally not submillimeter galaxies. Furthermore, we find no statistically significant excess of dust-obscured star-forming components within ~22 kpc of the LBGs.

Inner-shell K$\alpha$ x-ray lasers have been realized by pumping gaseous, solid, and liquid targets using the intense radiation from free-electron lasers (FELs). For gaseous targets, lasing depends on generating K-shell core-holes on a timescale shorter than Auger decay refilling. In contrast, for solid and liquid systems, collisional effects are critical, influencing both atomic populations and line-widths, thereby affecting overall gain magnitude and duration. However, these collisional dynamics have not been thoroughly investigated. We present initial simulations using the CCFLY code for inner-shell lasing in solid-density magnesium (Mg), which self-consistently models the interaction between incoming FEL radiation and atomic kinetics, encompassing radiative, Auger, and collisional processes. Our results indicate that the combination of collisional population of lower lasing states and line broadening prevents lasing on all transitions except the K$\alpha$ line of the initially cold system. Even with an instantaneous FEL pump, the gain duration in the solid system is found to be less than a femtosecond.

Source code similarity analysis has become a critical tool in application development for identifying clones, isolating bugs, and detecting copyright infringements. Similar code fragments pose significant challenges because any errors in the original must be corrected in every duplicate, and maintenance updates like patches or extensions must be reapplied across all instances. Additionally, the wide variety of coding styles and the flexibility of modern programming languages make manual inspection of large repositories both difficult and cost-prohibitive, rendering automatic detection techniques essential. We introduce an efficient and scalable method for identifying similar code fragments using fingerprinting based on source code control flow graphs. This process involves generating control flow graphs from the source code, which are then hashed to create unique fingerprints that capture both semantic and syntactic similarities. These fingerprints enable the efficient storage and retrieval necessary for performing similarity searches across code fragments. Experimental results from our prototype implementation validate the approach, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency compared to existing solutions.

It is established that intrinsic Abelian topological phases typically undergo phase transitions marked by anyon condensation and confinement. Conversely, non-Abelian topological phases exhibit more complex behaviors during such transitions, as the multiple degenerate degrees of freedom associated with non-Abelian anyons can evolve in various ways. This paper investigates these novel phenomena—specifically partial condensation, partial deconfinement, and anyon splitting (where a non-Abelian anyon divides into distinct new species)—utilizing projected entangled pair states (PEPS). Initially, we demonstrate that anyon splitting is detectable through topologically degenerate ground states. Subsequently, we develop a set of PEPS representing all possible degrees of freedom for a specific non-Abelian anyon; by analyzing the overlaps of these PEPS with the ground state, we extract data on partial condensation. We further define a central matrix based on the norms and overlaps within this PEPS set, from which information regarding partial deconfinement can be derived. Notably, this matrix enables the construction of an order parameter capable of directly identifying anyon splitting. We validate the efficacy of this methodology by applying it to several non-Abelian topological phase transitions, including transitions from the $D(S_3)$ quantum double to the toric code, from $D(S_3)$ to $D(Z_3)$ quantum doubles, from Rep($S_3$) string-nets to the toric code, and from the double Ising string-net to the toric code.

In the past twenty years, the detection of exoplanets has radically reshaped our understanding of the cosmos and our position within it. Emerging research suggests that the high-energy particle and X-ray environment of a solar system plays a critical role in shaping the atmospheres of nearby planets, including hot Jupiters and terrestrial worlds orbiting M-dwarf stars. X-ray imaging and spectroscopy offer unique and potent insights into the high-energy radiation fluxes affecting exoplanets, with X-ray photons also acting as indicators of transformative coronal mass ejections. Furthermore, when a host star emits sufficient X-rays, transit observations comparable to those in optical and infrared wavelengths become feasible, enabling the direct analysis of exoplanet upper atmospheres. This white paper outlines the potential contributions to exoplanet science and their surrounding environments that can be realized through increasingly high-quality X-ray data expected to be available in the next decade to a decade and a half.

Motivated by recent BESIII measurements of two-body nonleptonic $J/{\psi}$ weak decays, this study investigates charm-changing $J/{\psi}$ transitions to $D_{s,d}V$ modes using the perturbative QCD framework, with $V$ representing vector mesons ${\rho}$ and $K^{\ast}$. The results indicate that the branching ratio for the $J/{\psi}$ ${\to}$ $D_{s}{\rho}$ decay could be as high as ${\cal O}(10^{-9})$, a magnitude within the reach of future high-luminosity experiments.

Recent findings from the SH0ES Collaboration have established a $5\sigma$ Hubble tension between high-redshift ($z>1000$) and low-redshift ($z<1$) observations, with the latter yielding a higher value. This study introduces a particle physics framework designed to mitigate this tension through an out-of-equilibrium hidden sector interacting with the visible sector. The dark sector comprises a dark fermion serving as dark matter, a dark photon, a massive scalar, and a massless pseudo-scalar. Starting with no initial dark sector population, weak kinetic mixing couplings allow the dark sector to populate without ever reaching thermal equilibrium, maintaining distinct temperatures between the two sectors. We present a cosmologically consistent analysis utilizing coupled Boltzmann equations to model the correlated evolution of both sectors under a two-temperature formalism, calculating the dark matter relic density accordingly. This approach satisfies Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) constraints with minimal impact on $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$. Nevertheless, the out-of-equilibrium decay of the massive scalar into the massless pseudo-scalar near the recombination epoch increases $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$, offering a mechanism to alleviate the Hubble tension.

This paper introduces a stylish image captioning model based on the Multi-style Multi-modality (2M) mechanism. We demonstrate that 2M enables the creation of an effective stylish captioner, where the model's multi-references facilitate self-explanation by pinpointing erroneous input features in faulty cases. Furthermore, we illustrate how the 2M mechanism constructs these models and how they can be leveraged to explain likely errors.

Determining the socioeconomic profiles of social media users, specifically their occupation and income, is a critical challenge in computational social science. Automatically deriving these traits holds significant value for personalized recommendation engines, targeted advertising, and digital political campaigns. Although prior research confirms that linguistic cues can accurately forecast socioeconomic status on Twitter, leveraging data from users' social connections remains an unexplored avenue for such complex attributes. This study introduces a technique to predict occupational categories and income levels by analyzing extended network data through low-dimensional graph embeddings. These representations are utilized to train models for both prediction tasks. Evaluations on two public datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, integrating graph embeddings with textual features yields substantial performance gains, illustrating that social network structures and language data are complementary.

The Hadamard Extension of a matrix is formed by the collection of all Hadamard products derived from subsets of its rows. This construction is significant in the context of identifying mixtures of product distributions over binary random variables, as full column rank in these extensions is a crucial requirement for identification algorithms. We present several findings regarding the conditions under which a Hadamard Extension achieves full column rank.

In dynamic nuclear polarization, radicals function both as polarization sources and sinks. When the coupling between electron spins and various nuclear reservoirs exceeds the reservoirs' own couplings to the lattice, radicals facilitate hetero-nuclear mixing. This study reports on radical-enhanced $^{13}$C relaxation in pyruvic acid doped with trityl, observing a linear relationship between carbon $T_1$ and the magnetic field ranging from 5 mT to 2 T. By extending a model previously used for protons to carbon nuclei, we predict efficient proton-carbon mixing through the radical Non-Zeeman reservoir across fields from 20 mT to over 1 T. Differences between the observed carbon relaxation and model predictions are ascribed to enhanced direct hetero-nuclear mixing caused by trityl-induced linebroadening, alongside field-dependent carbon diffusion from the radical environment into the bulk. Measurements of hetero-nuclear polarization transfer up to 600 mT validate the predicted mixing, as well as the two effects deduced from the relaxation analysis.

We define digital cash as the digital counterpart to physical currency, possessing traits such as security, fungibility, decentralization, direct control, and privacy, while introducing qualitatively new capabilities. It enables highly efficient transfers and, crucially, transactional or contract-backed operations. This allows for the fully automated, guaranteed execution of atomic resource swaps and intricate contracts, bypassing numerous intermediaries and costly, slow manual processes. A key educational goal is to distinguish monetary characteristics from technical implementations, such as specific blockchains or distributed ledgers, thereby clarifying debates on digital money design separate from execution methods. We further examine the power and function of programmable, contract-backed digital money through case studies: tokenizing invoice debt via Ethereum smart contracts using stablecoins; ensuring transparent and reliable payment disbursement aligned with social laws; and a Danish e-krone application for crowdfunding public and private community projects. These insights are drawn from independent chapters by members of the 2018 and 2019 Working Group on Digital Cash at Copenhagen FinTech, which are previously unpublished. Collectively, these contributions demonstrate the design possibilities and potential of digital money empowered by smart contracts, which effectively eliminate counterparty risk (failure to pay or deliver) and settlement risk (failed trades requiring abortion) orders of magnitude faster than current financial practices.

Coastal erosion involves the shifting of sand driven by tidal, wave, or current movements, with certain wave behaviors modeled using Helmholtz-type equations. This paper aims to investigate optimal obstacle shapes designed to reduce sand transport while adhering to Helmholtz equation constraints. Additionally, the study addresses Dirichlet and Neumann spectral problems. We demonstrate the existence of such optimal shapes within a general class of quasi-open sets and establish first-order necessary optimality conditions within a regular framework.

This study introduces a method for segmenting pulmonary arteries from CT scans, utilizing a deep neural network architecture that combines Swin UNETR and U-Net. To generate the final segmentation masks, we ensembled six models—three based on Swin UNETR and three based on 3D U-Net with residual units—using a weighted average approach. Our team achieved a multi-level Dice score of 84.36% with this technique. The project code is accessible at https://github.com/akansh12/parse2022, and this work is part of the MICCAI PARSE 2022 challenge.

Turbulent convection is fundamental to numerous natural settings, spanning from Earth's oceans, mantle, and outer core to diverse astrophysical phenomena. For these flows characterized by intense thermal forcing, an ultimate scaling law for heat flux and velocity has been hypothesized. Despite extensive experimental and numerical investigations, definitive confirmation of this ultimate regime remains elusive. This study demonstrates that the ultimate scaling is fully achieved when the thermal boundary layer becomes completely decoupled from the viscous boundary layer and resides within the turbulent bulk. Consequently, the heat flux can increase by approximately an order of magnitude. Our findings offer solid evidence that the ultimate state emerges when the entire thermal boundary layer is embedded within the turbulent region, a scenario likely prevalent in many natural convection systems.

Scanning and transmission electron microscopy, electrical transport measurements, magnetization studies, quasiparticle spectroscopy, and real-time real-space magneto-optical imaging were employed to characterize niobium thin films on silicon substrates, which serve as the foundation for superconducting qubits. This work examines niobium films to demonstrate a comprehensive analytical framework that could advance superconducting circuits, including those integral to quantum computing. The films exhibit an excellent superconducting critical temperature of $T_{c}=9.35$ K, a relatively clean superconducting gap, and an enhanced superfluid density at intermediate temperatures. These findings align with recent theoretical models regarding anisotropic strong-coupling superconductivity in niobium. However, the magnetic response remains complex, characterized by pronounced irreversible behavior and inadequate thermal conductivity, which result in thermo-magnetic instabilities. These factors could hinder further enhancements in transmon quantum coherence, and potential mitigation approaches are discussed.

Clinical Text Notes (CTNs) capture physicians' reasoning processes in an unstructured, free-text format generated during patient examinations and interviews. Recently, numerous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of machine learning in predicting doctor diagnoses from CTNs, a process referred to as ICD coding. However, data annotation is labor-intensive, especially for medical data requiring specialized expertise. This paper introduces a method to augment a sparsely annotated dataset of Icelandic CTNs using machine-learned imputation within a semi-self-supervised framework. The approach involves training a neural network on a limited set of annotated CTNs to extract clinical features from unannotated ones; these features comprise responses to approximately one thousand potential questions a physician might encounter during a consultation. These extracted features are subsequently utilized to train a classifier for diagnosing specific diseases. The study evaluates this data augmentation technique across three tiers of data availability to physicians. Results indicate a significant positive impact of the method, though this benefit diminishes when clinical features derived from patient examinations and diagnostics are included. Consequently, the authors recommend this approach for augmenting scarce datasets in systems that rely on clinical features excluding examinations or tests.

We address the challenge of estimating the optimal transport map from a fixed source distribution $P$ to an unknown target distribution $Q$, utilizing samples drawn from $Q$. This estimation task has gained significant importance in contemporary statistical fields, including generative modeling. Currently, theoretical estimation rates are established only under restrictive conditions—such as when both $P$ and $Q$ possess bounded densities and the transport map belongs to a H\"older class—conditions that rarely align with practical scenarios. We introduce a unified framework for deriving estimation rates across general function spaces. Our theoretical requirements are notably less stringent than existing literature: we assume merely that the source measure $P$ satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality and that the optimal map is the gradient of a smooth convex function residing in a space with controllable metric entropy. While this approach recovers known rates for bounded densities and H\"older maps, it also yields nearly sharp results in many previously uncovered settings. Notably, we establish the first statistical estimation rates for cases where $P$ is a normal distribution and the transport map corresponds to an infinite-width shallow neural network.

We introduce the Fourier-domain transfer entropy spectrum, a new model-free causality metric that extends traditional transfer entropy. Unlike methods that treat systems as single entities, this approach systematically evaluates causal interactions among individual components within any arbitrary system. The resulting spectrum provides a comprehensive representation of time-varying latent causal relationships, effectively handling non-stationary processes and high-dimensional scenarios. We validate the method through analyses of parameter dependence, statistical significance, and sensitivity. Furthermore, an open-source, multi-platform implementation has been created and successfully applied to neuroscience datasets and diffusively coupled logistic oscillators.

The goal is to showcase the elegance and strength of Alexandrov geometry by deriving intriguing applications with minimal foundational work. The subjects covered include:
1. Evaluations of collision counts within billiard systems.
2. The creation of unusual aspherical manifolds.
3. The geometric properties of two-convex subsets in Euclidean space.

This work examines the category of diffeological vector pseudo-bundles and explores the extension of classical differential geometric concepts—specifically automorphism groups, frame bundles, the space of connection 1-forms, and the space of covariant derivatives—to this setting. A key distinction in this generalized framework is the non-isomorphism between connection 1-forms and covariant derivatives. The applications extend beyond finite-dimensional examples with singularities to include infinite-dimensional vector bundles where the base is not a smooth manifold equipped with an atlas, thereby pushing the boundaries of classical infinite-dimensional geometry.

Advancements in sports data science often rely on "big data," yet such extensive datasets are frequently unavailable, requiring specialized models capable of functioning with limited observations. A key domain in sport-science characterized by small sample sizes is the study of post-exercise recovery. In this field, models are usually fitted to data from exhaustive exercise tests that athletes can only undertake a few times. Recent discoveries indicate that conventional recovery frameworks, such as work-balance models, are overly simplistic and fail to adequately capture observed data trends. Consequently, we examined a hydraulic model that, like work-balance models, requires only a minimal number of data points but offers superior accuracy in predicting recovery dynamics.

To evaluate the hydraulic model against established work-balance models, we retrospectively applied both to datasets compiled from published literature. The comparison involved one hydraulic model and three work-balance models using data extracted from five studies. The hydraulic model surpassed all established work-balance models across every defined metric, including those that penalize models with higher parameter counts. These findings encourage further research into the hydraulic model as a promising alternative to existing energy recovery performance models.

We present findings from an unsupervised decomposition of the local stellar halo within the chemo-dynamical space defined by abundance data from APOGEE DR17 and GALAH DR3. Our Gaussian Mixture Model identifies four dominant independent components in the Solar neighborhood: three previously recognized groups—Aurora, Splash, and GS/E—and a newly identified component, Eos. Among these, only GS/E originates from accretion, reinforcing earlier assertions that it serves as the primary progenitor of the Galactic stellar halo. We demonstrate that Aurora's chemical properties align perfectly with the Heracles merger. Without applying any predefined chemical selection cuts, our analysis reveals that Aurora exhibits a broad range of [Al/Fe] and a metallicity correlation suggesting rapid chemical enrichment in a massive galaxy, specifically the young Milky Way. The newly discovered halo component, Eos, is classified as $in situ$ due to its high mean [Al/Fe]. Eos displays significant evolution across [Fe/H], transitioning from resembling GS/E at the lowest metallicities to becoming indistinguishable from the Galactic low-$\alpha$ population at the highest. We propose that at least a portion of the outer thin disk began its evolution using gas polluted by GS/E, with Eos serving as evidence of this process.

This work investigates a mass formula concerning Artin-Schreier curves of genus $g$ defined over a finite field $k$ with characteristic $p$. Specifically, for odd primes $p$ and small values of $g$, we calculate the number of $k$-isomorphism classes of these curves, weighting each by the size of the centralizer of the Artin-Schreier involution within the automorphism group. This research generalizes previous findings by various authors that were limited to the characteristic $p=2$ case.

Keywords: Artin-Schreier curve, finite field, automorphism, Mass formula, moduli space, arithmetic statistics

Vision and language models (VL) often rely on fragile cues within single modalities, caused by distributional biases, rather than focusing on pertinent information. When a unimodal model experiences a slight accuracy drop on a VL task, it indicates "unimodal collapse." However, reliably quantifying this collapse at both the dataset and instance levels remains a challenge for targeted diagnosis and mitigation. We introduce MM-SHAP, a performance-agnostic multimodality score that measures the extent to which a model utilizes individual modalities in multimodal tasks. Built upon Shapley values, MM-SHAP serves two purposes: (1) comparing models based on their degree of multimodality, and (2) assessing the contribution of specific modalities to a given task and dataset. Experiments involving six VL models—LXMERT, CLIP, and four ALBEF variants—across four VL tasks reveal that unimodal collapse varies in degree and direction, challenging the prevailing assumption that it is always one-sided. We recommend using MM-SHAP to analyze multimodal tasks, diagnose issues, and guide advancements toward true multimodal integration. Code is available at: https://github.com/Heidelberg-NLP/MM-SHAP

Shadow estimation offers a statistically guaranteed and efficient approach to predicting various observables of a quantum state. In the multi-shot regime, this involves performing projective measurements on a state prepared sequentially $K$ times following identical unitary evolution, a process repeated across $M$ rounds of randomly sampled unitaries, resulting in a total of $MK$ measurements. This work analyzes the performance of shadow estimation within this multi-shot context, specifically focusing on the variance associated with estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$. We demonstrate that, alongside the shadow-norm $\|O \|_{\mathrm{shadow}}$ established in [Huang et.al.~Nat.~Phys.~2020\cite{huang2020predicting}], the variance depends on a newly defined quantity termed the cross-shadow-norm $\|O \|_{\mathrm{Xshadow}}$. For both random Pauli and Clifford measurements, we derive upper bounds for $\|O \|_{\mathrm{Xshadow}}$. Notably, we obtain an exact variance formula for Pauli observables when subjected to random Pauli measurements. These findings provide theoretical insights to guide the practical application of multi-shot shadow estimation.

We introduce the Pseudo-Mallows distribution, defined over all permutations of $n$ items, to approximate a posterior distribution utilizing a Mallows likelihood. The Mallows model is established as a valuable tool in recommender systems, enabling the extraction of user preferences from highly sparse data. However, traditional inference via MCMC is computationally slow, hindering its application in real-time scenarios. The Pseudo-Mallows distribution is constructed as a product of univariate discrete Mallows-like distributions, constrained to the permutation space. The accuracy of this approximation relies on the sequence order used to factorize the $n$ items. Within a variational framework, we optimize the variational order parameter by minimizing marginalized KL-divergence. We propose an approximate algorithm for this discrete optimization and conjecture a specific form for the optimal variational order based on the data, a hypothesis supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical results. Sampling from the Pseudo-Mallows distribution facilitates rapid preference learning compared to MCMC-based alternatives, particularly when data consists of partial rankings or item clicks. Through simulations and a real-world case study, we demonstrate that the Pseudo-Mallows model effectively learns personal preferences and generates recommendations with significantly improved efficiency while maintaining accuracy comparable to the exact Bayesian Mallows model.

Analyzing orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems at the receiver with non-linear impulsive noise suppressors remains a difficult challenge in communication theory. While exact closed-form expressions for the output signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) exist for common impulsive noise models, deriving a theoretical expression for the symbol error rate (SER) has remained unresolved. Existing analytical SER approaches in the literature approximate time-domain impulsive noise as Gaussian in the discrete frequency domain. In contrast, this study offers a precise analysis of distortion noise at the nonlinearity output by utilizing a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). This GMM-based method unifies SER prediction for both unmitigated systems and mitigated ones employing non-linear suppressors such as blanking, clipping, clipping-blanking, and attenuating processors. We derive closed-form SER expressions for both non-fading and frequency-selective Rayleigh and Rician fading channels under impulsive noise modeled by GMMs, thereby encompassing Bernoulli-Gaussian (BG), Middleton Class-A, and (approximated) alpha-stable noise. Theoretical SER performance is validated against simulations, demonstrating excellent agreement across all impulsive noise scenarios and non-linear suppressor configurations.

The rapid expansion of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) for diverse computer vision applications has created significant opportunities to enhance their efficiency and utility. However, detecting objects in aerial imagery remains difficult due to inconsistencies in scale, pose, and visual appearance. Furthermore, autonomous flight systems, which are constrained by limited computational resources and memory, require detection algorithms that are both accurate and efficient enough for real-time processing. This study adapts the widely used YOLOv4 framework to identify objects and their locations in aerial scenes with high precision and speed. By employing transfer learning on the VisDrone DET dataset, we achieved faster model convergence. The resulting model attained a mean average precision (mAP) of 45.64% and an inference rate of 8.7 FPS on a Tesla K80 GPU, demonstrating strong performance in identifying truncated and occluded objects. We also analyzed how different network resolutions and training epochs influenced performance. Comparative experiments against other modern aerial detectors confirmed that YOLOv4 outperforms them, suggesting it is an ideal choice for integration into aerial platforms.

Standard pretrained language models process sequences of subword tokens, lacking direct access to the characters within each token's string. However, by examining the embedding layer of these models, we demonstrate that they surprisingly learn the internal character composition of both whole words and subword tokens, despite never observing characters paired with those tokens. Our findings indicate that the embedding layer of RoBERTa contains sufficient information to accurately spell up to one-third of its vocabulary and achieve high average character n-gram overlap across all token types. Additionally, we investigated whether enriching subword models with extra character data could boost language modeling performance, noting that this approach yields a learning curve nearly identical to training without spelling-based enrichment. Collectively, our results imply that language modeling objectives motivate models to implicitly acquire some concept of spelling, and that explicitly instructing the model on how to spell does not seem to improve its performance on these tasks.

We employed isobaric Monte Carlo simulations to chart the complete phase diagram of hard cylindrical particles characterized by length $L$ and diameter $D$, utilizing an enhanced algorithm for determining cylinder overlap. This study reports phase diagrams for both prolate ($L/D>1$) and oblate ($L/D<1$) geometries without assuming continuity. For prolate cylinders, we identified low-density isotropic (\textrm{I}) and high-density crystal (\textrm{X}) phases alongside intermediate nematic (\textrm{N}) and smectic (\textrm{SmA}) phases, featuring \textrm{I-N-SmA} and \textrm{I-SmA-X} triple points; an apparent columnar phase (\textrm{C}) is observed to be metastable, similar to findings in spherocylinder systems. In contrast, the oblate case reveals stable intermediate cubatic (\textrm{Cub}), nematic (\textrm{N}), and columnar (\textrm{C}) phases, with \textrm{I-N-Cub}, \textrm{N-Cub-C}, and \textrm{I-Cub-C} triple points. We compare these results with prior numerical and analytical investigations. By explicitly accounting for the cylindrical shape, this research facilitates the development of more advanced models with significant biological relevance, such as those describing viruses and nucleosomes.

Passive detection of individuals is possible by monitoring the signal strength of Wi-Fi and other communication signals. This study investigates how and when such detection can be thwarted through modifications to transmitted signal power and comparable techniques. The paper's primary contribution is the development of a formal framework for analyzing this issue, alongside the identification of various scenarios and protocols capable of preventing or restricting inference derived from passive signal strength monitoring.

Two functors associated with the direct and inverse limits of bidual Banach space systems are presented. These functors are adjoint and maintain key spectral characteristics, such as whether an operator is Fredholm or has a compact spectrum. Applications of this framework include findings regarding the supports of representing measures.

Stellar metallicity influences evolutionary outcomes by altering radii, luminosities, lifespans, and remnant characteristics. This study employs the binary_c population synthesis code to examine the impact of metallicity on novae within binary stellar evolution. We analyzed a 16-point metallicity grid spanning from $Z=10^{-4}$ to 0.03, presenting distributions for nova white dwarf masses, accretion rates, delay times, and initial system properties at the grid's extremes. Our results reveal a distinct anti-correlation between metallicity and nova production frequency, with the rate at $Z=0.03$ being roughly half that at $Z=10^{-4}$. While the white dwarf mass distribution exhibits significant systematic variation with metallicity, the accretion rate distribution's shape remains largely insensitive to it. We estimated the current Milky Way nova rate at approximately 33 events per year; this aligns with extra-Galactic observational estimates but falls short of those based on Galactic data. However, our predicted distribution of Galactic white dwarf masses differs markedly from observed distributions, likely due to our underlying physical assumptions. For M31, we calculated a rate of about 36 novae per year, which underestimates the recent observational figure of $65^{+15}_{-16}$. Ultimately, we conclude that for predicting observable nova rates in spiral galaxies or environments with long-past star formation, metallicity is likely secondary to uncertainties in binary stellar evolution.

For a sufficiently large prime $p$, we have classified nilpotent pre-Lie rings of order $p^4$, which consequently yields a classification of braces of the same order. Previous research established that for large enough $p$, nilpotent pre-Lie rings of order $p^n$ are in correspondence with strongly nilpotent braces of order $p^n$, where these braces are explicitly derived via the group of flows construction. Since the classification of non-right nilpotent braces of order $p^4$ has already been completed, our findings finalize the classification of all braces of cardinality $p^4$.

Experimental studies indicate that the brain's rapid electrochemical dynamics, known as neurodynamics (ND), are characterized by strong stochasticity, chaos, and dominance by instantons (neuroavalanches). These dynamics also exhibit partial scale-invariance, loosely linked to critical phenomena. Recently, the supersymmetric theory of stochastics (STS) was shown to provide a theoretical framework explaining these ND characteristics. Within STS, all stochastic models feature topological supersymmetry (TS), where the "criticality" of ND and similar processes arises from a noise-induced, spontaneous breakdown of TS. This breakdown occurs due to instanton condensation near the boundary with ordinary chaos, where TS fails because of non-integrability. This paper proposes a novel approach potentially valuable for constructing low-energy effective theories of ND. Its core component is a coarse-graining method for neural networks utilizing simplicial complexes and the concept of an "enveloping lattice." This method represents a neural network as a continuous, high-dimensional base space, whose rich topology mirrors that of the original network. The reduced one-instanton state space is defined by the de Rham cohomology classes of this base space, allowing the effective ND dynamics to be understood as instanton interactions, following the Segal-Atiyah formalism.

Blockchain protocols utilize total-order broadcast in permissionless environments where nodes can freely join or exit. To mitigate Sybil attacks in such settings, honest nodes depend on cryptographic proofs linked to specific resources to qualify for transaction ordering. For instance, Proof-of-Work (PoW) uses computation as the resource, requiring the solution of a computationally difficult puzzle, whereas Proof-of-Stake (PoS) relies on coin ownership, selecting participants via a secure lottery proportional to their holdings. Although numerous resource-based blockchain protocols have formal security proofs in existing literature, these proofs do not explain why specific resource types render protocols susceptible to distinct attack classes. For example, PoS systems face greater vulnerability to long-range attacks—where an adversary corrupts past nodes to rewrite history—compared to Proof-of-Work and Proof-of-Storage systems. Similarly, both PoS and Proof-of-Storage protocols are more prone to private double-spending attacks than PoW-based systems, where an adversary secretly mines a chain without broadcasting blocks until the attack concludes. This paper formally defines resource properties using an abstraction known as the resource allocator and provides a framework for analyzing longest-chain consensus protocols based on different resources. Furthermore, it employs this resource allocator to illustrate security trade-offs among various resources by examining well-known attacks, such as long-range and nothing-at-stake attacks.

Bessel-Gauss (BG) beams represent a promising alternative to Gaussian beams for strong field science, offering greater flexibility in spot size and working distance while being easily generated with standard optics. This study utilizes BG beams created via a lens-axicon system for high-order harmonic generation (HHG) within a thin gas jet. The finite interaction region enables scanning of the HHG yield along the propagation axis. By simultaneously measuring ionization yield and extreme ultraviolet (XUV) output, we distinguish between zones of peak ionization and optimal XUV generation. This differentiation is crucial for BG fields, as axicon-generated beams often exhibit on-axis intensity oscillations that can be leveraged for extended phase matching. For the first time, we observed these oscillations in both ionization and XUV flux along the propagation axis. Similar to Gaussian modes, the harmonic yield does not peak at the point of maximum ionization. Furthermore, despite the central hole characteristic of Bessel beams in the far field, the resulting XUV beam remains well-collimated, making BG modes an excellent choice when spatial filtering of the fundamental beam is required.

This paper examines various Boussinesq-type systems used to model surface water waves. These equations, developed by multiple researchers, describe the bidirectional propagation of long gravity waves. A key focus is the existence of specific solutions known as solitary waves. While numerous studies have employed a variational approach combined with concentration-compactness arguments, these proofs are technically complex and often differ significantly across systems. In contrast, our methodology utilizes the implicit function theorem, offering a more streamlined and unified treatment.

For more than ten years, physical and energy limitations have hindered clock speed advancements in standard microprocessors, prompting chip manufacturers to shift toward developing multi-core, low-power architectures like GPGPU, ARM, and Intel MIC. Significant efforts by both developers and vendors have aimed to make these systems accessible for general computing tasks. However, leveraging the performance of numerous cores alongside specialized vector or SIMD units demands meticulous algorithm design and code optimization. In high-energy particle physics, a particularly computationally intensive challenge during event reconstruction is the identification and fitting of charged-particle tracks. This task is projected to become the primary bottleneck at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). Currently, methods relying on the Kalman filter are the most prevalent for track finding; their proven robustness and high physics performance on real detector systems have led to their adoption at the LHC for both trigger and offline processing. In previous work, we documented substantial parallel speedups achieved by adapting Kalman filters for track building and fitting on Intel Xeon and Xeon Phi processors. This paper outlines our progress in understanding these architectures and details new developments in porting Kalman filters to NVIDIA GPUs.

We outline the gravitational-wave observation and astrophysics initiatives planned for the LIGO Scientific Collaboration (LSC) over the coming decade, utilizing data from the US-based LIGO Observatories alongside international partners in Europe, Japan, and India. This overview details the targeted gravitational wave signal types and the significance of gravitational waves within time-domain multi-messenger astronomy. Additionally, we provide a concise summary of the insights derivable from detected signal characteristics, such as astrophysical event rates and populations, tests of gravitational-wave properties and General Relativity in highly dynamical, strong-field regimes, investigations into matter under extreme neutron star conditions, and cosmological measurements enabled by gravitational-wave sources.

Efficiently utilizing the limited wireless spectrum is a primary goal, and spectrum sensing serves as a key mechanism to achieve this. This paper introduces a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) designed for wireless spectrum sensing and signal identification, leveraging the spectral correlation function as a robust characterization of cyclostationarity. Unlike classical methods, this approach performs signal classification without requiring prior knowledge or a statistical decision process. The method is evaluated across two distinct scenarios: CASE1, where sensing and classification occur simultaneously, and CASE2, where they are executed sequentially. Experimental results using real-world over-the-air signals from cellular bands demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing deep learning classifiers and traditional sensing techniques. Although tested on cellular signals, the proposed framework is adaptable to any signal exhibiting cyclostationary properties. Furthermore, the measurement-based dataset employed for validation is made publicly available to facilitate result replication and future research.

We have derived the formal solution for the auxiliary system of Non-Linear Sigma Models (NLSM) where the target space is a rank-1 symmetric space associated with the indefinite orthogonal group O(p,q). This solution corresponds to any arbitrary solution of the NLSM and encompasses Anti-de Sitter, de Sitter, and Hyperbolic spaces, which are significant due to their relevance in the AdS/CFT correspondence. This formal solution connects to the Pohlmeyer reduction of the NLSM, establishing an additional relationship between the NLSM and its reduced theory. In addition to deriving the solution, we provide a review of the Pohlmeyer reduction applied to these models and discuss the implications for the monodromy matrix and its eigenvalues.

This paper presents "speechocean762," a newly developed open-source speech corpus tailored for pronunciation evaluation. The dataset comprises 5,000 English utterances from 250 non-native speakers, including half of whom are children. Each utterance was annotated by five experts across sentence, word, and phoneme levels. To demonstrate the phoneme-level assessment workflow, an open-source baseline system has been released. The corpus is freely available for both commercial and non-commercial use, downloadable from OpenSLR, with the corresponding baseline system published within the Kaldi speech recognition toolkit.

This work addresses the challenges of automatically detecting comparative sentences and classifying their implied preference (e.g., transforming "Python has better NLP libraries than MATLAB" into the triplet (Python, better, MATLAB)). To achieve this, we manually labeled 7,199 sentences covering 217 unique item pairs across multiple domains, where 27% of the data features oriented comparisons indicating superiority or inferiority. Our experimental results show that a gradient boosting model utilizing pre-trained sentence embeddings attains an F1 score of 85%. This system can be deployed to extract comparative statements for use in pro/con argumentation within comparative search engines or debating technologies.
