This note addresses a gap in the author's earlier work, "Ricci-Flat Holonomy: a Classification," by examining irreducible holonomy algebras that function as subalgebras or real forms of $\mbb{C} \oplus \mf{spin}(10,\mbb{C})$. All such cases are found to be of Ricci-type.

This paper investigates Higgs and co-Higgs bundles on non-Kähler elliptic surfaces. We demonstrate that non-trivial stable Higgs bundles arise only if the base of the elliptic fibration has a genus of at least two, and we apply this existence criterion to derive explicit topological conditions guaranteeing the smoothness of moduli spaces for stable rank-2 sheaves on these surfaces. Furthermore, we establish that non-trivial stable co-Higgs bundles exist exclusively when the base genus is zero, corresponding to the case where the non-Kähler elliptic surface is a Hopf surface. Finally, we provide a comprehensive characterization of non-trivial rank-2 co-Higgs bundles; these structures serve as examples of non-trivial holomorphic Poisson structures on $\mathbb{P}^1$-bundles over Hopf surfaces.

For a given prime $p$, we investigate topological counterparts to Iwasawa invariants linked to $\mathbb{Z}_p$-covers of the $3$-sphere branched over a link. We establish explicit conditions for identifying these invariants and apply them to analyze links composed of two-component knots. With $p$ fixed, we derive statistical findings regarding the average behavior of $p$-primary Iwasawa invariants for $2$-bridge links expressed in Schubert normal form. Our primary result, which stands entirely without conditions, demonstrates that the density of $2$-bridge links where the $\mu$-invariant is zero and the $\lambda$-invariant equals $1$ is $(1-\frac{1}{p})$. Furthermore, we conjecture that the density of $2$-bridge links with a vanishing $\mu$-invariant is $1$, a hypothesis strongly supported by computational data. Although our findings are established within a topological framework, they carry arithmetic importance by opening new avenues in arithmetic statistics and arithmetic topology.

We introduce an efficient approach for uniformly sampling points on a hypersphere across any number of dimensions. By circumventing the need to calculate computationally intensive functions such as logarithms, trigonometric ratios, or higher-order roots, this technique outperforms existing methods in speed.

We introduce the concept of fibrantly generated model categories. Just as cofibrantly generated model categories extend CW-approximations to facilitate inductive cofibrant replacements, we construct inductive fibrant replacements using Postnikov towers. These constructions offer novel methods for calculating homotopy limits within model categories, illustrated through examples involving simplicial and differential graded comodules. Our primary application demonstrates a Quillen equivalence between simplicial comodules and connective differential graded comodules, showing that their derived cotensor products correspond accordingly.

This study examines bipartite quantum state discrimination through positive-partial-transpose (PPT) measurements, demonstrating that minimum-error discrimination via PPT measurements is intrinsically linked to the decomposability of entanglement witnesses. Leveraging the notion of decomposable entanglement witnesses, we derive specific conditions governing minimum-error discrimination using PPT measurements. Furthermore, we establish criteria for the upper bound of the maximum success probability achievable across all feasible PPT measurements. Finally, we validate these findings with examples involving multidimensional bipartite quantum states.

This study details Coulomb blockade transport measurements on InAs nanowires featuring epitaxial layers of superconducting aluminum and ferromagnetic EuS insulator on intersecting facets. By comparing experimental data with theoretical models, we link spin-polarized Andreev levels to cotunneling signatures observed in even-odd bias spectra. The findings indicate that zero-field spin splitting surpasses the induced superconducting gap, and the energies of subgap states can be tuned on both sides of zero using electrostatic gates.

Surrogate model-based uncertainty quantification has garnered significant attention across numerous engineering disciplines, with Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE) and Deep Learning (DL) emerging as robust techniques for model construction. However, PCE demands higher expansion orders to enhance accuracy, necessitating more labeled data to compute coefficients, while DL similarly relies heavily on extensive labeled datasets for training deep neural networks. To address these limitations, this study introduces adaptive arbitrary polynomial chaos (aPC) and establishes two key properties regarding its adaptive expansion coefficients. Leveraging these findings, a semi-supervised Deep Adaptive Arbitrary Polynomial Chaos Expansion (Deep aPCE) method is developed to minimize data requirements and boost surrogate model precision. First, Deep aPCE utilizes the two identified properties of aPC to train the DNN using a minimal set of labeled data alongside a large volume of unlabeled data, thereby drastically cutting training costs. Second, the approach employs the DNN to dynamically fine-tune the adaptive expansion coefficients, achieving superior model accuracy with a lower expansion order. Furthermore, Deep aPCE enables the direct construction of accurate surrogate models for high-dimensional stochastic systems, eliminating the need for complex dimension reduction or model decomposition. The efficacy of the proposed Deep aPCE method is validated through five numerical examples and a real-world engineering application.

Using a 143 fb$^{-1}$ data set from the CMS experiment at the LHC, the production cross-section ratios for B$_\mathrm{c}$(2S)$^+$ to B$_\mathrm{c}^+$, B$_\mathrm{c}^*$(2S)$^+$ to B$_\mathrm{c}^+$, and B$_\mathrm{c}^*$(2S)$^+$ to B$_\mathrm{c}$(2S)$^+$ have been measured in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV. These measurements cover the phase space region defined by $p_\mathrm{T} > 15$ GeV and $|y| < 2.4$, with the excited B$_\mathrm{c}^{(*)}$(2S)$^+$ states identified via the decay chains B$_\mathrm{c}^{(*)+} \to$ B$_\mathrm{c}^+ \pi^+\pi^-$, B$_\mathrm{c}^+ \to$ J/$\psi \pi^+$, and J/$\psi \to$ $\mu^+\mu^-$. The resulting cross-section ratios, which incorporate the unknown branching fractions for B$_\mathrm{c}^{(*)}$(2S)$^+$ $\to$ B$_\mathrm{c}^{(*)+}\pi^+\pi^-$, are determined to be (3.47 $\pm$ 0.63 (stat) $\pm$ 0.33 (syst))%, (4.69 $\pm$ 0.71 (stat) $\pm$ 0.56 (syst))%, and 1.35 $\pm$ 0.32 (stat) $\pm$ 0.09 (syst), respectively. No significant variation of these ratios with respect to the B$_\mathrm{c}$ meson's $p_\mathrm{T}$ or $|y|$ is observed, and the normalized dipion invariant mass distributions for the B$_\mathrm{c}^{(*)}$(2S)$^+$ $\to$ B$_\mathrm{c}^{(*)+}\pi^+\pi^-$ decays are also presented.

We demonstrate that the presence of a Gottlieb element in the rational homotopy of a simply connected space $X$ yields specific structural conclusions for the Sullivan minimal model, varying by parity. In the even-degree scenario, we establish that a rational Gottlieb element constitutes a terminal homotopy element. This finding enables us to finalize Dupont's argument, proving that an even-degree Gottlieb element generates a free factor within the rational cohomology of a formal space of finite type. Furthermore, we utilize the odd-degree result to confirm a particular instance of the $2N$-conjecture regarding Gottlieb elements of a finite complex. By synthesizing these outcomes, we advance the realization problem for the classifying space $B\mathrm{aut}_1(X)$. Specifically, we show that if a simply connected space $X$ satisfies $B\mathrm{aut}_1(X_{\mathbb{Q}}) \simeq S_{\mathbb{Q}}^{2n}$, then for $n = 1, 2, 3$, $X$ must possess infinite-dimensional rational homotopy and exhibit vanishing rational Gottlieb elements in degrees exceeding $2n-1$.

This survey aims to offer a rigorous introduction to the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra (FTLA) and its underlying theories, specifically targeting readers with prior linear algebra experience. It provides detailed explanations and proofs of key results from Strang (1993), explores the FTLA through multiple perspectives, and elucidates the properties and interconnections among these views. As a cornerstone in electrical engineering, computer science, machine learning, and deep learning, the FTLA is central to numerous disciplines; consequently, this survey summarizes the purpose and significance of the critical theories supporting it. The primary objective is to deliver a self-contained exposition of the concepts and mathematical tools necessary for a rigorous analysis of the FTLA's properties across four subspaces. However, we acknowledge the limitations of scope and cannot cover all pertinent or fascinating results, such as the separate analysis of orthogonal projection matrices. For a more comprehensive treatment of these related fields, readers are directed to existing literature, including works by Rose (1982), Strang (2009, 2019, 2021), and Trefethen and Bau III (1997).

This study examines the impact of robust electron-electron interactions and Wigner-molecule (WM) formation on the spectra of $2e$ singlet-triplet double-dot silicon qubits, utilizing a full configuration interaction (FCI) method that integrates the valley degree of freedom (VDOF) within a continuous effective mass framework. In our approach, the VDOF is treated as an isospin alongside standard spin, allowing for the assignment of a complete set of good quantum numbers for both spin and valley isospin to each energy level. This analysis uncovers an underlying SU(4) $\supset$ SU(2) $\times$ SU(2) group-chain structure in silicon double-dot spectra. Using parameters consistent with real experimental conditions, we show that for a (2,0) charge configuration, strong $e-e$ interactions significantly suppress the spin-singlet to spin-triplet energy gap ($E_{\rm ST}$) within the same valley. Consequently, this gap becomes comparable to the small inter-valley energy gap ($E_V$), a phenomenon we explore for both $E_{\rm ST} < E_V$ and $E_{\rm ST} > E_V$ scenarios. By varying detuning, we observe strengthened avoided crossings resulting from reduced interdot barriers and valley-orbit coupling effects. Additionally, we demonstrate the appearance of avoided crossings in the (1,1) configuration under an applied magnetic field, driven by spin-valley coupling. Finally, the developed valleytronic FCI method for two electrons in a tunable double quantum dot serves as a powerful tool for analyzing spectra in systems with multiple wells or electrons.

We examine the constraints of perturbative coupling constants and a metastable electroweak vacuum extending to the Planck scale within high-scale thermal leptogenesis, specifically under a type-I seesaw framework. Our analysis reveals a substantial region of the parameter space that simultaneously satisfies these conditions and generates the observed baryon asymmetry of the Universe. We show that these requirements imply an upper bound of approximately 0.66 for the trace of the neutrino Yukawa matrix squared, ${\rm Tr}[Y_N^\dagger Y_N]$. Furthermore, we explore this scenario in a context featuring a large number $N_F$ of coloured Majorana octet fermions, introduced to ensure the asymptotic safety of quantum chromodynamics in the ultraviolet regime.

This work investigates a boundary value problem on an unbounded domain linked to difference equations featuring the Euclidean mean curvature operator. The existence of solutions that remain positive throughout the entire domain and decay at infinity is established through newly derived Sturm comparison theorems for linear difference equations, alongside a fixed-point method utilizing a linearization technique. Additionally, the transition from the continuous to the discrete formulation is analyzed, highlighting specific discrepancies between the discrete and continuous scenarios.

Although language models (LMs) now underpin nearly all major language technologies, their capabilities, constraints, and risks remain poorly understood. To address this, we introduce Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to enhance transparency. First, we categorize the extensive landscape of potential use cases and desired metrics, then select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, highlighting gaps such as question answering for neglected dialects or trustworthiness metrics. Second, we employ a multi-metric strategy, assessing seven dimensions (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) across 16 core scenarios whenever possible (87.5% of the time). This approach ensures that metrics beyond accuracy are not overlooked and clearly reveals trade-offs. Additionally, we conduct seven targeted evaluations using 26 specific scenarios to examine particular aspects like reasoning and disinformation. Third, we perform a large-scale assessment of 30 prominent models (covering open, limited-access, and closed types) across all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were previously unused in mainstream evaluations. Before HELM, models were typically evaluated on only 17.9% of these core scenarios, with some major models sharing no common scenarios; we have improved this to 96.0%, ensuring all 30 models are densely benchmarked on identical core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation yields 25 top-level findings. To ensure full transparency, we publicly release all raw prompts and completions for further analysis, along with a modular toolkit. We aim for HELM to serve as a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.

This research presents comprehensive calculations of energies, hyperfine structure constants, Land\'e g$_J$ factors, and isotope shifts for the lowest 71 states of Na-like Ar$^{7+}$, Kr$^{25+}$, and Xe$^{43+}$ ions. Additionally, radiative parameters—including transition rates, wavelengths, oscillator strengths, and lifetimes for electric and magnetic dipole and quadrupole transitions—have been estimated among these levels. The study encompasses states with configurations $1s^2s^22p^6nl$ where $n$ ranges from 3 to 9 and $l$ spans from s to i. These calculations employ the fully relativistic multiconfiguration Dirac Fock method within the most recent version of a general-purpose relativistic atomic structure package. Furthermore, relativistic effects such as Breit interactions and quantum electrodynamics corrections were incorporated and analyzed for their impact on energy levels. To verify the reliability of the multiconfiguration Dirac Fock (MCDF) results, a separate set of calculations was conducted using the many-body perturbation theory method via the Flexi Atomic code. A rigorous comparison was made between these two computational approaches and existing theoretical and experimental data where available, revealing good agreement. The current work significantly expands upon existing knowledge for these Na-like ions, as many results are reported here for the first time. Moreover, the high accuracy of these findings is expected to prove valuable for spectral analysis and diagnostics in plasma and astrophysical contexts.

To date, single strontium atoms confined in optical tweezers have been imaged exclusively via the broad $^{1\hspace{-0.3ex}}S_0$-$^{1\hspace{-0.3ex}}P_1$ transition. In contrast, ytterbium has successfully utilized the narrow (183 kHz-wide) $^{1\hspace{-0.3ex}}S_0$-$^{3\hspace{-0.3ex}}P_1$ transition for simultaneous cooling and imaging within tweezers featuring a magic wavelength for that specific transition. We present high-fidelity imaging of individual Sr atoms using its even narrower (7.4 kHz-wide) $^{1\hspace{-0.3ex}}S_0$-$^{3\hspace{-0.3ex}}P_1$ transition, where the atoms are held in non-magic-wavelength tweezers. By detecting photons scattered during Sisyphus cooling, we maintain the atoms near the motional ground state throughout the imaging process. This method achieves a detection fidelity of 0.9991(4) and a survival probability of 0.97(2). An atom can remain trapped under these imaging conditions for 79(3) seconds, enabling hundreds of images to be captured, with the duration primarily limited by background gas collisions. We successfully detect atoms in an array of 36 tweezers using 813.4-nm light and trap depths of 135(20) $\mu$K. This trap depth is approximately three times shallower than that typically required for imaging on the broad $^{1\hspace{-0.3ex}}S_0$-$^{1\hspace{-0.3ex}}P_1$ transition. Narrow-line imaging offers the potential to further reduce trap depths, provided that all trap frequencies remain larger than the imaging transition linewidth. Furthermore, performing imaging on a narrow-linewidth transition within a non-magic-wavelength tweezer enables the selective imaging of specific tweezers. As a demonstration, we selectively image (and hide) a single tweezer from the array, providing a valuable tool for quantum error correction protocols.

Hodge numerical invariants associated with a variation of Hodge structure over a smooth quas-projective variety quantify the complexity of the global twisting of the limit mixed Hodge structure during degeneration. These invariants feature in Arakelov inequalities, which may include correction terms. Research often explores these correction terms to establish Arakelov equalities. In this study, we examine numerical Arakelov-type inequalities and equalities for a family of curve-fibered surfaces. Our approach leverages Arakelov identities within weight 1 and weight 2 variations of Hodge structure (referencing \cite{GGK}) inside a commutative triangle of fibrations. We propose correlating the degrees of Hodge bundles across the two families and compare their Fujita decompositions. Furthermore, we analyze various identities and relationships connecting Hodge numbers with the degrees of Hodge bundles at different levels.

Nomizu and van Est established a theorem calculating the cohomology of compact nilmanifolds, which corresponds to the group cohomology of an arithmetic subgroup within a unipotent linear algebraic group defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. We demonstrate an analogous result for the cohomology of a compact open subgroup of a unipotent linear algebraic group over $\mathbb{Q}_{\ell}$, utilizing coefficients from a complex of continuous $\ell$-adic representations. Our approach employs the triangulated categories introduced by Ekedahl, which serve as the "derived categories of continuous $\ell$-adic representations." This work is inspired by Pink's formula regarding the derived direct image of an $\ell$-adic local system on a Shimura variety within its minimal compactification, particularly concerning its application to automorphic perverse sheaves on Shimura varieties. The central technical achievement is the calculation of cohomology with coefficients in a unipotent representation and torsion coefficients via an explicit complex of polynomial cochains of finite type.

This study examines a double pair plasma system comprising cold inertial positive and negative ions alongside inertialess super-thermal electrons and positrons. By employing the reductive perturbation method, the standard nonlinear Schrödinger equation is derived to analyze the nonlinear dynamics of ion-acoustic waves (IAWs) and their modulation instability. Observations indicate that ion-acoustic dark (bright) envelope solitons emerge in modulationally stable (unstable) plasma regions. Furthermore, a high density of super-thermal electrons and positrons is found to expand (shrink) these unstable (stable) regions. Additionally, the super-thermality of either electron or positron species increases nonlinearity and accelerates the formation of bright envelope solitons. These findings are relevant to both laboratory and space plasma systems for elucidating the propagation of localized electrostatic disturbances.

This paper aims to analyze the isolated singularities of positive solutions to the Choquard equation in the sublinear regime where $q \in (0,1)$:
$$ \displaystyle \ \ -\Delta u+ u =I_\alpha[u^p] u^q\;\;
  {\rm in}\; \mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\}, \quad \displaystyle \lim_{|x|\to+\infty}u(x)=0, $$
with parameters $p >0$, $N \geq 3$, and $\alpha \in (0,N)$. Here, $I_{\alpha}[u^p](x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \frac{u^p(y)}{|x-y|^{N-\alpha}}dy$ denotes the Riesz potential, serving as a nonlocal component within the equation. We examine both the existence and nonexistence of isolated singular solutions across various ranges of the exponent pair $(p,q)$. Additionally, we derive qualitative properties for the minimal singular solutions.

This paper examines the Lambert-Tsallis function, a two-parameter extension of the Lambert function. We establish a condition on these parameters ensuring the existence of a complex domain that touches zero at its boundary and is mapped bijectively to the upper half-plane by the Lambert-Tsallis function.

This study investigates the origins of UV-excess in star clusters through N-body simulations of six clusters, featuring populations of 10k and 100k stars (including singles and binaries) across metallicities of Z=0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001, utilizing the PETAR code. Each model begins with a primordial binary fraction of 50%. Using GalevNB, we transform the simulation outputs into synthetic photometry and spectra tailored for the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the China Space Station Telescope (CSST). Analysis of the spectral energy distributions reveals three stellar sources contributing to the UV-excess: (1) second asymptotic giant branch stars, which dominate UV flux early on; (2) naked helium stars; and (3) white dwarfs, which provide long-term FUV contributions. Binary systems pairing white dwarfs with main-sequence stars are identified as cataclysmic variable (CV) candidates. The magnitude distribution of these CV candidates exhibits bimodality up to 2 Gyr, with the brighter population showing distinct FUV-NUV brightness. Our model clusters display FUV-NUV colors that are 1-2 magnitudes redder than UV-excess globular clusters found in the Milky Way and M 87, a discrepancy potentially caused by helium enrichment in observed systems. Our simulations rely on simple stellar evolution and omit variations in helium and light elements or multiple stellar populations. A positive radial color gradient is observed in CSST NUV-y for main-sequence stars across all models, with a color difference of 0.2-0.5 mag extending up to 4 half-mass radii. For NUV-g > 1 mag, the CSST NUV-g color correlates strongly with HST FUV-NUV, following the linear relation $FUV-NUV=(1.09\pm0.12)\times(NUV-g)+(-1.01\pm0.22)$. This relationship enables the conversion of future CSST NUV-g colors into HST FUV-NUV colors, which are sensitive to UV-excess features. We conclude that CSST will be capable of detecting UV-excess in galactic and extra-galactic star clusters older than 200 Myr.

This work investigates quantum soft covering and privacy amplification in the presence of quantum side information. Soft covering seeks to approximate a quantum state through sampling from a prior distribution and querying a channel, whereas privacy amplification focuses on extracting uniform, independent randomness secure against quantum adversaries. For both scenarios, closeness to the ideal target state is quantified using trace distance. We demonstrate that the minimum sample size required for an $\varepsilon$-covering corresponds to the $(1-\varepsilon)$-hypothesis testing information (plus logarithmic additive terms), while the maximum extractable randomness for an $\varepsilon$-secret extractor is defined by the conditional $(1-\varepsilon)$-hypothesis testing entropy. By analyzing independent and identical repetitions of these tasks, our one-shot results yield tight asymptotic expansions for these operational quantities. Specifically, we derive second-order rates determined by the variances of quantum mutual information and quantum conditional information, respectively. Furthermore, these findings apply to the moderate deviation regime, providing optimal asymptotic rates when trace distances decay at a sub-exponential rate. Our methodology relies on the direct analysis of trace distance, avoiding the use of smoothing techniques.

Two sets of positive integers, $A$ and $B$, are defined as \emph{exact additive complements} if their sumset $A+B$ includes all sufficiently large integers and the ratio $A(x)B(x)/x$ converges to 1. Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ be such a set, where $A(x)$ represents its counting function and $a^*(x)$ denotes the maximum element in $A$ up to $x$. Building upon the research of Ruzsa and Chen-Fang, we demonstrate that for exact additive complements $A$ and $B$ satisfying $\frac{a_{n+1}}{na_n}\rightarrow\infty$, the inequality $A(x)B(x)-x\ge \frac{a^*(x)}{A(x)}+o\left(\frac{a^*(x)}{A(x)^2}\right)$ holds as $x\rightarrow +\infty$. Conversely, we also construct specific exact additive complements $A$ and $B$ with the same growth condition $\frac{a_{n+1}}{na_n}\rightarrow\infty$ for which the bound $A(x)B(x)-x\le \frac{a^*(x)}{A(x)}+(1+o(1))\left(\frac{a^*(x)}{A(x)^2}\right)$ is valid for infinitely many positive integers $x$.

In the field of quantum cryptography, quantum secret sharing (QSS) serves as a foundational primitive essential for developing complex and secure multiparty quantum protocols. Current QSS schemes are limited to either the $(n, n)$ threshold level of 2 or the $(t, n)$ threshold level of $d$ relying on a trusted participant, where $n$ represents the total number of players and $t$ indicates the required threshold. This study introduces a novel, secure $d$-level QSS protocol designed for efficient secret sharing simulation. Compared to existing methods, including the $(n, n)$ threshold 2-level and the $(t, n)$ threshold $d$-level with a trusted player, our proposed protocol offers superior security, flexibility, and practicality. Furthermore, it ensures that no information regarding the secret is revealed to the players. Security analysis confirms the protocol's robustness against various threats, including intercept-resend, intercept, entangle-measure, forgery, collision, and collusion attacks.

In Quantum Field Theory, spectral functions like zeta functions are commonly employed to determine physical observables. This study applies zeta function regularization to calculate the electrostatic potential and field generated by an infinite discrete array of point charges, effectively eliminating divergences in the derived expressions. Our results indicate that the asymptotic behavior of both the potential and the field mirrors that observed in continuous charge distributions. Ultimately, this exercise serves as a valuable resource for graduate students seeking to investigate spectral and special functions.

Let $G$ be a $k$-connected graph with order $n$, where $k \geq 2$. If the chromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\chi(G)$, satisfies $\chi(G) \geq n - k$, then $G$ is either Hamiltonian or isomorphic to $K_k \vee (K_k^c \cup K_{n - 2k})$ under the condition that $n \geq 2k + 1$.

The demand for machine learning-driven anomaly detection methods is increasing to expand the search for Beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) physics at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and beyond. The initial phase of any such approach involves defining observables to identify anomalous events, with a prevalent strategy being the selection of events exhibiting low probability density. However, it is established that probability densities lack invariance under coordinate transformations, meaning detection sensitivity can vary based on the chosen coordinate system. The wider machine learning community has recently linked this coordinate sensitivity to anomaly detection, and our objective is to highlight this critical issue within the expanding high-energy physics literature. Beyond analytical insights, we present numerical examples drawn from simple random variables and the LHC Olympics Dataset, demonstrating how reliance on probability density as an anomaly score can result in events being classified differently depending on the coordinate frame used.

Consider the simple algebraic supergroup $\bar{G}$ defined over $\mathbb{C}$ as either $\mathrm{SL}(m|n)$ or $\mathrm{OSp}(m|2n)$. Let $\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Lie}(\bar{G})=\mathfrak{g}_{\bar{0}}\oplus\mathfrak{g}_{\bar{1}}$ denote its Lie superalgebra, and let $G=\bar{G}(\mathbb{C})$, where $\mathbb{C}$ is treated as a superalgebra with elements only in the even degree. Given a nilpotent element $e\in\mathfrak{g}_{\bar{0}}$, this work characterizes the centralizer $\mathfrak{g}^{e}$ within $\mathfrak{g}$ and its center $\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{g}^{e})$. Specifically, explicit bases are provided for $\mathfrak{g}^{e}$, $\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{g}^{e})$, and the $G^{e}$-invariant subspace $\left(\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{g}^{e})\right)^{G^{e}}$. Furthermore, the labelled Dynkin diagram $\varDelta$ associated with $e$ is determined, and the connection between $\left(\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{g}^{e})\right)^{G^{e}}$ and $\varDelta$ is elucidated.

The reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), a planar metasurface composed of numerous low-cost reflective elements, has garnered significant attention for its capacity to enhance both spectral and energy efficiency by dynamically adjusting the wireless propagation environment. This paper introduces an optimization approach for RIS phase shifts and base station (BS) beamforming designed to minimize uplink transmit power within an RIS-aided IoT network. The proposed method, termed Riemannian conjugate gradient-based joint optimization (RCG-JO), utilizes the Riemannian conjugate gradient technique to simultaneously optimize RIS phase shifts and BS beamforming vectors. By leveraging the product Riemannian manifold structure inherent to the sets of unit-modulus phase shifts and unit-norm beamforming vectors, the nonconvex uplink power minimization problem is transformed into an unconstrained one, allowing for the identification of the optimal solution on the product Riemannian manifold. Performance analysis and numerical results demonstrate that the RCG-JO technique reduces uplink transmit power by 94% compared to conventional schemes that do not utilize RIS.

The dynamics of internal fluid flow and surface oscillations within the melt pool during arc welding remain intricate and not entirely comprehended. This study utilizes high-fidelity numerical simulations to investigate how welding position, sulphur levels (ranging from 60 to 300 ppm), and travel speeds (1.25 to 5 mm/s) influence molten metal flow in fully penetrated pools. To achieve time-resolved frequency spectra of oscillation signals, a wavelet transform is applied, addressing the limitations of Fourier transforms regarding temporal resolution. By comparing the numerical findings with existing analytical and experimental data, the reliability of this approach in forecasting melt-pool oscillations is validated. The findings indicate that shifts in welding position alter surface morphology, which modifies the spatial distribution of arc forces and power density acting on the molten material, thereby changing flow patterns. Furthermore, under comparable conditions, varying sulphur concentrations impacts Marangoni flow, while increasing travel speed reduces pool dimensions and widens the offset between the top and bottom surfaces, consequently influencing surface flow structures such as vortex formation. Ultimately, fluctuations in internal flow patterns drive the evolution of the melt-pool's shape and its associated surface oscillations.

Previous research on ideology prediction has predominantly examined single modalities, such as text or images in isolation. This study introduces the task of multimodal ideology prediction, wherein a model forecasts binary or five-point scale ideological leanings based on paired text and images containing political content. We begin by assembling five new large-scale datasets comprising English documents and images with associated ideological labels, spanning news articles from diverse US mainstream outlets and social media posts from Reddit and Twitter. We carry out detailed analyses of these news articles, uncovering variations in image content and utilization across the political spectrum. Additionally, we execute comprehensive experiments and ablation studies that highlight the efficacy of specific pretraining objectives applied to various model components. Our top-performing model, which employs a late-fusion architecture pretrained using a triplet objective on multimodal data, surpasses the state-of-the-art text-only model by nearly 4% and exceeds a robust multimodal baseline without pretraining by more than 3%.

Continuously acquiring knowledge from new data without compromising understanding of prior classes remains a significant research challenge. Crucially, this process must adhere to strict memory and computational limits: (i) only a handful of training samples are available per class, (ii) the cost of learning new classes must remain constant, and (iii) model memory usage should increase linearly with the number of observed classes. To address these requirements, we introduce C-FSCIL, featuring a frozen meta-learned feature extractor, a trainable fixed-size fully connected layer, and a rewritable, dynamically expanding memory module that scales with the number of encountered classes. C-FSCIL offers three distinct update modes that balance the trade-off between learning accuracy and compute-memory efficiency. By leveraging hyperdimensional embedding, the method enables the continuous representation of a vast number of classes within a fixed vector space with minimal interference. Furthermore, the quality of class representations is enhanced by aligning them quasi-orthogonally using novel loss functions. Experimental results on CIFAR100, miniImageNet, and Omniglot demonstrate that C-FSCIL surpasses existing baselines in both accuracy and compression. Notably, it scales to unprecedented problem sizes in few-shot settings, successfully learning 423 novel classes atop 1200 base classes with less than a 1.6% accuracy decline. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/IBM/constrained-FSCIL.

Silicon-germanium heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) are promising candidates for low-noise microwave amplifiers because they offer competitive noise figures and lower costs compared to III-V devices. Consequently, understanding the fundamental noise limits of HBTs is crucial, with previous research suggesting that quasiballistic electron transport across the base causes cryogenic non-ideal IV characteristics that impact these limits. However, this hypothesis has not been rigorously validated against theory, as earlier studies relied on empirical models or approximate Boltzmann equation solutions. This work investigates non-diffusive transport in narrow-base SiGe HBTs using an exact, semi-analytic solution of the Boltzmann equation derived from an asymptotic expansion. Our results show that the calculated transport characteristics do not align with experimental data, indicating that quasiballistic electron transport is unlikely to be the source of these cryogenic IV anomalies. Ultimately, this study aids in identifying the mechanisms that determine the lower bounds of the microwave noise figure for cryogenic HBT amplifiers.

The extensive integration of Free/Libre and Open Source Software (FLOSS) indicates that maintaining numerous widely used software components increasingly depends on the collective work of volunteers who independently set priorities and select tasks. We contend that this dynamic has generated a novel risk termed 'underproduction,' defined as a misalignment between the available supply of software engineering labor and the demand from software users. We introduce a conceptual framework for detecting relative underproduction in software, alongside a statistical methodology applied to a comprehensive dataset from the Debian GNU/Linux distribution. This dataset encompasses 21,902 source packages and the complete history of 461,656 bugs. Leveraging this application, we conduct two experiments: first, demonstrating how the technique identifies at-risk packages within a large FLOSS repository, and second, validating these findings using an alternative risk indicator. Our analysis confirms the effectiveness of this approach and uncovers widespread underproduction among various widely installed components within Debian.

Causal structure discovery (CSD) models are increasingly applied across various fields, including Earth system sciences; however, their broad adoption is hindered by the frequent exclusion of expert domain knowledge and the need for iterative model adjustments. This paper introduces a workflow designed to integrate such expertise when applying CSD algorithms within Earth system sciences, while also highlighting open research challenges that remain. We propose a method for interactively refining CSD outputs, arguing that user interaction can be conceptualized as a greedy search for the local maximum-a-posteriori solution of a likelihood function. This function combines the likelihood of the causal model with a prior distribution that encodes the expert user's knowledge. Using a real-world dataset developed in collaboration with domain experts, we demonstrate that discovering maximally usable causal models in Earth system sciences or similar domains is a complex task fraught with unresolved questions. Furthermore, we contend that incorporating domain knowledge significantly influences the quality of the resulting causal models.

Data applications often face invariant constraints driven by practical requirements. Consequently, data curators utilizing differential privacy must adhere to these constraints as a fundamental utility requirement, as such invariants complicate the formulation, implementation, and interpretation of privacy guarantees. To address this, we introduce subspace differential privacy, which accurately describes how sanitized outputs depend on confidential data attributes. We present two design frameworks that adapt established differentially private mechanisms, including Gaussian and Laplace, into subspace variants that honor curator-specified invariants. For linear queries, we detail the construction of near-optimal mechanisms that minimize mean squared error. These subspace mechanisms eliminate the need for post-processing to satisfy invariants, maintain output transparency and statistical clarity, and support distributed execution. We demonstrate the efficacy of these mechanisms using the 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance data and a spatio-temporal dataset of mobile access point connections from a large university campus.

Electrostriction, defined as the deformation of dielectric materials in response to an electric field, remains a significant topic in optics. A notable discrepancy exists between the classic experiment by Hakim and Higham [Proc. Phys. Soc. 80, 190 (1962)] regarding stationary fields and the recent findings by Astrath et al. [Light Sci. Appl. 11, 103 (2022)] concerning optical fields, which support different formulas for electrostrictive force density. To investigate this divergence, this study develops a time-dependent covariant theory of force densities within photonic materials. When a light pulse traverses a bulk dielectric, the resulting field-induced force density comprises two components: (i) the optical wave momentum force density, which transports the light's wave momentum and propels a mass density wave associated with the covariant coupled light-material state; and (ii) the optostrictive force density, which stems from the dependence of electric and magnetic field energy densities on atomic density. This optostrictive component serves as an optical generalization of the Lorentz-force-based electro- and magnetostrictive force densities familiar from static electromagnetic fields, derived via the principle of virtual work. Because the work performed by the optostrictive force density does not equate to the change in field energy density during material contraction, optostriction-related dissipation terms are required to satisfy energy conservation, with the detailed physical model of such dissipation reserved for future research. Conceptually, the optostrictive force density can be interpreted as field-induced pair interactions within the material. Due to associated action and reaction effects, this force density does not contribute to the net momentum transfer of the optical field. Furthermore, the proposed theory is applied to simulate the propagation of a Gaussian light pulse through a dielectric medium.

This study establishes regularity properties for weak solutions to Robin problems governed by the well-known Orlicz $g$-Laplacian operator. Specifically, employing a tailored modification of the Moser iteration method, we demonstrate that all weak solutions to this problem are bounded. Furthermore, by integrating this finding with Lieberman's regularity theorem, we prove that any $C^1(\overline{\Omega})$-local minimizer is also a $W^{1,G}(\Omega)$-local minimizer regarding the associated energy functional of the Robin-Orlicz problem.

The transverse wobbling band observed in odd-mass $^{105}$Pd has been re-examined using the triaxial particle rotor model. By utilizing various sets of moment of inertia (MOI) parameters, multiple theoretical outcomes were found to align well with experimental data, which reveal distinct rotational excitation patterns. These patterns exhibit sensitivity to the ratio between the MOI along the intermediate and short axes. As this ratio increases, the wobble transitions gradually from occurring about the short axis of the total angular momentum to one about the intermediate axis. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that precession and tunneling represent two facets of quantum wobbling motion, with tunneling dominating in the yrare states of $^{105}$Pd. These findings regarding $^{105}$Pd underscore the intricate nature of the transverse wobbling mode.

The Galilei group serves as the foundational symmetry for nonrelativistic physics, encompassing both quantum and classical domains. However, our rigorous group-theoretic approach to quantum theory necessitates specific modifications. This overview outlines the complete framework, highlighting distinctions from conventional perspectives. Our analysis entails a more precise examination of the connection between exact mathematical structures and their application in dynamical theories, alongside a comprehensive implementation of mathematical logic often absent in standard physics literature. This article synthesizes our previous formulation while extending it, specifically refining the identification of basic representations where Newtonian mass acts as a Casimir invariant and the center of mass is defined by symmetry principles. Furthermore, we demonstrate the necessity of excluding time translational symmetry, as its inclusion would otherwise prohibit particle interactions.

Evaluating affective states and stress levels via ECG signals represents a critical area in biomedical signal processing. While current studies typically offer only binary stress classification, healthcare applications would benefit from a multi-level assessment approach. Additionally, although existing research analyzes ECG signals independently in either the spatial or transform domains, the potential of fusing these domains remains underexploited. To leverage this fusion effectively, we present a novel dataset capturing multiple stress levels, classified using a deep learning method that converts ECG signals into images based on R-R peaks without prior feature extraction. We further enhance these images by generating multimodal, multidomain representations through the Gabor Wavelet Transform (GWT) for time-frequency analysis and the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for frequency analysis. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) extract features from these distinct modalities, followed by decision-level fusion to boost classification accuracy. Experiments conducted on an in-house dataset from 15 users demonstrate that our proposed fusion framework, utilizing ECG-to-image conversion, achieves an average accuracy of 85.45%.

This paper describes the construction of symplectic foliations on 3-dimensional orientable Riemannian manifolds using harmonic forms, proposing a topological framework for addressing Poisson's equation and Newtonian gravity.

Determining mixed Nash equilibria (MNE) in two-player continuous zero-sum games represents a significant and difficult challenge within machine learning. A standard approach for locating these equilibria involves noisy gradient descent ascent, which, under the infinite particle limit, evolves into Mean-Field Gradient Descent Ascent (GDA) dynamics defined over probability measures. This paper investigates the convergence properties of a two-scale Mean-Field GDA aimed at solving entropy-regularized objectives. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any fixed positive temperature (regularization parameter), the two-scale Mean-Field GDA with a finite scale ratio converges exponentially to the unique MNE, without requiring the interaction potential to be convex or concave. Central to our proof is the development of novel Lyapunov functions that exhibit exponential dissipation along the Mean-Field GDA trajectories. Additionally, we examine the simulated annealing of Mean-Field GDA dynamics. We establish that employing a temperature schedule decreasing logarithmically with time allows the annealed Mean-Field GDA to converge to the MNE of the original unregularized objective function.

Multimodal sentiment analysis enhances diverse fields, including human-computer interaction and recommendation systems, by inferring users' bipolar sentiments through visual, textual, and acoustic signals. While researchers acknowledge the link between cognitive cues and emotional expressions, most existing multimodal approaches overlook user-specific factors. To address this, we introduce a novel method for multimodal sentiment prediction that incorporates cognitive cues like personality. Our framework builds an adaptive tree by hierarchically segmenting users and trains LSTM-based submodels, employing attention-based fusion to transfer knowledge oriented toward cognition within the tree structure. Following this, the system utilizes the aggregated knowledge from the adaptive tree to generate final sentiment predictions. Additionally, we developed a dynamic dropout technique to enable data sharing among neighboring nodes, thereby mitigating data sparsity. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms current leading approaches. Furthermore, compared to other ensemble methods, this transfer-based algorithm more effectively leverages latent cognitive cues to improve prediction results. Based on both intrinsic and extrinsic analysis, we find that our hierarchical clustering strategy groups users within the adaptive tree more effectively than other theoretical-based techniques.

This paper examines Kummer K3 surfaces situated near the orbifold limit, enhancing the estimates for Calabi-Yau metrics previously established by R. Kobayashi. Leveraging these improved metric bounds, the study investigates stable closed geodesics, demonstrating that their existence is typically subject to specific constraints. Furthermore, it highlights that under certain conditions of high symmetry, stable closed geodesics can emerge as a consequence of hyperkähler identities.

Inferring the properties of 3D objects from 2D images is difficult because appearance changes depending on the viewing angle. While tasks like object classification remain unchanged under 3D rotations (invariant), others like pose estimation change predictably (equivariant). However, enforcing equivariance with 2D inputs is generally impossible without knowing beforehand how images transform during out-of-plane rotations, a requirement currently met only by models using point clouds or voxels rather than 2D images. This paper introduces a new architecture utilizing icosahedral group convolutions that learns to project input images onto an icosahedron to reason in $\mathrm{SO(3)}$, achieving approximate equivariance to 3D rotations. Applied to pose estimation and shape classification, the model surpasses reasonable baselines. Project website: \url{https://dmklee.github.io/image2icosahedral}

The metric nearness problem involves identifying the closest distance matrix to a given dissimilarity matrix that adheres to triangle inequalities, a task with significant applications in fields like sensor networks and image processing. However, achieving even a moderately accurate solution is challenging due to $O(n^{3})$ metric constraints and a nonsmooth objective function, typically a weighted $\ell_{p}$ norm. To address this, we introduce a delayed constraint generation method where each subproblem is solved using the semismooth Newton-based proximal augmented Lagrangian method (PALM). By leveraging the specific structure of the matrix associated with metric constraints, our approach avoids the need to store the full constraint matrix, despite its high memory demands. Notably, the algorithm can handle problems with up to $10^{8}$ variables and $10^{13}$ constraints, as confirmed by numerical experiments. Theoretically, we first establish a primal-dual error bound under mild conditions, which is crucial for analyzing the local convergence rate of PALM. Second, we demonstrate the equivalence between the dual nondegeneracy condition and the nonsingularity of the generalized Jacobian for the inner PALM subproblem. Finally, when the objective involves the $\ell_{1}$ or $\ell_{\infty}$ norms, we prove that the dual nondegeneracy condition is equivalent to the uniqueness of the primal solution, even without assuming strict complementarity.

Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have gained traction for diverse natural language processing (NLP) applications. Their capacity to encode corpus-wide features within graph structures has made them particularly effective for tasks like document classification. However, a significant limitation of existing GNN models is their reliance on homogeneous graphs; representing text data typically necessitates multiple node types, resulting in a heterogeneous schema. To address this, we introduce a transductive hybrid framework that combines an unsupervised node representation learning model with a subsequent node classification or edge prediction model. This approach enables the processing of heterogeneous graphs to generate unified node embeddings, which are then applied to downstream tasks such as node classification or link prediction. Specifically, our model is designed to classify technical analysis reports in the stock market, marking the first known effort in this domain. Experimental results on a custom-built dataset validate the model's efficacy in both embedding extraction and performing these downstream tasks.

This paper investigates almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes within the polynomial ring $R = k[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ over a field $k$, where $I$ denotes a monomial ideal. Specifically, we characterize almost Cohen-Macaulay ideals of polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, and provide illustrative examples.

We examine positive solutions to semi-linear equations of the form $Lu = \varphi(\cdot, u)\mu$ defined on open sets $U$ within a space $X$. The operator $L$ can represent a second-order elliptic or parabolic operator (acting as the generator of a diffusion) or an integro-differential operator (generating a jump process). In this context, $\mu$ denotes a positive measure on $U$, and $\varphi$ is an arbitrary measurable real function on $U \times \mathbb{R}^+$ satisfying specific conditions: for each $x \in U$, the mapping $t \mapsto \varphi(x, t)$ must be continuous, increasing, and equal to zero at $t=0$.

Specifically, let $h$ be a non-negative measurable function on $X$ that is $L$-harmonic on $U$ (meaning $Lh=0$ on $U$ and $h$ is continuous on $U$). We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of positive solutions $u$ satisfying either: (Problem 1) $u=h$ on $X \setminus U$ while sharing the same boundary behavior as $h$ on $U$, or (Problem 2) $u \le h$ on $U$ with $u$ not identically zero on $U$. We demonstrate that these problems are equivalent to finding positive solutions to integral equations of the form $u + K\varphi(\cdot, u) = g$ on $U$, where $K$ serves as a potential kernel. These results are derived within the general framework of balayage spaces $(X, \mathcal{W})$, which, in probabilistic terms, corresponds to transient Hunt processes possessing a strong Feller resolvent.

This study examines the near-horizon geometry of the Kerr Vaidya metrics, the most basic axisymmetric space-time within their class. Derived from the Vaidya metric via a Newman-Janis complex coordinate transformation, these geometries exhibit an energy-momentum tensor classified as type 3 in the Segre-Hawking-Ellis scheme, yet with all Lorentz invariant eigenvalues equal to zero. We identify the apparent horizon location for quasi-stationary Kerr Vaidya black holes and demonstrate that these energy-momentum tensors violate the null energy condition. Furthermore, we show that for an infalling observer, the energy density, pressure, and flux diverge within the outgoing Kerr Vaidya metric. This divergence creates a firewall that results in the violation of a specific quantum energy inequality.

Standard domain adaptation techniques often fail when the disparity between source and target domains is substantial. To address this, gradual domain adaptation utilizes intermediate domains to progressively transition from the source to the target. Prior approaches relied on the assumption that numerous intermediate domains exist with minimal distance between adjacent ones, making self-training with unlabeled data feasible. However, in practical scenarios, gradual self-training often fails because intermediate domains are scarce and the gaps between them are significant. We propose employing normalizing flows to overcome this limitation within an unsupervised domain adaptation framework. By generating synthetic pseudo-intermediate domains through normalizing flows, we facilitate gradual domain adaptation. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method effectively resolves the identified issue and enhances classification accuracy.

This paper introduces a novel greedy algorithm for sparse approximation named SLS (Single L_1 Selection). The method employs a greedy forward strategy where each new component is chosen by solving a least-squares optimization problem penalized with the L_1 norm of the remaining variables, followed by selecting the component with the highest amplitude. Simulation results on challenging sparse deconvolution tasks using a highly correlated dictionary demonstrate the method's efficiency, showing that it surpasses popular greedy algorithms and Basis Pursuit Denoising when the solution is sparse.

**Motivation:** Peptides have garnered significant attention this century because of their exceptional therapeutic potential. While computational tools have been created to leverage existing data and present it simply for the general public, these systems often suffer from redundancy, lack clarity in data presentation, and sometimes fail to allow data downloads. To support drug design and other biotechnological endeavors, peptide information must be accessible in a straightforward format.

**Results:** We introduced Peptipedia, an intuitive database and web application designed for searching, characterizing, and analyzing peptide sequences. This tool consolidates data from thirty previously published databases, establishing it as the largest repository of peptides with documented activities to date. Additionally, we incorporated various services to enhance usability. These distinct features represent a major contribution to advancing biotechnological and bioengineering applications involving peptides.

**Availability:** Peptipedia is offered as open-access software for non-commercial use under the GNU General Public License (GPL 3.0). The web platform can be accessed at pesb2.cl/peptipedia, and both the source code and sample datasets are hosted on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/CristoferQ/PeptideDatabase.

**Contact:** david.medina@cebib.cl, ana.sanchez@ing.uchile.cl

Burgers' equation, a prominent model in applied mathematics linked to one-dimensional Navier-Stokes flows and traffic dynamics, is the focus of this study. Building on prior research, we investigate solutions within the complex plane, specifically examining the behavior of complex singularities and their impact on the real-line solution. Given an initial condition featuring simple poles in both the upper and lower half-planes, we employ formal asymptotics for small and large time scales to describe the singularities' evolution. The small-time analysis demonstrates that infinitely many singularities emerge at $t=0$, aligning increasingly near anti-Stokes lines in the far-field of the inner problem, while also determining whether the singularity nearest to the real axis migrates toward or away from it. For intermediate times, we utilize the exact solution combined with the method of steepest descents and AAA approximation to monitor the singularities, establishing a link between the trajectory of the closest singularity and the gradient steepness on the real line. Although Burgers' equation admits an exact solution, we intentionally combine various analytical techniques to create a methodology applicable to other nonlinear partial differential equations lacking such exact solutions.

This paper presents a contemporary formulation of classical concepts. It considers a Euclidean space $E$ of dimension $n$ and its associated vector space $V$, also of dimension $n$. A sliding vector is defined as a non-zero vector in $V$ constrained to move only along a specific line $L$ within $E$. The collection of such sliding vectors forms a set of dimension $2n-1$, which is naturally embedded in a vector space of dimension ${n+1 \choose 2}$. Elements of this higher-dimensional space are termed line bivectors, though they are also referred to as screws or wrenches in practical applications. The paper provides a clear description of line bivectors using Grassmann algebra within a projective framework and demonstrates that this abstract concept has a concrete realization via moment functions mapping $E$ to bivectors over $V$. While physics and engineering literature typically focus on the case where $n=3$, the findings presented here are applicable to this scenario and its most prevalent application: representing forces as vectors in $V$ and torques as bivectors over $V$. The work concludes by examining duality relationships, such as those between force and velocity, or torque and angular velocity.

We derive a general geometrical formulation of the supersymmetry conditions for D-branes within arbitrary type II supersymmetric backgrounds, alongside the corresponding BPS bounds. This comprehensive approach extends beyond static scenarios to include non-static configurations and D-branes with non-vanishing electric flux, thereby completing earlier partial findings. Specifically, our analysis elucidates how the concept of calibration can be generalized to accommodate the most extensive supersymmetric setups. As an initial demonstration of this methodology, we apply the procedure to fundamental strings.

Interactions between SARS-CoV-2 and human proteins drive information flow through biochemical pathways that contribute to the immunopathology of COVID-19. This study introduces a communication network model of the immune system designed to calculate the information transmitted by viral proteins, utilizing existing SARS-CoV-2 protein-protein interaction (PPI) data. The volume of transferred information is contingent upon the immune system's reference state—that is, its condition in the absence of SARS-CoV-2 PPIs—and serves to quantify the number of immune variables regulated by the virus. The information received by immune proteins from viral sources aids in pinpointing biological processes prone to dysregulation and estimating the duration of viral PPIs required for such dysregulation to manifest. Furthermore, calculating the reduction in information caused by viral PPIs when drugs are applied offers a direct metric for assessing therapeutic efficacy.

Nested named entity recognition (NER) has gained significant recent interest. While Fu et al. (2021) addressed nested NER by adapting a span-based constituency parser, treating nested entities as partially observed trees and utilizing the masked inside algorithm for partial marginalization, their approach fails to exploit entity heads, which are valuable for mention detection and typing. To overcome this limitation, our work employs more expressive lexicalized constituency trees, where constituents are annotated with headwords, to model nested entities. We utilize the Eisner-Satta algorithm for efficient inference and partial marginalization. Furthermore, we introduce three enhancements: a two-stage strategy, head regularization loss, and head-aware labeling loss, all aimed at improving performance. A comprehensive ablation study evaluates the contribution of each component. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on ACE2004, ACE2005, and NNE, competitive performance on GENIA, and maintains fast inference speeds.

We examine the competing entanglement dynamics within an open Ising-spin chain interacting with an external central ancilla qudit. Upon analyzing the real-time evolution following a quench from an initially unentangled spin-ancilla state, we observe that the ancilla's von Neumann entanglement entropy ($S_{vN;\mathcal{A}}$) mirrors the dynamical phase transition occurring in the spin system. In this composite setup, as the ancilla entanglement entropy increases, purely spin-spin entanglement metrics—including mutual information and quantum Fisher information (QFI)—decay. We introduce multipartite entanglement loss (MEL) as the discrepancy between collective magnetic fluctuations and QFI; this value vanishes in the limit of a pure spin chain. MEL effectively measures the ancilla's influence on the evolution of spin-spin entanglement. A key finding is that $MEL(t) \propto e^{S_{vN;\mathcal{A}}(t)}$. Our findings establish a platform for investigating entanglement dynamics in composite systems and indicate that MEL acts as a quantitative proxy for the information entropy shared between collective spins and the ancilla qudit. Furthermore, our work offers a novel framework linking physical spin fluctuations, QFI, and bipartite entanglement entropy across collective quantum systems.

We investigate the sensitivity of the Higgs boson ($h$) and top quark ($t$) coupling to new physics at high energy scales by analyzing the $pp\to t\bar{t}h$ process at the high-luminosity LHC. This approach probes the coupling across both time-like and space-like domains at high scales, offering complementarity to off-shell Higgs processes found in the time-like region. Using an effective field theory framework alongside a non-local Higgs-top form factor to parameterize beyond-Standard-Model effects, we focus on the boosted Higgs regime combined with jet substructure techniques. Our findings demonstrate that the current search can directly measure the Higgs-top coupling with high precision, thereby achieving strong sensitivity to the scale of new physics.

Enhancing model prediction accuracy and generating high-quality datasets relies heavily on feature engineering, yet this task demands substantial domain expertise and is often time-intensive. Consequently, automating this workflow has emerged as a significant focus for both research and industrial use. This paper introduces a new approach named Meta-learning and Causality Based Feature Engineering (MACFE), which integrates meta-learning, feature distribution encoding, and causality-driven feature selection. Within the MACFE framework, meta-learning identifies optimal transformations, while the search efficiency is boosted by pre-selecting original features based on their causal significance. Experimental results across popular classification datasets demonstrate that MACFE improves prediction performance for eight different classifiers, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods by an average of at least 6.54% and achieving a 2.71% gain over the best prior works.

Machine learning algorithms excel at detecting patterns across diverse datasets thanks to their adaptability. Nevertheless, expanding dataset size causes the computational time required for training and deploying these statistical models to increase rapidly. Quantum computing presents a novel approach that could address these computational challenges. In this study, we introduce a quantum version of K-means clustering, execute it on simulated superconducting qubits, and benchmark it against an existing quantum support vector machine. Our results show that the algorithm achieves accuracy comparable to classical K-means for both clustering and classification tasks. Furthermore, the method exhibits an asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$, where $N$ represents the number of data points, $K$ the number of clusters, and $P$ the data point dimension, delivering a substantial speedup over its classical counterpart.

Cosmic acceleration stands as one of the most profound cosmological findings of the past century. However, more precise data yields a more striking conclusion: recent analyses, particularly those involving Type Ia supernovae, suggest that time-varying dark energy provides a superior fit compared to a cosmological constant. Specifically, the equation of state parameter $w$ (the ratio of pressure to energy density) appears to cross the value of -1 at low redshifts. This crossing phenomenon poses a significant challenge to fundamental physics. This article reviews various approaches aimed at explaining this remarkable behavior. We first outline the key observational evidence supporting the crossing and then focus on theoretical advancements in dark energy models capable of realizing this -1 crossing. Three specific model categories are discussed: 1. two-field models (quintom-like), 2. interacting models (where dark energy couples with dark matter), and 3. models within modified gravity frameworks, with a focus on brane world scenarios.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has reported [1-3] the detection of multiple exotic cosmic ray-like events seemingly associated with thunderstorms. These occurrences are significantly larger in scale than standard cosmic ray events and exhibit distinct temporal characteristics. The underlying nature of this phenomenon remains an active area of research and debate due to the difficulty in explaining many of its unusual attributes. Notably, the occurrence rate of these exotic events is extremely low (fewer than two per year), which stands in stark contrast to the high frequency of conventional lightning strikes in the same region. We propose that these observations can be explained within the axion quark nugget (AQN) dark matter framework. This model suggests that AQNs could initiate a unique class of lightning strikes during thunderstorms by ionizing atmospheric molecules along their trajectory. Consequently, AQN-induced lightning flashes would display specific features absent in the far more common conventional flashes. We substantiate this proposal by showing that the observations [1-3], including event frequency and duration, are consistent with the AQN model. Additionally, we discuss potential connections between AUGER exotic events and bursts detected by the Telescope Array as well as terrestrial gamma-ray flashes. We outline several testable characteristics of AQN-induced events, such as specific radio pulses synchronized with these occurrences, for future experimental verification. Furthermore, we recommend employing distributed acoustic sensing instruments to detect the acoustic pulses that should be synchronized with the AUGER exotic events.

A trained Class T1 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) will be employed to assess its capacity to recognize motor imagery from pre-processed electroencephalography (EEG) data. Ideally, a correctly trained model should accurately classify and label these inputs. Subsequently, the model will be restored to test its ability to identify the same motor imagery class using significantly smaller datasets, thereby simulating conditions akin to live data.

This document was prepared by the HEP Software Foundation (HSF) Physics Event Generator Working Group (WG) to serve as input for the second phase of the LHCC review regarding High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) computing, scheduled for November 2021. It builds upon prior materials produced by the WG during the 2020 first phase of the LHCC review, most notably the WG paper addressing specific challenges in Monte Carlo event generator software for the HL-LHC. That earlier paper has since been updated and published, and is also being submitted as a core component of our contribution to the November 2021 review.

This study examines the radiation emitted by accelerating entangled two-level systems. By applying first-order perturbation theory, we calculate the transition rates for two entangled Unruh-DeWitt detectors rotating at an identical angular velocity while interacting with a massive scalar field. Our analysis covers decay mechanisms across various radii, angular velocities, and energy gaps. Furthermore, we explore the mean lifetime of these entangled states, as well as the phenomena of entanglement harvesting and its degradation.

This research examines the efficacy of Deep Learning (DL) in classifying planetary nebulae (PNe), specifically targeting their differentiation from other celestial objects and their morphological categorization. Employing a deep transfer learning strategy with three ImageNet pre-trained models, the study utilized data from the HASH DB and Pan-STARRS databases. Results indicate that the algorithms successfully distinguish genuine PNe from other object types without requiring parameter tuning, achieving a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.9. Among the tested models, DenseNet201 emerged as the most effective. Regarding morphological classification into Bipolar, Elliptical, and Round categories, the system correctly identified half of the objects, suggesting that further enhancement would benefit from additional data and training. The discussion outlines trade-offs and future directions, concluding that deep transfer learning is a viable method for classifying wide-field astronomical imagery.

While the principle of similarity, or homophily, frequently accounts for patterns in complex networks like transitivity and triangle density, numerous phenomena ranging from labor division to protein-protein interactions are actually driven by complementarity (differences and synergy). This study demonstrates that complementarity correlates with the prevalence of quadrangles (4-cycles) and dense bipartite-like subgraphs. We associate both principles with their specific motifs and introduce two families of coefficients: (1) structural similarity coefficients, which extend local clustering and closure measures to encompass the entire spectrum of similarity-driven structures; and (2) structural complementarity coefficients, defined similarly but centered on quadrangles rather than triangles. By analyzing various social and biological networks, we show that these coefficients effectively capture structural features tied to significant domain-specific phenomena. Our findings reveal that they can differentiate between distinct social relations and quantify the growing structural diversity of protein-protein interaction networks across the tree of life. We conclude that complementarity offers a superior explanation for certain relational types compared to homophily and holds promise for enhancing existing link prediction techniques. Additionally, we provide a Python package containing efficient algorithms for computing these proposed coefficients.

Traditionally, estimating the spectral density function $f(w)$ for $w \in [-\pi, \pi]$ has relied on kernel smoothing the periodogram and associated methods. This approach essentially performs local averaging, approximating $f(w)$ as a constant within a narrow window. While $f(w)$ is known to be uniformly continuous and periodic with a period of $2\pi$, this paper identifies that $w=0$ and $w=\pm \pi$ effectively function as boundary points in the context of kernel smoothing. It is established that local averaging can be suboptimal for kernel regression near or at such boundaries. Consequently, we propose using local polynomial regression—applied to either the periodogram or the log-periodogram—when $w$ is located at or near $0$ or $\pm \pi$. The scenario where $w=0$ holds particular significance because $f(0)$ represents the large-sample variance of the sample mean; therefore, accurately estimating $f(0)$ is essential for performing any inference regarding the mean.

This paper focuses on the asymptotic behavior of the finite differences of the logarithm of the overpartition function, specifically $(-1)^{r-1}\Delta^r \log \overline{p}(n)$. We achieve this by establishing the following inequality for $n \geq N(r)$:
$$\log \Bigl(1+\dfrac{C(r)}{n^{r-1/2}}-\dfrac{C_1(r)}{n^{r}}\Bigr)<(-1)^{r-1}\Delta^r \log \overline{p}(n) <\log \Bigl(1+\dfrac{C(r)}{n^{r-1/2}}\Bigr),$$
where $C(r)$, $C_1(r)$, and $N(r)$ are explicitly determined computable constants dependent on the positive integer $r$. This result provides a lower bound superior to $0$ for $(-1)^{r-1}\Delta^r \log \overline{p}(n)$, addressing a question raised by Wang, Xie, and Zhang. Consequently, we demonstrate that
$$\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}(-1)^{r-1}\Delta^r \log \overline{p}(n) =\dfrac{\pi}{2}\Bigl(\dfrac{1}{2}\Bigr)_{r-1}n^{\frac{1}{2}-r}.$$

Stripped envelope supernovae (SNe) frequently exhibit high-velocity material, identified by broad absorption lines in their spectra. This phenomenon occurs in SNe linked to both long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) and low-luminosity GRBs (llGRBs), as well as in those unrelated to GRBs. Recent hypotheses propose that this fast-moving material stems from a cocoon propelled by a relativistic jet; in LGRBs, the jet successfully penetrates the stellar envelope, whereas in llGRBs and non-GRB SNe, the jet is choked. This study employs numerical simulations to investigate the velocity distribution of outflows driven by choked jets and how they vary with jet and progenitor characteristics. The results indicate that whenever a jet is choked without being trapped too deeply within the star, the resulting outflow maintains a roughly constant energy per logarithmic scale of proper velocity across a broad velocity range. This characteristic depends primarily on the cocoon's volume at breakout and represents a universal trait of jet-driven outflows, distinguishing them from those in spherically symmetric explosions or cases where jets are choked very deeply. Consequently, we conclude that moderately choked jets offer a natural explanation for the high-velocity material observed in the early spectra of stripped envelope SNe not associated with LGRBs, and that analyzing this material could uncover details about the otherwise obscured jets.

Recent advancements in implicit neural representations, notably NeRF, demonstrate the ability to store high-fidelity scene and lighting data efficiently within compact networks. Nevertheless, the high computational burden of evaluating these networks repeatedly along view rays—often demanding dozens of petaFLOPS—hinders their application in real-time rendering. This work aims to bridge that gap, making compact neural representations viable for real-time synthetic content in domains like gaming and virtual reality. We demonstrate that image quality can be maintained even when the number of samples per ray is drastically reduced, provided samples are strategically positioned near scene surfaces. To achieve this, we introduce a depth oracle network that predicts optimal ray sampling locations with just a single network evaluation. Our findings indicate that classifying logarithmically discretized and spherically warped depth values is crucial for accurately encoding surface locations rather than estimating depth directly. These innovations culminate in DONeRF, a compact dual-network architecture comprising a depth oracle for initial sampling and a locally sampled shading network for ray accumulation. When conditioned on ground truth depth, DONeRF achieves up to a 48-fold reduction in inference costs compared to standard NeRF. Unlike concurrent raymarching acceleration techniques, DONeRF requires no extra memory for explicit caching or acceleration structures, enabling interactive rendering at 20 frames per second on a single GPU.

We share the methodology for migrating machine learning models to the TensorFlow framework at scale within a large online advertising environment. This presentation outlines the primary challenges encountered and details our successful strategies for overcoming them, specifically focusing on deploying models in TensorFlow and achieving low-latency inference through diverse optimization methods.

The Poincaré-Hopf Theorem acts as a conservation law for real-analytic vector fields that are tangential to closed surfaces, such as spheres or tori. Furthermore, the theorem applies to real-analytic vector fields on surfaces with smooth boundaries, provided the field points in the outward normal direction along those boundaries. This paper extends the Poincaré-Hopf Theorem to cover real-analytic vector fields that are tangential to surfaces with piecewise smooth boundaries, where the vector field is not necessarily parallel to the outward normal of the boundary.

The geometric trinity of gravity provides a framework where gravity can be described through three analogous methods: curvature, torsion, and nonmetricity. Consequently, general relativity can be represented in three dynamically equivalent forms, potentially illuminating distinct properties of these decompositions, including their Hamiltonian structures, numerical efficiency, and the classification of gravitational degrees of freedom. This study employs a $3+1$ decomposition of both the teleparallel and symmetric teleparallel equivalents of general relativity, both of which are dynamically equivalent to the curvature-based formulation. By separating the spacetime metric and associated tetrad into spatial and temporal components and deriving Gauss-like equations, a general foundation for various gravity formulations is established. Building on these findings, general evolution equations for the $3$-tetrad and $3$-metric are derived.
