Ultimately, by selecting specific connections, this approach recovers the metric $3+1$ formulation of general relativity, along with the tetrad $3+1$ formulation for the teleparallel equivalent and the metric $3+1$ formulation for the symmetric teleparallel equivalent. Fundamentally, this methodology is capable of identifying common features across different general relativity formulations and highlighting unique characteristics that may emerge in their extensions or alternatives.

Although the recently introduced pitch-controllable text-to-speech (TTS) system, FastPitch, is conditioned on pitch contours, its synthesized speech quality deteriorates significantly when pitch values diverge substantially from the average, thereby limiting its pitch control capabilities. To overcome this limitation, we introduce two algorithms designed to enhance FastPitch's robustness. First, we present a new timbre-preserving pitch-shifting algorithm for natural pitch augmentation; this approach ensures that pitch-shifted audio sounds more natural by maintaining the speaker's original vocal timbre. Second, we propose a training algorithm that leverages pitch-augmented datasets featuring varying pitch ranges for identical sentences to define FastPitch. Experimental findings confirm that these proposed algorithms effectively improve the pitch controllability of FastPitch.

We examine $k$ ($\ge 2$) independent populations, denoted $\Pi_1, \ldots, \Pi_k$, where each $\Pi_i$ adheres to an exponential distribution characterized by a hazard rate ${\sigma_i}$ for $i = 1,\ldots,k$. A random sample of size $n$, consisting of observations $Y_{i1},\ldots, Y_{in}$, is drawn from the $i$th population. For each population $i$, the sum $Y_i=\sum_{j=1}^nY_{ij}$ is calculated. The selection criterion involves choosing the population corresponding to the maximum sample sum; specifically, $\Pi_i$ is selected if $Y_i=\max(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)$. Following this selection, the hazard rate of the chosen population is estimated using the entropy loss function. Several natural estimators are introduced, and it is demonstrated that one possesses minimaxity. Furthermore, improved estimators that outperform the natural ones are derived. A numerical analysis is subsequently conducted to compare the proposed estimators based on their risk values.

The longitudinal collective modes of a bunched beam subject to repulsive inductive impedance (arising from space charge below transition or chamber inductance above it) are analytically characterized by reducing the linearized Vlasov equation to a parameter-free integral equation. For every multipolarity, the discrete spectrum comprises an infinite series of modes with real tunes, converging toward the incoherent zero-amplitude frequency. Consequently, despite RF bucket nonlinearity and potential well distortion, Landau damping is absent. This implies that even minimal coupled-bunch interaction induces beam instability, with analytically derived growth rates for all modes across arbitrary multipolarities. Practically, however, the finite threshold for this damping loss is determined by either high-frequency impedance roll-off or intrabeam scattering. Once this threshold is exceeded, the growth of the dominant collective mode leads to sustained nonlinear oscillations.

This study addresses noisy matrix completion, which involves reconstructing a low-rank matrix from incomplete and noisy data. Under assumptions of uniform sampling and incoherence, we demonstrate that a tuning-free square-root matrix completion estimator (square-root MC) attains optimal statistical performance for this task. Mirroring the square-root Lasso in high-dimensional linear regression, square-root MC operates without requiring prior knowledge of the noise magnitude. Although solving square-root MC involves a convex optimization program, our statistical analysis relies heavily on its close relationship to a nonconvex rank-constrained estimator.

This paper examines the validity of Farkas' lemma and associated propositions—including the Fredholm alternative for solving linear systems, linear programming optimality conditions, Stiemke's lemma, the Superhedging Duality in mathematical finance, and von Neumann's minimax theorem applied to constructive game theory—within the context of constructive mathematics (BISH).

Current debates in online platform research primarily focus on the degree to which these platforms can successfully intervene to mitigate societal harms occurring within their ecosystems. A central question remains whether platforms can implement effective, enduring solutions to issues like cyberbullying, or if more profound systemic changes are required. While empirical research is essential for answering these questions, it is often hindered by high costs, time constraints, and the limitations of company-defined inquiry scopes. To guide this empirical investigation, we propose an agent-based modeling (ABM) methodology. Specifically, we simulate an online dating environment to evaluate how various interventions influence the scarcity of long-term interracial relationships within an artificial society, noting that such relationship gaps often perpetuate real-world inequality. Our findings indicate that many hypothesized interventions have minimal impact and that their efficacy depends heavily on underlying sociocultural assumptions. Furthermore, strategies that successfully promote diversity in long-term relationships frequently conflict with platforms' profit-driven objectives. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the utility of ABM in elucidating both the potential benefits and unintended consequences of different platform interventions.

Deep learning frequently utilizes embeddings to encode categorical items like words, apps, and movies. An embedding layer assigns a distinct vector to each entity, resulting in memory usage that scales directly with the entity count. In recommendation systems, where a single category may encompass hundreds of thousands of items, embedding layers can consume gigabytes of memory, making deployment in resource-limited settings challenging. This paper introduces a novel method to shrink embedding tables while ensuring every entity retains a unique representation. Instead of storing a complete embedding table, the approach generates each entity's embedding dynamically using two distinct tables: the first uses hashing to map multiple entities to shared embeddings, while the second holds a trainable weight for each entity to differentiate those that share the same hash. Because these tables are trained together, the model learns unique embeddings per entity, preserving discriminative power comparable to uncompressed models. We refer to this technique as MEmCom (Multi-Embedding Compression). Evaluated against state-of-the-art compression methods across classification and ranking tasks, MEmCom demonstrated superior performance on four major recommender system datasets. It achieved compression ratios of 16x, 4x, 12x, and 40x with only a 4% relative drop in nDCG, whereas competing techniques suffered relative losses of 16%, 6%, 10%, and 8% at the same ratios. Furthermore, MEmCom successfully compressed a RankNet ranking model by 32x on a dataset involving millions of user game interactions, incurring merely a 1% relative loss in nDCG.

This work investigates the control of a free surface via fluid jets applied at the boundary of a two-dimensional solid domain, specifically within the framework of gravity waves and sloshing dynamics. Leveraging conformal mappings and the Dirichlet–Neumann operator, the system is recast as a second-order evolutionary equation defined on the free surface, which incorporates a self-adjoint operator. Furthermore, we identify the requisite Sobolev spaces that admit solutions for this system and establish exact controllability by deriving an observability inequality for the associated adjoint problem.

Label scarcity poses a significant challenge in various music information retrieval tasks, particularly melody extraction, where acquiring labeled data is often prohibitively expensive or time-consuming. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) offers a remedy by capitalizing on abundant unlabeled datasets. This study introduces an SSL approach employing teacher-student architectures for vocal melody extraction. In this self-training framework, a teacher model pre-trained on labeled data instructs a student model to produce consistent predictions on unlabeled inputs. We evaluate three distinct teacher-student configurations utilizing varied data augmentation techniques and loss functions. Addressing the limited availability of labeled data during testing, we synthetically generate extensive test sets with pitch annotations from unlabeled audio using an analysis-synthesis technique. Our findings indicate that the proposed SSL method substantially outperforms purely supervised learning, with gains contingent upon the specific teacher-student architecture, the volume of unlabeled data, the number of self-training iterations, and other hyperparameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ensuring the presence of vocal segments within the unlabeled audio is critical for success. Ultimately, we show that this SSL strategy allows a baseline convolutional recurrent neural network to reach performance levels comparable to state-of-the-art models.

Superoscillations represent a unique class of band-limited functions capable of oscillating at frequencies far exceeding those of their highest-frequency Fourier components. Initially observed in fields like optics and radar physics, these phenomena have recently attracted significant attention following their connection to a modern quantum measurement approach known as the weak value scheme. Within this theoretical framework, superoscillations have become a vibrant area of mathematical inquiry, with applications transitioning from abstract theory to practical implementation. Although our understanding remains incomplete, current analysis indicates that such extreme oscillations occur only where the function's amplitude is negligible, imposing a fundamental constraint on their utility. This paper offers a comprehensive review of both the theoretical and practical advancements in superoscillation research and introduces the two-state vector formalism, which provides the basis for realizing the weak value scheme.

This work examines the characteristics of mean-type mappings ${\bf M}\colon I^p \to I^p$ defined by ${\bf M}(x_1,\dots,x_p):=\big(M_1(x_{\alpha_{1,1}},\dots,x_{\alpha_{1,d_1}}),\dots,M_p(x_{\alpha_{p,1}},\dots,x_{\alpha_{p,d_p}})\big)$, where $p$ and $d_i$ are positive integers, each $M_i$ represents a $d_i$-variable mean on an interval $I \subset \mathbb{R}$, and $\alpha_{i,j}$ denotes an index from $\{1,\dots,p\}$. We demonstrate that, given certain natural conditions on the $M_i$ functions, the question of whether a unique $\bf M$-invariant mean exists can be simplified to determining the ergodicity of a directed graph with vertices $\{1,\dots,p\}$ and edges $\{(\alpha_{i,j},i) \colon i,j \text{ admissible}\}$.

This study examines Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequalities defined on the sphere, which serve as interpolations between the Poincaré and Sobolev inequalities, with the logarithmic Sobolev inequality appearing as a specific instance. By employing spectral decomposition methods and applying entropy and carré du champ techniques to nonlinear diffusion flows, we derive explicit stability results within the subcritical regime.

The efficiency of Markov chain Monte Carlo computations depends on two factors: the ensemble variance of the Monte Carlo estimator and the autocorrelation inherent in the Markov process. To investigate autocorrelation, binning analysis is frequently employed, estimating values from data grouped into bins of logarithmically expanding sizes. This paper demonstrates that binning analysis introduces a bias that can be removed by combining bin sizes. Furthermore, we show that this analysis can be executed in real-time with linear time overhead and logarithmic memory overhead relative to the sample size. We also establish that binning analysis reveals not only the cumulative impact of autocorrelation but also allows for the estimation of the autocorrelation length spectrum, thereby determining the height of phase space barriers. Finally, we revisit the Ising model to apply the proposed methodology and recover its autocorrelation spectra.

Based on semiclassical equations governing the phase space densities of Zeeman ground-state sublevels, we derive an exact series expansion for the average velocity of cold atoms in dissipative optical lattices under probe driving. This expansion utilizes the amplitudes of excited atomic density waves to pinpoint the specific current contributions from propagating atomic waves for a given driving condition and to establish the general threshold for transitioning into a regime of infinite density.

**Context:** While aligned dust grains are frequently used to determine magnetic field orientations, the precise physical mechanisms responsible for large-scale coherent grain alignment remain poorly understood.

**Aims:** This study investigates the effects of gas-dust drift on mechanical alignment of dust (MAD) and its influence on dust polarization.

**Methods:** We analyze fractal dust aggregates to statistically determine the average alignment behavior of various grain ensembles. Monte Carlo (MC) simulations are employed to calculate spin-up efficiencies for individual aggregates. These efficiencies are examined to identify stable alignment states along the drift direction and magnetic field lines, followed by the calculation of net dust polarization for each ensemble.

**Results:** Mechanical spin-up within the Cold Neutral Medium (CNM) is sufficient to achieve stable grain alignment, which is likely parallel to the drift direction. Roundish grains require supersonic drift for alignment, whereas rod-like grains can align under subsonic conditions. We predict a polarization efficiency near unity for MAD; however, supersonic drift may cause rapid rotation leading to grain disruption and a significant drop in polarization. In the presence of a magnetic field, the drift required for alignment is approximately ten times higher than in pure MAD scenarios. Under these conditions, polarization efficiency ranges from 0.8 to 0.9, suggesting that drift can provide the necessary conditions to probe magnetic fields. Conversely, alignment is inefficient when drift and magnetic field lines are perpendicular.

**Conclusions:** We conclude that MAD must be considered as an alternative driving mechanism, particularly where the standard Radiative Alignment Torque (RAT) theory fails to explain the full range of observed dust polarization.

This research examines the stability of Betti numbers for ideals within a local ring under minor perturbations. Specifically, for any natural number $p$ and an ideal $I$ in a Noetherian local ring $(R,\mathfrak m)$, we establish that there exists an integer $N>0$ such that any ideal $J$ satisfying $I\equiv J\bmod \mathfrak m^N$ and sharing the same Hilbert function as $I$ will possess identical Betti numbers $\beta_i^R(R/I)$ and $\beta_i^R(R/J)$ for all $0\le i\le p$. Additionally, we identify various scenarios where the condition $I \equiv J \bmod \mathfrak m^N$ alone necessitates that $J$ shares the same Hilbert function as $I$, and consequently, the same Betti numbers.

We have constructed a model to describe the Pc states detected by LHCb in $\Lambda_b^- \to J/\psi p K^-$ decays. By utilizing fewer parameters than competing approaches, our model achieves excellent fits to the $J/\psi$-$p$ invariant mass spectrum, successfully accounting for both the major peaks and broader structures across the entire mass range. A key distinction of our approach is that while $P_c(4312)$, $P_c(4380)$, and $P_c(4440)$ are identified as resonances with $\Sigma_c^*-D^*$ constituents, the $P_c(4457)$ state exhibits a different nature; it can be interpreted as either a $\Sigma_c^*-D^*$ threshold cusp, a $\Lambda_c(2595)$-$D$ enhancement arising from a triangle singularity, or a $\Lambda_c(2595)$-$D$ resonance. We suggest specific experimental measurements capable of distinguishing between these scenarios. Unlike other models, our production mechanism adheres to isospin symmetry and the empirical dominance of color-enhanced processes in weak decays, while also providing a natural explanation for the overall data shape. Furthermore, our model remains consistent with experimental constraints from photoproduction and $\Lambda_b^- \to \Lambda_c^- D^*{}^0 K^-$ decays, and it avoids predicting partner states whose non-observation remains unexplained in alternative frameworks.

Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data, promising significant advancements for cloud privacy, though its widespread use is currently hindered by substantial computational and memory demands. TFHE is a leading Torus-based FHE scheme that depends heavily on bootstrapping, a noise-removal process required after every encrypted operation. We introduce FPT, a Fixed-Point FPGA accelerator designed specifically for TFHE bootstrapping. As the first hardware accelerator to leverage inherent noise in FHE calculations, FPT replaces standard floating-point arithmetic with approximate fixed-point methods. Through a detailed analysis of noise propagation during bootstrapping FFT operations, FPT utilizes noise-trimmed fixed-point representations that reduce data size by up to 50% compared to previous floating-point or integer FFT implementations.

FPT's microarchitecture functions as a streaming processor modeled after traditional streaming DSPs, featuring cascaded high-throughput computational stages, simplified control logic, and streamlined routing. This streaming design achieves 100% utilization of arithmetic units and minimizes the need for bootstrapping key caches, delivering a compute-bound throughput of 1 bootstrapping operation per 35 microseconds. This performance stands in sharp contrast to classical CPU-based FHE acceleration, which is typically limited by memory and bandwidth constraints. Fully implemented and tested as an FPGA kernel on an Alveo U280 datacenter accelerator card, FPT delivers bootstrapping throughput nearly three orders of magnitude greater than existing CPU implementations and 2.5 times higher than recent ASIC emulation results.

Using the Green Bank Telescope, we report the accidental detection of widespread, faint, and exceptionally broad ($\Delta V_{LSR} \sim 150$ km/s) ground-state thermal OH emission at 1667 and 1665 MHz in the outer Galaxy's second quadrant ($R_{gal}$ > 8 kpc). Since its initial discovery in 2015, we have documented five years of rigorous experimental, observational, and data quality validations. The emission's longitude-velocity profile clearly indicates large-scale Galactic structure. Furthermore, the OH radial velocity distribution exhibits a smooth pattern morphologically consistent with HI in the outer Galaxy, revealing that molecular gas extends far more broadly in this region than previously thought. These findings suggest the presence of a previously undetected, thick ($-200 < z < 200$ pc) disk of diffuse ($n_{H_{2}} \sim 5 \times 10^{-3}$ cm$^{-3}$) molecular gas in the Outer Galaxy, which had escaped detection in all-sky CO surveys.

py-irt is a Python library designed for fitting Bayesian Item Response Theory (IRT) models. It estimates latent traits for both subjects and items, making it suitable for various IRT tasks and ideal-point models. Built on the Pyro and PyTorch frameworks, py-irt utilizes GPU-accelerated training to handle large datasets efficiently. The code, documentation, and examples are available at https://github.com/nd-ball/py-irt, and the library can be installed directly from the GitHub repository or via the Python Package Index (PyPI).

This study introduces recurrence relations for QCD dipole densities, enabling their determination from solutions to the BFKL equation. By solving these relations within the diffusion approximation for the BFKL kernel, we derive the summation of large Pomeron loops. This summation yields a scattering amplitude that diminishes at high rapidity values ($Y$).

The spatially varying tetragonality within martensite grains of a high-carbon steel (1.2 mass percent C) was characterized using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) achieving a spatial resolution of approximately 100 nm. In contrast to spatially integrating X-ray diffraction, which provided an average c/a ratio of 1.05, the EBSD technique conducted in a scanning electron microscope revealed local fluctuations in the lattice parameter ratio ranging from 1.02 to 1.07. This variation in local tetragonality was validated through two distinct EBSD data analysis methods relying on the fitting of simulated patterns to experimental data. The resulting tetragonality maps indicate a complex interplay between carbon concentration and local lattice distortions during the formation of martensitic structures.

We demonstrate a variable substitution that preserves the Mahler measure of a polynomial. This approach enables the creation of complex polynomials with specified Mahler measures, thereby resolving certain conjectured numerical formulas proposed by Boyd and Brunault.

Quantum tunneling is a core quantum mechanical phenomenon underlying numerous physical processes, where controlling it could significantly influence these processes and their associated technologies. We demonstrate that the probability of a particle tunneling through a potential barrier can be boosted to nearly one via quantum Zeno dynamics, achieved by frequently monitoring the particle's momentum direction. Initially, we modeled momentum direction measurements as selective von Neumann projections, followed by an analysis of nonselective, direction-sensitive interactions between the particle and probe particles. Our findings indicate that nonselective measurements are more effective than selective ones in enhancing the tunneling probability.

Question answering (QA) systems designed for extensive document collections usually rely on sequential pipelines that (i) retrieve potentially relevant documents, (ii) re-rank them, (iii) rank paragraphs or snippets from the top documents, and (iv) extract exact answer spans from the highest-ranked snippets. Although these pipelines are conceptually straightforward, errors tend to propagate from one stage to the next without allowing subsequent components to correct prior mistakes. We introduce an architecture for jointly ranking documents and snippets—covering the middle two stages—which is grounded in the premise that relevant documents contain high-quality snippets and vice versa. This framework is versatile and compatible with any neural text relevance ranker. We evaluate two primary instantiations of this architecture: one based on POSIT-DRMM (PDRMM) and another utilizing a BERT-based ranker. Experiments on biomedical data from BIOASQ demonstrate that our joint models significantly surpass traditional pipelines in snippet retrieval, which is the primary objective for QA, while requiring fewer trainable parameters and maintaining competitiveness in document retrieval. Moreover, our joint PDRMM-based model rivals BERT-based models despite employing orders of magnitude fewer parameters. These findings are further validated by human evaluations on two BIOASQ test sets. To verify our results on a different dataset, we adapted the Natural Questions dataset for use in both document and snippet retrieval tasks. On this modified dataset, our joint PDRMM-based model again outperforms the corresponding pipeline in snippet retrieval, although it trails the pipeline in document retrieval. We have made our code and the adapted Natural Questions dataset publicly accessible.

The Auger Engineering Radio Array (AERA) experiment has deployed FPGA/NIOS FIR filters utilizing linear prediction (LP) to mitigate radio frequency interference (RFI) at multiple radio stations. These stations detect coherent radio emissions from extensive air showers generated by ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, providing detailed insights into the electromagnetic development of such showers. This radio data complements information from Auger surface detectors, which primarily measure particle content at the ground level. The observed radio signals result from coherent emissions driven by geomagnetic and charge-excess mechanisms within the 10–100 MHz band. However, this spectrum is heavily polluted by narrow-band RFI and other anthropogenic distortions. Consequently, an FIR filter integrated into the FPGA logic of the front-end electronics significantly enhances the signal-to-noise ratio.

This paper reports initial findings on the efficiency of an adaptive LP FIR filter installed at a real AERA station in the Pampas, comparing its performance against the currently employed IIR notch filter with fixed coefficients. Laboratory testing verified the filter's stability; using constant LP coefficients maintains suppression efficiency for hours, equivalent to over $\bf 10^{12}$ clock cycles. Furthermore, various configurations of the LP FIR filter were evaluated under real-world conditions, differing in filter length and coefficient widths (dictated by fixed-point FPGA representations). The objective was to minimize power consumption for the radio station while ensuring adequate accuracy for noise reduction.

Recently, simultaneous translation has gained significant traction due to its utility in applications like live event subtitling and real-time video call interpretation. Certain systems permit partial translation editing, necessitating re-translation capabilities. Existing methods rely on autoregressive sequence generation models (ReTA), which produce target tokens sequentially. This sequential approach in ReTA models creates an expanding latency gap between incoming source input and the corresponding output as the source lengthens. Furthermore, the extensive number of inference operations required makes these models unsuitable for resource-constrained devices. To address these issues, this study introduces FReTNA, a faster re-translation system utilizing a non-autoregressive sequence generation model. Evaluations across multiple translation tasks demonstrate that FReTNA reduces inference time by several orders of magnitude while maintaining a BLEU score competitive with both ReTA and streaming (Wait-k) models. Specifically, FReTNA cuts average computation time by a factor of 20 compared to ReTA, accepting only a minor reduction in translation quality. Additionally, it surpasses the Wait-k model in both efficiency, achieving 1.5 times faster computation, and overall translation quality.

Physical networks, including biological neural networks, can acquire desired functions without a central processor by utilizing local learning rules across space and time to operate in a fully distributed manner. Techniques such as equilibrium propagation, directed aging, and coupled learning similarly leverage these local rules to enable learning in physical systems like electrical, flow, and mechanical networks. However, unlike some natural neural networks, these approaches have historically been confined to the quasistatic limit, where learning occurs on time scales significantly slower than the system's physical relaxation. This quasistatic constraint decelerates learning, thereby hindering their application as machine learning algorithms and potentially limiting the range of physical networks suitable as learning platforms. In this work, we investigate coupled learning within an electrical resistor network, demonstrating its implementation both computationally and experimentally at speeds ranging from slow to well beyond the quasistatic limit. Our findings reveal that learning accelerates without significant alterations in behavior or error levels up to a critical threshold defined by the ratio of the learning rate to the physical relaxation rate. Beyond this threshold, while the error displays oscillatory dynamics, the networks continue to learn effectively.

Human assessments are traditionally viewed as the benchmark for natural language generation; however, as model fluency advances, we must question the efficacy of evaluators in detecting and rating machine-generated content. This study investigates the capacity of non-experts to differentiate between human-written and machine-generated text (specifically from GPT2 and GPT3) across three genres: stories, news articles, and recipes. Results indicate that without prior training, evaluators performed at random chance when distinguishing GPT3 output from human writing. We tested three methods for rapidly training evaluators to improve detection (detailed instructions, annotated examples, and paired examples), observing accuracy gains up to 55%; yet, no significant improvement was achieved consistently across the three domains. Due to inconsistent performance across genres and the often contradictory rationales provided by evaluators, we re-examine the utility of untrained human judgment in NLG evaluation and offer recommendations for researchers aiming to enhance assessments of text produced by state-of-the-art models.

Long-term Optical Character Recognition (OCR) services strive to deliver high-quality results affordably. Given the intricate nature of user-submitted data, continuous model enhancement is critical. Providers incentivize users by rewarding contributions that challenge the OCR system, factoring in data complexity, legibility, and budget constraints. While previous OCR research typically trained models on standard datasets without addressing end-user needs, this study proposes a strategy for iteratively upgrading a Handwritten Hindi OCR model three times using data from 15 users. A fixed budget of four users is allocated per iteration. In the first round, the model trains directly on data from the initial four users. In subsequent rounds, the remaining users each contribute a page, from which service providers select the four highest-performing users based on their ability to generate human-readable predictions. These selected users then contribute an additional 23 pages to further refine the model. The model is enhanced using Curriculum Learning (CL) on current iteration data and compared against subsets from prior iterations. The final upgraded model is evaluated on a held-out set comprising one page from each of the 23 users. This work offers insights into the impacts of Curriculum Learning, user selection mechanisms, and data from unseen writing styles, providing a framework for long-term OCR services in crowd-sourcing environments for both providers and users.

This paper introduces a novel method for designing processor accelerators, proposing a new computing model alongside a specialized accelerator featuring a dynamic, end-user programmable architecture. In this model, a newly introduced supervisor layer manages core operations, enabling them to outsource portions of their tasks to neighboring cores based on parallelization data provided by the compiler and guided by the supervisor. These architectural and operational modifications offer significant advantages: they drastically boost computing throughput, improve efficiency in terms of performance per logic gate, reduce non-payload activity associated with operating system services, enhance real-time behavior, and simplify the integration of accelerators with processors. The discussion here focuses solely on specific architectural and operational details, with further descriptions available elsewhere.

Rhombohedrally stacked MoS2 demonstrates spontaneous polarization even at the bilayer limit and maintains a robust depolarization field when encapsulated by graphene. This field induces a spontaneous photovoltaic effect, eliminating the need for p-n junctions. Our study reveals that devices utilizing just two atomic layers of MoS2 achieve an external quantum efficiency of 10% at low temperatures and exhibit a picosecond-scale photocurrent response, corresponding to an intrinsic bandwidth of approximately 100 GHz. To achieve these insights, we employed a non-degenerate pump-probe photocurrent spectroscopy technique to separate thermal and charge-transfer processes, successfully uncovering the multi-component dynamics of the photocurrent. The rapid component reaches the theoretical limit of charge-transfer velocity at the graphene-MoS2 interface. These findings, highlighting both remarkable efficiency and ultrafast photoresponse in graphene-3R-MoS2 heterostructures, underscore the potential of ferroelectric van der Waals materials for next-generation high-performance optoelectronics.

This essay explores the opportunities and hurdles involved in searching for physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) at the FCC-ee, with a focus on rare decays of heavy-flavoured particles and long-lived particles. Within the Standard Model, specific suppression mechanisms render certain processes infrequent, thereby creating rare decay signatures. These decays are compelling because BSM physics may not be subject to the same constraints, allowing new phenomena to emerge naturally. This interest is further bolstered by recent measurements of $b$-flavoured rare decays that deviate from Standard Model expectations. We will demonstrate how the FCC-ee project is uniquely positioned to tackle these scientific inquiries and will examine the detector design challenges required to meet them. Additionally, we discuss processes yielding new particles with extended lifetimes, which travel significant distances within detectors before decaying. Models featuring long-lived particles offer solutions to unresolved Standard Model issues, such as the origin of dark matter and neutrino masses, while serving as a valuable complement to conventional searches. These particles often exhibit distinctive signatures, including displaced tracks and vertices, disappearing tracks, or anomalously charged jets. Consequently, they typically face minimal background interference, though they necessitate specialized reconstruction algorithms and triggers.

This study examines the one-photon process for $e^+e^-$ pair creation during collisions between nonrelativistic nuclei. We calculate the contribution of virtual photon electric quadrupole radiation to the cross section and thoroughly analyze the impact of finite nuclear size. Our results are compared against those from electric dipole radiation of virtual photons and the two-photon pair production mechanism. We demonstrate that electric quadrupole radiation dominates the cross section across a broad range of relative velocities. Additionally, we investigate the cross section for $e^+e^-$ pair production accompanied by the capture of an electron by one of the nuclei.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) is a well-researched task that involves determining if one text entails another, meaning its full meaning can be deduced from the source. While current datasets and models typically define entailment at the sentence or paragraph level, even simple sentences often comprise multiple distinct units of meaning known as propositions. Since these propositions can hold different truth values within a specific premise context, we argue that it is necessary to evaluate the entailment relationship of each proposition individually. To address this, we introduce PropSegmEnt, a dataset containing over 35,000 expert-annotated propositions. This corpus is designed for two primary tasks: (1) segmenting sentences into their constituent propositions, and (2) classifying the entailment relationship of each proposition relative to a different but topically aligned document, such as one describing the same event or entity. We establish robust baselines for both segmentation and entailment tasks. Furthermore, case studies on detecting summary hallucinations and document-level NLI demonstrate that our framework offers a valuable approach for understanding and explaining the compositionality of NLI labels.

This research investigates the gravitational collapse of a spherically symmetric, anisotropic relativistic star within the framework of Einstein's theory of gravity, utilizing a recently developed stellar model [{\it Astrophys. Space Sci.} {\bf361} 99 (2016)]. The analysis examines the final state of continuous collapse for massive stars under regular initial conditions, specifically focusing on black hole formation. To model the evolution of an anisotropic star during collapse, the dissipation process is assumed to manifest as a radial heat flux. The interior spacetime is defined by a static metric matched at the boundary to the Vaidya metric, which represents the exterior radiating region. The initial static configuration is based on the relativistic solution provided by Paul and Deb [{\it Astrophys. Space Sci.} {\bf354} 421 (2014)]. The study evaluates how anisotropy influences the dynamical gravitational collapse of massive stars. Furthermore, the relativistic causal heat transport equation, known as the Maxwell-Cattaneo equation, is employed to demonstrate the relationship between anisotropy and the temperature profile of the collapsing system.

This study examines the elementary reaction ${e}^{+}{e}^{-} \rightarrow{\mu}^{+}{\mu}^{-}$, occurring at leading order through electron-positron interaction with an intense circularly polarized laser wave. Utilizing the scattering matrix approach, we analytically derived the expression for the laser-assisted differential cross section. Our analysis explores the impact of the number and energy of exchanged photons on muon pair production during electron-positron annihilation across various center-of-mass energies, specifically encompassing the $Z$-boson peak. Consequently, we investigated a broad spectrum of high-energy center-of-mass values pertinent to future $e^{+}e^{-}$ colliders to evaluate cross section behavior. Our findings indicate that, for a fixed number of exchanged photons, as well as specific laser field strength and frequency, a circularly polarized laser field reduces the total cross section by several orders of magnitude.

Although reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant promise for advanced autonomous driving, existing RL approaches struggle with low data efficiency and training oscillations when dealing with high-dimensional tasks. To address these challenges, this paper introduces Learn to Drive with Virtual Memory (LVM). LVM addresses the issue by compressing high-dimensional inputs into compact latent states and training a latent dynamic model to encapsulate the agent's experiences. This model generates various imagined latent trajectories, which serve as a virtual memory. By propagating gradients through the learned latent model using these imagined trajectories, the policy achieves high data efficiency. Additionally, a double-critic architecture is implemented to minimize oscillations during training. The efficacy of LVM is validated through an image-based autonomous driving benchmark, where it surpasses current methods in data efficiency, learning stability, and control performance.

Simulating sediment transport remains a difficult yet critical task for understanding particulate geophysical flows. This study investigates sediment transport within the collisional regime, specifically targeting continuum models for granular flows. To achieve this, a hybrid frictional-collisional framework is created, merging a Coulomb model with kinetic theory for granular gases. This methodology relies on benchmarking against coupled fluid-discrete simulations, which standard kinetic theory models cannot accurately replicate. To refine the continuum model, the fluctuating energy balance derived from discrete simulations is calculated and rigorously compared with kinetic theory closure laws. The analysis reveals that inter-particle friction influences the radial distribution function and heightens energy dissipation, consistent with existing literature. Additionally, the presence of saltating particles—whose motion eludes kinetic theory—causes deviations from viscosity and diffusivity laws in the dilute regions of the granular flow. Furthermore, the quadratic nature of drag force is demonstrated to amplify granular fluctuating energy dissipation. Guided by these findings, adjustments to the kinetic theory closure laws are suggested. The resulting modified model accurately reproduces discrete simulations across the full depth structure of the granular flow. These enhancements are shown to alter the flow's rheological properties and enable the recovery of the {\mu}(I) rheology within the dense regime.

This paper derives the parametric equations for canal hypersurfaces in $E^4_1$, defined as the envelope of families of pseudo-spheres or pseudo-hyperbolic spheres centered on pseudo-null, partially null, or null curves. We calculate key geometric invariants, including unit normal vector fields, Gaussian curvature, and mean curvature. Additionally, we provide specific examples of these canal hypersurfaces and conclude by presenting characterizations for tubular hypersurfaces within $E^4_1$.

Deep neural networks have become a cornerstone technology for numerous demanding and actively studied computer vision tasks. Among these, the classical ResNet is recognized as a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) capable of extracting features with strong generalization capabilities. This study introduces a biologically inspired deep residual neural network that incorporates hexagonal convolutions within the skip connections. We evaluate the performance of various ResNet variants utilizing both square and hexagonal convolutions using the competitive training strategy referenced in [1]. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method enhances the baseline image classification accuracy of standard ResNet architectures on the CIFAR-10 dataset and performs comparably well across multiple subsets of the ImageNet 2012 dataset. Specifically, we observed average improvements of 1.35% and 0.48% in top-1 accuracy for ImageNet 2012 and CIFAR-10, respectively. Furthermore, the proposed biologically inspired deep residual networks exhibit superior generalization performance, suggesting a promising avenue for enhancing the discriminative capabilities of current state-of-the-art image classification networks.

The tidal evolution rate of asteroidal binaries is governed by the ratio of dynamical Love numbers to quality factors. A common, often invalid, simplification substitutes dynamical Love numbers with their static equivalents. Since static Love numbers are roughly inversely proportional to rigidity, a widespread misconception arises that the tidal evolution rate depends on the product of rigidity and the quality factor ($k_l/Q \propto 1/(\mu Q)$). In truth, dynamical Love numbers are functions of tidal frequency and all rheological properties of the affected body, not merely rigidity. We show that for asteroidal binaries, component rigidity has negligible impact on tidal friction, lag, and consequently on tidal torques, dissipation, and orbital changes. Instead, the critical determinant is the product of effective viscosity ($\eta$) and tidal frequency ($\chi$). The relationship between torque and this product hinges on the competition between viscosity and self-gravity, defining two distinct regimes: when $\eta\chi$ is high, $k_l/Q \propto 1/(\eta\chi)$, whereas for low values, $k_l/Q \propto \eta\chi$. This analysis assumes asteroids behave as Maxwell bodies; while valid for rigid rocks at low frequencies, this model is also applied to rubble piles due to the absence of superior alternatives. Future advancements in understanding granular mechanics under weak gravity may necessitate refining tidal theory to include additional rheological parameters beyond those describing viscoelastic bodies.

This study examines macroscopic behaviors and the conditions for initiating or suppressing collective oscillations within a diverse population of active rotators, which include both excitable and oscillatory components. Utilizing the continuum limit and the Ott-Antonsen reduction method, we identify states characterized by a constant mean field and map their stability boundaries based on the rotators' frequency distribution characteristics. The system exhibits three distinct macroscopic regimes: a homogeneous stationary state, an oscillatory state, and a heterogeneous stationary state. Transitions between these regimes feature a complex bifurcation structure centered on three codimension-two points: Bogdanov-Takens, cusp, and fold-homoclinic. Beyond monostable regions, the analysis uncovers two bistable domains, where solutions coexist either as two stationary states or between a stationary and a periodic state. We demonstrate that collective modes can arise through two primary scenarios—SNIPER or Hopf bifurcations—implying that the shift from a homogeneous to a heterogeneous stationary state under increasing diversity can follow either a classical path or a hysteretic one. Furthermore, we show that the fundamental bifurcation structure remains qualitatively stable in the presence of small noise or minor coupling delays, although the boundaries of these characteristic domains shift relative to the noiseless, delay-free scenario.

We propose a conjecture that forecasts surprising connections between the coefficients in the elliptic expansions of Klein's modular j-function near j = 0 and j = 1728. This conjecture draws inspiration from recent advances in mirror symmetry, specifically the work of Tu on categorical enumerative invariants of matrix factorization categories and the contributions of Li-Shen-Zhou regarding FJRW invariants of elliptic curves.

Transition path theory derives statistical insights from collections of reactive trajectories. A prevalent approach for sampling these trajectories involves managing the branching and pruning of paths to improve the coverage of low-probability regions. Nevertheless, applying transition path theory to data generated by such methods presents difficulties, as verifying whether specific configurations or trajectory segments belong to reactive processes necessitates examining both past and future time points. In this work, we demonstrate an efficient solution to this problem by implementing straightforward data structures. Although we illustrate this methodology using nonequilibrium umbrella sampling (NEUS), the proposed strategy is broadly applicable and can yield transition path theory statistics from other techniques that sample segments of unbiased trajectories.

This paper investigates commutative Krasner hyperrings that possess a nonzero identity. We introduce the concepts of $\phi$-prime, $\phi$-primary, and $\phi$-$\delta$-primary hyperideals, aiming to generalize the notion of $\delta$-primary hyperideals to the $\phi$-$\delta$-primary framework. Additionally, we provide characterizations for classifying these hyperideals. Let $L(\Re)$ denote the collection of all hyperideals in $\Re$, and let $L^{\ast}(\Re)$ represent the set of all proper hyperideals. Consider $\phi$ as a reduction function mapping $L(\Re)$ to $L(\Re) \cup \{\emptyset\}$ and $\delta$ as an expansion function mapping $L(\Re)$ to $L(\Re)$. For a proper hyperideal $N$ of $\Re$, we define $N$ as a $\phi$-$\delta$-primary hyperideal if $a \circ b \in N - \phi(N)$ implies that $a \in N$ or $b \in \delta(N)$ for some $a, b \in \Re$. Finally, we examine the relationships between $\phi$-$\delta$-primary hyperideals and other types of hyperideals.
It is demonstrated that every finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra defined over an algebraically closed field with characteristic 0 can be generated by two elements.

We investigate asymptotic invariants of metric spaces based on the travelling salesman problem, aiming to classify groups and spaces according to their ordering efficiency in this framework. We identify virtually free groups as precisely those admitting an order with specific efficiency properties for 4-point subsets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all $\delta$-hyperbolic spaces can be ordered with exceptional efficiency when considering subsets as the number of points approaches infinity.

We conducted a 130 ks observation using the Suzaku X-ray Imaging Spectrometer to study an extended X-ray emission that ROSAT and Chandra data suggested was linked to the globular cluster 47 Tucanae. The resulting $0.5-6$ keV spectrum was well-modeled by a redshifted thin thermal plasma emission model, yielding a rest-frame temperature of $2.2^{+0.2}_{-0.3}$ keV and a redshift of $0.34\pm0.02$. The derived parameters, including temperature, redshift, and luminosity, reveal that the source is actually a background galaxy cluster whose projected position coincidentally aligns with the proper motion direction of 47 Tucanae.

This study investigates packet management within discrete-time status updating systems, specifically aiming to determine the stationary Age of Information (AoI) distribution. Initially, we model the system as a Ber/G/1/1 queue. By defining a two-dimensional stochastic process that tracks both the receiver's AoI and the packet's age within the system, we derive the steady-state AoI distribution by solving for its equilibrium. This approach effectively analyzes a broader class of queues known as probabilistic preemption Ber/G/1/1, where packet service may be interrupted with a specific probability. As a particular instance, we also derive the stationary AoI distribution for a Ber/Geo/1/1 queue.

For systems with a buffer size of two, we examine two specific configurations: Ber/Geo/1/2 and Ber/Geo/1/2*. The fundamental methodology involves characterizing the random transitions of a three-dimensional vector comprising the receiver's AoI, the age of the packet currently in service, and the age of the packet waiting in the queue. This constructs a three-dimensional AoI process, from which the stationary AoI distribution is extracted as a marginal distribution. Explicit expressions for the AoI distribution are derived for both cases, providing a comprehensive description of the system's steady-state AoI. Furthermore, by solving for the steady state of this higher-dimensional process, we gain additional insights beyond just the AoI distribution. For the size-two systems, these include the distributions of system time and waiting time for packets, as well as violation probabilities regarding the AoI exceeding a defined threshold.

This study focuses on the $\bar{K}NNN$ system, an exotic configuration comprising an antikaon and three nucleons. By solving dynamically exact four-body Faddeev-type equations, the characteristics of the quasi-bound state were determined. Utilizing three antikaon-nucleon and three nucleon-nucleon potentials, the research examined how four-body pole positions depend on the specific two-body interaction models. The calculated binding energies, $B^{\rm Chiral}_{K^-ppn} \sim 30.5 - 34.5$ MeV using chirally motivated potentials and $B^{\rm SIDD}_{K^-ppn} \sim 46.4 - 52.0$ MeV using phenomenological potentials, align closely with results for the $K^- pp$ system derived from the same $\bar{K}N$ and $NN$ potentials; however, the four-body widths, $\Gamma_{K^- ppn} \sim 38.2 - 50.9$ MeV, are notably smaller.
We categorize irreducible homogeneous almost Hermite-Lorentz spaces with complex dimension 3.

Rising privacy and security demands within intelligence-native 6G networks necessitate Quantum Key Distribution-secured Federated Learning (QKD-FL), enabling data owners to collaboratively train global models via quantum channels without revealing local datasets. While architectural design and routing management are crucial for facilitating QKD-FL, practical implementation remains insufficient. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical architecture for QKD-FL systems that jointly optimizes QKD resources, specifically wavelengths, and routing for federated learning applications. Our approach emphasizes adaptive resource allocation and routing for FL workers to minimize the deployment costs of QKD nodes under various uncertainties, including security constraints. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed architecture and resource allocation model achieve a 7.72% reduction in deployment costs compared to the CO-QBN algorithm.

This study investigates numerical errors within large-eddy simulation (LES) for both isotropic and wall-bounded turbulence. We introduce a direct-numerical-simulation (DNS)-assisted LES framework, in which the subgrid-scale (SGS) term is derived from filtered DNS data. First, we confirm that this approach yields zero error when commutation errors between the filter and the numerical differentiation operator are absent. This technique enables the assessment of how numerical errors evolve over time across various schemes at grid resolutions pertinent to LES. The analysis reveals that numerical errors are typically of the same magnitude as modeling errors and frequently offset one another. Consequently, this suggests that supervised machine learning models trained on filtered DNS data may not be ideal for robust SGS model development, as such methods overlook the cumulative impact of numerical errors. Furthermore, the evaluation of errors in turbulent channel flow indicates that numerical errors near the wall are dominant, a finding with significant implications for the creation of wall models.

For any positive integer $n$, it is a known fact that triangles with rational side lengths $a$, $b$, and $c$ can always be found such that their area equals $n$. Under the assumption that the Shafarevich-Tate group is finite, we initially construct a family containing infinitely many Heronian elliptic curves of rank precisely 1, derived from a specific class of Heronian triangles. Additionally, we explicitly generate a distinct family of infinitely many Heronian elliptic curves whose 2-Selmer rank falls between 1 and 3.

Although advanced machine learning models are susceptible to data poisoning attacks aimed at compromising their integrity, current research predominantly relies on ad hoc methods tailored to specific models. Furthermore, existing literature restricts these attacks to binary classifiers or gradient-based algorithms. To overcome these constraints, this paper introduces a novel model-free label-flipping attack that leverages data multi-modality to target class clusters within a label-flipping budget. The proposed algorithm exhibits linear time complexity relative to dataset size and can double the error rate for a given attack budget. Additionally, a new defense mechanism utilizing the Synthetic Reduced Nearest Neighbor (SRNN) model is presented, capable of identifying and excluding flipped samples in real-time during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed attack severely degrades the accuracy of various models, while the corresponding defense technique significantly surpasses conventional methods in restoring the targeted model's accuracy under such attacks.

This paper investigates the existence of various vortex-wave systems within inviscid gSQG flow, where total circulation arises from point vortices and vortices with compact support. To address challenges stemming from singular formulations and infinite kinetic energy, we propose an adapted reduction technique. Additionally, several asymptotic characteristics of the system are presented.

In 2020, Bang-Jensen et al. extended the concept of the Hajós join from graphs to digraphs and broadened various vertex coloring results for directed graphs. Despite these advancements showing that digraphs can be generated through directed Hajós joins and the identification of non-adjacent vertices, the task of determining the specific sequence of Hajós operations required to construct a given digraph remains computationally difficult. Specifically, Bang-Jensen et al. highlighted the challenge of identifying the Hajós operations needed to build a symmetric 5-cycle from a complete symmetric digraph of order 3. We addressed this challenge by adapting a rank-based genetic algorithm, incorporating novel recombination and mutation operators derived from graph theory. In our approach, the Hajós join served as the recombination operator, while the identification of independent vertices functioned as the mutation operator. Consequently, we successfully derived a sequence of just 16 Hajós operations to construct the symmetric cycle of order 5.

Recent breakthroughs in optical coherence tomography (OCT) have facilitated high-resolution, noninvasive visualization of the human retina's substructures. Consequently, OCT examinations are now standard in clinical settings and a cornerstone of ophthalmic research. These scans empower ophthalmologists to comprehend the structural impact of diverse retinal and systemic diseases in unprecedented detail. However, detecting and analyzing minute, localized alterations in the retina during the early stages of disease remains difficult. This overview introduces innovative visual analytics methods designed for the interactive investigation of early retinal changes in individual and multiple patients, facilitating comparisons with normative datasets and the automated quantification of diagnostically critical metrics. Developed through close collaboration with ophthalmology researchers and experts from a leading OCT device manufacturer, these approaches have substantially decreased the time and effort needed for OCT data analysis, particularly in cross-sectional studies. Furthermore, they have enabled several novel discoveries that have been published in biomedical journals.

Monocular depth estimation remains a core challenge in computer vision that has recently gained significant traction. Lately, several approaches have reframed this problem as a classification-regression task to enhance performance, estimating continuous depth by combining discrete bins with predicted probability distributions through linear weighting. This paper introduces BinsFormer, a new framework specifically designed for classification-regression-based depth estimation. It concentrates on two pivotal elements: 1) the creation of adaptive bins and 2) robust interaction between bin predictions and probability distributions. Specifically, we utilize a Transformer decoder to generate bins, treating the process as a direct set-to-set prediction task. Additionally, a multi-scale decoder architecture is incorporated to capture comprehensive spatial geometric details and estimate depth maps using a coarse-to-fine strategy. Furthermore, an auxiliary scene understanding query is introduced to boost accuracy, enabling models to implicitly extract useful information from an environment classification task. Extensive evaluations on the KITTI, NYU, and SUN RGB-D datasets show that BinsFormer significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The code and pretrained models will be released publicly at \url{https://github.com/zhyever/Monocular-Depth-Estimation-Toolbox}.

This study introduces and examines a weak Galerkin finite element approach designed to solve the transport-reaction equation across $d$ spatial dimensions. The method offers significant flexibility by accommodating discontinuous finite elements on general meshes composed of arbitrary polygons or polyhedra. We establish an $L_2$-error bound of $O(h^{k+\frac{1}{2}})$ for the discrete solution when employing $k$th-order polynomials ($k \geq 0$). Furthermore, for a specific category of meshes, we derive an optimal $L_2$-error estimate of $O(h^{k+1})$. Additionally, we propose a derivative recovery technique to approximate the convection directional derivative and provide the associated superconvergence result. Numerical experiments conducted on both compatible and non-compatible meshes demonstrate the efficacy of this weak Galerkin method.

Label distribution learning captures the polysemy of an instance via label distributions; however, processing these distributions can introduce noise and uncertainty into the label space due to artificial or environmental influences. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a \textbf{L}abel \textbf{C}orrelation \textbf{G}rid (LCG) designed to model label relationship uncertainty. Specifically, we calculate a covariance matrix for the label space within the training set to capture inter-label relationships, then model the information distribution (using a Gaussian function) for each matrix element to construct the LCG. Subsequently, our network learns this LCG to precisely estimate the label distribution for every instance. Furthermore, we incorporate a label distribution projection algorithm as a regularization term during model training. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks confirm the efficacy of our approach.

Accurate assessments of extreme sea levels are crucial for coastal flood mitigation and the design of defensive infrastructure. As global climate change accelerates, the combination of rising seas and more frequent, intense storms heightens risks for coastal populations. This study introduces a novel approach to estimating extreme sea levels that captures climate change impacts on extreme events beyond simple mean sea level trends. Employing a joint probability framework, we analyze sea levels as the sum of peak tides and skew surges. We model extreme skew surges using a non-stationary Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD), incorporating covariates for climate change, seasonality, and the interaction between skew surges and peak tides. Additionally, we establish methods to efficiently detect trends in extreme skew surges across various coastlines and seasons. These techniques are demonstrated using data from four tide gauges in the United Kingdom.

Identifying patterns within massive, densely connected datasets is essential for driving value in business and scientific fields. This research addresses subgraph matching on streaming graphs, a capability vital for diverse applications such as social network analysis and cybersecurity. Since each domain requires unique control parameters—including match constraints, data stream types, and search granularity—existing problem-specific subgraph matching systems often lack the flexibility to serve multiple domains effectively. This paper introduces Mnemonic, a programmable platform offering a high-level API that democratizes the creation of various subgraph matching solutions. Beyond its flexibility, Mnemonic provides crucial data management features and optimizations designed to enable real-time processing of long-running, high-velocity, multi-relational graph streams. Experimental results highlight Mnemonic's versatility, showing it outperforms several state-of-the-art systems by up to 100 times.

This paper introduces a novel Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) on Natural Language Processing designed for non-English speakers. Spanning 12 weeks, the curriculum combines weekly lectures, practical sessions, and quizzes, with the final three weeks dedicated to Kaggle-style coding challenges. The course aims to achieve four key objectives: (i) acquaint students with fundamental NLP concepts and methods, including language modeling and word/sentence representations; (ii) demonstrate how recent breakthroughs, such as pre-trained Transformer models, rely on these foundations; (iii) present architectures suited for high-demand real-world applications; and (iv) cultivate practical skills for processing texts across various languages. Developed and recorded in 2020, the course launched by year's end and garnered positive feedback in early 2021.

Recent years have witnessed significant volatility in oil prices, causing conventional forecasting models to become ineffective. The primary reason for this failure is that traditional approaches rely on actual parameter values rather than their expected counterparts. This paper introduces a system dynamics framework that integrates expectational variables to determine oil pricing. In our model, price is derived from the interplay between expected and actual demand and supply. The core of our approach utilizes regression analysis on historical time series data, enhanced by the inclusion of numerous causal loops within the oil market. We simulated the proposed model across various historical scenarios, and the results aligned closely with the observed trends in oil prices for each case.

Social media recommendation systems frequently face criticism for trapping users in "rabbit holes" of increasingly ideologically skewed content. However, previous research on algorithmic radicalization has yielded inconsistent results, and existing studies lack systematic methods to reduce ideological bias within these algorithms. To address this, we performed a systematic audit of YouTube's recommendation engine using one hundred thousand sock puppets to assess three key factors: the presence of ideological alignment between recommendations and user beliefs, the magnitude of this bias (whether users are exposed to a growing number of aligned videos), and the potential for radicalization (whether recommendations become progressively more extreme). Additionally, we designed and tested a bottom-up intervention capable of minimizing ideological bias without requiring YouTube's cooperation. Our findings confirm that YouTube's algorithms do direct users—particularly those on the right—to increasingly biased and radical content across both homepages and suggested videos. While our intervention successfully mitigated this bias by promoting ideologically neutral, diverse, and dissimilar content, debiasing proved significantly more difficult for right-leaning users. Overall, our systematic evaluation demonstrates that although YouTube's recommendations foster ideological bias, this bias can be effectively reduced through our proposed intervention.

Max-point-tolerance graphs (MPTG), investigated by Catanzaro et al. in 2017, were previously defined as p-BOX(1) graphs by Soto and Caro in 2015. Our study focuses on central-max-point tolerance graphs (central MPTG), constructed by treating the points of an MPTG as the centers of their corresponding intervals. We demonstrate that the class of central MPTG coincides with that of unit max-tolerance graphs. Furthermore, we prove that unit central max-point tolerance graphs are equivalent to proper central max-point tolerance graphs, which in turn are identical to the class of proper interval graphs. Additionally, we introduce 50% max-tolerance graphs, distinguishing them from unit max-tolerance graphs, whereas for min-tolerance graphs, the 50% and unit categories represent the same class. Interval catch digraphs (ICD) were first proposed by Maehera in 1984, who conjectured a characterization of central interval catch digraphs (central ICD) using forbidden subdigraphs. This paper refutes that conjecture through counterexamples. We establish a close relationship between central MPTGs and central ICDs and characterize the latter by defining a mapping from vertices to the real line. Our analysis extends to oriented interval catch digraphs (oriented ICDs), where we characterize the augmented adjacency matrix for tournaments and identify oriented ICDs whose underlying graphs are trees. We also provide a characterization for the adjacency matrix of proper interval catch digraphs and offer a forbidden subdigraph characterization for proper oriented interval catch digraphs with chordal underlying undirected graphs. Finally, we examine the interrelationships among these various classes of graphs and digraphs.

This paper addresses spatiotemporal object-centric reasoning within video data, focusing on the concept of object permanence: the capacity to track an object's location despite occlusion, containment, or transport by other entities. While existing deep learning methods often encounter spatiotemporal biases in video reasoning tasks, we introduce Hopper, a system utilizing a Multi-hop Transformer to reason about object permanence. Given a video and a localization query, Hopper iteratively traverses image and object tracks, selectively skipping critical frames to determine the final position of the target object. We show that incorporating a contrastive loss effectively mitigates spatiotemporal biases. Evaluations on the CATER dataset reveal that Hopper achieves 73.2% Top-1 accuracy by processing only a few key frames at 1 FPS. Furthermore, we establish a CATER-h dataset to demonstrate Hopper's capability for long-term reasoning, requiring multi-step logic to correctly localize objects of interest.

High-coherence visible and near-visible lasers are essential for advanced position, navigation, and timing systems, as well as classical and quantum sensing applications. However, the bulky and complex nature of current bench-top lasers hinders their deployment outside laboratory settings. This study demonstrates a system-on-a-chip capable of emitting high-coherence visible and near-visible light. The technology utilizes an innovative method that integrates wavelength conversion and coherence enhancement via self-injection-locking within a single nonlinear resonator. Implemented in a hybridly-integrated device, this streamlined approach achieves a short-term linewidth of approximately 10–30 kHz and delivers on-chip converted optical power exceeding 2 mW. Furthermore, measurements indicate that heterogeneous integration can yield conversion efficiencies surpassing 25% with output powers greater than 11 mW. By combining mature III-V pump lasers with thin-film lithium niobate, this method offers a pathway for low-cost, scalable manufacturing of high-coherence visible sources. Additionally, the coherence generation mechanism is adaptable to other frequency conversion techniques, such as optical parametric oscillation, sum/difference frequency generation, and third-harmonic generation.

This paper aims to launch a mathematical investigation into the drivers of wage inequality, specifically examining their connection to consumption choices and production technologies within an economy. It develops a straightforward Heterodox Model for a closed economy, distinctly separating yet linking consumption and production sectors via a tatonnement mechanism. The equilibria achieved in this process mirror those found in a corresponding Arrow-Debreu model. This framework enables the identification of combinatorial relationships between the economic system's parameters and its equilibria, highlighting how consumer preferences affect wages. Furthermore, the model facilitates the explicit construction of a consumer choice game, where individual utilities act as strategies and wages (either total or relative) function as payoffs. Two examples are provided to demonstrate the mathematical intricacies of this game. The analysis reveals that consumer preferences, articulated through adjusted utility functions, permeate the entire economy, influencing not only prices but also production and wage levels. Consequently, consumer choice can serve as a potent instrument for redistributing wages.

This study examines the convergence properties of $\mathtt{Expected~Sarsa}(\lambda)$ when utilizing linear function approximation. We demonstrate that employing off-line estimates (multi-step bootstrapping) within this framework leads to instability during off-policy learning. Leveraging a convex-concave saddle-point approach, we introduce a convergent variant called $\mathtt{Gradient~Expected~Sarsa}(\lambda)$ ($\mathtt{GES}(\lambda)$). Theoretical analysis confirms that our proposed $\mathtt{GES}(\lambda)$ algorithm converges to the optimal solution with a linear rate, a performance comparable to leading gradient temporal difference methods. Additionally, we utilize a Lyapunov function technique to analyze how step-size parameters affect the finite-time performance of $\mathtt{GES}(\lambda)$; this methodology holds potential for extension to other GTD algorithms. Finally, experimental results are presented to validate the efficacy of our $\mathtt{GES}(\lambda)$ algorithm.

We introduce a parameter estimation protocol designed for generalized Pauli channels operating within $d$-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Key advantages of this approach involve the use of product probe states and measurements, a number of measurement configurations that scales linearly with $d$, minimal post-processing requirements, and a mean square error scaling that matches that of entanglement-based schemes for the same channels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when measuring generalized Pauli operators, errors induced by Pauli noise can be effectively modeled as measurement errors. This insight enables the application of measurement error mitigation frameworks to address errors stemming from generalized Pauli channels. Leveraging this result, we mitigate noise on the probe states to restore the scaling behavior of noiseless probes, albeit with a constant factor dependent on the noise strength. Additionally, this technique of representing Pauli channels as measurement noise holds independent significance for other NISQ applications, such as state tomography, variational quantum algorithms, and various channel estimation tasks where Pauli measurements are central.

The zero modes approach is utilized to derive the action of monodromy matrix elements on off-shell Bethe vectors within quantum integrable models featuring $U_q(\mathfrak{gl}_N)$-invariant $R$-matrices. These resulting action formulas facilitate the establishment of recurrence relations for both the off-shell Bethe vectors and the highest coefficients of their scalar products.

This paper addresses the existence of prescribed mean curvature (PMC) graphs with fixed graphical boundaries within the product manifold $N\times\R$. We introduce the concept of a Nc-f domain, defined as a region whose closure excludes specific subdomains where the boundary's mean curvature equals $f$. Using a blow-up technique originally developed by Schoen and Yau, we demonstrate the existence of such PMC graphs over bounded Nc-f domains under natural boundary conditions. These results have applications in solving the Plateau problem for PMC surfaces in 3-manifolds.

The Parker Solar Probe's (PSP) distinctive orbit enables unprecedented close-up observations of the solar wind. To further our understanding of solar wind and energetic particle origins, it is crucial to pinpoint the sources of PSP data. This study presents findings from the first two PSP solar encounters, utilizing the Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA) model driven by Air Force Data Assimilative Photospheric Flux Transport (ADAPT) maps. We determined the coronal magnetic field and the 1 Rs source regions corresponding to the solar wind observed by PSP, validating these results against observed solar wind speeds and magnetic polarity. When model reliability is high, we generated time series data for model-derived spacecraft separation from the heliospheric current sheet, magnetic expansion factor, coronal hole boundary distance, and photospheric field strength along field lines connected to the spacecraft. New results for Encounter 1 reveal the temporal evolution of a far-side mid-latitude coronal hole that PSP co-rotated with, discussing how this evolution aligns with observed variations in solar wind speed, density, and temperature. During Encounter 2, a newly emerged far-side active region complicated modeling; however, once this region rotated to the near-side, ADAPT-WSA outputs aligned well with PSP observations, allowing for reliable retrospective estimation of solar wind sources for most of the encounter. We conclude by highlighting how coronal modeling facilitates scientific interpretation of these encounters that would otherwise be unattainable.

Focusing solely on leading interactions, alongside excluded volume effects and a minimal alignment rule, we demonstrate that polar order exhibits characteristic features of second-order phase transitions within a two-dimensional disordered active system. In addition to inducing collective motion, the alignment interaction promotes the fluidification of the active glass and results in the dynamical slowing down of the polar phase. Furthermore, we find that polar order eliminates active phase separation, yielding homogeneous, disordered configurations in motion.

This work investigates optimization problems concerning probability measures in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with cost functionals derived from multi-marginal optimal transport. Within a framework of $N$ interacting particles, similar to Density Functional Theory, the interaction cost is repulsive and defined by a two-point function $c(x,y)=\ell(|x-y|)$, where $\ell: \mathbb{R}_+ \to [0,\infty]$ is a decreasing function vanishing at infinity. Because mass loss at infinity can lead to non-existence, it is essential to relax the initial problem to sub-probabilities. This paper characterizes the relaxed functional by extending the findings of \cite{bouchitte2020relaxed} and introduces a duality approach to compute the $\Gamma-$limit as $N\to\infty$ under broad assumptions on the cost $\ell(r)$. We demonstrate that this limit corresponds to the convex hull of the direct energy. Furthermore, we analyze the limiting optimization problem under a continuous external potential, providing conditions and explicit examples regarding when minimizers are probabilities or possess a mass strictly less than one. Finally, we examine the scenario of short-range interactions $\ell_N(r)=\ell (r/\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon\ll 1$, illustrating how the duality method determines the limit energy as $\varepsilon\to 0$ for a large ensemble of $N_\varepsilon$ particles.

Classifying pickup and delivery transactions based on unstructured customer text presents significant challenges, as it requires mapping diverse user inputs to a fixed set of categories while accommodating varying writing styles. This classification is critical for businesses, enabling the analysis of market trends and the creation of personalized experiences for different customer segments. Therefore, capturing these category trends at scale with high precision and recall is essential. This paper addresses a specific use case where a single category defines each transaction, proposing a cost-effective approach leveraging semi-supervised learning and knowledge distillation. The method determines transaction categories from free-text customer inputs by utilizing weak labels, achieving performance comparable to that of human-annotated data. Experiments on a large internal dataset and the 20Newsgroup dataset demonstrate that RoBERTa excels at this categorization task. Furthermore, by employing an ALBERT model—which possesses 33 times fewer parameters than RoBERTa—as a student model with RoBERTa serving as the teacher, we achieve results similar to RoBERTa and superior to a standard ALBERT model. This framework, designated as R-ALBERT, is currently deployed in production, assisting the business in tracking evolving trends and making informed decisions.

The excitation spectra of the deformed nucleus $^{232}$U were investigated using the (p,t) reaction at the Munich Tandem accelerator's Q3D spectrograph. Triton angular distributions were recorded for 162 excited states observed in the spectra, extending up to 3.25 MeV.
