Using a simulated pCT imaging system, we found that this reduction yields RSP resolutions as low as 0.2% for cortical bone and up to 1% for lung tissue. Additionally, further improvements are possible for various materials by selecting the beam's residual energy to align with the detection mechanisms that offer the best RSP resolution.

Building upon recent research [J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 44, 495201 (2012); Eur. Phys. J. D 67, 179 (2013)], we introduce a novel family of generalized coherent states associated with Landau levels, designed to serve as finite Fock subspaces for the $su(2)$ Lie algebra representation. We elucidate the connection between these states and deformed truncated coherent states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that they fulfill the resolution of the identity condition via positive definite measures over the complex plane. A detailed analysis of their nonclassical and quantum statistical characteristics—including quadrature squeezing, higher-order $su(2)$ squeezing, anti-bunching, and anti-correlation effects—is provided. Specifically, we examine how this generalization impacts the nonclassical behavior of two-mode systems.

Interlacing is a common technique in television broadcasting and video recording that doubles the perceived frame rate without increasing bandwidth, yet it introduces distracting visual artifacts like flickering and serrated silhouettes during playback. Current state-of-the-art deinterlacing approaches either sacrifice visual quality for real-time performance by ignoring temporal data, or improve quality through motion estimation at the cost of high computational demands. This paper introduces a novel deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) method that achieves both high visual fidelity and real-time performance. Unlike existing super-resolution models that depend on translation-invariant assumptions, our DCNN leverages temporal information from both odd and even half-frames to reconstruct only the missing scanlines while preserving the original ones to generate complete frames. Furthermore, a layer-sharable architecture enables real-time processing on a single GPU. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses all existing techniques in both reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency.

This research extends the findings presented in [Fittouhi and Joseph, Parabolic adjoint action, Weierstrass Sections and components of the nilfibre in type $A$]. Consider a parabolic subgroup $P$ of an irreducible simple algebraic group $G$, with $P'$ denoting its derived group and $\mathfrak m$ representing the nilradical of the associated Lie algebra. According to Richardson's theorem, the subalgebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$, which consists of $P$-semi-invariants within $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]$, is polynomial. A linear subvariety $e+V$ within $\mathfrak m$ is defined as a Weierstrass section for the $P'$ action if the restriction map creates an isomorphism between $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$ and $\mathbb C[e+V]$. While the existence of such a section necessitates that the ring of invariants be polynomial, this condition alone does not guarantee existence. A general combinatorial method was developed to establish the existence of a canonical Weierstrass section $e+V$ in $\mathfrak m$ for all cases; notably, $e$ resides in $\mathscr N$ and is constructed as a sum of root vectors corresponding to linearly independent roots. Although the specific form of $e+V$ varies depending on the choice of parabolic subgroup, the construction remains uniform. It was previously announced in [Fittouhi and Joseph, loc. cit.] that $e$ can be augmented to an element $e_{VS}$ by adding root vectors, where the linear span $E_{VS}$ of these vectors lies in $\mathscr N^e$ and its closure equals $\mathscr N^e$. This result indicates that $\mathscr N^e$ does not necessarily possess a dense $P$ orbit, though this was only confirmed for the specific case yielding the counterexample. This paper provides a general proof of that theorem. Finally, a map from compositions to the set of distinct non-negative integers is introduced, with its image determining the canonical Weierstrass section.

Although imitation learning effectively addresses numerous real-world challenges, methods like behavioral cloning are hindered by data mismatch and compounding errors. The DAgger algorithm was developed to mitigate these issues by having the novice's state distribution guide the sampling of corrective actions from an expert. However, such sampling protocols necessitate that the expert supply action labels without full system control, which can compromise safety and, when humans serve as experts, reduce label quality due to perceived actuator lag. To address these challenges, we introduce HG-DAgger, a DAgger variant tailored for interactive imitation learning with human experts in real-world settings. Beyond training a novice policy, HG-DAgger learns a safety threshold for a model-uncertainty-based risk metric to forecast the trained novice's performance across various state space regions. Evaluations on both simulated and real-world autonomous driving tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms both DAgger and behavioral cloning.

While classical Fourier series decompose functions into sinusoidal waves, Vilenkin (Walsh) functions utilize rectangular waves. Although the development of Vilenkin-Fourier series has been heavily shaped by the classical theory of trigonometric series, significant distinctions also exist. This master thesis aims to explore, advance, and apply recent advancements in this intriguing field within the context of modern harmonic analysis. Specifically, we examine Nörlund means under the condition of monotone coefficients, demonstrating convergence at both Lebesgue and Vilenkin-Lebesgue points. Given that these points occur almost everywhere for any integrable function, we establish the almost everywhere convergence of these summability methods.

Using the phenomenological relativistic quark model (RQM) incorporating coupled channel effects, the mass spectrum of $c\bar{b}$ states was calculated. The investigation employed a Hamiltonian featuring a confinement potential alongside the confined one gluon exchange potential (COGEP). Within this RQM framework, M1 and E1 radiative decays of these states were analyzed, and weak decay widths were estimated under the spectator quark approximation. The results demonstrate satisfactory agreement with experimental data regarding both masses and decay widths.

Bayesian optimization (BO) serves as a powerful method for optimizing costly black-box functions by balancing exploitation (targeting likely maxima) with exploration (investigating uncertain regions). In scenarios where direct objective function measurements are unavailable—limited instead to binary outcomes like success/failure or pairwise comparisons—efficient exploration requires distinguishing between two uncertainty types: epistemic uncertainty regarding the unknown function and aleatoric uncertainty arising from irreducible observation noise. We demonstrate that only epistemic uncertainty drives effective exploration. Leveraging this insight, we introduce several novel acquisition functions that surpass current state-of-the-art heuristics in both binary and preferential BO contexts, offering rapid computation and straightforward implementation. Furthermore, we extend these acquisition rules to batch learning settings, enabling simultaneous multi-query performance.

To accommodate users' diverse data requirements, various global mobile network operators have introduced mobile data trading markets (DTMs), enabling users to exchange data quotas among themselves. This paper investigates the significance of DTMs by examining user operator selection and trading behaviors alongside the operator's profit-maximization strategy. We formulate the interaction between the operator and users as a three-stage Stackelberg game. In Stage I, the operator determines the fee charged to sellers to maximize profits. In Stage II, users select their preferred operator. In Stage III, DTM participants make their trading decisions. We derive a closed-form expression for the unique Nash equilibrium (NE) in Stages II and III, noting that all users propose an identical price where total demand equals total supply. Additionally, we demonstrate that the optimization problem in Stage I is convex and calculate the optimal operation fee. Our analysis and numerical results indicate that operators with a small initial market share can enhance their profits by implementing a DTM, a finding consistent with real-world scenarios in Hong Kong.

Understanding the plastic deformation state within metallic structures is essential for preventing failure, which has driven the development and widespread use of non-destructive acoustic testing based on first-order elastic constants. However, these methods often fail to detect spatially heterogeneous plastic deformations if the resulting changes in elastic constants are negligible. Recently, digital image correlation techniques, combined with finite element modeling, have successfully provided insights into interior plastic deformation using surface measurements. In contrast, acoustic waves can penetrate deeply, offering the ability to probe the bulk of plastically deformed materials. We previously established that nonlinear acoustic methods are significantly more sensitive to variations in dislocation density than linear ones. In this study, we demonstrate that the nonlinear Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) method is sufficiently sensitive to identify distinct zones of von Mises stress and effective plastic strain in centimeter-sized aluminum specimens. This capability was validated through ultrasonic measurements on a sample subjected to a three-point bending test. Given the relatively low stress levels and minor deformations, plasticity in the sample arose from dislocation proliferation. Consequently, we conclude that the nonlinear parameter measured by SHG is also highly sensitive to dislocation density. Our experimental findings align with numerical results derived from Finite Element Method (FEM) modeling. Furthermore, X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) measurements, despite being intrusive and less accurate, corroborate the acoustic data and the plastic deformation patterns observed in the finite element simulations.

Multicellular organisms thrive only when their constituent cells balance cooperation with competition. Cooperation entails sacrificing individual fitness for the collective good, yet too much cooperation renders the community vulnerable to aging. Conversely, competition removes unfit, senescent cells through natural selection, thereby slowing aging, but excessive competition invites cheaters, such as those found in cancer. These dynamics imply that an optimal degree of intercellular competition maximizes organismal vitality by postponing the onset of aging. Using a statistical mechanical framework, we model this concept as a generalized replicator dynamical system where somatic mutations alter cell vitality and cooperation levels, increasing susceptibility to aging and cancer. By analyzing the costs of cooperation and the intensity of competition within a minimal model, we demonstrate that our framework predicts a specific optimal level of competition that enhances vitality and delays the inevitability of senescence or malignancy.

Given the significant risks and ethical challenges associated with advanced technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI), their regulation has become increasingly critical. While the potential benefits of rapid deployment are substantial, the pressure to accelerate development often leads to overlooked safety measures and societal implications, fostering a competitive "race" among developers. This study utilizes a game-theoretical model of an idealized technology race in a fully connected environment to examine how varying interaction structures among participants influence collective decisions and regulatory necessities. Our results demonstrate that when participants exhibit strong diversity in connectivity and peer influence—such as within scale-free networks—conflicts typically seen in homogeneous settings are markedly diminished, thereby reducing the demand for regulatory intervention. Moreover, our findings suggest that technology governance can leverage global patent heterogeneity and inequality among firms and nations to implement targeted interventions on a select minority of actors, effectively steering the entire population toward the ethical and sustainable utilization of advanced technologies.

Achieving high-quality experimental evaluation of debugging and testing methods for quantum programs requires realistic benchmarks featuring reproducible bugs and their fixes. However, until now, no appropriate benchmark suite has existed to systematically assess these methods. This paper introduces Bugs4Q, a benchmark comprising thirty-six real, manually verified Qiskit bugs drawn from four major Qiskit components (Terra, Aer, Ignis, and Aqua), each accompanied by test cases to reproduce the faulty behaviors. Bugs4Q offers interfaces to access both buggy and corrected versions of the Qiskit code and to execute the relevant tests, thereby enabling reproducible empirical research and comparative analysis of debugging and testing tools for Qiskit. The benchmark is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Z-928/Bugs4Q.

This letter computes the gravitational waves (GWs) radiated by a small binary (SB) by solving the Teukolsky equation against the backdrop of a massive exotic compact object (ECO), modeled phenomenologically as a Schwarzschild geometry featuring a reflective boundary at its "would-be" horizon. The "continuous echo" waves that propagate to infinity, resulting from the ECO's reflectivity at this "would-be" horizon, offer a precise probe into the fundamental nature of the ECO's horizon.

Matrix models exhibit phase transitions where variable distributions undergo topological changes akin to the Gross-Witten-Wadia transition. A recent numerical investigation identified similar splitting and merging behaviors in the distributions of dynamical variables within a tensor-vector system. This paper analyzes the system exactly under certain large-$N$ limits, where these distributions consist of discrete configuration sets instead of continuous ones. Our findings reveal cascades of first-order phase transitions for fixed tensors, alongside both first- and second-order transitions for random tensors, all defined by specific replica symmetry breaking patterns. The system holds significance in at least three distinct fields: splitting dynamics are crucial for the emergence of classical spacetimes in tensor models of quantum gravity; the same dynamics inherently identify tensor rank in data analysis via tensor rank decomposition; and the system offers a variant of the spherical $p$-spin model for spin glasses, introducing a novel non-trivial parameter. We explore implications of these results from these viewpoints and compare our analytical findings with numerical simulations to verify large-$N$ convergence and validate the underlying assumptions.

Achieving learning goal-conditioned control in real-world robotics remains a difficult open challenge. While reinforcement learning allows for autonomous trial-and-error learning, practical deployment is often hindered by the high costs of manual reward engineering, safe exploration guarantees, and hyperparameter tuning. Conversely, imitation learning simplifies real-world control acquisition but typically relies on expensive curated demonstrations and lacks mechanisms for continuous refinement. Recent iterative imitation methods have demonstrated the ability to learn goal-directed control from undirected data and improve via self-supervised goal reaching; however, these results have so far been confined to simulations. This work provides evidence that iterative imitation learning can scale to goal-directed behaviors on a physical robot within dynamic environments, specifically high-speed, precision table tennis (e.g., landing the ball on a specific target). We demonstrate that this approach enables straightforward, continuous on-robot learning without the complexities of reward design or sim-to-real transfer. Furthermore, the method is highly sample-efficient, capable of training on a physical robot within just a few hours. In real-world evaluations, the resulting policies perform as well as or better than randomly selected amateur human players from a robotics lab at returning balls to designated targets. Finally, our analysis reveals that the size of the initial undirected bootstrap dataset significantly impacts performance; even a modest amount of unstructured demonstration data drastically accelerates the convergence of a general-purpose goal-reaching policy. Videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/goals-eye.

Beam-induced ionization injection (B-III) is currently under investigation as a technique to introduce an electron beam with a regulated density profile into a plasma wakefield accelerator (PWFA). This mechanism is triggered by the fields of an unmatched drive beam when its slice envelope attains its minimum, known as the 'pinch.' To effectively manage the characteristics of the injected beam, it is essential to analyze beam-slice envelope oscillations, particularly regarding pinch location and size. This proceeding introduces an ansatz grounded in harmonic motion to derive an analytical solution for beam-slice envelope evolution within the nonlinear regime. The pinch size is subsequently determined by applying energy conservation principles in the transverse direction. The derived analytical expressions demonstrate strong alignment with numerical results.

The Deep Noise Suppression (DNS) challenge aims to drive innovation in noise suppression techniques to attain high-perceptual speech quality. Following special sessions at INTERSPEECH and ICASSP 2020, we have released open-source training and test datasets for wideband conditions, along with a subjective evaluation framework adhering to the ITU-T P.808 standard, which was utilized to assess challenge participants. Although numerous researchers from both academia and industry have significantly advanced the field, the best noise suppressors still fall short of delivering superior speech quality in difficult environments. For the INTERSPEECH 2021 iteration, we are expanding our datasets to include full-band scenarios. This challenge features two tracks dedicated to real-time denoising for wideband and full-band cases. Additionally, we are providing participants with DNSMOS, a dependable non-intrusive objective speech quality metric, to aid in their development process.

Most stars in the Milky Way's stellar halo were probably acquired through a few ($\lesssim$3) significant dwarf galaxy mergers. Nevertheless, the timing of these events remains uncertain, relying mainly on indirect dynamical mixing evidence or imprecise age estimates of stars within debris structures. This study seeks to derive reliable stellar ages for stars linked to galactic substructures to more directly refine our understanding of the Galaxy's merger history. By integrating kinematic, asteroseismic, and spectroscopic data where possible, we determined ages for 10 kinematically selected red giant stars associated with the stellar halo, including some from the Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage substructure, and compared them to 3 red giants in the Galactic disk. Despite systematic variations in both absolute and relative ages found in this work, the age rankings within the sample remain robust. Using multiple stellar age determination packages with identical observable inputs, we calculated a weighted average age for the Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage stars in our sample as 8 $\pm$ 3 (stat.) $\pm$ 1 (sys.) Gyr. We also established hierarchical ages for Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage, in situ halo, and disk populations, yielding a Gaia-Enceladus-Sausage population age of 8.0$^{+3.2}_{-2.3}$ Gyr. While our limited data and small sample prevent distinguishing between hierarchical population ages for halo or disk structures, this methodology promises to enable distinct characterization of Galactic substructures with larger samples and additional data in the near future.

This research investigates particle creation induced by an external electric field's Coulomb potential within the gravitational field of a static cosmic string. By solving the generalized Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations and applying the Bogoliubov transformation, we determine the probability and number density of generated particles. We then examine how the cosmic string affects the pair production rate driven by the Coulomb potential. Specifically, for grand unified theory (GUT) cosmic strings, spinless particle production occurs when the Coulomb potential nucleus charge satisfies $Z\geq206$, whereas spin-1/2 particle production requires $Z\geq275$.

Recent decades have witnessed major advancements in both deep learning and quantum computing, sparking growing interest in their convergence. This synergy has recently yielded techniques such as quantum deep learning and quantum-inspired deep learning. This paper provides an overview of progress at this intersection by examining the technical contributions, strengths, and commonalities of various studies in the field. Specifically, we review and summarize the diverse schemes proposed for modeling quantum neural networks (QNNs) and related architectures like quantum convolutional networks (QCNNs). Additionally, we briefly outline recent developments in quantum-inspired classical deep learning algorithms and their applications to natural language processing.

An analysis has been conducted to search for new phenomena in final states characterized by at least one isolated high-momentum photon, jets, and missing transverse momentum, utilizing proton-proton collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The dataset, gathered by the ATLAS experiment at the CERN LHC, represents an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. These results are interpreted within a supersymmetric framework where pair-produced gluinos decay into neutralinos; subsequently, the neutralinos decay into a gravitino, accompanied by at least one photon and jets. No significant deviations from Standard Model predictions were found. Consequently, upper limits on the visible cross section for physics beyond the Standard Model were established, alongside lower limits on the masses of gluinos and neutralinos, all determined at a 95% confidence level.

Mafia, alternatively known as Werewolf, is a party game where participants split into two rival factions: citizens and mafia. The goal for each side is to eliminate the other. The gameplay unfolds over two alternating phases—day and night—featuring specific actions such as daytime lynching. While the citizen faction is larger in number, mafia members possess special abilities, including mutual knowledge and nighttime killing.

We introduce a straightforward mathematical framework for this game, modeled essentially as a pure death process occurring in discrete time steps. Our analysis yields closed-form solutions for the probability of mafia victory, denoted as w(n,m), and tracks the game's progression. Additionally, we examine the discrete characteristics of these outcomes alongside their continuous-time approximations.

Results indicate that the mafia requires a relatively small number of members to achieve an equal chance of winning against the citizens; specifically, this number scales with the square root of the total player count. Moreover, the game's outcome is heavily influenced by whether the total number of players is even or odd.

We provide a mathematical formalization of `generalized data parallel' operations, encompassing frequent scientific kernels like matrix-vector multiplication, multi-grid coarsening, load distribution, and others. We demonstrate that from a concise specification, computational elements such as MPI messages or task dependencies can be automatically generated.

We explore the scenario where $\mu^-\to e^+$ conversion is observed before $\mu^-\to e^-$ conversion, analyzing its consequences for new physics investigations. Our study centers on a model featuring mixing between $SU(2)_L$ doublet and singlet scalar leptoquarks, a framework that generates both lepton flavor and lepton number violation. This structure is inspired by R-parity violating (RPV) supersymmetry, where sbottom particles mediate these conversion processes. We derive the $\mu^-\to e^+$ rate by drawing an analogy to muon capture within muonic atoms and perform numerical evaluations across various target nuclei. The test of lepton flavor universality in pion decay imposes strict constraints on the $\mu^-\to e^+$ rate, limiting the maximum branching ratio to approximately $10^{-18}$ given current bounds on RPV parameters. We demonstrate that either $\mu^-\to e^-$ or $\mu^-\to e^+$ signals could be detected in upcoming experiments, suggesting that concurrent searches for these processes will yield crucial insights into the pattern of coupling constants.

Over recent decades, mobile robot navigation has been the subject of extensive research, with a growing focus on human-robot collaboration in shared workspaces. To gain acceptance from human collaborators, future mobile robots must adhere to social norms; however, defining compliance formally remains challenging. Conversely, empowerment has proven effective for artificial agents to learn complex, generalized behaviors and serves as a strong model for biological systems. This paper extends beyond classical reinforcement learning by equipping our agent with intrinsic motivation through empowerment. Unlike methods focused on self-empowerment, our approach prioritizes empowering humans in the environment, ensuring the robot's presence and movement do not disrupt them. Experimental results demonstrate that this method positively impacts humans by minimizing the robot's distance to them, thereby reducing human travel time while the robot efficiently reaches its goal. Furthermore, an interactive user study indicates that participants perceive our approach as more socially compliant than current state-of-the-art methods.

The high R/X ratio in typical distribution networks renders system voltage susceptible to active power injections from distributed energy resources (DERs). Additionally, the intermittent and unpredictable nature of DER generation introduces new complexities for voltage regulation. To address voltage violations in distribution systems with high photovoltaic (PV) penetration, this paper introduces a two-stage stochastic optimization approach for the optimal placement of PV smart inverters equipped with Volt-VAr capabilities. This strategy provides guidance for upgrading existing inverters to smart variants during the planning phase while accounting for Volt-VAr operational characteristics. A key benefit of this approach is its reliance on the local control features of smart inverters, which eliminates communication delays and failures. Furthermore, the optimization model incorporates Volt-VAr control characteristics as internal constraints, enhancing the accuracy of placement decisions. The optimization aims to minimize upgrading costs and the quantity of required smart inverters while ensuring the voltage profile remains within acceptable limits. Validation through case studies on a 12.47kV, 9km Arizona utility feeder using OpenDSS confirms the strategy's effectiveness in both static and dynamic simulations. Index Terms

Significant advances in quantum technology now allow for the creation of quantum states involving more than a dozen entangled qubits. Fully characterizing these systems requires tailored approaches based on their specific nature and intended applications. We introduce a method for characterizing stabilizer states that scales linearly with the number of qubits. This approach enables the simultaneous measurement of fidelity, entanglement, and nonlocality, making it highly practical. We validate the method's efficiency by experimentally characterizing a photonic four-qubit cluster state, as well as three- and four-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states. Our scheme can be readily extended to larger-scale quantum information tasks.

Distance metric learning algorithms are designed to accurately quantify the similarities and distances among data points. Within clustering applications, these methods often rely on expert-provided side information, typically represented as must-link and cannot-link constraints. Under this framework, the algorithms adjust data point pairs to be closer together when linked by must-labels, and push apart pairs subject to cannot-link constraints. For these algorithms to succeed, the chosen distance metric must align with expert knowledge, expectations, and beliefs, while the resulting transformations should maintain the dataset's underlying geometric properties. Additionally, filtering expert constraints to retain only the most beneficial ones while discarding potentially harmful ones is a valuable strategy. To tackle these challenges, we propose leveraging the dual information inherent in the pairwise constraints of semi-supervised clustering. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating this dual information significantly enhances the performance of distance metric learning algorithms.

The initial section provides a general overview of the $\gamma / \phi_3$ extraction and compares the respective experimental environments. Subsequently, I examine the existing results from the CDF experiment. Finally, the third part introduces early findings from the LHCb experiment, which represent promising initial progress toward a future $\gamma / \phi_3$ measurement.

Current research on transportation network uncertainty and reliability emphasizes the need to model both probabilistic origin-destination (O-D) demand and network flows. Leveraging extensive historical traffic data, this study proposes a new theoretical framework to estimate the mean and variance-covariance matrix of O-D demand, accounting for day-to-day fluctuations caused by travelers' independent route selections. Furthermore, it derives the probability distributions for link and path flows and their associated travel costs, attributing variance to three distinct sources: O-D demand, route choice, and unobserved errors. The proposed method iteratively estimates O-D demand parameters, a process equivalent to iterative generalized least squares (IGLS) in statistics, while employing Lasso regularization to achieve a sparse covariance matrix that enhances both interpretability and computational speed. Although the probabilistic O-D estimation operates within a significantly larger solution space compared to deterministic models, the study demonstrates that its estimator for the O-D demand mean performs at least as well as the optimal estimator, with estimation error diminishing as sample size grows. Validated on two small-scale and two large-scale real-world networks, the probabilistic O-D estimation yields quick convergence under the IGLS framework, producing results that are compelling, satisfactory, and computationally feasible. However, the application of Lasso regularization to covariance estimation tends to underestimate most variance-covariance entries; therefore, selecting an appropriate Lasso penalty is crucial to balance estimation bias and variance effectively.

This paper investigates recommendation systems framed as contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems. We introduce a graph-based approach that leverages the geometric structure of user data to form meaningful clusters within the user domain. This strategy lowers the dimensionality of the recommendation task without compromising MAB accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze how graph sparsity and cluster size influence MAB performance, supported by comprehensive simulations on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art MAB algorithms.

This paper introduces a Bayesian simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) approach grounded in multipath modeling, which continuously adjusts interacting multiple models (IMM) parameters to characterize mobile agent state dynamics. The evolution of these IMM parameters follows a Markov chain and is integrated into the factor graph structure that encodes the SLAM problem's statistical properties. The proposed belief propagation (BP)-based method adaptively handles time-varying system models in real time by jointly estimating model parameters alongside the agent and map feature states. Finally, the algorithm's efficacy is assessed through a simulated scenario. Our numerical results demonstrate that this multipath-based SLAM algorithm effectively manages strongly varying agent state dynamics.

This paper addresses the challenge of obtaining semi-global solutions for optimal feedback control and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. While implementing a feedback control law derived from an HJB solution allows for real-time execution with minimal computational effort, traditional numerical methods fail for general nonlinear systems with more than three state variables due to the curse of dimensionality. To overcome this, we propose a novel computational approach that mitigates the curse of dimensionality. Rather than directly discretizing the HJB equation, we introduce a sparse grid within the state space and apply Pontryagin's maximum principle to formulate a set of necessary conditions as a boundary value problem (characteristic equations) for every grid point. This spatially causality-free method supports perfect parallelism on the sparse grid. Compared to dense grids, the reduced size of a sparse grid makes it feasible for higher-dimensional systems, as demonstrated by a 6-D example. Once solutions are computed at each grid point, high-order polynomial interpolation approximates the feedback control at arbitrary locations. We establish and numerically estimate an upper bound for the approximation error. Finally, the efficacy of this sparse grid characteristics method is validated through two examples of rigid body attitude control utilizing momentum wheels.

The Internet has increasingly become a primary target for security breaches and intrusions, which can result in system failures, network disruptions, and data corruption or theft. Network Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) function by monitoring network traffic to identify unauthorized and malicious activities. Current state-of-the-art IDS solutions typically detect attacks by analyzing comprehensive attack information, meaning they can only identify an intrusion after it has been executed and potentially caused damage. In this paper, we introduce an end-to-end early intrusion detection system designed to mitigate network attacks before they inflict further harm, thereby avoiding unexpected downtime and interruptions. Our approach utilizes a deep neural network-based classifier for attack identification, which is trained in a supervised manner to extract relevant features directly from raw network traffic data, eliminating the need for the manual feature selection processes common in existing methods. Additionally, we propose a novel metric termed "earliness" to assess how promptly our method detects attacks. Empirical evaluation on the CICIDS2017 dataset demonstrates that our approach performs effectively, achieving an overall balanced accuracy of 0.803.

Over the past ten years, political discourse has increasingly migrated to social media platforms. This shift allows researchers to capture and analyze the rhetorical strategies used by online participants and groups, enabling a statistical examination of societal controversies and their argumentative dynamics. This paper introduces a five-step methodology designed to extract, categorize, and investigate the hidden argumentation structures within online debates. Focusing on Twitter data regarding a potential "no-deal" Brexit scenario, we examine the anticipated consequences of such an event. Initially, we utilize Regular Expressions targeting verbs associated with Creation, Destruction, and Causation to identify cause-effect claims in tweets. Subsequently, we classify these extracted effects using a Structural Topic Model based on unigrams and bigrams. We then isolate controversial topics and analyze argumentation differences between self-identified partisan factions. Topics are typed by estimating covariate effects on topic propensities, and a correlation network is used to map the debate's topological structure, revealing coherent thematic constellations. Finally, we investigate temporal dynamics to infer lead/follow relationships among factions. The results demonstrate that this methodology facilitates a statistical rhetorical analysis of debates and maps the architecture of controversies over time. Specifically, the "no-deal" Brexit debate exhibits an assortative argumentation structure dominated by factional argument clusters and polarized narrative frames expressed through Creation and Destruction verbs. These findings underscore the advantages of a systemic approach to debate analysis, which reveals the topical and factional dependencies inherent in online arguments.

Deep learning advancements depend heavily on access to extensive, well-annotated datasets. In the medical imaging domain, however, labeling such vast amounts of training data demands the scarce time of skilled radiologists. To mitigate this challenge, few-shot learning has emerged, delivering competitive results with minimal labeled examples. Despite this, a critical yet previously neglected aspect of few-shot learning concerns the pre-learning selection of template images, which significantly influences final performance. We introduce a novel Sample Choosing Policy (SCP) designed to identify the most valuable images for annotation within few-shot medical landmark detection. SCP comprises three components: 1) self-supervised training to develop a pre-trained deep model for feature extraction from radiological images, 2) a Key Point Proposal mechanism to localize informative regions, and 3) a Representative Score Estimation module to identify the most representative samples or templates. Extensive experiments across three prominent public datasets validate SCP's effectiveness. Specifically, for one-shot medical landmark detection, SCP reduces mean radial errors on the Cephalometric and HandXray datasets by 14.2% (from 3.595mm to 3.083mm) and 35.5% (from 4.114mm to 2.653mm), respectively.

Machine learning has demonstrated significant efficacy across diverse domains, including speech and object recognition on mobile devices. Given that access to extensive training data is crucial for success, numerous datasets are now being made publicly available. From the perspective of data managers or consumers, assessing data quality serves as a vital initial step in the learning workflow, enabling informed decisions about dataset selection, updates, and maintenance. However, practical methods for evaluating data quality remain scarce, particularly for large-scale, high-dimensional data like images and videos. This paper introduces two novel metrics designed to calculate class separability and in-class variability—two fundamental dimensions of data quality—for any given dataset. While traditional measures often concentrate solely on class separability, we argue that in-class variability is equally significant. We present efficient algorithms, leveraging random projections and bootstrapping, to compute these metrics with statistical advantages when handling large-scale, high-dimensional data. Experimental results demonstrate that our measures align with classical approaches on small datasets while offering substantially improved computational efficiency for large-scale, high-dimensional scenarios.

We establish a precise link between reflexive modules over a one-dimensional ring $R$ and its birational extensions that are self-dual as $R$-modules. This connection demonstrates that a complete local reduced Arf ring possesses only finitely many indecomposable reflexive modules up to isomorphism, which can be explicitly represented by the local rings infinitely near it. Furthermore, we characterize Arf rings by the condition that every reflexive module is self-dual. Our findings include applications to the dimensions of subcategories and the existence of endomorphism rings with small global dimension (non-commutative desingularizations). Ultimately, our results highlight remarkable parallels between one-dimensional Arf rings and two-dimensional rational singularities from both representation-theoretic and categorical viewpoints.

The socially optimal placement of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs), such as rooftop solar, relies heavily on existing retail electricity frameworks. Ongoing discussions regarding DER regulations, particularly variations of Net Energy Metering (NEM), focus on creating compensation mechanisms that reflect true value, aiming to accelerate DER adoption while mitigating cost burdens shifting between adopters and non-adopters. Nevertheless, these dialogues largely overlook the time- and location-specific value of DERs, as well as market inefficiencies like information asymmetry among stakeholders and externalities such as carbon emissions. This paper introduces a game-theoretic model incorporating information asymmetry to evaluate the efficiency impacts of implementing granular DER compensation strategies, such as value stacks and distributional locational marginal prices, as alternatives to NEM's flat retail rates. Our findings demonstrate that granular compensation policies yield more efficient market results than NEM, even when information asymmetry exists, thereby eliminating the necessity for regulatory interventions. Furthermore, when paired with granular DER compensation, carbon pricing offers the most precise price signals to DER investors and aggregators, ultimately maximizing social welfare.

We investigate a system of nearest-neighbor coupled nonlinear autonomous oscillators featuring quenched random frequencies and purely conservative interactions. Our analysis demonstrates the emergence of global phase-locked states within finite lattices and explores their numerical destabilization. As model parameters vary, these states lose stability, giving rise to localized periodic and chaotic oscillations. In cases of weak nonlinear frequency dispersion, the system exhibits metastability similar to that observed in almost-conservative systems. Furthermore, we contrast our findings with the phase-approximation approach, where amplitude dynamics are adiabatically eliminated.

Recent observations suggest that the center of the Milky Way contains a supermassive entity possessing an extremely intense radial magnetic field (Eatough et al., 2013). We show that the radiation detected near the Galactic Center (GC) (Falcke and Marko 2013) cannot originate from the accretion disk's gas because the abnormally strong radial magnetic field prevents the plasma from approaching the GC. Consequently, these fields block the infalling accretion flow from both the inner disk region and the central massive black hole within the standard model, implying that the central black hole cannot generate the observed radiation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ultra-strong radial magnetic field near the GC cannot be produced by Parker's turbulence dynamo mechanism, as preliminary qualitative estimates yield a field strength six orders of magnitude weaker than observed. However, replacing the central black hole of the standard model with a supermassive stellar object containing magnetic monopoles (SMSOMM; Peng and Chou, 2001) resolves these issues. Our theoretical prediction for the thermal radiation power peak aligns well with observations, and the discovery of the strong radial magnetic field is naturally explained and consistent with our model. Additionally, the presence of such a strong magnetic field near the GC may serve as astronomical evidence for the existence of magnetic monopoles, as predicted by the Grand Unified Theory of particle physics.

We introduce an ALMA 870 $\mu$m continuum survey with 0.15$^{\prime\prime}$ resolution (equivalent to 21 au), covering 25 pointings of 31 young stellar objects within the Ophiuchus molecular clouds. Utilizing dust continuum emission as an indicator for both circumstellar disk radius and dust mass, we find mean masses of 2.8$^{+2.1}_{-1.3}$ and 2.5$^{+9.2}_{-1.1}$ M$_{\oplus}$, along with mean radii of 23.5$^{+1.8}_{-1.2}$ and 16.5$^{+2.8}_{-0.9}$ au, for Class I and Flat spectrum protostars, respectively. Furthermore, we analyze the multiplicity statistics of dust around these young stellar objects in Ophiuchus. Based on this study alone, the multiplicity fraction (MF) and companion star fraction (CSF) for the combined Class I and Flat samples are 0.25 $\pm$ 0.09 and 0.33 $\pm$ 0.10, respectively, aligning with values observed in Perseus and Orion. Although distinct differences in mass and radius exist between the Ophiuchus surveys and those of Perseus/Orion, no significant variations are detected in the multiplicities across these regions. We suggest that star formation conditions in Ophiuchus differ in ways that strongly influence disk size (and thus disk mass) without affecting system multiplicity, potentially indicating important variations in planet formation processes.

Error bound analysis, which quantifies the distance from a point to the solution set of an optimization problem via the optimality residual, serves as a potent instrument for analyzing first-order optimization algorithms. This paper employs global error bound analysis to investigate the iteration complexity of a first-order method designed for linearly constrained nonconvex minimization. We introduce a novel "decomposition" technique to establish a global dual error bound for a regularized variant of this nonconvex problem. Leveraging this global dual error bound, we demonstrate that a specifically constructed primal-dual first-order method can produce an $\epsilon$-stationary solution for the linearly constrained nonconvex minimization problem within $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations, achieving the optimal iteration complexity known for this class of nonconvex problems.

The $Aldous\text{-}Broder$ and $Wilson$ algorithms are prominent methods for generating uniform spanning trees (USTs) using random walks. This study examines their interplay to accelerate the construction of random trees. By analyzing $branches$—specific paths produced by both algorithms at defined stopping times—we demonstrate that the trees generated on a complete graph are statistically identical at these moments. This finding enables a hybrid algorithm that creates USTs for complete graphs more rapidly than either standalone method. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient two-stage framework to extend this hybrid strategy to graphs beyond the complete class, validating its utility across various examples, including transitive graphs where it reduces generation time by 25% compared to the $Wilson$ algorithm.

For $G=GL(n,\mathbb{C})$ with a parabolic subgroup $P=LN$ featuring a two-block Levi subgroup $L=GL(n_1)\times GL(n_2)$, the space $G\cdot (\mathcal{O}+\mathfrak{n})$—where $\mathcal{O}$ denotes a nilpotent orbit of $\mathfrak{l}$—constitutes a union of nilpotent orbits within $\mathfrak{g}$. The initial segment of our primary theorem employs geometric Sakate equivalence to demonstrate that $\mathcal{O'}\subset G\cdot (\mathcal{O}+\mathfrak{n})$ holds if and only if certain Littlewood-Richardson coefficients are non-zero. Furthermore, the second segment of our main theorem elucidates the geometry of the space $\mathcal{O}\cap\mathfrak{p}$, a critical domain for investigating Whittaker supports and annihilator varieties associated with representations of $G$.

Routing remains a critical and persistent challenge in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs), primarily because protocols must minimize communication overhead to conserve sensor energy. Hierarchical routing protocols are widely recognized as the most energy-efficient solutions for WSNs. This paper introduces a generalized hierarchical routing protocol based on tree data structures, where clustering forms a general tree constructed adaptively according to sensor distances. The results demonstrate that this proposed tree-based protocol offers significant advantages in energy consumption and network lifetime compared to existing hierarchical methods.

When a TeV-scale leptoquark possesses a significant Yukawa coupling, its primary production mechanism at hadron colliders involves partonic lepton-quark fusion. Although the parton distribution functions for leptons within protons are negligible, this deficit is offset by resonant enhancement. This work presents the initial calculation of higher-order radiative corrections to the resonant leptoquark production cross-section at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD and QED corrections are comparable in magnitude but exhibit opposite signs. We determine NLO $K$-factors across a broad spectrum of scalar leptoquark masses, covering all viable combinations of quark and lepton flavors and leptoquark charges. Additionally, we quantify theoretical uncertainties arising from renormalization and factorization scale variations, as well as from limited parton distribution function knowledge. Finally, we examine strategies for distinguishing the flavor structure of leptoquark interactions by leveraging the interplay among various production channels.

Multiscale entropy (MSE) evaluates signal complexity across varying timescales. Originally developed for biomedical applications, it has recently been effectively employed within a supervised machine learning framework to characterize light curves and classify stellar variability. This study investigates the algorithmic properties of MSE in the context of stellar variability and connects it with conventional astronomical time series analysis methods. We then utilize MSE as the foundation for an interpretable, unsupervised clustering framework capable of distinguishing hybrid pulsators (exhibiting both p- and g-modes) from stars with exclusive p-mode pulsations, such as $\delta$ Sct stars, or those with only g-mode pulsations, like $\gamma$ Dor stars. Our findings indicate that MSE is a potent tool for capturing variability patterns in stellar light curves, offering insights into a star's pulsation structure by revealing the interaction between short- and long-term variability based solely on time-domain data. Furthermore, we demonstrate a correlation between MSE and the frequency content of stellar signals, particularly regarding the near-core rotation rates of g-mode pulsators. The proposed clustering framework successfully identifies hybrid pulsators within datasets of $\delta$ Sct and $\gamma$ Dor stars. A key advantage of this approach is its unsupervised nature, which eliminates the need for pre-labeled data and avoids biases inherent in prior knowledge.

The quantum Hall (QH) effect serves as an exceptional platform for leveraging electron quantum coherence across diverse applications, ranging from metrology to quantum computing. Within the fractional regime, this phenomenon supports anyons—emergent quasiparticles exhibiting neither bosonic nor fermionic behavior, but rather fractional statistics. Detecting and controlling these particles are critical steps toward realizing topologically protected quantum computation. By capitalizing on the high phase coherence found in QH edge states, researchers have designed and built electronic interferometers to probe the coherence and statistical nature of the interfering components. This review examines the two primary interferometer geometries utilized in the QH regime: Mach-Zehnder and Fabry-Perot devices. We outline their operational principles, fabrication techniques, and key findings obtained in both integer and fractional QH contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate how recent technological progress enabled the direct experimental verification of fractional statistics for Laughlin quasiparticles using a Fabry-Perot interferometric configuration.

The electroencephalogram (EEG) serves as a widely utilized instrument for investigating brain activity. This data is typically acquired by positioning electrodes on the scalp to record the oscillating currents that flow through them. The interpretation of these oscillations can vary based on factors such as the subject's health status, the specific experimental protocol, the sensitivity of the equipment, and manual adjustments. When collected over time, this information constitutes a time series. Existing literature suggests that EEG data associated with epilepsy may exhibit chaotic behavior. Regardless of this, embedding theory within dynamical systems indicates that, under appropriate conditions, time series from complex systems can be employed to reconstruct their phase space. This paper introduces a novel analysis of epilepsy EEG time series based on an approach termed "complex geometric structurization." This method derives complex geometric structures by first constructing strange attractors using embedding theory from dynamical systems and subsequently applying a geometry tool known as $\alpha$-shapes from shape analysis. Preliminary results demonstrate a proof of concept, showing that these structures effectively capture anticipated changes in brain lobes. Furthermore, deeper analysis indicates that these complex structures have the potential to function as biomarkers for detecting seizure-related changes.

This research examines two counter-propagating electromagnetic waves in a vacuum within the Born-Infeld framework of quantum electrodynamics. By selecting the crossed-field configuration where ${\bf E}\cdot{\bf B}=0$ (implying $\mathfrak{G}^2=0$), the Born-Infeld Lagrangian simplifies to the Born Lagrangian; consequently, this specific scenario allows for an analysis identical to that of Born electrodynamics. We demonstrate that, for ordinary wave conditions, the non-linear field equations decouple when utilizing self-similar solutions, enabling an investigation into shock wave steepening. Our findings indicate that the sole solutions are exceptional traveling waves moving at a constant velocity, which do not evolve into shocks. Furthermore, we discuss the associated phase shifts and cross-sections, alongside our proposed direct detection methods for photon-photon scattering \cite{KadlecovaKornBulanov2019,KadlecovaMine2019}. This study serves as a preliminary step toward analyzing waves under the more general conditions of Born-Infeld theory.

Generating and gathering labeled data represents a significant hurdle in machine learning workflows, a challenge that has been intensified by the rise of automated feature generation methods like deep learning, which typically demand vast amounts of training data. Although weak-supervision approaches have offered a workaround, current frameworks present their own limitations: systems like Snorkel necessitate that users manually craft diverse, high-quality labeling rules, while tools like Snuba require an initial labeled subset to automatically derive such rules. Manually writing these rules is often laborious and time-intensive, whereas assembling a labeled subset can be prohibitively expensive or unfeasible in imbalanced scenarios, as random sampling in such cases frequently yields too few positive instances.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce Darwin, an interactive system designed to simplify the process of writing labeling rules for text within weakly-supervised contexts. Starting with an initial rule, Darwin automatically produces a set of candidate rules for the specific task and refines them based on feedback from the annotator. Darwin is both scalable and versatile, capable of processing extensive text corpora (exceeding one million sentences) and supporting a broad spectrum of labeling functions defined by context-free grammars. Furthermore, experiments across five real-world datasets demonstrate that Darwin allows annotators to create weakly-supervised labels efficiently and cost-effectively. Specifically, our results indicate that rules discovered by Darwin identify approximately 40% more positive instances than those found by Snuba, even when Snuba is given 1,000 labeled instances.

The study derives fundamental constraints on enhancing rotor angle stability through local frequency or phase angle measurements. Analysis using a two-machine power system model reveals that while inter-area oscillation damping can be improved, it inevitably reduces transient stability margins, independent of the specific control design. These limitations arise because external disturbances exciting inter-area modes cannot be reliably estimated using only local frequency data. Validation on a modified Kundur four-machine, two-area test system with active power modulation on an embedded high-voltage DC link confirms these findings. Specifically, damping control based on local phase angle measurements inevitably results in larger rotor angle deviations following certain load disturbances, which can precipitate transient instability in highly stressed systems. Consequently, the identified limitations underscore the necessity for wide-area measurements in power oscillation damping strategies.

Passivity serves as a foundational requirement for any quantum system to reach thermodynamic equilibrium and for temperature to become defined. Although significant research has leveraged this concept, the specific transition from single-shot passivity to the completely passive Gibbs state remains technically understood but lacks a cohesive intuitive framework. This work redefines passivity in quantum systems using purely geometric language, rendering the emergence of the Gibbs state from passive states entirely clear. By clarifying established findings, the study also offers new insights into non-equilibrium quantum systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that every passive state corresponds to a simple convex shape within a two-dimensional plane, where the area of this shape quantifies the system's deviation from the equilibrium manifold. This approach introduces a novel geometric metric for athermality, establishing connections to both ergotropy and $\beta$-athermality.

We present Amortized Neural Networks (AmNets), a network architecture designed with compute efficiency and low latency in mind, making it ideal for sequence modeling. By integrating AmNets into a Recurrent Neural Network Transducer (RNN-T) for automatic speech recognition (ASR), we significantly lower computational costs and latency. This architecture allows the system to dynamically toggle between different encoder branches on a frame-by-frame basis, where each branch offers varying levels of computational expense and model capacity. We demonstrate this variable compute capability using two established techniques: sparse pruning and matrix factorization. An arbitrator network, which imposes minimal computational overhead, decides which branch to activate for each frame. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech dataset confirm that this approach can cut inference costs by as much as 45% and achieve near real-time latency without compromising accuracy.

Formal verse poetry is characterized by rigid constraints regarding meter and rhyme schemes. While previous research on generating such poetry typically relies on existing poems for supervision—a resource that is scarce for many languages and forms—this study introduces an unsupervised method capable of creating poems adhering to any specified meter and rhyme without needing training data. The proposed technique involves segmenting a standard, non-poetic text corpus into phrases, attaching control tokens that specify each phrase's length and ending rhyme, and then training a transformer language model on this augmented dataset. At inference time, the system constructs control tokens corresponding to the target meter and rhyme scheme, conditioning the model on these inputs to produce formal verse. Experiments conducted in Spanish and Basque demonstrate that the approach successfully generates valid poems, often achieving quality levels comparable to human-written works.

Stripping extraction of hydrogen molecular ions has become increasingly relevant in the cyclotron sector owing to its superior extraction efficiency. Nevertheless, magnetic fields can induce unwanted Lorentz dissociation of hydrogen anions and molecular ions during the acceleration phase. Research regarding dissociation under electric fields equivalent to a Lorentz-transformed magnetic field in a standard cyclotron (approximately a few MV/cm) remains limited. Consequently, to provide essential data for cyclotron design, this study consolidates and summarizes investigations into the Lorentz dissociation of H$^-$, H$_2^+$, and H$_3^+$ specifically for stripping extraction applications.

We confirm the conjecture proposed by F. Qi and R. Agarwal in "On complete monotonicity for several classes of functions related to ratios of gamma functions," published in J. Inequal. Appl. (2019), demonstrating that the function $1/\arctan$ is logarithmically completely monotonic on $(0,\infty)$, yet it does not qualify as a Stieltjes transform.

The "redshift desert" refers to the range between 2.2 and 3, where quasars are notoriously difficult to detect in optical surveys because their optical colors closely resemble those of normal stars. However, a candidate known as SDSS J085543.40-001517.7 was identified spectroscopically as a new quasar with a redshift of 2.427. This discovery, made by LAMOST in December 2009 and confirmed by the NAOC/Xinglong 2.16m telescope in March 2010, utilized a selection criterion based on near-IR $Y-K$ and optical $g-z$ colors. Although this object fell within the stellar locus on optical color-color diagrams—leading to its omission from SDSS spectroscopic surveys—it was clearly distinguished from stars in the $Y-K$ vs. $g-z$ diagram. With an $i$ magnitude of 16.44, this quasar stands out as the brightest known in the 2.3 to 2.7 redshift range. Spectral analysis revealed a central black hole mass of $(1.4\sim3.9) \times 10^{10} M_\odot$ and a bolometric luminosity of $3.7\times 10^{48}$ \ergs, classifying it as one of the most luminous quasars in the universe. This finding validates the effectiveness of using near-IR color criteria to locate quasars within the redshift desert. Future LAMOST spectroscopic surveys are expected to recover many more such missing objects, which is crucial for understanding the cosmological evolution of quasars at redshifts exceeding 2.2.

This presentation examines various models that expand the Standard Model's scalar sector through the addition of new matter states. Specifically, I concentrate on recent findings concerning singlet extensions, updating results from earlier studies. In greater detail, I will briefly overview methods for probing a strong first-order electroweak phase transition via precision electroweak measurements, as well as production cross-sections for non-standard scalars at Higgs factories.

Designing the architecture of software systems is a complex undertaking that demands substantial experience and years of accumulated knowledge. To facilitate this process, reference architectures have gained traction, aiding in both the standardization and evolution of such systems. Despite the significant time and effort invested in creating these architectures, many still contain outdated descriptions, leading to their eventual abandonment. This article offers guidelines for updating reference architecture descriptions, tailored to various stakeholder types and specific tasks. To validate that these guidelines are sound—being grounded in the widely recognized ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 international standard and existing literature—we also provide a brief qualitative comparison against ad hoc approaches commonly found in reference architectures. We contend that implementing such guidelines is essential and will significantly enhance the sustainability and longevity of reference architectures.

This study investigates the existence and asymptotic mass behavior of positive solutions to the coupled system:
\begin{equation}\label{eqA0.1}\nonumber \begin{cases} -\Delta
u+\lambda_1u=\mu_1u^3+\alpha_1|u|^{p-2}u+\beta v^2u\quad&\hbox{in}~\R^4,\\
-\Delta v+\lambda_2v=\mu_2v^3+\alpha_2|v|^{p-2}v+\beta
u^2v\quad&\hbox{in}~\R^4,\\ \end{cases} \end{equation}
subject to the mass constraints $$\int_{\R^4}u^2=a_1^2\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\R^4}v^2=a_2^2,$$
where $a_1,a_2$ are fixed constants, $\mu_1,\mu_2,\beta>0$; $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in \R$, $p\!\in\! (2,4)$ and $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\!\in\!\R$ function as Lagrange multipliers. Initially, we demonstrate non-existence for the repulsive interaction scenario, where $\alpha_i<0$ for $i=1,2$. Subsequently, examining the attractive case ($\alpha_i>0$), we establish that for $2<p<3$, the problem possesses both a ground state and an excited state, identified respectively as a local minimizer and a mountain-pass critical point of the associated energy functional. Furthermore, we derive precise asymptotic profiles for these solutions as $(a_1,a_2)\to (0,0)$ with $a_1\sim a_2$. To our knowledge, this represents the first work addressing multiplicity and synchronized mass collapse in normalized Schrödinger systems featuring Sobolev critical exponents. For the range $3\leq p<4$, we prove existence results for ground states, alongside non-existence results specifically when $p=3$, characterizing these states as constrained mountain-pass critical points. Additionally, we obtain detailed asymptotic behaviors for ground states as the masses of both components vanish, whether clustering toward an upper bound or diverging to infinity.

Multiple planetary systems contain several giant planets, yet the influence of a second planet on the gas accretion of both during simultaneous formation remains uncertain. This study utilizes long-term 2D isothermal hydrodynamical simulations (exceeding 0.5 Myrs) with the FARGO-2D1D code to examine two non-migrating planets drawing from the same gaseous disk. Our results indicate that the evolution of the planets' mass ratio is contingent upon gap formation; however, when accretion begins simultaneously, the planets invariably converge to nearly identical masses ($0.9 < m_{p,out}/m_{p,in} < 1.1$) after 0.5 Myrs. If the onset of accretion for one planet is delayed, the initial mass ratio can become more disparate, but the values rapidly converge to a similar range ($0.8 < m_{p,out}/m_{p,in} < 2$) within $10^5$ years. To account for the diverse mass ratios observed in exoplanets, accretion must commence at different times and cease shortly after runaway gas accretion begins (within less than 0.5 Myrs), likely due to disk dispersal. Consequently, the evolution of the mass ratio significantly influences system dynamics and may offer constraints on the formation history of Jupiter and Saturn.

Despite the inherent ambiguity of natural language, identifying semantic similarities between sentences remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a straightforward method for recognizing semantically equivalent questions by integrating the advantages of word embeddings with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Furthermore, we illustrate the efficacy of using cosine similarity to compare feature vectors. The proposed model was trained on the Quora dataset, comprising more than 400,000 question pairs. We evaluated various embedding techniques, including Word2Vec, FastText, and Doc2Vec, to analyze their impact on performance. Our approach yields competitive results on the Quora dataset, further supporting the established utility of CNNs for paraphrase detection.

A perpetual calendar determines the day of the week for any specific date through arithmetic calculations involving congruence. Zeller's congruence is a widely recognized algorithm for this purpose across both Julian and Gregorian systems. Conversely, a less famous but historically significant perpetual calendar has been utilized by Javanese communities in Indonesia for nearly 400 years. This unique system integrates the Saka Hindu, lunar Islamic, and western Gregorian calendars, featuring cycles beyond the standard seven-day week, lunar months, and lunar years. These include the five-day *pasaran*, the 35-day *wetonan*, the 210-day *pawukon*, the eight-year *windu*, and the 120-year *kurup* cycles. Beyond its temporal functions, the Javanese calendar serves cultural and spiritual roles, such as guiding marriage decisions. This chapter examines the intersection of mathematics and Javanese culture, specifically focusing on how the calendar's arithmetic principles influence daily life. Furthermore, we introduce a novel congruence formula designed to calculate the *pasaran* day. We anticipate that this exploration will offer valuable insights for teaching and learning congruence within number theory.

Real-world networks often exhibit inherent incompleteness or inaccuracies, which can degrade the performance of downstream machine learning tasks such as community detection. To mitigate this, effective preprocessing is essential. This paper introduces HAP, a novel link prediction strategy grounded in community attributes, alongside a two-step community enhancement algorithm featuring an automatic evolution process driven by HAP. The primary goal is to clarify ambiguous community structures by adding links. The HAP approach leverages neighborhood uncertainty and Shannon entropy to pinpoint boundary nodes, subsequently establishing connections based on both node community attributes and community size. Experimental evaluations across twelve real-world datasets with known community ground truths demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses baseline approaches, and the resulting community enhancements adhere to the anticipated evolutionary trajectory.

The ab initio Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) method, widely used for investigating excitons in materials, is traditionally solved under conditions that account only for static electronic screening. In this work, we extend this framework to incorporate dynamical screening from phonons at the lowest order of electron-phonon interaction. Applying this generalized BSE approach to a range of inorganic lead halide perovskites (CsPbX₃, where X = Cl, Br, and I), we observe that including phonon screening substantially lowers the calculated exciton binding energies. By deriving a simplified expression for phonon screening, we identify general trends regarding its significance in semiconductors and insulators using a hydrogenic exciton model. Furthermore, we show that the magnitude of the phonon screening correction in isotropic materials can be accurately predicted using four specific parameters: the reduced effective mass, static and optical dielectric constants, and the frequency of the most strongly coupled longitudinal optical (LO) phonon mode. This framework clarifies the role of phonon screening and its connection to excitonic properties across a wide variety of semiconductors.

This study utilizes the $\bar{\partial}$-steepest descent technique to analyze the Cauchy problem for the complex short pulse (CSP) equation, given initial data within the weighted Sobolev space $H^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})=\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}): f',xf\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\}$. Within a fixed space-time cone defined as $S(x_{1},x_{2},v_{1},v_{2})=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}: y=y_{0}+vt, ~y_{0}\in[y_{1},y_{2}], ~v\in[v_{1},v_{2}]\}$, we establish the long-time asymptotic behavior of the solution $u(x,t)$. Leveraging these asymptotic results, we confirm the resolution conjecture for the CSP equation, which features an $N(I)$-soliton contribution from the discrete spectrum and a $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ decay term associated with the continuous spectrum, with a residual error bounded by $O(t^{-1})$.

This study presents an engineering approach that enables the realization of a complete classification table for topological insulators using passive acoustic crystals. Specifically, we design an acoustic crystal that exhibits all the defining features of a Class D topological insulator, including non-trivial Chern numbers and precise particle-hole symmetry governing both bulk and edge dynamics. This is achieved through a specific resonator geometry that ensures eight independent couplings of equal strength, thereby maintaining the accuracy of mode-coupling theory. This setup allows for the high-fidelity implementation of a de-complexified tight-binding model that generates two-dimensional Class D topological phases, a model previously introduced by Barlas et al. in PRB (2018). Successfully creating this Class D topological acoustic crystal opens the door to observing Majorana-like modes stabilized by pi-fluxes.

Transformer models have demonstrated remarkable success in numerous NLP tasks; however, prior research on automated ICD coding suggested they do not surpass earlier approaches like CNN-based models. This paper contests that finding by introducing a straightforward, scalable technique for handling long text using established transformers such as BERT. Our results indicate that this method substantially enhances the performance of transformer models in ICD coding, successfully exceeding the capabilities of a leading CNN-based approach.

High-speed camera imaging serves as a potent method for examining the spatiotemporal characteristics of unsteady plasma processes, typically relying on the assumption that light fluctuations mirror plasma density variations. This study systematically contrasts high-speed imaging with concurrent measurements of key plasma parameters—density, electron temperature, and floating potential—within a weakly magnetized Argon plasma column operating at low pressure (1 mTorr) and magnetic fields between 160 and 640 G. Spectral filtering was applied at wavelengths of $488\pm5$~nm, $750\pm5$~nm, and $810\pm5$~nm. The findings demonstrate that light intensity cannot serve as a direct proxy for plasma density and that electron temperature must be accounted for when interpreting high-speed imaging data, applicable to both time-averaged profiles and fluctuations. The investigation explores plasma parameter fluctuations, specifically highlighting ion acoustic waves (approximately 70 kHz) at low magnetic fields and low-frequency azimuthal waves (several kHz) at higher fields. An exceptional correlation was observed between high-speed image fluctuations and an Arrhenius law function that integrates variations in both plasma density and electron temperature. These insights clarify previously reported discrepancies between ion saturation current and narrow-band imaging measurements found in existing literature.

Currently, there are no practical quantum computing applications for power grids. This paper explores solving a core grid challenge, DC power flow, using quantum computing. As the most prevalent power system analysis method—used either independently or integrated into other tools—rapid and precise power flow solutions are critical for grid operators. Our research relies on the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) quantum algorithm, which offers a theoretically proven speedup over classical methods for solving linear equation systems. Practical experiments were performed on a quantum computer utilizing the WSCC 9-bus system.

Inspired by the recent identification of a continuous ferromagnetic quantum phase transition in CeRh$_6$Ge$_4$ and its contrast with other U-based heavy fermion metals like UGe$_2$, we construct a unified theoretical framework for their distinct ground state properties using an anisotropic ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg model. Utilizing an enhanced large-$N$ Schwinger boson method, we forecast a comprehensive phase diagram that features a continuous ferromagnetic quantum phase transition at high magnetic anisotropy and first-order transitions at lower anisotropy. Our computations identify three distinct ferromagnetic phases, including a half-metallic spin-selective Kondo insulator characterized by constant magnetization. We observe abrupt changes in Fermi surface topology across these phases, aligning with observations in UGe$_2$. At finite temperatures, our predictions indicate that Kondo hybridization emerges well before the onset of ferromagnetic long-range order and relocalizes near the phase transition, matching band structure measurements in CeRh$_6$Ge$_4$. These findings underscore the critical role of magnetic anisotropy and offer a cohesive theory for interpreting ferromagnetic quantum phase transitions in heavy fermion metals.

While state-of-the-art language models frequently perform accurately on question-answering benchmarks featuring well-defined queries, real-world scenarios often involve questions that cannot be answered without user clarification. We demonstrate that current models typically fail to request such clarification when faced with imprecise questions, instead offering incorrect answers or hallucinations. To resolve this, we present CLAM, a framework that leverages the model to identify ambiguous queries and subsequently prompts it to seek clarification from the user when necessary. Additionally, we detail a scalable and cost-effective method for automatic evaluation, utilizing an oracle language model with privileged information to supply clarifying details. Our approach yields a 20.15 percentage point increase in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models on a novel dataset of ambiguous questions derived from TriviaQA.

This study introduces a hybrid classical-quantum framework designed for density estimation and supervised classification. Implemented as a quantum circuit within a high-dimensional quantum computer simulator, the proposed protocols demonstrate the capability to estimate probability density functions and perform supervised learning predictions. Furthermore, this model can be extended to calculate the expected values of density matrices in high-dimensional quantum systems. Experimental evaluations across diverse datasets confirm that the method serves as a viable strategy for executing both density estimation and supervised classification on high-dimensional quantum computers.

We propose and analyze an additive autoencoder designed for dimensionality reduction, which sequentially performs bias estimation, linear trend estimation, and nonlinear residual estimation. Computational experiments demonstrate that this architecture, utilizing a shallow network to capture nonlinear dynamics, can successfully identify a dataset's intrinsic dimension with minimal autoencoding error. This finding prompts a comparative study of shallow versus deep network structures and their respective training methods. Our conclusion is that while deeper networks achieve lower autoencoding errors during intrinsic dimension identification, the detected dimension itself remains unchanged compared to that of a shallow network.
