In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a leading approach within the computer vision community. However, as a data-driven method, deep models demand vast quantities of accurately labeled training data, which is frequently unavailable in many real-world scenarios. Data Augmentation (DA) offers a solution by artificially generating new images from existing samples. Since augmentation strategies must often be tailored to specific datasets to accommodate different data types, the traditional design of DA policies relies heavily on human expertise and domain knowledge, a process that is often subjective and prone to errors. To address this limitation, a new direction known as Automated Data Augmentation (AutoDA) has arisen, which aims to automatically learn augmentation policies directly from the dataset. The objective of AutoDA models is to discover optimal policies that maximize performance improvements. This survey examines the factors driving the rise of AutoDA technology specifically within image classification. It identifies three core components of a standard AutoDA framework: a search space, a search algorithm, and an evaluation function. By analyzing their architectures, the paper presents a systematic taxonomy of existing AutoDA methods. Furthermore, it reviews major contributions in the field, evaluates their strengths and weaknesses, and suggests several promising avenues for future research.

Correlation functions serve as fundamental entities in quantum field theories, often defined within high-dimensional space-time domains. However, their numerical analysis is impeded by the curse of dimensionality, which restricts the practical application of advanced many-body theories to significant problems. To address this, we introduce a quantum-inspired Multi-Scale Space-Time Ansatz (MSSTA) for these correlation functions. This approach maps space-time dependencies onto auxiliary qubit degrees of freedom that represent exponentially varying length scales, under the assumption of scale separation. We numerically validate the ansatz across diverse equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems, achieving compression rates spanning several orders of magnitude for difficult scenarios. Furthermore, we formulate essential components of diagrammatic equations, including convolutions and Fourier transforms, within this compressed framework. Numerical results confirm the stability and efficiency of our proposed methods when applied to the Dyson and Bethe-Salpeter equations. Ultimately, MSSTA offers a unified framework for the efficient computation of quantum field theories.

This paper outlines our approach to the AVA-Kinetics Crossover Challenge at the CVPR 2021 ActivityNet workshop. Our method employs various relation modeling techniques for spatio-temporal action detection and implements a training strategy that integrates these methods through end-to-end training on two extensive video datasets. We also explore the use of memory banks and fine-tuning for long-tailed distributions to enhance performance. This work details the implementation of our solution, presents experimental results with corresponding analysis, and reports a final test set mAP of 40.67 on the AVA-Kinetics dataset.

This paper introduces a Borsuk-Ulam-type property for homotopy classes of maps from a topological space $M$ to $N$ relative to a proper free action $\tau$ of a group $G$ on $M$, extending the classical antipodal Borsuk-Ulam theorem for maps from $\mathbb{S}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$. Specifically, when $M$ is a finite pathwise-connected CW-complex, $G$ is a finite, non-trivial Abelian group acting properly and freely via cellular maps, and $N$ is either $\mathbb{R}^2$ or a compact boundaryless surface distinct from $\mathbb{S}^2$ and $\mathbb{RP}^2$, we provide an algebraic criterion based on braid groups to determine if a free homotopy class $\beta \in [M,N]$ satisfies this property. Applying this criterion, we analyze the case where $M$ is a compact boundaryless surface with a free action by the finite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_n$. By considering the orientability of the orbit space $M_\tau$, the value of $n$ modulo $4$, and an algebraic condition on the first homology group of $M_\tau$, we establish conditions under which the unique homotopy class of maps from $M$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ possesses the Borsuk-Ulam property with respect to $(\mathbb{Z}_n,\tau)$. Finally, we present examples of surfaces acted upon by the symmetric group and derive partial results concerning the Borsuk-Ulam property for maps into $\mathbb{R}^2$ in these scenarios.

Existing research demonstrates that Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) possess the ability to encode factual knowledge; however, certain analyses indicate that this capability lacks robustness, particularly regarding sensitivity to prompt variations during fact extraction. To address this vulnerability, we propose enabling PLMs to learn the deterministic relationship between the available context and masked information. This approach ensures that masked facts can be inferred with certainty based on contextual clues, offering more stable learning patterns compared to random masking strategies. We introduce two specific pre-training tasks designed to encourage PLMs to rely on these deterministic relationships when filling in masks. In practice, an external Knowledge Base (KB) is utilized to identify these relationships, and PLMs are continuously pre-trained using our proposed methodology. Probing experiments on factual knowledge reveal that continuously pre-trained models exhibit superior robustness in capturing facts. Additionally, experiments on question-answering datasets demonstrate that learning these deterministic relationships through our methods also benefits other knowledge-intensive tasks.

Inspired by prior research on the Floquet PXP model [Mukherjee et al., Phys. Rev. B 102, 075123 (2020); Phys. Rev. B 101, 245107 (2020)], we investigate a one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ lattice featuring three-spin interactions within an identical constrained Hilbert space, which forbids configurations containing two adjacent $S^z=\uparrow$ spins. We demonstrate that this system exhibits extensive Hilbert space fragmentation, resulting in the failure of thermalization during unitary evolution from a broad range of simple initial states. Although the Hamiltonian is non-integrable, many high-energy eigenstates can be described using quasiparticles. We identify two categories: "bubble eigenstates," characterized by integer eigenvalues (including mid-spectrum zero modes) and strictly localized quasiparticles, and a second class featuring mobile quasiparticles that create momentum-space dispersion. Additionally, we examine anomalous eigenstates arising from a secondary fragmentation mechanism, such as those producing flat bands in momentum space via destructive quantum interference. We further analyze the effects of introducing a staggered magnetic field and a PXP term; while the former maintains fragmentation, the latter eliminates it. A Floquet variant with a time-dependent staggered field also avoids thermalization, exhibiting unique behaviors like the freezing of exponentially many states at specific drive frequencies. Finally, we map the model to a $U(1)$ lattice gauge theory coupled to dynamical fermions, interpreting certain anomalous states in this framework. We observe that a subset of gauge-invariant states displays reduced mobility for elementary charged excitations, with only specific charge-neutral objects remaining mobile, suggesting a link to fracton physics.

Operated by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) is a ten-year project scheduled to begin in 2022, designed to capture images of half the sky every three nights. LSST generates approximately 20TB of raw data nightly, requiring near real-time calibration and analysis. Due to this massive data volume, the conventional approach of downloading subsets for reprocessing encounters significant hurdles. This paper outlines the initial development of an astronomical science gateway that will allow researchers to process images and catalogs at scale. Specifically, this first phase focuses on running the Rubin LSST Science Pipelines—a suite of algorithms for image and catalog processing—on Amazon Web Services (AWS). We also present our preliminary observations regarding the performance, scalability, and costs of deploying such a system in the cloud.

The deployment of smart manufacturing systems is accelerating due to their capacity to process diverse sensed information and act upon derived insights. Primarily, these systems aim to quickly identify or predict failures to minimize operational expenses and eliminate downtime, which often requires detecting anomalies within sensor data. However, this domain presents distinct technical challenges, including the presence of various sensor types with differing costs and capabilities, as well as data characteristics that fluctuate based on operating conditions, such as motor RPM. Consequently, anomaly detection must be calibrated relative to specific operating points. This paper analyzes four datasets from manufacturing testbeds, evaluating both traditional and machine learning-based forecasting models for predicting sensor time series. Furthermore, addressing sparse data from certain sensors, we utilize transfer learning from high-data-rate sensors to classify defect types. Collectively, these efforts demonstrate the feasibility of predictive failure classification, thereby advancing the path toward predictive maintenance.

Pretrained language models (PLMs) frequently struggle to fairly represent users from specific global regions due to the scarcity of such regions in their training data. Assessing biases in modern PLMs, which are trained on massive datasets, remains challenging because of their opaque architecture and the sheer volume of information involved. This study introduces a Geographic-Representation Probing Framework that utilizes self-conditioning and entity-country mappings to investigate geographic bias and knowledge within these models. Our results indicate that while PLM representations align remarkably well with real-world country associations, this knowledge is distributed unevenly across languages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that although large PLMs capture concepts of geographical proximity, they tend to excessively amplify geopolitical favoritism during inference.

Current state-of-the-art techniques for 2-player zero-sum imperfect information games primarily utilize linear programming or regret minimization, excluding dynamic programming (DP) and heuristic search (HS)—methods that are central to solving other sequential decision problems. In partially observable or collaborative contexts, such as POMDPs and Dec-POMDPs, DP and HS necessitate the introduction of a sufficient statistic to render the problem fully observable, alongside convex approximators to bound the optimal value function. While this strategy has worked for specific subclasses of 2-player zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs), its application to the general case remains unresolved. We resolve this by (i) formally defining an equivalent game for analysis, (ii) establishing mathematical properties of the optimal value function that enable the derivation of bounds coupled with solution strategies, (iii) introducing, for the first time, an HSVI-like solver guaranteed to converge to an $\epsilon$-optimal solution in finite time, and (iv) conducting an empirical evaluation. These contributions pave the way for a new class of promising methods that complement existing approaches based on linear programming or iterative algorithms.

Although major white matter tracts are central to neuroscience and medical research, manually dissecting them from diffusion MRI tractograms in large cohorts is labor-intensive, demands expert expertise, and lacks reproducibility. Our prior work introduced Tract Orientation Mapping (TOM), a novel bundle-specific tractography method that learns a mapping from original fiber orientation distribution function (FOD) peaks to tract-specific peaks known as tract orientation maps, where each map defines the voxel-wise principal orientation of a specific tract. This study extends TOM by integrating precise segmentations of tract outlines along with their start and end regions. Additionally, we developed a custom probabilistic tracking algorithm that samples from a Gaussian distribution with a fixed standard deviation centered on each peak, facilitating more comprehensive tracking on these maps compared to deterministic methods. These enhancements allow for the automatic generation of bundle-specific tractograms with unprecedented accuracy. Evaluations across 72 bundles using high-quality, low-quality, and phantom data demonstrate that our approach is faster and yields more accurate results than seven state-of-the-art benchmark methods, while eliminating cumbersome steps such as whole-brain tractography, non-linear registration, clustering, or manual dissection. Furthermore, testing on 17 datasets confirms that the method generalizes effectively across various scanners, acquisition settings, and pathological conditions. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/TractSeg.

This paper introduces an embedding method designed to estimate standard model $\tau\tau$ backgrounds using minimal simulation input. By removing muons from reconstructed $\mu\mu$ events in the data and substituting them with simulated tau leptons sharing identical kinematic properties, the study generates hybrid events that rely on simulation only for tau decay. This approach circumvents difficulties associated with simulating underlying events or associated jet production. Developed for the CMS experiment, the technique's validation and associated uncertainties are examined. Performance is demonstrated using a sample of proton-proton collisions recorded by CMS in 2017 at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 41.5 fb$^{-1}$.

Reference \cite{key-1} details the application of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) for distinguishing neutrino events from backgrounds in reactor experiments. While that study utilizes photoelectron counts from PMTs as inputs, the current work employs reconstructed event energy and position. Using Monte-Carlo simulations of a toy detector, neutrino events and three primary backgrounds were generated within the signal region. Compared to the approach in Ref.\cite{key-1}, the BNN method presented here achieves superior rejection of $^{8}$He/$^{9}$Li and uncorrelated backgrounds, resulting in significantly improved ratios for both relative to the signal. However, this method fails to identify a larger fraction of fast neutron backgrounds, leading to a slightly higher fast neutron-to-signal ratio than observed in Ref.\cite{key-1}.

Although various BDI logics have been introduced within Agent Programming, the connection between these logics and the specific agent programs they are intended to describe remains unclear. Furthermore, because these logics rely on modal logic, their associated reasoning problems are generally intractable, which restricts their application to real-world scenarios. This research employs Dynamic Preference Logic to establish a semantic foundation for BDI agent programming languages and examines tractable expressive subsets of this logic for reasoning about agent programs. Consequently, our goal is to enable the implementation of semantically grounded agent programming languages that feature efficient reasoning cycles.

Gaining a quantitative grasp of bee colony dynamics is vital for advancing global initiatives to bolster bee health and strengthen pollination services. While conventional methods rely either on theoretical modeling or data-driven statistical analysis, we contend that integrating both approaches is necessary to derive interpretable insights into colony states. Specifically, we demonstrate this synergy using time series data on intra-day weight fluctuations. By employing ordinary differential equations to simulate how bee foraging and food processing influence overall hive weight, we establish a method to estimate reliable ranges for the model's ten parameters using data from a single day. Analysis across ten hives at various times reveals that key health indicators—such as foraging success (total food collected) and the count of active foragers—are robustly estimated and align with previously reported findings. These metrics can serve as early warning signals for potential colony collapse.

Transferring composite data structures containing variable-length fields frequently demands the creation of complex, non-uniform protocols that lack compatibility across different hardware architectures. When individual projects develop proprietary data formats and communication protocols, collaboration among hardware developers is significantly hindered, a problem that is particularly acute within the open-source community. Furthermore, the high-level intent of a protocol often becomes obscured when translated into low-level languages during custom design, necessitating extensive documentation; interpreting this documentation introduces additional opportunities for errors.

To address these challenges, the Tydi specification (Tydi-spec) was introduced to standardize composite and variable-length data structures through a formal type system and a unified protocol for transferring typed data between hardware components. The Tydi intermediate representation (Tydi-IR) builds upon this by defining typed interfaces, components, and the connections linking them.

This paper introduces Tydi-lang, a high-level hardware description language (HDL) tailored for streaming designs. Tydi-lang integrates Tydi-spec to define typed streams and offers templates for describing abstract, reusable components. We have implemented an open-source compiler that translates Tydi-lang into Tydi-IR. Leveraging an existing Tydi-IR to VHDL compiler, we also present a simulator blueprint designed to detect streaming bottlenecks. We provide several Tydi-lang examples that translate high-level SQL queries into VHDL, demonstrating that Tydi-lang can effectively increase the level of abstraction and reduce design effort.

A pseudo Nambu-Goldstone boson, exemplified by axion-like particles, serves as a theoretically robust inflaton due to its naturally flat potential, a feature known as natural inflation. This stability arises because Goldstone's theorem shields the potential from significant quantum corrections. However, such corrections typically induce an $R^2$ term in the action, introducing the scalaron as an alternative inflaton candidate; this term is equivalent to a scalar field possessing a quasi-flat potential, characteristic of Starobinsky inflation. This study explores a novel multifield framework where both the scalaron and a pseudo Nambu-Goldstone boson actively drive inflation, termed natural-scalaron inflation. To ensure generality, the model incorporates a non-minimal coupling, which is shown to originate from microscopic theories. The analysis demonstrates that a stable inflationary attractor persists even when the masses of the two inflatons are comparable. Furthermore, the inclusion of the scalaron enables compliance with all observational constraints across a broad parameter space, a capability that pure-natural inflation lacks.

Black solitons in the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation with intensity-dependent dispersion share identical characteristics with those in the cubic defocusing NLS equation. However, we demonstrate that intensity-dependent dispersion yields novel features in the stability analysis of these black solitons. Specifically, the spectral stability problem admits only isolated eigenvalues along the imaginary axis. Furthermore, energetic stability arguments remain valid within Sobolev spaces equipped with exponential weights. Additionally, the black soliton survives the addition of a small decaying potential and retains spectral stability when anchored at the minima of the effective potential. The model also supports a continuum of traveling dark solitons across all wave speeds; consequently, we integrate properties of these dark solitons, particularly those with low wave speeds, into the analysis of the black soliton's orbital stability.

Quintessential inflation encompasses models where one scalar field accounts for both the inflationary epoch and the current acceleration of the universe. This review examines the formalism of this unified framework, emphasizing its fundamental components. Achieving a consistent unification requires a scalar field potential that begins shallow, transitions to a steep region, and returns to a shallow state near the present day. To ensure the scalar field does not disrupt the thermal history, the potential must remain steep after inflation, while late-time dynamics must be independent of initial conditions. The paper details scaling and asymptotic scaling solutions, along with the transition mechanism from these regimes to late-time acceleration. A fresh analysis of scaling solutions is provided, as they are pivotal to the unification theme. Regarding the exit mechanism, significant focus is placed on the dynamic coupling between massive neutrinos and the scalar field, which can drive late-time acceleration. We offer a comprehensive analytical treatment of scalar field dynamics under such coupling. Finally, we briefly address a unique characteristic of quintessential inflation: the generation of a blue spectrum of gravitational waves during the shift from inflation to the kinetic regime.

This research examines various domination scenarios involving attacking and non-attacking rooks and queens on polyominoes and polycubes across all dimensions. Our primary finding establishes that determining domination for non-attacking queens on polyominoes and non-attacking rooks on three-dimensional polycubes is NP-complete. Furthermore, we investigate these problems within the subset of convex polyominoes, proposing and providing preliminary support for the conjecture that they remain NP-complete for both piece types. Additionally, we calculated new values for classical queen domination on standard chessboards by formulating the problem as an integer linear programming task. Leveraging this computational approach alongside the Godot game engine, we created a video game featuring minimal domination strategies for queens and rooks on randomly generated polyominoes.

We outline the deployment of a quantum network utilizing existing fiber infrastructure in the Chicago region. This work details the network's topology and control architecture, while demonstrating initial findings regarding quantum teleportation and the simultaneous transmission of quantum and classical data over a shared fiber link.

Machines capable of interpreting human actions can utilize sign language semantics to bridge communication gaps between hearing-impaired individuals and the general public. Sign Language Recognition (SLR) represents a pivotal and engaging domain within computer vision and pattern recognition. Although SLR applications are expanding rapidly, system performance remains highly sensitive to environmental conditions, image resolution, input modalities, and dataset characteristics. Consequently, many researchers are dedicated to developing generic, real-time SLR frameworks. This review offers a thorough examination of SLR, addressing its requirements, obstacles, and associated issues. We analyze existing literature covering both manual and non-manual features, diverse modalities, and various datasets. Furthermore, we evaluate the decade-long progress and current state-of-the-art SLR models. By identifying research gaps and limitations, we propose future directions. Ultimately, this paper serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers and readers seeking insight into SLR and the evolution of advanced SLR architectures.

Difference equations, exemplified by the Ricker map, become unstable and transition into deterministic chaos when the parameter value increases. To stabilize these systems, various methods can be employed. Proportional Feedback control involves reducing the state variable proportionally at every $k$th step. Specifically, if $k \neq 1$, this approach stabilizes a cycle rather than an equilibrium. Furthermore, the model can include an additive noise term to represent environmental variability and a multiplicative noise term to account for fluctuations in control intensity. This paper addresses both aspects, demonstrating the feasibility of achieving a stable blurred $k$-cycle. The study utilizes examples from the Ricker model and equations with unbounded functions, such as bobwhite quail population models. Although theoretical results confirm stabilization only with either multiplicative or additive noise individually, numerical simulations show that a blurred cycle can be stabilized even when both types of noise are present.

The magnetic field is crucial to the formation of highly collimated jets in active galactic nuclei (AGN). However, relativistic effects make it impossible to directly reconstruct the magnetic field direction as being transverse to electric vectors in radio maps. Consequently, we established the \textbf{B}-field topology by modeling the transverse distributions of total and linearly polarized intensity, polarization degree, and the deviation of the polarization direction from the local jet axis, subsequently comparing these models with observational data. We evaluated two scenarios: (i) a helical field with varying twist angles, and (ii) a toroidal field along the jet axis encased in a sheath containing a longitudinal field, where we varied the sheath thickness relative to the spine. In this second scenario, the sheath velocity was assumed to be equal to or less than that of the spine. Relativistic effects were accounted for in a general case where the jet axis and velocity vector do not align with the radial direction. Our simulations successfully replicate the primary features of observed transverse polarization profiles in parsec-scale AGN jets. We found that the shapes of these theoretical transverse distributions are heavily influenced by the outflow's kinematic and geometric parameters. This was demonstrated across three AGNs exhibiting distinct yet typical polarization patterns on radio maps. For each object, we identified model parameters that yielded a qualitative match between theoretical profiles and observations, indicating that the \textbf{B}-field remains strongly ordered on parsec scales.

This work demonstrates the application of realization theory to determine solutions for the Carath\'eodory extremal problem within the symmetrized bidisc, defined as \( G = \{(z+w,zw):|z|<1, \, |w|<1\} \). It is established that, in the generic case, solutions are unique modulo composition with disc automorphisms. Additionally, explicit formulae are derived for extremal functions corresponding to tangents of non-generic types in the Carath\'eodory problem.

Certain meta-stable polymorphs of bismuth monolayers (bismuthene) possess topologically nontrivial phases, yet it is currently unknown whether substrate interactions can stabilize these structures, maintain their topological characteristics, or guide the design of optimal substrates to enhance robustness. Leveraging first-principles methods, we reveal that bismuthene polymorphs achieve stability when interfaced with silicon carbide (SiC), silicon (Si), and silicon dioxide (SiO2). Furthermore, we find that proximity effects in these heterostructures significantly alter the monolayer's electronic structure, even in cases of weak bonding. Our analysis identifies van der Waals forces and the disruption of sublattice symmetry as the primary drivers of these electronic modifications. Ultimately, this study confirms that substrate interactions can fortify the topological properties of bismuthene polymorphs, rendering them viable for experimental study and technological implementation.

We tackle the challenge of calculating operator norms for matrices induced by specific norms defined on both the input and output spaces. While it is established that computing these norms is NP-hard in most scenarios—except for a limited number of solvable instances, primarily when both norms are Euclidean—we define broad families of input and output norms (specifically "ellitopic" and "co-ellitopic") that enable reasonably tight and computationally efficient upper bounds on the associated operator norms. We further extend these findings to bound the "robust operator norm" of an uncertain matrix subject to box uncertainty, defined as the maximum operator norm across all matrices expressible as a linear combination of a given set with coefficients having a magnitude no greater than 1. Finally, we explore applications of these norm-bounding techniques, including: (1) the computationally efficient synthesis of affine, non-anticipative, finite-horizon control for discrete-time linear dynamical systems with constraints on peak-to-peak gains; (2) signal recovery in the presence of uncertainties within the sensing matrix; and (3) the identification of parameters for time-invariant discrete-time linear dynamical systems using noisy state and input observations over a specified horizon, assuming "uncertain-but-bounded" noise that varies within a box.

Current automatic GUI test generators frequently produce tests lacking semantic relevance, leading to the omission of critical test scenarios. To mitigate this, test adaptation techniques can automatically derive semantically meaningful GUI tests by leveraging test cases from applications with comparable functionalities. This paper introduces ADAPTDROID, a method that frames test adaptation as a search problem and employs evolutionary testing to adapt both GUI tests and oracles across similar Android applications. Evaluation across 32 popular Android apps demonstrated that ADAPTDROID successfully adapted semantically relevant test cases in 11 out of 20 cross-application scenarios.

We examined the tamper-resistant attributes of Blockchain and its efficacy within IoT environments. Specifically, we constructed an IoT testbed integrated with Blockchain technology. Multiple experiments were performed and analyzed to verify the block validation mechanisms, confirming the tamper-resistant nature of Blockchain in establishing trust for IoT systems. A demonstration video is available at [1].

Various dynamical processes occurring on networks can be characterized by the spectral properties of specific linear operators, which encode the dependence of dynamical rules on network topology. While these spectral features are often derived theoretically using only local node attributes, such as degree distributions, many networks exhibit large-scale modular structures that significantly alter their spectral characteristics and are overlooked in simplified models. In this work, we derive the spectrum for a broad family of operators—including adjacency, Laplacian, and normalized Laplacian matrices—for networks with generic modular structures in the limit of large degrees. We investigate the conditions under which isolated eigenvalues merge with the continuous spectral band, rendering the planted modular structure undetectable via spectral methods. This critical transition determines when a modular structure is sufficiently robust to impact a specific dynamical process. We demonstrate that this transition occurs at distinct points for different matrices, implying that the detectability threshold varies considerably depending on the operator selected. Consequently, even with identical large-scale structures, the sensitivity of dynamical processes associated with each matrix to modular features differs. Furthermore, we show that, except for the Laplacian matrix, these distinct transitions converge to a single point when modules are homogeneous, but remain separate otherwise.

For the BraTS 2021 segmentation challenge, we utilized an ensemble comprising a modified TransBTS, nnU-Net, and a hybrid of both. We enhanced the original TransBTS architecture by integrating Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks, increasing the number of CNN layers, and substituting positional encodings in Transformer blocks with learnable Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) embeddings to ensure adaptability to varying input sizes during inference. These adjustments significantly boosted TransBTS performance. Drawing inspiration from the nnU-Net framework, we integrated our improved TransBTS by replacing its internal architecture with our custom model. On the BraTS 2021 Validation set, this ensemble achieved Dice scores of 0.8496, 0.8698, and 0.9256, and HD95 values of 15.72, 11.057, and 3.374 for enhancing tumor, tumor core, and whole tumor, respectively. Our code is publicly available.

This research explores the practical implementation of privacy-preserving ticketing systems for public transit. The proposed protocols are derived from existing, privacy-compromising global transit systems. The first protocol mimics traditional paper tickets, while the second utilizes a pay-as-you-go model where fares are calculated at check-in and check-out. Both approaches rely on smartphones as the primary device for storing tickets or travel credit. We view this work as a foundational step toward designing common infrastructure with privacy in mind, with specific focus on handling system failures.

The cross section for top quark pair production was measured during proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. Data gathered during a dedicated 2017 LHC run characterized by low energy and intensity yielded an integrated luminosity of 302 pb$^{-1}$. This analysis focused on events containing one electron and one muon with opposite charges, accompanied by at least two jets. The initial cross section measurement was determined to be 60.7 $\pm$ 5.0 (stat) $\pm$ 2.8 (syst) $\pm$ 1.1 (lumi) pb. To mitigate statistical uncertainty, this result was combined with data from a single lepton + jets channel collected in 2015 at the same energy level, which provided 27.4 pb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The final combined value is 63.0 $\pm$ 4.1 (stat) $\pm$ 3.0 (syst+lumi) pb, consistent with the standard model prediction of 66.8 $^{+2.9}_{-3.1}$ pb.

Health mention classification focuses on identifying diseases within text that includes disease-related terminology, a task complicated by non-medical and figurative usage. Recently, adversarial training has become a popular regularization technique in various NLP applications. This paper introduces a novel method for training language models to classify health mentions in tweets by incorporating adversarial training. We create adversarial examples by injecting Gaussian noise into the transformer model representations at multiple levels. Additionally, we utilize contrastive loss as a secondary objective function. The proposed approach is evaluated on an extended version of the PHM2017 dataset, with results demonstrating a significant performance improvement over baseline methods. Our analysis reveals that introducing noise at earlier layers enhances model performance, whereas noise at intermediate layers degrades it. Furthermore, adding noise to the final layers yields better results than adding it to the middle layers.

Molecular communication (MC) facilitates collaboration among spatially distributed molecular robots via feedback control driven by diffusing signal molecules. Yet, traditional analysis frameworks for MC channels primarily address unidirectional communication, often overlooking the impact of feedback interactions. This paper introduces a comprehensive control-theoretic modeling framework for bidirectional MC systems that systematically captures the dynamics of feedback control through MC. The proposed approach accounts for both molecular diffusion dynamics and the boundary dynamics at the robots, thereby modeling the latency at the interface between the communication channel and the robots. This enables the systematic analysis of bidirectional communication systems using established control theory methods. Furthermore, we conduct a frequency response analysis based on this framework to establish a general design guideline for MC systems aiming to transmit signals with a specific control bandwidth. Finally, we illustrate these findings by detailing a step-by-step design procedure for a specific MC channel that meets a given specification.

Currently, gender diversity within the technology industry has not achieved a balanced equilibrium between men and women. Numerous women face barriers to entering computer science stemming from social, cultural, structural, and socialization-related factors, with implicit gender bias playing a significant role. The scarcity of female representation in the field hinders the cultivation or expansion of interest in these areas. To encourage women to pursue these careers, it is essential to provide female role models and greater transparency regarding job roles. Furthermore, leaders can actively foster gender diversity by implementing tailored initiatives.

Although multi-task and transfer learning have recently achieved significant success in natural language processing (NLP), there has been a lack of systematic investigation into how increasing the number of pre-training tasks affects performance. To address this gap, we introduce ExMix (Extreme Mixture), a vast dataset comprising 10^7 supervised NLP tasks spanning diverse domains and task categories. Leveraging ExMix, we examine multi-task pre-training at an unprecedented scale and investigate transfer relationships among common task families. Our analysis reveals that manually selecting an optimal set of tasks for multi-task pre-training is complex, and that scaling up multi-task training alone can substantially enhance model performance. Furthermore, we present ExT5, a model pre-trained using a combination of self-supervised span denoising and supervised ExMix tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ExT5 surpasses strong T5 baselines on SuperGLUE, GEM, Rainbow, Closed-Book QA, and various tasks beyond ExMix, while also significantly improving sample efficiency during pre-training.

We examine the max-type equation
$$x_{n+4}=\max\{x_{n+3},x_{n+2},x_{n+1},0\}-x_n,$$
starting from arbitrary real initial values. We provide a full characterization of its period set $\mathrm{Per}(F_4)$ and its associated periodic orbits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that there exists a natural number $N \notin \mathrm{Per}(F_4)$ such that the set $\{N+m : m \geq 1, m \in \mathbb{N}\}$ is contained within $\mathrm{Per}(F_4)$.

Automatic songwriting, an engaging field in both academia and industry, involves composing lyrics and/or melodies using machines. This process relies heavily on two critical tasks: generating melodies from lyrics and generating lyrics from melodies. Both tasks face significant hurdles: first, the scarcity of paired lyric-melody data limits generation quality, as the weak correlation between the two modalities necessitates large training sets; second, the requirement for strict lyric-melody alignment depends on specialized modeling techniques. To overcome these issues, we introduce SongMASS, which utilizes masked sequence-to-sequence (MASS) pre-training and attention-based alignment modeling for bidirectional generation. Specifically, SongMASS extends sentence-level MASS pre-training to the song level to capture long-range contextual information, employing separate encoders and decoders for each modality. Furthermore, it enhances alignment during training by combining sentence-level attention masks with token-level constraints. During inference, a dynamic programming approach establishes alignment between lyrics (words/syllables) and melodies (notes). Trained on unpaired datasets, SongMASS achieves superior generation quality in both objective and subjective evaluations compared to baseline methods lacking pre-training or alignment constraints.

Bell inequalities serve as effective witnesses for device-independent applications even when faced with quantum or post-quantum eavesdroppers, though this capability is currently limited to single entangled systems. Our objective is to investigate device-independent frameworks for quantum networks. We introduce a novel Bell inequality designed to confirm genuine multipartite nonlocality in connected quantum networks, encompassing cyclic architectures and universal resources for measurement-based quantum computation. Furthermore, this approach enables the construction of a new monogamy relation within a fully device-independent setting utilizing multisource quantum resources. Finally, we apply this model to multiparty quantum key distribution, blind quantum computation, and quantum secret sharing. This framework holds the potential to inspire diverse large-scale, device-independent applications across quantum networks.

We examined fundamental correlations among various structural parameters of galaxies using data from diverse literature samples across different passbands. Our discussion covers disc scaling relations and addresses contentious aspects of the "Photometric Plane" for bulges and ellipticals, as well as various iterations of the renowned Kormendy relation. We demonstrate that while certain correlations are merely artifacts (self-correlations), others genuinely uncover new essential details regarding galactic structural properties. Our primary findings are as follows: (1) Currently, we cannot assert that faint stellar discs are, on average, thinner than those in high surface brightness galaxies; the observed correlation between central surface brightness and thickness arises solely from using a transparent exponential disc model to describe real discs. (2) The Photometric Plane lacks independent physical significance; its various forms are essentially sophisticated variations of the Kormendy relation or self-correlations involving central surface brightness and the Sersic index $n$ for bulges/ellipticals. (3) The Kormendy relation represents a physical correlation, likely reflecting differences in the origins of bright versus faint ellipticals and bulges. To substantiate our main hypothesis, we present arguments utilizing the creation of artificial samples.

Real-world networks are typically complex and evolving, making it essential to analyze how network topology influences traffic dynamics and congestion. To address this, we developed a time-varying network model in which new nodes join the existing network with a probability proportional to a node's degree and exhibit disassortativity relative to its neighbors. Betweenness centrality (BC) is crucial for identifying influential nodes and determining users' shortest paths, as these routes often pass through hub nodes where congestion is more likely. Consequently, BC-BC correlation is employed to trace user routes. A link connecting two hub nodes is more prone to reduced data forwarding capacity. Additionally, nodes displaying disassortativity with their neighbors are more likely to forward packets and be selected for routing. Finally, we calculated the optimal data sending rate and critical packet generation rate for the proposed model, demonstrating improved performance compared to the classical scale-free network model.

Reference [1] derived the impulse response for the first arrival position (FAP) channel in both 2D and 3D molecular communication (MC) environments but left its Shannon capacity unresolved. The primary challenge in calculating this capacity stems from the FAP density transforming into a multi-dimensional Cauchy distribution as drift velocity vanishes. Consequently, standard mutual information maximization techniques fail because the first and second moments of a Cauchy distribution are undefined. This paper presents a complete characterization of the zero-drift FAP channel capacity for 2D and 3D spaces. The resulting capacity formula resembles that of a Gaussian channel under a second-moment power constraint. Notably, the 3D FAP channel capacity is double that of the 2D case, indicating that capacity increases with spatial dimension. Furthermore, our technical advances involve substituting the conventional power constraint with a modified logarithmic constraint and replacing the input signal constraint with an output signal constraint to ensure a concise final formula.

This study examines the stability of Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) when applied to noisy data. To ensure stability, we integrated truncated total least squares (T-TLS) regression with optimal truncation level selection into the TLS DMD framework. By incorporating truncation regularization, the T-TLS DMD method enhances computational stability without sacrificing the accuracy of the original TLS DMD. We assessed the performance of T-TLS DMD using wake analysis behind a cylinder and practical pressure-sensitive paint (PSP) data regarding the buffet cell phenomenon. The findings underscore the critical role of regularization within DMD algorithms. Regarding eigenvalues, T-TLS DMD demonstrated greater resistance to noise, yielding stable and accurate results, in contrast to the significant variations observed in TLS and subspace DMD due to noise. Additionally, we noted that both standard and exact DMD eigenvalues exhibit a tendency to shift toward the damping side, a phenomenon previously documented. Concerning eigenvectors, T-TLS and exact DMD successfully captured distinct flow patterns even amidst noise, whereas TLS and subspace DMD failed to do so clearly under similar conditions.

For any real number $k$, let $\pi_k(x) = \sum_{p\le x} p^k$. We establish that for $k>0$, the difference $\pi_k(x) - \pi(x^{k+1})$ is $\Omega_{\pm}\left(\frac{x^{\frac12+k}}{\log x} \log\log\log x\right)$ as $x\to\infty$, and demonstrate an analogous result for the range $-1<k<0$. These findings improve upon and rectify a proof error in a previous paper by J. Gerard and the author. Furthermore, we provide quantitative measures supporting the observation from that earlier work that $\pi_k(x) - \pi(x^{k+1})$ is typically negative when $k>0$ and typically positive when $-1<k<0$.

This study employs numerical simulations to investigate advective-diffusive scalar transport within three-dimensional porous media featuring high-contrast, discontinuous permeability fields, which were generated using a truncated pluri-Gaussian geostatistical method. By varying permeability contrasts, correlation lengths, and Péclet numbers, we characterize the shift toward non-Fickian transport behavior. This deviation is primarily caused by significant permeability differences between zones and is amplified by connected high-permeability channels characterized by elevated advective velocities. Consequently, the overall transport dynamics diverge from the macroscopic advection-dispersion model grounded in Fickian analogy. The simulations utilize an Eulerian approach within a novel unified numerical framework built on the \of finite-volume library, designed to: i) generate random pluri-Gaussian porous media, ii) solve steady-state Darcy-scale flow, iii) solve the advection-diffusion equation, and iv) compute post-processing metrics including first-order statistics, spatial probability density functions, and breakthrough curves. Our analysis reveals a hierarchy of factors driving non-Fickian transport, with permeability contrast strength acting as the primary determinant. The Péclet number and the characteristic length of facies transitions serve as secondary influences. Transport adheres to Fickian principles when facies conductivities differ by no more than one order of magnitude; however, greater permeability contrasts intensify the formation of fast-flow channels, thereby promoting non-Fickian transport.

The ALICE detector's muon spectrometer at the LHC has measured $\Upsilon$ meson production in Pb-Pb collisions at a nucleon pair center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5$ TeV. In the forward rapidity range of $2.5<y<4.0$, yields and nuclear modification factors were analyzed as functions of rapidity, transverse momentum, and collision centrality. Results indicate that $\Upsilon$(1S) production is suppressed by approximately a factor of three compared to proton-proton collisions. Additionally, a significant $\Upsilon$(2S) signal was observed for the first time at forward rapidity, showing a suppression roughly 2-3 times greater than that of the ground state. These findings are contrasted with predictions from transport, hydrodynamic, comover, and statistical hadronisation models.

Pater's main article makes a compelling argument for deepening the connection between theoretical linguistics and connectionism (deep learning). This commentary broadens those arguments to cover semantics, with a specific focus on challenges related to learning, compositionality, and lexical meaning.

We introduce a self-improving algorithm designed to compute Voronoi diagrams under a fixed convex distance function, operating with constant description complexity. The $n$ input points are sampled from a concealed mixture of product distributions; we are provided with an upper bound $m = o(\sqrt{n})$ on the count of these distributions and the guarantee that each distribution contributes an input instance with a probability of at least $\Omega(1/n)$. For any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, following a training phase requiring $O\bigl(mn\log^{O(1)} (mn) + m^{\varepsilon} n^{1+\varepsilon}\log(mn)\bigr)$ time, the algorithm achieves an expected runtime of $O\bigl(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}n\log m + \frac{1}{\varepsilon}n2^{O(\log^* n)} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon}H\bigr)$ with a success probability of at least $1 - O(1/n)$, where $H$ represents the entropy of the Voronoi diagram output distribution. This expectation accounts for both the input distribution and the algorithm's randomized choices. Specifically, when utilizing the Euclidean metric, the expected runtime is refined to $O\bigl(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}n\log m + \frac{1}{\varepsilon}H\bigr)$.

Building upon a prior demonstration that electric charge quantization naturally emerges in renormalizable $SU(3)_c \otimes SU(n)_{L} \otimes U(1)_{Y}$ gauge theories, this work advances the same framework to derive the exact quantization of weak charges. This is achieved by first establishing a viable boson mass spectrum through an appropriate parametrization of the Higgs sector. Subsequently, diagonalizing the neutral boson mass matrix yields the quantized neutral weak charge operators. The resulting model fully reproduces Standard Model phenomenology, as the electroweak scale ($v_{SM}=246$ GeV) is decoupled from the higher unification scale ($V\sim$ 10 TeV) characteristic of our generalized electro-weak theory.

Piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) offer a powerful framework for modeling intricate industrial dynamical systems. However, the computational expense associated with simulating these processes renders traditional Monte Carlo methods ineffective for reliability assessment. This challenge can be addressed through an adaptive importance sampling (AIS) approach grounded in a cross-entropy (CE) procedure, which significantly reduces variance. The efficacy of this AIS method hinges on selecting an appropriate family of approximations for the PDMP's committor function. The text introduces several such families, specifically designed for high-dimensional industrial contexts, with functional forms derived from fault tree analysis concepts like minimal path sets and minimal cut sets. The proposed methodology is thoroughly examined and validated through applications to both academic models and a realistic nuclear industry system.

Co-adaptive guidance seeks to facilitate efficient human-machine collaboration within visual analytics, a concept supported by various theoretical frameworks. This paper connects these conceptual models to practical application by presenting an accessible guidance model and a companion library that translate theory into practice. We offer a system-provided guidance model grounded in design templates and derived strategies. This model is instantiated in a library named Lotse, which enables the specification of guidance strategies via definition files and automatically generates executable code. Lotse represents the first library to utilize this approach; it supports the development of reusable guidance strategies for retrofitting existing applications and encourages the formation of general guidance strategy patterns. We validated its efficacy through initial case studies with visual analytics researchers possessing varying levels of expertise in guidance design, demonstrating that Lotse allows for the effective and rapid implementation of guidance. Additionally, we analyzed the framework's cognitive dimensions to assess its expressiveness and provided a summary of open research questions aimed at aligning guidance practices with its complex theoretical underpinnings.

The local diffusion of strictly hyperbolic higher-order partial differential equations with constant coefficients at all simple singularities of associated wavefronts can be understood and identified through just two local geometric characteristics. We firmly refute the intuitive conjecture that this principle extends to arbitrary singularities by providing counterexamples: instances of diffusion occurring at all non-simple singularity classes of generic wavefronts in odd-dimensional spaces, which cannot be reduced to diffusion at simple singular points.

This research investigates the short-time and long-time existence, finite propagation speed, and finite-time blow-up of nonnegative solutions to long-wave unstable thin film equations defined as $h_t = -a_0(h^n h_{xxx})_x - a_1(h^m h_x)_x$, where $n>0$, $a_0 > 0$, and $a_1 >0$. The findings regarding existence and finite speed of propagation broaden the scope of results established in [Comm Pure Appl Math 51:625--661, 1998]. Specifically, for the range $0<n<2$, we demonstrate the existence of a nonnegative, compactly supported, strong solution on the real line that exhibits finite-time blow-up. This construction necessitates initial data that are nonnegative, compactly supported in $\R^1$, belong to $H^1(\R^1)$, and possess negative energy. Furthermore, the blow-up phenomenon is proven across a broad spectrum of $(n,m)$ exponents, extending previous work found in [Indiana Univ Math J 49:1323--1366, 2000].

Iterative algorithms play a critical role in decision-making and control systems. As the proliferation of new, distributed, and proprietary algorithms accelerates, the demand for effective classification and comparison methods has likewise increased. By modeling these algorithms as discrete-time dynamical systems and applying Koopman operator theory, we can detect (semi-)conjugacies among them based on their spectral characteristics. This approach establishes a comprehensive framework for categorizing and evaluating such algorithms.

The stability of high-performance piezo-acoustic drop-on-demand (DOD) inkjet printers is often hindered by air bubbles trapped within the ink channel. This study investigates the mechanism of bubble detachment from an acoustically actuated meniscus in a transparent DOD printhead, varying the driving waveforms. We demonstrate that bubble detachment arises from low-amplitude higher-order meniscus oscillations superimposed on the primary high-amplitude motion responsible for droplet ejection. Within a specific range of control parameters, phase inversion between low and high-frequency components triggers the encapsulation of an air cavity and subsequent bubble detachment. Despite phenotypic similarities, this process differs from capillary wave interactions seen during drop impact on liquid pools. Instead, we identify geometrical flow focusing as the underlying mechanism: initially, an outward jet forms on the retracted concave meniscus. When a subsequent high-frequency pressure wave strikes the now toroidal meniscus, it propels the toroidal ring outward, creating an air cavity capable of pinching off. The critical parameters governing this detachment are pulse timing and amplitude. To mitigate bubble entrainment, the threshold for detachment can be raised by suppressing high-frequency acoustic waves via optimized waveform design. Consequently, this research enhances inkjet printer stability by providing a physical understanding of meniscus instabilities.

Addressing the COVID-19 pandemic presents an urgent global challenge, where the rapid geographic dissemination of SARS-CoV-2 mirrors underlying social structures. Prior to the widespread availability of effective vaccines and treatments, public health must depend on non-pharmaceutical interventions such as social distancing, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, contact tracing, and frequent testing to curb transmission. Among these measures, frequent testing is paramount when other alternatives are unavailable. We propose a network-based approach to identify optimal pool testing strategies tailored for low-resource settings, capable of detecting infected individuals using a minimal number of tests and testing rounds, particularly at low virus prevalence. By simulating stochastic infection trajectories within quarantined societies, we demonstrate that while limited social interaction can help flatten the curve, comparable outcomes are achievable through the strategic identification and isolation of infected persons to maintain a healthier social structure. This analysis evaluates the most effective containment strategies using an algorithm that combines sample pooling with group testing [1]. A critical parameter for flattening infection curves with this method is the frequency of testing in zones reporting high infection rates. Conversely, the algorithm's efficiency diminishes significantly when relying on random searches for infected individuals.

This paper introduces Hamilton's equations for the Teleparallel Equivalent of General Relativity (TEGR), a reformulation of general relativity utilizing a connection that is curvatureless, metric-compatible, and torsionful. By employing an irreducible decomposition of phase space variables into vector, antisymmetric, symmetric, and trace-free components, we derive the TEGR Hamiltonian. For the first time in existing literature, we present this Hamiltonian within a covariant formalism, utilizing a spin connection dependent on Lorentz matrices. We establish the requisite mathematical framework to calculate Hamilton's equations in both the Weitzenböck gauge and the covariant formulation; the latter requires the introduction of new fields, specifically Lorentz matrices and their conjugate momenta. Furthermore, we derive explicit relationships between the conjugate momenta of the tetrad and those of the metric as traditionally defined in General Relativity, facilitating a comparison between the two formalisms.

Anomaly detection (AD), which distinguishes anomalous instances from normal data, finds widespread utility across diverse fields, including security and healthcare. Although prior research has largely focused on scenarios with fully or partially labeled data, such settings are rare in practice because labeling is extremely labor-intensive. This paper addresses fully unsupervised AD, where the training dataset comprises both normal and anomalous samples without any labels. To solve this challenge, we propose enhancing the robustness of one-class classification models trained on self-supervised representations through a data refinement process. Our refinement strategy utilizes an ensemble of one-class classifiers (OCCs), where each classifier is trained on a distinct subset of the training data. Furthermore, the self-supervised representations are iteratively updated as the data refinement progresses. We evaluate our method on various unsupervised AD tasks involving both image and tabular datasets. On the CIFAR-10 image dataset (10% anomaly ratio) and the Thyroid tabular dataset (2.5% anomaly ratio), our approach surpasses the state-of-the-art one-class classifier, achieving improvements of 6.3 in AUC, 12.5 in average precision, and 22.9 in F1-score.

We gathered both anonymized individual-level and aggregated publicly accessible data from multiple sources concerning suspected and confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases, vaccination rates, government non-pharmaceutical interventions, human mobility, and population inequality across Brazil. Furthermore, we created a data framework designed to facilitate real-time collection, curation, integration, and extract-transform-load (ETL) workflows tailored for various purposes. With granularity extending from the state to the municipal level, this dataset supports individual and ecological epidemiological research, statistical and computational modeling, data visualization, and the scientific communication of information regarding the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil.

We demonstrate how to derive integral representations for the measures associated with free-probability Voiculescu transforms, which serve as counterparts to hyperbolic characteristic functions. This derivation requires knowledge of these transforms solely along the imaginary axis, differing from complex analysis where information across specific domains of the complex plane is necessary.

This study proposes a novel $p$-dependent coercivity condition that enables the derivation of $L^p$-moments for solutions across a broad range of SPDEs within the variational framework. When $p=2$, this condition aligns with the classical coercivity requirement, which is limited to establishing second moments. The abstract findings are demonstrated to be optimal. Additionally, these results are utilized to secure $L^p$-moments for various well-known SPDEs, including stochastic heat equations with Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, Burgers' equation, and the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. Moreover, our unified coercivity condition allows for the recovery of recent findings regarding systems of SPDEs and higher-order SPDEs.

Causality has recently become a focal point in quantum information research. This study investigates the single-shot discrimination of process matrices, which serve as a universal framework for defining causal structures. We derive an exact formula for the optimal probability of correctly distinguishing these matrices and offer an alternative derivation utilizing convex cone structure theory. Furthermore, we formulate the discrimination problem as a semidefinite program (SDP). Consequently, we developed an SDP algorithm to calculate the distance between process matrices in terms of the trace norm; as a significant by-product, this program also identifies an optimal strategy for the discrimination task. Additionally, we identify two classes of process matrices that allow for perfect distinction. However, our primary contribution addresses the discrimination of process matrices corresponding to quantum combs. We analyze whether adaptive or non-signalling strategies should be employed, proving that the probability of distinguishing two quantum comb process matrices remains identical regardless of the chosen strategy.

In 2016, Leclerc proposed conjectural cluster structures for open Richardson varieties by utilizing preprojective algebra representations. M\'enard later derived a version featuring more explicit seeds in his thesis. This paper demonstrates that M\'enard's seeds indeed generate *upper* cluster algebra structures on these open Richardson varieties and addresses the outstanding challenges required to establish them as full cluster algebra structures.

Research demonstrates that the infinite series of tree-level soft graviton symmetries within asymptotically flat 4D quantum gravity can be unified into a single chiral 2D Kac-Moody symmetry derived from the wedge algebra of w(1+infinity). Furthermore, the infinite towers of soft photon and gluon symmetries also exhibit irreducible transformations under w(1+infinity).

Although neural networks can be trained to map specific datasets, they typically fail to learn generalized transformations that accurately extrapolate beyond their training data. For example, a generative adversarial network (GAN) trained solely to convert images of black-haired men to blond-haired men may not produce similar results for black-haired women. This limitation arises because neural networks excel at generating content within the data manifold they were trained on, whereas generating samples outside this manifold or extrapolating "out-of-sample" remains a difficult, under-researched challenge. To overcome this, we introduce "neuron editing," a technique that learns how neurons encode specific edits within a latent space. By employing an autoencoder to decompose dataset variations into distinct neuronal activations, we generate transformed data by applying editing rules to these neurons. Performing transformations in this latent space allows us to encode complex, non-linear data changes through relatively simple shifts in neuronal activation distributions. We first demonstrate this approach in the image domain before applying it to two primary biological use cases: eliminating batch artifacts (unwanted noise) and modeling drug treatment effects to predict drug synergy.

This study investigates anomalous interactions involving the Higgs boson, specifically examining its $CP$ characteristics. The analysis focuses on Higgs boson candidates primarily generated through vector boson fusion and gluon fusion, which subsequently decay into pairs of $\tau$ leptons. Data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC in 2016, with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, were utilized. A matrix element method was applied to analyze these anomalous interactions. By combining these findings with previous results from the H $\to 4\ell$ decay channel, the study establishes the most restrictive limits to date on anomalous Higgs couplings to electroweak vector bosons, expressed as effective cross-section fractions and phases. The derived constraints are $f_{a3}\cos(\phi_{a3})$ $=$ $(0.00 \pm 0.27) \times 10^{-3}$ for the $CP$-violating parameter, and for $CP$-conserving parameters: $f_{a2}\cos(\phi_{a2})$ $=$ $(0.08 ^{+1.04}_{-0.21}) \times 10^{-3}$, $f_{\Lambda1}\cos(\phi_{\Lambda1})$ $=$ $(0.00 ^{+0.53}_{-0.09}) \times 10^{-3}$, and $f_{\Lambda1}^{\mathrm{Z}\gamma}\cos(\phi_{\Lambda1}^{\mathrm{Z}\gamma})$ $=$ $(0.0 ^{+1.1}_{-1.3}) \times 10^{-3}$. The current dataset does not provide precise constraints on $CP$ properties within the gluon fusion process, and the results remain consistent with Standard Model predictions.

Multilayer graphene (MLG) films were synthesized via chemical vapour deposition (CVD) on molybdenum carbide ($MoC_{x}$) substrates, which were prepared using plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PEALD). The study investigates the graphene growth mechanisms on both amorphous and crystalline $MoC_{x}$ films and highlights the distinct benefits of PEALD for catalytic substrates through two device fabrication methods. First, a complete bottom-up, resist-free patterned graphene growth was achieved on pre-patterned $MoC_{x}$ at 50$^{\circ}C$; this selective CVD approach removes the necessity for patterning or transferring the graphene, thereby maintaining its pristine, as-grown properties. Second, MLG was directly fabricated on PEALD $MoC_{x}$ supported by a 100 nm suspended SiN membrane. The resulting MLG quality was evaluated using Raman spectroscopy, with further sample analysis conducted via optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and X-ray diffraction. The manufacturing techniques demonstrated here establish a pathway for the large-scale production of graphene-based applications.

Let $\mathbb{K}$ denote a discrete field and $(V, \phi)$ represent a flow within the category of locally linearly compact $\mathbb{K}$-spaces. This section provides the formulas for calculating the topological entropy of $(V, \phi)$ under operations involving the extension or restriction of scalars.

Accurate resonant differential scattering cross sections are essential for modeling radiative transfer in the intense magnetic fields ($\sim 10^{12}$ G) observed in X-ray pulsars, though existing formulas are often complex. This study compares the cumbersome quantum-mechanical (relativistic) expressions with their classical (non-relativistic) counterparts and proposes a method to utilize the simpler classical formulas with high precision. By expanding the quantum cross sections to first order in $\epsilon \equiv E/m_ec^2$ and $B \equiv {\cal B}/{\cal B}_{cr}$—where $E$ represents photon energy and ${\cal B}_{cr}$ is the critical magnetic field—we derived the classical cross sections alongside terms accounting for spin flips, a purely quantum phenomenon. When these spin-flip terms are manually added to the polarization-dependent classical cross sections, the results align excellently with the full quantum mechanical predictions across all energies near resonance and scattering angles. Our plots confirm this strong agreement, and we provide a specific prescription for employing classical cross sections that ensures very accurate outcomes.

The semi-Markov model represents a highly versatile framework for analyzing stochastic dynamic systems. This study investigates a two-player zero-sum game involving semi-Markov processes, specifically targeting an expected discounted payoff criterion where discount factors depend on both state and action. The analysis assumes that both state and action spaces are Polish spaces, with the payoff function being $\omega$-bounded. Initially, a comprehensive model for semi-Markov games is established under a specified semi-Markov kernel and strategy pair. Subsequently, utilizing standard regularity and continuity-compactness conditions inherent to semi-Markov games, a "drift condition" for the semi-Markov kernel is derived. Assuming the discount factors maintain a positive lower bound, the existence of a value function and a pair of optimal stationary strategies is proven via the Shapley equation. Furthermore, when the state and action spaces are finite, a value iteration-based algorithm is proposed to compute the value function and an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with its convergence rigorously demonstrated. The paper concludes with numerical examples that validate the primary findings.

This study examines almost paracontact almost paracomplex Riemannian manifolds of minimal dimension, constructing these structures on hyperspheres within both 4-dimensional Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean spaces. The resulting manifolds are analyzed and characterized according to the applicable classification system and their specific geometric attributes.

Although camera-based loop closure yields excellent results on benchmark datasets, it often falters in real-world adverse weather, such as direct sunlight, rain, fog, or nighttime darkness. In automotive contexts, 3D LiDAR sensors offer complementary data to cameras. This article evaluates camera-only, LiDAR-only, and fused camera-LiDAR loop closures using a consistent neural network pipeline under various weather conditions, leveraging the newly released USyd dataset. Experiments conducted over 50 weeks on identical trajectories demonstrate that a 16-line 3D LiDAR effectively enhances image-based loop closure performance. These findings underscore the necessity for further research into multi-sensory loop closure systems.

This study presents a robust analysis of the stellar-halo mass relation (SHMR) at high masses ($10^{11.3}{\rm M_{\odot}}<M_{\star}<10^{11.7}{\rm M_{\odot}}$) and redshift $z_s\sim0.6$, examining its dependencies on morphology, color, and galaxy size. Using the Photometric objects Around Cosmic webs (PAC) method, previously applied to CMASS and HSC-SSP data, we measured the excess surface density ($\bar{n}_2w_p(r_p)$) of satellites around massive central galaxies categorized by their S\'ersic index $n$. Our findings indicate that more compact central galaxies (higher $n$) host a greater number of satellites. By employing abundance matching to estimate halo masses, we observed a monotonic increase in halo mass with $n$, providing strong evidence for a morphology-dependent SHMR. Specifically, the most compact galaxies ($n>6$) reside in halos approximately 5.5 times more massive than disk galaxies ($n<2$). Furthermore, utilizing effective radius $R_e$ and rest-frame $u-r$ color, we determined that red (larger) galaxies inhabit halos averaging 2.6 times (2.3 times) more massive than those containing blue (smaller) galaxies.

This study investigates how an external mechanical load influences a periodic structure characterized by band gaps generated via an inertial amplification mechanism. Unlike conventional Bragg scattering or standard local resonant metamaterials, we observe a more pronounced shift in the dispersion curve, achieved through significant yet fully reversible compression or stretching of the unit cell. This modulation results in a substantial (up to double) expansion or contraction of a specific band gap width. Additionally, selective vertical shifts of certain dispersion branches at specific wavenumbers are noted, indicating that such variations can induce negative group velocities across broader or narrower wavenumber ranges. An analytical model elucidates a non-monotonic trend in the lower bound of the first band gap under increasing prestrain, demonstrating that this behavior stems from distinct variations in the unit cell's effective mass and stiffness. To examine the prestress impact on the dispersion diagram, a two-step computational approach was developed: first, an Updated Lagrangian framework incorporating static geometrically nonlinear analysis of a representative unit cell under external load, followed by the application of Floquet-Bloch decomposition to the linearized acousto-elasticity equations for the deformed unit cell. These findings offer new insights into inertial amplification-induced band gaps and suggest potential for real-time tunable wave manipulation.

T-cell receptors identify foreign peptides presented by MHC class-I proteins, initiating the adaptive immune response; consequently, predicting which peptides bind to MHC class-I molecules is essential for developing peptide vaccines. Although various computational approaches, such as the leading allele-specific tool MHCflurry, exist for estimating peptide-MHC binding affinities, this manuscript introduces two novel allele-specific Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) methods: ConvM and SpConvM. These models address the binding prediction challenge by employing ranking-based learning objectives to optimize peptide-MHC binding orders. This ranking-focused approach offers greater robustness against measurement errors in binding affinities, thereby facilitating more precise prioritization of potential binders. Furthermore, we implemented a new position encoding strategy within ConvM and SpConvM to enhance the identification of critical amino acids involved in binding. Experimental evaluations show that our models substantially surpass current state-of-the-art methods, including MHCflurry, achieving an average improvement of 6.70% in AUC and 17.10% in ROC5 across 128 different alleles.

The application of tropical geometry within max-plus algebra to statistical learning models on tree spaces is driven by the advantageous properties of the tropical metric, particularly its convexity. However, a significant hurdle in utilizing tropical geometry for tree spaces remains the challenge of interpreting statistical model outcomes under this metric. This paper investigates the combinatorial structure of tree topologies along a tropical line segment—an intrinsic geodesic connecting two phylogenetic trees within tree space—and highlights specific characteristics of such segments. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any number of leaves exceeding four, the probability of a tropical line segment between two randomly selected trees passing through the origin (the star tree) is zero. Furthermore, we show that if two trees differ by only a single nearest neighbor interchange (NNI) move, then any tree topology encountered along the tropical line segment between them must correspond to the topology of one of the original two trees, potentially with zero branch lengths.

We identify symplectic Weyl group elements ensuring that the FFLV basis aligns with the PBW filtration on symplectic Demazure modules, thereby generalizing type A findings by the second author. Remarkably, the count of these elements is independent of whether the Lie algebra is of type A or C, relying solely on the rank.

This study examines Klein-Gordon (KG) oscillators within the (1+2)-dimensional G\"{u}rses spacetime framework under position-dependent mass (PDM) conditions. We find that KG-G\"{u}rses oscillators naturally emerge from the intrinsic structure of the G\"{u}rses spacetime. Our analysis reveals that the energy levels of these oscillators exhibit correlations between vorticity and energy, alongside degeneracies linked to the spacetime itself (STAD). We critically evaluate the results presented by Ahmed \cite{Ahmed1 2019} for KG-G\"{u}rses oscillators, identifying flaws in his approach and demonstrating that his findings should instead align with the results reported here. Furthermore, we propose a new class of KG pseudo-G\"{u}rses oscillators that share isospectrality and invariance with the standard KG-G\"{u}rses oscillators, while also retaining their vorticity-energy correlations and STADs.

Although significant advancements have been made in creating new sentiment lexicon generation (SLG) methods for English, effectively adapting these techniques to other languages and domains remains an unresolved challenge. This paper addresses this issue by systematically comparing semi-automatically translated English polarity lists against the outcomes of original automatic SLG algorithms applied directly to German data. The evaluation utilizes a corpus of 7,992 manually annotated tweets. Furthermore, we aggregate results from both dictionary-based and corpus-based SLG methods to determine which paradigm is more effective for the inherently noisy social media environment. Our experiments demonstrate that semi-automatic translations significantly outperform automatic systems, achieving a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.589. Additionally, dictionary-based techniques yield substantially superior polarity lists compared to corpus-based approaches, which reached best F1-scores of 0.479 and 0.419 respectively, even when applied to the non-standard Twitter genre.

**Background:** The transverse densities $\rho_{1, 2}(b)$ characterize the distributions of electric charge and magnetic moment at a specific light-front time, serving as a bridge between nucleon elastic form factors and their partonic structure. Through a dispersive representation, the form factors $F_{1, 2}(t)$ express these densities via $t$-channel hadronic state exchanges, enabling analysis through hadronic physics techniques.
