Current methodologies face several constraints: prior studies employing CDRs often ignore cell tower transmit power during user localization and rely on overly simplistic models to handle load-sharing effects. Additionally, these earlier works treat the entire user population as a single homogeneous group, failing to account for variations in mobility patterns across different user segments. This study proposes a novel methodology for localizing user positions from CDRs by enhancing the detection of load-sharing effects through the inclusion of transmit power data and by segmenting users into distinct groups to learn model parameters. Furthermore, the research addresses existing limitations and validates its findings using nearly 4 billion CDR data points, cross-referenced with travel survey data and voluntarily collected mobile data.

Recent debates indicating a reproducibility and replication crisis in machine learning (ML) imply that certain published findings should not be accepted without scrutiny. These issues draw parallels to similar crises in the social and medical sciences and have prompted calls to merge statistical methods for causal inference with predictive modeling. By examining the shared roots of reproducibility concerns in supervised ML and the replication crisis in experimental science, researchers can better contextualize these challenges and avoid the pitfalls of indiscriminately adopting methodologies from explanatory modeling or vice versa. This paper offers a comparative analysis of inductive learning issues within causal attribution (as seen in psychology) versus predictive modeling (as seen in ML). We highlight recurring themes in reform discussions, such as an excessive dependence on asymptotic theory and unrealistic assumptions about real-world data generation. We argue that in both domains, claims of generalizability beyond the specific study environment are often unrefutable due to hidden variances in the learning pipeline. Specifically, acknowledged errors in ML challenge the belief that massive datasets and predictive accuracy optimization eliminate the need to understand true data generating processes or formally quantify uncertainty. Finally, we address the risks of misdiagnosing error sources and emphasize the necessity of recognizing the role of human inductive biases in both learning and reform efforts.

We examined the microlensing event KMT-2021-BLG-0322, which displays three unique sets of caustic-crossing characteristics in its light curve. Although a binary-lens (2L1S) model roughly captures the overall light curve features, it leaves significant residuals. To account for these discrepancies, we evaluated several interpretations, discovering that the residuals can be resolved by either incorporating nonrectilinear lens-source motion driven by microlens-parallax and orbital effects or by introducing a low-mass companion within a three-lens (3L1S) configuration. A severe degeneracy exists between the higher-order 2L1S and 3L1S models, making it challenging to determine the correct solution from photometric data alone. This specific degeneracy has previously plagued two other events (MACHO-97-BLG-41 and OGLE-2013-BLG-0723), leading to erroneous planetary detections in binary systems. Consequently, recognizing this degeneracy in KMT-2021-BLG-0322 highlights that such ambiguities are not only frequent but also extreme, underscoring the necessity of evaluating both deviations from 2L1S models. Bayesian analysis using the event timescale, angular Einstein radius, and microlens parallax yielded component masses of $(M_1, M_2) = (0.62^{+0.25}_{-0.26}~M_\odot, 0.07^{+0.03}_{-0.03}~M_\odot)$ for both the 2L1S and 3L1S scenarios, while the tertiary component mass in the 3L1S solution is estimated at $M_3=6.40^{+2.64}_{-2.78}~M_{\rm J}$.

This study refines the asymptotic formulae for the probability distribution of a test statistic, building upon G. Cowan et al.'s work~\cite{asimov} from a novel perspective distinct from the previous arXiv submission. The approach taken here is considered more intuitive. The probability distribution function under hypothesis $H$ is expressed as:
$f(T_\mu | \mu_H) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}f(T_\mu|n,\mu_H)P(n|b+\mu_Hs)$
$= \sum_{n=0}^{n_{\text{small}}}f(T_\mu|n,\mu_H)P(n|b+\mu_Hs) +
\sum_{n>n_{\text{small}}}f(T_\mu|n,\mu_H)P(n|b+\mu_Hs)$
$\approx
\sum_{n=0}^{n_{\text{small}}}f_{\text{LS}}(T_\mu|n,\mu_H)P(n|b+\mu_Hs) +
(1-\sum_{n=0}^{n_{\text{small}}}P(n|b+\mu_Hs))f_{\text{LS}}(T_\mu|n_{\text{small}},
\mu_H)$.
In this context, $P(n|\nu)$ denotes the Poisson distribution, and $n_{\text{small}}$ represents the threshold separating small statistics (SS) from large statistics (LS), requiring careful selection. When the event count exceeds $n_{\text{small}}$, the distribution of $T_\mu$ is governed by a single function, $f_{\text{LS}}$, which essentially constitutes the standard asymptotic formula with a correction. For event counts at or below $n_{\text{small}}$, the distribution $f_{\text{SS}}$ is derived from a simplified 6-bin model of the observables:
$f_{\text{SS}}(T_\mu|n,\mu_H) =
\sum_{k_0+k_1+k_2+k_3+k_4+k_5=n}\frac{n!}{k_0!k_1!\cdots
k_5!}\Pi_{i=0}^5(\frac{b_i+\mu_Hs_i}{b+ \mu_Hs})^{k_i}
\times f_{\text{binned}}(T_\mu|n_i=k_i,i=0,1,\cdots,5;\mu_H)$.
This methodology enables accurate prediction of bump structures arising from small sample sizes. Consequently, the new asymptotic formulae offer a significantly improved differential description of the test statistics.

Reentrant superconductivity has been detected in the potential spin-triplet superconductor UTe$_2$ under magnetic fields applied along the hard axis. Resistivity data indicate that a widened superconducting transition occurs near the lowest $T_c$, underscoring the significance of superconducting fluctuations in this region. We offer a phenomenological analysis based on a field-induced first-order transition between two superconducting phases. Our findings demonstrate that quenched randomness can naturally explain both the reentrant superconductivity and the broadened transition through inhomogeneity-enhanced fluctuations near the critical point.

This paper begins by extending Fresnel integrals through a modification of the integration path within the proof of the Cauchy integral theorem. Subsequently, leveraging the concept of oscillatory integrals, we derive a further generalization of these extended Fresnel integrals. Utilizing this finding, we establish an asymptotic expansion for an oscillatory integral featuring a positive real parameter, a phase function with a degenerate critical point expressed via positive real powers (including moderate oscillations), and a suitable amplitude function. This outcome provides a more refined extension of the stationary phase method in one variable, which traditionally applies to phase functions with non-degenerate critical points.

Leveraging the extensive datasets from the HotQCD Collaboration, which employ the HISQ action for light and strange quarks while applying a quenched approximation to the charm sector, we investigate the second and fourth-order cumulants of charm fluctuations alongside their correlations with lighter conserved flavor quantum numbers. This study utilizes a dataset 100 times larger than previous efforts on $N_\tau = 8$ lattices, a configuration previously unexplored for charm fluctuation analyses. By examining the correlations between charm fluctuations and those of baryon number and electric charge, we isolate charmed baryon and meson correlations to compare against calculations from an extended hadron resonance gas model incorporating quark model effects. Our objectives include achieving a precise measurement of the dissociation temperature for charmed hadrons and assessing the sensitivity of these fluctuation observables to the existence of multiple-charmed baryons.

Quantum state discrimination is a fundamental issue in quantum measurement theory, with applications ranging from quantum computing to communication. Conventional approaches typically focus on minimizing the probability of error or achieving unambiguous discrimination by accepting a certain rate of inconclusive results. In contrast, an optimal inconclusive measurement—a type of non-projective measurement—minimizes error for a specified probability of inconclusive outcomes. This broader framework subsumes standard paradigms and offers a significantly more versatile tool for quantum information processing. In this work, we experimentally realize the optimal inconclusive measurement for distinguishing binary coherent states using linear optics and single-photon detection. Our setup employs coherent displacement via interference, single-photon detection, and rapid feedback to execute the optimal non-projective quantum measurement policy with high fidelity. This generalized approach enables a seamless transition between standard measurement strategies, optimizing the shift from minimum-error to unambiguous detection for binary coherent states. Specifically, we apply this general method to implement the optimal minimum-error measurement for phase-coherent states, which represents the ideal modulation scheme under average power constraints. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid measurement strategy that combines the binary optimal inconclusive measurement with sequential, unambiguous state elimination to achieve higher-dimensional inconclusive measurements of coherent states.

This study presents a measurement of off-shell Higgs boson production within the $ZZ\to4\ell$ and $ZZ\to2\ell2\nu$ decay channels, where $\ell$ denotes an electron or muon, utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. The ATLAS experiment gathered this data in 2015 and 2016 at the Large Hadron Collider, accumulating an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$. At a 95% confidence level, the analysis establishes an observed (expected) upper limit on the off-shell Higgs signal strength—defined as the event yield normalized to Standard Model expectations—of 3.8 (3.4). By assuming that the ratio of Higgs boson couplings to Standard Model predictions remains constant regardless of the momentum transfer in the production mechanism, and combining these results with on-shell signal-strength measurements, an observed (expected) 95% CL upper limit on the total Higgs boson width of 14.4 (15.2) MeV is derived.

This study examines the ground state of antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models on L × L clusters connected by a single bond alongside balanced Bethe clusters, utilizing quantum Monte Carlo simulations and modified spin-wave theory. The research employs Sandvik and Evertz's enhanced Monte Carlo approach, analyzing observables such as valence bond and loop valence bond metrics introduced by Lin and Sandvik, along with valence bond entropy and second Renyi entropy. Regarding the bisecting of Bethe clusters, both the valence loop entropy and second Renyi entropy scale logarithmically with the number of sites; this finding aligns with modified spin-wave theory but contradicts earlier results. For L × L clusters linked to L × L clusters, the valence bond entropy scales linearly with L, whereas loop entropy and entanglement entropy scale as ln(L). The coefficient of the logarithmic term for entanglement entropy, representing half the number of Goldstone modes, proves universal and serves as the analogue to the sub-leading term in an L × L cluster. These conclusions were reinforced by modified spin-wave calculations on the ferromagnetic X-Y model. Collectively, the results indicate that connecting high-entanglement objects does not significantly increase total entanglement. Consequently, simulating the ground states of clusters joined by a few bonds should not present substantially greater difficulty than simulating a single cluster's ground state.

Following the LHC's highly productive initial operational phase, the LHCb experiment implemented an enhanced trigger strategy for Run II featuring real-time reconstruction, alignment, and calibration. This approach leverages offline-quality track reconstruction within the high-level trigger, thereby eliminating the need for a distinct offline event reconstruction step. To support this method and manage the increased event rates resulting from accelerator upgrades, the duration of track reconstruction was significantly reduced. Timing enhancements were partly realized through parallel computing techniques, which are detailed in this document via two specific examples. Despite the reduction in computation time, reconstruction quality—specifically regarding efficiency and fake rates—was improved in several areas. Additionally, the document highlights two applications of rapid machine learning techniques used to refine track candidate selection during the early phases of reconstruction.

We report far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three FUV filters—BaF2 (F154W), Sapphire (F169M), and Silica (F172M)—on the Ultra-Violet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) aboard the \mbox{{\em AstroSat}} satellite. Cluster membership for the UVIT-detected sources was verified using proper motions from Gaia Data Release 2 (GAIA DR2). Analysis of UV-optical color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) revealed 37 blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars, one blue straggler star (BSS), and 15 variable stars. Our findings indicate that all FUV-luminous BHBs belong to the second-generation population. By examining UV-optical CMDs, we distinguished two sub-populations among the FUV-bright BHBs, designated BHB1 and BHB2, with a star count ratio of 24:13. Effective temperatures ($T_{\mathrm{eff}}$) for both sub-populations were determined using the BaSTI-IAC zero-age horizontal branch (ZAHB) color-temperature relation. Furthermore, BHB1 stars exhibit greater central concentration than BHB2 stars. Finally, we derived the physical parameters of the identified FUV-bright BSS by fitting younger-age BaSTI-IAC isochrones to the optical and UV-optical CMDs.

This study examines how the scattering of conduction electrons by dynamic spin fluctuations influences thermopower in metals approaching a thermal transition into an antiferromagnetic state, specifically focusing on room-temperature transitions observed in IrMn heterostructures. While electrical resistivity displays a narrow, low-amplitude peak at the transition that can be easily obscured by contributions from phonons and impurities, the thermopower reveals a distinct, prominent peak both when plotted against temperature $T$ for a fixed antiferromagnetic layer thickness $t_{\text{AFM}}$ and when plotted against $t_{\text{AFM}}$ for a fixed $T$. We propose that the transition temperature $T_c$ depends on both $t_{\text{AFM}}$ and the Fermi energy $E_F$, resulting in a sharp peak in thermopower near the transition as either variable changes. Furthermore, the predicted magnitude of this peak for three-dimensional longitudinal spin fluctuations aligns well with experimental data.

Visual Salient Object Detection (SOD) focuses on identifying objects that draw human attention, whereas Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to uncover objects concealed within their surroundings. This paper introduces a framework that utilizes the contradictory nature of these tasks to boost detection performance for both. We begin by repurposing easy positive samples from COD datasets as hard positive samples for SOD, thereby enhancing the robustness of SOD models. Subsequently, we implement a similarity measure module to explicitly capture the conflicting attributes inherent to both tasks. Additionally, addressing labeling uncertainties in both datasets, we propose an adversarial learning network to achieve higher-order similarity assessment and improved confidence estimation. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets confirm that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance for both SOD and COD.

As the most recent video coding standard, Versatile Video Coding (VVC) demonstrates strong capabilities in maintaining pixel quality. To unlock further compression potential for video conferencing under ultra-low bitrate constraints, this paper introduces a bitrate-adjustable hybrid compression scheme tailored for face videos. This hybrid approach merges the pixel-level precise recovery of traditional coding methods with the generative power of deep learning utilizing condensed information. By integrating Pixel-wise Bi-Prediction, Low-Bitrate-FOM, and a Lossless Keypoint Encoder, the system achieves a PSNR of up to 36.23 dB at an ultra-low bitrate of 1.47 KB/s. In completely fair comparative experiments that incur no additional bitrate overhead, our method outperforms VVC, validating the efficacy of the proposed scheme. Furthermore, the scheme is adaptable to any existing encoder or configuration to meet diverse encoding needs, with the ability to dynamically adjust bitrates in response to network conditions.

This study investigates tree-level celestial correlators of light-transformed gluon operators and examines how these operators transform under four-dimensional translations. The two-, three-, and four-point functions derived from MHV amplitudes in terms of these operators obey translation invariance, are non-distributional, and feature standard CFT power-law terms. A novel channel-dependent term appears in the three-point function. We demonstrate that the three-point light-transformed correlation function achieves conformal covariance once contributions from all three channels are combined. Furthermore, we analyze the OPE limits of the various three-point channels to explore the construction of a mapping between the OPE in the Mellin basis and that in the light-transformed basis.

The recently introduced quality-based principle for prediction intervals (PIs) aims to find the narrowest intervals that meet specific coverage probability standards, thereby extracting high-quality PIs that effectively summarize predictive certainty in regression tasks. This approach has been widely adopted to address numerous practical issues, with current state-of-the-art methods relying on deep neural networks or linear models. In this paper, we introduce the Highest Density Interval Regression Forest (HDI-Forest), a novel quality-based PI estimation method grounded in Random Forests. Unlike other approaches, HDI-Forest eliminates the need for additional training by directly reusing the trees from a standard Random Forest model. By leveraging the unique characteristics of Random Forests, HDI-Forest can optimize PI quality metrics more efficiently and directly. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that HDI-Forest significantly outperforms existing methods, reducing the average PI width by over 20% while maintaining equal or superior coverage probability.

Light plays a pivotal role in guiding atomic motion in free space, facilitating the cooling and trapping of matter waves via ponderomotive forces and Doppler-mediated photon scattering. Similarly, interactions between light and free electrons have recently become a flexible method for shaping electron wave functions, with applications in ultrafast electron microscopy. This study unites these two domains by theoretically showing that matter waves can be optically controlled through inelastic interactions with optical fields. This approach enables the modulation of translational wave functions and the generation of atomic beam pulses that are compressed both temporally and spatially. Specifically, we achieve this modulation through stimulated photon absorption and emission by atoms moving through phase-matching evanescent fields created by light scattering off nanostructures, as well as via stimulated Compton scattering in free space without any material medium. These findings underscore optical manipulation of matter waves as a potent instrument for microscopy, spectroscopy, and investigating new fundamental phenomena linked to light-atom interactions.

Despite the recent publication of a catalogue offering synthetic RGB magnitudes for 1,346 bright stars, its utility remains constrained by the limited number of reference stars distributed across the sky and the restriction to Johnson V < 6.6 mag. This study introduces synthetic RGB magnitudes for approximately 15 million stars brighter than Gaia G = 18 mag, utilizing a calibration derived from the RGB magnitudes of the bright star sample and high-quality G, G_BP, and G_RP photometry from Gaia EDR3. The calibration is restricted to stars with -0.5 < G_BP - G_RP < 2.0 mag and targets prediction accuracy within ±0.1 mag. Given that the reference sample is dominated by nearby, slightly metal-poor stars, systematic variations in predictions are anticipated and modeled using stellar atmosphere models. These deviations are confined to the ±0.1 mag range when applying the calibration to stars with minimal interstellar extinction and metallicities consistent with the median of the bright star sample. The abundance of Gaia sources in every sky region should ensure high-quality RGB photometric calibrations.

Indoor localization and location-based services have increasingly relied on Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology, driving recent efforts to minimize ranging errors. However, research into achieving more reliable and energy-efficient communication remains underexplored. The IEEE 802.15.4 UWB physical layer offers various configurable settings that impact energy usage, range, and reliability. By leveraging link state diagnostics available from UWB devices, it becomes possible to dynamically adjust these PHY settings according to environmental conditions. To capitalize on this opportunity, we introduce a deep Q-learning approach designed to ensure reliable UWB communication by maximizing packet reception rate (PRR) and minimizing energy consumption. Deep Q-learning is particularly suited for this task due to its inherent adaptability to changing environments. Validation conducted in a realistic office setting demonstrated that this algorithm outperforms traditional Q-learning, linear search methods, and fixed PHY layer configurations. Our findings indicate that deep Q-learning achieves a higher average PRR and reduces ranging error while consuming only 14% of the energy required by a fixed PHY setting in a dynamic office environment.

This paper explores novel connections between string theory, four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills (SYM) theory, and the Riemann hypothesis. Since the Riemann hypothesis is mathematically equivalent to a specific inequality governing the sum of divisors function $\sigma(n)$, we leverage existing literature to examine how $\sigma(n)$ arises in the context of counting supersymmetric states within $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM featuring an $SU(3)$ gauge group. Specifically, the Schur limit of the superconformal index serves as a generating function for $\sigma(n)$. Under the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis holds, we derive constraints on the information contained within $1/8$-BPS states in this SYM model. Furthermore, the AdS/CFT correspondence links the Riemann hypothesis to type IIB superstring theory on $AdS_5 \times S^5$, where the hypothesis necessitates an unexpected cancellation among Kaluza-Klein modes of the supergravity multiplet and D3-branes wrapping supersymmetric cycles. Finally, we consider potential avenues for deriving fresh insights into the Riemann hypothesis through physical perspectives.

Motivated by the recent discovery of the $a_0(1817)$ by the BESIII Collaboration, we identify a coherent Regge trajectory comprising the $a_0(980)$, $a_0(1450)$, and $a_0(1817)$, which classifies these particles as members of the isovector scalar meson family. This classification is reinforced by their two-body strong decay modes permitted by the Okubo-Zweig-Iizuka rule. Within this framework, we predict the third radial excitation of the $a_0(980)$, labeled as $a_0(2115)$, which can be probed in future experiments to validate this assignment. Additionally, we uncover another Regge trajectory consisting of three isoscalar scalar states: $f_0(980)$, $X(1812)$, and $f_0(2100)$. The observed strong decay patterns for these states, also allowed by the Okubo-Zweig-Iizuka rule, align reasonably well with experimental data, supporting their grouping into the isoscalar scalar meson family. Notably, both Regge trajectories exhibit comparable slopes. In conclusion, this work establishes a scheme for organizing the scalar meson family using these reported states. Furthermore, the identification of $f_0(1710)$ as a scalar glueball candidate remains viable despite the discovery of $a_0(1817)$, as the latter is better suited as the isovector partner of $X(1812)$.

Eccentricity has become a promising indicator for tracing the origins of black hole mergers, yet calculating the amplitude of eccentric signals demands many harmonics, rendering template generation computationally prohibitive and complicating statistical comparisons between different formation channels. This paper presents a method for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of inspiraling binaries at low frequencies, such as those targeted by LISA and DECIGO, with applicability extending to other quasi-periodic sources. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that the SNR evaluated near the power spectrum's peak frequency can be accurately approximated using a constant noise curve, despite the reality of power-law noise strain profiles. We refine this initial approach to account for frequency-dependent noise, thereby broadening the range of eccentricities and frequencies where the approximation holds. We illustrate how to apply this technique to achieve accuracy within a factor of two across nearly the entire projected observable frequency band. We emphasize that this method complements rather than replaces detailed signal processing; its primary value lies in identifying theoretically meaningful discriminators among various populations and providing reasonably accurate estimates of their efficacy. Additionally, this approximation offers a computationally efficient way to constrain parameter spaces when events are detected. Finally, we reveal a unique method for identifying events with extreme eccentricity, where the signal is unexpectedly enhanced at high frequencies compared to naive expectations.

We have analyzed the probability distributions of spacings between the nearest and next-nearest neighbors relative to a specific energy level for interacting fermion and boson systems, both with and without spin, constructed via an embedded Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) incorporating one-body terms and random two-body interactions. Our numerical findings show strong agreement with the analytical formulas recently derived by Srivastava et al. using a $3 \times 3$ random matrix model and related quantities [J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. **52** 025101 (2019)]. This confirms definitively that local level fluctuations arising from embedded ensembles adhere to the predictions of classical Gaussian ensembles.

Despite their differences in the physical domain, digital video and audio share several key traits, including being temporal data streams typically stored as 8-bit values in buffers. This paper explores a technique for generating harmonic audio from video input. A musical instrument is proposed that employs video not only for sound synthesis but also as a controller interface to select notes based on specific velocities. The author informally concluded that while the resulting instrument produces pleasant and intriguing sounds, it is difficult to control, making it well-suited for synth pad textures.

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin ensembles in diamond serve as a sophisticated magnetic sensing platform applicable to both physical and life sciences. Although isotopically engineered $^{15}$NV diamond offers magnetometry benefits over naturally occurring $^{14}$NV due to its simpler hyperfine structure, it presents a challenge when sensing modalities require a bias magnetic field misaligned with the NV axis. In such scenarios, the lack of a quadrupole moment in the $^{15}$N nuclear spin causes significant envelope modulation in time-dependent spin evolution measurements. While these effects in spin echo experiments are well understood, their impact on Ramsey measurements and magnetometry remains largely unexplored. This work derives the modulated $^{15}$NV Ramsey response to a misaligned bias field using a straightforward vector model of the effective magnetic field acting on the nuclear spin. Comparing these predictions with experimental data reveals substantial magnetic sensitivity loss if this modulation is not corrected. We further demonstrate that double-quantum coherences within the NV $S=1$ electronic spin states effectively suppress these envelope modulations, while also showing resilience against other parasitic factors like strain heterogeneity and temperature fluctuations.

Measuring the longitudinal charge distribution or bunch shape presents significant challenges for temporally short, non-relativistic bunches. In such beams, the electromagnetic field profile extends longitudinally more than the charge profile itself, which hinders the capability of field-sensing instruments like phase pick-ups or wall current monitors to accurately determine the charge distribution. This study assesses the viability of utilizing coherent transition and diffraction radiation from non-relativistic beams to perform bunch shape measurements.

We present a phenomenological framework describing entanglement dynamics in monitored quantum many-body systems characterized by distinct quasiparticles. In this model, entanglement propagates ballistically via non-Hermitian quasiparticles that undergo stochastic resets due to the measurement protocol, occurring at a rate determined by their finite inverse lifetime. By formulating a renewal equation for the entanglement entropy statistics, we demonstrate that varying quasiparticle decay spectra can lead to diverse scaling behaviors, including sharp entanglement phase transitions. When applied to a Quantum Ising chain with transverse magnetization measured through quantum jumps, our theory forecasts a critical phase exhibiting logarithmic entanglement scaling, an area law phase, and a continuous phase transition between them, where the effective central charge vanishes as a square root at the transition. Comparisons with exact numerical simulations of the same model reveal excellent agreement with these predictions.

Emotions play a vital role in human interaction, conveyed through verbal cues, vocal tone, facial expressions, and body movements. Despite advancements, brain-computer interface (BCI) technology has not yet achieved the capability necessary for accurate emotion interpretation. However, recent progress in machine learning, dry electrode methods, and practical BCI applications for non-clinical users has significantly increased interest in classifying emotions from electroencephalogram (EEG) data. EEG signals are particularly valuable because they authentically reflect emotional states and are readily processed by computers. This study identifies EEG patterns corresponding to positive, neutral, and negative emotions through channel selection preprocessing. While the precise connections between these emotional states were previously unclear, this work addresses that gap by applying discrete wavelet transform alongside machine learning models, specifically recurrent neural networks (RNN) and k-nearest neighbors (kNN). The process began with classifier-based channel selection to generate final feature vectors by combining EEG segment data from selected channels. These vectors, representing the three emotional categories, were then independently classified using both the RNN and kNN algorithms. A comparative analysis of the two techniques revealed average overall accuracies of 94.844% for RNN and 93.438% for kNN.

Video streaming has become a dominant media format, prompting this work to introduce a novel technique for real-time video stabilization that mimics the smoothness of gimbal-based recording. Unlike previous approaches, our framework operates in a self-supervised manner, eliminating the need for specialized hardware such as stereo rigs or motion sensors. The system functions through a sequential pipeline: first, a transformation estimator applies global stability adjustments between frames; second, a scene parallax reduction module utilizes spatially smoothed optical flow; and finally, a margin inpainting module reconstructs the empty areas generated during stabilization to minimize cropping. This multi-step process significantly reduces distortion and edge cropping while maximizing stability, allowing our method to surpass both state-of-the-art real-time techniques and offline solutions relying on camera trajectory optimization. Furthermore, the procedure achieves a processing speed of approximately 24.3 milliseconds, delivering 41 frames per second consistently across various resolutions, including 480p and 1080p.

Scientific software frequently demands specific usability standards that are often neglected. With computational science evolving into a distinct field separate from theoretical and experimental disciplines, it has imposed new demands on the development of future scientific software. This paper examines the origins of these challenges and outlines nine key dimensions of effective usability, emphasizing best practices tailored to applications in computational science.

This study computes the mass spectrum of strangeonium up to the $3D$ multiplet using a nonrelativistic quark model with a linear potential. Leveraging the derived wave functions, we subsequently analyze the strong decays of these states via the $^3P_0$ model. Building on our successful descriptions of established states including $\phi(1020)$, $\phi(1680)$, $h_1(1415)$, $f'_2(1525)$, and $\phi_3(1850)$, we explore potential assignments for experimentally observed strangeonium-like candidates by integrating our theoretical findings with empirical data. Our analysis suggests that certain resonances, such as the $f_2(2010)$ and $f_2(2150)$ listed by the Particle Data Group, as well as the newly identified $X(2062)$ and $X(2500)$ from BESIII, could be interpreted as strangeonium states. Additionally, the possibility that $\phi(2170)$ represents the $\phi(3S)$ or $\phi(2D)$ state remains viable. We anticipate that these results will offer valuable guidance for future searches for missing $s\bar{s}$ states.

Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) have shown marked performance gains in creating diverse discrete objects $x$ based on a reward function $R(x)$, suggesting potential for using supervised learning to predict a desirable property $y$ from $x$ independently. However, we hypothesize that separating the inductive optimization biases of training $R$ and the GFlowNet can cause incompatibility, resulting in suboptimal samples and sluggish adaptation to distributional shifts. To address this, we extend recent efforts on jointly learning energy-based models with GFlowNets to handle multiple variables, introducing Joint Energy-Based GFlowNets (JEBGFNs)—for instance, to model peptide sequences alongside their antimicrobial activity. By training the energy-based model, which serves as the GFlowNet's reward, jointly with the sampler, we eliminate the aforementioned incompatibility issues. Our findings indicate that this joint training approach significantly enhances the generation of anti-microbial peptides. Since sequences often evolve or are artificially selected for high antibiotic efficacy, their distribution likely contains structural information revealing activity levels, offering a distinct advantage to joint generative modeling over purely discriminative methods. Furthermore, we assess the JEBGFN within an active learning framework aimed at discovering new anti-microbial peptides.

In the context of limited feedback design for Full Dimension Multi-Input Multi-Output (FD-MIMO) systems, two pivotal challenges are the quantization of Channel State Information (CSI) with low complexity and the exploitation of vertical freedom within three-dimensional (3D) channels. This paper introduces an efficient limited feedback scheme. Initially, we utilize a Kronecker Product-based Codebook (KPC) to investigate the vertical dimensions of 3D channels, thereby extending limited feedback capabilities from two dimensions (2D) to three dimensions (3D). Subsequently, we apply Noncoherent Sequence Detection (NCSD) to quantify CSI, encompassing both vertical and horizontal channel data. This quantization approach leverages the duality between codebook searching and NCSD to convert CSI quantization on KPC into two parallel NCSD processes. Consequently, complexity decreases from exponential to linear relative to the number of antennas. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed scheme maintains full diversity order without compromising the system's diversity gain. Monte Carlo simulations indicate that the proposed method achieves at least 1.2 dB in coding gain over traditional 2D limited feedback schemes. Additionally, under conditions of high spatial correlation, the proposed scheme surpasses other FD/3D CSI quantization methods by 0.8 dB in coding gain while maintaining moderate complexity.

We present $^{77}$Se NMR measurements taken on a single crystal of FeSe in both its normal and superconducting phases across various magnetic field orientations. While the Knight shift is suppressed by in-plane fields in the superconducting state, it fails to disappear entirely at zero temperature. Conversely, fields applied perpendicular to the plane show little to no reduction below $T_c$. These findings indicate that spin-singlet pairing develops from a nematic state characterized by significant orbital susceptibility and spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, spectral and spin-relaxation data highlight electronic inhomogeneity that intensifies in the superconducting state, potentially due to an increased density of states within vortex cores. Despite the spin polarization of these states, no signs of antiferromagnetic fluctuations were detected.

Investigating the sub-structure formation of dissipative dark-matter halos, which could contain compact objects like black holes, necessitates molecular cooling. In this study, we examine the reaction rates governing the formation, dissociation, and transitions of hydrogenic molecules across various physical parameters, including the coupling constant, proton mass, and electron mass. We normalize these rates relative to standard molecular hydrogen for every scenario, ensuring applicability whenever dark matter exhibits weak coupling and one fermion is significantly more massive than the other. These findings facilitate a rigorous numerical analysis of cosmic structure, specifically targeting mini-halos where molecular cooling plays a critical role within a dissipative dark matter framework.

A version control system tracks modifications to files over time, enabling the monitoring of changes and the retrieval of specific historical versions. Consequently, it is a vital component of reproducible workflows and warrants inclusion as a learning objective in statistics and data science curricula. This paper details the experiences and implementation choices of four faculty members who teach diverse courses at various institutions. Each instructor has established version control as a learning goal and successfully incorporated a system like Git into one or more statistics courses. The approaches outlined cover a spectrum of implementation strategies tailored to student backgrounds, course types, software selections, and assessment methods. By showcasing these varied methods for teaching Git, the paper aims to serve as a valuable resource for instructors at any level within undergraduate or graduate statistics and data science programs.

Efficiently processing and extracting features from large-scale point clouds is crucial for computer vision and cyber-physical systems. This study explores point cloud resampling via hypergraph signal processing (HGSP) to more effectively uncover relationships between points and isolate contour-enhanced features. Specifically, we develop hypergraph spectral filters to capture multi-directional interactions among point cloud signal nodes while better maintaining surface outlines. Unlike traditional methods requiring the construction of an underlying hypergraph, our low-complexity approach directly estimates the hypergraph spectrum by utilizing hypergraph stationary processes derived from observed 3D coordinates. Evaluation using multiple metrics confirms the high effectiveness of this hypergraph characterization and demonstrates the robustness of HGSP-based resampling even under noisy conditions.

Object-centric processes, also known as artifact-centric processes, operate on a paradigm where process instances do not function in isolation but instead interact with other instances of the same or different processes through bridging events that facilitate data exchange. This approach is increasingly popular in both academic and industrial sectors due to its prevalence in various application scenarios. However, the complex intricacies of these interconnected instances, characterized by many-to-many associations, present significant challenges for predictive analytics. Current research struggles to leverage these interactions, which restricts prediction accuracy. This paper introduces a method to integrate object interaction data into predictive models. Evaluated using real-world event data and various Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), the proposed approach is benchmarked against a naive method that ignores object interactions, demonstrating the substantial improvements in prediction quality achieved by accounting for these interactions.

Although recently introduced BERT-based evaluation metrics achieve strong performance on standard benchmarks, they remain susceptible to adversarial attacks, particularly those targeting factuality. We contend that this vulnerability arises partly because these models rely on semantic similarity. In contrast, we propose evaluation metrics grounded in Natural Language Inference (NLI), which we consider a more suitable modeling approach. By designing a preference-based adversarial attack framework, we demonstrate that our NLI-based metrics exhibit significantly greater robustness compared to recent BERT-based alternatives. While our NLI metrics surpass existing summarization metrics on standard benchmarks and fall slightly short of state-of-the-art machine translation metrics, integrating them with current metrics yields dual benefits: enhanced adversarial robustness (increasing by 20% to 30%) and improved quality scores on standard benchmarks (ranging from 5% to 25%).

By combining the effective field theory approach for extended bodies with the coset construction, we construct the leading-order effective action for the most general compact object within an effective theory of gravity akin to general relativity. Identifying the symmetry breaking pattern of a charged, spinning compact object allows us to derive all necessary covariant building blocks and constraints required to formulate relevant invariant operators in the action to all orders. This symmetry breaking necessitates the introduction of Goldstone bosons, which serve as fundamental components via their derivatives. Given that gravity represents a space-time symmetry, the inverse Higgs constraint is applied to eliminate redundant bosons. The resulting building blocks, composed of Goldstone fields, correspond to degrees of freedom such as acceleration and angular velocity. By analyzing permissible invariant operators, we derive the effective action for spinning extended objects, enabling state-of-the-art post-Newtonian calculations and corrections to the point particle due to charge. Furthermore, we develop operators that incorporate the internal structure of these extended objects, including tidal effects, polarization, and dissipation. These invariant operators are paired with coefficients that encapsulate the specific properties of the compact object. We align these coefficients with established values from the literature and identify those that remain unknown and require derivation.

The Toda lattice serves as a model for nonlinear wave equations that support exact soliton solutions, physically realized through an electric circuit comprising transmission lines, inductors, and variable capacitance diodes. This model has been extended to the dimerized Toda lattice by incorporating alternating bondings defined by a parameter $\lambda$, such that the system reverts to the standard Toda lattice when $\lambda = 0$. This study examines the topological dynamics of voltage propagation along the transmission line. Numerical results indicate that the system exhibits topological characteristics for $\lambda < 0$, whereas it becomes trivial for $\lambda > 0$, with the phase transition occurring at the original Toda lattice limit ($\lambda = 0$). These behaviors are effectively described using the chiral index known from the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. The topological phase transition is evident from the distinct voltage dynamics between the two phases, attributed to the emergence of topological edge states, which represents a bulk-edge correspondence within nonlinear systems. The validity of these topological arguments stems from the fact that the dimerized Toda lattice can be adiabatically connected to a linear system. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological edge state remains robust against random perturbations.

This paper investigates the challenge of reverse image filtering, where a black-box filter $g(\cdot)$ generates an observation $b$ from an unknown input $x$. The objective is to recover the original signal $x$ given the filter and the resulting observation. We re-examine and enhance existing state-of-the-art techniques through the lenses of fixed-point iteration and gradient descent, while also investigating acceleration strategies for both approaches. Comprehensive experiments and comparisons demonstrate that applying acceleration methods to these iterations significantly improves the convergence speed of current state-of-the-art solutions.

This study presents a search for long-lived particles decaying into opposite-charge lepton pairs ($\mu\mu$, $ee$, or $e\mu$), utilizing 32.8 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV by the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis requires candidate leptons to originate from a displaced vertex within the inner tracking volume, separate from the primary interaction point. No lepton pairs with an invariant mass exceeding 12 GeV were observed, a result consistent with background estimates derived from data. Detection efficiencies for generic resonances with lifetimes ($c\tau$) ranging from 100 to 1000 mm decaying into dileptons with masses between 0.1 and 1.0 TeV are provided as functions of $p_T$ and decay radius, facilitating the calculation of upper limits on production cross-sections for theoretical models. These findings are also interpreted within a supersymmetric framework where the lightest neutralino, produced through squark-antisquark pair production, decays into $\ell^{+}\ell^{'}-\nu$ ($\ell, \ell^{'} = e, \mu$) with a finite lifetime induced by R-parity violating couplings. Cross-section limits are established for specific squark and neutralino mass combinations. Specifically, for a 700 GeV squark, neutralinos with masses from 50 to 500 GeV and proper lifetimes ($c\tau$) between 1 mm and 6 m are excluded. Similarly, for a 1.6 TeV squark, $c\tau$ values ranging from 3 mm to 1 m are excluded for neutralinos with a mass of 1.3 TeV.

Thorin originally introduced the class of generalized gamma convolutions while investigating the infinite divisibility of log-Normal and Pareto distributions. While these distributions have been thoroughly examined in univariate settings, the literature has largely overlooked their multivariate extensions and associated dependence structures. Additionally, prior to this work, only a single projection method existed for the univariate case, with no available estimation techniques. By representing multivariate generalized gamma convolution densities within a tensorized Laguerre basis, we address these gaps and develop efficient estimation procedures for both univariate and multivariate scenarios. This study offers performance insights for these methods and derives a convergent series for multivariate gamma convolution densities, demonstrating superior stability compared to the univariate series proposed by Moschopoulos and Mathai. Finally, we illustrate these concepts through several examples.

This study introduces SketchMeHow, an interactive general instruction framework designed to guide everyday users in completing real-time daily tasks. Unlike traditional augmented reality systems that rely on pre-defined markers, SketchMeHow leverages user sketches as input to infer production intentions directly from drawing interfaces. Once a sketch is provided, the system analyzes the intended task by breaking it down into sub-tasks and applying spatial localization. Spatial augmented reality technology, implemented via a projector-camera setup, delivers these instructions to the end-users. To validate the framework, we performed two case studies involving domino arrangement and bento box preparation. Our user studies demonstrate that the system enables novice users to complete tasks efficiently with high satisfaction. We believe SketchMeHow has the potential to expand research in sketch-based real-world applications within human-computer interaction.

For a long time, identifying a combinatorial property that defines Cohen-Macaulay binomial edge ideals has been a challenging task. A recent conjecture proposes a connection between the Cohen-Macaulayness of a binomial edge ideal $J_G$ and specific vertex sets of its underlying graph $G$, known as \textit{cut sets}. Specifically, the conjecture asserts that $J_G$ is Cohen-Macaulay precisely when it is unmixed and the family of $G$'s cut sets forms an accessible set system. This paper provides a theoretical proof of the conjecture for all graphs containing up to $12$ vertices and introduces an algorithm capable of verifying the conjecture computationally for all graphs with up to $15$ vertices, as well as all blocks with whiskers where the block contains at most $11$ vertices, thereby substantially broadening earlier computational findings.

The NPDGamma experiment quantifies parity-violating asymmetry in gamma-ray emission resulting from the capture of polarized neutrons by liquid parahydrogen. In extracting the physics asymmetry from experimental data, the sensitivity of each detector within the array serves as a critical parameter. While the detector array exhibits approximate cylindrical symmetry around the target and a step-wise sinusoidal function was previously employed to model sensitivity, deviations from perfect symmetry require a Monte Carlo model to calculate necessary corrections for geometrical factors. To achieve this, the source code for MCNPX was modified to compute the sensitivity of individual cesium iodide detectors to the physics asymmetry. This paper details the MCNPX model, presents the calculation results, and explains how these findings are validated by measuring the parity-violating asymmetry of gamma rays from neutron capture on chlorine.

Deep neural networks have greatly enhanced predictive accuracy in classification tasks but often produce over-confident predictions in real-world scenarios involving domain shifts and out-of-distribution (OOD) instances. While most uncertainty estimation research targets computer vision to allow for visual verification, few studies address the natural language processing domain. Unlike Bayesian approaches that infer uncertainty indirectly via weight variations, evidential methods explicitly model class probability uncertainty using subjective opinions. These methods further account for inherent data uncertainty stemming from different causes: vacuity (lack of evidence) and dissonance (conflicting evidence). This paper introduces the first application of evidential uncertainty for OOD detection in text classification. We propose a cost-effective framework that utilizes both auxiliary outliers and pseudo off-manifold samples to train models with prior class knowledge, which exhibits high vacuity for OOD data. Extensive experiments show that our evidential uncertainty-based model surpasses existing counterparts in detecting OOD examples. Furthermore, this approach is readily deployable on traditional recurrent neural networks and can be fine-tuned for pre-trained transformers.

Various extensions of the Standard Model predict that neutrons can oscillate into hidden sector particles. Experimental tests of this additional neutron disappearance channel have not yet covered significant regions of the oscillation parameter space. Recent initiatives have aimed to refine oscillation time limits for low mass-splitting in ultra-cold neutron (UCN) storage setups and for higher mass-splitting in wall-penetration experiments. This study outlines the anticipated sensitivity of an experiment designed to probe neutron hidden oscillations at intermediate mass-splitting by utilizing magnetic fields ranging from $B_0=30-1100$ $\mu$T. Conducted at the Institut-Laue-Langevin, the experiment employed a new UCN counter to track beam flux. Based on the measured UCN rate and the data acquisition method, the study forecasts a sensitivity to the oscillation time on the order of a few seconds.

Determining significant point cloud features and estimating the pose between them remains a difficult challenge, primarily due to the lack of inherent structure and ambiguous ordering within point clouds. Although deep learning has significantly advanced most 3D computer vision tasks—including object classification, segmentation, and registration—the consistency of features remains a weak point in current learning-based frameworks. This paper introduces a novel learning-based alignment network for complex scenarios, named Deep Feature Consistency, which comprises three core components: a multiscale graph feature merging network that transforms geometric correspondences into high-dimensional features, a correspondence weighting module that generates multiple candidate inlier subsets, and a Procrustes-based method called deep feature matching that provides a closed-form solution for relative pose estimation. A critical aspect of the deep feature matching module involves constructing a feature consistency matrix for each inlier subset to derive principal vectors as inlier likelihoods. We rigorously evaluate the robustness and effectiveness of our approach on the 3DMatch and KITTI odometry datasets. For large indoor scenes, results on 3DMatch show that our method surpasses both state-of-the-art traditional and learning-based techniques. In KITTI outdoor scenes, our approach significantly reduces transformation errors. Furthermore, we demonstrate its strong generalization capabilities across different datasets.
This paper establishes that any Ricci shrinker which is sufficiently close to $(\mathbb C P^N,g_{FS})$ in the Gromov-Hausdorff topology is necessarily isometric to $(\mathbb C P^N,g_{FS})$.

The transmission of contagious diseases is fundamentally tied to the timing of interactions between infected individuals and others, yet the specific interplay between contact schedules (time of day, day of week) and the latent or infectious phases of a disease remains poorly understood. By analyzing real-world physical proximity data, we demonstrate that actual human contact patterns destabilize epidemic outbreaks and non-trivially alter the basic reproduction number compared to randomized scenarios. Through simple generative models constrained by this empirical data, we attribute these findings to specific temporal statistics of contact behavior. Specifically, outbreak destabilization arises from a high likelihood of extreme events—such as super-spreading and zero-spreading—which our models replicate by incorporating temporal clustering of contacts. Additionally, contact patterns can either elevate or suppress the basic reproduction number depending on the length of the latent period; this modulation results from the alignment of the infectious period with recurring daily and weekly fluctuations in the conditional rate of secondary contacts, a mechanism reproduced by implementing a cyclostationary contact rate in our models. Consequently, by identifying and simulating these relevant non-Markovian contact statistics, our research paves the way for systematically investigating the non-equilibrium physics of realistic disease transmission and non-Markovian spreading processes in general.

Android enforces a security protocol mandating that applications explicitly request permission to access sensitive user data, such as contacts and SMS messages, or utilize specific system capabilities like the camera and internet connectivity. Despite this, Android applications frequently exhibit overprivilege, a condition where they demand more permissions than actually required, creating a significant security vulnerability. To address this issue, the paper introduces MPDroid, a method integrating static analysis with collaborative filtering to determine the essential permissions for an app by examining its description and API usage. The MPDroid process begins by using collaborative filtering to establish an initial set of minimum permissions, followed by static analysis to pinpoint the precise permissions the app genuinely requires. Subsequently, the system assesses the risk of overprivilege by analyzing the app's excess privileges, which are the unnecessary permissions requested. Experimental validation was performed on a dataset of 16,343 popular applications sourced from Google Play, demonstrating that MPDroid significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions.

Given suitable technical assumptions, simple-loop theory enables the derivation of various asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues of Toeplitz matrices $T_{n}(f)$ generated by a function $f$. However, this theory is currently unavailable in the preconditioning context, which involves matrices of the form $T_{n}^{-1}(g)T_{n}(l)$ where $l$ and $g$ are real-valued, $g$ is non-negative, and not identically zero almost everywhere. Independently, and under the milder hypothesis that $f=\frac{l}{g}$ is even and monotonic on $[0,\pi]$, matrix-less algorithms have been created for efficiently computing the eigenvalues of large preconditioned matrices of this type with linear complexity relative to the matrix order. The high efficiency of these algorithms stems from expansions similar to those when $g\equiv 1$, combined with extrapolation techniques; consequently, numerical evidence strongly suggests that simple-loop theory must be extended to this new setting. This work focuses on a change of variable followed by the asymptotic expansion of the transformed variable, introducing new matrix-less algorithms tailored to this specific case. Numerical experiments demonstrate significantly higher precision, reaching machine precision, while maintaining the same linear computational cost compared to previously proposed matrix-less procedures.

Handling uncertainty has become just as critical, if not more so, than raw predictive performance in machine learning models. This is especially relevant during crises like the pandemic, where government policies and individual choices are constantly shaped by unknown variables. Addressing this need, Neural Process Families (NPFs) have emerged as a promising approach by integrating Gaussian processes with neural networks to enable uncertainty-aware predictions. Among these, Latent Neural Processes are noted for their capacity to capture both local uncertainties at specific points and global uncertainties inherent in function priors. However, several key issues remain open, including a rigorous definition of global uncertainty, the causal mechanisms driving it, and its manipulation within generative frameworks. To address these gaps, we introduce GloBal Convolutional Neural Process (GBCoNP), a model that achieves state-of-the-art log-likelihood among latent NPFs. GBCoNP employs a global uncertainty representation, $p(z)$, defined as an aggregation over a discretized input space. We further investigate the causal relationship between global uncertainty levels and intra-task diversity. Our learned priors are evaluated across diverse scenarios, ranging from 1D and 2D data to a newly introduced spatial-temporal COVID dataset. By manipulating global uncertainty, our method not only facilitates the generation of targeted samples for few-shot learning but also allows for probability assessments of functional priors.

We introduce mesoscale numerical simulations of Rayleigh-Bénard convection within a two-dimensional emulsion model. The investigated systems consist of finite-sized droplets, with their concentration ($\Phi_0$) systematically adjusted from low levels (characteristic of Newtonian emulsions) to high levels (non-Newtonian emulsions). Our primary focus is on characterizing heat transfer properties near the transition from conductive to convective states. While homogeneous Newtonian systems display steady flows and time-independent heat fluxes in this regime, emulsions exhibit non-steady dynamics marked by heat flux fluctuations. This study aims to characterize such non-steady behavior through detailed analysis of time-averaged heat flux and its fluctuations. To understand the time-averaged flux, we propose a comparative study between the emulsion and a single-phase system with viscosity derived from the emulsion's shear rheology. We demonstrate that this local closure approach is effective only when a specific degree of coarse-graining at the droplet scale is applied to the local viscosity. To further investigate heat flux fluctuations, we compare Newtonian and non-Newtonian emulsions at a fixed time-averaged heat flux. This comparison reveals that finite-size droplets and non-Newtonian rheology interact to induce enhanced heat-flux fluctuations at the droplet scale. These amplified fluctuations stem from the emergence of spatial correlations among distant droplets, which we identify through direct measurements of droplet displacement and the analysis of the corresponding correlation function. The findings provide valuable insights into heat transfer characteristics for confined systems containing finite-size constituents.

Modern networks increasingly utilize drones as mobile base stations (MBSs) to enhance coverage flexibility, yet this deployment introduces significant challenges, particularly the high power consumption of drones. To address this, we propose a novel architecture featuring "charging drones" capable of supplying energy to MBS drones. Since these charging drones also require power, we incorporate ground-mounted charging towers to replenish them. This study formulates an energy-efficiency maximization problem divided into two independent optimization tasks. The first task involves a two-stage charging matching process: the initial stage schedules connections between ground towers and charging drones, while the second stage coordinates between charging drones and MBS drones. We also demonstrate how to transform the original formulation, which contains non-convex terms, into an equivalent convex optimization problem. The second task focuses on minimizing time-average transmit power for each MBS drone while ensuring system stability through Lyapunov optimization. Our proposed solutions effectively extend the operational lifetimes of MBS drones, thereby increasing the overall network coverage duration.

Investigating neutron star mergers through gravitational wave detection represents one of the most promising avenues for understanding dense nuclear matter at extreme densities. Currently, however, there is no compelling evidence confirming that these stars possess zero temperature during their final pre-merger orbits; conversely, theoretical models suggest temperatures could reach several MeV. According to the prevailing theory, tidal interactions transfer mechanical energy and angular momentum from the orbit to the star, with internal friction converting this energy into heat. While these effects during the inspiral phase are potentially observable, varying methodologies for estimating energy transfer and tidal friction sizes have led to divergent conclusions regarding the significance of pre-merger tidal dynamics. This study specifically examines how temperature influences the tidal deformability of neutron stars immediately preceding a merger. By applying a class of hot equations of state derived from diverse nuclear models, we determined that even at low temperatures ($T<1$ MeV), the impact on the fundamental components of tidal deformability is non-negligible. Nevertheless, our primary finding indicates that the effect of temperature on tidal deformability remains indistinguishable, a surprising result whose implications are analyzed and discussed herein.

This study applies Polchinski's exact renormalisation group equations to multicritical fixed points found in scalar theories across dimensions ranging from two to four, utilizing both the local potential approximation (LPA) and its derivative expansion extension. By demonstrating that non-linear differential equations can be linearized at each multicritical point to treat the $\epsilon$-expansion perturbatively, the authors compare their findings with standard perturbation theory results for critical exponents. These comparisons serve to validate the LPA and the derivative expansion. Furthermore, an alternative truncation of the exact RG equation yields equations resembling the derivative expansion but achieving accuracy for critical exponents up to order $\epsilon$ and for the field anomalous dimension up to order $\epsilon^2$. Finally, an exact marginal operator for the complete set of RG equations is derived.

Numerous efforts have aimed to create countermeasure techniques to bolster Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) systems against spoofing attacks. However, as demonstrated by the ASVspoof 2019 challenge, current ASV models lack sufficient generalization to handle unseen attacks. Further analysis suggests that a comprehensive three-tiered approach—encompassing the classifier, feature extraction, and loss function—could partially mitigate this issue. Consequently, this study introduces the Efficient Attention Branch Network (EABN), a modular architecture paired with a combined loss function, to tackle the problem of generalization.

Interpretable machine learning (IML) focuses on the behaviors and characteristics of machine learning models. However, researchers primarily view models merely as means to understand underlying phenomena. This work bridges these viewpoints by demonstrating how to construct IML property descriptors. These descriptors function as IML methods that offer insights not only into the model itself but also into the properties of the phenomena the model aims to represent. We contend that IML is essential for scientific inference using machine learning because individual model components do not directly represent phenomenon properties; rather, the complete model does. Nevertheless, existing IML research frequently merges two distinct objectives of model analysis—model auditing and scientific inference—rendering it ambiguous which interpretations are valid for learning about phenomena. Leveraging statistical decision theory, we demonstrate that applying IML property descriptors to a model grants access to relevant facets of the data's joint probability distribution. We delineate the types of questions these descriptors can answer, offer a framework for constructing suitable descriptors, and measure their epistemic uncertainty.

By applying ultraproduct methods, we introduce a nonstandard Minkowski dimension applicable to all bounded sets, characterized by the property $\dim(A\times B)=\dim(A)+\dim(B)$, meaning it is product-summable. To demonstrate this result, we extend Falconer's example to prove that neither the standard upper Minkowski dimension nor the Hausdorff dimension satisfies product-summability.

With the growing integration of autonomous and semi-autonomous agents into society, ensuring their safety has become increasingly critical. However, the complex scenarios in which these agents operate often make formal verification unfeasible, leading to the adoption of simulation-based methods designed to falsify complex systems. While recent approaches leverage reinforcement learning, they are susceptible to over-exploiting known failure modes, thereby restricting the coverage of the failure space. To address this limitation, the proposed work introduces a class of Markov decision processes called the "knowledge MDP," which operates on both the learned model and its associated metadata, such as sample counts. Specifically, by utilizing the "knows what it knows" (KWIK) framework, the learner evaluates its understanding of the underlying system, including model estimates, confidence levels, and assumptions. This approach is validated through a novel algorithm that extends bidirectional learning across multiple simulator fidelities to the domain of safety validation. A case study involving the training of an adversary to intercept a test model within a grid-world environment demonstrates the method's effectiveness. Monte Carlo trials compare the proposed algorithm's sample efficiency against single-fidelity learning, highlighting the benefits of incorporating knowledge about learned models into decision-making processes.
We investigate endomorphisms and derivations within infinite-dimensional cyclic Leibniz algebras.

While Grammatical Error Correction systems are typically judged by the quantity of errors they fix, it remains unexplored whether every error category holds equal significance. We introduce and implement a technique to measure how distinct grammatical error types impact human perception. Our findings reveal that certain infrequent errors are perceived as more disruptive than frequent ones, which should influence strategies for enhancing both the systems and their evaluation metrics.

This paper investigates a model of mass enhancement within N=2 supersymmetric quantum mechanics. Its simplicity allows it to serve as a quantum simulation for the mass enhancement that occurs during spontaneous supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking. The model is derived from a prototype based on the quantum Rabi model. While the original mathematical prototype facilitates the transition from N=2 SUSY to its spontaneous breaking without exhibiting mass enhancement, recent trapped-ion experiments have successfully realized this transition using a specific experimental method. The proposed model explains how a single-mode heavy boson gains mass from the excitation of a single-mode light boson during SUSY breaking. Although the interaction lacks a Higgs potential, the mass is radiatively enhanced through the exchange between bosonic and fermionic states. This mass-enhancement transition is achieved under the conditions established in the aforementioned trapped-ion experiment.

The failure to forecast the 2014-2015 "Monster"/"Super" El Ni\~no a year in advance was attributed to the rising significance of El Ni\~no Modoki, a variant known for its low predictability using traditional models. However, this study demonstrates that, as of now, this new El Ni\~no type can largely be predicted with a lead time exceeding 10 years. This capability is achieved by identifying the predictability source through an information-flow-based causality analysis, a method rigorously grounded in first principles over the last decade. We reveal that information originating from solar activity 45 years ago influences sea surface temperatures, creating a causal structure that mimics the El Ni\~no Modoki mode. Utilizing this insight, we construct a multidimensional system based on sunspot number series with time delays ranging from 22 to 50 years. By selecting the first 25 principal components as predictors and applying information-flow-based causal deep learning, the model accurately reproduces these events with a 12-year forecast horizon.

Weakly supervised person search has recently been introduced to eliminate the need for human-annotated identities, training models exclusively on bounding box data. A common approach decomposes this task into detection and unsupervised re-identification (Re-ID) stages; however, this method overlooks two critical cues found in unconstrained scene imagery. First, current unsupervised Re-ID models utilize only cropped images, neglecting rich contextual details. Second, real-world scenes contain numerous unpaired persons; treating them as distinct identities creates a long-tail distribution, whereas discarding them causes significant information loss. To address these issues, we present the Context-Guided and Unpaired-Assisted (CGUA) weakly supervised person search framework. This framework employs a novel Context-Guided Cluster (CGC) algorithm to integrate contextual information during clustering and an Unpaired-Assisted Memory (UAM) unit to differentiate between unpaired and paired individuals by separating them. Comprehensive experiments indicate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art weakly supervised techniques, achieving over a 5% mAP improvement on the CUHK-SYSU dataset. Furthermore, by utilizing a wider range of unlabeled data, our approach matches or exceeds the performance of current supervised state-of-the-art methods. The code and models will be made available shortly.

This study introduces a novel consensus-based distributed algorithm designed to address learning problems characterized by feature partitioning and non-smooth convex objective functions. Because these problems are inherently non-separable—meaning the objective functions cannot be decomposed into a simple sum of agent-specific terms—we reformulate the original optimization task into a dual convex problem that is amenable to distributed optimization via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Subsequently, we propose a technique to solve the minimization component of the ADMM update step without relying on conjugate functions, which can be computationally prohibitive or infeasible for non-smooth objectives. Instead of calculating conjugates, we resolve the optimization problem for each ADMM iteration within the dual domain using the block coordinate descent algorithm. Distinct from existing approaches, our proposed method operates in a fully distributed manner and eliminates the need for objective function conjugates. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the algorithm converges to the optimal centralized solution, a finding further supported by simulation results confirming network-wide convergence.

This paper introduces an alternative Kalman filter implementation for track fitting in the LHCb experiment, utilizing simplified parametrizations for particle trajectory extrapolation within the LHCb dipole magnet's field and for modeling multiple scattering effects in detector materials. This approach achieves a performance improvement of over fourfold without compromising the accuracy of the estimated track parameters, making it suitable for the software-only trigger system planned for the LHCb upgrade.

This article constructs six-quark currents with quantum numbers $J^P=0^+$, $0^-$, $1^+$, and $1^-$ to investigate $\Lambda_c\Lambda_c$ dibaryon and $\Lambda_c\bar{\Lambda}_c$ baryonium states using QCD sum rules. The analysis incorporates vacuum condensates up to dimension 16 and truncates contributions at order $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^k)$ where $k\leq3$. The resulting predicted masses are $5.11_{-0.12}^{+0.15}$ GeV, $4.66_{-0.06}^{+0.10}$ GeV, $4.99_{-0.09}^{+0.10}$ GeV, and $4.68^{+0.08}_{-0.08}$ GeV for the $J^P=0^+$, $0^-$, $1^+$, and $1^-$ states, respectively. These values can be compared with future experimental data, particularly given the high integrated luminosity expected at the BESIII facility around a center-of-mass energy of $4.8\,\rm{GeV}$. Furthermore, we observe that terms with $\frac{3}{2}< k \leq 3$ contribute negligibly and may be safely neglected in the QCD sum rule calculations.

The mechanism behind the unexpectedly high radiative production rate of pseudoscalar mesons in $J/\psi$ decays has long remained unclear. This study introduces the inaugural lattice QCD computation of the partial decay width for the transition $J/\psi \to \gamma\eta$, aiming to verify that the QCD $U_A(1)$ anomaly strengthens the coupling between gluons and flavor-singlet pseudoscalar mesons. The simulation employs $N_f=2$ lattice QCD gauge configurations with a pion mass of approximately 350 MeV, utilizing the distillation technique to compute light quark loops. The analysis yields an $\eta$ mass of $718(8)$ MeV and a decay width of $\Gamma(J/\psi\to\gamma \eta)=0.385(45)$ keV. Based on the assumption that the $U_A(1)$ anomaly dominates, alongside a flavor singlet-octet mixing angle of $\theta=-24.5^\circ$, the predicted production rates for the physical $\eta$ and $\eta'$ in $J/\psi$ radiative decay are $1.15(14)\times 10^{-3}$ and $4.49(53)\times 10^{-3}$, respectively. These findings align closely with experimental measurements, confirming the significant influence of the $U_A(1)$ anomaly in this decay process. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that lattice QCD is a promising method for investigating light hadrons produced via $J/\psi$ radiation.

We introduce a novel framework for trajectory planning along predefined paths designed for general N-link manipulators. Unlike prior methods that rely on open-loop minimum-time controllers or pre-tuned motion profiles via time-scaling, we develop analytical algorithms capable of identifying all initial conditions that can be steered to a desired target set while respecting environmental constraints. Furthermore, we characterize families of safe state-feedback controllers possessing several advantageous properties. A central component of our approach is a state feedback template that establishes ordering properties among trajectories within the resulting closed-loop system. This structure enables direct operation on the nonlinear system for both analysis and synthesis. The proposed architecture ensures that both offline computations and online execution scale efficiently with the number of manipulator links. Numerical experiments on a commercial robotic arm confirm the feasibility of efficient online implementation, suggesting potential applications for a range of challenging tasks.

Recent attention has focused on solving nonconvex min-max optimization problems because of their extensive applications in machine learning, networked resource allocation, and distributed optimization. The most widely adopted first-order approach for these problems is the simultaneous (or single-loop) gradient descent-ascent algorithm, favored for its implementation simplicity.
