The advent of fifth-generation (5G) mobile communication systems and software-defined networks (SDN) has not only enhanced the performance of vehicular networks but also created a demand for new applications, such as autonomous vehicles, within future transportation. To address the requirements of intelligent transportation systems, this paper proposes a novel vehicular network architecture that integrates 5G technologies with SDN. Furthermore, fog cells are introduced to flexibly serve vehicles and minimize frequent handovers between vehicles and road side units (RSUs). Based on this proposed 5G SDN framework, transmission delay and throughput are analyzed and compared. Simulation results demonstrate that 5G SDN vehicular networks achieve a minimum transmission delay across varying vehicle densities. Additionally, the throughput provided by fog cells in this architecture surpasses that of traditional transportation management systems.

Sequential Monte Carlo represents a suite of algorithms designed to sample from evolving distributions. Certain methods within this family, including particle filters, are extensively utilized in physics and signal processing research. Recently, their utility has expanded to broader inference tasks, such as Bayesian modeling. In recent years, these algorithms have garnered significant attention due to their capacity for natural and scalable parallelization. Nevertheless, they are often regarded as challenging to implement. Furthermore, while parallel programming is conceptually attractive, particularly for fields involving sequential Monte Carlo, it remains unfamiliar to many researchers. To address these challenges, a C++ template library has been developed to facilitate the implementation of general sequential Monte Carlo algorithms on parallel hardware. The library's capabilities are demonstrated through two examples: a basic particle filter and a traditional Bayesian modeling problem.

Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in Game AI research, especially within Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, despite these successes, existing games often rely on fixed environments and mechanics, hindering researchers' ability to prototype varied scenarios. Yet, evaluating RL agents across diverse game settings is essential for investigating generalization and preventing overfitting. This paper introduces Griddly, a novel platform for Game AI that offers a distinctive blend of highly customizable games, multiple observer types, and a high-performance C++ engine. Furthermore, we present a series of baseline experiments designed to examine how different observation configurations impact the generalization capabilities of RL agents.

Insertion tasks are fundamental to most robotic assembly processes, with the peg-in-hole (PiH) scenario being a particularly prominent area of study within both academic and industrial manipulation fields. This category encompasses a wide range of challenges, where difficulty varies based on factors such as the nature of misalignment and contact dynamics during insertion attempts. This paper details the development and evaluation of adaptive compliance controllers tailored for insertion-based assembly, including learning-driven approaches capable of handling uncertainties in goal positioning. Initially, we introduce compliance controllers designed to guarantee safe robotic operation by capping contact forces during engagement. Subsequently, we analyze the resulting force signatures to derive corrective actions necessary for successful insertion. Finally, we integrate these controllers and learned models to formulate a policy capable of achieving insertion in novel test conditions with near-perfect reliability. The proposed methodology is validated through experiments on a physical robotic testbed utilizing a 6-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm.

The achievements of text-based pre-training have recently been successfully expanded to encompass vision, audio, and cross-modal contexts. Current pre-training models across these diverse modalities are increasingly adopting similar architectural structures, creating an opportunity to unify them within a single framework. This paper introduces TencentPretrain, a toolkit designed to support pre-training models across various modalities. Its primary advantage lies in a modular design that categorizes pre-training models into five distinct components: embedding, encoder, target embedding, decoder, and target. Since nearly all standard modules are available within each component, users can freely combine elements from different parts to construct complete pre-training models. This modularity allows for the efficient reproduction of existing models or the creation of novel ones. Evaluations on text, vision, and audio benchmarks demonstrate that the toolkit achieves performance comparable to original implementations.

The coalgebraic $\mu$-calculus offers a versatile semantic foundation for fixpoint logics applied to systems with branching structures extending beyond standard relational models, such as probabilistic, weighted, or game-based systems. Prior research established an exponential-time upper bound for satisfiability checking, contingent upon the existence of tableau rules for next-step modalities that meet specific formal criteria: rule matches must be encodable in polynomial size, and their sequent duals must support cut absorption. Although such rule sets exist for certain significant cases, they remain unproven for others, notably those involving integer weights in the graded $\mu$-calculus or real-valued weights combined with non-linear arithmetic. This work demonstrates the same exponential complexity bound under broader conditions, specifically by leveraging the complexity of the underlying one-step logic's simpler, nesting-free satisfiability problem. The bound is achieved through a generic global caching algorithm enabling on-the-fly satisfiability verification. A key advantage of this method is its direct handling of unguarded formulae, thereby eliminating the need for guardedness transformations. Practical applications include deriving new exponential-time upper bounds for satisfiability in the graded $\mu$-calculus extended with polynomial inequalities (such as positive Presburger arithmetic) and in the two-valued probabilistic $\mu$-calculus augmented with polynomial inequalities.

We establish the global existence of weak solutions for a dissipative variant of the one-velocity Baer-Nunziato system, which models a mixture of two non-interacting, viscous, compressible fluids within a piecewise regular Lipschitz domain subject to general inflow and outflow boundary conditions. The chosen geometric framework is sufficiently broad to encompass most application-relevant domains, such as (curved) pipes featuring piecewise regular and axis-dependent cross-sections. Regarding the proof of existence, we adapt the contemporary classical Lions-Feireisl methodology for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, integrating it with a generalization of the renormalized solutions theory for transport equations inspired by Vasseur, Wen, and Yu. Furthermore, the results concerning the families of transport equations presented herein extend and refine existing statements within the theory of renormalized solutions, thereby holding independent interest.

Sparse modeling has been a central focus in signal processing and machine learning for more than twenty years. Supervised sparsity-aware learning primarily follows two trajectories: discriminative methods and generative methods. The latter, often referred to as Bayesian approaches, are particularly valuable for assessing prediction uncertainty, leveraging prior information effectively, and enhancing model robustness through the marginalization of parameter estimation uncertainties. Additionally, hyper-parameters for these priors can be learned directly from training data. A critical factor in implementing sparsity-aware learning involves selecting an appropriate regularizer for discriminative methods or a suitable prior distribution for Bayesian learning. While the last decade has seen a surge in research emphasizing discriminative techniques due to the rise of deep learning, there is a renewed interest in Bayesian methods. This resurgence offers fresh perspectives on designing deep neural networks, strengthens connections between neural networks and Bayesian models, and paves the way for new unsupervised learning avenues, such as Bayesian tensor decomposition.

This article aims to achieve two objectives. First, it provides a unified review of recent progress in integrating sparsity-promoting priors into three prominent data modeling frameworks: deep neural networks, Gaussian processes, and tensor decomposition. Second, it examines the associated inference techniques, covering both evidence maximization via optimization and variational inference methods. The discussion also addresses key challenges, including the small data dilemma, automatic model structure search, and the natural evaluation of prediction uncertainty, illustrated through typical signal processing and machine learning tasks.

High harmonic generation (HHG) offers a proven method for creating compact setups that produce coherent, ultrafast pulses with short wavelengths. These table-top sources are increasingly employed to image biological and physical systems through advanced techniques like ptychography and coherent diffraction imaging. Since these methods rely on coherent illumination, it is crucial to analyze the spatial coherence of high-harmonic beams and identify the factors limiting this property. This study examines the near- and far-field spatial characteristics of high-harmonic radiation produced within a gas cell. Using the SCIMITAR technique, we measured the far-field intensity profiles, wavefront curvature, and complex coherence factors across different harmonic orders. By applying the Gaussian-Schell model, we deduced the beam properties at the generation plane. Our findings indicate that the order-dependent spatial coherence aligns with partial coherence caused by both the intensity-dependent variation of the dipole phase and the finite spatial coherence of the driving radiation. These results provide strategies to enhance the coherence of harmonic beams, which would directly improve imaging capabilities using high-harmonic radiation.

Several prior neural network-based approaches excel at removing salt-and-pepper noise but rely on the assumption that noise values are strictly 0 and 255, an idealization that does not hold in real-world scenarios. Consequently, these methods produce significantly degraded results when noise values deviate from these extremes. To address this limitation, our proposed method employs a convolutional neural network to identify noise pixels across a broader spectrum of values. A filter is then applied to reset these detected pixels to 0, facilitating subsequent processing. Furthermore, a second convolutional neural network is utilized to perform the actual denoising and image restoration.

Large pre-trained language models have revolutionized the natural language processing (NLP) field, becoming the standard approach for various tasks even when annotation data is scarce. However, deploying these models in production environments, whether on the cloud or at the edge, remains difficult due to their substantial memory requirements and inference expenses. As an alternative, recent advancements in efficient NLP demonstrate that small, weight-efficient models can deliver competitive performance at significantly reduced costs. We present pNLP-Mixer, an embedding-free model built on the MLP-Mixer architecture that achieves high weight-efficiency through a novel linguistically informed projection layer. Our evaluations on two multi-lingual semantic parsing datasets, MTOP and multiATIS, show that on MTOP, pNLP-Mixer nearly matches the performance of mBERT while using 38 times fewer parameters and surpasses the state-of-the-art tiny model (pQRNN), which has three times fewer parameters. Furthermore, on a long-sequence classification task (Hyperpartisan), our unpretrained pNLP-Mixer outperforms RoBERTa, which contains 100 times more parameters, highlighting the architecture's potential.

Recommender systems are essential for online platforms because they can integrate individual user preferences. While accuracy is crucial, diversity is equally important for expanding users' perspectives and boosting corporate sales. Nevertheless, balancing accuracy with diversity remains a significant challenge, particularly regarding unexplored data and user biases. This paper introduces an adaptive learning framework designed to achieve both precise and diverse recommendations. We adapt a recent bilateral branch network from computer vision, originally used for image classification, to the domain of item recommendation. Specifically, we encode domain-level diversity by dynamically balancing accurate predictions in a standard branch with diverse predictions in an adaptive branch. Additionally, we capture user-level diversity using a two-way adaptive metric learning backbone within each branch. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show that our method consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art baselines.

This paper examines forgetting within disjunctive logic programs, a process that reduces the program's signature by removing a specific atom. We aim to establish a syntax-independent methodology, ensuring that if two programs are strongly equivalent, the outcomes of forgetting an atom in both remain strongly equivalent. Our primary definition of forgetting, though theoretically sound by characterizing the set of Strong Equivalence (SE) consequences that exclude the target atom, is impractical. Consequently, we introduce an equivalent and practical definition: forgetting an atom $p$ involves retaining all rules that do not mention $p$, alongside rules derived via a single inference step from rules that do. We demonstrate that this approach possesses appropriate properties and yields a finite characterization with a manageable (at most quadratic) computational blowup. Additionally, we have developed a prototype implementation of this forgetting mechanism.

We introduce a mesh-free deep learning approach to address nonconvex energy minimization problems associated with martensitic phase transitions and crystal twinning. These challenges are analytically and computationally demanding due to multiwell gradient energies characterized by numerous local minima and topologically complex microstructures featuring free boundaries with gradient discontinuities. Our method employs the Deep Ritz framework, representing minimizer candidates via parameterized deep neural networks and optimizing energy with respect to these parameters. A key innovation is the introduction of SmReLU, a novel smoothened rectified linear unit that effectively captures minimizer structures where standard activation functions fail. Being mesh-free, the approach naturally approximates essential free boundaries without specialized handling and is straightforward to implement. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

In numerous fields, sequential data often exhibit variable lengths, including extremely long sequences, necessitating that neural attention mechanisms effectively capture long-range dependencies. However, most current attention models are limited to short sequences or rely on chunking and padding to standardize input dimensions. To address this, we introduce ChordMixer, a straightforward neural component designed to handle variable-length sequences of any magnitude. Each ChordMixer block comprises a parameter-free, position-wise rotation layer paired with an element-wise MLP layer. Stacking these blocks creates a robust network backbone that efficiently blends input signals toward learning objectives. We evaluated ChordMixer on the synthetic addition task, long document classification, and DNA sequence taxonomy classification. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses other neural attention models.

We introduce a new approach to address a chemical diffusion master equation characterized by birth and death processes. This framework consists of an infinite set of Fokker-Planck equations, with components interconnected through reaction dynamics that mirror those of a chemical master equation. Originally formulated in [3], this system models the probabilistic evolution of chemical reaction kinetics alongside the spatial diffusion of individual particles. Leveraging fundamental concepts from infinite-dimensional Gaussian analysis, we recast this infinite system of Fokker-Planck equations into a solitary evolution equation governed by a generalized stochastic process, expressed via Malliavin derivatives and differential second quantization operators. Through this alternative formulation, we establish a connection between specific finite-dimensional projections of the original solution and the solution to a single partial differential equation of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck type, where the number of variables corresponds to the dimension of the projection space.

We simulated six binary-merger progenitors of Supernova 1987A (SN 1987A), characterized by properties similar to the blue supergiant Sanduleak -69 202. These models underwent 3D neutrino-heated explosions and evolved post-shock breakout before transitioning to spherical symmetry for light-curve calculations. Our findings align with previous studies on single-star progenitors: (1) 3D neutrino-driven explosions with energies matching SN 1987A produce Ni-56 masses consistent with the radioactive light-curve tail; (2) hydrodynamic simulations mix hydrogen inward to velocities below 40 km/s, consistent with spectral data; and (3) for a fixed explosion energy, the efficiency of outward Ni-56 mixing is primarily driven by high growth factors of Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities at the (C+O)/He and He/H interfaces, alongside weak interactions between fast plumes and the reverse shock beneath the He/H interface. All binary-merger models feature presupernova radii matching the photometric radius of Sanduleak -69 202 and outer-layer structures capable of reproducing the initial luminosity peak observed in the first week. Models mixing approximately 0.5 solar masses of hydrogen into the helium shell and exhibiting strong outward Ni-56 mixing with peak velocities exceeding 3000 km/s (the observed bulk velocity) yield light-curve shapes that closely match the dome of the SN 1987A light curve. A comparative analysis of the best 3D neutrino-driven explosion models based on single-star and binary-merger progenitors indicates that only one binary model satisfies all observational constraints, with the exception of one.

We examine general charged Kasner-like solutions within the framework of five-dimensional supergravity coupled to Abelian vector multiplets, applicable across any space-time signature. Depending on the coordinate system selected, these solutions serve as extensions of Melvin/Rosen cosmologies, flux-branes, and domain walls.

Pascal Baseilhac and Stefan Kolb recently established a PBW basis for the $q$-Onsager algebra $\mathcal O_q$, defining its elements recursively, which obscures their closed-form representation. To address this challenge, we utilize the universal Askey-Wilson algebra $\Delta_q$. By employing the natural algebra homomorphism $\natural \colon \mathcal O_q \to \Delta_q$, we apply it to the aforementioned PBW basis and derive closed-form expressions for the resulting images. These findings rely extensively on Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind.

In many online bipartite matching scenarios, including edge-weighted matching and those involving two-sided vertex arrivals, current fractional algorithms surpass their randomized integral versions. This discrepancy is notable because the bipartite fractional matching polytope is integral, theoretically permitting lossless rounding. However, Devanur et al. (SODA'13) demonstrated that lossless rounding is unfeasible in an online context.

Notwithstanding this limitation, we commence an investigation into lossless online rounding for online bipartite matching. Our primary insight is that although general lossless online rounding is impossible, randomized algorithms generate fractional counterparts with identical competitive ratios, which are inherently losslessly roundable online. This suggests introducing constraints to reduce the "online integrality gap," thereby enabling lossless online rounding. We identify a collection of non-convex constraints that facilitate such rounding and achieve competitive ratios superior to those of deterministic algorithms.

Applying our lossless online rounding framework yields two significant results: (i) a doubly-exponential enhancement alongside a precise threshold for the randomness (or advice) required to beat deterministic online algorithms for vertex-weighted bipartite matching, and (ii) an optimal semi-OCS, aligning with recent findings by Gao et al. (FOCS'21) that addressed a query posed by Fahrbach et al. (FOCS'20).

During the 1970s, Berge defined 1-extendable graphs, also known as B-graphs, as graphs where each vertex is part of a maximum independent set. Driven by applications in wireless network design, this study examines the computational complexity of determining 1-extendability. We demonstrate that, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, this problem cannot be solved in $2^{o(n)}$ time for general graphs, where $n$ represents the number of vertices. Furthermore, 1-extendability remains NP-hard even within subcubic planar graphs and unit disk graphs, the latter being a standard model for wireless networks. Despite the apparent proximity between 1-extendability and the Maximum Independent Set problem, we prove that there exist 1-extendable graphs for which finding a maximum independent set is NP-hard. Additionally, we explore a parameterized variant of 1-extendability.

Photoluminescence (PL) spectra of monolayer (1L) semiconductors display peaks corresponding to various charge-carrier complexes. We utilized diffusion quantum Monte Carlo simulations to calculate the binding energies of these complexes and investigated their reactions to electric and magnetic fields. Our analysis centers on quintons (charged biexcitons), as they represent the largest free charge-carrier complexes found in transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). To evaluate the accuracy of the Rytova-Keldysh interaction potential, we compared the binding energies of charge-carrier complexes in 1L-TMDs against those derived from *ab initio* interaction potentials. Magnetic fields below 8 T alter binding energies (BEs) by approximately 0.2 meV per Tesla, a finding consistent with experimental data, where different complexes exhibit similar variations in BE. These findings will assist in identifying specific charge complexes within the PL spectra of 1L-semiconductors.

Recent progress in laser technology has made it crucial to examine fundamental laser-assisted processes within extremely intense laser fields. This study, situated within the framework of laser-assisted quantum electrodynamics (QED), analyzes electron-proton scattering under a strong, circularly polarized electromagnetic field. Initially, we investigate the process considering only the relativistic dressing of the electron, excluding the proton. Subsequently, to assess the impact of proton dressing, we account for the relativistic dressing of both the electron and proton using Dirac-Volkov functions. Analytical expressions for the differential cross section (DCS) are derived for both scenarios at the lowest order of perturbation theory. The results indicate that the laser field significantly reduces the DCS. Furthermore, proton dressing effects become significant at laser field strengths of $10^{10}~\text{V/cm}$ or higher, necessitating their inclusion. The study also details how laser field strength and frequency influence the DCS and provides a comparison with Mott scattering and laser-free outcomes.

Millions of internet users engage in diverse discussions across Question-and-Answer (Q&A) platforms, yet attention varies significantly; some communities flourish and sustain themselves, while others struggle to gain traction, remaining small niches or becoming dormant. Consequently, it is crucial to identify and understand the specific factors and rules that determine the sustainability of Q&A platforms. Our objective is to equip community managers with quantitative tools to better comprehend, regulate, and nurture their communities, thereby enhancing the efficiency of information exchange online. To achieve this, we extracted, modeled, and clustered user activity time series from 50 randomly selected Q&A sites within the Stack Exchange network to analyze user behavior. Our analysis revealed four distinct temporal patterns of user activity, primarily differentiated by activity frequency. Furthermore, by decomposing total activity in these 50 instances according to these identified user profiles, we classified the platforms into three distinct activity categories. This streamlined categorization reflects the developmental stage and maturity of the underlying communities and offers practical value to operators. Beyond quantitatively assessing the progress of Q&A platforms, our approach provides actionable insights for optimizing community building, such as recommending which user types to prioritize at various stages of a community's development.

Air pollution has emerged as a significant global threat to nearly all major metropolitan areas. In response, atmospheric scientists are developing various models to better comprehend air quality issues. This paper introduces a novel metric known as the Delhi Similarity Index (DSI), which calculates the geometric mean of trace gases including ozone, sulfur dioxide, and carbon monoxide. The DSI scales from 0 (indicating dissimilarity to Delhi's pollution levels) to 0.9–1 (indicating similarity). The study also examines the tool's limitations regarding nitrous oxide data and provides graphical GIS projections illustrating the role of PM2.5 in Indian cities. Furthermore, DSI results from 2011 to 2014 reveal that Bengaluru is approaching Delhi's pollution threshold, with values between 0.8 and 0.9 (80–90%), while Jungfraujoch recorded values ranging from 0.65 to 0.7 (65–70%).

Taylor's findings demonstrate that triple Massey products pull back non-trivially via non-zero degree maps between rational Poincaré duality spaces. This raises the broader question of whether formality, or the absence of specific obstructions to it, is maintained under such maps, consistent with the heuristic that a domain of a dominant map is typically more complex than its codomain. However, we establish that Taylor's result does not extend directly to quadruple Massey products; specifically, we construct a non-zero degree map between rational Poincaré duality spaces where a non-trivial quadruple Massey product on the target becomes trivial upon pullback to the domain. To facilitate this construction, we develop a method for converting a cdga into one satisfying Poincaré duality, a process that is natural in particular contexts.

Hebrew's morphological complexity makes it more challenging to model than simpler languages. However, recent advancements, particularly the Transformer architecture and BERT, have enabled Hebrew models to achieve state-of-the-art performance, matching the results of non-Morphologically Rich Language (MRL) counterparts. This study investigates the forefront of this domain by conducting style transfer, text generation, and classification tasks on news articles sourced from online archives. Additionally, news portals serve as a compelling corpus for analysis; examining them may uncover valuable insights regarding societal structures and public discourse.

This study investigates a triple-star configuration in which a compact neutron star (NS) - NS binary penetrates the envelope of a red supergiant (RSG) and spirals inward toward the core. Within this common envelope, the two neutron stars accrete matter via disks and generate jets, driving an exceptionally luminous and prolonged transient known as a common envelope jets supernova (CEJSN). Dynamical friction subsequently causes the binary to merge, either within the RSG envelope or its core, releasing a total energy output exceeding 10^52 erg in both radiation and kinetic forms. The resulting light curve remains bright for months to years, potentially producing detectable gravitational wave signals. The ejected material includes newly synthesized r-process elements, originating not only from the final NS-NS merger akin to kilonovae but also possibly from pre-merger jets formed inside the core, as proposed in the r-process CEJSN model. This mechanism accelerates the timeline for NS-NS mergers compared to standard kilonovae and may alleviate challenges in explaining early Universe r-process nucleosynthesis. I estimate the frequency ratio of CEJSN events relative to core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) to be between 10^-6 and 2x10^-5; however, due to their superior luminosity, their detection fraction is expected to be significantly higher. Consequently, this research advocates for incorporating CEJSN scenarios within binary and triple star systems when interpreting peculiar and puzzling superluminous supernovae.

This study presents a performance evaluation comparing Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to cardiac mechanics on both structured and unstructured finite element meshes. Myocardial mechanical behavior is modeled using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, which are discretized via finite elements to generate large-scale nonlinear algebraic systems. These systems are solved using a Newton-Krylov method, with BDDC/AMG preconditioners accelerating the resolution of the Jacobian linear systems. To ensure a fair comparison, we comprehensively investigate key BDDC parameters, specifically examining the performance of various direct solvers for local and coarse problems, the effects of different choices for BDDC primal degrees of freedom, and the impact of finite element order. Scalability assessments were conducted on Linux clusters utilizing up to 1024 processors, culminating in a performance analysis of a realistic electromechanical simulation.

This study addresses measure estimation within the barycentric coding model (BCM), where an unknown measure is defined as a Wasserstein-2 barycenter of a finite collection of known measures. In this framework, estimating the measure is equivalent to determining its barycentric coordinates. The paper offers new geometrical, statistical, and computational perspectives through three primary contributions. First, it utilizes the Riemannian geometry of Wasserstein-2 space to formulate a quadratic optimization problem for recovering barycentric coordinates, assuming access to true reference measures; the parameters for this problem are derived from inner products of the optimal displacement maps between the target measure and the reference measures. Second, the authors present an algorithm to compute these coordinates when only empirical i.i.d. samples of the measures are available, proving precise convergence rates that depend on the measures' smoothness and dimensionality, thus ensuring statistical consistency. Finally, the practical value of the BCM and its estimation methods is illustrated across three domains: covariance estimation for Gaussian measures, image processing, and natural language processing.

Reconstructing past states in Partial Differential Equation (PDE) analysis is frequently challenging, requiring both robust prior knowledge and efficient computational techniques. Our objective is to localize heat sources within a three-dimensional domain based on subsequent measurements, assuming these sources are small and discrete, such as hot fragments from a milling tool. This scenario necessitates a Prior that encodes such a priori information. Given that sparsity-inducing hyperpriors have been effective in similar contexts involving sparse signals or image reconstruction, we integrate a hierarchical Bayesian framework with gamma hyperpriors to enforce sparsity. Furthermore, we employ low-rank computations for PDE systems formatted as tensor trains to facilitate this approach.

This work extends the framework presented in [arXiv:2005.13198 [hep-th]] to the context of heterotic strings. Specifically, beginning with generic Gepner models for Calabi-Yau 3-folds, we build non-supersymmetric heterotic string vacua that exhibit a vanishing cosmological constant at the one-loop level. Our primary focus is on asymmetric orbifolding derived from discrete subgroups of a chiral $U(1)$-action, which simultaneously operates on both the Gepner model and the $SO(32)$ or $E_8\times E_8$ sectors. We provide a classification of these relevant orbifold models that yield vacua with the specified properties. In certain instances, the resulting vacua are constructed similarly to those in [arXiv:2005.13198 [hep-th]] for type II strings, utilizing orbifold groups with two generators and discrete torsions. Conversely, we also identify simpler models realized as asymmetric orbifolds of cyclic groups involving a single generator.

Relying on automatic evaluation metrics that can substitute human judgment is essential for accelerating the development of new methods, prompting significant research into creating such tools. This study takes a step back to examine recent advancements by comparing the collective body of existing automatic and human metrics. Since metrics function by ranking systems, the analysis occurs within the space of system rankings. Our comprehensive statistical investigation yields surprising insights: both legacy and contemporary automatic metrics are far more alike to one another than they are to human judgments. These automatic metrics are not complementary, as they tend to rank systems similarly. Remarkably, human metrics predict each other with greater accuracy than the aggregate of all automatic metrics used to forecast a human metric. This is unexpected because human metrics are typically engineered to be independent, targeting distinct quality dimensions such as content fidelity or readability. We offer a discussion of these discoveries along with recommendations for future research in the field of evaluation.

This work explores several generalizations of the string class within loop group bundles. The string class represents the obstruction to lifting a bundle with a loop group $LG$ structure group to one with a Kac-Moody central extension of $LG$ as its structure group. We introduce the concept of higher string classes for bundles where the structure group consists of based loops, $\Omega G$. Specifically, we derive a formula for characteristic classes in odd dimensions for these bundles, which are associated with $G$-bundle classes in a manner analogous to how the string class relates to the first Pontryagin class of a $G$-bundle linked to the loop group bundle. This establishes a theory of characteristic classes for $\Omega G$-bundles that mirrors Chern-Weil theory in finite dimensions and offers a geometric interpretation of the standard transgression map $H^{2k}(BG) \to H^{2k-1}(G)$.

Additionally, we examine the obstruction to lifting a bundle whose structure group is the semi-direct product of the loop group and the circle, $LG \rtimes S^1$, rather than the loop group itself. By reviewing bundle gerbes and their role in central extensions and lifting problems, we derive an explicit de Rham representative for the obstruction to lifting such bundles. Furthermore, we connect this to a generalization of the "caloron correspondence"—which typically relates $LG$-bundles over a manifold $M$ to $G$-bundles over $M \times S^1$—extending it to a correspondence that links $LG \rtimes S^1$-bundles over $M$ to $G$-bundles over $S^1$-bundles on $M$.

Utilizing the Wigner function under local equilibrium, we obtain hydrodynamical quantities for polarized spin-1/2 systems, specifically the particle number current density, energy-momentum tensor, spin tensor, and dipole moment tensor. In contrast to ideal hydrodynamics lacking spin, these derivations include additional terms at first and second orders of the Knudsen number $\text{Kn}$ and average spin polarization $\chi_s$. The Wigner function is formulated using matrix-valued distributions, with equilibrium states defined by thermodynamic parameters within quantum statistics. Furthermore, the equations of motion for these parameters are established via conservation laws at both the leading and next-to-leading orders of $\text{Kn}$ and $\chi_s$.

This study examines recent findings regarding Ultra High Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECR), focusing on their clustering, composition, and sky distribution from several EeV up to the highest energies, including the dipole anisotropy. Reaffirming a proposal made in 2008, we conclude that UHECRs in the 40–70 EeV range are predominantly composed of light and lightest nuclei. The observed absence in the Virgo region and the scarcity of localized nearby extragalactic sources, such as CenA, NG 253, and M82, can be explained by the fragility and opacity of these lightest nuclei over Mpc distances. We also discuss the potential contribution of a few galactic UHECR sources at 10 EeV to the Auger dipole anisotropy. Furthermore, recent anisotropies in the spectral composition of lightest and heavy nuclei, both outside and along the galactic plane, may serve as initial validation of our earlier claims from 2012. Ultimately, the interaction between heavier, high-energy galactic UHECR nuclei and the dominant local (Mpc-scale) extragalactic signal driven by lightest nuclei appears to account for the primary components of the UHECR puzzle.

This paper introduces the concept of pseudo-triangular norms (pseudo-t-norms) as weakly associative operations defined on trellises, extending the notion of triangular norms (t-norms) to bounded trellises. We examine their various properties, offer constructions of pseudo-t-norms on bounded trellises, and investigate T-distributivity within this context. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between pseudo-t-norms and isomorphisms on bounded trellises, noting that this relationship becomes more complex when the meet and join operations lack the property of (transitive) associativity.

We introduce a novel method that does not rely on a specific cosmological model to derive the Hubble constant ($H_0$) using localized Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) and Hubble parameter measurements. Applying this approach to data from eighteen localized FRBs and nineteen Hubble parameter measurements within the redshift interval $0<z\leq0.66$, we achieve the first such determination: $H_0=70.60\pm2.11~\mathrm{km/s/Mpc}$, featuring an uncertainty of approximately 3.00%. This model-independent result falls between the values obtained from Planck CMB observations and nearby type Ia supernovae (SN Ia). Simulations indicate that utilizing mock data from 500 localized FRBs and 25 Hubble parameter measurements across the redshift range $0<z\leq1$ could reduce the $H_0$ uncertainty to match the precision of nearby SN Ia data. Given the anticipated large-scale detection of localized FRBs, our method promises to provide a more accurate and reliable $H_0$ determination in the near future, aiding in the resolution of the Hubble constant tension.

We demonstrate that Nesterov acceleration functions as an optimal-order iterative regularization method for linear ill-posed problems, assuming the parameter is selected based on the solution's smoothness. This finding is established using both an a priori stopping rule and the discrepancy principle. The key instrument enabling this result is the representation of residual polynomials through Gegenbauer polynomials.

This paper investigates non-fragile finite-time stabilization for linear discrete mean-field stochastic systems, assuming that uncertainties in control parameters follow a Bernoulli distribution. A novel "state transition matrix method" is proposed, yielding necessary and sufficient conditions to address the stabilization issue. Furthermore, the application of Lyapunov theory via the state transition matrix advances discrete finite-time control theory. Finally, a practical example demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed control strategy.

Currently, monitoring urban environmental data, such as air quality, primarily relies on fixed static sensors. However, achieving dense spatial coverage with this approach necessitates a vast number of devices, resulting in high costs. An alternative known as drive-by sensing utilizes a fraction of sensors mounted on moving vehicles to achieve dense spatiotemporal coverage. By leveraging the redundancy in air quality data, matrix completion techniques can impute missing values from these sparsely sampled observations. Nevertheless, the accuracy of this imputation hinges on how well the moving sensors capture the inherent structure of the data matrix. Consequently, the core challenge lies in selecting vehicle paths that ensure representative spatiotemporal sampling. Existing literature often focuses on maximizing coverage by simply increasing the number of samples at various locations and times, a strategy that fails to guarantee representative sampling. We introduce a regressive facility location-based drive-by sensing framework, an efficient vehicle selection method that accounts for spatial smoothness and temporal autoregressive correlations to identify an optimal set of vehicles. We demonstrate that this drive-by sensing problem is submodular, enabling the use of a greedy algorithm with performance guarantees. Evaluating our framework on Delhi's public transport fleet reveals that our method captures representative spatiotemporal data more effectively than baseline approaches, significantly reducing extrapolation errors in simulated air quality scenarios. Thus, our approach offers a potential pathway to generating cost-effective, dense air quality maps.

In federated learning systems, parameter gradients are exchanged between participants and a central coordinator, yet the raw data remains within its secure local domain. Despite this, gradients can inadvertently contain sufficient details to allow adversaries to accurately reconstruct the original data, exposing client datasets to inference attacks when shared with a central server. This paper introduces a quantitative metric grounded in mutual information, enabling clients to assess the potential risk of data leakage within their gradients. While mutual information has gained significant traction in machine learning and data mining recently, current estimation techniques struggle with high-dimensional variables. To address this, we propose a novel approach to approximate the mutual information between high-dimensional gradients and batched input data. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed metric effectively quantifies the degree of information leakage in federated learning. Furthermore, by utilizing this metric, we analyze the factors influencing risk levels, proving that the susceptibility to inference attacks depends on both the state of the task model and the intrinsic data distribution.

In recent years, the proliferation of fake news has inflicted significant damage on society, making rapid detection a critical imperative. While existing approaches often treat news articles and related entities as static heterogeneous information networks (HINs) relying on computationally intensive message-passing algorithms, they fail to account for the dynamic nature of real-world networks where nodes and edges evolve over time. To address this, we introduce a novel Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (DHGNN) designed for efficient fake news identification. Our method begins by employing fine-tuned BERT to generate semantic representations of news content and author profiles, which are then transformed into graph data. We subsequently construct a heterogeneous news-author graph to capture contextual nuances and relational dynamics. Furthermore, by integrating personalized PageRank propagation and dynamic propagation techniques tailored for heterogeneous networks, we significantly reduce the computational complexity associated with back-propagation across numerous nodes. Empirical evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that DHGNN surpasses other GNN-based models in both performance and efficiency.

This white paper concisely outlines the significance of investigating relativistic cosmic rays, highlighting their role as a fundamental component of the universe and their influence on the evolution of stars and galaxies. The discussion centers on the scientific potential of ground-based gamma-ray observations spanning 20 GeV to 300 TeV over the next ten years. Most content is derived directly from "Science with the Cherenkov Telescope Array," which details the broader scientific case for CTA. We ask that any authors citing results from this paper refer to the original source.

User-generated content is fundamentally altering the landscape of the World Wide Web. Consequently, numerous systems are emerging to accommodate the rising demand for creating, sharing, and managing content. Tagging systems represent a specific subset of these platforms, enabling users to collaboratively annotate and share items like photos and URLs. This collective activity and the resulting repository of user-generated metadata offer avenues for enhancing existing platforms and developing novel mechanisms. However, unlocking this potential requires a deep understanding of how current systems are utilized. This study tackles that challenge by analyzing three tagging systems—CiteULike, Connotea, and del.icio.us—through three key dimensions: i) the patterns of information production regarding tags and items; ii) the temporal evolution of users' tag vocabularies; and iii) the social dimensions inherent to tagging systems.

This study establishes that any 11-channel sorting network requires a minimum of 35 comparators and that a 12-channel network requires at least 39 comparators. These findings definitively confirm the optimality of the sorting networks presented in *The Art of Computer Programming*, Volume 3, and resolve the two smallest remaining open cases of the Bose-Nelson sorting problem. By extending a result originally by Van Voorhis from standard sorting networks to a broader class of comparator networks, we developed a dynamic programming algorithm capable of calculating the optimal size for a sorting network with a specified number of channels. Executing this algorithm generates a certificate that documents the derivation of the corresponding lower bounds, which we validated using a program formally verified with the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant.

Recent proposals suggest that protocell growth and division can be modeled as a chemically active droplet undergoing simple reactions fueled externally; this framework is known as the continuum model. Numerical simulations of this model demonstrate a shape instability causing the droplet to split into two equal-sized parts, mimicking cell division [1]. This paper examines a simplified version of the continuum model, termed the effective model, analyzing it across both linear and nonlinear regimes. We begin with a linear stability analysis of a flat interface, followed by the development of a nonlinear theory based on the longwave approximation. Our findings indicate that the leading-order interface dynamics are governed by the modified Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, which implies a logarithmic blow-up of the interface within a finite time. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the local velocity of the interface.

Zero-shot image classification involves scenarios where training data lacks images from certain novel classes, yet provides alternative information like natural language descriptions or attribute vectors. This approach is vital for real-world applications where collecting images for every possible class is often infeasible. Unlike prior methods that attempted to map attribute spaces to image spaces via transfer functions, our approach utilizes a conditional variational autoencoder to synthesize samples from given attributes, which are then employed to classify unseen classes. Through extensive evaluations on four benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our model surpasses state-of-the-art performance, especially in the more realistic generalized setting where training classes appear alongside novel classes during testing.

In local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), hot, dense plasmas composed of intermediate or high-Z elements exhibit an immense number of electronic configurations that significantly influence macroscopic properties like spectral opacity and the equation of state. This study introduces systematic approaches to analyze the count of relativistic electronic configurations within such plasmas. Although the total combinatorial number of configurations remains vast even for mid-Z elements, the subset with non-negligible populations is considerably smaller and varies complexly with temperature and density. We examine two effective methods for estimating the number of populated configurations: (i) performing exact calculations of the total combinatorial configurations within superconfigurations using a converged super-transition-array (STA) model, and (ii) estimating the multidimensional width of the probability distribution for electronic population across bound shells, which follows a binomial distribution when electron exchange and correlation are ignored. These methods are evaluated, and the underlying mechanisms driving the large number of populated configurations are explored in detail. Furthermore, comprehensive finite-temperature density functional theory (DFT) average-atom calculations are conducted across a broad spectrum of temperatures and densities for various low, mid, and high-Z plasmas. The results provide a detailed discussion and explanation of how temperature and density affect the number of populated configurations.

This study constructs and computes non-perturbative path integrals within a multiply-connected space-time by summing over distinct homotopy classes of paths. The space-time's topology arises from Einstein-Rosen bridges (ERBs) generated by the entanglement of virtual black holes within the quantum foam. According to the $ER=EPR$ conjecture, these entangled "bubbles" are linked by Planck-scale ERBs, resulting in a space-time with a large first Betti number ($B1$). Consequently, for any compact 2-surface in this manifold, the topology and homotopy are non-trivial due to the numerous Planckian ERBs traversing it. We conjecture that quantizing space-time with this specific topology, combined with an appropriate selection of 2-surfaces, enables a non-perturbative path integral formulation of quantum gravity over the manifold.

We introduce PORT, a software platform designed for the local extraction and analysis of digital trace data. Although data collected by both private and public entities offers immense potential for social scientific discovery, its most valuable components have remained inaccessible to academics due to privacy restrictions and prohibitive API costs. However, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) ensures that all citizens can obtain an electronic copy of their personal data. Major data controllers—including social media platforms, banks, e-commerce sites, loyalty programs, and public transit systems—comply by supplying clients with a "Data Download Package" (DDP). Building on a previously proposed conceptual workflow where citizens donate their data to researchers, this process involves locally processing DDPs on users' machines before obtaining informed consent to share a subset of the processed information. This paper presents PORT, the newly developed software that executes the local processing phase of this workflow. By keeping sensitive data entirely on the user's device, PORT prevents any contact with external observers, including researchers, thereby safeguarding privacy. Consequently, PORT unlocks a wide array of applications for social data science using data that was previously unobtainable.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have surpassed human-level performance in image classification and are extensively used in practical applications. However, these models remain susceptible to adversarial perturbations, which are specifically crafted noise patterns designed to deceive classification algorithms. To mitigate this vulnerability and enhance the adversarial robustness generalization of state-of-the-art CNNs trained via adversarial training, the Adversarially Trained GAN (ATGAN) has been introduced. ATGAN integrates adversarial training into the standard Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework to eliminate obfuscated gradients—a phenomenon often found in existing GAN-based defenses that creates a misleading sense of security. Furthermore, ATGAN employs an image-to-image generator for data augmentation, thereby reducing the sample complexity required to achieve robust generalization during adversarial training. Experimental evaluations on the MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that the proposed method operates without reliance on obfuscated gradients and delivers superior global adversarial robustness generalization compared to current adversarially trained CNNs.

Attention regarding explanation techniques for multivariate time series prediction in sequential models is growing within machine learning research. Although existing approaches excel at instance-level explanations, they face difficulties in accurately and efficiently attributing causes over extended durations and amidst intricate feature interactions. We introduce WinIT, a framework designed to assess feature importance in time series forecasting by measuring shifts in the predictive distribution across multiple instances within a windowed context. Extensive empirical results indicate that our method surpasses the previous state-of-the-art, FIT, by effectively capturing temporal dependencies in feature significance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that WinIT enhances the accurate attribution of features within specific time steps, a capability often lacking in current interpretability techniques. Evaluations against baselines on both simulated and real-world clinical datasets reveal that WinIT outperforms FIT and other feature importance methods by 2.47x on the real-world MIMIC-mortality task. The project code is accessible at https://github.com/layer6ai-labs/WinIT.

Source code separation into vocals and accompaniment has become a prominent research area, with supervised deep learning techniques showing significant performance gains in recent years. We introduce a method that leverages visual data reflecting singers' vocal actions to enhance the fidelity of separated vocal tracks. Specifically, a video frontend model processes mouth movements and integrates them into the feature embeddings of an audio-centric separation system. To enable the network to learn the correlation between audio and visual singing cues, we augment the training audio mixture with vocal signals unrelated to mouth motion. We established two audiovisual singing datasets for training and evaluation: one sourced from online audition recordings and another captured in-house. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses audio-only methods in separation quality across most test recordings. This superiority is particularly notable in scenarios involving backing vocals within the accompaniment, a condition that presents a substantial challenge for audio-based techniques.

We construct a complex linear Weil representation $\rho$ for the generalized special linear group $G={\rm SL}_*^{1}(2,A_n)$, where $A_n=K[x]/\langle x^n\rangle$, $K$ is the quadratic extension of the finite field $k$ with $q$ elements ($q$ odd), and $A_n$ carries a second class involution. Following the specification of certain data, the representation is defined on the generators of a Bruhat presentation of $G$ using linear operators that satisfy the presentation's relations. We also describe the structure of a unitary group $U$ associated with $G$ and utilize this group to derive an initial decomposition of $\rho$.

We present Hocalarim (MyProfessors), the most extensive student review dataset currently available for the Turkish language. This collection comprises more than 5,000 online professor evaluations where various educational dimensions are rated on a five-star scale. The study analyzes the dataset's characteristics and provides its statistical overview, while also exploring how the type of student institution influences ratings and examining the correlation between student bias and the tendency to provide positive or negative feedback.

The complex dynamics arising from the interplay of interaction, disorder, and dissipation exhibit a rich phenomenology. This study examines a disordered XXZ spin chain coupled to a bath that, in isolation, would drive the system toward a highly delocalized and coherent Dicke state. We demonstrate that there are regimes where, despite strong disorder, the natural orbitals of the single-particle density matrix in the steady state remain localized, occurring under both weak and strong interaction conditions. Furthermore, we find that for weak interactions, the averaged steady-state occupation in the eigenbasis of the open system Hamiltonian follows an exponential decay at intermediate disorder strengths, whereas it becomes more uniformly distributed under strong disorder or strong interactions. Finally, we observe that strong dissipation enhances the coherence of steady states, thereby diminishing localization signatures. These localization effects are also captured using a concatenated inverse participation ratio, which simultaneously quantifies the localization of the Hamiltonian's eigenstates and the proximity of the steady state to an incoherent mixture of distinct energy eigenstates.

We develop models for differential $KO$-theory and twisted differential $KO$-theory by enhancing Karoubi's $KO$-theory [Kar78] through the use of gradations on Clifford modules. To achieve this, we establish a generalized Clifford superconnection formalism that extends Quillen's superconnection formalism [Qui85]. One of the resulting models serves to classify "fermionic mass terms" within physics.

The Jupiter Trojan asteroid 128383 (2004 JW52) was recently suggested to possess optical colors inconsistent with its dynamical classification, but fresh and archival data demonstrate this is inaccurate. This highlights the necessity of excluding the possibility that a minor planet's Point Spread Function (PSF) is blended with a background star in survey images before accepting the colors listed in the survey catalog as reliable.

Various models are employed to investigate diverse natural and technical phenomena. Typically, researchers are constrained to a single modeling approach, often unaware of or unable to utilize alternative methods. The authors argue that a comprehensive analysis of any phenomenon requires the integration of multiple modeling perspectives. This paper outlines several approaches applied to the study of the Random Early Detection algorithm for active queue management, detailing the approaches themselves, their implementations, and the resulting findings.

This paper introduces a numerical approach for div-curl systems subject to normal boundary conditions, utilizing the primal-dual weak Galerkin (PDWG) finite element method. The proposed PDWG scheme for div-curl systems distinguishes itself through two key attributes: it delivers accurate and dependable numerical solutions under the assumption of low $H^\alpha$-regularity ($\alpha>0$) for the exact solution, and it effectively approximates normal harmonic vector fields irrespective of the domain's topology. Seven numerical experiments are provided to illustrate the algorithm's performance, featuring one specific case study on computing discrete normal harmonic vector fields.

The Coon amplitude represents the unique solution satisfying duality constraints with logarithmic Regge trajectories. Notably, this solution bridges the gap between the Veneziano amplitude and a scalar particle amplitude. Although an analytic demonstration of its unitarity remains elusive, this brief note explicitly calculates the partial wave coefficients for the leading Regge trajectory in D=4. Our findings show that these coefficients are invariably positive, despite their magnitudes diminishing as spin increases. Given that subleading trajectory coefficients are empirically larger than those on the leading trajectory, our results suggest that the full Coon amplitude in D=4 maintains positivity.

The scaled standard Wigner matrix, characterized by symmetric, mean-zero entries with unit variance, and its limiting eigenvalue distribution—the semi-circular law—have been subjects of significant interest. It is a known fact that the $2k$-th moment of this limit corresponds to the count of non-crossing pair-partitions of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2k\}$. While various extensions of this principle exist in the literature, this paper introduces a unifying extension that also generates further insights.

We examine an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix $W_n$ with independently distributed entries. Under appropriate conditions on these entries, we demonstrate that a limiting spectral distribution exists either in probability or almost surely. The moments of this limit are characterized by a specific set of partitions that is generally broader than the set of non-crossing pair-partitions, thereby creating intriguing enumerative combinatorial challenges.

Our framework encompasses several established results on limiting spectral distributions, including those for the standard Wigner matrix, the adjacency matrix of a sparse homogeneous Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner matrices, certain banded Wigner matrices, and Wigner matrices featuring a variance profile. Furthermore, our main results yield new findings for these models and their extensions.

This study presents the first direct, model-independent determination of the absolute values of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix elements $|V_\mathrm{tb}|$, $|V_\mathrm{td}|$, and $|V_\mathrm{ts}|$, utilizing final states dominated by single top quark $t$-channel events. The analysis relies on proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, gathered in 2016 at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Processes directly sensitive to these elements are examined at both the top quark's production and decay vertices. Under the standard model's assumption of CKM unitarity, a lower bound of $|V_\mathrm{tb}|$ $>$ 0.970 is established at the 95% confidence level. Furthermore, considering various theories beyond the standard model and relaxing constraints among the relevant parameters, the study measures $|V_\mathrm{tb}| =$ 0.988 $\pm$ 0.024 and $|V_\mathrm{td}|^2 + |V_\mathrm{ts}|^2 =$ 0.06 $\pm$ 0.06, where the uncertainties encompass both statistical and systematic contributions.

We demonstrate that a set equipped with an action of a locally finite-dimensional free partially commutative monoid, along with its associated semicubical set, possess isomorphic homology groups. Furthermore, we construct a finite-length complex designed to calculate the homology groups of any asynchronous transition system possessing a finite maximum number of mutually independent events. Finally, we provide examples illustrating the computation of these homology groups.

The classical Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm can be adapted to produce non-reversible Markov chains by modifying the acceptance probability through the use of a vorticity matrix. This approach yields non-reversible chains, and the text discusses existing literature on asymptotic variance, large deviations, and mixing times, adapting specific large deviation results to highlight the superior performance of non-reversible chains in these areas. Furthermore, an application of Non-Reversible Metropolis-Hastings (NRMH) is presented in a continuous setting, involving the development of the requisite theory and its initial application to Gaussian distributions in three and nine dimensions. Empirical results regarding autocorrelation and estimated asymptotic variance for these examples demonstrate significant improvements over standard MH when using the same stepsize.

This study examines neutrino data collected by the Baikal NT200 telescope to search for associations with gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), finding no correlated neutrino events. Under the assumption of a Waxman-Bahcall spectrum, we established an upper limit on the neutrino flux of **$E^2 \Phi < 1.1 \times 10^{-6}cm^{-2}s^{-1}sr^{-1}GeV$**. Additionally, we provide a Green's Function fluence limit for this search, which surpasses the energy range of the Super-Kamiokande limit by two orders of magnitude.

Magnetometer data from Saturn's magnetotail reveals magnetic reconnection products mainly via distinct anomalies in the north-south magnetic field component. These deflections result from reconnection-generated plasma structures sweeping past the spacecraft. Historically, detecting these signatures relied on visual inspection or semi-automated techniques that necessitated human validation. This study introduces a fully automated, supervised feed-forward neural network designed to detect reconnection evidence in the Kronian magnetosphere using the three magnetic field components measured by Cassini in KRTP coordinates. The model was trained on a three-year catalog containing 2,093 classified reconnection events, including plasmoids, travelling compression regions, and dipolarizations. When tested against the entire year of 2010, the network demonstrated rapid detection capabilities with high accuracy (87%), a true skill score of 0.76, and a Heidke skill score of 0.73. Consequently, comprehensive cataloging and analysis of magnetic reconnection throughout Cassini's mission near Saturn are now feasible.

This study investigates the asymptotic stability of a composite wave formed by two viscous shocks subjected to spatially periodic disturbances within the one-dimensional full compressible Navier-Stokes framework. The analysis demonstrates that, as time progresses, the solution converges toward the background composite wave, albeit with a distinct shift for each shock; these shifts are uniquely identifiable provided that both the periodic perturbations and the shock strengths remain sufficiently small. The core of the proof relies on constructing an appropriate ansatz that enables the application of the anti-derivative method.

This research introduces a new experimental approach to determine the profile of interactions induced between impurities in a trapped gas of ultracold Fermi/Bose atoms, commonly known as Fermi/Bose polarons. The proposed method involves a two-body collision experiment where impurities and host atoms interact weakly. Numerical simulations of the quantum dynamics demonstrate that measuring the polaron wave packet at various time snapshots can reveal information about the non-local induced interaction between two polarons. This inference is possible because, when the WKB approximation is valid for the relevant Schrödinger equation, the potential of the induced interaction is effectively balanced by the quantum potential.

Promotional videos have quickly emerged as a favored tool for influencing behavior across various domains, such as e-commerce and social enterprises. While traditionally created by professionals—a process that demands significant time, labor, and resources—the rise of AI-empowered persuasive video generation (AIPVG) has made large-scale content production more feasible. As an interdisciplinary field, AIPVG can be difficult for newcomers to navigate, and to date, no comprehensive survey has addressed it. This paper fills that void by examining essential AI techniques for automatically crafting persuasive videos. We present an original taxonomy categorizing AIPVG into three core stages: 1) visual material understanding, which identifies relevant information from visual assets; 2) visual storyline generation, which selects and sequences high-quality assets to construct a compelling narrative; and 3) post-production, which includes generating background music and animating stills to improve the viewer experience. Furthermore, we outline standard evaluation metrics and datasets used in this area, critique the strengths and limitations of current approaches within these stages, and explore promising avenues for future research.

We examine constraints on the leading higher-dimension operators contributing to the four-graviton amplitude in four dimensions, derived from perturbative unitarity and crossing symmetry, specifically accounting for various helicity configurations. Our analysis centers on the leading-order effects arising from the exchange of massive degrees of freedom, which ensure the infrared finiteness of the relevant amplitudes. Specifically, we establish a bound on the coefficient of the $R^3$ operator, which corrects the graviton three-point amplitude, expressed in relation to the $R^4$ coefficient. To validate these constraints, we generate nontrivial effective field-theory data by calculating the large-mass expansion of the one-loop minimally-coupled four-graviton amplitude involving massive particles with spin up to 2 circulating in the loop. Notably, we find that the leading EFT coefficients derived from both string theory and one-loop field-theory amplitudes cluster within small, distinct regions or "islands." The geometry and position of these islands can be predicted using a dispersive representation for the Wilson coefficients, based on crossing symmetry and the assumption that lowest-spin spectral densities dominate. Our findings suggest that the Wilson coefficients in weakly-coupled gravitational theories face significantly tighter constraints than those predicted by standard dispersive analyses of $2 \to 2$ scattering. The one-loop four-graviton amplitudes utilized to derive this EFT data were computed employing modern amplitude techniques, such as generalized unitarity, supersymmetric decompositions, and the double copy.

The category of special generic maps represents a significant group of smooth mappings that includes Morse functions on spheres with precisely two singularities, as well as standard projections of unit spheres. This study establishes novel constraints on such maps for closed, simply-connected manifolds of dimension six or greater when mapped into $\mathbb{R}^5$. Notably, spheres that are not diffeomorphic to standard unit spheres generally fail to support maps with negative codimensions. These restrictions significantly influence both the homeomorphism and diffeomorphism classifications of manifolds. Conversely, certain basic manifolds, such as those formed by connected sums of products of unit spheres, do admit special generic maps into appropriate Euclidean spaces. This observation drives the investigation into the existence or non-existence of these maps on other elementary manifolds, including projective spaces and specific closed, simply-connected manifolds. In this renewed exploration, detailed analyses of cohomology rings serve as a primary tool.

We conducted a high-resolution investigation of $0^{+}$ states in $^{134}$Ba through the $^{136}$Ba($p,t$) two-neutron transfer reaction. Our findings reveal that a substantial fraction of the $L = 0$ pair-transfer strength is localized at excited $0^+$ levels in $^{134}$Ba. We briefly address the potential implications of these results for calculating the neutrinoless double beta decay matrix element of the $^{136}$Xe $\to$ $^{136}$Ba transition.

Targeting the acquisition and analysis of high-dimensional (HD) data, Snapshot Compressive Imaging (SCI) captures 2D compressed measurements via optical systems and recovers HD data using compressive sensing algorithms. Although the Plug-and-Play (PnP) framework presents a promising approach for SCI reconstruction, its core denoising step remains a significant challenge. Current denoisers within the PnP framework often struggle with either suboptimal performance or a heavy reliance on extensive training datasets. This paper introduces an efficient, shallow-learning-based algorithm for video SCI reconstruction. By revisiting dictionary learning techniques, we integrate Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD) as a novel denoiser into the PnP framework. Leveraging KSVD, our method achieves a balanced trade-off between reconstruction quality, computational speed, and training complexity. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across various datasets confirm the method's effectiveness. Compared to a standard baseline utilizing total variation, our approach yields approximately $2$ dB higher PSNR and an SSIM improvement of 0.2. We anticipate that the proposed PnP-KSVD algorithm will establish itself as a new benchmark for video SCI reconstruction.

Accurate nearshore bathymetry, which maps the seafloor topography in coastal areas, is essential for forecasting surf zone hydrodynamics and planning navigation routes to avoid underwater hazards. Consequently, it has become increasingly critical for diverse applications such as maritime operations, coastal governance, and risk evaluation. Nevertheless, obtaining high-resolution bathymetric data directly is often hindered by budget limitations and logistical challenges. When only sparse observations exist, Gaussian Process regression (GPR), also known as Kriging, serves as an alternative; however, it struggles to identify sharp gradients characteristic of sand bars and submerged objects, particularly with limited data. This study introduces several deep learning approaches to estimate nearshore bathymetry using sparse, multi-scale measurements. We propose a Deep Neural Network (DNN) for calculating posterior estimates and a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) for sampling from the posterior distribution. Our models are trained on synthetic data derived from nearshore surveys conducted by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Field Research Facility (FRF) in Duck, North Carolina. Comparisons between our methods and Kriging, using both real surveys and those with artificially introduced sharp gradients, demonstrate that direct DNN estimation yields superior predictions in this context. Furthermore, we employ bootstrapping with the DNN for uncertainty quantification and introduce a hybrid approach termed DNN-Kriging, which integrates deep learning with Kriging to achieve further enhancements in posterior estimates.

Spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy were employed to investigate the electronic structure of the semimetal MoTe$_2$, aiming to explain its diverse response characteristics. Researchers identified a new spin-texture within the bulk Fermi surface of the non-centrosymmetric structural phase, aligning with first-principles predictions. This texture exhibits three-dimensional properties regarding both momentum dependence and spin orientation, remaining partially intact above the temperature at which centrosymmetry is broken. Additionally, two distinct types of surface Fermi arcs were observed to persist significantly above the transition temperature. The emergence of a prominent Fermi arc is highly sensitive to thermal history, with electron quasiparticle lifetimes markedly increasing during the initial cooling phase. These findings suggest that a polar instability driven by strong electron-lattice interactions occurs near the surface, even when the bulk remains largely in a centrosymmetric state.

For $1<p\leq q$, we demonstrate that the Poisson semigroup $e^{-t\sqrt{-\Delta}}$ on the $n$-sphere is hypercontractive from $L^{p}$ to $L^{q}$ within dimensions $n \leq 3$ if and only if $e^{-t\sqrt{n}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{p-1}{q-1}}$, whereas this equivalence does not hold in sufficiently large dimensions.

This study examines the MGT equation with memory, defined as $\partial_{ttt} u + \alpha \partial_{tt} u - \beta \Delta \partial_{t} u - \gamma\Delta u + \int_{0}^{t}g(s) \Delta u(t-s) ds = 0$. We demonstrate existence and uniqueness results without requiring the convexity assumption on the convolution kernel $g$, a condition typically found in existing literature. Specifically, in the subcritical regime where $\alpha\beta>\gamma$, we prove that energy decays exponentially. This result is achieved without relying on the standard differential inequality $g'+\delta g\leq 0$ (for $\delta>0$); instead, it suffices that $g$ exhibits exponential decay.

We introduce a systematic framework for analyzing continuous substitutions over compact Hausdorff alphabets. By examining the consequences of irreducibility and primitivity, we elucidate key characteristics of the topological dynamics within their subshifts. Furthermore, we translate ergodic theory inquiries into questions regarding the spectral properties of an associated substitution operator. This endeavor necessitates extending standard Perron–Frobenius theory to encompass Banach lattices. Leveraging this development, we establish computable conditions that ensure the quasi-compactness of the substitution operator, thereby guaranteeing the unique ergodicity of the resulting subshift.

The Cadmium Zinc Telluride Imager (CZTI) on AstroSat, functioning as an open detector for energies above approximately 100 keV, serves as a valuable instrument for studying the hard X-ray properties of $\gamma$-ray pulsars. Previously, we introduced a custom algorithm capable of identifying pulsars through long-duration (years-long) archival data integration. This study expands that methodology by incorporating an additional ~20% of CZTI pixels that were previously excluded due to low gain values. Recent advancements have established more robust calibration for these pixels, revealing higher detection thresholds and an extended energy reach up to ~1 MeV. By utilizing data from these newly included pixels, we can now construct pulse profiles across a broader energy spectrum. Analysis of the Crab pulsar's profiles across various sub-bands confirms that the observed behavior aligns with this expanded energy coverage. Although detailed spectroscopy across the full band remains challenging due to low count rates, we have developed hardness ratios that, when combined with AstroSat Mass Model simulations, allow us to constrain the power-law index of the radiation spectrum. We present phase-resolved spectral results for PSR J0534+2200 and the total pulsed emission of PSR J1513-5908, with recovered photon indices accurate to within ~20%.

The swift spread of information and the uptake of social behaviors are vital across varied scenarios, including collective movements, pandemic control, and marketing campaigns.
