While the mechanics of large cascades have been widely investigated in different settings, few studies have methodically analyzed how network topology influences the efficiency of information diffusion. In this work, we utilize the linear threshold model on networks featuring communities to show that a key network characteristic—the modular structure—significantly impacts the velocity of information diffusion within complex contagion. Our simulations reveal that an optimal level of network modularity always exists to maximize spreading efficiency; beyond this threshold, both increased and decreased modularity impede diffusion speed. These findings are validated by an analytical approximation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the optimal modularity shifts depending on both the size of the initial seed group and the desired cascade size, ultimately varying based on the specific network in question. We highlight the relevance of these insights for applications ranging from marketing and epidemiology to neuroscience and engineering, where understanding the structural design of complex systems is crucial for optimizing information propagation.

Recent studies have highlighted the prevalence of gradient masking within proposed adversarial defenses. Although defenses relying on this trait are deemed ineffective and vulnerable to bypass, there remains a significant gap in methods for quantifying gradient masking and comparing its magnitude across various networks. This work shifts the perspective from viewing gradient masking as a binary condition to analyzing it through the lens of measurability. We introduce and justify multiple metrics for this phenomenon, supported by extensive empirical evaluations on defenses suspected of varying degrees of masking. These metrics are computationally efficient compared to robust attacks, facilitate inter-model comparisons, and eliminate the need for resource-intensive, custom attacks tailored to specific architectures. Our findings demonstrate that these proposed metrics effectively capture the extent of gradient masking across different networks.

Transparent objects pose a significant challenge in computer vision because their lack of clear boundaries makes segmentation and classification difficult, and the scarcity of real-world data hinders the training of deep neural networks. Consequently, existing approaches rely on rigid synthetic datasets that lack flexibility and suffer from poor performance in real-world applications, primarily because rendering pipelines often omit critical features like refraction, dispersion, and caustics. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SuperCaustics, a real-time, open-source simulation tool for transparent objects tailored for deep learning. SuperCaustics incorporates extensive modules for stochastic environment generation, leverages hardware ray-tracing to accurately render caustics, dispersion, and refraction, and facilitates the creation of massive datasets with multi-modal, pixel-perfect ground truth annotations. To demonstrate the system's efficacy, we trained a deep neural network from scratch to segment transparent objects under challenging lighting conditions. This model achieved performance on par with state-of-the-art methods on real-world data using merely 10% of the training set and in a fraction of the required time. Additional experiments confirm that models trained with SuperCaustics can successfully segment various caustic patterns, even in images containing multiple overlapping transparent objects—a capability, to our knowledge, previously unattainable with models trained solely on synthetic data. Our open-source code and experimental datasets are publicly available.

Polynomial interpolation using the monomial basis is frequently deemed unsuitable for numerical work due to the ill-conditioning of the associated Vandermonde matrix. This paper challenges that assumption, demonstrating that in many relevant scenarios, this method achieves accuracy comparable to interpolation in better-conditioned bases. Moreover, we establish that the monomial basis outperforms alternative polynomial bases across several practical applications.

Although self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models have revolutionized speech representation learning, several questions regarding their capabilities remain unresolved. This study investigates two specific inquiries: (1) Can SSL speech models process non-speech audio effectively? and (2) Do different SSL speech models capture distinct aspects of audio features? To address these questions, we performed extensive experiments using diverse speech and non-speech audio datasets to evaluate the representation capabilities of state-of-the-art SSL models, specifically wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT. These experiments were conducted within the NeurIPS 2021 HEAR Challenge, utilizing the official standard evaluation pipeline. Our results indicate that (1) SSL speech models can extract meaningful features from a broad spectrum of non-speech audio, though they may struggle with specific dataset types; and (2) various SSL models offer insights into different dimensions of audio features. These findings lay the groundwork for ensembling representation models. Consequently, we propose an ensemble framework designed to fuse embeddings from speech representation models. This framework surpasses current state-of-the-art SSL speech and audio models, demonstrating superior performance across numerous datasets compared to other participants in the HEAR Challenge. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/tony10101105/HEAR-2021-NeurIPS-Challenge -- NTU-GURA.

It is a well-established principle among experts that resonances within nonlinear systems generate novel invariant structures, which in turn give rise to new dynamical behaviors. This paper aims to investigate the invariant sets produced by resonances specifically under foliation-preserving torus maps. These are maps acting on a torus that maintain a foliation of irrational lines defined as $L_{\theta_{0}}=\{\theta_{0}+\Omega t | t\in\mathbb{R}\}\subset\mathbb{T}^{d}$. Foliation-preserving maps occur naturally as reparametrizations of linear flows on the torus and are significant in various applications, including coupled oscillators, delay equations, and resonators with moving boundaries. The invariant objects identified in this work provide predictive insights into the behavior of such models. Given the intention to apply these findings to other problems, we have established highly quantitative results that offer explicit descriptions of the phenomena and the invariant structures governing them. The architecture of phase-locking regions for foliation-preserving maps differs markedly from that of generic torus maps. To ensure completeness, we also conducted a similar analysis for generic torus maps, demonstrating that the objects arising in foliation-preserving maps are both qualitatively and quantitatively distinct from those in generic cases, a distinction with implications for applications.

Spiking neural networks (SNNs) leverage their binary, event-driven architecture to achieve ultra-high speed and ultra-low energy consumption on neuromorphic hardware, making them ideal for edge-based generative tasks like high-quality image creation. This study presents a Spiking Variational Autoencoder (VAE) designed for image generation. While VAEs are renowned for their stability and recently improved quality, standard implementations require floating-point calculations for sampling from a normal distribution in the latent space, which is incompatible with the binary constraints of SNNs. To overcome this, we constructed the latent space using an autoregressive SNN model, enabling the random selection of samples that adhere to a Bernoulli process and support variational learning. Consequently, we developed the Fully Spiking VAE, where every module consists entirely of SNN layers. To our knowledge, this represents the first implementation of a VAE using exclusively SNN layers. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our model generates images with quality equal to or superior to conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs). The source code is accessible at https://github.com/kamata1729/FullySpikingVAE.

Neutrino charged-current quasielastic-like scattering, a process frequently employed in neutrino oscillation studies, investigates nuclear effects that dictate neutrino-nucleus interactions. This Letter presents the inaugural measurement of the triple-differential cross section for $\nu_{\mu}$ quasielastic-like reactions within the hydrocarbon medium of the MINERvA detector, utilizing a wide-band beam with energies ranging from 2 to 20 GeV. The study examines correlations between transverse and longitudinal muon momenta and the total proton kinetic energy, contrasting these findings with predictions from a state-of-the-art simulation. Observed discrepancies likely indicate limitations in modeling pion and nucleon intranuclear scattering as well as the ejection of spectator nucleons from struck nuclei. Furthermore, the independent determination of leptonic and hadronic variables may guide experimental strategies for neutrino-energy estimation.

This experiment aimed to employ established analytical methods to investigate the generation, simulation, and measurement of molecular Hamiltonians. The approach utilized the Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO), the Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU), and the Phase Estimation Algorithm (PEA). The study focused on $H_2$ (both with and without spin) and $He_2$ (without spin). Hamiltonians were initially constructed within the LCAO basis and subsequently reconstructed via the Jordan-Winger transform to form linear combinations of Pauli spin operators. A significant increase in Hamiltonian length was observed when moving from spinless $H_2$ to $He_2$, which diminished the capacity for ideal simulation. Consequently, the LCU-based expansion of the Hamiltonian was restricted to low orders, specifically $l = 1$ and $l = 2$. The resulting Hamiltonians were measured using PEA, with data plotted as a function of $\frac{2\pi(K)}{N}$ alongside the probability distribution for each register; graph resolution varied depending on the number of registers, $N$. Notably, reducing the order had minimal impact on the visual representation of the $H_2$ graphs. Finally, qualitative comparisons were conducted across the three molecular systems.

To gain insight into the unexpectedly low-frequency vibrational modes in structural glasses, we analyze the spectra of a large collection of sparse random matrices, with disorder regulated by bond weight distributions and network coordination. Our results reveal that the density of states $D(\omega)$ consists of three distinct regimes: a very-low-frequency range predictable via extremal statistics, an intermediate region featuring quasi-localized modes, and a plateau where $D(\omega) \sim \omega^0$. Specifically, when bond weights are uniform, the intermediate regime exhibits a $D(\omega) \sim \omega^4$ scaling that remains independent of both network coordination and system size, aligning with recent simulation findings for structural glasses.

We present four methods for solving linear Diophantine equations over natural numbers: lexicographic enumeration, a completion procedure, a graph-based approach, and the Slopes algorithm. It is well-established that the enumeration and completion methods lag behind the other two in performance. This study provides a detailed comparison between the graph-based and Slopes algorithms. Unlike prior studies, our findings indicate that while both perform similarly on small inputs, the graph-based algorithm significantly outperforms the Slopes algorithm as input size increases. Consequently, we recommend using the graph-based algorithm for AC-unification implementations to achieve optimal efficiency.

This paper introduces a new haptic teleoperation method designed to ensure both the safety and stability of the system. Building on prior research into haptic shared control, we utilize control barrier functions (CBFs) to create reference haptic feedback that alerts the human operator to the system's internal state, enabling safe navigation without relinquishing control authority. A critical distinction in our approach is that the force rendered to the user does not directly dictate the robot's motion, which remains under direct user control; however, earlier studies often ignored the feedback loop involving the user, potentially leading to unstable closed-loop trajectories. To address this, we impose a differential constraint on the rendered force that guarantees finite-gain $L_2$ stability. This constraint formulates a Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program (QCQP), for which we derive a closed-form solution. Our proposed constraint is comparable to, yet less restrictive than, the standard passivity constraints found in existing literature. We validated the method through an experimental simulation where a human operator piloted a UAV near an obstacle.

Counterfactual Regret Minimization (CFR) is a robust algorithm for solving extensive games with imperfect information (IIEGs); however, it is restricted to known environments where the transition functions of chance nodes and terminal rewards are predefined. In uncertain settings, such as those encountered in Reinforcement Learning (RL), the Variational Information Maximizing Exploration (VIME) framework offers a mechanism for exploration driven by information gain. This paper introduces VCFR, a novel approach that integrates CFR with information gain to compute Nash Equilibria (NE) within IIEGs under RL conditions. By incorporating information gain into the reward signal, the average strategy derived by CFR can serve directly as an interactive strategy, substantially enhancing the algorithm's exploration efficiency in uncertain environments. Experimental results indicate that this method not only significantly reduces the number of environment interactions but also successfully identifies an approximate Nash Equilibrium.

We examine Lepton Flavor Violation (LFV) within a general Standard Model extension defined by gauge-invariant dimension-6 operators. Our analysis covers three-body charged lepton decays and the $Z$ boson decay into a lepton pair, contrasting our derived analytical expressions with existing experimental data. Furthermore, we establish numerical constraints on the Wilson coefficients that characterize the permissible magnitude of New Physics effects.

Semantic segmentation of LiDAR point clouds is a fundamental challenge in 3D computer vision, particularly for autonomous driving, yet achieving accurate results remains difficult due to the inherent sparsity and noise in single-sweep data. This paper introduces a new framework for sparse LiDAR semantic segmentation that leverages learned contextual shape priors. The approach begins with an initial semantic segmentation of a single sweep using a standard network, which then serves as input for a semantic scene completion (SSC) module. By utilizing multi-frame LiDAR sequences as supervision, the SSC module learns contextual shape priors to reconstruct the sparse point cloud into a dense representation, thereby enhancing the initial segmentation through fully end-to-end training. Additionally, a Point-Voxel Interaction (PVI) module is developed to improve knowledge fusion between the segmentation and completion tasks, facilitating interaction between the incomplete local point geometry and the complete global voxel structure. Notably, the auxiliary SSC and PVI components can be omitted during inference without incurring extra computational costs for segmentation. Extensive experiments on the SemanticKITTI and SemanticPOSS benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed JS3C-Net achieves superior performance, yielding improvements of 4% and 3%, respectively.

Networks-of-networks (NoN) serve as a graph-theoretic framework for interdependent networks featuring distinct dynamics within each layer. By incorporating specialized edges to model relationships between nodes across different layers, NoN offers a unified approach to analyzing complex, intertwined systems. Although NoN-based models have previously been suggested for cyber-physical systems, this position paper advances toward a three-layered NoN architecture designed for enterprise cyber systems, where each layer represents a unique aspect of such a system. Furthermore, we provide a detailed examination of four key graph-theoretic applications to illustrate how this three-layered NoN model can be utilized for continuous system monitoring and mission assurance.

Conventional automatic metrics, such as BLEU, prove unreliable for evaluating machine translation at the document level. These metrics fail to differentiate between sentence-level and document-level quality improvements and cannot pinpoint discourse phenomena responsible for context-agnostic translations. To address this, we present BlonDe, a new automatic metric that expands MT evaluation from the sentence to the document level. By classifying discourse-related spans and computing an F1 score based on similarity, BlonDe incorporates discourse coherence into its assessment. Extensive comparisons using our newly developed BWB dataset demonstrate that BlonDe offers superior selectivity and interpretability at the document level while being more sensitive to document-specific nuances. Furthermore, a large-scale human evaluation confirms that BlonDe achieves a significantly higher Pearson's r correlation with human judgments than prior metrics.

This work introduces two distinct definitions of temperate almost periodic distributions within Euclidean space. Leveraging the characteristics of distributions and measures with discrete support, we explore the relationship between these distributions and their Fourier transforms. Additionally, we examine the link between the Fourier transform of an almost periodic distribution and its Fourier coefficients. Furthermore, we present several nontrivial examples of measures that do not qualify as almost periodic distributions. Notably, we construct a crystalline measure on the real line that is neither an almost periodic distribution nor a Fourier quasicrystal.

Artificial neural networks are currently achieving state-of-the-art results across an expanding range of applications, addressing a vast array of problems. However, issues such as biases within training data challenge the generalization capabilities of these models. This work introduces EnD, a regularization strategy designed to stop deep models from internalizing undesirable biases. Specifically, EnD implements an "information bottleneck" within the neural network to separate bias-related information from task-relevant data, allowing the latter to continue forward while the former is filtered out. A significant benefit of EnD is its efficiency; it does not increase training complexity by requiring extra layers or decoders, as it functions as a direct regularizer applied to an already trained model. Experimental results demonstrate that EnD successfully enhances generalization on unbiased test sets and is effective in real-world applications, such as eliminating hidden biases in COVID-19 detection from radiographic images.

We examine the destruction of charged and rotating black holes within Einstein-Maxwell-(dilaton) theory. Our findings indicate that a test particle possessing specific properties can exist within the black hole's background and transform it into a naked singularity. In this study, we disregard self-force, self-energy, and radiative effects, which are factors often accounted for in other literature. Consequently, we demonstrate that both Kerr-Newman and Kaluza-Klein black holes can be destroyed by such a test particle. Additionally, regarding Kaluza-Klein black holes, we explore the possibility of overspinning them using a neutral test scalar field.

Bug localization seeks to shorten debugging durations by identifying program components pertinent to specific bug reports. Historically, researchers have tackled this challenge using information retrieval methods that exploit similarities between bug reports and source code. However, as modern software development accelerates toward faster changes and continuous delivery, existing localization techniques struggle to keep pace with the latest software versions, rendering them increasingly insufficient. This paper introduces an online bug localization approach that supports models capable of rapid updates. Specifically, we present a streaming technique grounded in an ensemble of online topic models, designed to handle both concrete bug reports containing explicit code references and more abstract descriptions. By utilizing changesets (diffs) rather than source code snapshots as input, the model inherently incorporates defect prediction and co-change data into its analysis. Preliminary findings demonstrate that this approach enhances bug localization performance in 42 out of 56 evaluated projects, achieving an average Mean Average Precision (MAP) improvement of 5.9%.

Automatically generating natural language descriptions from images is a difficult challenge in artificial intelligence that demands a robust grasp of visual and textual signals, as well as the relationships between them. Current state-of-the-art image captioning methods struggle to match human-level performance, particularly when data is scarce. This paper introduces a method to enhance existing image captioning models by integrating two sources of prior knowledge: (i) conditional latent topic attention, which employs latent variables (topics) as anchors to generate highly probable words, and (ii) a regularization technique that leverages inductive biases within the syntactic and semantic structures of captions to improve model generalization. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields more human-interpretable captions and achieves significant performance gains on the MSCOCO dataset across both full and low-data scenarios.

Creating skyrmionic devices necessitates precise tuning of material parameters to ensure skyrmion stability and regulate their density. Recent studies have shown that heterostructures combining ferromagnets, ferrimagnets, and heavy metals can simultaneously stabilize distinct skyrmion types at room temperature, presenting a novel approach to encoding binary data via skyrmion type rather than simply their presence or absence. In this work, we manipulate the energy landscape of these two skyrmion types within such heterostructures by customizing the geometrical and material attributes of each layer. Our findings indicate that finely adjusting the thickness of the ferromagnetic layer—and consequently its magnetic anisotropy—enables the trilayer system to host either a single skyrmion type, both types coexisting, or varying densities of each.

High-order harmonic generation (HHG) represents a core phenomenon where intense laser fields induce the emission of high-energy photons from matter, offering profound insights into the electronic structure and dynamics of gases, solids, and liquids. Recently, HHG in solids has garnered significant interest from attosecond science and condensed matter physics communities because its spectral signatures encode details about electron-hole interactions and both inter- and intra-band current flows. This study investigates how interlayer coupling and symmetry influence HHG in two-dimensional materials by examining monolayers and two distinct stacking configurations of bilayer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The simulations demonstrate that high-order harmonic emission patterns are critically dependent on crystal inversion symmetry, rotational symmetry, and the strength of interlayer coupling.

The flux reconstruction (FR) methodology provides a versatile framework for characterizing various high-order numerical schemes, such as nodal discontinuous Galerkin and spectral difference methods. This capability is achieved via the application of specific correction functions. In this research, we utilize a weighted Sobolev norm to establish a novel extended class of FR correction functions, with their stability confirmed through Fourier analysis. Several schemes within this new family demonstrate diminished dissipation and dispersion overshoot. Additionally, many of these schemes achieve higher CFL limits while preserving the anticipated convergence rates. Numerical experiments involving homogeneous linear convection and Burgers turbulence were conducted, with the outcomes aligning with the theoretical predictions.

Graph databases have undergone substantial research and development, with issues like modularity, centrality, alignment, and clustering being formalized and resolved across diverse contexts. This paper concentrates on databases where graphs possess a spatial foundation, termed "rigid graphs," in which nodes maintain preferred positions relative to their neighbors. Examples include abstractions of large biomolecules, human brain functional connectomes, and logs from mobile device or sensor communications. When analyzing these networks, accounting for edge lengths is crucial; for instance, identifying conserved patterns via graph alignment requires not only topological similarity but also correlated edge lengths. Unlike extensive work on topological graph alignment, rigid graph alignment concurrently aligns both the network and its underlying structure defined by edge lengths. We formulate this problem and introduce a meta-algorithm grounded in expectation-maximization that iteratively aligns the network and its structure. Our findings demonstrate that this meta-algorithm markedly enhances alignment quality in target applications compared to using topological or structural aligners independently. We apply rigid graph alignment to functional brain networks from 20 subjects in the Human Connectome Project (HCP), achieving more than a two-fold improvement in alignment quality over state-of-the-art topological methods. Furthermore, through an evaluation on synthetic graphs, we characterize the performance impact of various input dataset parameters. Our results hold broad applicability for other applications and abstracted networks embeddable in metric spaces, such as those achieved via spectral embeddings.

We present a novel Legendrian isotopy invariant applicable to any closed orientable Legendrian surface $L$ situated within a closed contact $5$-manifold $(M, \xi)$ that supports an "admissible" open book $(B, f)$ containing $L$. We demonstrate that for any such $L$ and a specific page $X$, an integer denoted as $M\mathcal{P}_{X}(L)$—termed the "Relative Maximal Page Crossing Number of $L$ with respect to $X$"—can be assigned, remaining invariant under Legendrian isotopies of $L$. Furthermore, we establish that this concept extends to a page-independent invariant, allowing the assignment of an integer $M\mathcal{P}_{(B,f)}(L)$, known as the "Absolute Maximal Page Crossing Number of $L$ with respect to $(B, f)$," which is likewise invariant under Legendrian isotopies of $L$. Notably, this new invariant is capable of distinguishing Legendrian surfaces in the standard five-sphere that remain indistinguishable via the Thurston-Bennequin invariant.

Spiking neural networks (SNNs) utilizing the Leaky Integrate and Fire (LIF) model are employed for energy-efficient spatiotemporal and temporal tasks. While the bio-plausible dynamics and simplicity of LIF-SNNs enable event-driven processing, they often suffer from diminished performance due to reliance on spike-based information transmission. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a Leaky Integrate and Analog Fire (LIAF) neuron model that allows neurons to exchange analog values, forming the basis of a deep architecture named LIAF-Net for efficient spatiotemporal processing. In the temporal domain, LIAF adheres to conventional LIF dynamics to preserve temporal capabilities, whereas in the spatial domain, it integrates information via convolutional or fully-connected mechanisms. As a versatile spatiotemporal layer, LIAF can also operate in conjunction with traditional artificial neural network (ANN) layers. Experimental results demonstrate that LIAF-Net matches the performance of Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models on bAbI Question Answering tasks and achieves state-of-the-art results on spatiotemporal Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS) datasets—such as MNIST-DVS, CIFAR10-DVS, and DVS128 Gesture—with significantly fewer synaptic weights and lower computational overhead compared to networks based on LSTM, GRU, Convolutional LSTM, or 3D convolution. Furthermore, LIAF-Net exhibits a substantial accuracy improvement over traditional LIF-SNNs across all experiments. Ultimately, LIAF-Net offers a framework that merges the strengths of ANNs and SNNs for lightweight and efficient spatiotemporal information processing.

This research investigates the vertical variations of wave periods for magnetoacoustic two-fluid waves within the partially ionized lower solar atmosphere. This environment comprises ion (proton) and electron fluids coupled with neutral atomic hydrogen through ion-neutral collisions. The study identifies wave period cutoffs and their atmospheric variations, clarifying how these cutoffs influence wave propagation. The model assumes a uniform vertical magnetic field and employs one-dimensional numerical simulations based on a two-fluid framework. In this setup, plane waves are generated by a harmonic driver acting on vertical ion and neutral velocities at the base of the solar photosphere. Our simulations reveal the excitation of waves possessing cutoff periods alongside those directly driven by the source. Notably, certain driver-excited waves can penetrate into the solar corona. Although the model has limitations, including the absence of non-adiabatic and non-ideal terms and its simplified one-dimensional structure, it offers new insights into how cutoffs dictate wave propagation conditions and determines which wave periods can transport energy from the solar surface to the corona.

We integrate infectious disease transmission dynamics with non-pharmaceutical intervention (NPI) responses to disease incidence within a unified closed model. This framework utilizes two coupled delay differential equations to describe the incidence rate and the time-varying reproduction number. The model relies on three adjustable parameters: the initial reproduction number, the intensity of the intervention, and the lag time between infection onset and the implementation of NPIs. Specifically, the NPI response is defined by a rule where the rate of change in the reproduction number is proportional to the negative difference between the current incidence rate and a specific intervention threshold. This delay-based dynamical system displays damped oscillations in certain parameter regions and growing oscillations in others, with a boundary surface separating these behaviors where the system exhibits strictly periodic nonlinear oscillations. For parameters pertinent to the COVID-19 pandemic, the transition from damped to growing oscillations occurs at response delays of approximately one week. This finding implies that effective control and mitigation of successive epidemic waves are unattainable unless NPIs are adopted proactively rather than merely reacting to current incidence levels.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) represent highly energetic radio wave sources detected across cosmological distances. By applying a detailed observational model of FRBs—fully described in an accompanying study—to extensive datasets from ASKAP and Parkes (which include seven FRBs with confirmed host galaxies), we have constrained key population parameters. Our analysis reveals that the FRB population evolves with redshift at a rate consistent with, or exceeding, the star-formation rate (SFR), effectively excluding a non-evolving population at a 99.9% confidence level. Assuming a 1 GHz bandwidth, our estimated maximum FRB energy is $\log_{10} E_{\rm max} [{\rm erg}] = 41.84_{-0.18}^{+0.49}$ (68% C.L.), accompanied by a cumulative luminosity distribution slope of $\gamma=-1.16_{-0.12}^{+0.11}$. Additionally, we determine a log-mean host contribution to the dispersion measure of $145_{-60}^{+64}$\,pc\,cm$^{-3}$, superimposed on a typical local contribution (from the ISM and halo) of approximately 80\,pc\,cm$^{-3}$, a value notably higher than most previous estimates. These findings align with models positioning FRBs as the high-energy limit of magnetar bursts while permitting progenitor evolution that outpaces the SFR.

Let $p$ denote a prime number, where $K$ represents a finite unramified extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ and $\mathbb{F}$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{F}_p$. By employing perfectoid spaces, we assign to every finite-dimensional continuous representation $\overline{\rho}$ of ${\rm Gal}(\overline K/K)$ over $\mathbb{F}$ an étale $(\varphi,\mathcal{O}_K^\times)$-module, denoted $D_A^\otimes(\overline{\rho})$, defined over a completed localization $A$ of $\mathbb{F}[\![\mathcal{O}_K]\!]$. We propose that for any smooth representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{GL}_2(K)$ found within a Hecke eigenspace of the mod $p$ cohomology of a Shimura curve, one can similarly construct an étale $(\varphi,\mathcal{O}_K^\times)$-module $D_A(\pi)$. Furthermore, we conjecture that $D_A(\pi)$ is isomorphic (up to a twist) to $D_A^\otimes(\overline{\rho})$, with $\overline{\rho}$ being the associated $2$-dimensional representation of ${\rm Gal}(\overline K/K)$. Leveraging prior research by the same authors, we establish this conjecture under the conditions that $\overline{\rho}$ is semi-simple and sufficiently generic.

We present an ultrafast, high-repetition-rate (250 kHz) monochromatic extreme ultraviolet (21.6 eV) source based on high-order harmonic generation (HHG), featuring polarization tunability and designed for multi-modal dichroism in time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. By utilizing an annular beam to drive HHG, we spatially separate the high-power 515 nm driving laser from the XUV beamlet while maintaining the ability to adjust the linear polarization angle. This approach permits control over the XUV radiation's polarization state using a fixed, all-reflective phase-shifter. Consequently, the system achieves a source brightness of 5.7×10¹² photons/s at 21.6 eV (delivering up to 4×10¹¹ photons/s on target) with ellipticities reaching as high as 90%.

Simulating particle physics data serves as a critical yet computationally demanding component in Large Hadron Collider analyses, where observational set-valued data is produced based on incoming particle configurations. To expedite this process, we introduce a new generative model utilizing graph neural networks and slot-attention modules, which outperforms current baseline methods.

Although recently introduced bianisotropic acoustic metagratings hold significant promise for passive acoustic wavefront control—especially for flat lenses and ultra-high-frequency ultrasound imaging—they have historically been unable to operate at the MHz frequencies standard in medical imaging. A primary obstacle has been the fabrication of microscopic, complex structures; however, two-photon polymerization now enables the precise creation of sub-wavelength features within this frequency band. Despite this advancement, miniaturization introduces substantial thermoviscous losses that must be accounted for in design. This study presents three microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves to $-35^{\circ}$ at 2 MHz. To achieve metaatoms resistant to thermoviscous effects, we employed shape optimization based on linearized Navier-Stokes equations solved via the finite element method. We report the first manufacturing of microscopic acoustic metamaterials using two-photon polymerization and validate their performance experimentally, utilizing a capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducer as the source and an optical microphone as the detector across a 1.8–2.2 MHz range. Our results demonstrate that, even in the presence of thermoviscous losses, a microacoustic metagrating only 0.29$\lambda$ thick can successfully redirect normally incident waves and concentrate 90% of the transmitted energy into the $-1$st diffraction order.

This study examines the connection between cellular phone data and housing prices in Budapest, Hungary. We derived mobility metrics from one month of Call Detail Records (CDR) to characterize the socioeconomic status of Hungary's capital using property price data. Initially, we validated our methodology by comparing estimated home and work locations, along with commuting patterns from the cellular network dataset, against reports from the national mini census. We then analyzed statistical relationships between mobile indicators—such as the Radius of Gyration, the distance between home and work, and the Entropy of visited cells—and economic status measures based on housing prices. Our findings indicate a significant correlation between mobility and socioeconomic status. Furthermore, we applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to combined vectors of mobility indicators to characterize how mobility habits depend on socioeconomic status. The PCA results revealed a remarkable correlation between housing prices and mobility patterns.

This paper investigates various time-fractional extensions of both the nonlinear Jordan-Moore-Gibson-Thompson (JMGT) equations and their linear Moore-Gibson-Thompson (MGT) counterparts within the field of nonlinear acoustics. Utilizing the methodology outlined by Jordan (2014), these fractional acoustic equations are derived from four fractional adaptations of the Maxwell-Cattaneo law presented in Compte and Metzler (1997). Beyond establishing well-posedness for each formulation, the study examines the behavior of these equations as the fractional order approaches unity, thereby recovering the classical third-order-in-time (J)MGT equation.

This study demonstrates that Takens' celebrated Embedding Theorem is merely a specific instance of a broader principle: randomly generated linear state-space models derived from generic observations of an invertible dynamical system inherently facilitate the embedding of the system's phase space dynamics into the selected Euclidean space. This embedding aligns with a natural form of generalized synchronization occurring within this framework, establishing a topological conjugacy between the dynamics of the state-space model and the original dynamical system. Consequently, this finding offers new methodologies for representing, learning, and analyzing chaotic attractors, while also providing deeper insights into the reservoir computing phenomenon observed in recurrent neural networks.

This paper presents "MOVESTAR," an open-source model designed to compute fuel consumption and pollutant emissions for motor vehicles. Built upon the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Motor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES), the model delivers precise emission estimates across diverse, user-defined scenarios. While the original MOVES software necessitates the input of numerous parameters—such as vehicle categories, temporal and geographical settings, specific pollutants, operating characteristics, and road types—MOVESTAR functions as a streamlined alternative. It requires only second-by-second vehicle speed data and vehicle type as inputs. To facilitate seamless integration, the model's source code is available in multiple programming languages, including Python, MATLAB, and C++. Furthermore, the paper includes a case study demonstrating the model's efficacy in advancing vehicle technology.

For a long time, link prediction within knowledge graphs (KGs) was exclusively transductive, failing to support reasoning over unseen entities. Recently, significant research has shifted toward semi- and fully inductive settings to facilitate inference on new and emerging entities. However, existing methods have primarily focused on triple-based KGs, neglecting their more complex counterparts, hyper-relational KGs (such as Wikidata). This study categorizes various inductive scenarios and investigates the advantages of utilizing hyper-relational KGs for semi- and fully inductive link prediction tasks, leveraging recent progress in graph neural networks. Experimental results on a newly created benchmark suite demonstrate that incorporating qualifiers on typed edges can yield absolute performance gains of 6% (measured by Hits@10) compared to triple-only baselines. The project's code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/mali-git/hyper_relational_ilp}.

Legged robots are uniquely suited for search and rescue, inspection, and exploration tasks due to their ability to navigate difficult terrain, perceive surroundings, and plan safe footholds. However, maintaining stability while traversing such environments remains a critical challenge, often necessitating gait transitions. Because classical PID control struggles with the complex dynamics of quadrupeds, advanced techniques like Model Predictive Control (MPC) are required. MPC leverages system models and terrain characteristics to predict stable body poses and correct for external disturbances that alter desired behavior. This MPC controller, designed in MATLAB for full-body torque control, was validated using Boston Dynamics Spot within the Webots simulator. The results demonstrate that the controller can counteract external perturbations of up to 150 N and prevent falls from heights as high as 80 cm.

Palomar 5 stands out as one of the sparsest star clusters within the Milky Way's halo, renowned for its extensive tidal tails that stretch across more than 20 degrees of the sky. N-body simulations indicate that these distinct characteristics arise from a population of stellar-mass black holes making up approximately 20% of the cluster's current mass. According to this model, Palomar 5 originally formed with a typical black hole fraction of a few percent; however, stars were depleted at a faster rate than black holes, causing the black hole proportion to rise over time. This expansion inflated the cluster, intensifying tidal stripping and tail development. In roughly one billion years, the cluster will fully dissolve, leaving behind a system composed entirely of black holes. Conversely, clusters that were initially denser retain lower black hole fractions, remain more compact, and fail to produce visible tails. Consequently, extended star clusters dominated by black holes are considered the probable origins of the recently identified thin stellar streams in the Galactic halo.

Reconfigurable Broadcast Networks (RBN) represent a distributed computation framework where agents disseminate messages across a communication topology that may undergo arbitrary changes during execution. This paper presents a parameterized analysis of RBN, focusing on "cubes"—infinite sets of configurations defined by lower and upper bounds on the agent counts within each state. We demonstrate that evaluating boolean combinations of these cubes and their associated reachability sets falls within PSPACE, with the specific problem of determining reachability between two cubes being PSPACE-complete. To establish this upper bound, we derive structural properties regarding reachability sets and the symbolic graph abstraction of RBN, findings that hold independent interest. We validate these results through two applications: first, by proving that the almost-sure coverability problem for RBN is PSPACE-complete, thus resolving a complexity gap identified in prior research; and second, by introducing "RBN protocols," a computation model inspired by population protocols, and precisely characterizing the set of predicates computable by these protocols.

The Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) represents the next generation of ground-based gamma-ray observatories, promising to enhance the sensitivity of existing instruments by a factor of ten. The LST-1, the initial prototype constructed at the Canary Islands' La Palma site, has been collecting data for several years. Functioning as an Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope (IACT), the LST-1 detects light generated by the Cherenkov effect when high-energy particles traverse the atmosphere. By analyzing camera snapshots, researchers can distinguish gamma photons from hadrons and reconstruct the physical properties of the selected photons. Developing models for discrimination and reconstruction, as well as estimating telescope response through simulations of atmospheric showers and optical/electronic systems, necessitates extensive Monte Carlo simulations. These trained models subsequently process data from actual observations. The `lstMCpipe` is an open-source Python package designed to manage the various stages of Monte Carlo file analysis on computing facilities. Currently in production status, it schedules the full pipeline within a SLURM cluster. This tool streamlines the analysis workflow by introducing an abstraction layer, enabling users to execute the entire pipeline via a straightforward configuration file. Furthermore, LST collaboration members can request analyses with customized parameters by submitting pull requests to the project repository. This mechanism facilitates peer review by other collaborators, ensures centralized management of productions, minimizes human errors, and optimizes computing resource utilization.

Dry Eye Disease (DED), affecting 5% to 50% of the population, is a primary cause for visits to ophthalmologists. Currently, diagnosing and quantifying DED depends on slit-lamp examinations to analyze the ocular surface, yet these assessments are often subjective and lack reproducibility. To enhance diagnostic accuracy, we propose a two-step approach: first, tracking the ocular surface in 3D using video recordings captured during exams, and second, grading severity by registering these frames. Our registration technique employs unsupervised image-to-depth learning, which derives depth from lighting and shadows to estimate pose via depth maps. However, DED examinations present unresolved challenges, such as moving light sources and the transparency of ocular tissues. To address these issues and calculate ego-motion, we developed joint CNN architectures with multiple losses that integrate prior knowledge—specifically the eye's shape—through semantic segmentation and sphere fitting. Our method achieves tracking errors that surpass state-of-the-art performance, recording a mean Euclidean distance as low as 0.48% of the image width on our test set. This improved registration boosts DED severity classification by a 0.20 AUC difference. Notably, this is the first approach to address DED diagnosis using supervision derived from monocular videos.

This study introduces a nonparametric method for detecting change points in multivariate time series without relying on prior distributional assumptions. We propose a structural subsampling technique that transforms observations into multiple sequences of Bernoulli variables. To identify change points within each Bernoulli process, we combine a maximum likelihood approach with a novel searching algorithm. Subsequently, we introduce aggregation statistics to synthesize results from these individual univariate series into consistent and stable location estimates. Additionally, we investigate a weighting strategy to assess the relevance of different subsampled groups. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methodology outperforms existing popular nonparametric methods across various complex settings. Finally, the approach is applied to real-world data involving categorical, ordinal, and continuous time series from genetics, climate, and finance domains.

The NASA TESS mission is anticipated to identify hundreds of planets through single transits detected in light curves. Establishing the orbital periods for these single-transit candidates usually demands extensive follow-up observations, such as capturing a second transit or measuring radial velocity orbits. In Yao et al. (2019), we created simulations showing that combining archival photometric data with TESS could "precover" orbital periods for these candidates with minute-level precision, provided the orbits were circular. This study integrates updated models for TESS single transits that account for eccentric orbits, alongside an improved methodology to enhance result reliability. Furthermore, we investigate the application of radial velocity (RV) observations for single-transit events using strategies different from those used when the orbital period is already known. Our findings indicate that scheduling reconnaissance RV observations based on an estimated period derived from a circular orbit can effectively separate eclipsing binaries from planets. For candidates that pass these initial checks, we simulate RV monitoring campaigns capable of yielding approximate orbital solutions. We conclude that this approach can regularly determine orbital periods for planets exceeding 0.5 M_J, even with periods extending up to 100 days.

Although neural networks have achieved remarkable success in modeling system dynamics from data, they frequently function as physics-agnostic black boxes. In the context of physical systems, this often leads to physically inconsistent predictions, rendering them unreliable in practical applications. This paper introduces Physically Consistent NODEs (PC-NODEs), which utilize the framework of Irreversible port-Hamiltonian Systems (IPHS)—capable of describing most multi-physics systems—to learn parameters from data via Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs). Because IPHS models inherently align with the first and second laws of thermodynamics, the resulting PC-NODEs share this consistency. Additionally, the NODE training process enables the seamless integration of prior knowledge regarding system properties into the learned dynamics. We validate the method's efficacy by modeling the thermodynamics of a building using real-world measurements and simulating a gas-piston system. Leveraging the modularity and flexibility of the IPHS framework, PC-NODEs offer the potential to extend to physically consistent models for multi-physics distributed systems.

This study introduces a mathematical model to evaluate how salinity and inundation impact the long-term growth and carbon sequestration of monospecific *Rhizophora mucronata* mangrove plantations in the Philippines. The model utilizes allometry for growth equations and stochasticity to simulate population-level developmental events. It identifies an index, $\xi$, which helps determine strategies for maximizing long-term carbon accumulation. When the initial plot configuration yields $\xi > 1$, *R. mucronata* plantations can reach approximately 1000 t/ha of above-ground biomass (AGB), equivalent to 500 tC/ha, within 200 to 250 years. Conversely, current restoration efforts in the Philippines align with $\xi < 1$, meaning restored mangroves cannot sustain stable growth without expensive human intervention, such as repeated replanting. Without such support, AGB declines over time until the trees perish. Therefore, mangrove restoration should be strategically planned to avoid wasteful and costly practices. The proposed index $\xi$ acts as an early warning signal for the success or failure of restoration projects.

Class imbalance is a prevalent challenge in numerous NLP tasks, intrinsically linked to bias, as training data skewness often results in superior accuracy for majority groups while disadvantaging minority groups. Historically, research addressing class-imbalanced learning and bias mitigation has operated in separate silos, with a unified perspective emerging only recently. This study evaluates long-tail learning techniques for classifying tweet sentiment and occupations, extending a margin-loss framework with mechanisms to enforce fairness. Through controlled empirical experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed methods effectively address both class imbalance and demographic biases.

This study analyzes long-term torque noise fluctuations in persistent X-ray binaries—specifically Her X-1, Vela X-1, GX 301-2, CEN X-3, 4U 1538-53, OAO 1657-415, and 4U 1626-67—by utilizing historical pulse frequency data from CGRO/BATSE and Fermi/GBM. Our findings indicate that known disk-fed sources display a saturated $1/\omega^{2}$ red noise component in their power density spectra. Conversely, wind-fed sources exhibit a distinct white noise component, whereas wind-fed systems with intermittent disk formation show $1/\omega$ flicker noise. We discuss these long-term timing noise characteristics by modeling the power density spectrum of pulse frequency derivative fluctuations as a combination of monochromatic and colored noise processes. Additionally, we explore the relationship between measured noise strengths and other independently derived physical parameters. Although the sample size is limited, we propose that noise strengths correlate with luminosity but remain uncorrelated with magnetic field strength, suggesting that accretion is the primary mechanism driving these noise fluctuations.

Semantic Technologies, especially the Semantic Web, have proven to be highly effective for modeling cultural heritage and artistic practices. Nevertheless, the landscape of ontologies for musicology remains narrow and often confined to niche applications. This research introduces HaMSE, an ontology designed to represent musical features to support musicological inquiry. Specifically, HaMSE tackles long-standing challenges in the field, namely the representation of music and the integration of quantitative and qualitative data. By enabling the alignment of diverse music representation systems and defining a comprehensive set of musicological features, HaMSE facilitates music analysis across various levels of granularity.

The World Health Organization has officially classified the novel coronavirus, COVID-19, as a pandemic. Since vaccine availability is currently lacking, managing social contact networks through extensive social distancing remains the most effective strategy for controlling transmission. This study employs an age-structured SIR model, utilizing social contact matrices derived from surveys and Bayesian imputation, to analyze the progression of the epidemic in India. We calculated the basic reproductive ratio ($R_0$) and its time-dependent variant using case data, age demographics, and social contact patterns. The research evaluates the efficacy and optimal duration of various social distancing interventions, including school closures, workplace non-attendance, and lockdowns. Results indicate that a three-week lockdown is inadequate to prevent a resurgence; instead, we recommend sustained lockdowns with periodic relaxations. We provide forecasts regarding the reduction in age-specific morbidity and mortality resulting from these measures. Ultimately, this study highlights the critical role of age and social contact structures in determining the country-specific impact of social distancing protocols.

This study provides a comprehensive examination of harmonic longitudinal and Hall voltage measurements for in-plane magnetized Pt/Co/Ta and Ta/Co/Pt trilayers, comparing them against Pt/Co and Ta/Co bilayers. By incorporating a second heavy metal (HM) with an opposing spin Hall angle, we observe an enhancement in both spin-orbit torques (SOTs) and unidirectional spin Hall magnetoresistance (USMR). The calculated SOT efficiencies for these trilayers exceed those of the bilayers, validating previously reported improvements in perpendicularly magnetized Co trilayers. Notably, the Pt/Co/Ta trilayer achieves a maximum effective spin Hall angle of $\theta_{SH}$ = 20%. Furthermore, the USMR effect in the trilayer is up to 27% greater than in the corresponding bilayers, with the Pt/Co/Ta structure exhibiting the largest effective USMR amplitude of -0.32 $\times$ 10$^{-5}$ at a charge current density of 10$^{7}$ A/cm$^2$.

Mobility is a cornerstone of contemporary urban life, as the organization and efficiency of transport systems directly influence how residents navigate the city, access essential services, and engage in civic activities. Municipalities confront significant challenges: they must ensure citizens' right to move freely and reach local amenities while simultaneously reducing the economic, social, and environmental burdens of current mobility patterns. Issues such as traffic congestion, road safety risks, energy reliance, and air pollution are becoming increasingly prevalent, making the promotion of sustainable, active mobility practices—particularly cycling for routine trips like commuting to work or school—vital. Addressing commuter traffic effectively requires a collaborative approach involving both public and private sectors that balances infrastructure supply with transportation demand management. This paper introduces an end-to-end solution designed to enhance urban cycling. It empowers corporate Mobility Managers to advocate for active commuting, assists city planners in identifying necessary urban interventions, and encourages citizens to adopt sustainable travel habits. To assess the solution's impact, we conducted two analyses: the first evaluated the user experience and behavioral shifts resulting from the BIKE2WORK initiative, while the second demonstrated how the gathered data can guide the Municipality of Ferrara, Italy, in improving local cycling infrastructure and policies.

Using the mean-bacterial-velocity model, we examine the \textit{irreversibility} of two-dimensional (2D) \textit{bacterial turbulence} and contrast it with 2D fluid turbulence. Through extensive direct numerical simulations of Lagrangian tracer particles advected by the model's velocity field, we identify a key qualitative distinction: when the \textit{friction} parameter is large and positive (or the \textit{activity} parameter is large and negative), the probability distribution functions of energy increments or power along tracer paths exhibit \textit{positive} skewness. Consequently, irreversibility in bacterial turbulence can, on average, result in \textit{particles gaining energy faster than they lose it}, a phenomenon that stands in direct contrast to the behavior of tracers in 2D fluid turbulence.

Following the identification of COVID-19, triggered by the SARS-CoV-2 virus in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China, in late December, the disease spread rapidly worldwide. Given the clinical resemblance between COVID-19 and other flu-like conditions, patients are routinely tested for various influenza pathogens. Reports have documented co-infections among COVID-19 patients involving bacteria such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, and *Legionella pneumophila*, as well as viruses including influenza, rhinovirus/enterovirus, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, and influenza B. In this study, we constructed and analyzed a compartmental Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) model to investigate the dynamics of COVID-19 co-infection with other influenza-type illnesses. To reflect the constraints of limited treatment resources, the model incorporates a saturated treatment rate. We derived the basic reproduction number for the system and conducted numerical simulations across different parameter spaces to evaluate the model's solutions.

Bienvenu, Lambert, and Steel recently introduced the class of ranked tree-child networks, which are defined by an evolutionary process with a fixed planar embedding. Having established counting results for this class, the authors now provide bijective proofs for three of their findings. Furthermore, two of these bijections address specific questions posed in their original paper.

Since its inception, quantum mechanics has lacked a universally accepted interpretation, with many alternatives remaining viable because they are difficult or impossible to falsify experimentally. This paper demonstrates how to experimentally differentiate between theories positing tiny, localized particles and those advocating for realistic, non-local wave functions. This distinction becomes possible through a recently developed model describing the optical transmittance of ultra-dilute gases, which accounts for the impact of individual gas particle wave functions on transmitted light. The model's quantitative predictions vary depending on the specific interpretation of quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we reference a recent experiment based on this theory; its results align with the model's predictions, lending credibility to the framework. If confirmed, such findings would exclude pilot-wave interpretations. The paper provides a brief overview of both the experiment and the underlying model, while also addressing the significance of the Born rule.

This study applies fundamental physical laws to analyze human relationships by modeling them through worldlines (WLs) integrated with social networks (SNs). We examine the most elementary unit of society: a married couple, whose stability arises from a dynamic equilibrium between attraction and repulsion. By constructing worldlines and worldsheets, we establish a two-tiered coordinate system: one level describes the behavior of the string-like binary pair, while the external level tracks the couple's motion within the surrounding medium, generating a string-like sheet or brane. This methodology is demonstrated through simple, semi-quantitative toy models of worldlines and sheets, which are designed for future extension, refinement, and generalization. Our key innovation lies in adapting basic physical principles of attraction and repulsion to explain human conduct. The paper includes illustrative examples incorporating empirical inputs derived from intuition and observation. This work represents an initial, open-ended attempt with potential for broad application.

Addressing multi-agent path finding in dynamic, crowded settings holds significant academic and practical importance for real-world multi-robot systems. To enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of communication and learning during path planning in such environments, we propose AB-Mapper: an Attention and BicNet based Multi-agent path planning algorithm with effective reinforcement, grounded in the actor-critic reinforcement learning framework. Within this framework, the actor-network employs BicNet to facilitate intra-team coordination, while a centralized critic network selectively allocates attention weights to neighboring agents. This attention mechanism enables individual agents to automatically refine their action evaluations by incorporating the behaviors of surrounding agents. Compared to the state-of-the-art Mapper method, AB-Mapper demonstrates superior performance in solving general path finding problems with dynamic obstacles, achieving an 85.86% success rate versus 81.56%. Furthermore, in crowded scenarios, our approach significantly outperforms Mapper, achieving a substantial margin of over 40% in each experiment.

In both graph theory and 3-manifold topology, various "width" parameters are used to quantify the simplicity or thinness of a graph or manifold. Metrics like pathwidth and treewidth for graphs, or thin position for 3-manifolds, are crucial for algorithmic studies. Specifically, many computationally difficult problems in 3-manifold topology become solvable in polynomial time if the dual graph of the input triangulation has bounded treewidth.

Given these algorithmic findings, it is natural to inquire whether every 3-manifold possesses a triangulation with bounded treewidth. We demonstrate that this is false: there exists an infinite family of closed 3-manifolds that do not admit triangulations of bounded pathwidth or treewidth (note that bounded treewidth implies bounded pathwidth, though we provide distinct proofs for each).

Our conclusions stem from the work of Agol, Scharlemann and Thompson, and Scharlemann, Schultens, and Saito by establishing explicit links between the topology of a 3-manifold $M$ and the width parameters of the dual graphs of its triangulations. This addresses a recurring question in computational 3-manifold topology. Specifically, we prove that for a closed, orientable, irreducible, non-Haken 3-manifold $M$, the existence of a triangulation with treewidth (respectively, pathwidth) $k$ implies that the Heegaard genus of $M$ is at most $18(k+1)$ (respectively, $4(3k+1)$).

Hybrid mesons constitute a component of the exotic spectrum within the standard model. The recent discovery of the isoscalar hybrid, identified as $\eta_1(1855)$, represents a significant advancement toward completing the $1^{-+}$ nonet. In this study, we investigate the masses and two-body decay modes of the nonet's members through a model-based hadronic Lagrangian. While the isovector $\pi_1(1600)$ has been extensively examined via both experimental and lattice methods, we leverage existing data from these sources to determine the coupling constants. Utilizing these derived parameters, we then examine potential decay channels for hybrid kaons.

Image deblurring is a significant challenge across numerous scientific and engineering disciplines. While various techniques have been developed to address this issue, variational methods remain particularly prominent. These approaches replace the original problem with a minimization task involving a functional that combines a data fidelity term and a regularization term. This paper introduces a novel application of the graph Laplacian as the regularization operator within the classical $\ell^2-\ell^1$ minimization framework, subject to non-negativity constraints on the solution. First, we detail the construction of the graph Laplacian derived from the observed noisy and blurred image. Subsequently, we efficiently solve the proposed minimization problem by employing the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to separate the convolution operator from the graph Laplacian. Selected numerical experiments demonstrate the strong performance of the proposed algorithm.

Embedding-based retrieval (EBR) serves as a core component in numerous web applications, yet within sponsored search, it presents unique technical challenges distinct from generic scenarios due to its dual objectives: retrieving ads with high relevance to user intent and securing high click-through rates (CTR) to maximize engagement. This paper introduces Uni-Retriever, a novel representation learning framework developed for Bing Search that unifies knowledge distillation and contrastive learning to address both goals. Specifically, the system leverages a "relevance teacher model" via knowledge distillation to ensure high-relevance retrieval, while optimizing for high-CTR retrieval by training the model to distinguish user-clicked ads from the broader corpus. These two modes operate jointly within a multi-objective learning framework, ensuring that generated embeddings prioritize ads with both high relevance and CTR. Beyond the learning strategy, we detail an optimized EBR serving pipeline built on DiskANN, enabling massive-scale retrieval with competitive efficiency in time and memory while maintaining high quality. Comprehensive offline and online evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of these techniques, offering valuable insights for future EBR system development. Consequently, Uni-Retriever has become the primary retrieval path in Bing's production environment, delivering significant improvements in both representation quality and serving performance.

Addressing toxic content remains a paramount challenge for contemporary social media platforms, a necessity underscored by India's 518 million social media users in 2020. To ensure a positive environment for creators and audiences, it is essential to identify and flag toxic comments and their authors. However, detecting toxicity in low-resource Indic languages is particularly difficult due to multiple textual representations of the same content. Additionally, the informal nature of social media posts, which often lack consistent formatting, grammar, or sentence structure, further complicates abuse detection on multilingual platforms. This paper outlines the system developed by the 'Moj Masti' team for the \emph{IIIT-D Multilingual Abusive Comment Identification} challenge, utilizing data from ShareChat/Moj. Our approach leverages multilingual transformer-based models that were pre-trained and fine-tuned to handle code-mixed and code-switched classification tasks. Our top-performing solution was an ensemble of XLM-RoBERTa and MuRIL, which achieved a Mean F-1 score of 0.9 on the test set and leaderboard. We observed performance gains by incorporating transliterated data, and further improvements were realized through the use of weak metadata, ensembling, and post-processing techniques, ultimately securing first place on the leaderboard.

We report high-angular resolution observations of OH maser emission directed at the high-mass star-forming region IRAS 06056+2131. Utilizing the UK's Multi-Element Radio Linked Interferometer Network (MERLIN), we targeted the main OH lines at 1665 and 1667 MHz, as well as the satellite line at 1720 MHz. The study detected emission solely in the 1665 MHz line, with a total intensity estimated at approximately 4 Jy, while no emission was found in the 1667 or 1720 MHz lines.

Given MERLIN's full polarization capabilities, we were able to analyze the magnetic field within the OH maser region. Our findings indicate that IRAS 06056+2131 is a source of strong circular polarization. Analysis of the Zeeman pair in this transition yields an inferred magnetic field strength of roughly -1.5 mG. Furthermore, the orientation of the linear polarization vectors suggests that the magnetic field lines at the site of the OH maser emission likely align with the direction of the associated outflow. The evolutionary stage of the embedded proto-stellar object is also addressed.

It is well established that the specific output of the Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT) for a set of strings largely depends on the order in which those strings are provided in most implementations. Changing this input order influences the count of equal-letter runs ($r$), a critical metric for BWT-based structures like the FM-index and the $r$-index. In 2020, Bentley, Gibney, and Thankachan proposed a linear-time algorithm to determine the optimal string permutation that minimizes the resulting number of runs.

This paper introduces the first tool, named optBWT, which ensures a BWT with the minimum possible number of runs. It achieves this by integrating three components: an algorithm for constructing the BWT from a string collection (utilizing either the SAIS-based method from Cenzato et al., SPIRE 2021, or BCR from Bauer et al., CPM 2011); the SAP array data structure described by Cox et al. in Bioinformatics (2012); and the optimization algorithm developed by Bentley et al.

Experimental results on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the reduction in $r$ achieved through optimal ordering is substantial, while the computational overhead remains negligible. Consequently, the tool is competitive with existing BWT generators regarding both execution time and memory consumption. Specifically, on real data, optBWT reduces the number of runs by up to 31 times with only a $1.39\times$ increase in runtime. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/davidecenzato/optimalBWT.git.

The Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv theorem states that given any set of 2n-1 integers, one can always find n of them whose sum is divisible by n. This work links that theorem to Ramsey-theoretic large sets and establishes an infinitary extension of the result. The proof employs ultrafilter methods, though alternative approaches using topological dynamics are also possible.

We introduce a lattice model for superconducting fermions on a $d$-dimensional hypercubic lattice ($\mathbb{Z}^d$, where $d\ge 3$), featuring nearest-neighbor two-body interactions of the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) type. While such electron-electron interactions are typically attributed to electron-phonon coupling, our model assumes short-range interactions between electrons without involving phonons. We demonstrate that this system exhibits long-range superconducting order at low temperatures and possesses gapless excitations above the infinite-volume ground state. Specifically, a Nambu-Goldstone mode emerges due to the spontaneous breaking of U(1) symmetry. The corresponding Nambu-Goldstone boson is identified precisely as a Cooper pair, comprising an electron with spin up and another with spin down.

SpGEMM kernels, a critical component of sparse matrix computations, are ubiquitous in diverse fields ranging from graph-based pathfinding to machine learning models like neural networks. A primary bottleneck in optimizing these kernels is the strain placed on DRAM memory. While inner product methods mitigate the generation of intermediate results, they often saturate memory bandwidth due to excessive redundant fetching of input elements. Conversely, outer product approaches reduce redundant fetches but incur significant overhead from additional computation and memory operations required to manage partial products.

This thesis proposes a novel SpGEMM implementation utilizing a row-wise product strategy. By employing atomic instructions to merge intermediate partial products during their generation, this approach eliminates the necessity for creating explicit partial product matrices. To validate this method, we mapped an optimized SpGEMM kernel onto PIUMA, an experimental custom accelerator developed by Intel for graph-based workloads. PIUMA offers distinctive capabilities such as rapid context switching, user-configurable caches, globally addressable memory, non-coherent caching, and asynchronous pipelines, all of which our kernel is tailored to exploit.

The study evaluates our implementation against existing solutions within the PIUMA framework, beginning with an overview of the architecture's key features before detailing the optimized kernel. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves a 9.4x speedup compared to competing methods.

This study examines the fundamental definitions and characteristics of trapped surfaces within the framework of the Kerr-Vaidya metric. Our analysis reveals that an apparent horizon is not universally present in axisymmetric spacetimes because the surface defined by geodesic null tangent vectors does not necessarily coincide with the surface where the expansion of such vectors vanishes. Consequently, calculating an approximate apparent horizon for spacetimes where one is guaranteed to exist appears to be the only viable solution to this issue. However, this approximate horizon proves to be non-unique; selecting shear-free null geodesics, particularly at the leading order, seems to resolve this ambiguity. Furthermore, we introduce a novel definition for the black hole boundary.

We introduce the inaugural cosmological constraints derived from a simulation-based inference (SBI) analysis of galaxy clustering, utilizing the novel ${\rm S{\scriptsize IM}BIG}}$ forward modeling framework. ${\rm S{\scriptsize IM}BIG}}$ harnesses high-fidelity simulations to offer an inference method capable of extracting cosmological data from small, non-linear scales that remain out of reach for conventional analyses. Applied to the BOSS CMASS galaxy sample, this study examines the power spectrum, $P_\ell(k)$, extending up to $k_{\rm max}=0.5\,h/{\rm Mpc}$. We generated 20,000 simulated galaxy populations using a forward model grounded in high-resolution ${\rm Q{\scriptsize UIJOTE}}$ $N$-body simulations, incorporating detailed survey realism to thoroughly address observational systematics. Subsequently, we performed SBI by training normalizing flows on these simulated datasets to infer the posterior distributions of $\Lambda$CDM parameters: $\Omega_m, \Omega_b, h, n_s,$ and $\sigma_8$. Our results yield significant constraints on $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$, aligning with prior research. Specifically, our $\sigma_8$ constraints achieve $27\%$ greater precision compared to standard analyses, an improvement statistically equivalent to analyzing a galaxy sample roughly $60\%$ larger than CMASS using traditional methods. This gain stems from accessing additional cosmological information on non-linear scales beyond the limits of current analytic models ($k > 0.25\,h/{\rm Mpc}$). Although this work focuses on $P_\ell$ for validation and literature comparison, ${\rm S{\scriptsize IM}BIG}}$ establishes a versatile framework for analyzing galaxy clustering with any summary statistic, with anticipated further enhancements in cosmological constraints from future applications of ${\rm S{\scriptsize IM}BIG}}$ to statistics beyond $P_\ell$.

Let $B^{H_1}$ and $\tilde{B}^{H_2}$ denote two independent fractional Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$ with Hurst indices $H_i \in (0,1)$ satisfying $H_1 \leq H_2$. This study investigates their intersection local time, $\ell_t(a)$. We establish that $\ell_t(a)$ is spatially differentiable when $\frac{1}{H_1} + \frac{1}{H_2} > 3$. Furthermore, we define the "hybrid quadratic covariation" denoted by $[f(B^{H_1}-\tilde{B}^{H_2}),B^{H_1}]^{(HC)}$. Specifically, for $H_1 < \frac{1}{2}$, we construct a Banach space ${\mathscr H}$ of measurable functions ensuring that this covariation exists in $L^2(\Omega)$ for any $f \in {\mathscr H}$, thereby validating the Bouleau-Yor type identity:
$$ [f(B^{H_1}-\tilde{B}^{H_2}),B^{H_1}]^{(HC)}_t=-\int_{\mathbb R}f(a)\ell_t(da). $$
In the case where $H_1 \geq \frac{1}{2}$, we demonstrate that the quadratic covariation likewise exists in $L^2(\Omega)$, and the aforementioned Bouleau-Yor identity remains valid for all H\"older continuous functions $f$ with order $\nu > \frac{2H_1-1}{H_1}$.

This study examines the monitored recurrence of a one-parameter family of three-state quantum walks on a line, where calculations are significantly streamlined by selecting an appropriate basis for the coin space. We demonstrate that the Polya number—representing the site recurrence probability—is a function of both the coin parameter and the initial probability of the walker occupying a specific coin state, under conditions where the walk returns to the origin with certainty. Additionally, we provide a preliminary analysis of exact quantum state recurrence.

Recent reports indicate that the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) detected thousands of very-high-energy photons, reaching energies of approximately 18 TeV, originating from GRB 221009A. This study investigates the survival probability of these photons by accounting for their absorption by the extragalactic background light. Through $10^6$ Monte-Carlo simulations, we examined the parameter space consistent with existing observations, determining that the likelihood of LHAASO detecting at least one $\sim$18 TeV photon from GRB 221009A within 2000 seconds is 80\% and 25\% for spectral indices of $-2$ and $-3$, respectively. Consequently, standard physics remains capable of explaining LHAASO's observations in the several-TeV energy range.
